The picture looks like good. Huge respect for ammount of bosses and they have really interesting mechanics. From this points, there absolutely 0 positive words about this game at all. One of the worst optimized game ever with "souls-like" bugged system. If you have something less than RTX5080 or his equal of AMD - forget about 2k/4k smooth gameplay. I already told that the picture looks like good, but for what price? Absolute 0 end-game content - only some grinding events, PVP(more describtion later), and if you have a guild with high activity maybe some guild wars(30 VS 30). Now about optimization - every single update is a mess that including "shadow/hidden" fixes that most of time brings more bugs. The new content is always just looks fantastic and spectacular, but feels too "raw" while you playing it. Problems of textures, laggs, frame drops and sudden crashes are best friends of this game. And worst of that - devs doesnt give a F@@@ about your reports/reviews/requests about fixes and logs you send. About gameplay - 100500 of menus/windows that are not new players frienly. If you want to be strong is this game welcome to the GRINDING MACHINE: - Every single location has an "oddity" - some items that you submiting for 0.5 points of max/min damage, persicion and more. Ammount of that oddity is more than 150-200 of each region (for now is more that 4 regions). - Each path of weapon you choose has their "inner ways" - system of bonus effect of abilities/bonus damage/any other wich giving you a huge bonus of power, BUT each of them can be updated up to level 6 and the biggest problem is that "inner ways" is gives to you randomaly - now is 10 weapon paths(marshal arts), each of them has 4 inner ways - 3 purple and 1 gold, that is already 40 different inner ways. Then we have "gray" inner ways that giving you any bonus but every class can use this. There`re about 15 purple non-classified 2 gold and 5 blue inner ways. "Amd for dessert" - if you want to have lvl 6 of one single inner way, you need to submit 400 pages. - All "achievement" people can walk past because 30%-40% of achievements is alright like "beat this boss in 30 sec" or "complete maint quest of this region" but then... oh boy... 800 chests and its only one region... hidden quests with 0 rewards (like 15k gold and 5 stone not worthing it at all), pet all cats (yes its cute, but not to search about 200 cats) and there lots of achievements like this - Every 1-2 weeks this game has some "events" that gives you some new gameplay(often). There is no way you can restore that in each way - only a limited quantity of pills that restores 60 energy each, but this thing doesnt affect on anything at this system... So you need to grind items BUUUT only a couple times a week - THANK YOU. Same thing works at GVG where your team of 30 fighting other 30 to get the"flag" - tree to your base, and there much more bugs that I saw half year before and seeing today ! Donation system - this is only ONE THING that works properly of course. every week we get some new skins to buy, every new week I have letters from devs like "hey donate to us and buy skins" that my Gemini is automated to spam folder. Every entrance in game you got pretty banner that says "hey there we know that you want to get this skin with new animation that will frops your and all who sees it fps to 20 so pls donate here" or some kind of trash like that. Ok, WE GOT THIS, you have skins, and its only way you getting money, alright. Final conclusion - if you have like 10 hours a day about week and strong pc - this is good game for play like to beat bosses, complete main quests and do basic world exploration. For you this game can give you kind of challange. For those, who wanted more content and exploring online system, chill game, pc specs like 2060/core i5 7th gen and else - this game is not for you at all. Bad game, and like from 3 month of release is started to die, it`s still dying with eventually("big"update days) of good online and then dying more. 2/10 P.S. dont search at youtube something about this game like if it worth. mostliy you will see payed videos where people with happy faces playing like not more than 40 hours and recs it.

review_text: I want to love this game so much. Unfortunately, I really don't have the time nor the storage on my computer to play it anymore. This game had one of the only story sequences in any game period to make me genuinely cry. The environmental storytelling and lore is genuinely impressive and very intriguing, and if you simply played it through like a singleplayer PvE game, there would be nothing wrong with it. You could just run through the game like it's Sekiro, and the bossfights are spectacular, challenging enough (legend difficulty), but not extremely tough, and can actually be eased by just changing your own build. It's very enjoyable. I stopped playing a long time ago, a few weeks after release, due to the fact that PvP was mainly just a check of whoever lived closest to the game servers, and it was really the only thing I was playing for at that time. So, unfortunately, I did not have the joy of playing through the game's newer content (ending of Kaifeng onwards). I think if I never got deep into PvP and just played for the environment, music, story, people, I would still be playing it regularly to this day. It's really a shame. This game is worth checking out, as long as you have the storage for it. It's free.

review_text: This game, besides the reference, character design like InJoy or whatever-the-f*ck-that-game-name-is and shi*, its overall beyond BORING. It doesn’t have that anime look like Genshin or Wuthering Waves. It’s not a gacha game, there are no character rolls, and no waifu collecting system. What really shocked me is how much content is in the game. There are 1v1 arenas, guild arenas, and even a battle royale mode that feels similar to Naraka Bladepoint. There are raids and bigger MMO-style challenges. You can build structures and decorate your own world. There is a huge open world filled with things to do. review_text: I really love the concept of this game. Everything about it is so well thought out from a visual and game design standpoint. There's so many tiny little details you miss the first play through that you catch the second time, like a certain characters dual life, you can see in every scene a tiny hint of their real hair color. My only and biggest issue with Where Winds Meet is the absolutely awful limitations set on cooperative play. My wife and I wanted to play together so badly but at every single point where the two of us playing together in say boss fights, story line missions, ect. the game blocks co-op play. There's so much forced solo content that it's really hard to consider this an MMO for the first 100 hours of game play. For that reason, I cannot recommend this game if you intend to share the experience with someone which is what the game is marketed as. Don't misconstrue this as me having an issue with the story its self, the game play, the crafting, the deep systems, the visuals, the lore, and events, all of it is absolutely top tier. My issue lays solely with the lack of design intention for co-op gameplay.

review_text: Only issues I've ever had is the coop experience in anothers world is a little lack-luster, the community post-launch has slowly dwindled so queue-times are longer and personally I find the odd visual or gameplay bug here or there, but nothing major/unfixable so far. Overall, have loved the learning experience in this game but for those thinking about downloading to play - this game definitely takes time to learn, progress and feel like you're apart of the community - you'll feel bare-boned for a few months until you've been in some events and have collected some unique cosmetics as well as hopefully purchasing some through the free game to fit in with everyone else - again, things like this take time so make sure you're willing to spend the time, and maybe some money down the line! Originally downloaded it as a coop experience which was a little bit of a letdown seeing I enjoyed the game more than my duo, and as we were stuck having to complete our own campaigns within our own solo worlds, instead of being able to progress through that together, watching solo scenes as if we're the only one there but then loading in as two players would have been a simple way around this despite the story being solo-focused - this was my main issue, as now I'm level 100, my duo is level 45 (having left the game), and it doesn't seem very cooperative anymore, being in two different places and states on the game. Cosmetics are always flawless but they cost an arm and a leg for some of the more premium ones, better to spend money on a free game like this when you have an actual cash-flow coming into your account that isn't going to be compromised buying the odd $20-30 cosmetic - of course they have things to buy for those who spend even more though; definitely be wary of the "Gacha" system and how gambally it can truly be, just like a casino. The community has always been friendly here too, but in chat, you'll mostly see requests and invitations to join things like guilds rather than text chats - I do wish there was a filter to get rid of the random pictures that pop up, invitations etc in the settings for chat as it would make seeing each message only a lot easier and feel more like a community talking rather than players mindlessly posting their new picture hoping to get likes instead! again, overall - definitely have enjoyed the experience and will be returning every time a new chapter has been added - I find I quit the game entirely after completing the majority (all the main/lost/sidequests) of a chapter, leaving most smaller activities for another time when I hop on next time around! (which bare in mind, makes me miss many unique events and cosmetics - returning as a day one player, peoples "elegance" scores which racks up through owning cosmetics were double if not triple mine and I had spent a fair chunk of money and time on this game!) Hope this helps for anyone thinking of downloading the game, going on about my experience - still playing it myself and finding new things to do every day as it is the more I try to look so the game definitely isn't empty with content, always *something* to do, can just get draining :) --- TL;DR - Overall, I like this game, but there's a lot of work that goes into it, and the cooperative side (story/solo world specifically) isn't worth dabbling in if you're looking to play with a friend, only the Online/Social stuff really is!

review_text: I had a conversation with a friend on Discord recently about Where Winds Meet and they asked my thoughts on it, so instead of a standard review I'm just going to post that reply here: Saebin — 22:26 I think "Online RPG" describes Where Winds Meet accurately. Kinda like the original Guild Wars. Online, but you actually can ignore that element almost entirely and choose not to interact with it. It's not unheard of, just kind of rare in more well-known games or games that have/had a budget behind them. Overall to me it's built like a mobile game in terms of it's sub-menus and sub-systems (Maybe even worse). The gameplay and story are solid up until endgame, delivering exactly on what the game sells itself as and shows in trailers. You can do just about anything in this game, even pretty much fly and ontop of that even build. However, the wild and over the top eastern mythology here at play and the story is what will keep most invested and wanting to continue playing in the end. There is a currency limitations in Where Winds Meet (WWM) and I believe the currency limitation actively holds back WWM since players cannot do things at their own pace - this is probably done to create a returning playerbase more than anything, but that strategy is likely to also see players leave like I did in the end. It's a fun game at least worth checking out since it's free, but, if you do reach endgame you'll find very little reason to stay when you ask yourself "What am I actually doing this for?" because the answer to that is "Just to see larger numbers in a mostly singleplayer experience." or "Just to unlock a hard to obtain skill that'll just increase my numbers slightly and change part of my rotation and style in combat for a bit." and those novelties wear off pretty quickly in a mostly singleplayer adventure when you're done with the storylines and the mystery of exploration and learning new mechanics. While I do recommend the game, I don't think it's worth keeping installed once you're "Done" due to the significant amount of real estate it demands from a hard drive (Nearly 200gb), especially when you are limited in currency gains which you don't truly feel until endgame. So to me... It's a one and done game. (Reply ends here.) Note to the Devs: Do a currency crunch, it was getting a little silly when I last played - probably worse now. What I mean is unify many of the existing currencies into a singular one and remove the limitations on gaining them. Good luck and all the best. It was a fun and wild experience which definitely delivered, especially for a free game.

review_text: I'm not gonna act like it's a flawless game. A lot of the cons others are listing are accurate, even if some may feel disingenuous. That said, I feel like the Pros still outweigh the cons. I'll start listing them both and let you make your own choice based on these. 1. Free to play game with no pay-to-win. 2. The only Microtransactions are purely aesthetic - clothing, fashion, etc 3. 10/10 Beautiful Graphics and Background scenery. Too beautiful to not be immersed in. 4. You can change the time - and in some areas the season - of the setting you're in. Speaking of which... 5. The game gives you your own world similar to games like Genshin Impact and Wuthering Waves, but with way better features compared to when those games started out. 6. Best/Most Detailed facial character creation settings in gaming history to date. 7. Gives you at least a dozen different fun ways to traverse the world you're in; from riding different kinds of mounts to literally flying and gliding. 8. Also gives you countless ways to make resource gathering/management fun. 9. GOATed Wuxia-style story for your main character. 10. Souls-like Combat Mechanics - stamina (endurance) bar, rewarding deflects, dodges, perfect dodges, stagger meters (Qi bar), powerful 'magic' abilities (Mystic Skills), Executes, etc. 11. Despite this, it allows you to choose the difficulty of content in your own world. Not something souls-like games allow. If you personally want hardcore content, the game has that available too. 12. Recently introduced a system to help newer players get caught up faster to veteran players. 13. Low-stress grind systems with limits and weekly limits rather than the seamingly endless grinds from games like Warframe or FF14. 14. Playerbase is a mixed bag of hostile and friendly, but from my experience, it's been 70% more friendly... when you ignore the wild world chat at least. 15. The game allows you to join fun Sects/Factions that usually help other players determine what kind of player you are. Highly advised you look into these before choosing. 16. Like most Chinese games, it does have gacha elements, but the paid gacha system is strictly for fashion. 17. The game highly supports PvP and PVE modes. PvE is super fun for people that like team-based fights against bosses like me. 18. PvP, while full of issues, is still almost addicting to do anyway even when you know you may lose a fight. 19. The game has a lot of different PvP modes. Even allowing for 30v30 combat. 20. The various systems (gear, inner ways, mystic skills, etc.) while they 'seem' complex, are actually very easy and simple to understand. 21. The game allows you to bounty hunt and be bounty hunted (the latter usually done if you choose to commit crimes in your world like murder or theft). 22. The game lets you form marital partnerships. For those that care, same sex marriages are also a thing. 23. If you join the Velvet Shade Sect, you can have a whole harem of up to 5 partners (with some strings attached of course if they choose to divorce you). 1. The Gacha and Fashion, when purchased normally, are somewhat expensive. Especially so for gacha. An outfit with glowing effects or special VIP victory animations could cost you several hundreds if it's gacha. And that's with guaranteed rolls/pity. There are some methods involved to make it cheaper though. 2. Multiplayer content, especially PvP, is extremely ping reliant. If your ping or upload speed is poor, even with the game's official ping booster (GearUp), you may find yourself struggling horribly in PvP scenarios. 3. PvP is very unbalanced with builds revolving around tenacity being the absolute meta. 4. There are a lot of menus. Easy to navigate, but still A LOT of menus. 5. The game has two versions; a CN-only version and a Global Release (this one). Sometimes, with the lingering issues we have had since season 0, it feels like the devs care more about their CN counterpart than the Global. Some of which I'm about to describe. 6. The game, especially in very congested multiplayer modes, have a lot of lag when simply trying to roam about. This I suspect is more of an Unreal Engine issue than a WWM one, but it's still noticeable enough to ruin immersion at times. 7. Controller gameplay in the game is fun, but there are fixes and input lag issues with it that the game needs to fix. 8. Sometimes, in congested PvP modes with 12+ players, players won't properly load on your screen. When they perform certain ranged attacks, for example, they might not be immediately visible on your screen. 9. Some Sects, particularly Velvet Shade, actually require you to look as fashionable as possible if you want to excel in them. This is due to player voting-related systems passively created by the game. 10. The game needs more PvE group fight Modes. Modes that don't have an energy system or only exist as temporary events. 11. If you avoid joining a guild, or avoid multiplayer content entirely, build optimization will become much slower. Optimally getting the best gear requires team-based battles that cost energy. 12. If playing solo and grinding as a newer player, it can be a bit more challenging for players that prefer solo mode. 13. A lot of issues are not being fully fixed until the game catches up with the CN version. But that version is still leaps and bounds ahead of us in content so real fixes could take at most a year. At minimum 6-8 months. Alas this is purely speculation. It could take longer or shorter. Overall though, I still feel the game is absolutely worth playing, but only if you're willing to be patient and spend at least 1-3 months catching up with other players.

review_text: Where Winds Meet is the wuxia game I have been waiting my whole life to play. It does not borrow the look of old China and paste martial arts on top. It builds a Jianghu you can walk through, and then lets a story of family, honor, and a breaking empire grow inside it. You begin as an orphan raised in Qinghe by Aunt Han and Uncle Jiang, a wine-maker’s household that is also a school of the sword. The opening already tells you the stakes: a flight through bamboo, a child carried out of danger, a life that was never as ordinary as it looked. When that home comes apart, the road opens. You go looking for the people who raised you, and the search carries you out of villages and reed beds into Kaifeng, a city of lanterns, markets, and imperial intrigue sitting on poverty and conspiracy. The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era is the right century for this. The Tang has fallen, the Song has not yet settled the map, and power is a thing clans and courts tear at in the open and in the dark. History is not a lecture. It is the weather the story moves through. What I loved most is that the tale keeps offering you a self to become. Chivalry is not a menu perk. You can be the wanderer who rights a wrong, or the one who takes what the road offers and lives with the stain. Side stories branch in ways that sting. A keepsake returned to a waiting wife does not guarantee mercy. A ghost that needs guiding home asks you to sit with someone else’s grief before the sword comes out. The main campaign has the sweep of a serial — palaces, haunted ground, mechanical wonders, masters who treat the air like a road — and the endings of its quieter tales are where it becomes personal. I finished chapters feeling I had chosen a kind of person, not just cleared a quest log. The world earns that feeling. Qinghe is water, mist, and working villages. Kaifeng is density: shopfronts, alleys, theaters, people who sleep when the light goes and argue when it returns. Hundreds of them have trades, stations, and gossip. Patients need healing. Puppet shows play. Martial masters wait on ridgelines for a duel that is also a conversation. The Jianghu here is the old idea, not just a combat zone: a place outside the suffocation of court, where reputation answers to no emperor. Society is visible in who bows, who won’t, who is hungry under the grandeur. And the color. This is the most painterly landscape I have moved through. Ink-wash mountains go violet at dusk. Bamboo is a hard, living green. Kaifeng golds and crimsons pool under lantern light. Rivers take the sky. Nothing is the desaturated “ancient” filter so many games use as shorthand. It looks like a scroll that remembered it was also a place: wet stone, dyed silk, kiln smoke, festival red against grey water. The accuracy of the land and the people sits under that beauty. Architecture, dress, faith, craft, and the political fracture of the tenth century are treated as craft problems, not costume. You do not need a dynasty chart to feel it. You feel it in who holds a street and who is hiding under it. The fights are the sieges of this world. Movement is the fantasy: walls, rooftops, bamboo, the brief lie that a body can fly. Duels are operatic without turning into noise, and the larger clashes — cities under strain, set pieces that collapse around you — land because the quiet hours taught you what a reputation costs. Side quests kept me longer than the critical path. Some are short. The good ones are full stories, better written than plenty of main campaigns, and they are how the map becomes a society instead of a backdrop. I have played a lot of open worlds that gesture at history. Where Winds Meet is the one that made the Jianghu feel inhabited. The story stayed with me. The colors stopped me on ridgelines. The side roads were the point. It belongs with the games I will go back to for years. Gameplay not reflected on steam, I have over a 1000 hours between mobile and PS5.

review_text: The Ultimate Time-Gated Time Sink. Great setting, pretty good gameplay. This is not a traditional 'action-adventure rpg'. This is like a single-player MMO. The setting is beautiful and there's lots of exploration. And, it's free. However here's what you need to know before investing your time. Progression is time-gated. You can only level your character so many times before needing to 'breakthrough' to the next tier. These breakthroughs are time gated. The first couple are once a day. But at level 40, I now have to wait two days before I can 'breakthrough' and level again. All xp gained in the meantime is 'stored' until your next breakthrough. The bigger problem is that many quests, the ability to progress 'the story' and move to different areas, are dependent on your level. EDIT: I'm seeing from a lot of people that the time-gates are a temporary part of the season, I hope this is true. Now lets talk about the Wuxia gameplay elements. The cinematics in this game are cool. And the combat system is alright -everything looks cool, but it requires more thumbs if you're playing with controller. The gameplay is nowhere near as simple as the previews make it look. As for the 'flying kung fu' that fans love... it's not available until you've explored most of a given map... which is self-defeating to say the least. It's also extremely janky and you can't really control it, just basically which general direction you want to go. There are other less overt 'Lightness' skills like wall striding, running fast, running across water, etc. However, for most quests you can't use any of these skills. All the Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon stuff seems to be for exploration only. It's extremely jarring and immersion-breaking when you're exploring the world and all of the sudden you're grounded to bunny hops because you found yourself in a quest area. The last thing you need to know, is that this game is tucked inside a menu simulator. There are menus within menus within menus. There is an enormous amount of tracked challenges, collectibles, resources, skills, talents, shops, events, etc to unlock. This thing is a lot like an MMO. I started having flashbacks to Warframe with the ungodly amount of resources and various things to 'level up'. You have to level up your character, your gear, your martial arts, your mystic ways, inner ways, harmony, your profession, your profession's skills, and no I'm not even kidding -even your gear slots. The main reason this is billed as an rpg is because there is a singular story arc specific to your character. But hey, it's free. The game is beautiful. The boss fights and cinematics are cool. I nearly shed a tear during the Velvet Shade's Revelry Hall cinematic. The game shoots itself in the foot on a few things, but I'm enjoying it. It's loads of free content that's obviously kept me entertained many hours.

review_text: At first I wasn’t really sure what to think about this game. A F2P RPG with no P2W sounds way too good in 2025, so I expected another forgettable game, but it honestly surprised me in a good way. The F2P model is very clean. Everything you can buy is cosmetic and the battle pass is also purely cosmetic. There’s no P2W at all, which is still rare these days. The only thing some people might consider “P2W” are the mounts you can buy in the cash shop, since they gather resources for you, but honestly the impact is very small, so it feels more like a QoL feature than anything else. The first thing you need to know is that this is not an MMO, even if it has an “MMO mode” with world bosses, dungeons, GvG and online activities. The core of the game is an open world RPG with lots of systems, minigames and small interactions everywhere. There’s also a co-op mode, but this one is only for exploring, doing side missions and other activities together. The main story is singleplayer. The combat feels good, dynamic and fluid. You combine two weapons and play classic archetypes like tank, melee DPS, ranged DPS or even healer. There’s no upgrade system based on probabilities. You simply get the materials and level up your gear in a consistent way. You also have mystical abilities on top of your weapon skills, plus a talent tree, although it’s a simple one. For PvP you get a 1v1 arena, a 50-player battleroyale-style mode, duels and GvG. One interesting feature is the AI chat system, which lets you gain friendship with NPCs. It’s pretty basic, don’t expect deep conversations, but it’s well integrated and helps you unlock tasks and extra rewards. Some NPCs can give you items if you listen to what they say and help them, even though they don’t have markers or indicators. It adds a nice sense of discovery. There are also a lot of activities: the jar game, dialectic duels, musical minigames, puzzles and many small things that make the world feel alive. You can play most of these with friends. On the first day I played a card game similar to “liar’s dice” with several friends. We had a good laugh and even leveled up a couple of times. The game can run on both DirectX 11 and DirectX 12, but it’s clearly better on 12, with frame generation and more consistent visuals. So make sure to select the right option on Steam when you launch the game. (A small window appears when you click play, so it’s easy to find.) It also has tutorials for almost everything. Each system, mechanic and feature is explained, so it’s hard to get lost even with the amount of things the game offers. The biggest issue when you start is the number of menus and different currencies you get. Even though the menus unlock progressively, the first hours can be a bit confusing, but you get used to it after playing for a while. Some translations are also a bit rough and need to be polished, but it’s not a big deal. In short, Where Winds Meet is a F2P RPG that really surprises. It offers a world full of activities, fun combat and an online mode that, while not a real MMO, adds variety without making things complicated. If you enjoy RPGs with tons of things to do and no pressure to spend money, give it a try. I’m pretty sure you’ll like it.

review_text: Pros + Visually stunning animations and environments + Fun and reasonably challenging combat (choose your difficulty) + Bosses are pretty well designed + A TON of fun and varied optional side content + Plenty of flexibility in how you choose to approach the game + Easy switching between solo and co-op mode + Interesting incorporation of AI for NPCs + Paid content is mostly cosmetics; other paid content don't offer significant gameplay advantages + Doesn't constantly bombard you with ads for paid content + Geese are so strong that your power level is measured relative to them (goosepower) + Game is free! Cons - Menus are all over the place and can be very confusing - English localisation is understandable, but still needs a lot of improvement - Story feels kinda bland, but it might be partially due to localisation - English voices aren't great; many sound AI generated - Latency can make pvp a challenge Neutral +/- Some time gated stuff so you can't keep grinding, but nothing that really cripples gameplay +/- Plenty of content, but it can get overwhelming and a turn-off One of the most ambitious games I've ever played Where Winds Meet is a wild game. I don't think I've ever seen a game where you can roleplay as a villain and go around killing NPCs, have bounties placed on you, get hunted by other players, get jailed if you get caught, and then to cut your sentence short, get paraded around town while other players hurl cabbages and eggs at you. Oh, and this game also has raids, pvp, and a whole ass battle royale system built into it. This game tries to do a bit of everything and amazingly, it kinda pulls it off! There's enough content packed into this one game that anyone should be able to find something they like. Don't want to fight? Just explore, take screenshots, play musical instruments (players have figured out Linkin Park on the Guzheng), heal NPCs or other players, dance, wrestle, play chess, quiz, wrestle, build houses ... the list goes on. Want hardcore fights? Fight challenging bosses solo or co-op (Legend difficulty is no joke), take out enemy camps head on or stealthily, tune your gear, experiment with different builds, join raids etc... You get the idea. There is a ridiculous number of things you can do in this game. And it's all free , so what's there to lose by giving it a try?

review_text: Review at 250hrs. Best Persistant Multiplayer Dungeon game. MMORPG WORLD SYSTEM (8/10): EXCELLENT, but too many menus "Where wind meet" is a hybrid Multiplayer game with a game lobby and a interactive world, that have character progression based on a Single Player mode. Your quests/level progression mainly happens in a single player world. It is here the narrative and plot unfold, where you fights the soul-like bosses. Combat is fluid and smooth, comparable with the likes of BDO. The game lobby is a series of menus that open up various activities where you can join queues to fight dungeons, bosses (5man and 10man), or engages in PVP contest (1v1 and multiple player groups). The interactive world is just like a MMORPG, you can travel around, kill stuffs, collect resources and see everyone else. This world allows open world PVP and all manners of freedom. COMBAT SYSTEM (9/10): Combo based combat similar to most soullike/action combat game. Each character can equip 2 weapon, each with 4-6 moves. With around 10 odd weapons to choose, you can work out various combi. In addition, you can obtain various universal moves known as Mystic Arts (I see them as a series of addons, with some skills to improve combat mobility/durability/CC/counters). You can only equip 8 of these skills to your arsenal to further expand your combat option. PAY TO WIN/GRIND TO WIN/GROVEL TO WIN (10/10): BEST in MARKET Probably the best feature of this game. Any poor dude will get close to the whales. So no way to pay for power. No excessive grinding will gain you overwhelming resources, that will give you super distinct advantage. No grovel to your guild leaders to get first dips on loots, and maneuver in guild politics. GEARING Gearing is casual, just play 30min-1hr daily, you should get to level cap and gear cap in no time. DEATH PENALTY Close to nil, since everytime you die u lose 1 durability for each gear. Each gear has 100 durability and the repair is cheap. COSMETIC (10/10 or 0/10): Depends if you get jealous over someone else outfit They have quite detailed and beautiful free outfits, with a few dollars you can get some outfits. These are pretty cool too. Then you suddenly goes from few tens of dollars to whale class. These are outfits that cost till $800, and weapons close to $2k. Then again, since it is just to "Pay to Look Beautiful", I am fine, since they are paying the server uptime.

review_text: After around 150 hours in this game, i think I'm qualified to write an actual review here. First things first. As a souls player who loves the challenge, is this game worth your time? No. Don't get me wrong. It DOES have challenging parts and challenges, but it isn't a souls game. Even as a souls-like, it's definitely on the easier side of games, which makes sense since it's ment to attract casual gamers who want to play with their friends as well. So, if you're a souls veteran who wants the hardest challenges there are, you'll be disappointed with this. Anyone else - Come in! It also isn't your typical MMORPG. Yes, it does have MMO aspects, but for like 90% of your progress, you stay offline and explore your world, do story quests etc. You CAN play with friends to boost your exploration progress together, at the same time, which is huge. But, story missions are the ones you can not play in co-op, sorry guys. The "online mode" also isn't like a big open map with enemies everywhere for people to slay, no. It's more of a hub. Like, a lobby for players to meet and make up parties who then go into someones individual world together, or to form up for raids. It's also not your typical F2P game. Buying the battlepass DOES grant you a small advantage, yes. But, it's basically almost meaningless, and all you can truly do with real money is buying cosmetics. This game isn't Pay 2 Win, it's essentially Pay 2 Flex. I am F2P with a 0.90€ cosmetic, not a single battlepass, and my power level is close to 20k at this point, which puts me above basically 99% of the players at the point of writing this. Individual skill also matters a lot more than gear in most cases, unless the difference in gear is extreme. Progression is quite fast. A friend of mine who started just 2 weeks ago caught up with us day 1 endgame players already, currently at 17k power, and max level on their account. The game is time efficient, beginner friendly and honestly optimized pretty well. Now, the negatives. As long as you're offline, everything is fine, crisp, and responsive. As soon as you play with others, however, expect massive desync and input lag. Me and my friends live close to each other, we all have a ping of between 5 and 20 - and still, no matter who's world we join, there's massive delays. The servers definitely are on the lower end of things I've seen within 20+ years of gaming, but that's something that could always change in the future. All in all, the game is a solid 8/10. It's a F2P game that doesn't offer huge advantages from spending money. The gameplay is satisfactory and the progression is very good. However, there's negatives, like the poor server performance and a pretty weak main story plot (as of now). All fixable, of course. If you like souls like games but aren't one of these basement dwellers who need it to be the be-all end-all of souls likes, you'll love this game, especially with friends to play with. Even if you're a casual player who can't get their footing into souls games, this game might be for you. It's easier than most of them, it's online meaning your friends can help you get into it, and the only difficult part is learning and understanding the stats system of this game. But, YouTube is your friend, and with the willingness to look things up here and there, it won't be too much of an issue. I have to say though, the translation is terrible in some places, but that does lead to some funny moments. "Look, so many money!"

review_text: My first hours in this game were an unhinged sitcom starring me, a bear, and several medical emergencies. I began by crafting a character so horrifying the character creator begged for mercy and the game politely pretended he was normal. Cutscenes paired my goblin-faced mess with perfect K-pop angel NPCs like a before-and-after skincare ad. It only got worse from there. I witnessed a bear practicing tai chi to steal a beehive, copied the move like a shameless tourist, and immediately punted the bear into the sky like a furry space program. Bees then proceeded to dismantle my will to live, leaving me bruised, poisoned, and looking like expired fruit. I accidentally stole a horse, got clotheslined by its previous owner, and realized I was one more injury away from becoming medically classified as soup. Then salvation arrived, a stranger joined my session. His name might as well have been Asian John Wick. He rolled in, healed my collection of crippling ailments, bowed politely and then beat me into paste. Never took a scratch. Left like Batman. I was humbled. Enlightened. Traumatized. And inspired. Thus began my medical career. I healed geese. I cured villagers. I stress-tested guildmates by practicing chakra healing on them at random intervals like an overly enthusiastic chiropractor. Eventually, I was curing depression, bone fractures, and probably childhood trauma. Requests poured in endlessly. World chat named me The Green-Faced Duelist Doctor, the healer who cures first and challenges later. A legend with 100 flawless medical-violence house calls. Then he returned. The one who birthed my journey... Asian John Wick. He asked me to cure a Soul Bind. I succeeded. We fought. I won with a single HP left and the spirit of every goose I ever healed behind me. He bowed one final time and vanished. I sat there realizing: I have become the monster healer I feared. Best free game ever. Edit: Thank you for the support! I am gobsmacked.

review_text: It’s not often I play a free game and don’t feel like it’s quietly checking my credit score in the background. But Where Winds Meet? It actually feels... generous. Which is wild. Most “free-to-play” games start friendly and then slowly turn into a toll booth. This one honestly feels better than a bunch of $60 AAA titles I’ve bought, played for a week, and then quietly uninstalled. Now, if you’re anything like me and the word “multiplayer” makes your blood pressure tick up a little, you’ll get this. I love big, living worlds. I do not love the idea of being the guy who wipes a 10-person raid and gets that long, awkward silence in chat. Instant alt-F4 energy. This game fixes that. The absolute MVP feature for me is Solo Mode. You can do almost everything in your own private instance. Just you, the scenery, and whatever poor boss is about to catch a sword to the face. For tougher fights, you bring AI companions. Are they elite esports champions? No. Do they stand in fire sometimes? Yep. But they get the job done and, more importantly, they don’t judge you. No pressure. No random stranger sighing into their mic. It makes the whole experience feel way more welcoming than most MMOs for someone like me. What surprised me is that the game still gently nudges you toward other players without shoving you off a cliff. When I finally dipped a toe into multiplayer, it was... chill. Like, suspiciously chill. Guilds are actually built around different playstyles. Want to explore? Fight other players? LARP as a traveling musician or doctor? There’s a lane for that. Honestly, the rewards alone make joining worth joining a guild (or even switching between them for the unique rewards in each). And co-op is another sweet spot. One or two other humans exploring together is manageable. Ten is a committee meeting. Small group content feels relaxed, and it makes special events way easier without turning the game into a part-time job. There’s also always something going on. Daily and weekly stuff keeps you moving, and it feels like there’s constantly some event happening. The world never really feels dead. And let me be clear: this is not pay-to-win. You don’t need to spend money to compete or succeed. Most of the paid stuff is cosmetic, which is fine. If someone wants to spend money to look like a legendary silk-robed demigod, good for them. There’s a monthly pass that speeds up materials a bit, but it’s optional. If you’ve got patience, you can earn everything (that matters for play) just by playing. I haven’t run into toxicity or cheating, though I also avoid the ultra-hardcore PvP and multiplayer stuff, so your mileage may vary. But if you want a gorgeous, sprawling martial arts epic and you’re allergic to forced social chaos, this is absolutely worth a try.

review_text: Honest Review After 500+ Hours (Long Read) I have tried every aspect of this game 100% progress in some things, tried both high end pvp and leaderboard rankings. So here's an honest truth about the game. A wuxia styled F2P MMORPG with insane potential, beautiful worldbuilding, very similar to Wukong and Sekiro/Dark souls elements mixed in. Customization The character creator is insanely detailed easily one of the best parts of the game. You can tweak faces to perfection and create almost any look you want. However, it’s limited: • No body customization (height, build, proportions locked) • Only face + skin tone customization You can look unique but only from the neck up. Animation & Movement Movement is smooth, sprinting, parkour, climbing everything feels fluid. You can climb trees, mountains, buildings basically anything if you have stamina. Photo Mode The photo mode in this game is insanely good and honestly one of the most underrated features. It offers: • Advanced camera controls • Lighting adjustments (intensity, direction, tone) • Depth of field and focus tweaks • Filters and color grading • Pose and angle control • Also newly added custom poses and dancing by tracing with AI from a source Weapons & Combat Huge variety of weapons: • Dual blades • Umbrellas • Spears • Katanas • And more Each weapon has its own: • Unique mechanics • Combos • Playstyle identity • Role in team fights No weapon feels useless but here’s the catch: At high end PvP or leaderboard play, the meta becomes extremely narrow. If you want to compete, you’re forced into specific builds and weapon combinations. Freedom exists — until you want to be competitive. Playstyles Three main roles: • DPS • Healer • Tank These can be mixed depending on your build. Each role comes with: • Unique abilities • Combo systems • Team synergy You can also freely re-spec your gear if you get tired of 1 playstyle but limited amount of times in a season World Building (best part) The world is: • Beautiful • Deeply inspired by Chinese history, folklore, and legends • Filled with handcrafted environments You’ll find: • Unique dungeons and cave systems • Massive mountains to climb • Fully interactive NPCs • Animals (cats, dogs, etc.) • Even AI NPC-chatbots Every location feels carefully crafted and alive. Exploration Exploration is heavily rewarded so try and reach 100% for each part of the map, you will get: • Hidden loot • Lore • Character progression buffs There’s also a compendium system that tracks everything you discover from plants to NPCs, bosses etc. Social Features This is one of the most social MMOs out there. You can: • Hire players (healers, scholars) • Place bounties on players • Help others through bounty systems • Become a disciple or mentor • Form sworn groups • Get married/build relationships • Break players out of prison or capture them • Join guilds and sects • Play minigames • Dance, play instruments, relax in saunas The game is designed to reward social interaction heavily with most cosmetics rewards behind it. F2P & Monetization The good • No pay to win • Gear cannot be bought with real money • Cosmetics can be earned in game • Free gacha pulls exist with guaranteed rewards over time The bad • Gacha is extremely expensive (150–300$ for premium cosmetics) • Strong FOMO elements • Global version lacks trading systems (like China's Black Market) Cosmetics Very different from western MMOs: • No oversexualized designs • Modest, elegant, wuxia style outfits • Unique designs for male/female • Full dye system Voice Acting & Translations This is one of the weakest aspects: • Poor English voice acting • Missing or broken translations • Some things remains in Chinese Recommendation: Play in Chinese with subtitles but even those aren't perfect. Now for the bad part Since I mentioned a lot of pros here are the cons and why it's primarily bad and might affect current and future players 1. Timegated Progression You hit caps and must wait 1-3 weeks for breakthroughs. No grinding your way forward you’re forced to wait. 2. Global vs China Version China gets: • Better QoL • Better pricing for gacha • More features 3. Gacha & Pricing • Extremely expensive • Worse pricing than Chinese version • Encourages FOMO heavily 4. No Black market No trading system like China's Black Market less player freedom, more monetization pressure. 5. Server Issues The game only has 4 dedicated server locations • Players will lag and affect others gameplay • Host based sessions 6. Meta Problems • One dominant meta for PvP/leaderboards • Little room for experimentation at high level 7. New Player Disadvantage • New players almost have no chance to catch up • Missed events = fomo and less progression • New players probably won't find enough people for old activities without looking into discord or other places for help 8. UI & Complexity Menus inside menus inside menus. Hidden stats everywhere. Very overwhelming for new players. 9. Endgame Difficulty • The late game mechanics are too confusing for new players • Requires knowledge and coordination • You will get the most braindead teammates who won't help you or leave after you failed to do a raid mechanic or failed to heal enough 10. Sect System If you don't have 10+ friends that will willingly give you a vote your not reaching max rank and staying there No social circle = no progression. Final Verdict A beautiful, deeply immersive wuxia MMORPG with one of the best social systems in the genre. But it’s also: • Timegated • Unbalanced • Regionally unfair • Overly complex If you: • Don’t care about meta • Don't care about being top tier • Enjoy exploration and social gameplay You will love this game. Rating: 8/10

For me, it's just a bit too much noise.

review_text: TLDR: A triple-A gaming experience for free without pay-to-win. Worth it alone for the excellent game world and superb graphics. PROS: ➕Graphics ➕Amazing exploration ➕Lots of minigames CONS: ➖Bad UI can make it very difficult to locate specific menus ➖Combat is rather shallow ➖Translation issues Content (Game world/Narrative) – [8/10] The game world is set in a vast and beautiful Chinese land with a heavy Wuxia inspired setting. The world is a massive focus of the game itself, and exploration is king here, both in progressing your character and as a player interacting within the world. It seems like in every direction there is something for the player to engage in, whether it's combat, a minigame, or exploration/lore, there is SO MUCH to explore and find. As a point of reference, Elden Ring comes to mind as having awesome exploration, and in my opinion, this is even better here. This might be the best exploration-focused game I have ever played. The game also advertises its narrative as a core element. Right from the start, there is a strong focus on the story. As I progressed, I felt the story get a bit weaker, but still above average, especially for an online “MMO”-esque game. I think it's a solid story, but the hardest part might be the Chinese influence - names can be very hard to follow. I should mention, In my 40+ hours, I did not finish the story fully, but I did catch up almost to the end of the gated content (the story is time-gated as they release new content frequently). Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [7/10] The gameplay entirely revolves around exploration. Everything is connected to exploration. Exploring progresses your character, and gives you various currencies through things like chests, combat, gathering, and hunting. There are frequent minigames, puzzles, and collectables as you traverse the area. If you walk in a single direction, it wouldn’t take more than 30 seconds before you find something of interest. Let’s talk about the combat. I found it interesting, but a bit shallow. There are around ~10 different weapons, that act as classes. Most weapons are tagged as DPS, like swords and spears. There are a few that are classified as tank and healers, using large heavy weapons, or fans, respectively. At its core, the combat only consists of using 5 skills from weapons and 4(+4) skills that anyone can use. The 5 weapons I played around with, I found all fairly simple and consisted mostly of building up resources and then dumping them via a spender. To expand on the RPG aspects slightly, there are various systems that improve your stats as you level and builds you can create using passive abilities. The difficulty in this game can range from easy to very hard, and when you are doing solo content, like the story, you can set the difficulty level to what you are comfortable with. I found it to be close to something like Sekiro or Dark Souls on the higher difficulties, but lower was much easier. Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [9/10] Amazing. This game looks obscenely good many times. By far one of the best looking games I’ve ever seen. There surprisingly isn’t a lot of graphical options, maybe ~15ish, but I was able to max it and get around ~100 FPS with occasional dips. Ironically, I experienced the worst performance with indoor dungeon-like environments, not the outdoor world with the draw distance. Seems backwards, I know. Still, it runs good on a technical side. I did run into a few bugs with getting stuck in walls, but was able to get out via teleporting. My biggest complaint graphically is the menu UI. Often times I’ll find a screen and then will never be able to find it again if I need to access it. Super frustrating, but the menu is just awful. There are waaay too many menus. The gameplay HUD is fine, and the top-level menu is good, but its when you start digging you really notice the issues. i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | Windows 11 installed on SSD Audio – [7/10] Good audio, very reminiscent of the Wuxia era. All the music is from that period. There are instruments that players can play and even compose their own music (mostly using programs). There is voice acting, but in English, it's often not very good and doesn’t match the subtitles a good portion of the time. Replay Factor (Longevity) – [7/10] There is a LOT to do here and more content is releasing frequently. I haven’t gotten deep into the end game grind yet, so I can’t say if it is worth it dumping hundreds of hours into this, but I’ll say that with the content I’ve played, I haven’t gotten bored yet. Final Verdict – [8/10] Where Winds Meet (WWM) is a Chinese action RPG game with a heavily inspired Wuxia setting. This is a sort of “Lobby-based’ MMO-lite where you can play solo or online with others. This is not a true Massively Multiplayer Online game - you won’t see hundreds of people at once. Instead, you have the option to complete PVE content with players, like boss fights, or play solo player, where the majority of the game is focused on. Despite the single player focus, I really like how WWM incorporates online aspects into the game. Whether it's through world chat, Dark Souls-like sign posts, or joining groups for healing/cultivation, there’s enough of a community focus where I never really felt alone. WWM is built around exploration, which greatly appealed to me. I found myself taking much longer to get from point A to B due to being constantly distracted by the amazing world and exploration. There are frequent mini-games and rewards for exploring that not only give you currency, but also develop your character by providing stat bonuses and improvements. Overall, I do recommend WWM. Despite some translation issues, this is a bona fide AAA-game that is free, respects players time, and is not P2W. I can see some issues in getting past the Chinese culture, translations, and I do question the longevity of the end game, but this is an experience and world absolutely worth spending some (free!) time in. review_text: A very good free-to-play game with some flaws. I’ll start first with the combat: It feels like Naraka combat with Sekiro’s posture break and Wukong’s talent/weapon system, which is a good thing. There are some issues, though. The feedback on deflecting isn’t satisfying enough for me, purely in terms of audio and visual. I can’t even tell sometimes if I successfully deflected because the audio and visual feedback aren’t that good. The visual cue is passable, but the audio cue for attacks is nowhere to be found. If you want a good example of perfect audio and visual cues/feedback, I highly recommend checking out E33 or Sekiro (GOAT). Visuals are good. The introduction of the story is cinema. Last thing: dark patterns. The game’s login rewards counts the day you missed, but the cap for your level doesn't. So I’ve gotta wait for some days to level up. It should be a global cap, not a player cap. If someone who started the game earlier can hit level 50 today, then someone who also started today should be able to hit that level too. Monetization so far seems to be purely cosmetics. Overall, it’s enjoyable and a great game. I would recommend checking it out.

review_text: Already 100 hours of gameplay and I still haven’t even started chapter 3, which pretty much says it all about how much content this game has! The world looks amazing and is just fun to explore. There’s always something to do and I keep getting distracted but in a good way. I love running around, gathering oddities and chests and discovering side quests. The story is actually pretty cool too, even if it can be a bit hard to follow at times. The translation and localization are decent overall, not perfect at all times but definitely good enough to enjoy what’s going on. The UI is definitely messy at first, not gonna lie, but you get used to it and I actually kind of enjoy clicking around everywhere and randomly unlocking stuff and discovering features I didn't know where there. I know it's probably an unpopular opinion but it works for me! The game runs super smoothly and I don't have crazy PC specs at all! I haven't even really encountered any major bugs at all, some minor ones here and there but like getting stuck in a rock from time to time and it's really just so minor. The combat feels really satisfying and lets you build your own style instead of locking you into one way of playing. I didn't try all of the weapons and martial arts and abilities yet but I like the idea that I can switch at any time. I also like the social aspect a lot. Playing with a friend and jumping into each other’s world to clear bosses is a lot of fun. Even with random players: you can ask for help with healing, reputation, or fights, and people actually show up. The music is great and fits the vibe really well. I especially like those mini games where you gotta play a track to earn the music sheet! There are indeed a lot of microtransactions but honestly I just ignore them. They’re mostly cosmetic and don’t feel pay-to-win at all, so they never really bothered me. Overall I just really love this game and the fact that it’s free makes it even better so if you're looking for a good RPG, just go for it and hey if you don't like it, you don't even have to ask for a refund! Isn't that great?

review_text: My early journey in this beautifully chaotic game: I began by sculpting a character so disturbingly misshapen that any divine being would request a refund, then immediately had to watch my monstrosity share screen time with flawless, idol-tier NPCs. Witnessed a bear attempting a mystical t’ai chi routine to nab a beehive, learned the same move, punted the bear into orbit, nearly died from bees and bruises, accidentally stole a horse, and got my skull rattled by its furious owner — leaving me with a collection of painful injuries. Out of nowhere, a stranger with a Chinese username — essentially Asian John Wick — joined my world, purged my ailments with a chakra battle straight out of a shonen anime, then politely asked to duel and proceeded to fold me like laundry before bowing and disappearing. Spiritually defeated, I swore to train as a healer, unlocked basic poison remedies, and practiced on a wounded goose because I wasn’t competent enough to treat actual players. Started experimenting on my guildmates with the chakra healing mechanic, slowly building expertise until I could mend everything from fractures to full-blown emotional collapse. Took on healing requests from random adventurers, entered their sessions, cured them, challenged them to honorable combat, and vanished like a wandering sage. Eventually reached such absurd medical proficiency that I could bypass the mini-game entirely and instantly fix even the nastiest conditions — still insisting on duels afterward out of ritual. Climbed to the top of the healer leaderboard, gained the nickname “the green-faced dueling physician” in world chat, and began receiving requests at a constant, almost comical pace. After more than a hundred successful healings — and zero duel losses — I got a message for a level 4 Soul Bind, one of the hardest afflictions in the game. The sender? Asian John Wick. I cured him once more, we clashed in an incredibly tight duel, I survived with literally 1 HP, and he knelt, offered a deep, respectful bow, said “GG,” and departed — confirming that I had officially become the game’s supreme healer.

review_text: My first hours in this game were an unhinged sitcom starring me, a bear, and several medical emergencies. I began by crafting a character so horrifying the character creator begged for mercy and the game politely pretended he was normal. Cutscenes paired my goblin-faced mess with perfect K-pop angel NPCs like a before-and-after skincare ad. It only got worse from there. Bees then proceeded to dismantle my will to live, leaving me bruised, poisoned, and looking like expired fruit. I accidentally stole a horse, got clotheslined by its previous owner, and realized I was one more injury away from becoming medically classified as soup. Then salvation arrived, a stranger joined my session. His name might as well have been Asian John Wick. He rolled in, healed my collection of crippling ailments, bowed politely and then beat me into paste. Never took a scratch. Left like Batman. I was humbled. Enlightened. Traumatized. And inspired. Thus began my medical career. I healed geese. I cured villagers. I stress-tested guildmates by practicing chakra healing on them at random intervals like an overly enthusiastic chiropractor. Eventually, I was curing depression, bone fractures, and probably childhood trauma. Requests poured in endlessly. World chat named me The Green-Faced Duelist Doctor, the healer who cures first and challenges later. A legend with 100 flawless medical-violence house calls. Then he returned. The one who birthed my journey... Asian John Wick. He asked me to cure a Soul Bind. I succeeded. We fought. I won with a single HP left and the spirit of every goose I ever healed behind me. He bowed one final time and vanished. I sat there realizing: I have become the monster healer I feared. Best free game ever.

Besides the battle pass, you can also exchange 【First Clear of Strongholds(Medicinal Tales)】 rewards to increase potion carrying limits (current Chinese server cap is 7 bottles). Of course, I understand spending habits may differ by region. If a $10 seasonal battle pass makes you feel like fighting NPCs is P2W, then I suggest lowering the game difficulty. That way you can win more, because you can save on potion materials, save time collecting materials, and save crafting gold. 2. 【Cash Shop】 As a free-to-play game, it needs to make money, but I think what you really want to know is: 【As a casual player, spending little or even nothing, can I get cool items?】 The answer is definitely YES. —2.1 【Cash Prize Pools】 Quests give a small number of draw tickets (e.g., 1v1 duels with NPCs), and the developers also give some away. Accumulate for 6-8 months and you can get an outfit worth $500 for free (I got one for free). Please note: this pool is meant for players with money to spend(whales), not for casual players. This pool is key to keeping this game running! —2.2 【Seasonal Prize Pools】 The green currency in the top-right corner of the interface can be exchanged for draw tickets. This currency is obtained through all gameplay activities: gathering / opening chests / quests / collections... (Acquisition speed is related to exploration progress. I've obtained it for free twice). —2.3 【Direct Purchase Shop for Casual Players】 Item prices range from $1-40. I think the pricing is reasonable. If you still find it expensive, the daily login rewards include 1-2 "10% off" coupons per month. You can stack up to 5. As long as you have patience, you can get items for half price. PS: Thanks to all the big spenders in the 【Cash Prize Pools】! You let us play a good game for free 3. 【Voice Acting】 If English dubbing isn't a must, I strongly recommend using the Chinese voiceover! I think the English dub quality is indeed subpar; the Chinese dub has better voice actors and emotional delivery. I also strongly advise against skipping the story — this is a masterpiece of a narrative. If you just want mindless combat, you might as well go play 《Naraka: Bladepoint》 directly. 4. 【Story】 Don't give a negative review just because a character diesthe game is set in an era of war and famine, where tragedies like "swapping children to eat" were common. In this desperate setting, any character's death is an inevitability of the times. 5. 【Quests & Quest Comment Section】 You can find in your exploration log that quests are divided into two lines. Many people haven't noticed this. One line is the overt main story, told through cinematic narration. The other is a hidden, fragmented narrative. The two lines converge into the complete plot and unlock the final storyline.After completing certain quests, a comment section opens. I strongly recommend reading it — even as a Chinese server player, I often gain new insights into the story from "history fan" comments! 6. 【Currency System】 Many players complain there are too many currency types and are confused why each map has different currencies (except the shop currency). First, the reason: different gameplay categories earn different currencies. It ensures players with different playstyles get corresponding rewards. Second, why do map currencies differ? Because the game is set during the transition between the Tang and Song dynasties in China, when multiple currencies circulated in parallel. As the main story reveals — when dynasties change, common people's lifelong savings often turn to nothing. 7. 【Road Signs & Chat Box】 You can customize in settings: display of road signs / chat box / flying chat messages. Solo players can also get a clean experience. (The chat box settings are within the chat box itself, not in the ESC settings.) 8. 【Mount System】 unless you really like them. Your parkour (Lightness skill) is far more powerful than any mount. If you want a functional mount, then 【Gathering】 and 【Treasure Chest Finding】 mounts are somewhat useful, making things a bit easier for you. But honestly, they're not as good as doing it yourself. The 【Sprint】 mount in the shop is decent: 1. cheap, 2. it has the fastest startup speed before you have parkour, even though it's still "slow". The reason mounts feel "slow" is because at low exploration levels, collectibles are very dense, so you don't want to repeatedly mount and dismount. 9. 【Parkour (Lightness skill) Adjustment】 Be sure to switch to another camera mode in the settings! It greatly improves the flying experience, so you don't have to keep watching that close-up animation!!! (Wind Rider is the highest and farthest, recommended.) 10. 【Multiplayer Modes】 I don't think this is a good MMO; I think it can only be called 【Co-op】. Actually, it leans more towards a single-player game, but I'll still explain the difference. —Solo Mode: Up to 5-player co-op. Quest progress is NOT shared (similar to GW2's personal story). Exploration rewards & world boss kills within 300m are shared by the party. —Multiplayer Mode: Reduced number of NPCs, cannot complete quests. Contains exclusive content like cruise parties. 11. 【Network Latency】 The developers are optimizing it, but I don't think it will improve much. Because as a Chinese player who has played foreign games for years, I know how terrible latency can be. Unless someone is willing to act as a local agent for this game and set up servers locally. 12. 【Inventory System】 Abandon your habit of organizing your inventory from MMOs! Don't try to organize your bag. What you should do is forget its existence, unless you pick up a letter and want to read its contents, or if you miss the pop-up notification when picking up an equipment chest. Otherwise, there's no need for you to organize anything. When you need to use something, that interface will automatically fetch items from your bag. Finally, if you have other questions, feel free to leave a comment. I'll try my best to help.

review_text: This wallpaper generator is also a fast-paced RPG but it's also an interactive lesson in Chinese history however we can't forget that it's also a collection of multiplayer mini-games and an online fashion show. Oh, right, I forgot, it's also tactical PvP fighter with combos and huge build variety. I've played pretty much since launch and haven't been able to put it down. Single-player mode reminds me of Wukong and Sekiro mixed in. Beautiful scenes, diverse bosses and great variety. Legendary difficulty (which can only be selected at the start of the game but can be turned down if needed) offers a solid challenge with different approaches being viable. I've struggled early on and called in friends via co-op for some of the bosses but as I've learned my build and got used to the systems the fights transformed into cinematic masterpieces. While some bosses can down you in only a few hits, they are designed very fairy with clear understanding after each loss of where exactly you messed up. Only PvE Raids with 5 and 10 man groups can be difficult in pick-up groups as there are boss mechanics that players will need to learn and a small level of coordination is required. Running them in a pre-made Guild team is almost trivial but still fun and unlockable talents (achievements) give you something to work towards. From previews of Chinese server it seems like the difficulty of Raids will pick up even more and better teamwork will be required. PvP - there are currently 4 forms of it in Where Winds Meet. The meatiest and deepest is 1v1 Arena. It's like Black Desert Online and Tekken had a baby. It's very fast but extremely tactical. Spamming gets you nowhere and knowledge rules supreme. 3v3 Arena is a fun, less demanding format. Some builds clearly stand out for it and you're less able to brain your way out of trouble. Perception Forest is a battle royale with all the common systems in-place. Lastly, there's open world PvP via the Bounty system. Fun, but not particularly flashed out. (There's Prison Break PvP as well but that's more of a "For Fun" mode) Free to Play. It really is. Completely void of any Pay to Win mechanics. All paid content is cosmetic and while Gacha is pretty expensive, you also get plenty of draws for free with guaranteed Legendaries after a certain amount of draws. There's a ton of cosmetics which are earned in-game and you can be the show-stopper without ever spending a dime. Once I passed 600 hours I couldn't stop myself from buying a few skins and as I continue to enjoy this game, I'm sure I'll Pay-to-Slay again. The devs deserve my money. Lastly let's mention performance. I started playing WWM on a 3060 laptop and was able to run it smoothly over 60FPS except for some very dense areas. I never tried the Lite client which tones visuals more because it was always running well enough to enjoy. Currently I'm on a 5070Ti and I can comfortably max out all settings and still not get any framedrops at 140+ FPS. The game is gorgeous and there's so much eye candy that I spend a few hours per week in Photo Mode. Highly recommend to try this game out and perhaps I'll see you where winds meet.

review_text: Quick Summary Story: Surprisingly emotional and engaging for a free game. Some moments genuinely caught me off guard. Gameplay & Mechanics: Smooth combat with a mix of Ghost of Tsushima, Assassin’s Creed, and a bit of Sekiro-like learning (even though I never played Sekiro). Boss fights are visually impressive and satisfying once you learn the patterns. Exploration: Beautiful world with strong visual style, especially if you enjoyed Ghost of Tsushima’s art direction. Atmosphere: Strong presentation, memorable characters, and a story that lands harder than expected. Monetisation: Mostly cosmetic. You can play the full story and progress without spending anything. Overall: A surprisingly polished experience for a free-to-play title. One of those hidden gems worth trying at least once. Important Notes Before You Start Remember when the game asks you to set your character’s name: it must be unique and it is permanent. You cannot change it later, so choose carefully. The game has multiple difficulty modes. You can switch freely between Story and Expert at any time. But the highest difficulty, Legend , can only be selected at the very beginning when you create your username. If you lower the difficulty later, you can never return to Legend unless you make a new account. I chose Story to enjoy everything peacefully and switched to Expert for some bosses when I wanted a challenge. Where Winds Meet – A Free Game That Surprised Me in the Best Way I went in with the mindset of avoiding online free games, mainly because many of them end up turning into pay-to-win or heavy grind traps. But after seeing a few reviews saying “just try it, it is free,” I gave it a chance. And honestly, I was shocked by how good it turned out. People compare it to Ghost of Tsushima, Assassin’s Creed, Black Myth, and Sekiro. I only know the first two, but even then the comparisons make sense. The visuals instantly reminded me of Ghost of Tsushima’s atmosphere, especially during key story moments. Story and Emotional Moments I did not expect a free game to hit this hard, especially so early on. The ending of Chapter 1 genuinely caught me emotionally. It set the tone for the rest of the journey and felt far better than many paid games I played this year. Chapter 2 also had one of my favourite twists: Little Fu saying “I’m the Dao Lord,” then switching to “I work for the Dao Lord,” had everyone confused. And when the truth came out at the end, I laughed so hard because the community reaction online was exactly the same as mine. Only two chapters are available right now, but both have solid closure and feel complete on their own. Gameplay, UI, and World Feel Combat feels smooth once you learn enemy patterns. Some boss fights look incredible, especially for a free game. One side-boss took me hours, but once I learned everything, beating it felt extremely satisfying. The UI can look busy at first, especially if you prefer clean single-player setups. Thankfully, you can hide almost everything in the settings and even turn off world chat on the side. The world itself looks beautiful. The colours, animations, and overall presentation reminded me of modern AAA titles. Online System and Why Everything Is Connected The game is always online, but the reason seems to be tied to how saves and progression work. From what I understand, saves are on the server possibly to prevent people from modifying files and skipping progression. At the same time, it looks like the developers wanted all modes — solo, co-op, and multiplayer — to share one character with the same stats. I personally do not know the full technical reason, but that feels like the intention. It also means maintenance time can stop you from playing, which might feel odd if you prefer purely offline story games. Progression, Resources, and Level Gates There are level gates. For example, to begin Chapter 2 you need to be level thirty. At first, I thought it would feel like a wall, but by the time I finished Chapter 1 I was already level twenty-eight. Doing two side missions pushed me to thirty, so it did not waste my time. The only thing that bothered me slightly is how healing items and resources do not reset when you reload a save, since everything is online. If you run out of medicine, you have to go farm more and come back. Not a dealbreaker, but something to be aware of. Monetisation and What You Actually Need The game mainly sells skins and a battle pass. The cosmetics do not give big stat advantages, and you can play smoothly without spending. Grinding is enough to keep up with main story requirements. Final Thoughts Even though only two chapters exist at the moment, both are strong and enjoyable. The world looks beautiful, the story has emotion and twists, and the combat impressed me far more than I expected from a free title. It is one of those games where the phrase “just try it, love or hate, up to you” actually fits perfectly. I stayed away from these types of games for years, and this one surprised me in the best way.

review_text: Where Winds Meet is a good free to play game. You can spend a lot of time in it, and it looks amazing. Unfortunately, a lot of that time will be spent ever so slightly frustrated. Frustrations start right away with menu design. Where even after 1k hours you won't know where all the menus lead as it is an entangeled web of unintuative paths. And that's just the beginning. First, if you try to play co-op with a friend, you'll quickly realize that only a handful of quests (none of the main quests) actually work in co-op. More often than not, something will break, so even content that should work together suddenly doesn't. And if the host gets too close to certain, seemingly random areas, the other player gets kicked. So you decide to play solo. Great, except some of the best rewards are locked behind multiplayer activities, especially events. Fine, you play the events with other people. Except many of them are essentially reskinned versions of popular games (Slay the Spire, Dark and Darker, Resident Evil, TFT, etc) and often don't work properly. Their mechanics often don't ever get looked at again. You don't have to play the events, though. How about something permanent and core to the game like PvP. 1v1s tend to have one of two outcomes. you combo your opponent, or they combo you. Thankfully, whichever happens, it usually ends quickly. Is it at least fair? Well money is involved so.. players who can afford better routing to the servers, which the game openly advertises in its launcher have a noticeable advantage. And like in many games new weapons tend to be a little stronger than the old ones, conveniently accompanied by fresh skins. GvG is an interesting take on large scale MOBA, that is overshadowed by the amout of stutters that 60 shiny skins fighting with special VFX moves brings. There are other PvP options too. Perception Forest is an extraction (not) shooter with a surprisingly good feel to it... as long as you don't fight near walls, cliffs, trees, or boulders. If you do, the winner may simply be whoever manages to unstuck their character from the vertical surface first. New weapons can dominate here too, sometimes by simply staggering you indefinitely. And that's really the core problem with PvP in Where Winds Meet: stagger. It's direct interference with your inputs, taking control away from you rather than rewarding your ability to play. TLDR: The game has a lot of potential, and around the same amount of flaws. There is a genuinely good game buried underneath all of this. but it's constantly fighting against its own design and technical problems.
