review_text: I honestly don’t understand how this game is free. Where Winds Meet feels like the kind of project where someone should be knocking on my door to charge me for “unauthorized enjoyment.” It’s one of the most generous free titles I’ve touched in years. The opening hours hit like a tidal wave. The game throws an entire arsenal of systems at you combat styles, cultivation abilities, mobility techniques, crafting, hunting, stealth, exploration tools, even social interactions and it doesn’t always do the best job explaining any of them. About two hours in, I was confused but also curious, because the game practically encourages you to poke around and discover things through trial and error. The learning curve is steep, but once you start piecing things together, the freedom becomes the appeal. The game leans hard into those classic Asian design sensibilities layered mechanics, busy UI, fast pacing which gives it personality, even if it’s a lot to absorb at first. Combat is good, even if it’s not quite the Sekiro like precision some people expected. The auto parry system is a bit cheap in my opinion (thankfully you can disable it), but the real strength here is the variety. There are tons of weapons, martial arts disciplines, stances, and movement abilities that let you build your character in wild ways. The combat sandbox is flexable, you can double jump off projectiles, redirect arrows, kick enemies across rooftops, or switch from elegant swordplay to brutal spear combos. It’s not the deepest combat in the genre, but it’s creative and satisfying. This is where the game starts feeling suspiciously premium. The cutscenes are shockingly well produced great direction, expressive facial animation, and a level of polish I didn’t expect for a free to play title. The world itself is gorgeous, full of scenic landscapes and small environmental details that make exploration feel rewarding. A common point from other reviews is that the world feels alive, with random events, wildlife, hidden quests, parkour routes, and interactable objects everywhere. It’s the kind of world design western studios used to be known for, but haven’t delivered consistently in years. I was genuinely surprised by how much cosmetic content you get just by playing. Outfits, dyes, accessories far more than I expected, and without feeling nickel-and-dimed. The game is surprisingly fair, especially compared to the usual F2P model. Asia has been on a massive upswing with recent releases, and Where Winds Meet continues that trend. It’s no surprise that western gamers are migrating toward these titles these developers seem hungry, creative, and connected to their audience in a way many western studios have drifted away from. Is the game perfect? No. It’s messy, overwhelming, inconsistent, and sometimes unpolished. But it’s also bold, stylish, generous, and packed with ideas more than most full-priced games offer. For an open-world martial arts adventure? It’s one of the most interesting ones in years. "This bear knows martial art's, I must learn from it." Adequate response, this sums up the game.

review_text: Memories are like water in your palm; it doesn’t matter whether you have your hand open or holding it tight, it will still leak drop by drop until it’s all gone. However, the coolness of the water is unforgettable. - Wang Lin Where Winds Meet is an unforgettable game. Not only is it free to play, and runs on relatively low system requirements even with the full install (there is a smaller install available; not on Steam) but it manages to look amazing while doing so. I have noticed the odd occasional graphical glitch, and some low res rendering of my character in cut scenes (but its still the costume and appearance I set up) but these are only occasional and despite this flaw, are subsidiary issues compared to the incredible atmosphere the game manages to create. Being an RPG the game is expansive with many hours of content to explore. Although there is your standard increase in exp to level you, there are additional ways to customise your character and their traits, through playing various minigames or completing exploration tasks. Your character essentially becomes what they do, which feels like the very essence of roleplaying. For instance petting cats raises your charisma whilst running and training with disciples increases your endurance. Additionally,, interactions with NPCs include interactions with individualised chatbots for each NPC this harkens back to the days of MUDs where you were able to freely enter info and receive responses. The chatbot then processes the info and after hitting dialogue points increases your acquaintance with that character. Likewise regularly buying form merchants also increases your friendliness with them. It's a fun way to puzzle through and engage with freefrom dialogue. The story itself is phenomenal and ranges from the absurd (rabid geese, kung-fu chickens), to tragic (a love never spoken for an entire lifetime, past losses) and sometimes switches between these abruptly to keep the audience engaged and lighten or tone down the mood to create moments of contrast. Its well worth playing, and there is lots of lore to discover... Combat is incredible for a wuxia game. Not only is each attack beautifully choreographed making you feel like a skilled professional from the get go ,but the souls light combat is fun to play (if you're ping isn't killing you). Most of combat consists of parrying and dodging and counterattacking when enemies are in a weak or vulnerable state. To press them you have a plethora of weapon options (linked to your RP within the sect you choose, or steal the skills ,or be disloyal and leave and join sects). This is further expanded on with passive Inner Way customization. The game does rely on the tank/healer/dps setup. But a skilled DD good at dodging and parrying can still carry a group with a tank unable to taunt properly. Co-op includes running through Outposts killing mobs until the boss arrives ,specific Boss fights with fleshed out mechanics that rely on awareness and co-operation between team mates. There is also a PVP mode in the Arena which I haven't attempted. Exploration is an absolute joy,,, with things that you stumble over at every corner from amusing encounters with a lonely child who is being bullied (til she gets a doll) to enraged bears that you can lure into an enemy camp, and even a mystical deer. I can barely scratch the surface in this short review. The multiple mini games are fun and offer a variety so if becoming frustrated in one area, ,hope over to another activity for a bit, ,these games also allow you to level them up such as levelling healing skills, or dialogue cards for the argument minigame. There are issues here though, most likely browsing other reviews youll see complaints over the menu complexity ,which is a large issue,, once you have started to figure them out there are some neat tricks to quickly jump around, and the map also is quite complex but once youve figured out the way to set waypoints and track items it becomes a lot easier... it is ridiculous that this can take so many hours of play to figure out. Upgrading weapons and abilities is also unintuitive, there is a lot to upgrade and this can also become confusing. The game offers tutorials but they are bareboned and dont offer a lot of guidance or help. As a free game (that so far is not P2W) and only really raking in cash from cosmetics, I'd advise anyone to download this, it has the best elements of exploration, combat and social, and offers something for everyone. Just be aware you may need to invest time in learning... menus! Come join us in the Jianghu!

review_text: Where Winds Meet (WWM) is an open world RPG set in a Chinese martial arts world with light fantasy elements. review_text: This game tries to do allot of different things, but it has a consistent theme across all its systems. Imagine you’re a famous painter, you’ve painted a masterpiece. A work of art. A mere glance at it dazzles the eyes. And then you draw a gigantic red line through the painting. Why? Who knows. Now, instead of trying to paint over that red line and fix the drawing, you offer people temporary glasses that hide the color red every time they view it. A band-aid solution to something you’ve done intentionally, with no benefit to you, only harm. This is Where the Winds Meet. Let me break down the systems of the game, as well as its pros and cons, to show you the marred painting I mean. I’ll try to keep it organized into systems and subsystems. The Combat: At a glance, combat seems very fun in WWM. It’s flashy, parry-based, all weapons have their own playstyle and combinations, and you can mix and match! Not really. As you go deeper, you realize every “combo” is a reskin of the same style, with very few exceptions. Almost every available combination boils down to “this is your main weapon, use it 24/7” and “this is your secondary weapon, used only for a single ability or buff/debuff.” You’re not really using both. Every build boils down to a 10–15 second buff/debuff window while spamming 1–2 attacks. Your combat rotation is 1–3 abilities, chained or spammed every 10–15 seconds. Any weapon effects that significantly change how a weapon looks or feels are locked behind a €300 pity gacha, with awful rewards that make it a money sink. Thematically, many weapon combinations don’t make sense or have boring playstyles. Demonic twin blades that push you into rage paired with... rats? And actively using two weapons from different paths is shooting yourself in the foot. PvE: For some reason, the devs looked at Genshin Impact and said “that energy system limiting players from playing looks fun.” You have an energy system that takes 3 days and 3 hours to fully charge. It caps at 500, with ~1 energy every 9 minutes. There are three forms of group PvE: • 10-man raids: On paper, fun. In reality, rewards are capped once per week. With 9 people you know, it’s surprisingly fun to coordinate. Bosses are repetitive, sometimes buggy, and can outright kill you regardless of execution. Don’t have 9 people? Welcome to gambling. A large portion of players don’t read mechanics. Before fights, during fights, ever. So 10-man (and 5-man) becomes gambling on randoms knowing how to read. My success rate was about 20%. You’ll spend hours queuing, watching people die to mechanics that could be read in 30 seconds, and leaving. Rinse, repeat. • 5-man raids: Energy-limited. Each reward claim costs 60 energy, or 180 for triple rewards, once every 20 hours. PvE boils down to a raid every day or two, allot of gambling, and mediocre rewards. Progression: Probably the worst system I’ve seen in a very long time. Progression in WWM is multilayered, with each layer locked behind something more inane than the last. Mystic skills—some of your hardest-hitting abilities—are leveled by picking flowers. Each flower has a very low chance to give 1 rare material. You need around 108 to max a skill. No markers. You just search greenery for tiny petals. The game then offers limited weekly chests and food buffs to increase drop rates. Red line painting once more. You also need to run outposts—the third PvE mode—which offer almost no rewards besides iron for mystic skills and random gear. They scale, so you can’t prefarm. You use around 10–12 skills total, each requiring a different plant, meaning you’re farming multiple rare materials in some of the most boring content I’ve played. Then comes gearing. You open random gear chests hoping for legendary gear with usable stats (many don’t make sense). You can spend months not getting one. Then you gamble again tuning it, needing good rolls on 6 random stat slots. Bad roll? Start over. Lastly, Inner Ways. You can equip up to 4. They require escalating amounts of notes, awarded randomly from content chests. You constantly reroll instead of the system just not being random. They’re integral to player power, and falling behind cripples your character. PvP: If you’re not near central Europe, don’t bother. Above ~40 ping, input delay kills animation cancels, reactions, parries, and combos. Opponents fall out of combos due to ping differences, and you’re playing with a 1–2 second delay. PvP also uses a separate upgrade system and Inner Ways, meaning you’re maintaining two characters and halving your progression speed. The Story: The story is surprisingly good—if you understand it. It follows Dark Souls-style storytelling while relying heavily on ancient Chinese history. Between awful localization and obscure references even many Chinese players don’t know, you’ll probably skip it and watch it on YouTube later. The Content: Global releases are slower than China’s. Level caps and progression are drip-fed every 15 days, forcing you to repeat the same progression grind. New content arrives even slower, so once you’re done, you mostly log in to dump energy every few days. Most systems are weekly-limited. Finish them in a few hours and that’s it. Need upgrades? Too bad—weekly coin cap. Co-op is limited, laggy, and often only counts for the host. Online presence has little point outside of dailies. This isn’t even touching on shop pricing, gacha odds, or reward quality. The game had an insane amount of potential, but the devs keep designing great systems and then crippling them. Maybe this design works better in China, but it clearly doesn’t hit the same mark here.

review_text: I am only reviewing this as a Solo-mode player, and I will say it delivers an amazing single-player experience. I see a lot of the criticisms seem to come from PVP players, so if you are looking for a single player game, do not be discouraged, you can get so much out of this. I genuinely feel like most of the critiques that I’ve seen for this game are form people who don’t actually want to play the story quests or engage with the world, they just want the multiplayer content, which is not the bulk of the game, and are upset that the game doesn’t solely focus on PVP and multiplayer content. If you are playing a female character, the English audio will often refer to your character as “Him/He,” even if the text will say “She/Her” (or not having a gender pronoun at all, instead having a blank space). If that is something that might be distressing to you, use the Chinese audio (better voice acting too!) or avoid the game. My main gripes as a solo-mode player come from decisions that I believe were made to try and attract a PVP audience. Bosses scale with your level, it is therefore impossible to raise your level and come back to a boss fight later and have an easier time beating them. Additionally, all the weapons classes are weighted for multiplayer use. And with all the different elements you need to build a set of a specific type (gear types, gears of various levels with maxed out stats for passive bonuses, leveling up the weapon skills and mystic skills specific to your gear type). That means that if you find a specific playstyle that works for you, and it’s not the weakness of the boss, you will be at a horrible disadvantage for the fight and changing out your gear will involve days, if not weeks, of playtime to build up the right set, let alone getting used to the new fighting style. It takes so much time because the weapons are locked behind progression systems designed for multiplayer games, not solo-player games, which is a bizarre choice given how most of the quests and storyline are solo-mode content to begin with. Lastly, if you want to join a sect as a solo-mode player (not the same a guild which is the multiplayer thing) to get rewards or just because it feels right to your character, you’ll probably be forced into engaging with multiplayer content if you don’t want to get auto-kicked out after a month. There is also a stock market that heavily incentivise going to other players’ worlds to take advantage of their solo-world stock market prices and other things like that which try to force single-players to engage with the multiplayer content in non-meaningful and annoying ways. Other than that, I honestly have no complaints. The writing for the main quest lines blew me away. I am so invested in my character’s journey to the point where I am wearing a mask in certain areas after the end of Act I to stay in character and plan outfits around sentimental outfit pieces. When it comes to quests, the only things that’s found a bit annoying as someone who is invested in my character’s story is the fact that it’s very easy to do quests “out of order” so to speak, which leads to confusing moments when the game assumes you know some lore and you don’t, or your character is going around saying their full name and where they’re from when it’s now supposed to be information they’re trying to hide. Or characters will refer to a situation that you have solved or be coy about information that you have already learnt. It is a bit frustrating, but I do understand that it gives the player a lot more freedom to run around and mess about in the world. I do not understand all the critiques that the quests do not have good rewards. There is so much lore to uncover in the world, even talking to characters can unlock lore nodes. I also love the Wandering Tales, which rely on you paying attention to what the characters are saying instead of just following quest marker blindly. Additionally, this game implements character stats that go up as you collect oddities (the main secret collectibles of the game). These stats will allow you to use advanced gear better, unlock passive skills, and the collectibles can be exchanged for more health, skill improvements, and some outfit pieces. In most games, they are types of collectibles just exist in a “number go up” type of way, and have no actual value to gameplay, so I find that lack of reward critique absolutely wild. I would assume they mean lack of multiplayer specific rewards. Everything you do in this game will reward you with lore, skill progression, etc. Even running around has the chance of triggering Encounter quests if the right conditions have been met, so it is worth it to travel in map instead of fast travelling. One feature I would love to see if taking care of horses. Riding horses is so satisfying, and I love travelling the world on horseback. The main horse that the game gives you is tied to the story and is thankfully protected form being accidentally sold, but it has zero stats for good travelling. Since there is already a house/base building mechanic, I would love to be able to build a stable and make a little home for Clip-Clop, so I know he’s doing well and safe while I am off on adventures with the beefy black horse I tamed in the wilderness (I also LOVE the horse taming feature, so much fun, there is a lot of potential here for a horse game if the devs implement a few things). If you are playing on the Steam Deck, the Quinghe area runs okay, but the other two areas (Kaifeng and Hexi) are too much for it. Lastly, this game is free, so you have nothing to lose trying it out.

review_text: TL;DR: A near-perfect open-world wuxia game where I can chill after a ♥♥♥ day at work, with a slight Soulsborne feel in the combat. After ages, I’m finally writing another Steam review because this game deserves it. Before the FreeFire crowd jumps in, here’s my take on its current state. The Good: • The world is filled with loot and collectibles that you can grab immediately or return to later, and either way you’re rewarded. As a loot addict, I really appreciate this. Doing this will reward you, doing that will reward you. its perfect for a loot ♥♥♥ like me. • Conversation speed system lets you fast-forward those low-res dialogue scenes without skipping the actual content. Super convenient. • AI-generated NPC chats are fun to play around with. Easy to exploit, but still a new cool feature. • Gear farming feels fair and not overly grindy. We’re level-gated for now, but so far RNG is fine. • Paid content is mostly cosmetic, and nothing feels pay-to-win. • Every moveset, item, or currency shows exactly where to get it in the Inspect menu of that particular item or moveset. Super helpful for an old guy like me. • Graphics look beautiful even on the lowest settings. • Tons of content: main quests, side quests, minigames, challenges, caves, dungeons, customization—always something to do. • Optimization is surprisingly good. My potato PC still hits around 60 FPS most of the time. The Bad: • Ping/hosting system feels terrible. I don’t know how it works, but whatever it’s doing right now is hurting PvP a lot. • Combat still feels shallow. It’s not close to Soulsborne depth (obviously), but PvP especially needs more counterplay. Stunlock is too easy and too common. • Audio didn’t feel that good to me or maybe I’m just new to Chinese games. The Ugly: • Menus are all over the place and can be very confusing. They really need to fix this—I keep getting lost in the interface. Conclusion: I had tons more stuff to say to praise this game, but to keep this review from getting even longer, I’ll stop here. If they keep this up and continue dropping content like this in the years to come, this game will be a landmark for the F2P game industry.

review_text: First of all WWM is a good game. It's got a cool Wuxia setting, action based combat with a lots of weapons to choose from, and an interesting system to drive players to interact with each other. However the microtransaction practices has so many predatory things about it that I can't whole heartedly recommend. It's got a lot of the red flags, multiple premium currency, you can't buy the specific amount of currency you need and different gacha with different rules that can easily mislead you. On top of all of it they're retroactively release outfits from the CN version at a far higher cost and putting it behind a misleading Gacha.' I don't care if people don't like this review because they think I'm attacking the game. I like the game and want to support the game without feeling mislead by shady tactic. This review is here to warn people so they do not end up falling for misleading gacha tactics like many others did. To future players, especially those that never played a gacha games you should follow these rules. - Read the details and rule of the gacha banners so you can make an informed decision. I know this sounds extremely obvious but most who don't play gacha are used to pricing transparency. Most do not expect a sudden change in rules especially between banners. - If a deal looks too good to be true it probably is. Check if there is something else is going on. - Don't fall for sunk cost fallacy or fomo. They almost always bring time-limited stuff back and often easier to obtain later. For those who don't know, recently they released a new scratch (Unseen Veil) that appears to be cheap. However the price of the gacha actually jumps significantly with every scratch and many only found out after already invested a lot of money into. Only the first scratch is 60 pearl. The price jumps significantly with every scratch. It actually adds up to 7440 pearl (over 100 USD, jumping from 60 to 180, 400, 800 all the way to 2600 pearl). It's not 7 scratch at 60 pearls each like a lot of people were mislead into thinking. You would not know this if you did not see the extremely easy to miss information in the details. The rule is a tiny icon down near the corner for you to click on and it's even misspelled as "intro" not "info". This resulted in a lot of people to spend money on the scratch only to find out that its far more expensive than their initial price point. At lot of the time people would have already spend 30 50 dollars without said costume and will fall for sunk cost fallacy trying to finish the scratch. This is extremely concerning as the outfit in question CAN BE PURCHASED DIRECTLY on the Chinese server and significantly lower price too at 2580 pearl for the entire set. Meaning they made this outfit retroactively more expensive and put it behind gacha for the international release. I do not know what Netease is trying to pull but its nothing good for the long term health of the game. Netease is notorious for it's microtransaction practice but this was a first for me. There is more than a fair share of players who just want to enjoy the game on a budget fell for this. Why not just make the price upfront? Why resort to misleading people? You got whales spending over 40k on a ship on the 5th day of release, this isn't even about keep a game alive, your game is alive and well. Did you really have to start using this kind of tactic so soon? You already have the legendary banner that cost over 300 dollar to hit pity (Not even the specific item you want, it's double if you want to costume), regular costumes reaching 40 USD and a bunch of other weapons skins and animation changes. Did you really have to make an existing outfit that sold for 2580 pearls and lock it behind a 7440 Gacha instead? This is on top of the fact that the NPC for f2p or budget players to earn cosmetics is not in the international version as well as coupons being cut back from 2 a month to 1 through the login bonus. The currency for the monthly pass do not give a player to player trading currency but rather regular coins. Why are so many features missing and items being cut back? You can't even access some existing multiplayer function because of the missing currency. I want to love this game, the combat is great, the world is great, the story is great, but it's this kind of practice that cause people to leave games in the first place. Most don't mind spending money on games they enjoy, most don't want to feel like they're being tricked into it.

review_text: Still trying to wrap my head how this game is actually free since the game really blew me away and exceeded all my expectations. I was here for the story and immersion, but the actual gameplay from exploration to combat are also very satisfying. It's pretty goofy too with lots of Kungfu Hustle references. I've tried many of these F2P open world games in the past decade, and most of them bored me to tears after the first hour or day at most. But I'm still looking forward to play and explore more of this beautiful world after 16 hours playing over the weekend.

review_text: This game is a mashup of a bunch of different games and genres, it feels like they tried to put every open world game mechanic into this and for the most part it succeeds. Combat alone lets you equip 2 different weapons at the same time, each of which has regular and heavy attacks and 2 different abilities, then you can block, parry or dodge, you have mystic abilities (spells) and can have 8 of those slotted at a time (they are also used out of combat in puzzles, mini games and traversal) and then you have passive abilites you can equip to enhance abilities or play styles. And that's just combat, there are an absolute load of mini games to play, sumo wrestling, 2 different card games, playing musical instruments with guitar hero mechanics, and a number of others. You can build your own house and base and even hire NPCs to work for you, you can start a guild and have raids against bosses, tournaments or guild on guild pvp battles. All this any way more than I'm not going to go into as this review is already long enough. All in all, this game is very impressive in that it stuffs so much into a game without completely falling apart. It's not as good in any one category as the best games of that genre but it does do a solid job in most things it does. The game's monetization is all focused around cosmetics btw, so if you don't care about that you can easily play the game entirely for free. Just be warned, cosmetics can get very pricey if you are trying to chase down a particular outfit, so just be wary of that. But honestly, it's been a while since I got so into an open world game, and that fact that this can be played both single player and in a multiplayer server is very impressive. My one complaint is that the UI is such a mess, there are menus within menus with more sub-menus within those, and more gets added as you keep playing. I'm still seeing new menus pop up that I've never seen before and I'm almost 40 hours into the game.

review_text: Review written after 1,600 hours of gameplay and having experienced a wide range of situations in the game: - Several bugs: broken world map textures, glitched interactions, bugged building items... - Reports and bug reports are ignored: Bugs remain unresolved no matter how many times they are reported, and players reported for violations listed in the report options—including spam, inappropriate audio, cheating, and other disruptive behavior—are never punished. - Extremely expensive cash shop: Want to look fancy? You have to pay real money to get Pearls. There is absolutely no way to earn premium currency for free (not even a small monthly allowance for F2P players). - Instead of fixing these structural issues, every new patch just adds more cosmetics to the cash shop and shallow, cash-driven events. - Terrible PvP system: Horrible balance that forces the player base to use the exact same rigid META builds and weapons. - Insane lag and terrible optimization. - Confusing UI: Cluttered menus that lack any proper explanation. - Boring story quests: Long, tedious conversations and forced slow-walking segments that completely kill the pacing. - Lack of content variety: Repetitive NPC models and a complete lack of voice acting. - A Toxic Community: Because it is a free MMORPG, it attracts many toxic, weird, creepy, and attention-seeking players. The community is one of the strangest and most toxic in the MMO genre. Many guilds have an unhealthy, cult-like mindset where defending the game’s flaws matters more than criticism. Leaving a guild feels like being erased — friendships often end instantly. The game revolves around social status, creating endless drama and ego clashes. - Global chat is constantly flooded with spam: Players beg continuously for shop outfits, Pearls, gallery exhibition votes, and sect rank votes, often repeating the same requests through unsolicited DMs. This creates an endless 24/7 scroll that makes the chat channels annoying, intrusive, and practically useless. - A special mention goes to the Velvet Shade sect, which is by far the worst offender for community and spam issues. It embodies all of the aforementioned problems and also has a high volume of unsolicited marriage proposals and flirtatious requests that add to the overall annoyance. Conclusion: The game constantly tries to hook you into spending money. The shop is updated weekly with new outfits, flashy FX animations, mounts, weapon skins, and limited-time items—often wrapped in fake "special discounts" designed to trigger FOMO. Before you play, keep this in mind: They don't care about the community. They don't care about optimization or stability. They don't care about balance or fixing game-breaking bugs. They only care about bleeding your wallet dry. At this point, it feels less like a martial arts RPG and more like a social status simulator driven by whoever puts on the best show and spends the most money in the cash shop. Ultimately, many players forget a harsh reality: when this pseudo-MMORPG inevitably shuts down, everything they spent real money on just to look fancy and show off will disappear forever along with the servers.

review_text: WWM impressed me with its beautiful graphics, fair monetization model, great customization options and massive amount of content. It definitely sets a new standard for free-to-play games. It takes a bit of time to wrap your head around all the pop-ups, sub-menus and different currencies, but it's well worth it once you do. At its core, the game is single-player and is packed with a solid main story and varied side quests. Right from level 10, you unlock two new modes: Co-op and MMO. The latter acts more like a social lobby, with both modes dedicated for group content, including dungeons and raids. Is it a Souls-like experience? Not really, but it's close enough. The combat revolves around parries and dodges, yet it remains fast-paced thanks to the martial arts and various weapon combinations. The world map is immense and exploration is engaging with lots of minigames and secrets to discover. Gear progression follows a mobile-style energy system, with the energy refill not being a daily thing: this is definitely a blessing for anyone with a busy schedule since it lets you play at your own pace and still keep up. There are gacha elements in the game, but they are all focused on cosmetics items that offer no gameplay advantages. If you're looking for a free MMO-ish game with lots of options, including both PvE and PvP, this might be your next game to try.

review_text: This game is delightfully strange right up until level 32, when you venture into the second zone. The English "localization" was always a bit wonky, but things take a nosedive after that point. I went from understanding what was being asked of me at any moment, to genuinely questioning my sanity as NPCs read aloud punctuation marks, hashtags, etc. in the middle of dialog while things inexplicably happened around me. Maybe things make sense in the original Chinese, and maybe they don't, but I just can't handle it anymore. Added more for the trolls: Where Winds Meet is a delightful, weird experience for the entire duration of the first zone, then takes a nosedive in quality in the second, to such a degree that I cannot recommend the game because of the stark differences in QA and care that the developers have put into it. It goes from a solid B to an F in an instant when the quests devolve from "weird, but charming" into "so badly machine-translated that the original intent has been lost to all time, and it's actively harming the experience." There are multiple clue/deduction quests that are actually incomprehensible, using what I can only assume are stories and idioms that once made sense in the original Chinese, now butchered in an affront to both Chinese culture and the English language. If there was ever any meaning, they have now been relegated to wandering around aimlessly until one stumbles on the conditions to satisfy the quest. It is an inconsistent, baffling experience BECAUSE the first zone is so delightful. So yes, not recommended. I'm not surprised nuance is outside the reach of gremlins who have to go diving into Steam profiles for ammunition when they can't process their emotions.

review_text: Recommended, but with caution Where Winds Meet surprised me in the best way. The game looks and plays like a full triple A title and it is honestly hard to believe it is basically free to play. The world is stunning, the combat feels great, the character creator is outstanding and there is a huge amount of exploration and side content. Let me point out the big things though. First, it is not pay to win. The shop is cosmetics only. The problem is the gacha. The rates are terrible and it feels like a very old school mobile system. Some costumes have fixed prices, which is fine, but the random pulls are rough. Second, the game throws a ton of menus, systems and features at you at the beginning. It feels overwhelming to the point of confusion. The good part is that once you get used to it, everything becomes easy to navigate. The onboarding could be much better, but you do get over that hurdle. Now for the biggest issue I have. The leveling gatekeeping is awful. At the time of writing, I have to wait six more days to go from 55 to 60. I do not understand the logic behind this. You keep earning XP anyway, so when the gate is lifted you blast through the next levels in about twenty minutes. It makes the gate pointless. During this forced downtime I fully cleared almost the entire first zone. 98 % of all quests, exploration and objectives done. That is when it hit me. At this pace I will probably clear most of the game before I even reach max level. After that, all that is left is a short list of activities. Five bosses per zone - Qinghe and Kaifeng, one trial, a pseudo battleground and one arena. PVP is terrible. It is a stunlock fiesta. It could have been fun, but right now it is just frustrating, although I still play it for the rewards. I already maxed out my mastery at this level, reached almost thirteen thousand power, started collecting books for inner ways and I can already see the long term loop forming. If you remove the mini games, the game becomes three repeating activities. Farm the same bosses, farm the same arena, farm the same outpost. That is basically it. After checking the CN version I am honestly not sure how long the game will stay alive in the West. It feels like the time gating was brought over for retention, not for any creative reason. I expected proper dungeons and raids, not just straight boss fights. The game needs engaging endgame content, not repetitive farming. Overall I am still satisfied and I enjoy my time with it. The world and the presentation are that good. But unless the endgame improves, I worry the game will fade as fast as it appeared.

And, you can submit visual or auditory data, whether it is purely your own or something copyrighted that you don't have the rights to use, feed it into a generative-AI tool that can make your character look a certain way, sound a certain way, or even do emotes lifted from video footage. Gross. I can already imagine the possibilities of abuse just on the end of the players, let alone the legal disaster this will result in on the side of the devs. But hey, the USA and China are not going to care about this at all on a governmental level, because they have vested interest in the AI bubble and the US even went as far as to put a moratorium on the regulation of these AI tools. What a contrast. And now because of their lack of disclosure, I am doubting every asset I see in the game, wondering if it was truly made by a human, partly, or not at all. Honesty is dead. review_text: Pros: The game looks really nice, it has a very large open world that you can explore and seems to have quite a bit to do. For a "free game" it really gives you a lot of options and it's easy to just get lost in the world. The combat is pretty fun, it's fluid and it feels good with a good variety of techniques. Cons: It's just too convoluted.. ridiculously so. The game is an over complicated mess, everything you do introduces a new system and that system is buried in a menu beneath the menu for the last thing you did. It's insanely hard to find what you're looking for in menus, even just trying to change a setting or something on your character means a trip through 50 menus and you might find it.. you might not. If you don't.. then just try again because you will likely get different menus the next time you look. This game isn't without it's strengths, I feel bad giving it a thumbs down, I wish Steam gave us a middle of the road option, I would pick that. As good as parts of this game are, it's just way too much of a mess.. way too many systems and menus buried in menus buried in menus. After about 4 hours I started to realize that I wasn't going to run out of new systems to learn anytime soon and I just quit. It's a cool enough game if you have a lot of patience.. I however, do not.

There are a hundred different things you can claim every three steps you take, and they are all hidden under a hundred different sections of the menus, half of them accessed from different places. The shop prices are predatory, period.

review_text: Where Winds Meet is one of those games where you start with a simple quest, and an hour later you’re standing on top of a mountain you don’t remember climbing, holding five screenshots of a random tree, and wondering when exactly your life went off-track. That’s how pretty the game is, it constantly distracts you on purpose. The story and characters are charming too. At one point an NPC told me something deep and philosophical, and all I could think was: “Yes, wise elder, very inspiring, but could you also point me in the right direction? I’ve been lost since the tutorial.” Exploration is where the game really shines. You start walking, notice a shiny rock, go to check it out, then find a hidden pond, then chase a butterfly, then somehow end up on top of a hill you weren’t supposed to reach yet. The game doesn’t stop you, it just silently approves your chaos. You can interact with cats in the world, and sometimes they even pretend to like you. It’s a small, charming detail that makes wandering around even more fun, especially when they completely ignore you in the middle of a serious quest. There are a few quirks: the pacing slows down occasionally, some objectives are explained with the confidence of someone giving directions while half-asleep, and I had a couple of small performance snags, nothing major, just small pauses for dramatic effect. Overall though, it’s a lovely, relaxing adventure. If you enjoy exploring, getting (very) lost, and accidentally creating your own side stories, you’ll love it. I came, I wandered, I got lost gloriously!

review_text: 500 hours in Where Winds Meet and I’m still locked in—but I really need to talk about the translation and historical context. The game is gorgeous, the wuxia vibe is strong, and the combat still makes me feel like a martial arts legend (right before I get folded by some random NPC named “Hungry Bandit #3”). But the English translation definitely needs work. A lot of dialogue feels awkward or unclear, and important story moments sometimes lose impact because the wording just doesn’t hit right. The historical references are also interesting but under-explained. For example, when the game touches on regions like the Hexi Region, it clearly expects you to already understand the significance—but for most players, there’s not enough in-game context to connect the dots. I’ve had to pause multiple times just to look up what was actually being referenced. If the devs improve translation quality and add better historical grounding, this game goes from amazing to truly unforgettable. Still 10/10 experience—but I’m basically playing Where Winds Meet + Wikipedia simulator at this point.

review_text: Where Winds Meet has genuinely surprised me with how much there is to do and how easy it is to get lost in the world. The open-world setting is beautiful, with some fantastic scenery, detailed environments, and moments where I’ve found myself stopping just to look around instead of rushing to the next objective. One of my favorite parts is the freedom to switch between solo open-world play and co-op/online play. I can explore at my own pace when I want a more immersive RPG experience, then jump online when I feel like playing with other people. That flexibility makes the game feel much less restrictive than a lot of other online RPGs. There’s also an impressive amount of variety. You’re not just running from fight to fight. There are side stories, exploration, puzzles, martial arts, different weapons and builds, NPC relationships, professions, healing, collecting, housing, mini-games, hidden areas, and all kinds of strange little encounters scattered around the world. I’m still discovering systems I didn’t even realize were there. Combat has been fun too, especially once you start experimenting with different Martial Arts and Mystic Skills. The ability to switch styles and build a character around the way you actually enjoy playing gives the game a lot of room to grow. It can definitely throw a lot of systems at you early on, and some mechanics aren’t explained as clearly as they could be, so there are moments where you may find yourself wondering what you’re supposed to do. But once things start clicking, the sheer amount of freedom becomes one of the game’s biggest strengths. Overall, Where Winds Meet feels like a world meant to be explored rather than simply completed. I can spend one session progressing the story, another wandering around finding secrets, and another doing side activities or playing online. Between the gorgeous world, martial-arts atmosphere, open-ended exploration, and the ability to move between solo and co-op play, I’ve been having a great time with it. Definitely recommended if you enjoy open-world RPGs where wandering off the main road is half the fun.

review_text: So, I wanted to come back to the review I wrote and give a bit of a spitshine. This is that! TL;DR: if you like the idea of this game, play it! It's a very fun game and my hours show how much I really do like it. But be prepared to deal with both game-breaking and annoying bugs, a very touchy quest system, a playerbase that's nice and funny as best, & annoying and toxic at worst, insanely expensive fashion, no real tutorials past first 5 hours, shoehorned in generative AI, absolutely no moderation + reporting being pointless, and a very restrictive multiplayer. - The good of WWM: The design of the world overall is wonderful, and it's a very alive place even if you play solo. There's so many NPCs to talk to and learn from at all different in-game times, and you're encouraged to do so so you can collect anecdotes! Love this system. It's also a very pretty game, and the photo mode is pretty good for what it is! The fashion of this game is both accurate and non-sexualized. Of course, there's gonna be a little bit of slut in any MMO's clothes regardless of what game it is, but overall everything is very appropriate while still looking beautiful. I really appreciate this in an era of eastern gaming where everyone needs to be dressed like a stripper. Outfits are gender locked, but given that WWM is a Chinese game I'll leave that be. The combat is super fun! I think it's a good mix between Sekiro (which this game is very Souls inspired) and simplicity. There's lots of weapons to pick from, and even more martial art styles (combat styles), though you will have to level up each martial art individually. There's also a good set of accessibility options for people that struggle with things like parrying/countering - but some points get knocked off because that accessibility is NOT available for Martial Fellowship (NPC duels), some event fights, and PVP. PVP I understand, but... the other two being excluded is very, very stupid. Most minigames are fun! Gift of Gab, most of the Meow Meow puzzles, Archery competitions, NPC healing, Pitch pot, and Graceful melodies are all great little momentary distractions. review_text: While I would like to recommend this game to practically anyone, it's a matter of taste and personal preference, I can't in good faith tell anyone to play a live service Gacha Game. While the Sekiro inspired combat and Wuxia elements are fantastic, the underdeveloped MMO aspect of the game will likely wear a lot of players down over time. Three month long seasons, weak battlepass offerings, month-long stretches of time with nothing to do made up of time gated, drip fed, and buggy content that largely is comprised of mini games and weekly/daily runs of the same thing. Nearly every resource or incremental point of progress you make towards unlocking a free cosmetic/accessory is capped out. The resource farming is capped daily, coins are capped, everyday drops from monsters, crafting. I don't think there is a single system that doesn't have an internal limit to progression, even if it has no direct impact on PVE or PVP combat. I think the biggest killer of this title, for me, is the fact you run out of engaging solo content pretty early on, so you resort to trying PVP, Raids, and Abyss challenges. The raids can only be completed once per week, PVP is laggy and inconsistent (filled with bots), and the abyss trials are a fun challenge with little to no reward. Worst of all, outside of drip fed, time gated, energy capped content, is the abysmal integration of the Gacha system and no end-game trading system. I do appreciate it isn't explicitly pay-to-win, but the fact that it is so disconnected from the main gameplay loop makes it feel tacked on. Once again, you're capped to purchasing 3 premium pulls a week without forking over hundreds of dollars to get a single skin. The shop skins are 3x the price of CN servers, the Gacha is also wildly over priced (30 dollars for a single 10 pull btw) and a hard pity set at 150 which means virtually nothing. Hard pity doesn't guarantee the outfit, hitting hard pity then hitting pity again doesn't guarantee the banner reward. You have to spend on average around 400 dollars for a single item and there is no other way to purchase the premium currency without spending your college fund and selling your kidney. Here's my advice, play Sekiro, or Elden ring, Dark souls, or an actual MMO if you're into that. While I appreciate some of the potential depth of combat and the aesthetics, don't play aggressively monetized live service games like this. The lack of content, end game systems, and repetitive boring grind isn't worth it when the chance to get something good is less than .014% and the free outfits pale in comparison and take months to grind for (only because of hard caps.) I'll still revisit this game from time to time, and am willing to change my mind if the developers adapt, but I don't see that happening considering we aren't the main player-base. Until then, I'll be treating this game as if it's in maintenance mode for the next couple months (at least until Hengdao comes out.)

review_text: Heyo! I have around 360 hours in this game, and unfortunately, I can’t really recommend it in its current state. To start with the positives: the game is genuinely f2p friendly. There are no p2w mechanics, and players cannot purchase stronger gear with real money. That’s a big advantage and something more games should strive for. However, the overall experience is held back by several major issues. PvP feels unbalanced, and the presence of cheaters further undermines any sense of fair competition. (And no there is no skill issue or anything like that... I am quite good at PvP) Systems like the bounty mechanic add frustration rather than meaningful engagement. U often get a bounty for no reasons, often you don't even realize when and when that happens... You will get an annoying invasion from a REAL player. Which even when u manage to defeat, u won't get anything and you still gonna have a bounty in ur head. It's better to just log off for a minute then come back to be in jail to get out, because this mechanic is really bad. The outfit pull system also feels unnecessary and out of place, especially given how much of the social environment revolves around it. You must be very lucky to get an outfit from limited banner. Speaking of social features, the global chat is rarely used for actual interaction. Instead, it is dominated by guild recruitment spam and players begging for outfits, which makes the game world feel less alive than it should. Even within guilds, activity tends to be inconsistent — many players join briefly, then leave or stop playing altogether. Over time, this makes it difficult to maintain any stable or active community. While the world itself is large, there isn’t enough engaging content to support it long-term. Many events feel repetitive or uninteresting, which contributes to a gradual loss of motivation to keep playing. For me personally, the main reason I stayed as long as I did was because I was playing with close friends. Once they lost interest and stopped playing, it became much harder to find reasons to continue. Eventually, I reached the same point. In summary, *Where Winds Meet* has a strong foundation and a fair monetization model, but it currently struggles with balance issues, weak social systems, and a lack of engaging content. With improvements in these areas, it could become a much better experience — but as it stands now, I cannot recommend it.

review_text: I now have almost 1,500 hours of playtime, and this is probably one of the first truly negative Steam reviews I have ever written. If you want to pick flowers, explore the world, and casually follow an AI-generated story, then go ahead and play the game. However, if you want to do boss runs or take on genuinely difficult challenges, stay away from it. Almost every boss is bugged, and it feels as though every animation or cutscene has the potential to interfere with the fight. The game features a challenge mode with hitless runs, which was originally the part that interested me the most. However, you are not simply fighting the boss and learning its attack patterns. You are fighting against developers who apparently do not play or properly test their own game. You are given unfinished bosses whose actual attacks sometimes do not match the animations being shown. Some attacks are so inconsistent and off-rhythm that it can take ten hours or more to memorize them. Not because the mechanics are particularly challenging, but because the timing, animations, and actual hit detection do not reliably match. Once you have finally memorized every pattern, every delayed rhythm, and even every misleading animation, you still have to deal with input registration issues. The game sometimes fails to recognize that you dodged or parried an attack. During phase transitions, the fight can also freeze and prevent you from entering the second phase altogether. The worst part is that some of these bosses have already been in the game for more than a year. Despite that, their existing issues are rarely—if ever—fixed retroactively. The gear system is also a complete disaster. Yes, the game is not directly pay-to-win. Instead, your progress is artificially restricted by an energy system. You are only allowed to improve your equipment at the pace dictated by the game. Once you have spent your energy, it feels as though you are being starved of resources, because you may only make around two percent progress on your gear in an entire day. At the moment, completing a single gear set takes approximately two to three weeks. I have now reached the point where I am gearing my third class. This means it takes around six to nine weeks just to build three complete sets. And what happens after six to eight weeks? The level cap increases, and you need an entirely new gear set. Your previous set may not even be finished before you are forced to start all over again. Proper min-maxing is nearly impossible because the game constantly starves you of materials. Class balancing also only happens roughly once every two months—if it happens at all. At the same time, there is a class called “Nameless,” which is clearly the developers’ favorite child. This class attacks safely from range, mainly uses charged attacks, and still consistently achieves the highest damage. Almost no risk, very little mechanical skill required, yet always the highest DPS. As I said before: if you simply want to play casually, collect flowers, and explore the world, you may have a good time. However, if you expect a fair challenge, technically polished boss fights, and reliable mechanics, stay away from this game. You are better off investing your time in a more polished game made by developers with enough experience to properly test their own content. I will not say much about the gacha system. If someone wants to spend €300–€500 on a legendary skin with generic animations that ultimately does little more than glow slightly brighter, they are free to do so. That is for everyone to decide for themselves.

Expect around 150–200 hours to clear currently available content. Gameplay revolves around blocking, reflecting, and repeating the same actions. You technically have two weapons, but in practice you use one and swap to the second only for buffs or debuffs. The interface is one of the worst I’ve encountered in an MMO. Navigation is painful, even after extensive playtime. The sheer number of systems and items is overwhelming, and many of them never become relevant. COMBAT Likely enjoyable for younger players or controller users. On keyboard & mouse, combat feels like input gymnastics rather than actual fighting. Endless key combinations, awkward positioning, and timing windows turn encounters into something closer to playing a piano than engaging combat. Souls-like? Maybe. Fun? Not for me — at least not on keyboard and mouse. PvE Some areas look great visually. World size is below average to average, but presentation is solid. The main story feels unfinished and abandoned. Instances and raids are decent mechanically, but energy caps and seasonal restrictions kill momentum. 10-player raids with pugs are mostly wipe-fests. Boss mechanics are repetitive, and most players simply ignore them. 5-player content is more tolerable, depending on caps and available energy. PvP Not tested.Not interested in trying it on keyboard & mouse. SOLO / CO-OP / MMO SYSTEMS Switching between modes is buggy, annoying, and often requires unnecessary regrouping. Ping and region differences matter a lot. Healing bounties are nearly impossible to grab — by the time they appear, they’re already taken. Chat is constantly filled with healing requests for targets that are already healed. Sects and reputation systems feel unrewarding compared to the time investment. Rewards (e.g. Silver Needle) don’t justify the grind. Many progression systems are weekly capped, limiting how much you can actually play. SHOP The shop feels aggressive. In the very beginning of the game you are not allowed to change any settings except MMORPG or ARPG so meanwhile enjoy the ear cancer from the game since you cant lower the volume till you know which button opens the settings. In summary: I do recommend people to play the game, its great and very well made for today standard which means games nowadays are getting released and they're barely even working properly or empty also, pay to play. review_text: I was a beta tester for this game and often defended it because of its fluid and satisfying gameplay (and because it was marginally more enjoyable than thps3+4 I guess), but more and more the devs seem to want to push long term players who've already earned everything and seen everything the store has to offer away. After dedicating myself to beating the first season pass I was rewarded with very little incentive to play because I'll only keep a "portion of my premium currency" when the second season arrives. My silly efforts to do the same in the second season have been justly rewarded with the "incentive" being completely removed upon the arrival of the new season, namely any of the season pass currency you earned (or paid for if you were REALLY stupid) not being carried over. To explain, the latest update to the purchasable/earnable currency used to earn items and unlock new pages in the battlepass's will auto-spend at the end of each season, going from a system that let you retain SOME semblance of reward for your previous playtime, into a new one that essentially says to the player: "Oh? you were saving your currency for stuff that isn't this garbage? What a shame, we just bought it all for you. No, you can't keep the change. No, I don't care that you spent real money on it. You can have some more worthless AI-generated crap if you give me $10 though." Are you guys being held at gunpoint or something? You're sat on one of the most fluid and satisfying skate games ever made and you seem intent on making everyone who enjoys playing it feel like an imbecile for giving it more than a moment of their time. I enjoy playing this game. I want to support it. Please give me a single reason to.

review_text: Every season has made the game more fun to play, but at the tradeoff of a vastly worse user experience. I've tried to stay at least neutral, because the gameplay is genuinely fun. But I've gotten to the final straw when I finally fell victim to EA's scam as well. NOTHING you spend premium currency/real money on has a confirmation dialog. You hold the button long enough and it's yours, whether you actually wanted it or not. It's appalling that they still haven't changed this, even after months and months of users complaining about accidentally spending premium currency on items they didn't want. I intentionally bought the pass last season, and had to play dozens of hours over the course of the season, every single day just to finish it, and I barely made it. Because the developers made the inane decision to not only completely wipe battle pass currency every season, but they also greatly increased the total cost of items while also greatly decreasing the amount of battle pass currency available. I usually stay away from battle passes because they're a plague upon the industry, but I had saved enough premium currency from the free sections of the previous passes to buy it. Never before have I had to spend so much of my time to unlock stuff in any battle pass. It's mind boggling how they've made it worse and worse every season so far. Nevermind that this is an EARLY ACCESS GAME and it's now in its 5th "season", with literally hundreds of dollars worth of overpriced, paid cosmetics shoved in the user's face at every opportunity. I really do enjoy the gameplay, it's why my playtime is so high, but the business practices on display have always disgusted me and it just keeps on getting worse.

review_text: I installed the game and tried to launch it it got an error involving Javelin Anticheat, It asked me to get rid of some old driver so I did and tried launching it again. This went on for several minutes of issues... I removed every program it asked me to, until it demanded I remove the driver for my wireless headset (Corsair iCUE), which I am absolutely certain shouldn't be an issue. At that point, I knew it was a hard "no" for me, but I uninstalled iCUE temporarily just to see if the game would start... i restarted my PC and tried launching the game again it then showed an error regarding my GPU's fan control software... and immediately after that, i got a Blue Screen of Death All this hassle just to run a skateboarding game... I uninstalled the game immediately after all that. I spoke to a friend who said he had encountered similar errors (except for the Blue Screen), and he gave up on the game too. I googled to understand why Javelin is so aggressive towards absolutely everything installed on the PC... And to my lack of surprise I discovered that Javelin operates at the Windows kernel level and likely has more system privileges than even you, the Administrator, do. Not only is that way too much especially for the game in question but it also ensures I will never launch a game with this anticheat again. I will never buy or play anything that uses this system. It’s disappointing, especially considering this was a specific game I really wanted to play. The use of anti-cheat software is understandable, but there’s a limit to how intrusive these things should be on a user's computer. After dealing with a Blue Screen of Death and spending minutes uninstalling a bunch of drivers/programs only to find out that the next time I launch, it’s going to take issue with some other random stupid program that has nothing to do with cheating I never want to go near a game that uses this Javelin system, never again.

review_text: This is my first ever skating game, so I have no connection to the other skates or other skating IPs. But I do hate this game and here is why: -EA is the publisher (no more needs to be said about that) -Always online... WHY?? Why cant we just have a single player skating game that has a multiplayer lobby?? How does always being online make the game better?? -Buggy azz mess that seems to get worse over time the more you play. The stuttering 20 min into skating is frustrating, especially when you try to get challenges done. I cant even do a simple kickflip without the jankyness. Dont let your player bump anything because then they will dramatically ragdoll (which would be funny if it didnt happen over the dumbest ♥♥♥ ALL THE TIME). -A lack luster verity in challenges and the rewards they give you. This one is more of a subjective statement, but I feel like doing the challenges of the day become very unfun and similar because they just seem to cycle through the same ones week after week. They do add a few new ones (I want to give them flowers where they deserve it, but its not enough to bring me back or care to get it done). I also feel like they are always in the same places and never in spots or areas you dont skate. The rewards are very hit and miss. Some of the stuff is pretty rad (like the sponsored stuff), but the rest is barely worth getting in my opinion. It feels like you are collecting to just collect (which I normally love), but in this game is very unsatisfying. I do appreciate that they made opening boxes less time consuming, but It doesnt motivate me to care or continue to open them any longer. -The map kinda sucks. I feel like San Van isnt a bad map, it does have some great skate spots, but I wish we had more verity in terrain, scenery, structures. It almost feels empty and void of real live. The cars and people are there, but they really dont add life to the city. One part of the city still isnt even open and this season (Season 2) they finally added a few challenges over there, but not enough to get people to hangout. Also when you turn off cars and people in the settings, they just go invisible, but they are still there! Vee will still say the stupid lines when you "bump" into them. I wish they just had multi maps that we could choose from instead of being trapped on this hell island called San Van. Other random gripes: -The tutorial people are annoying as hell, all of them!! Also the devs missed an opportunity to make them real people in the game you meet up with. Its kinda lame to have them just pop up as a picture with a speech that I could care less about. -You get all these cool skating props (the one fun thing to collect), but can only place 5 down, which is lame -The music is okay, I just listen to my spotify most of the time -The skating its self is fun and feels good at times, but the rest of the game is not and it makes it hard to care or want to get on to play anymore. -No Afros! (that one is a personal personal gripe), but really??? To summarize, this game has pissed me off so bad that Im done playing. Thankfully I can skate in real life, so Im going to go do that! Thank you for coming to my Ted talk! Tchau!

review_text: it's fun, satisfying to hit tricks/clean lines, physics/animations are pretty good. a solid choice if you're into skating & just want a chill casual game to play! cons: always online no main story/lacking mission variety (no hall of meat) battle-pass/store in early access no pro skaters roaming base cosmetics are boring compared to previous titles after a few updates; it still lacks life. they gave us copy/pasted game-mode w/ a timer attached to it (zzz). tutorial island is back, boring after a few hours if you prefer street spots. grom is tied behind a pay-wall though, so it's essentially pointless & there to further more prove how anti-consumer EA is. nothing but zumez mall-skater brands continue to plague the game. rewards for premium are hilariously bad. where's the skate culture? 90% of the 'good' clothes are in the store/not obtainable w/ in-game currency. way too slow to fix bugs. 3 months is too long for seasons in the current state of the game, there's no way after YEARS of tech-demo, you still need that much time to bring back features that were in the demo. slow-dripping miniscule updates every 3 months is not good-live service, you need to provide sustainable content like bringing back popular game-modes, bringing back old skate maps (FREE NOT PAID) , 1:1 replicas of popular spots (not these weird half-baked edited spots) remove the awful AI voice & other "skaters" who yap non-sense in your ear, at least give them personality... you know, like the previous titles? lol i usually enjoy the VO on games, but from the first boot i have set the volume to 0. the player numbers reflect these issues, i still play. but man, it's getting harder to find joy in this w/ each update. through these problems however , the game has still improved in other places. the anims are smoother/refined, more optimized, better fidelity, cleaner art-style, less buggy, more tricks, the best one imo is the camera effects for keyframes. i chalk up these issues as a publisher sticking their hand into the devs candy bowl & deciding which ones the devs eat. let the devs do their job w/o micro-management & watch the money pour in. it's not rocket science.

review_text: I'm new to skate franchise and from a fresh perspective; i enjoy the controls to a point, but sometimes the game doesn't register the move i've done as being correct even though my input was correct, so some challenges become bricked. When it works, it feels great. Unfortunately there are glaring issues that are heavily affecting my review. The infinite loading screens and black screens requiring an alt-f4 to solve: (Disclaimer, don't mess with your bios unless you know what you're doing) Following a not too far away bios/gpu update, there was an overclocking/compatibility issue that i noticed since a couple other heavy games were having crash to desktop issues including this game. Upon defaulting the overclock then re-engaging it (DOCP1), things were running fine (beside the occasional blackscreen/loading-screen-lock which i know is an optimization issue with this game because the other heavy games stopped having CTD issues after disabling and re-enabling the PCs overclock). It could also be the GPU 50 series or bios having stability issues after certain updates, but what's frustrating is how long these issues continue on after further updates. I'm not sure what limitations would exist for an incredibly wealthy company such as EA, but their track record isn't great so i'm not expecting any improvement. So the performance and aggressive microtransactions are the major deterrent for me continuing to enjoy this game.

review_text: I never leave negative reviews on early access games, but the fact that they created a season pass at this stage opened the door for me. Firstly, for a game that requires you to play online, the co-op systems barely work. An open party will be listed as closed to other players, so you usually have to go in and either manually invite people or change your settings back and forth, so you can actually play with your friends. Half of the time your other party members are invisible. When you can see them, the desync causes you to see any movements of party members several seconds late. You also can't see your friends on the map anymore, forcing you to teleport in a game about skating places. The challenges are also incredibly broken. A lot of the time, goals won't register that you're completing them, both while you're in the challenge and after you complete it. You can do a line flawlessly, and you'll have to keep doing it, hoping that the game suddenly decides to register that you're completing a certain action. There's one challenge that half the time won't allow you to complete a triple kickflip in the designated area. This isn't a skill issue. You can hit it on the way to the scoring area, but once you're actually in the highlighted area, the game won't let you get your board off the ground. Then after a challenge's completion, you'll see on the map that there's one random goal that's still missing. There's absolutely no reason that "All goals in one attempt" should be checked off but one of the other goals isn't. Also when you try to queue co-op challenges, a lot of the time it just doesn't bring your party members in with you, giving you another reason to have to keep quitting and restarting. The physics are wildly inconsistent. You can speed into a rail head on, and sometimes it just kinda bounces you back a bit while you stay on the board. Alternatively, you can slightly graze against a rail at a shallow angle, and it might send you flying off your board at a higher speed than you were going in the first place. The map isn't terrible, but as some other reviews say, it feels very corporate and soulless. It has a handful of good spots and parks, but there's just something about it that feels like it wasn't made with love. The crashes are also one of this game's many mysteries. Sometimes you can hop on and play for an hour or two completely without issue. Other days you'll try to play, and you can't go ten minutes without your game deciding to close. As I opened with, I get that this game is in early access, and it understandably still needs some polishing. A lot of these issues are things they're working on, and can be fixed relatively easily. In fact, a lot of these things didn't even happen after the game was freshly released. I don't even mind the fact that they're selling cosmetics, the game is free. But EA being EA, they prioritize selling cosmetics that don't even look good instead of ironing out fundamental issues with their game that somehow get worse every update. This game has a lot of potential, and there's a decent amount of fun to be had in it (when it works). But unless EA learns what to focus on, this game is gonna be dead on arrival.

review_text: This game is probably the worst game they could have made as part of the skate series for a few big reasons. Firstly, the target demographic. They made a new skate game because all the fans of the first three games wanted it. Then they switched it up and targeted children who have no idea how skateboarding works. Why? That is the most counter-intuitive choice that they could have made. And now this game has no resemblance of what the sport means to most people. Skateboarding is supposed to be difficult, requiring you to risk injury in order to do something cool. And with this "Impervatek" bs, they completely nuked that idea to the floor just to lower the age rating and get more kids to give them money through microtransactions. Secondly, the map. The whole place just feels like a few big spots scattered throughout the most boring, repetitive map possible. I hope you enjoy skating in a city, because that's all you get. The districts are all practically identical, with no variation of decoration or features, no elevation changes, and no medium sized obstacles. Everything is just either a megaramp, or a bench. While playing this game, I haven't seen a single person after the first few weeks of the game skate anything other than their giant ramps. Every important spot is just so huge and impressive, that they all feel so artificial and samey. Thirdly, the game being live service. Live service has to be the worst trend ever conceived by game developers. All I want out of a game, is to be able to hop on and mess around for half an hour when I have a bit of free time. What I don't want, is to be waiting 5 minutes to get into a server, just to play the same poorly playtested missions and challenges that only work half the time. The problem is, they are adding low-effort temporary content instead of permanent stuff to make the game better. I can only do one of their 4 types of missions, which get stale extremely quickly and are just recycled every time they refresh (I will give them some slack as the game is still early-access). Some more (well thought out) mission types - such as races or competitions against AI - in future updates would be appreciated. Finally, their "early access" claims. If a game has seasons, its own version of a battle pass, and microtransactions, then this is not early access. This is a full game. The devs are just using this facade to give excuses for why the game is incomplete, yet they put their efforts onto making seasons (e.g. what they just released for Halloween). Where are dark catches and slides, where are underflips, where are other mission types and where is the replay editor from Skate 3? All we have now is just a buggy piece of crap that has no keyframes whatsoever, and can't even record at 60fps smoothly. They ruined my favourite part of 3: being able to film my tricks in a cool way. And now they put all their efforts making "seasons" as if the game is Fortnite or something. Cheers Full Circle. However, the game does feel smoother and less buggy than Skate 3, and the art style isn't the most horrendous thing like some other people say. All of this criticism is just for now, but if they don't make some pretty drastic changes, then the game will forever be bad. tl;dr: they made the game for kids, not who wanted it the map is extremely boring with only a few interesting spots the devs add low-effort content as the game is live service the they are adding seasons to the game, not actual permanent content I'll be surprised if anyone is still playing this after a few months. This game is destined to be forgotten.
