review_text: FragPunk brings a fresh twist to the hero shooter genre with its fast-paced gameplay, vibrant visual style, and unique Shard Card system that changes the rules of every match. The gunplay feels responsive, matches move at a thrilling pace, and the card mechanics create unpredictable moments that keep rounds exciting. At its core, FragPunk has all the ingredients of a standout competitive shooter. The weapons feel satisfying, the characters are distinctive, and the constant gameplay variety helps it avoid feeling repetitive. Unfortunately, the game's biggest weakness is its apparent reliance on bots. Many players have reported matches that feel filled with AI-controlled opponents rather than real competitors. Whether these bots appear in beginner lobbies, casual matchmaking, or other situations, their presence can make victories feel hollow and raise questions about the competitive integrity of the experience. When you're matched against real players, FragPunk shines. The strategic use of Shard Cards combined with quick gunfights creates some genuinely memorable moments. However, it's difficult to fully invest in the competition when you're unsure if the enemy team is made up of actual players or scripted bots. Despite this issue, the game remains fun for those seeking a casual shooter with a unique identity. The foundation is solid, and if the developers continue improving matchmaking transparency, FragPunk could become a much stronger competitor within the hero shooter market. Pros - Fast and engaging gunplay - Creative Shard Card system - Stylish visuals and presentation - Matches rarely feel repetitive Cons - Bots can make matches feel artificial - Competitive experience lacks trust and consistency - Victories sometimes feel less rewarding Final Score: 7/10 FragPunk is a creative and entertaining shooter with excellent gameplay foundations, but the perception of bot-filled matches prevents it from reaching its full potential. Great ideas and plenty of fun are here, but the multiplayer experience needs more authenticity to ensure long-term success.

review_text: I rarely leave reviews on Steam since I find them pointless. But these reviews are too harsh for a f2p game. Now... My hands are full with FragPunk, shilling and defending this game 100%, putting my full support behind it. As of September 2026. Nowadays, people love to hate games for any reason, disregarding the work of everyday programmers, artists, and player support agents. The problem!! greedy executives, stockholders, and lawyers who want to milk every penny from this industry. I was pleasantly surprised with FragPunk, and above all, it's a 100% free game with cosmetic skins and almost no pay-to-win (some Operator unlocks, but these are mechanically complex / hard to play). The developers and NetEase should keep it this way. In my short time playing this game, I did encounter some problems that many have already pointed out: Player Population- Sluggish matchmaking - A bigger player pool would fix this. Cheaters (just two in my playtime) - Since it's a game from NetEase, this is mostly handled by the latter, not the game developers. Bots - A bigger player pool would fix this. Overall, this is 100% on both the publisher and developers, mostly due to marketing. Gameplay / UI / UX- Extremely broken game modes - I actually liked this, but I understand why this would be a negative for a lot of people. Unlocking some Operators / Heroes - Pretty self-explanatory. Ranked mode extremely dependent on team play, team economy, team decisions, teamwork, team everything. It's ambitious, but people in most games hate to play in teams. Still, heavy team-oriented quirks define ranked, ESPECIALLY choosing card augments. Card augments! - Cool. I would make them even crazier. Overcrowded "mobile-first" UI/UX - A bunch of coins, materials, battle passes, chests, etc., etc. Very overwhelming. Other- The art style is outdated and looks very generic / bland. I would simply go full generic and copy CoD / BF6 like all modern FPS games. Found it fun with the overpowered mechanics, movement, and gunplay. Hope the devs can get more chances to fix the mess. My general advice is: "More streamlined and focused game." Recommended but with caveats Note: It's an UE game but my crap pc ran it well.

review_text: Season 1 was great, now the game is just disappointing. FRAGPUNK was genuinely a lot of fun during Season 1. The gameplay was fast, chaotic and simply felt good. I actually enjoyed the game enough to spend money on it. But the fact that you cannot disable crossplay on PC and are basically forced to play against players on other platforms using aim assist is honestly ridiculous. In a competitive shooter, PC players should at least have the option to choose whether they want to play against controller players or not. Playing with mouse and keyboard against aim assist can feel incredibly unfair, especially when the game is supposed to be competitive. The game also feels completely different compared to Season 1, and unfortunately not in a good way. At this point, I honestly feel like the money I spent on this game was wasted. Season 1: 🔥 FRAGPUNK now: ❌ It's a shame, because this game had so much potential.

review_text: Admittedly, I really enjoy Fragpunk! The game is oddly overstimulating with the powerful and brightly coloured visuals seemingly SHOUTING at you through the screen.. the UI seems like wayyy to much when you're just starting ( you are faced with an army of red exclamation points), however, looking past all that shimmer and shine, you see a game which really tries to stand apart from the regular shooter scene, which I suppose also lead to its sadly small player base. I see a lot of people complaining that the real reason Fragpunk fell off is because it just tries to do too much, being a Hero shooter is great but adding the Shard cards makes it a whole new game, and that game is of course Fragpunk, there is a lot of discourse about the execution of this idea and I think people are just overwhelmed. Oddly enough, I enjoy it, for example, I tried FINALS and that game was too much for me, whereas Fragpunk felt like a breath of fresh air! Funky, colourful, fun!! Having an oddly toxic relationship with shooter games like Valorant, this game doesn't feel that serious, and a shooter game that isn't really that serious is hard to come by. Fragpunk for me is a chill game where you basically just take the piss, the shooting feels really smooth, headshots feel great and if you understand hero shooters, you will understand Fragpunk, the shard cards just add a fun spin to it. And well of course the use of AI is horrible, and I don't support it at all, and in all fairness I have no idea how big their dev team is, but with their lack of advertising, it almost seems like they are leaning into the games death. Sadly, the queue times are a bit of a downer sometimes, but we digress.. The game is shamefully addictive for me and if you're looking for a stupid hero shooter with a stupid spin on it, this game is for you!

review_text: I honestly love this game. FragPunk has been a lot of fun, especially because the cards give every match a different feel. It keeps the game from getting crazy repetitive, and every game can play out differently. You get the occasional sus shot here and there, but overall I have a great time playing it. I started playing solo once in a while, and I finally got one of my friends to try it. Now we have been playing nonstop for the last two weeks. i got a group together so much more fun, Once you get a group together, this game is seriously fun. I did run into an issue trying to connect my accounts between PS5 and Steam. I can't get my account onto my PS5. I'm not sure if I messed something up by trying to connect everything through the game first, but hopefully this can be fixed because I would really like to play on both. My biggest complaint is the pricing. The battle pass is expensive, and the credits are pretty crazy too. I ended up getting the monthly option because I wanted to support the game and get the upgraded battle pass, but by the time everything is added up, I'm spending over $20. I don't mind spending money on a game I enjoy. I actually WANT to support the developers because me and my group have been having a great time. But I think the prices are going to hurt the game in the long run. If you want FragPunk to have longevity, I really think lowering the prices would help. More reasonable prices could mean more people buying things, more players sticking around, and more players coming back season after season. I also really think there should be a rotating skin shop, or some way to buy skins that you missed. It is honestly pretty annoying seeing some really cool skins and characters locked behind a battle pass and knowing you might never be able to get them again. Gameplay wise, FragPunk reminds me more of Halo than CS:GO or Valorant. It feels more forgiving when moving and shooting, and I personally really like that. It makes the game feel more fun and less punishing while still having plenty of skill involved. Overall, I really enjoy FragPunk and I want to see this game succeed. The cards, gunplay, characters, and overall gameplay make it something I keep coming back to. Me and my friends have been having a blast. Devs, if you really care about the longevity of the game, please take another look at the pricing and how skins are sold. Give players more reasonable prices and more ways to get the skins they actually want. I honestly think you'll keep more players around that way. Great game. Just please don't price your players out of it.

review_text: Fragpunk, my beloved. I have been on a kick lately of trying all the free-to-play tactical shooters out there, including Valorant. Fragpunk has been BY FAR the one that has held my attention the longest, with its stylish abilities, great TTK, and amazing gunplay. The heroes feel like they've been well-thought-out, and barriers to entry aren't too high, unlike other tactical shooters. Unfortunately I can't at this time recommend it, as the game went from over 100,000 players to now just around 1000, and the devs don't seem interested in reviving it. One thing they do is match you with entirely bot lobbies without telling you, instead of just giving you a slightly longer wait. review_text: I took a break from the game for a while, and when I came back I barely recognized it. Despite the fact that many new servers were added, it honestly feels like they switched to cheaper hosting overall. Why do I say that? Because the character models in the game feel even faster than before, but if you analyze demo recordings and look closely at hit registration, you can clearly see opponent models lagging. On top of that, the hit registration has become absolutely awful. This used to be one of the things that set the game apart from other shooters. In my personal ranking it used to be number one for hit registration, followed by Valorant and then CS2. The player base also feels much smaller now, which is not surprising considering the issues I mentioned. Replacing players with bots in different modes is simply ridiculous. The bots are clearly unfinished — they can kill poor newcomers while being completely blinded, for example. From the outside they even look like blatant cheaters because their aim sticks to you when they shoot. Watching it in demos is honestly cringe. What is even more noticeable is the quality of character skins and weapon skins. It feels like most of the game’s budget and development time is going into cosmetics. Yes, everything looks beautiful, but what’s the point when there’s nobody to play with (except bots), and when the game barely functions properly when you finally do get real opponents? Then there’s crossplay with console players. In about 70–80% of my matches, those poor console players are just struggling to even aim at people in time, not to mention using abilities properly. If you’re wondering about ranks — I’ve tried them all. I’ve been PunkMaster, Master, Diamond, and Platinum, and it’s the same everywhere. I even tested it on my second account, and it’s exactly the same story. As for skins, I also tried the gacha system and got a good feel for its randomness and somewhat predatory design. I pulled the top skins for Pathogen and Crown, but in both cases I had to completely roll through the banner to get them. It honestly felt like a Genshin Impact simulator. Sure, they occasionally throw you some freebies and basic skins, but all the top-tier items are very expensive. The only thing I can genuinely praise is the battle pass. If you buy it once and don’t spend the currency on anything else, you can keep renewing it indefinitely. Were you expecting something else? Of course not — the only real upside is tied to battle pass money. Everything else follows the same monetization philosophy. Finally, the anti-cheat. It’s basically a scarecrow in a field — maybe it scares the crows a little, but they still eat the corn and crap all over your garden. In other words, it’s complete garbage, even though it runs at the kernel level. I had huge hopes for this game. At the beginning it looked amazing. But now it just feels like another disappointment. Aside from the old, worn-out shooters, there’s honestly nothing new worth playing right now — because FragPunk has turned into a complete mess.

review_text: This may be a long review but its my genuine look on this game and I feel people should take it for consideration when playing. Fragpunk deserves more credit than it is given. The gameplay is enjoyable with good gunplay and character mechanics that all feel well balanced. The main negative reviews ive seen are mainly about ai generated content, bots-cheaters, and micro transactions As for ai content. The only content I can tell would be the showcase picture of skins. for example the battle pass banner for 2 premium skins. other than that the art in the game is great and has a lot of character. Stickers for example would be the guess for ai use. but i cant tell and I enjoy a lot of them. I can care less if a game uses a little ai if its done right. They shouldnt get a negative review for that. Bots and Cheaters. Ive been going through ranked and have not experienced any bots or cheaters. now for casual and arcade idk, but so far its been fun. Play with friends to get the most out of the arcade game modes, there a great addition for casual play and are well made. They added a tower defense game mode with around 100 or more cards just for it and I was suprised how fun it was. Now for Micro Transactions. By far the most important because people give the most negative reviews about it. Upfront im going to say Fragpunk is by far one of the best games to do micro transactions right and Ill explain why. First lets address free content. ill use the current season events for example. You get 3 character skins and 4 weapon skins 25 ultra pop cans with stickers, charms, head and arm ornaments, and profile stuff for free. Now these skins have different variants and vfx, different sound effects, cross hairs, tracers, and animations. I like how even rare and epic skins look good and make me want to use them instead of letting them rot. Not to mention you can use stickers and charms to make your own skins. I added a animated flaming sticker to my knife, last game to come close to that was bo3 and i miss it, but fragpunk brought it back. Ive even gotten random free promos that gave me ultra pop cans and frag coins. the premium currency, a free character unlock and a battle pass voucher thats $10 free. Which brings me to the currencies of the game. review_text: **Level 50 | Gold Ranked | Free to Play** --- I's basically Valorant but actually enjoyable to open imo ngl. The colours are loud, the sound design goes hard, and it just feels alive in a way Valorant stopped feeling like years ago. The big thing is the Shard Cards. Every round your team picks cards that change the rules. Giant heads, lifesteal bullets, removing a bomb site entirely. It's chaotic but it's the good kind of chaotic where you're laughing instead of fuming. They're all stupid but intresting and add a very nice strategic feel to the game, deffo objectyly, as u can see the opponets shard cards as welll and need to be aware of them. Matches are first to 7 wins. Not 13 rounds. Not a whole commitment. You can lose a couple early and still be totally fine. That alone makes it so much less stressful to queue into after a long day. Higher ranks scale up to first to 11 iirc, which is still nothing crazy. This maters laot to me cuz the first to 13 in val was just LOOONG. meant Val matches took an hour just for one. at least 40+ mins. On that note, the wait time. Idk why Val doesn't have smth o do while you're waiting but at least in Fragpunk u can enter training grounds or DM or smth while waiting. wait times really depends. sometimes i get many matches in under 30 seconds, and i also waysp lay solo, sometimes I'll be waiting for 30 mins. deffo due to the low playerbase but i think this sshould be noted as well. Customization is another REALLY good reason i love the game. unlike val customs aren' limied to only guns. even skins have parts that can be customized, as in headpiece, bracelet etc. even gun cuztomization aone is alot more than val. its not so much tahat it distracts mid game and voicelines mean hat I'll always know who is who (small characer cast as well but ironically more agents than val). **Performance wise**, my PC is kind of terrible and it runs. Minimum specs are pretty forgiving for a competitive shooter. That said there's a difference between running it and running it well, so if your rig is on the weaker side just drop the settings and chase the frames. The game still feels good on low. A few cards are clearly better than others and you'll notice your team defaulting to the same picks after a while. Small complaint. But honestly? It's just fun. Straightforward fun. Really hope the game gets decently popular. really fun, unique. **8.5 / 10**

review_text: Let's start off by saying that I absolutely recommend FragPunk. Even though FragPunk is not as popular as other games in the genre, it is the most fast-paced and fun one in my opinion. For one, the "shard card" system allows creative gameplay - every round can be played different based on the shard cards chosen by the team. However, like any other game FragPunk does have problems - mostly the overwhelming amount of gamemodes. Apart from the regular gamemode (called Shard Clash), there are several TDM modes, the Outbreak mode (a zombie vs. survivors kind of gamemode), duels, solo death matches etc. While a big amount of gamemodes isn't necessarily a problem, it is to be acknowledged that most of these modes are rarely played. Considering that the amount of gamemodes is the only major negative point I can think of, while being able to mention several positive points (e.g. fun gameplay, short rounds, nice graphics, a mostly nice community) I fully recommend playing FragPunk, especially with friends!

review_text: Genuinely one of the best competitive shooters I have ever played Generally reaching the top rank in a game is an absolute slog and painful. Hitting champ on R6 years ago took a mental toll, hitting Pred on Apex broke me and made me uninstall after getting it, etc. Reaching Punkmaster on Fragpunk was genuinely fun the ENTIRE way through. Every game feels different with the card system, and it's the only shooter where you continually see players doing things and causing interactions with abilities and cards that make you stop and think "why didn't I think of that?" or "wow, that's cool". I'm really not sure where the review bombers come from that call it a cash grab or Valorant clone, when in reality the only thing it shares in common with Valorant is that it is a 5v5 bomb mode. There are a TON of games like that, and this game does a good job carving a unique identity in that genre. You'll also notice EVERYONE who says those things have under 20 hours, and this game takes 50+ to really start to grasp and get used to. The cash grab accusations are braindead, considering the only paid things are cosmetics, and everything can be earned for free with enough playtime. If you don't have the self control to not spend money on every pretty skin you see, maybe stick to single player games, as Fragpunk's microtransactions are objectively less predatory than games like Apex, Overwatch, CS2, Valorant, etc. The real shortcoming of this game is the marketing team. Please for the love of god advertise this game, do a collab, SOMETHING. This game has SO much potential behind it, and it is being wasted by a marketing team who clearly has no idea what they are doing. Also, who decided this game needed a "Hentai" tag??? There is ZERO nudity or sexually suggestive material, the most you'll see is a character's midriff or thigh. Is this middle school? If you are like me and have the "Hentai" tag blocked from showing up on steam recommendations, this game would never appear for you unless searched for directly. tldr; Great game, awful marketing team, review bombed by low play time Valorant dudes who are mad they cant find any 15 year olds to groom

review_text: One of, if not the weirdest game I've ever played. Even though this experience is only around 1 and a half hour to play through; it feels lot longer and I mean that the best way possible. There's so much quality stuff here, it's so captivating and overwhelming and the game acts like it's nothing. So many interesting characters with all sorts of styles, animations and voices; so many diverse places with so much personality and ideas, it feels like they could go on forever, but they still manage to feel connected and consistent. It all feels like a trip, it's so out there, I don't even know where to begin or what to say about it; you just have to see it for yourself, you'll get it the first minute you boot it up. I'll say this though, it feels one of the bests out of the bunch that are aiming for a similar experience. It does not feel cheap at all; there's so much quality here with it's presentation, it's surreal, humorous, uncanny, existential tone. If I would have payed for this game I still would have been satisfied; but with no price tag it actually feels criminal playing this for free, even if it's not your cup of tea. So what do you have to lose; it's free, might as well try it! It's only one chapter so far, it's clear there's more content and chapters planned in the future; but it still feels like a compact experience with some conclusion, but with mysteries and lore still open. I really hope they are still working on it and make it a full game eventually; I'd happily pay for it once it's out. Even though I haven't played LSD: Dream Emulator; that seems like the closest comparison in terms of weirdness and style, but this one feels a bit less cryptic and more straight forward with tasks and objectives. If that one or Jazzpunk, Kid A Mnesia Exhibition, Manifold Garden, Antichamber or any other trippy, weird experiences are up your alley; this seems like an obvious choice!

review_text: I used to think that surrealism was just really random. I still liked it, but thought it was randomness. ENA and her world is proof that randomness couldn't make a great surrealist world. My personal favorite thing about this game is just seeing how creative and fluid each animation can be. This is not free slop. The idea that this is free is baffling to me. Please take the time for yourself to experience the world that ENA dream bbq manages to create. It may not make a ton of sense at first (or ever). review_text: I don’t want to spoil you of anything. So, I’m not gonna review the game normally. But I’m not gonna tell you to “just get it already” either. Instead, I’m gonna tell you WHY you should play it, but with ZERO spoilers. What this game is: Dream BBQ is season 2 of “ENA”. Season 1 is a series of four YouTube videos which you can watch for free (and should; they’re great!) and season 2 is this video game; “ENA: Dream BBQ”. Like with most things, it’s best to finish season 1 before starting season 2. Dream BBQ will release in multiple chapters. Chapter 1 is free and out now, but the rest will cost money when they release individually. I’m not sure if the game be a one-time purchase or if you’ll need to buy each chapter individually. This isn’t a half-baked experience, though, and you’ll get to go on a smaller-scale adventure for a couple of hours with a beginning and end, which is part of one overarching narrative. (Although, like most things ENA, the narrative is pretty strange, vague and confusing, although that’s all part of the fun.) Why you should play it (after season 1): ENA season 1 had beautiful, unique, and bizarre visuals, characters with great, varied designs and distinct personalities, and is generally full of absurd and dark humor. All of which are things I love. Dream BBQ takes that and turns it into a walking simulator with a few simple platforming elements (although one section so far is kind of difficult), which it translates very well into. I personally like season 2’s protagonist more than season 1’s, even if I liked 1 too. Conclusion: So yeah, go and watch season 1 if you haven’t already. Like it? Play Dream BBQ chapter 1 for free! Like chapter 1? Play it again for the route that you didn’t pick! Want more chapters? Wait! 🫠 Great game. My score: 9.7/10.

review_text: I thought ENA: Dream BBQ was just going to be another weird indie game. I was wrong. The world makes absolutely no sense. The characters talk like they're from completely different realities. The environments look like someone put a dream, a fever dream, and an old computer together and somehow made it playable. And somehow, it works. At first, I was mostly laughing. Then I started getting uncomfortable. Then I started wondering what the hell was actually happening. And somehow, I was doing all three at once. What I love most about ENA is that it never feels like it's trying to explain itself to you. It just throws you into its world and expects you to keep up. One moment you're talking to a completely bizarre character about something that makes absolutely no sense. The next, you're walking through an environment that feels strangely beautiful despite looking like it shouldn't exist. And then something happens that makes you stop and think: "Wait... what?" The humor is ridiculous, the visuals are unforgettable, and the soundtrack somehow makes the entire thing feel even more like a dream. I've played games with clearer stories, better graphics, and much more conventional gameplay. I don't remember most of them. I'll remember ENA. I'll remember the strange characters. I'll remember the bizarre places. I'll remember constantly wondering whether I was supposed to understand what was happening. Some games tell you exactly what their world is. ENA throws you into its world and lets you figure out what it means to you. It's confusing. It's funny. It's beautiful. It's unsettling. And I have absolutely no idea what I just experienced. 100% recommended.

review_text: I installed ENA: Dream BBQ expecting a quirky surreal indie game. Instead I accidentally injected pure digital schizophrenia directly into my frontal lobe. This game does not use normal human logic. Every conversation feels like two broken AI chatbots arguing inside a microwave. Every NPC speaks like they know something horrible about you personally. One second you’re walking through a beautiful dreamscape. The next second a creature shaped like a tax fraud accusation asks you to collect meat cubes for spiritual reasons. And somehow it all makes sense. The Steam page says you “explore strange worlds” and “meet sweet and sour characters.” That is the biggest understatement since “the ocean is somewhat damp.” The worlds in this game look like a PS2 fever dream that escaped containment. The art style feels like someone fed 2004 internet culture, public access television, lost Flash animations, and a cursed geometry textbook directly into a neural network powered by emotional trauma. And ENA herself? ENA is not a protagonist. ENA is a psychological condition. She talks like a customer support bot moments away from a nervous breakdown. Half the time she sounds deeply concerned. The other half she sounds like she’s about to explode into confetti and unpaid taxes. The soundtrack deserves investigation by international authorities. It sounds like haunted elevator music broadcast from a shopping mall floating in deep space. Somehow every song feels nostalgic for a childhood nobody actually had. The funniest part is that the game is FREE. Free. Joel G and the ENA Team created one of the most visually unique games on Steam and then released it onto the internet like an escaped laboratory specimen. The reviews are “Overwhelmingly Positive,” which makes sense because nobody who survives this experience remains mentally capable of leaving a negative review. People online genuinely debate the lore like they’re decoding ancient scripture. Some fans think ENA committed war crimes. Others think the entire game is symbolic. At one point I laughed. At another point I stared at a floating object for ten minutes because I wasn’t sure if it was an NPC, a building, or a philosophical statement. 10/10. This is not an indie game.

review_text: Such an oddball game. It's so extreme and zany in some of its presentation, but yet it's so entrancing in its very surreal and artsy nature. I'm a sucker for stuff that's out there like this game and I think watching the ENA series on YouTube beforehand definitely helped ease me into the vibes, but it's not a necessity for this game. I love the unnecessary amount of attention to detail this game has. There was a point where I interacted with a hole in the ground that had a skeleton in it and the game said "A body could fit in here." and my brain for some reason thought of the non-interactable mannequins around the map. So imagine my surprise when I tried interacting with one immediately after and it told me "Not that kind." like it knew where my brain was going. There's also details like many characters having several additional lines/voice lines that you would normally miss out on if you don't keep on talking to them after some of their main dialogue. One thing I have to give a massive compliment to is the art department. The character designs are so unique, fun, and a lot of the animations are really well done, some almost feeling straight out of an anime with how fluid they're presented at times. Most of my time spent with this game I was either in awe, laughing at what the hell was going on, or I was just straight up dumbfounded, but in the best way. So yeah absolutely play this if you're down for a very outlandish experience!

Its worlds are packed with strange imagery and references that feel straight out of the late '90s internet era everything from LSD Dream Emulator to the Zelda CD-i games and obscure webcore aesthetics. It certainly has a unique art direction, experimental storytelling, and it captures the spirit of digital nostalgia. However I can see how some found it confusing or directionless more of an “experience” than a traditional game. If you enjoy surreal exploration games, vaporwave style visuals, or the feeling of wandering through a digital dreamscape, ENA Dream BBQ is absolutely worth your time. It’s weird, it’s wild, and it’s unlike anything else out there.

review_text: It's a free first-person adventure you might think is complete but is actually just chapter one with other chapters not released as I write this. Totally different art styles and animations for different characters, sometimes the same one. The landscapes are delightfully strange, like naked legs in a sea of red liquid with a huge eye in the sky. It's like a mash-up of different art directions and the designers couldn't agree on what the final look would be. But it was all intentional, part of the appeal and it has that quirky Japanese vibe that I like... even though it's not Japanese. A bunch of characters speak in different languages with subtitles and the writing, while not being completely nonsensical, definitely has absurd, surreal vibes. In fact, it feels like a few characters are bipolar or have multiple personalities, the main character Ena being the most obvious example. The characters also usually have more than one line of text so click on them more than once. The gameplay is mostly exploring, talking to people and getting what they want. The best part for me was planting board members' heads in holes to make their body grow (into a board) and reach higher plateaus. However that section also had the most frustrating part that might make people rage quit: a jumping section on platforms while wind constantly blows you to the left. The game takes between 1.5 to 2 hours depending how much you mess around and if you get stuck (like I did in the labyrinth under a building). Color me intrigued for the follow-ups.

review_text: I mean, how do I even describe this experience? This game is a bit impenetrable. It's like jumping into a tv show that's 7 seasons in. You have no context, even though there is a lot of context. And any context you uncover is not only layered beneath heaps of mulch, but is also tinged with so much enigma, sarcasm, and irony. This is like a soup of weirdness. And that's the selling point, this game is meant to be weird and strange. The game oozes artistry. I was delighting over every new character I met. So many weird designs, so many detailed animations, so many unique voice acting lines in so many different languages and deliveries. There is so much to love here in the presentation. As a game, however, this flounders. It's a basic puzzler meets walking sim. The entertainment is the experience itself, encountering all the strange characters, and with only minor challenges here and there. But outside of some very simple puzzles and some platforming, the actual game here doesn't have too much to offer. It almost feels like a narrative adventure, choices-matter game, à la Life is Strange or Detroit Become Human, but they decided to shift focus toward puzzles and interactivity instead of character interaction and narrative. But the game just doesn't have enough muscle to lift anything outside of its extremely dynamic presentation. Which is why it's so hard for me to have a strong opinion about this. I love the artstyle and animation; if this was just an online series like Amazing Digital Circus, I would be enthralled. Alternatively, if this were a game with more meat on its bones, I could praise that. But this is all style and no substance. It is too impenetrable to understand without context, and even though I loved everything I experienced, it's really hard to evoke that love for something that is so absolutely confounding and confusing. I'd be excited to see where they take this in the future.

review_text: I happened upon this game while watching VODs of a streamer I follow. Minutes after I saw the fluidity of the animation, differing styles of said animation and art on display, and excellent audio mixing and voice acting, I had to turn the video off and pick it up for myself. I feel that this is a game akin to an interactive artistic showcase in first person than something to complete or win. There does seem to be a broader narrative/goal, and my understanding is that it's based on a web series that I was aware of but have not watched yet. However, my own experience with this game is marveling at the surprises whether they're a shift in tone, location, style, or objective. You're not always "rewarded" for interacting with things per se, but when you do something usually happens. Thing is, I could never guess what it would be each time. There's something striking about the character of ENA, too. Not really a hero in any traditional sense, but more of a tasktaker who lives (exists?) and works(?) in a surrealist dimension. There's just something delightful about the duality of her personality. Also, there's something very amusing or humorous about her (even if I don't "get" the joke) that drives me forward. And her design is unique in this way that is hand drawn, flat, yet simultaneously and unmistakably dimensional. It's clear from the jump that this game's core is rooted in unbridled artistry and passion for creating something to express ideas, or feelings, or thoughts, or something else entirely. But in a lot of ways you just kind of get out of it what you get out of it. I'm very interested to see how development of this progresses toward its full completion. Until then, download and play it. First chapter is free, so there's absolutely no reason not to give it a shot.

Guerra and his team showcase their imaginations and take the player on a surrealist rollercoaster with strange characters, some returning from the web series, some new, and even stranger circumstances. Wearing its influences on its sleeve, the game's level design is very much akin to LSD Dream Simulator and its progeny, but offers "concrete" objectives to guide the player in the form of jobs. Each job has quirky set-up and payoff that is sure to either tickle, confuse, or horrify players throughout the one-to-three-hour experience. Even though it's only the first episode of the full experience (with the release of subsequent episodes being currently unknown), ENA Dream BBQ is the perfect preview for those wanting a glimpse inside the crazy and imaginative world that Joel Guerra has to offer. The fact that it's free should give players even more incentive to give it a shot. I very much enjoyed the whole experience, and the only issue I had was improper glyph display for Nintendo Switch controllers (though the fact that it has controller support is a big plus) Help ENA get to the Bathroom!

review_text: TL/DR: WORTH IT I'll try to be concise and avoid spoilers, enjoy :3 Intro My experience, as almost everyone else's, began with original series and I fell in love with the concept. The surrealistic mix of 3D and 2D visuals, languages and audio in the setting of 90s games felt refreshing. The idea of turn it into a real game was just a matter of time Details Dream BBQ is one of those games, where your curiosity is rewarded. You want to explore those strange holes? Yeah, go ahead. Wanna let this annoying guy suffocate? Why not lol. The list goes on, Joel made sure to fulfill all our intrusive thoughts. I have 40 hours on record and still haven't seen all gimmicks (yeah I like to prolong the pleasure) How to play it: Don't speedrun your first playthrough, pay attention to small details and let your inner child do shenanigans. Explore locations, seek for secrets and catch references Dry ratings: Gameplay: 5/10 - mostly 3D exploration, responsive controls, not source-like (almost no inertia), no serious timings Visuals and style: 10/10 - mixed 2D/3D, shift to ps1-like graphics, many hand-drawn sprites, contrasting colorscheme Audio: 10/10 - impactful sound effects, location-based, doesn't feel repetetive, most of the dialogues are voice-acted, stereo Story/writing: 6.8/10 - the protagonist aims to find the boss but first has to get rid of the annoying smoke. Along the way, you encounter sidequests that lead to different routes, but eventually you reach the goal. The ending gives a hint at future chapters. Characters are unique, with various attitudes toward the player, leading to funny and surreal interactions. Dialogue, unfortunately, can't brag about interactivity or impact; if you're not a great fan of yapping, can always skip the cutscenes Performance: 9/10 - runs at 60 fps on my 10-year-old laptop, actually impressive Support: If you're already fan of Ena or enjoyed the time spent in this game, the DLC floods you with backstage content and hella new secrets, recommended for observation and to support devs Honorable mention: One extra feature of this game is language. Specific vocabulary, uncommon phrases and overall speech sometimes feels comically exaggerated in some way. Since english isn't my mother tongue, I found it quite helpful; I actually learned handful useful phrases. Even tho most of them sound silly out of context, that makes it even better Ps: That was not concise afterall lol. If you're still reading this, thanks, but fr give this game a chance. If I missed sth or made mistakes, you know what to do. That was fun Bless you for your business!

review_text: I finally uninstalled today. The betas were better. For SO long, the balance was pretty all over the place over the games life span. The bots really do kill a lot of the fun because they're always present with no way to avoid them. You have to grind your ass off to get to player matches only EVERY season, and the casual mode rarely has any players. The Extraction shooter mode was an honest to god mistake to add or focus on and took away time and resources that could've been better allocated elsewhere. The 3v3 mode should've just been a custom room option. And for whatever reason they nerfed character creation from the betas into launch which probably put off all the dress up people since they could no longer make THEIR character their own. In the betas you used to be able to pick custom colors for so much stuff, such as a key one being eye color. In the launch and to this day they changed it to only preset color options. The microtransactions were more like macro ones, we now have a gacha system for skins on top of that, they introduced a whole new paid currency just for that new gacha system, and finally the bots were never addressed once despite being brought up as a massive pain point before the game even launched during the betas. I hope this game at least gets a private server like Gundam Evolution did, because I don't think this game really has much time left in it before its canned by the developers, who are clearly trying to extract as much money as they can from the few dedicated players remaining before they inevitably shut it down. Which I hate to say because its a REALLY solid game despite balance being all over the place. No other mech game really gave me the same feeling as playing Falcon and zipping around in the air barely avoiding death and often getting away with so much while holding on by a shred of health. I'll miss this game, but the developers kind of brought it on themselves.

review_text: As a high-quality free game, I want to recommend it, but not without major caveats. Unfortunately, the developers have made some frustrating design choices: -Inventory Clutter: Storage space is limited, and cosmetic items count directly toward that cap. -Paint & Pattern System: There are dozens of colors and patterns, yet every single mecha requires a separate unlock for each paint or pattern. -Marketplace Restrictions: Player-to-player sales of acquired cosmetics are restricted to real-life currency (corite) with unreasonable minimum price floors. -Exorbitant Pricing: Premium striker and pilot skins cost around $50, dropping only to $30 during discounts. If you're looking to grind the ranked VERGE queue, be advised that the low active player count means high-rank wait times stretch to 5–10 minutes. If these top issues were resolved, I would gladly give it a thumbs-up. But in its current state, I can't recommend it wholeheartedly. I thumbsed up because it's a free game and that would give you the chance to try it for yourself.

The gameplay and combat is good but repetitive with lot of things to keep track of. Multiplayer has a lot of issues and none of them are easy to understand. Its a good game overall, but outside the main focus, there is zero focus and doesn't hold up well when push comes to shove.

review_text: # Mecha BREAK: A Competitive Game That Somehow Forgot to Build a Competitive Scene Mecha BREAK is a spectacular-looking game wrapped around one of the most poorly thought-out competitive ecosystems I have seen in a PvP game. The actual mech combat can be fun, but almost everything surrounding it feels like the developers had absolutely no idea what kind of competitive game they were trying to build. Amazing Seasun had plenty of experience with online games, but they had never established themselves as developers of a serious arena-based PvP game. Yet Mecha BREAK came out swinging with ranked systems, competitive aspirations, and even the apparent ambition of building an esports scene almost immediately. And it failed hard. Instead of spending years building a healthy competitive ecosystem, establishing matchmaking, understanding player behavior, refining ranked progression, and then seeing whether an esports scene naturally develops, the game seemed determined to shove competitive gaming down everyone's throat from day one. The result is a competitive scene that is difficult to take seriously. ## Ranked Matches With Bots Having bots in a PvP game is already questionable. Having bots in ranked matches is absurd. Having bots in ranked matches while simultaneously trying to present the game as a serious competitive title is next-level stupidity. Then there is the complete lack of meaningful rank decay at the top. Watching a supposedly competitive leaderboard where players can sit in the Top 100 without meaningful rank decay is one of the dumbest competitive systems I have ever seen. A leaderboard is supposed to represent who is actively competing and performing well, instead Mecha BREAK can turn it into a museum exhibit. And somehow this gets even worse. ## The Blocklist Problem The fact that players can influence matchmaking through their blocklists is genuinely baffling. If your matchmaking system allows competitive players to manipulate who they are matched against by strategically blocking people, then your competitive integrity is already hanging by a thread. This becomes catastrophic in smaller regions. EU is the perfect example. When the active high-level population becomes small enough that the same players repeatedly encounter each other, top players can share blocklists and effectively manipulate the matchmaking pool. At that point, what exactly are we measuring? Mechanical skill? Team coordination? Who can manipulate the matchmaking system most effectively? Who has the right people blocked? Who can avoid the players they don't want to fight? Congratulations, you have accidentally turned ranked matchmaking into social engineering. This makes statements from Kris, who apparently believes he knows what gamers want better than the gamers themselves, increasingly difficult to take seriously. If this is the direction the competitive design is heading, perhaps making mobile games would have been the more appropriate career path, because whatever Mecha BREAK is trying to accomplish competitively clearly isn't working. ## The "Competitive Scene" Is a Joke The smaller the region, the worse this becomes. When you have fewer than 100 genuinely active players in a competitive region and those players can influence matchmaking through blocklists, the entire ranking system becomes questionable. You cannot build a legitimate competitive environment out of a population that small while simultaneously allowing players to manipulate the matchmaking pool. Yet apparently this is supposed to become an esports game. An esports game needs a stable player population, strong matchmaking, transparent competitive rules, meaningful ranking systems, serious anti-abuse mechanisms, and a healthy ecosystem. Mecha BREAK has managed to make several of those things optional. But don't worry, at least we have another overpriced cosmetic bundle. ## Progression and Currency Systems The progression system is another mess. There are too many currencies, too many systems, and too many layers between the player and the actual content they want. Instead of making progression feel rewarding, it often feels like the game is constantly trying to figure out which currency it can put between you and the thing you actually want. The player should be thinking: **"What do I want to unlock?"** Instead, Mecha BREAK frequently makes you think: **"Which ♥♥♥ currency do I need for this?"** That is not satisfying progression. That is an accounting department disguised as a game. ## Communication From the Developers The communication doesn't exactly inspire confidence either. Competitive games require developers who understand that their community needs clear explanations, especially when it comes to matchmaking, ranking, progression, seasonal systems, and competitive integrity. Instead, players are frequently left trying to figure out what the developers actually intend. When developers appear convinced that they understand what players want better than the players themselves, the disconnect becomes even more obvious. A developer can disagree with its community, that's fine, but if the community repeatedly tells you that something is broken and your response is essentially "you don't know what you want," eventually you have to consider the possibility that the problem isn't the customers. ## Too Many Modes, Not Enough Players This might be the most obvious mathematical problem in the entire game. You have multiple game modes, ranked, different team sizes, extraction, different regions, and then a shrinking player population. What could possibly go wrong? Everything. Instead of concentrating the remaining players into a healthy matchmaking pool, Mecha BREAK spreads them across multiple queues and then apparently has to use bots to fill the holes. This creates a death spiral: **fewer players → longer queues → bots → worse matches → players leave → fewer players.** And then the solution apparently is another game mode. Fantastic. ## The Biggest Problem The biggest problem with Mecha BREAK isn't that the game is terrible. That's actually what makes it frustrating. There is a genuinely fun mech game buried underneath all of this. The combat can be fantastic, the mechs look incredible, and the core concept is strong. And yet the developers seem determined to surround that good foundation with questionable competitive design, bloated progression, excessive monetization, fragmented matchmaking, and a baffling approach to player feedback. The studio had never established itself as a serious arena PvP developer and nevertheless seemed eager to push Mecha BREAK toward esports immediately. Instead of building the foundation first, they tried to build the trophy room. Now the foundation is cracking: bots in ranked, no meaningful top-rank decay, matchmaking that can be influenced through blocklists, tiny regional populations, players manipulating who they encounter, multiple queues splitting the remaining population, progression systems designed like a spreadsheet, overpriced cosmetics, oversexualized character monetization, repetitive content, poor communication, and balance problems. Mecha BREAK didn't need to become an esports game on day one. It needed to become a good competitive game first. Instead, the developers tried to sell us the esports fantasy before proving they could build the ecosystem. The result is a competitive scene that increasingly feels less like professional PvP and more like a private lobby with a leaderboard attached. The sad part is that the mech combat deserved better.

review_text: "A beautiful titan of steel, thoroughly choked by the weeds of greed." How tragic it is to witness an engine of such immense potential brought low by the petty architectures of modern commerce. Every time I dare to step inside the cockpit, expecting the roaring symphony of an iron giant, I am instead assaulted by a relentless barrage of pop-ups. In-game solicitations, desperate and vulgar, screaming for attention to sell who knows what. They refuse to simply let me play. ## The Gacha Rot The entire foundation of this experience has been warped into the likeness of a low-effort gambling house. * * The Irrelevant Vessel: Instead of a battle-hardened commander, I am forced to look at a hyper-skinny, fragile pilot who feels completely divorced from the heavy metal they operate. * Nonsensical Design: The interface is a labyrinth of bloated, goofy features I will never have use for. It is a system built not for depth, but for distraction. * ## Confusion as a Commodity The game treats information like a weapon to be used against the player. * * Unexplained Mechanics: Vital features are left completely shrouded in mystery, unexplained and abandoned. * The Pop-Up Tutorial: When the game does condescend to explain its systems, it does so through the most irritating pop-ups imaginable—breaking whatever fragile immersion remained. * ## A Soulless Spectacle I am confident there is a certain breed of modern consumer that thrives on this endless cycle of blinking lights and micro-transactions. Yet, I cannot help but look at the undeniable effort, visual fidelity, and mechanical polish that went into the core of this game and marvel at how utterly soulless the final product feels. Anyone can construct a playground of flashy make-believe, but true artistic triumph is broken by these greedy, limiting boundaries. --- Verdict: Great bones buried under a mountain of cheap mobile-game garbage.

review_text: I guess it's time to finally put my opinion into words as I'm constantly asking others to do. This game is extremely fun! Being someone who is a bit older I tend to struggle with keeping up with the snap pinpoint aiming that many other PC users are able to do in PvP which causes me to dislike most of these types of games on the market. Along comes Mecha Break with a generous aim assist system and the whole thing is turned on its head. I can now actually enjoy a competitive shooter again and man does it deliver. The moment to moment action is fast and engaging. The match ups between strikers is simple at a base level but can turn into a bit of a mind game the further up the ranks you move. The graphics are fantastic and barring an occasional server lag spike runs perfectly at 165FPS consistently. The customization of paint is very exciting to do and gives you a lot of freedom to make your striker look cool/pretty/dumb as hell. The game of course doesn't come without it's drawbacks. -The menu designs can be confusing to navigate at times. -The balance could use a bit of fine tuning for a few strikers (but what game isn't like this?). -The corite (premium currency) system definitely needs to be earn able in some way in game so that people can actually choose to use the marketplace. -The game modes that aren't the premiere 6v6 mode tend to have a small player pool and very long queue times accordingly. -The game tends to fill lobbies with bots a lot in lower ranks or if you get on a lose streak which would be ok if they actually had to play by the same rules as a player and if the game would tell you who is actually a bot or a real player. It is unfortunate that this game is flooded with so many negative reviews because they are scaring people off of coming to one of the most fun shooters I've played since Titanfall 2. A lot of negatives tend to be overblown or sometimes not true and it really kills a lot of people's want to try something out with such a low steam score. So at the end of the day I'd like to say this one simple thing. Just try it. Who cares what I or anyone else says about the game. Try it for yourself and if after a few hours you're not vibing with it you can just uninstall. It's a free to play game that is not pay to win so what is there to lose? Have fun!

review_text: Another mech game where you dream of what could have been. Poor decisions by the developers have hamstrung this one out of the gate, with aggressive microtransactions, poor perception handling on 'pay to win' (it's not, but communication is the larger issue) mechanics, and progression that is not competitive with other free-to-play games in this category. Now that the game has hemorrhaged players, most games are filled with bots up until you hit Grandmaster Tier (not impressive, it does not take very long to get there). Bots are a double-edged sword, and easily one of the biggest threats to the game's longevity. They are necessary to even play nowadays, given the shrunken playerbase. What is a problem is how they are handled - specifically, the experience of slogging through a team full of bots - your own teammate bot AI significantly worse. All bots have exceptional auto-aim, are able to pivot onto your mech from one attack to pinpoint where you are, and have frame-perfect movement and the ability to see through stealth. Again - if you have a group of six players vs. bots, you will be fine. If you are 1-2 players and 4-5 bots, this is like pulling teeth with a visually flashy pair of pliers. The experience of grinding through your matches with your own bots staring at walls or sluggishly moving back and forth while the enemy bot team works in perfect coordination is discouraging at best and rage-inducing at worst. What remains of PVP balance errs on the side of caution rather than reactivity - however, the devs are not striking this balance correctly, with some strikers remaining an issue across seasons. They are planning to re-release this game in July as an 'updated' version addressing some of the issues. This was announced in November 2025. What they have not done since then is provide a roadmap as to what changes they will have. I personally do not have high hopes. Alright, fine. What do I like about this game? The design language of the strikers is fantastic and the gameplay is fun. I love mechs. This is unapologetically flashy, visually appealing, and though the customization is not nearly as in-depth as Armored Core VI, it's still what you want in a mech game (albeit putting paints into the gacha economy feels outdated). If the prospect of a mecha-themed Overwatch brawler appeals to you, you'll love this. What will hurt is watching it die a slow death with the other 2000 of us left due to poor decisions across the board. I want to like this game so much. It's a shame that it's so disappointing.

review_text: I'll start by saying a lot of these reviews are wrong about some fundamental things (like PvE content). I explain a little furthur in. Anyway, I waited for the devs to announce their plans for season 4 before trying this game. From the outside looking in, with dozens upon dozens of amazing games vying for my attention, I just don't have the time to invest into a game that isn't going to be around in another 3 months. I also found the strong PvP focus a turn-off. Thankfully, the Season 4 changes look promising (assuming they follow through with a greatly reduced team). Also, the game is damn good fun, pretty, and responsive. I want to clear up some misinformation I'm seeing in the other reviews: 1) There IS solo PvE content (and not just the prologue). You can join Mishmak in covert ops (no enemy teams) and launch without matchmaking. It isn't the same as a full-fledged story mode (or horde mode, roguelite mode, etc), but it allows you to progress and practice using some of the mechs in various scenarios. Additionally, you can try any Striker in training mode whether you own them or not. 2) The monetization is not aggressive. It just isn't. There are things that are outrageously expensive, but they're also cosmetic (and, if I'm brutally honest, most are hideous beyond all reason). For the, "I wish I could pay once and get everything" crowd. You can drop 10 bucks on the season pass, get a premium Striker right away and, within a few hours, get another one. I'm well on my way to a third and I literally just started. That gives me seven Strikers to play (and I made informed decisions on who to pick thanks to training mode) and each will take dozens of hours to truly master. There are some things I find frustrating, but that's true of any high-skillcap game I've ever played. The biggest is the number of bots in online PvP matches. However, without them, lower ranks would be completely barren. TLDR: This game isn't for everyone, but there are a ton of players who would love it who are missing out due to an insane amount of misinformation. It's mostly a PvP game, but there is plenty of PvE to do as well (once you find it) and the monetization is not nearly as bad as everyone makes it out to be. I recommend if you're even remotely interested.

review_text: I picked up this game a year after release. As far as I can tell, most people consider it a dead game. Well, it may be on life support, but it's not dead and I hope it doesn't die. The truth is that this is a pretty fantastic game. If you're looking for a game that merges a Gundam-esque theme with Overwatch style gameplay, you've found it. I'll break down my experiences into some pros and cons for you to consider if it's right for you: Pros The visuals are phenomenal They nail the aesthetic of Gundam-like mechs. The particle effects are well done, and the environments are generally well constructed to place you in the themes of the shows and games many have enjoyed before. The gameplay is sharp Abilities feel crisp and movement feels reliable. Certain mechs aren't just fast, but feel fast. Abilities that provide indicators before delivery do a good job of cutting through the chaos to give everyone time to react, allowing for counterplays. Timing of abilities feel like they keep the pace of the battle flowing well. I also like that there aren't a million different crowd control effects that last too long. What exists is disruptive without being overbearing. The customization is deep I love that I can customize my mech's colors across so many areas, making it feel unique and fresh. It gives me something to do when I'm waiting in queue. The pilot is pretty goonin', but the same is still true. This is something I've come to appreciate over time. Cons The menus are messy There's just too many menus and places to click. You also go down chains that you'd expect to link back on their own, but don't. It's a minor thing, but one you notice and feel frustration with. It's the result of a game that seemed like they had developers come up with good ideas and slammed them into the game without cohesion, resulting in menu hell in some cases. For the most part, this is a minor gripe, but enough time spent and it wears you down. Bots in matchmaking This sounds like it was a contributing cause of the game's decline, but became a necessary evil with just 1,300 active people. However, the game does everything it can to mask whether or not you're partied with or against bots. It does this to hide the fact that the game is kinda empty. The frustration with this is that sometimes the bots are really good and other times they're absolutely braindead. Some modes like Ace Arena seem to amplify this. If they're going to keep the bots in matches, then they need to improve the consistency of the AI. Do the challenge missions as a new player and you'll discover that the bots can be challenging! Ranks need to be reduced There's just too many of them with no point. It isn't until you reach grand master that you can only be paired with humans, which actually becomes detrimental due to the volume of people playing (so sad). You go through a somewhat lengthy climb just to arrive at a point where ranked leads to super long queues. You end up just running casual mode most of the time. Currencies are confusing Because the game also has in-game purchases and pve modes, there are other currencies that I don't even understand. The game doesn't do a good job of explaining things here or helping to get me involved in the pve side of the game. It feels pretty half baked, and the marketplace where you list off stuff feels extremely incomplete. It's like they have the elements for a foundation, but nothing actually put together for a well-rounded player experience. Fries in the basket This game is just fun. It's been an absolute blast getting some buddies together and experiencing it as a group. We've had such a great time and we'd love to see more people join in. We live in a time where we expect games to be better than this, but it's often the window dressing that we make a big deal about. The core aspects of the game are great, and worth seeing succeed. I'm kinda shilling the game a bit because the potential for greatness is all right there. IF they pump the right modes and cut the fat, relaunch to bring in fresh blood, I think we'd have the mech game many of us wanted and didn't know it. Give it an honest try, but grab 1-2 friends.

review_text: Over 800hr played this game, I still can’t recommend this game. this is not a skill issue — it’s a balance issue. The main problem isn’t a “skill issue” — it’s the complete lack of balance between units. The imbalance significantly reduces the overall enjoyment of the game. No matter how skilled you are, when the game isn’t balanced, it just doesn’t feel fair. Players who focus on completing objectives have an extremely hard time. The DPS output is way too high. Tanks and healers can barely survive when attacked by melee units. Once melee units manage to stun-lock someone, they can keep attacking endlessly without ever running out of energy. The more I play, the less fun it becomes — especially since most players only care about kill counts and completely ignore objectives. The developers have the ability to rebalance the game every patch or update, but they choose not to. Instead, they release overpriced skins. It’s already been four seasons, and nothing has changed. Honestly, skins should cost around 50–250 Corite at most. On top of that, there’s no Raid mode or meaningful story content. The gameplay design shouldn’t be overly punishing, and the game should include proper difficulty options like Easy, Normal, and Hard modes. Until the developers acknowledge and address these problems, I can’t recommend this game. They should take notes from Final Fantasy XIV, where tanks and healers can sustain themselves and provide strong crowd control effectively. I’ll wait and see if improvements are made. If the game gets properly updated and balanced, I might change my mind.

review_text: This game is a lot of fun, in that the gameplay feels solid, its fast paced and action packed. There are cool mechs to play with all different playstyles, and the lack of mission types doesn't seem too repetitive for how many way to play. That being said, there are things that make this game very irritating to play, and from what I understand, the Devs seem to be completely tone def to these problems because of money. You still find bots, and not just a few, like a lot, and they will absolutely ruin your game. You also find players who aren't competitive, because of paid "rank loss prevention." This means that if you're playing poorly, you can stay at the same rank, and continue climbing instead of having to be stuck with your poor gameplay. And the game will award you with these prevention "cards" via loot boxes and season passes (called contracts). It ruins any sort of meaning to ranked structure, and I've played many games competitive games (AOE2, StarCraft series, Halo series, League of Legends, Overwatch, CoD, BF, and more...). There is nothing but seasonal cosmetics that make playing ranked worth it, despite the competitive potential for this game. 2. There are so many transactions, and the menus are infinite. Understanding what currency unlocks what is a nightmare, and navigating the menus to do so would make any navigator lose their way. I have over 80 hours of actual at keyboard time with this game, and I still don't know where to consistently find customizations, or certain missions. 3. You don't keep your game-earned currency through the next season. At the end, it goes away. No more free-to-play cosmetics, or unlocking mechs. if you forgot to. tough luck. 4. Voice acting: honestly this is a nit pick as far as Im concerned, but holy hell is this incredibly repetitive. If you're into anime (I am not), then this won't be a bother to you but jeeezus is there sooo much anime high pitched, over-the-top voice acting. ughh. If it weren't mutable, I wouldn't play it. I would give this game a glowing review if Ranked were actually ranked and not garbage/impossible to beat bots or have an actual work-to-progress (EARN YOUR RANK LIKE EVERY OTHER GAME EVER) system in place that actually works. Bots don't belong in any ranked match ever.

review_text: If you grew up watching Armored Core, Gundam, or Zone of the Enders and wanted a game that captures that blistering, high-speed tactical robot warfare in a modern multiplayer format, Mecha BREAK is an absolute masterpiece in the making. It delivers pure, unadulterated adrenaline. The Good: Breathtaking Speed and Combat: The movement mechanics feel incredible. The transition between high-speed aerial dodging, ground dashing, and shifting into jet forms is seamless. Every melee clash feels heavy and impactful, while long-range artillery strikes feel devastating. Diverse Mecha Lineup: The game doesn't just offer skin swaps; every single mech (Striker) has a completely distinct archetype and mechanical identity. Whether you want to play a massive, shield-bearing heavy tank, a stealthy sniper, a flying support healer, or a lightning-fast melee assassin, there is a mech tailored to your exact playstyle. Insane Customization: The paint and cosmetic customization suite is incredibly detailed. You can modify specific armor plates, weathering effects, glows, and matte/metallic finishes to build your dream custom rig. Tactical Team Play: The 3v3 and 6v6 modes require genuine coordination. It’s not just a mindless deathmatch; combining a heavy defender's shield with a sniper's covering fire to protect an objective feels highly rewarding. The Mixed: The visual chaos can be overwhelming at first. With missiles, lasers, and thruster plumes filling the screen, it takes a few matches to develop the spatial awareness needed to track fast-moving targets. It is easily one of the most fluid, visually spectacular, and mechanically satisfying mech games on the market right now. If you want high-octane metal-on-metal violence, this is a mandatory download. Rating: 9/10

review_text: I come from a background of Overwatch and Heroes of the Storm, so I am familiar with team gameplay. Mecha Break is a fantastic game, especially if you enjoy mecha. The game has many modes and they are constantly adding more. There are some single player missions, a PVE mode where you can play by yourself or in a team and there is an entire island that you can explore, loot, get items and upgrades, fights bosses, etc. You can run around and explore the base as one of your pilots which is a great way to learn a bit of the lore. I do wish there was maybe some secret items to find and collect to make exploring more worthwhile. The PVP is split into a 3v3 brawl and a 6v6 objective based mode. Both of these are fun to play and there is enough variety to familiarise yourself with each map but to have some flavour. The gameplay with the different strikers is where the game really shines, there is a great range of Strikers to choose from that fulfill different roles. Each Striker has a set of skills and one thing I like is that they don't have overpowered "ults" designed to flip an engagement. The way to flip an engagement is to get good with your striker and know when to engage and stay at a distance. There is a lot of customization options, so far I have made Char Aznable, Asuka and Sephiroth for a laugh. They have spent a lot of time making changes this season to the way the store works, adding a new wave clearing mode and more and the changes seem to be good improvements. If you like mecha and want a game to try out, this is the best one out there atm by far.

review_text: As a devout 'single player games will always be better than online multiplayer ones' kind of guy, I gotta say, Mecha Break is pretty fun. In terms of moment-to-moment gameplay, Mecha Break is really fun. Fast combat, snappy controls, and there's actually quite a bit of variety in the mechs, to the point that I can't say any of the current lineup is any similar to any other ones. You've got the drill-spear mech, the stealth sniper mech, the air sniper mech, the absolute tank mech, plane mech, heal mech, the list goes on. I want to say that some could use a bit of tuning (looking at you Welkin), but it's possible that I just suck at certain matchups. The mechs and moment-to-moment gameplay carries the whole game, I think. Because outside of that, I wouldn't say Mecha Break sets any standards. For the content, I admit I'm not sure I can be a proper judge for it, because I usually hate multiplayer online PvP games and am not very familiar with them, but by itself, Mecha Break feels a tad lacking. You've got the default 6v6 mode with several different types of missions, you've got the 3v3 arena that's basically just a Deathmatch mission from the 6v6 mode, and you've got the extraction shooter mode that seems to have hardly any players and also seems to be the only feasible way to earn any amount of the premium currency as an F2P, because you can sell your loot in the in-game marketplace and pray to the mech gods that someone will buy. That's also my main criticism, I suppose: there's hardly any way for F2P to earn premium currency; not even a pittance. Most cosmetics, notably outfits, can only be bought with premium currency too, so as someone who loves cosmetic options in games, I can only ask the mech gods why. Back to the game modes, specifically the ranked 6v6 one. It is ranked, and you get rewards at the end of every season. The rewards? Lootboxes. Yeah, grind your weekend away, place well, and you get a chance of rolling...something. Is this the standard for online PvP games? I wouldn't know, but if it is, good lord. I'm not even sure what significant thing you can get out of the lootboxes. Most I've gotten out of them are paltry amounts of seasonal points and dupes upon dupes of paintjobs for the mechs that I'll never use because I already have a favourite--and also most of them look like old carpet. The seasonal points are used as currency, by the way; you use them to buy newly-released mechs (not the default lineup; those are free), items for the extraction mode, and that's about it. There are cosmetics that you can buy with them, but they're locked behind the premium pass. Yeah, you need to spend money to get the privilege to spend in-game money. And that's about it, I suppose. Good gameplay, everything else is ehhh. I've been picking it up from time to time since launch, and while I enjoy my short bursts of mech on mech action, there isn't really much incentive to keep playing. Still, I recommend at least to check it out, if not only for the mechs and gameplay.

review_text: Honestly the most fun team hero/class shooter I've ever played in the gameplay department. There is strong mecha influence in the lock-on system (FCS), fluid armor, and energy bar (EN) mechanics. There is a lot of interesting mobility as well, as literally every mech in the game can boost and hover around. The game is free-to-play, so be ready to see a lot of cosmetics microtransaction options like in other hero shooters, but it is not pay-to-win. Word of warning: the game is somewhat harsh and pretty difficult to master. There are no ultimate abilities, healing is a lot lighter than in other hero shooters, and the aforementioned FCS, fluid armor, and EN mechanics are extremely unforgiving when they are disrupted. Looking forward to the PlayStation release adding a bunch of new players. Note: There are 3 modes of gameplay, Operation VERGE (6v6 PvP with objectives), Operation STORM a.k.a 'Mashmak' (Extraction Shooter-esque PvPvE), and Ace Arena (3v3 PvP deathmatch). Pretty much 90% of my time playing is in VERGE, so that's most of what this review is for. A lot of people have fun with the Mashmak, but it's not really my cup of tea. Ace Arena is somewhat like the 3v3 mode in Armored Core 6, if you're familiar with that, but it kinda falls flat in comparison, in my opinion.
