review_text: Absolutely fantastic, underrated game. It's Entirely F2P friendly, not a single cent spent provides any sort of power or upgrades that cannot be earned within a VERY reasonable time through just playing the game casually. I'll tell you up front. Ignore the complainers that hover around the game. Sadly, and this is true of so, so, SO many facets of media these days, there are people who will bash anything and everything. According to the internet, 90% of videogame developers are idiots who don't know how to program games and "Waste potential" because they don't make the game EXACTLY the way each individual person wants. You can ask 10 different people and get 10 different answers as to "Why the game is failing" Meanwhile, it's the best performing Mecha game on the market right now, and a completely unique game in it's own right. Games like Cosmic Break and Starward play more like a fighting game in their way. Slower, more "frame data" centric style stuff. Mecha break will obviously pull comparisons to Armored core 6, but the main difference between Mecha break and Armored core is a big one: Mecha break is faster paced, and doesn't rely on you grinding for days or longer to unlock "the good parts" that you can actually use to play online, nor does it suffer from AC6's biggest flaw, the stamina system. No, not the ENERGY system. The stamina-break system. The stamina break system limited AC6 in SO many ways, and while it's absolutely possible to have a few fun rounds with friends using meme parts, if you go into any form of quickplay, you'll run into legions of the same minmaxed AC's. Mecha break snaps that in half by making each mech it's own unique hero, more akin to something like overwatch or titanfall, where it plays more like a hero shooter, with each Mecha (called strikers) having a unique, interesting kit that stands them apart from the rest. But what this does is encourage players to pick something that suits their sensibilities and playstyle, but offers a few variants on that style, usually by weight class. The game features a PLETHORA of modes, and by this time tomorrow as of the time of posting this review, we'll also have a co-op roguelike mode. So you have: • 6v6, Ranked and Unranked. • 3v3, Ranked and Unranked. • 1~3 player PVE co-op Roguelike modes. • 1~3 player extraction-shooter style modes, as well as a 1~3 Co-op PVE variant where the AI is more dangerous. • A 12 player free-for-all mode. Oh and from time to time they also run events that include things like co-op boss raids. So you have A PLETHORA of modes that allow you to pick what you're in the mood for, PVP or PVE, and you could absolutely play the game entirely in one mode or the other if that's all you want, or mix-and-match across the gamut to maximize your rewards and boost your credits up faster. If you're even REMOTELY competent, you can scrounge up the credits you need to unlock one of the handful of locked strikers in a few hours. You do have the option to skip the "wait" but it's barely a wait, honestly. There's paid games out there that make you grind more for unlocks and not by a little. This game is GENEROUS, with a striker unlock having a cost of 15'000, and each individual game you play averaging around 300~600 depending on your performance, and if double-credit weekend bonuses are going, and each mission gives you an extra 1000 which you can do 6 of a week. So if you do your weeklies, by the time you finish those, you'll EASILY have enough for a new Striker every single week and that's assuming you're taking your time. In the time I've been playing, I've already got 4 of them. OH AND THEY GIVE YOU A FREE TRIAL OF ONE OF THE LOCKED STRIKERS EVERY WEEK FOR YOU TO PLAY AND EVEN IF YOU OWN THEM ALREADY, YOU CAN DO BONUS MISSIONS WITH THEM FOR EVEN **MORE** free credits. You can easily, if you play consistently and diligently, milking every single credit out of the game you can, get every single locked striker for free in a month. review_text: So, first things first, I am biased because, as I suspect most of the playerbase is, a massive Mecha fan, much like the developers themselves. Gameplay is good, fluid, and fast. Each of the individual Strikers feel unique, even if they have overlaps in their niches - Skyraider is more suited to direct combat while Falcon is more suited to hit-and-runs, Aquila's sniping is meant to be done at a much closer range as compared to Narukami's, Stego and Inferno are both Ultra-Heavy Attackers but have entirely different playstyles, etc... It's also a passion project - with all the pros and cons that implies. On the one hand, it means that this game is liable to get a lot of updates and regular support; on the other hand, balance patches and big game-changers may be long in coming. Now, there are very few games that manage to correctly convey the feeling of controlling a Mecha (that is to say, those giant robots that lie on the more humanoid side of the scale) - and unfortunately most Mecha games make it rather difficult to distinguish between a mecha and a powered armor. And I can confidently say that Mecha BREAK is not one of them, On the gameplay side, while movement feels fluid, it also feels weighty and satisfying. High TTK even for the light Strikers helps sell the fact that these things are technically heavy weapons by infantry metrics. Every Striker usually has some form of mounted weapon and/or ability entirely separate from their handheld weapons, often multiple. On the aesthetic side, you're always reminded that these things are, in fact, weapons platforms - many have elements that would be impossible or inconvenient on a suit, the Strikers in general resemble robots more than they do armor (likely courtesy of having veteran mechanical designers on-board), scattered around every map are human-scale objects that your Striker dwarfs, actual sustained flight is something only a select few Strikers are actually capable of, etc - It all helps convey that sense of "this is a giant robot" that, to my knowledge, only Armored Core has mananged to nail before.

During defense there is no cooldown however should it be destroyed in an initiated invasion it is locked for both modes for a certain time or you can use your in game points to repair it right away. review_text: Mecha BREAK is fairly easy to get started with, but difficult to get really good at. While mechs within the same class have some overlap, each one still has its own mechanics that you need to learn. There is a bit of a rock-paper-scissors feel between different mechs, but skill matters a lot. If you're better with your mech than the other player is with theirs, you can absolutely win even when the matchup isn't in your favor. The game looks simple at first, but there's a surprisingly high skill ceiling. New players will probably need some time to figure things out. The unfortunate part is that matchmaking doesn't seem to care much about account age or experience. It's not uncommon to end up against players who have been playing much longer than you, which can be frustrating when you're still trying to learn the basics. There's also a PvE mode, and it's honestly a good way to build up currency and unlock mechs that fit your playstyle better. The catch is that you need an item earned through PvP to enter, so new players can't completely avoid PvP if they want to progress that way. I originally played this on PC but didn't stick with it for long. I only really got back into the game after getting a Steam Deck. Surprisingly, it runs pretty well. Cap it at 45 FPS and the experience is smooth enough for a competitive game. What I ended up liking most is how well it fits handheld gaming. Most matches last around 10–15 minutes, so it's easy to squeeze in a game during a break, while waiting for something, or whenever you have a bit of free time. Overall, if you enjoy mecha games and don't mind learning mechanics, Mecha BREAK is worth trying. The gameplay is fun, each mech feels distinct, and I'd definitely recommend giving it a shot on Steam Deck. That said, I really think the game needs better ways for new players to learn and play against others at a similar experience level. The biggest obstacle right now isn't the gameplay, it's surviving long enough to learn it.

review_text: I was pretty excited for this game when it was first announced. A shiny new fast-paced mecha action game for me to sink my teeth into. The graphics looked great, and most importantly, the mech designs were awesome (Falcon, my beloved). But upon hearing about the disastrous launch, I decided to refrain from downloading the game. It sounded to me like just another poorly thought-out live-service cash grab (and my hunch was proven correct). Fast forward to the recent dev update. Hearing about how the team had been filtered down to only developers who truly care about this game and want it to succeed gave me a bit of hope. They sounded so genuine, filled with passion to improve, to course-correct, and to bring out the game’s true potential. The addition of the PvE roguelike mode sealed the deal. I would finally try out Mecha Break. After finishing character creation, I was wowed by the tutorial mission. What a bombastic way to start a mech game. Sure, it was a bit janky. The animations were stiff at times, and the cutscenes were locked at 30 FPS for some reason. But the heart was there. I was once again reminded of how much wasted potential there was in releasing this game as a PvP experience instead of a single-player one. They could have told far more interesting stories in the world they created. Hell, it might have even spawned a whole new IP. Nevertheless, this is the game we got, and I continued on to try out the PvP mode. It’s pretty decent. Fast-paced, the mechs all do different things, and there’s room for strategy and skill expression. Nothing amazing, but nothing horrible either. My one question is: if this was supposed to be a highly competitive esport game, then why does account/PvE progression give players an advantage in PvP matches? This was one of the biggest questions I had at launch, and one of the main reasons I was put off by the game. But PvP aside, now it was time for the most important part of the update: the roguelike mode. It’s a training simulation... Imagine my disappointment when I found out that the roguelike mode is merely a virtual training simulation. A horrible decision both gameplay-wise and immersion-wise. For one, it completely isolates the mode from the rest of the game’s story landscape, relegating it to little more than a side activity. Second, it drops you into a bland training map where you shoot at basic enemies standing around on flat ground. It also seems that the devs have, for some incomprehensible reason, decided to balance the mode around mod progression, as my weapons deal little to no damage against enemies without any mods equipped. Why force mod progression in a game mode that already has built-in stat progression? Why add evasion chance and crit rate to the mode? This isn’t an RPG, this is an action game. Victory and defeat should be determined by the player’s skill, not the roll of a dice. Overall, I’m extremely disappointed in this roguelike mode, which was the main draw for me. There’s also something to be said about how every aspect of the game forces you to grind for mods, which, as far as I’m aware, are obtained through loot boxes. It’s the same song and dance we’ve seen so many times before. Exploit the gambling dopamine, get players addicted. Not surprising, just disappointing. In the end, whether due to incompetence or a lack of time and resources, the game failed to meet my expectations despite all the big talk from the devs. If it’s the latter, I genuinely hope that, given enough time, they manage to turn this ship around. It might already be too late, but I hope they try their best. I’ll leave the game on my PC for a couple more days and see if I feel interested in booting it up again. If not, I’ll uninstall it and wait for further improvements.

review_text: 1,249 hours since day 1. Uninstalled today. I really tried to like this game. At launch it was great, there were tons of people everywhere and it felt alive. But after a few months you start to see what it actually is: a mobile gacha game with an MMO built around the cash shop. I can't recommend anyone to start playing now. The good parts The movement is honestly great. Multiple jumps, flying, gliding, it feels better than riding a mount. And the Homestead flower breeding is the one system where you can tell someone cared, the genetics in it are actually pretty well done. That's about it. Pay to win The whole progression system is designed to cater to Chinese whales, and everyone else just gets dragged along. The devs list items in the trading store themselves, and some of them you can't get anywhere else in the game. So it's not really a player market, it's a shop that rewards people who spend. Refinement is the old enhancement system with a % chance to fail. When it fails you lose the materials and get a 2% better chance next time. Some of the materials that lower the fail chance only come from those dev listings, you can't craft them and no player can sell them. You can buy skills, will materials and unbound luno with paid currency, so anyone with a credit card can just skip months of grinding. There are more than 20 currencies. You can properly farm maybe 3 or 4 of them. A few of the ones you need for your character are basically paid only. Free players can't really trade with each other because of the bound/unbound split. Only stuff made with Focus or bought with money can be traded. The mounts that look good cost hundreds of dollars, and the seasonal leaderboards are literally for who bought the most cosmetics. Progression is RNG on top of RNG Everything is time gated. You finish what there is to do, then you wait for the next gate, and then you wait again. To craft a boss will you need the drop from the boss plus 15 crafting materials, nobody knows the drop rates, and you only get 2 keys a day. The best part is that the materials don't drop from the same boss, so you have to burn your keys on a different one. More than 90% of the purple battle images and materials are useless. Gold replaces all of it and you can't even sell the purple stuff because nobody wants it. Gold modules can roll three healing stats when you're a DPS, and if you scrap one you get back about a quarter of a new one. Then every new season brings some new power mechanic that makes the gear you spent hundreds of hours on worthless, and you start over. The season gimmick itself is just leaving your game running AFK for hours to farm mob drops. The raids don't even use it. It's there to inflate playtime numbers and your AS. And because AS is the only thing people can look at, groups ask for ridiculous numbers for content you can clear with much less. A simple clear counter per boss would fix that, but nobody can sell you a clear counter. Endgame and dailies The endgame is the same few raid fights on different difficulties, and the same dungeons from release with more HP and more damage. Dailies feel like chores. The chests have a chance of giving you nothing useful, gold materials drop at single digit %, and boss wills at less than 1%. Commissions are the worst I've seen in any game, the same boring minigames over and over for bound luno you can't even use in the trading center. Events are either standing AFK somewhere for 30 minutes or logging in to claim something. The story is go here, talk to this person, screen goes black, and a text tells you what happened instead of showing it. Professions Everything that matters is locked behind Focus. A recipe that costs Focus gives 80 XP, one that doesn't gives 2 XP, and going from 1 to 50 takes 163k XP. And after all that, the gold gear you craft is much worse than dropped gear because it's missing a whole stat buff. Players and servers There aren't enough people left for the dungeon queues. On master difficulty you wait 10 minutes or more and some queues never pop. The game wants you to fill the group with AI teammates, but the bots can't do the wipe mechanics, so the higher master dungeons are impossible with them. They also cut the number of map lines by a lot, which made farming elites and bosses nearly impossible. If you're not in NA you play with constant lag and dropped inputs. When the EU server finally came, there was no account migration. They expected people who played for a year to start from zero just to have decent ping, so obviously it was dead from the first day. Regions are locked too, so a playerbase that was already shrinking got split in half. UI, chat and bugs Only one chat channel can be fully customized. MMOs had custom chat tabs 20 years ago. The chat filter is so strict you can't even type the names of items that are in the game. The UI is a mess, with several different shop tabs, two season pass tabs and two gacha tabs. World chat is full of bots and script sellers all day and nobody bans them. Meanwhile the anti-cheat mostly just keeps non-Windows players out. How the devs treat players They sent premium rose orbs to everyone by mistake. When they noticed, the servers went down for emergency maintenance faster than they've ever reacted to an actual game-breaking bug. Then instead of doing a rollback, they took the orbs back from people who had already spent them and left those accounts with a negative balance that has to be paid off before buying anything else. No explanation and no apology.

review_text: Finally decided to write a review after 3 seasons of the game not getting any better. Here are SOME of the issues I have with this game: Lack of content, everything is just time-gated so you're forced to do the little content there is over long periods of time. Nothing is farmable. You can get around some of it by paying but the prices are extremely expensive (thousands of dollars for a weapon, hundreds of dollars to level up imagine skills only 1 level, thousands if you want to max them out). These can be attained for free but you can only get the materials a couple times per day/week with very little chance of a drop (takes around a full season or longer to get ONE of your BIS imagines to max level without paying money, You need two for every class and they get power crept by new ones every season). Class balancing is horrible, some classes might be good one season, then absolutely useless the next. Endgame content requires lots of damage (which you get by paying more money) and people won't even accept you in their party if you're one of the bad classes for that season or don't have the super expensive weapon. (Not because they're being mean, but because its literally impossible to clear with you in the party.) Switching classes will require another full season or two for your BIS imagines, or spending more money to be strong/useful enough for endgame content. There are catch up systems in place for new players, or people switching classes, which basically gives them everything you spent the last season or two doing dailies/weeklies every day/week for free. (Big selling point for the game; you don't even have to play it!) Outfit and mount gacha have extremely low chances of pulling until hitting pity, expect to spend $100-200 or more if you want it (everybody will have it the first day it drops). Extremely aggressive, shameless monetization, but game is laggy, content that does get added is slop that was lazily made with bugs everywhere, dev team seems nonexistent when it comes to listening to player feedback, The only time they'll fix anything is when the issue is directly losing them money. (Or when the bugs are allowing people to clear high level content without spending enough money first!) The game is only "free" if you like to sit around afk with nothing to do all day. Basically just a bad mobile gacha game disguised as an MMO. The community is fun and friendly, but as a game it's terrible. Not just pay to win, it's basically pay to play with high prices. Seems like what was supposed to be a quick cash grab that's only still going because people haven't stopped buying.

Character Creation & Customization (The High Point)** * **The Good:** The character creator is a standout feature. It’s robust, offers deep customization (including body type adjustments), and lets you create great-looking anime-style characters with options like ears, tails, and easy preset importing/randomizing. * **Flexibility:** You can change your appearance later, which is a big plus for vanity lovers. ### **2. Progression, Boosts, & Account Systems** * **Instant Level 60 Boost:** The game gives you a free instant level 60 boost pack right at the start. Since the game has level/content guardrails and your skills start at level 1 anyway, it’s best to use it early to skip the grind, boost survivability, and make combat smoother. * **Character Isolation:** Accounts don't function traditionally—each character is essentially in their own separate world. Money, items, and purchased goods are not easily shared or banked across characters. * **Currency & Skills:** In-game currency (like Luna/Luma) is earned through quests, mobs, and chests, and is used to level up skills. However, you have to choose upgrades carefully rather than just dumping resources into everything with a notification badge. ### **3. Gameplay, Combat, & The Story Wall** * **The Grind/Story Loop:** The core game revolves heavily around a massive, long-winded story mode. You can spend hours just running back and forth doing quests before ever really getting loose in the open world. * **The Dialogue Issue:** There is an overwhelming amount of reading. While some parts are voice-acted, a large portion is text-only, which can quickly become tedious and lead to players spamming the skip button just to play the actual game. * **QoL Features:** Navigation and movement are well-handled once unlocked, featuring automated pathfinding/teleportation that works great—especially if playing on desktop or mobile devices. * **Multiplayer & Social:** Features like built-in local area voice chat in dungeons add an interesting layer to grouping up, alongside fun emotes and actions. ### **4. Economy & Population Concerns** * **Marketplace:** The trading center feels sparse. Listings are extremely low (e.g., only a couple of items or vegetables for sale, and zero/minimal high-end appearance items, mounts, or gear available), suggesting a thin player-driven economy. * **Player Population:** The open world feels largely empty—you'll only run into a handful of players—raising questions about the long-term health and ongoing developer support for the game. ### **5. Final Verdict / Summary Takeaway** * **Potential:** The game has a lot of roleplaying potential and strong stylistic charm. * **Drawbacks:** Plagued by excessive unvoiced dialogue, isolated character economies, and a worryingly quiet player base. * **Recommendation:** Worth a quick look if you love character creators and anime MMOs, but temper your expectations regarding community activity and the heavy story barrier to entry. --- Let me know if you want to tweak any of these points, shift the tone, or expand on a specific section for your written review! review_text: This is the shortened version of the review as the original one was over the character review limit by 6.5K characters. The review mainly talked about the bad points of the game TLDR: The game prioritizes a good short term experience, where they make the player spend as much on the game as possible At the time of writing, the current season is 3 (S3). Everything is subject to change (and let's hope it will (for the better)) This is what you'll be greeted by when you start (assuming you start at the beginning of a season): The main story quest which you don't have to engage with at all (despite being an MMORPG). The devs worked very hard to make it just an MMO. You'll see that your character is already at the max level because they wanted to make newbies be able to catch up to the latest content as quick as possible. The next thing you'll notice is a friend request from Maria, an infamous bot account made for scamming people. Yes, people do complain about the bot problem in the official discord server and yet, they don't get banned. Now, you take a glance at the world chat where you'll see players discussing how nice the newly implemented QoL features are (that they could've implemented anytime but decided to wait until the start of the next season.) Some of them should've been there since the start of the game and others make you wonder whether they made some parts of the game bad on purpose just so they could later fix it like this The game wants to make the initial impression as nice as possible and get new players up to speed. There's a special store that let's you buy all the rewards you would've got from content you missed. The currency for it is earned by just playing the game normally. Any items from the previous season become obsolete. Do you remember Maria, whom you've probably blocked? You should have gotten another friend request from them by now, which is your first encounter with the broken features and the lack of basic QA testing this game has to offer You get non-raid gear from dungeons. You'll quickly come to hate them as you'll have to grind these a lot to get the gear you want. So far, each season added QoL fixes to make them more bearable S2: guaranteed gold gear S3: you'll only get gear for a the class you select You only need gold gear from almost right off the bat Some dungeons from S1 got reused in S3 with barely any changes made to them There are other ways to acquire gear craft them, but crafted gear is way worse raids (these get you raid gear, which is what you'll be using) When it comes to gear, you only need to care about the illusion breaking strength stat, which I'll be calling ILSTR. Anything besides that is just optimization. If you have less of it than your enemy then you'll deal greatly reduced damage and receive significantly more damage. Having more has less impact Next, you'll want to upgrade your gear. There's 3 kinds of upgrades Reforging; you'll quickly notice that you have a limited amount of the items needed for reforging and there's not a lot of ways to get them. You can buy them from the trading center or wait for the weekly refresh Refining (expensive, obsolete, no ILSTR): you upgrade the gear slots. Can fail; you can use items to boost your chances of success Embedding: Became worse rather than better over time. You used to embed gems to your gear until you hit the major stat boost that you have a 5% chance to get. Now, you embed sigils. These are random boss drops which you can only get by using your keys (you get 2 a day and can carry up to 6 at a time.) You still have to craft gems to embed those sigils Crafting upgrade materials require you to use focus (AKA stamina; you get 400 a day and can store up to 2000) and materials you have to gather using focus. Even better, the amount of materials you get are random Gathering and crafting involves a lot of RNG for the amount of items received and for the level of the potions and foods By design, the game makes sure that you cannot get enough materials at a decent pace; and that's where the trading center comes in. You can buy and sell unbound materials for unbound Luno. You can also buy the the moss mech shard, which cannot be crafted (but is still listed under the life skills -> smithing category). And then there's the materials for the "whale weapon" that becomes obsolete by the time you can acquire it without buying the materials from here There are 2 more subsystems for character progression Modules (the gear that is technically not gear): the upgrade button has been unimplemented since S1, RNG, limited amount, buy more from the trading center Imagines (summons): get will and other materials to craft & upgrade them (low drop rate from bosses and you need keys for it) or buy them from the trading center or the gacha or from the guild hunt. You can also get them from stimens vault (the most hated game mode. so much so, that one of the QoL features that they've added is that you don't have to start from the very first floor after the reset) You can buy/sell unbound items for unbound Luno (the normal currency). The only exception to this are rose orbs (the premium currency.) When you buy rose orbs, they become bound items for a greedy reason You can it now, can't you? You buy rose orbs for real money, sell them to get unbound Luno and buy any materials you need to get stronger. bound roser orbs are used for the will gacha and some items in the store. Unbound rose orbs used for the outfit gacha. Customization is the only decent feature this game, so you bet they'll monetize the heck out of it. This is why you cannot get unbound rose orbs from the trading center. You can buy 3 pulls a week for bound rose orbs as well, which is nowhere near enough. You can buy gacha outfits and mounts from the trading center for a lot of unbound Luno Now let's talk about the gameplay. The good parts: the MMO aspect (guilds, chatting and friend system); the customization (character and homestead) (no edits needed for this part) And with those out of the way, back to talking about the majority of the game * Raids: lot's of full party wipe mechanics and DPS checks. The former wouldn't be that bad if people were willing to learn the mechanics * Poorly explained mechanics: The game does its absolute worst to properly explain raid and dungeon mechanics, you need a 3rd-party site to get a decent explanation * Almost every feature has a bug * CN/Global: the CN is way ahead. Despite that, the collaboration events happen at the same time. Both servers receive the same content, balanced for CN. Currently, they are trying to sync global up to CN, which includes giving us lots of valuable materials, so they locked those behind challenging gameplay * Main story: It's being neglected (and it is pretty meh to begin with) * Some of the maps are a bit too alike: we have a lot of maps that are just a big dense forest so I hope you like them * For most classes, the skill tree has only one optimal build * Class balancing is bad and there are classes that are barely played but I don't know the details And for the finale, an example just how they only care about squeezing money out of the players: Once, every player received a gift from the mail that contained unbound rose orbs. This was unintentional as they quickly locked the mail feature so players cannot claim it and removed it from the inventory of those who already have Apart from that, the only time they ever quickly fixed a bug is when it involved enabling the players to get more materials for outfit customization than intended. They removed either the excess items or the amount of rose orbs they are worth from the inventories of the players And the worst part is, if you find a good guild, you can enjoy the MMO aspect of the game enough to keep playing

review_text: Beautiful presentation, hollow endgame, this one nails the classic gacha-MMO trap of looking incredible on the surface while the actual loop underneath wears thin fast. Pros ✔ Visuals are genuinely excellent, the anime art style is polished and the character creator gives real room to make something unique. ✔ Fashion and cosmetics are a major draw, with a wide variety of outfits and collab content like Monogatari and Fairy Tail. ✔ Strong initial presentation makes the first stretch of the game genuinely enjoyable for casual players. ✔ Good as a seasonal, low commitment anime MMO if you're not expecting long term depth. Cons ✘ The dye system is surprisingly restrictive, several collab outfits don't allow full recoloring, undercutting the customization the game is otherwise praised for. ✘ Story is largely forgettable, more about moving between zones than giving you a reason to care. ✘ Endgame loop is shallow and repetitive, the same daily gather, craft, and boss run routine with minimal variation. ✘ Progression heavily gatekept by Ability Score requirements in group content, making it hard to advance without already being carried. ✘ Dungeon design recycles the same handful of layouts across difficulty tiers rather than offering real variety. ✘ Seasonal resets wipe progress and restart the grind, turning what should feel rewarding into a treadmill. ✘ Best cosmetics are locked behind limited-time gacha banners, adding a monetization layer on top of an already repetitive structure. Overall Blue Protocol: Star Resonance has a genuinely strong foundation, gorgeous presentation, solid character customization, and an inviting first impression. But the endgame doesn't hold up, seasonal resets undercut long-term investment, and progression leans too heavily on gatekeeping and gacha luck. Worth trying for a season if you want something casual and pretty, not worth committing to as a long-term MMO. Rating 4/10

review_text: When this game initially came out, I would have probably given it an 8/10. I personally enjoy the Hoyoverse-like art, the raid mechanics, and the building of community for BPSR. In Asian servers, this game has a decent reputation with more involvement with the development team. They get the love and the respect. Many people spent the orbs as fast as they could before the servers shut down and were rolled back. Those who spent the unpaid for currency were in "debt" for the rest of the time on their account, but they were at least able to keep the cosmetics. This final situation where the dev team could have been like "that's our fault, you can keep the orbs, no reason to punish the user for our mistake" would have maybe kept the player base, but they opted to maintain the "integrity" of the currency system. Sometimes the right corporate response ends up being the worst decision to keep, maintain, and grow an online MMO community. If you're looking for a singleplayer Hoyoverse-like game that's void of microtransactions, try DragonSwored: Awakening . review_text: I put over 400 hours into Blue Protocol: Star Resonance, so I definitely got my money's worth in terms of playtime. I enjoyed the game for a while, but I can't honestly recommend it to anyone looking for an MMO they can invest in long-term. Let's start with the positives. The visuals are excellent. The anime art style is beautiful, and the character creator gives you plenty of options to make a character that feels unique. Fashion is also one of the game's biggest draws—but it comes with a major caveat. While there are a lot of great cosmetics, many of the best outfits are locked behind limited-time gacha banners. On top of that, the dye system is surprisingly restrictive. Several outfits, including collaborations like Monogatari and Fairy Tail, don't let you freely recolor every part of the costume, which makes customization feel far more limited than it should. Unfortunately, that's where most of my praise ends. The story is incredibly forgettable. It mostly feels like you're moving from one area to the next without much reason to care about what's happening. The biggest issue is the endgame. Once you reach it, you realize just how shallow the gameplay loop really is. Every day becomes the same routine: gather and craft until you run out of stamina, either stop playing or burn potions to keep gathering, run your daily boss run (Unstable fights which take around 20 seconds with an AI party), and farm bosses hoping for imagines drops so you can play. I spent 6 months doing the same boss everyday and only had 1 imagine drop. ( Don't even bother tanking unless you have Tempest Ogre. He feels mandatory) That's... pretty much it. There are weekly raids, but unless you're in an active guild, you'll either struggle to find a group or hope you get lucky with a decent PUG. Progression is also frustrating because many groups refuse to accept players unless they already have an absurdly high Ability Score. It's a classic case gatekeeping. I joined a few guilds that simply carried me through the harder content. While I appreciated the help, it also made progression feel hollow because I wasn't really earning anything. The dungeon design doesn't help either. Most seasons simply recycle the same few dungeons across three different difficulty levels. New dungeons are added each season, but they usually boil down to pulling as many enemies as possible, AoEing everything down, and then fighting a boss. Seasonal events aren't much better. Most are either AFK events or small minigames that lose their appeal after a handful of runs. Eventually, I realized I was logging in every single day just to complete my dailies without actually having fun. Then the next season would arrive, wipe most of my progression, and send me back to square one. Instead of feeling rewarded for my time, it felt like I was on a treadmill that never went anywhere. I haven't logged in for a few weeks now, and honestly, it's been a relief. I don't miss the daily checklist. This game has a fantastic foundation. The visuals, character customization, and overall presentation are genuinely good. But the repetitive endgame, seasonal resets, shallow progression, restrictive cosmetic systems, and overreliance on limited-time gacha keep it from reaching its potential. I don't regret the time I spent with it, but I can't recommend it unless you're simply looking for a casual anime MMO to play for a season or two without expecting much depth.

review_text: blue protocol is honestly a massive joke that completely kills off the spirit of a true online mmo just to push mobile-first, predatory garbage, showing exactly why you are a million times better off spending 10 eur a month on final fantasy xiv, which is a literal masterpiece of a game. look into the general player consensus and data trends, and it becomes blindingly obvious how fundamentally broken its core design is. analysis across global forums reveals that the entire game acts as a cheap puppet show; it is not even a real pc mmo, but rather a clunky mobile title that was hastily ported to desktops with an restrictive user interface overlay that completely ruins custom scaling. independent player evaluations highlight that the overworld difficulty is completely non-existent, featuring mob artificial intelligence that just stands there blankly while you click repetitive, automated keys, completely removing any sense of achievement or mechanical skill from the combat loop. while the anime visuals look kinda cute when you first log in, the moment-to-moment gameplay is weighed down by clunky cross-platform combat limitations, messy menus, and a completely empty endgame that treats you like a servant, forcing you into automated shallow daily chores and brain-dead time-gating instead of letting you go out and explore a real world. the whole progression loop is actively ruined by a multi-currency trap and pay-to-win gacha elements that gatekeep basic combat skills and essential quality-of-life features behind massive paywalls, creating a toxic loop where the team designs annoying roadblocks just so they can sell you the fix. local players are also getting totally screwed over by regional matchmaking issues and severe routing lag because instead of setting up normal cross-play matchmaking or smart cloud lines using flexible aws architecture, the studios locked everything down with archaic server divides that split up the dwindling community even further. there is zero respect for your time here because the progression relies on awful layers of rng stacked on top of more rng meant exclusively to milk whales who buy cosmetic rewards and weapon rolls; they drip-feed minor updates and pretend it is fresh content, while every single season drops lazy power-creep mechanics like "illusions" that instantly trash the high-tier weapons and hard-earned items you grinded hundreds of hours for. steam community user tracking shows that the daily active player base has completely plummeted to devastatingly low numbers, and corporate greed is so wild that the developers only run to patch glitches if it threatens their direct profits. they completely ignore broken, automated guild leadership bugs that ruin active social communities by randomly transferring control to inactive accounts without warning, while stealthily dipping into player inventories to adjust premium currency errors, leaving innocent players buried under massive negative coin debts. moving your time over to final fantasy xiv for a flat monthly subscription changes everything because it is incredibly good, beautifully written, and square enix treats your efforts with actual respect; every piece of high-end raid gear and a good 80% of every beautiful mount is unlocked purely through merit-based gameplay, and the genius single-character multi-job system lets you level up and master every single tank, healer, and dps class on one solo avatar without ever dealing with a paid wall, an automated bot-like gameplay layout, or a greasy gacha pop-up window. its absolutely embarrassing and pathetic how a giant like bandai namco wasn't able to deliver this title themselves after hyping it up for years as the next big anime mmo, only to completely drop the ball, run away from their own project, and hand the broken remains over to external mobile studios who turned it into an unoptimized trash fire. so... yes: this game is a dead-on-arrival, predatory clown show that strips away every ounce of what makes a real gaming experience fun just to milk your wallet, so save yourself time and go play real mmos.

review_text: tl;dr: Game's literally dead for MMORPG standards. No players, poor management and heavy p2w endgame. The premise looks amazing. High quality anime graphics, fun action combat and you can dress up your character - what else would you want from an MMORPG? Well, this game did not have any EU servers until very recently, so the "global" launch was not global at all. Now that they added them, they did not add a simple feature: server migration. In a game where you can play any job on one character, every progression is incredibly time gated, you unironically expect the few players to start over? I was a returning player so I did not mind starting from scratch, but the server is absolutely dead. I have met one person in the entire open world in a couple of hours of playing and two unique players talking in global chat in russian. The NA server is basically a couple of whales and new players being gatekept by them in the only multiplayer aspects of the game. I really wished for this game to succeed. The anime MMORPG market is basically free real estate. The only competition in the genre are games that are literally 20 years old that are on life support since a decade. All this game had to do was to use its fun combat, add a somewhat fun progression system and sprinkle in some proper social mechanics into the game. Top it off with loads of p2w skins and you'd own this part of the market. What we get instead is the pinnacle of mismanagement and wasted potential. There is a million other reasons why you should not play this game, but other reviews cover the reasons already.

review_text: PROS - Great potential at launch, fun early game when it came out. CONS - Severe lack of endgame and guild content. - Extreme repetition and small, restricted maps. - Terrible automated systems (losing ownership of your own guild without any warning/email). - Rapidly dying player base and heavily monetized. Honest review: I looked forward to Blue Protocol for a really long time (since 2023), and when it finally came out, I was genuinely enjoying it. But after a while, the gameplay loop became incredibly repetitive and boring. The "open world" was basically just one part of the map, and the other locations that unlocked later on were quite small and mostly space-restricted. I was running a guild, but eventually, there was absolutely nothing left to do. The game lacks any real guild content that would add substance for members or give guild members something to work on together. Naturally, inactive players started piling up, and Blue Protocol's player base began to tank hard. After a while, I decided to take a break. But guess what happened? I logged back in after two months or so, only to find out that the guild I built—where I had so many memories and tons of screenshots taken with my guildmates—had been handed over to someone else. To make matters worse, it was given to an inactive player who just happened to log in once, got auto-assigned as the Guildmaster, and then never logged in again. So, I did the only thing that made sense at that moment: I closed the game and uninstalled it. I was never warned anywhere that my guild would be transferred to someone else due to inactivity. I didn't even get an email notification saying, "Log in or lose your guild"—if I had, I would have easily logged in for a minute to keep it. This game had massive potential, but after numerous bugs and a severe lack of content, it just became a chore. The guild situation was the final nail in the coffin that convinced me this game isn't worth my time. It has turned into a total cash grab that only survives because a few people, for some reason, keep throwing money at it. At this point, it’s completely pointless to keep playing or even keep it installed. They only keep the servers running because it’s still making them a bit of cash. Averaging around 900 players a day for a game like this is devastating, and I'm just waiting for the day they announce the shutdown, which is inevitable. P.S. Unfortunately, because of what happened to my guild, I genuinely regret ever downloading and playing this game.

review_text: After around 100 hours in Blue Protocol, I have several thoughts that I feel need to be considered. This game is trying to strike a balance between popular MMOs like WoW, FF14, GW2, and ESO and, most notably, the Hoyoverse games. In some ways I do think that it succeeds in making a "Hoyoverse MMO", but in other ways, it has a lot to improve. Graphics Quality: 8/10. I think that the quality is good, though there are some instances even on high graphics where NPCs' teeth don't load in during cutscenes and such. Sound/Music Quality: 7/10. Like the graphics, I think the quality is perfectly fine, though I do think that the generic battle theme is highly repetitive and could have been a bit less of something that I'd rather mute and play my own music over after several hours. Story: 3/10. Way too fast-paced. I won't go into spoilers, but the story for this game moves at 100 miles an hour, to the point that most "important" character moments for the cast of NPCs fall flat because we've only known them for five minutes. I think that the developers focused way too hard on having a story that they could reasonably deliver during the opening hype for the game. If you didn't keep up the story with the small daily chunks they timegated off during the first two weeks of the game, I think a playthrough of the first arc could maybe be only 6 hours long, with you only being familiar with the main villain for 1.5-2 hours of that. The characters also, in medias res, act like major things have happened in-universe in the span of you doing a 2 minute puzzle. I genuinely wonder if there were plans for there to be like 30-50% more quest content and they just cut it for some reason or another. Localization: Tied to story. My GOD the locatlization in this game is ROUGH. Most of the localization is fine, if not a little awkward, but some of them are just atrocious. I think one of the text boxes I found with placeholder "Type Here" text just said "Please". PLEASE have someone go over the text before it gets shipped. Quality Assurance: 6/10. Not great. I learned that apparently dialogue in the game is built in HTML since I noticed one of the lines of dialogue had a ? instead of a > to line break. Some sentences are missing spaces between words, it's not uncommon to randomly disconnect at times, and I noticed a sound bug in one of the high-level areas where the sound randomly starts and stops. This game REALLY needed another month or two of QA testing before release. Class Design: 9/10. I actually really like the classes in this game and look forward to any future releases they may put out. While most of them have clear analogues to other MMOs (Frost Mage being WoW frost mage, Wind Knight being FFXIV Dragoon, etc.), I don't think that's a bad thing. They're aesthetics that people are familiar with and already like. Also, THIS GAME GIVES YOU TIPS AND USE CASES FOR YOUR INDIVIDUAL CLASS ABILITIES! How have the other big MMOs not done this yet? Massive props from me. Fight Design: 9/10. The Master difficulty fights aren't out yet, but I've been pleasantly surprised with what I've seen so far in the "casual" content. AoE dodges, add phases, rot passes from FFXIV, and more. If the high-end combat was more accessible to the average player, I'd give this a 10/10. Economy: 2/10. Garbage-tier. There are approximately 8 different currencies to keep track of, each with their own weekly/monthly lockouts, and two of them are just "unbound/f2p" versions, with one being presented as the "general currency" and the other being the "freemium". Ironically, for the purposes that you need them for, the "general currency" feels like the most you want and is harder to obtain in meaningful amounts. In other MMOs, you'd just supplement this by using crafting and gathering to make things to sell and vendor mob drops. THERE IS NO VENDOR TO SELL SURPLUS MOB DROPS. YOU WILL BE STUCK WITH THEM FOREVER. I'll get into crafting and gathering next, but the game systems have essentially culminated in the classes needing massive amounts of the "general currency" to progress your character, but not having enough to actually do anything for it. This is probably my biggest complaint in the entire game aside from the crafting and gathering. Crafting / Gathering: 1/10. This game has a stamina system for crafting and gathering. It's shared between all of the "life skills", so you have to pick and choose what you want to do every day. If you don't use stamina, you gain 1/40 of the exp you would have if you used stamina. This is honestly just not acceptable. Other MMOs have tried to do this and it hasn't really worked out. This needs to not be a thing. What happens if you have a raid group that needs food and "serums", but you're capped on your stamina or don't have enough to make what you need? It's bad enough trying to level one of them, but there's around 8 life skills in total. If you're like me and like having one of every crafter and gatherer in MMOs, this is going to be a LONG grind for you. Fashion: 4/10. I like making my characters look good in MMOs. I like DOING CONTENT that lets me get things that make my characters look good in MMOs. 99% of the fashion choices in this game are paid. I do like what's on offer, but I'm not inclined to spend upwards of $10 for an outfit in this game for the sake of just not being in the default outfit. I don't know how the CN players reacted to a lot of the problems in the game, particularly since localization presumably wasn't much of a thing that they had to consider, but I genuinely wonder why the developers thought some of these decisions were acceptable. That being said, the F2P in this game is quite reasonable, I'd just have much rather paid to buy this game than deal with the stamina and currency woes. Otherwise though, great game. I'd recommend for at least something to enjoy yourself in, but the developers have made it hard to consider this as a "daily driver". My main recommendations for improvement are: Remove the stamina system from crafting and gathering so the player economy can start to grow instead of whatever it's doing now. Open up vendors so players can sell mob drops to make some pocket change or at least exchange them for something usable. Condense the 8 different currencies - or at least just merge the bound and unbound ones. Spend more time proofreading the lines of dialogue in the game. Spend some time crafting a story rather than drip-feeding it and acting like major things have been happening. I want to like this game and I will play for the foreseeable future, but if this game wants to survive long-term, there are changes that need to happen.

review_text: 22/05/2026 - The game's publisher has recently demonstrated serious incompetence in handling major issues within the game. The day before this edit, all players received an in-game mail containing roughly $100 worth of premium currency, with the message clearly indicating it was a gift . It was later revealed that the mail had been sent globally by mistake instead of to a single intended recipient. Around 30 minutes later, the game entered maintenance, and over the following 24 hours, players who claimed this "gift" had the equivalent amount of premium currency deducted from their accounts, regardless of whether that currency had already been spent on in-game purchases. As a result, many players who reasonably assumed this was a legitimate gift have effectively ended up with over $100 worth of negative premium currency (which, mind you, can only normally be obtained through real-money purchases). Choosing this approach instead of issuing a rollback, especially given how little time had passed, is baffling from every angle. It also remains unclear whether carrying a premium currency debt may eventually result in account bans. === Day 1 player here. I really wanted to enjoy this game. I genuinely tried to put aside the initial negative reviews and my own doubts, just to give it a fair shot and find something to like. That lasted until around the middle of Season 2. Once you’ve seen one season, you’ve basically seen them all. The loop is predictable: new gear drops that immediately invalidate whatever you’ve been working toward, seasonal activities that feel designed more to keep the game open than to be engaging, the same structure of three raid bosses across difficulties, and a handful of dungeons recycling rewards with slight variations. On top of that, there’s a constant stat crunch, new paid “summons” that overshadow older ones, and more fashion sets locked behind an overpriced gacha system. At its core, it’s a gacha game that doesn’t respect your time or your investment. It tries to appeal to hardcore MMO grinders, but the systems are too shallow to support that, while simultaneously being too demanding for a more casual audience. It ends up stuck in an awkward middle ground where neither playstyle feels satisfying. Even the one strong point I initially enjoyed the game for, fashion, is starting to feel stale. Recent additions lean heavily into repetitive, cutesy designs, with little variety or creativity, and the male options in particular feel like like they were created with random additions and seeing what sticks. It’s just not worth the time commitment, and definitely not worth the money. Both feel wasted here. Stay away.

review_text: I think after almost 80 hours... I'm good. I really wanted to love this game. I spent so long waiting for it. I was heartbroken when I saw the original game was shut down. Was ecstatic to hear it was coming back, in one form or another. I played it for all this time, joined a guild with nice people, even spent money to pick up an outfit or two. But I don't know, this game makes you feel kind of empty. When such-and-such character dies, it's kind of sudden and there was no real attachment there because we only knew them for maybe 3-4 quests, and I found myself not feeling anything particular about it even though it was treated as something super sad for the other characters. I think that was probably the first moment I started wondering if I was actually enjoying the story. Cutscenes are incredibly cheaply made, sometimes they're just slideshows with blurbs of text in between, or sometimes they're just 5 seconds of a character turning to look your way. Dialogue is okay if you engage in it, but there's no incentive to, and you'll reach the same end every time. Movement speed is incredibly slow, even on a mount. It's hard playing this game and swapping back to one that's faster paced. Your character sprints at full tilt, but it never really seems like you're going anywhere. Thankfully there's auto navigation for most content, so you can do something else while your character travels to wherever you pointed to. Combat's... okay, but I stopped bothering to watch my cooldowns and use skills myself and opted to just use the auto-combat after a while. Fighting started feeling like a chore. Boss fights are fine though, it wasn't hard to understand mechanics, and if you played with bot teammates, they'd handle most of the mechanics themselves, leaving you to focus on dealing damage. Other reviews have already mentioned how the cash shop currency doesn't carry over between your 3 characters, nor does any other purchase you make. It was a little jarring finding that out AFTER buying an outfit. The daily loop was probably the most draining part about the game. It's all about grinding and gearing and busting your butt thinking you've finally earned all the best gear-- right before an update invalidates it all by adding in a tier higher. I get that it's a "Welcome to MMO's" moment and I shouldn't be surprised by it, but the amount of work you had to put to get fully geared was A Lot. Add to that daily/weekly limits and you'll almost always end up behind somehow. Log in, do a boss fight or two, do your guild dailies, log out. It's easy to burn out unless you've got people you're playing with doing it with you. While I appreciate that the game came back at all, it just feels soul-crushingly average at best.

review_text: Okay, I like waiting to review games to give them a fair review & not make rash judgements based on superficial whims. With that said, and nearly 500 hours clocked into this game I cannot in good faith recommend this game. I *really* wanted to give a positive review as well. The game is p2w, what you win: superiority and bragging rights of being top dps, if you pick the right class. Sink time and money into the wrong class and you’ll be just above average. The gatekeeping and community is 90% of what killed the player base. People treated this like a hardcore MMO, when the reality is you have 5 buttons, a few basic PvE mechanics that are nothing new, and relies on team work. People in world chats upset that they can’t find groups to clear content a week old being met with “uninstall” “baby’s first MMO”. There is an “auto battle” feature, which is awesome as you can toggle skills to be on auto or not. Really great for stuff that you constantly have in rotation that needs to be used the moment it’s off CD. The auto battle does not “battle” it just activates skills, and even times certain spells to maximise dps. Great feature for when there’s a lot of movement or aoe happening, however that of course is a problem. Many players call for “auto battle banned in dungeons and raids” “will be kicked if on auto”. The lack of content. When the game first released, this was not a problem what so ever as there was a *ton* of stuff unlocking so no biggie that the story is time gated, no worries that life skills have a cap. However, now that the game is towards the end of the season there’s no more random chests scattered around as they’ve been found, there’s no more books to find, there’s no more maps unlocking, you can’t grind you skills because limited stamina, all content is reclears, helping others. There’s literally nothing to do if you’ve been playing since day 1 and clearing content semi casually each week. Further more exacerbated by p2w carrying entire parties and making what should take an hour or so a 5 minute raid or dungeon. Everyone just leaves parties as quickly as possible. The social aspect of the game is abysmal. There’s no way to chat locally and have it make sense, if you’re in a map, then the “current” channel is for the entire map, not local to a current radius. There’s no social hang outs, no idle games or events, literally nothing that helps players connect beyond guilds. I was a guild leader, had tons of quality players, good personalities, smart people, engaging with building a good community. Was awesome the first couple weeks, then the drop offs started happening, no problem recruited more players, then they fell off. Okay, recruit more players, okay now maybe recruit lagging guilds... and the cycle never stops as there are literally thousands of players each week who fall off. I never struggled to find a group, knew how to ask in world chat for groups, make friends, find players. That was never an issue. There are dozens of players I know who quit because they didn’t put in that effort, and it was difficult to get parties together, would take me a good 10-15m sometimes for dungeons, 30 or so minutes for raids. The “dailies” are an absolute joke. You can buy over priced items from a mystery shop, you must buy the battle pass to get an extra refresh, and the item pricing doesn’t even make sense, it’s completely random. Sometimes you’ll find stamina potions for 100 orbs, or you’ll find them for 10,000 luno. There’s 10+ currencies in game, half expire at the end of the season, they don’t roll over and they don’t tell you which ones expire. I didn’t mind any of these glaring flaws because my friends were playing and we were all having fun. The fun is now now feels like a daily grind / chores, almost all my friends have stopped playing, in game and the ones out of the game. I was holding out for season 2 but have read multiple sources saying there will be p2w weapons and items that further the dps gaps, AND 0 balance changes. This info was the nail in coffin for me. Cannot recommend this game, sadly. I stuck through the bugs, I dealt with the drops offs, I “made my own community”, I cleared content at a normal pace. Now that the newness has worn off, this game is literally just click some items, clear ez mode dungeons, teleport to a location, afk farm.

Below, I outline the primary concerns based on expert analyses and documented cases, drawing from security discussions and technical evaluations. 1. Security Vulnerabilities Kernel-level access provides anti-cheat software with unrestricted control over critical system components, making it a high-value target for exploitation. A flaw or bug in the anti-cheat driver can lead to system-wide instability, such as crashes (e.g., Blue Screen of Death on Windows) or complete compromise. For instance, if hackers identify a vulnerability, they could leverage it to gain kernel privileges, enabling malware installation, data theft, or remote code execution. Privacy Concerns These systems often collect extensive data to function effectively, including hardware details, running processes, and user behavior patterns. This level of intrusion raises privacy issues, as the software can potentially access sensitive information unrelated to the game, such as personal files or browsing history. Developers gain unprecedented oversight, which could be misused for data aggregation or shared with third parties without explicit user consent. In regions with varying data protection laws, this amplifies risks of unauthorized surveillance. 3. Performance and Stability Impacts Operating at the kernel level can degrade system performance by consuming resources for constant monitoring. Users have reported reduced frame rates, increased latency, or conflicts with other software, such as antivirus programs. Moreover, incompatibilities—particularly on non-Windows platforms like Linux—can cause frequent crashes or prevent games from launching, as seen in your experience with Blue Protocol Star Resonance. 4. Broader Systemic Risks Granting kernel access to third-party software deviates from best practices in operating system design, where such privileges are reserved for essential drivers. This increases the attack surface of the entire device, potentially affecting non-gaming activities. Experts, including kernel developers, argue that no game justifies this level of control, as it shifts trust from the operating system to potentially unvetted game publishers. Counterarguments and Mitigations Proponents note that well-implemented kernel-level anti-cheats can be stable and effective against sophisticated cheats, with minimal impact if no malicious activity is present. Some developers, like those behind Valorant, implement safeguards such as regular audits and limited data collection. review_text: It’s a shame that this is how it ended, because the game actually had a lot of potential. The management made a long series of bad decisions and ended up ruining it. The game had a lovingly crafted world, great enemies, interesting raids, cute costumes, and in the beginning even the monetization felt acceptable. I was there from day one, I had a great guild, made Friends, but the game became uninteresting to me very quickly because of the timegating. It clearly wanted to be accessible and make it easy for players to jump back in, even if they had missed a week. But what it actually achieved was punishing active players. Someone who logged in once a week could get the same gear in half an hour as a player who had invested several hours every day. Even raid rewards that were supposed to be difficult to earn were basically handed out to everyone at the end of the week, regardless of whether they had even attempted the raid. Because of the heavy timegating, you quickly ran out of things to do, and the only remaining goal became the seasonal costumes from dungeons. But since there was no pity system at all, you could grind a dungeon over 100 times and still never get the skin you wanted. Progress was so heavily restricted that within just a few weeks, you could complete nearly every achievement, and in the end fishing and gathering became the only things left to do. But since botting was not punished, even there a player who left a fishing bot running for a few nights was far ahead of a normal active player. And now there’s apparently even going to be a button that boosts you straight to level 60. They wanted to attract casual players, but instead they drove away the active player base. What came out of it is a dead game that could have been a truly great experience otherwise.

Regardless of the many issues I have, I poured (what I consider to be) an unhealthy amount of hours the past weekend to this MMORPG, which I almost never do nowadays. review_text: The game has always been just decent- a fun way to pass the time with friends but nothing revolutionary and had plenty of room for improvement. The kind of game where you stick around because your friends make it fun, not because the game itself is amazing. But on May 21st, the publisher sent out 8,165 premium currency in the mail to all players, with a message stating it was a gift. Something didn't feel right, so while I claimed the mail, I refused to spend any of them. Sure enough; roughly within an hour or two, the servers were taken down for immediate emergency maintenance- it turns out the mail had been sent accidentally. Upon the servers going back up, it was assumed they were just going to roll back everything, but those who did not spend the orbs had them removed, along with any paid for orbs in their account without explanation. Those who spent the orbs kept whatever they obtained using said orbs. The next day; anyone who spent the gifted orbs had their accounts placed in the negatives for the amount spent, while keeping the items; giving them a boost over those who had not used them, while also needing to spend roughly 100 USD to get back out of debt. The supposed gift turned into a loan, and when confronted by players they said they were looking into it. Individuals who asked about their paid orbs in the official discord were told to use customer support- an AI chatbot, to get their paid for orbs back and one of the discord bots was changed to make Ba Sing Se memes whenever someone typed May 21st. Several days later, nothing has changed and no further communication on the subject has come from the publisher or the individual who sent the "gifted" orbs, making it seem as they intend to sweep the entire situation under the rug. Constant feedback is ignored in the official discord about the subject, making it feel as they're just going to sweep everything under the rug. I no longer feel this is a game worth playing or spending money on, and I don't recommend you spend any money or time on it either. The gifted orbs is one thing, but taking orbs out of an account that spent actual money on them and refusing to resolve the situation, while putting everyone else into debt for something given freely, is a trust breaker. Do not give these publishers money. They will take it and run.

review_text: The good: Art, music, dungeons, boss fights, plenty to do The bad: Currencies, gacha, class variety, class switching, auto combat existing The ugly: Ability score, players The primary issue with this game that is going to kill this game is players who do not understand how ability score works. It is very easy to game the system and inflate your AS by means that have nothing to do with skill or experience. As a result, you have bad players with high AS that advertise high AS requirements for content that doesn't require even close to the numbers they are asking for. The general population constantly sees these requirements and either just assume that's what's actually needed and either repeat those requirements or don't bother asking to join groups because they "don't meet those requirements". You literally have people requiring 19k AS for normal raid pugs. Long term, this is going to bleed the game of its player base because they are being gate kept. I think the most surprising thing about this MMO is the fact that using a DPS meter is less useful gauging personal performance or group performance. It's a better tool for identifying imposters with 19k AS who barely do more dps than the healer and tank. If you are thinking about starting the game, I wouldn't advise it. You are already way behind most of the pack. You might have some fun for a while, but you are going to get locked out of later content by 90% of the player base.

review_text: We had an amazing 50 hours—unfortunately, the game didn’t give us a reason to stay for 51. ** below are all based on first few weeks of launch ✅ Charming visuals and strong artistic direction ✅ Fun world events and boss hunts at launch ✅ Detailed environments that made exploration enjoyable ✅ The holy trinity system (rare these days) felt great, with surprisingly thoughtful healer design ✅ Solid character customization ⛔ Too much content was time-gated for too long at launch (main reason my gf and I eventually quit) ⛔ Gear grind felt meaningless since upgrades were quickly invalidated once new tiers unlocked ⛔ Overwhelming amount of menus and sub-menus ⛔ Heavy microtransactions, with some feeling pay-to-win Grade: C+ After waiting years for Blue Protocol , it was so incredibly disappointing to hear it had been cancelled just when it finally seemed close to release (F U Amazon). When a mobile version, Blue Protocol: Star Resonance was announced, I immediately knew I wanted to give it a try. At launch, it was such a fun experience. My gf and I had a great time exploring the world, figuring out which elites and bosses to farm, and just learning the game together. There’s always something special about the early days of an MMO, and this one captured that magic well. Unfortunately, the longer-term systems didn’t hold up. Time-gated content dragged on too long, and the gear grind quickly started to feel pointless when our hard-earned upgrades were replaced almost immediately once new content unlocked only a few days later. Eventually, we both just stopped feeling the urge to login. In the end, I’m glad I didn’t force myself to keep playing past that point. The experience never soured and we just stopped when the fun stopped. It was a good, fun 50 hours, and honestly, that’s enough for me. At this point, it’s probably not worth jumping into—at least not as a long-term game—but for a brief moment, it was a genuinely good time.

review_text: I was a little bit debating about this review of mine, but here it is. Please, take into consideration that I am a female player and I see things -also- under this view. ⭐ Pros 1. Beautiful anime visuals. The art direction is really good. Characters look expressive and vibrant, and the world feels like an interactive anime. If you enjoy that aesthetic, the game is a treat. 2. Smooth, responsive combat. The combat is fast, stylish, and satisfying. Dodging, timing, and chaining abilities feels fluid. Boss fights are especially fun & flashy, challenging, and rewarding. 3. Good character customization. As a female player, I appreciated the variety of hairstyles, outfits, and accessories. The game lets you build a character who actually feels like you instead of locking options behind gender stereotypes. 4. Social features and co-op feels natural. Grouping up never feels forced. The game is designed for quick cooperation without awkward pressure. There is a nice balance between solo freedom and shared moments. If you join an active guild, that's even better. I was lucky. 5. Epic soundtrack. The music is cinematic and uplifting, especially during story beats and big encounters. ❌ Cons 1.Heavy grinding. A lot of progression is locked behind repetitive tasks. If you don’t enjoy farming materials or repeating the same dungeons, the game can feel exhausting. 2. Story pacing is inconsistent Some story chapters are emotional and engaging, but others drag on or feel thin. The narrative sometimes struggles to hold the same level of excitement that the visuals promise. 3. Monetization needs polish. While the game isn’t fully pay-to-win, cosmetics and convenience items are very obviously pushed. It occasionally breaks immersion when the shop feels more polished than the quest system. 4. Limited variety in enemy types. Many enemies feel similar despite the different zones. The world is beautiful, but the mobs don’t always match that level of creativity. 5. Performance issues on certain devices. Even with good hardware, the game sometimes stutters in crowded areas or large battles. Optimization still has room to grow. Final Thoughts Blue Protocol: Star Resonance is a beautiful and charming MMO with satisfying combat and a strong visual identity. As a female player, I loved the customization, the expressive characters, and the sense of adventure. However, the game still leans too hard on grinding, has unstable pacing, and shows some rough edges in monetization and performance. If you love anime aesthetics and action-combat MMOs, you will enjoy it. If you want rich storytelling or deep variety, you might find it lacking.

review_text: Blue Protocol: Star Resonance is a by-the-numbers anime MMO that doesn't do anything special to stand out. One of the game’s biggest highlights is the art style; it offers strong anime visuals, a colorful world, stylish characters, and pretty detailed environments. It also offers almost all of the MMO activities you'd expect: some world exploration, fighting world bosses, crafting, fishing, and dungeons/raids. The combat is also ok-ish, but nothing to write home about; it's action-oriented, and you get a handful of skills for each class. But everything else about BP:SR is really dull and uninspired. The story is the most generic and clichéd stuff you can think about and puts you to sleep real fast (there's an option to skip most dialogue and cutscenes, but reading any of the interactions is really tiresome - I've only completed the first 3 chapters of season 1, but it was more than enough to convience me that the game is garbage); all cutscenes look stilted and robotic, and the mouth animations are not synced to the dialogue; the story pacing is all over the place, and story beats feel hastily put together; activities around the world are just filler and feel repetitive fast; the world traversal is abysmal, it's slow and sluggish and none of the 3 mounts I got for free or any of the traversal skills available made it any more fun; controls in general (walking/traversal and combat) feel unresponsive and there's always a delay to all your actions; the camera sometimes feels broken and you can't move it easily enough to see the world around you. Also, there's an instant level 60 boost for new players, which I found weird, but at least you can still progress through the initial story if you are so inclined. Plus, like in any Asian MMO, there are a billion different menus that you must open 1 at a time and collect every single reward manually (or at least I didn't find a Collect All button). The performance isn't great; I had FPS dips at times for no reason, and the game sometimes crashed after leaving it idle for 15-20 minutes. It also has a season pass (free and paid), a monthly subscription pass, and a cash shop. There are also multiple currencies, some of which I don't even know what they are used for and just make the game more confusing. I personally can't say if the game's P2W, as I got bored before reaching end-game, but from what I've read online, it's a very gacha-heavy MMO and feels more like a mobile MMO (the interface is also very ugly and very mobile-ish, and the UX is not great at all). On top of everything, there's also apparently time-gated content, which just feels like another nail in the coffin.
