review_text: The Mr. Rabbit Magic Show developed and published by Rusty Lake is a short but delightfully inventive puzzle experience that serves as both a playful celebration of the studio’s distinctive style and a clever theatrical showcase for its signature surreal storytelling. Designed as an interactive magic performance, the game invites players to step into the audience of an unusual stage show hosted by the enigmatic Mr. Rabbit, a character longtime fans of Rusty Lake will instantly recognize from earlier titles. Rather than presenting a traditional narrative adventure with exploration across multiple locations, the game focuses on a tightly structured series of magical “acts,” each built around a small puzzle that captures the feeling of witnessing a trick unfold in real time. The structure of the game revolves around a sequence of bite-sized challenges presented as stage illusions. Each act places a set of props on the stage—top hats, playing cards, cages, mirrors, or other mysterious devices—and asks the player to interact with them in order to help Mr. Rabbit complete his trick. The mechanics are simple on the surface, relying mostly on point-and-click interactions, but the puzzles frequently require a bit of lateral thinking. Rusty Lake’s design philosophy has always leaned toward experimentation rather than strict logical deduction, and that approach is very much present here. Solutions often emerge from observing subtle visual hints, manipulating objects in unusual ways, or understanding the playful logic behind a magician’s performance. Some tricks feel like classic puzzle-box challenges, while others rely on visual illusions that cleverly mimic real magic tricks. Although the game is relatively short, its presentation carries the unmistakable style that defines Rusty Lake’s catalog. The visuals combine minimalistic illustrations with a slightly eerie tone, blending whimsy and unease in equal measure. The stage itself feels like a surreal theater where the boundaries between performance and reality blur. Characters and props are rendered in a clean, hand-drawn style, but their movements and transformations often take on strange or unsettling qualities. Mr. Rabbit himself acts as a charismatic host, silently guiding the player through each act with theatrical gestures and exaggerated expressions. The overall aesthetic reinforces the sensation that something mysterious is always happening just behind the curtain. Sound design and music contribute significantly to the atmosphere. The soundtrack is playful yet slightly uncanny, echoing the mood of an old magic show mixed with the dreamlike tone Rusty Lake is known for. Subtle sound effects accompany every successful trick or interaction, giving each puzzle the satisfying payoff of a completed illusion. Even though the game does not rely heavily on dialogue or exposition, the audiovisual presentation gives each act a sense of personality and rhythm, making the experience feel like a continuous performance rather than a collection of disconnected puzzles. While the focus is clearly on puzzle interactions, the game also carries a layer of narrative significance for fans of Rusty Lake’s broader universe. Mr. Rabbit is not simply a random stage performer but a character tied to the surreal mythology that appears throughout the studio’s other games, including titles in the Cube Escape and Rusty Lake series. The magic show occasionally hints at this larger world through subtle references and symbolic imagery. These small touches create a sense that the show is more than just entertainment—it is part of the strange and mysterious timeline that Rusty Lake fans have been piecing together for years. One of the most memorable elements of the experience arrives when the game begins to break the illusion of the stage itself. What initially appears to be a straightforward sequence of tricks gradually evolves into something more self-aware and experimental. Without revealing too much, the game eventually introduces a playful meta twist that shifts the perspective from a simple stage show into something that feels like a celebration of Rusty Lake’s creative journey. This moment transforms the game from a collection of puzzles into a charming tribute to the studio’s history and its relationship with its audience. The main drawback of the game lies in its length. Most players will likely complete the entire magic show in less than an hour, and some puzzles may feel too simple for experienced Rusty Lake fans. A few acts end just as they begin to feel interesting, leaving players wishing there were more elaborate sequences or additional layers of challenge. However, the game’s brevity is somewhat intentional. It is designed as a compact, celebratory experience rather than a full-scale adventure, and its pacing reflects the quick, surprising nature of stage magic itself. Despite its short runtime, the game succeeds in delivering a memorable and creative experience. It captures the playful imagination, surreal charm, and clever puzzle design that have defined Rusty Lake’s identity for years. For longtime followers of the studio, it feels like a lighthearted gift packed with references and personality. For newcomers, it serves as a welcoming introduction to Rusty Lake’s unique blend of mystery and puzzle storytelling. In the end, The Mr. Rabbit Magic Show may be small in scope, but it demonstrates how much creativity can be packed into a brief interactive performance. Its imaginative presentation, charming puzzles, and clever meta elements make it an entertaining little spectacle that is well worth experiencing, even if only once. Rusty Lake manages to transform the simple idea of a magic show into a memorable interactive vignette that feels both playful and slightly mysterious. Rating: 9/10

review_text: Rusty lake/Cube Escape Review After finally revisiting and catching up with this series from my last played game being Hotel I believe, I'm going to attempt to review the 18 entries as a whole. I feel it's the best way to look at the series. They are talked about roughly in the intended play order so read to where it's appropriate, some further thoughts on the whole series at the bottom. Mr magic rabbit show was an okay fluff piece. At least it's free. I don't fund the puzzles very good (I'd struggle to call some of them puzzles, which makes it feel like a poor celebration of Rusty lake) And that's kind of why I felt like I had to Tackle the game like this, you aren't just buying into one game but an over arching narrative that sadly in 13 years and 18 games we've seen so little forward momentum in, it feels like Roots was the last to really give any. They do easily could provide some answers close the odd mystery while keeping the rest alive but not only are we reiterating the same mystery the same point in the story but tacking on another mystery to the same thing. I'd be like if kingdom hearts one never had us save kairi and face ansem. Sure there was plenty more mystery but it was a self contained story that brought itself to a close. So do I recommend it. Yes? Probably, there's some really great bits and even as a whole it adds up to a pretty okay price. The puzzles feel like they getting increasingly obtuse though, I'm not a fan of all this multimedia cross socials nonsense, the games should contain their own answers. It's very fad like but also wasn't it a fad before rusty lake was even a thing and wasn't popular then. But to sum up my thoughts I want to discuss the games plot so mega spoilers maybe. To me the game is not to be taken at face value anywhere, it's all just a vehicle for it's narrative and a glimpse into a mind that doesn't cope with the reality they've been dealt. So paradoxically the game has told us exactly what it was about from game 1. Mental health (rusty lake mental health), depression (van Gogh Laura even dale), nostalgia (the wallpapers the furniture the phones it's all so nostalgic even if a time you may not have experienced) and letting go, of the past, of paradise (even though it was never good), of anger (Albert) of guilt (Dale for both Laura and his parents, he's clearly seeing his failure to provide justice for her as him harming her, even though there is no mystery she took her own life it was her own dark self). Robert couldn't let go of something he didn't own and "lost it all". The Vanderbooms don't want to let go of life so badly they ruin multiple generations of their family with their nonsense. So I am going to take a que from this series and let go, of it, the developers might not be ready to yet and are stuck in this holding pattern, slapping in fads that don't move things forward but after 13 years I'm ready to let go, frankly I struggle to see how Servant of the lake being based when it is, will provide any answers we hadn't already seen in past games. review_text: R.E.P.O. — A Friendships-Destroying Simulator ⭐⭐⭐ 10/10 would ruin my friendships again. R.E.P.O. is genuinely one of the most cancerous games you can play with your friends, and I mean that in the most beautiful way possible. You load into this game thinking you're going to have a fun little gaming session with the boys, collect some valuables, make some money, and get out alive. Sounds simple enough, right? WRONG. Within 5 minutes, your entire squad has turned into a bunch of screaming idiots, someone has accidentally thrown a priceless object across the room, another guy is laughing so hard he can't breathe, and somehow I'm already ♥♥♥ dead. I genuinely don't understand how I manage to die in literally every possible situation. It doesn't matter what we're doing, where we are, or how carefully I play. I could be standing in the safest corner of the map, minding my own business, and some horrific abomination from the deepest depths of hell will materialise directly behind me and send me straight to the ♥♥♥ shadow realm. Meanwhile, my friends are somehow running around like professional exterminators, surviving things that should have killed them instantly, while I'm lying on the floor questioning every decision I've ever made in my life. And GOD FORBID you play this game with friends who have absolutely zero brain cells. You have one friend who thinks he's the main character and tries to fight every monster he sees. One friend who touches EVERYTHING despite being repeatedly told not to. One friend who accidentally destroys half the building while trying to carry a ♥♥♥ lamp. And then there's the friend who laughs at everyone else's deaths but somehow becomes the biggest liability the moment something actually happens. The worst part is that you can't even be mad at them properly because they're usually too busy laughing at your corpse to hear you screaming into the microphone. You could be desperately begging for help while a monster is actively ripping you apart, and instead of saving you, your friends will stand 10 metres away laughing like they've just witnessed the funniest event in human history. They'll watch you get folded like a lawn chair, wait until you're completely dead, and THEN decide to ask if you need help. THANKS, MATE. REALLY APPRECIATE THE SUPPORT. And don't even get me started on carrying valuables. Apparently, transporting a single object from point A to point B requires the coordination of a NASA space mission. Someone bumps into a wall, the object flies across the room, the physics engine decides gravity is optional, and suddenly everyone's screaming because we've just lost more money than we made in the last three rounds. Every single mission turns into a disaster. You start off organised, communicating, and working together like a proper team. Five minutes later, everyone is separated, the building sounds like a war zone, and I'm watching the rest of my squad from the afterlife because I somehow managed to die doing absolutely nothing. I swear this game has a personal vendetta against me. The monsters don't even want the valuables anymore. They just want ME. They see me enter the building and immediately clock in for their shift. My friends aren't teammates. They're unpaid funeral directors. The amount of times I've heard my friends say, "It's fine, he's probably safe," right before I get obliterated is genuinely concerning. I could have the entire squad protecting me, and somehow the one monster we haven't seen in 20 minutes will appear out of nowhere and erase me from existence. And the betrayal? UNFORGIVABLE. You think you've built trust with your friends after hours of playing together. You think you know them. Then one of them decides it's a good idea to throw something at you, lure a monster into your room, or leave you behind while they escape with all the money. Suddenly, you're not playing a co-op horror game anymore. You're participating in a psychological experiment designed to determine how quickly friendships can collapse under extreme pressure. The funniest part is that despite all this suffering, all the screaming, all the deaths, and all the times I've threatened to uninstall the game, I STILL COME BACK FOR MORE. Because every once in a while, you get that perfect round. Everyone's alive, the loot is valuable, the teamwork is immaculate, and you're finally convinced that maybe, just maybe, you're actually good at this game. Then you turn around, walk into a room, and immediately ♥♥♥ die. Honestly, R.E.P.O. is an incredible game if your goal is to develop trust issues, lose your sanity, and discover which of your friends would leave you behind during an actual apocalypse. The horror isn't the monsters. The horror is knowing that the people standing next to you are the same idiots who would sell your soul for an extra $200 worth of loot. Final verdict: Would I recommend this game? Absolutely. Would I recommend playing it with friends? Only if you hate them. Will I continue playing despite somehow being the first person to die in every single round? Unfortunately, yes. I came here to collect valuables. I left with emotional damage, a ruined friendship, and absolutely no money. 10/10. Five stars. Someone please revive me. I'm begging you.

review_text: R.E.P.O is the kind of game that starts with “okay, let’s do one quick run” and ends with everyone screaming, laughing, and questioning their teamwork skills. It somehow turns simple objectives into absolute chaos in the best way possible. One moment you’re calmly trying to do your job, and the next you’re running for your life while your friends are making *very* unhelpful decisions. What really makes R.E.P.O shine is how naturally funny it is. The physics, timing, and unexpected disasters feel perfectly designed to create comedy without trying too hard. You don’t even need to be good at the game to have fun—in fact, being bad might make it even better. Every failed attempt feels like a story worth retelling. The atmosphere is tense enough to keep you on edge, but never so serious that it stops being fun. It balances suspense and humor perfectly, turning panic into laughter almost instantly. And when you play with friends, the game becomes a nonstop highlight reel of mistakes, heroic sacrifices, and blaming each other for everything that goes wrong. Overall, R.E.P.O is pure fun. It’s goofy, stressful, unpredictable, and endlessly entertaining. If you enjoy games that create unforgettable moments, inside jokes, and lots of laughing (and yelling), R.E.P.O is absolutely worth playing.

review_text: Bought R.E.P.O. thinking it was a co-op horror game. What I got instead was: a piano that weighs approximately the same as the moon a friend who dropped a priceless ceramic vase down the stairs immediately a monster that only activates when someone says "is it safe" and a cart we lost in the first two minutes and never spoke of again. The objective is simple. Carry valuable items carefully to extraction. Do not break them. We have never once done this. The physics system is a masterpiece of human suffering: "Okay, careful, careful—" The vase flies sideways into a wall. It was worth $4,000. We needed $4,000. Dave is no longer allowed to touch things. The proximity voice chat adds incredible immersion. You can hear your friends whispering in real time as you creep through a dark mansion. You can also hear the exact moment someone starts screaming because a monster that looks like a rejected Pixar villain walked through a door at 2% speed and somehow this is the most terrifying experience of our collective lives. The monster AI is elegantly simple. It hears noise. We make noise. This is our entire relationship with death. The upgrade shop offers meaningful progression. We bought better lungs. We needed better lungs because we keep screaming. We are still screaming. We just have more health while we do it. 10/10. We never hit quota. We're going back in. Someone find the cart.

review_text: Probably the only "lethal company-like" (or whatever you wanna call it) that I like, including the original Lethal Company. While Lethal Company is still a good game and commendable for popularizing the gameplay loop it has, it's still primarily a game where you're meant to die in various ♥♥♥ ways for laughs. REPO still expects you to die eventually, but the tools you have are way stronger, and how you play the game can vary a lot on the gear you buy and the party you have. Early game REPO is more faithful to the original genre since you have very little gear, but once you get your first weapons the game really sets itself apart. You can absolutely play the game like a horror game and run away/hide from every enemy, but you can also play the game like it's DOOM and go around trying to kill every monster on the map. Weapons aside, there's a lot of very useful equipment that feels good to use. The point being is that the REPO devs do a great job of making the gameplay itself fun and engaging, instead of it essentially being a way to kill the player and make your friends laugh. Also, unlike plenty of other games in the genre this game gets consistent, and quality, updates. I can't think of a single update since launch that I thought was bad.

review_text: R.E.P.O. is an absolute hit. It's called "Retrieve, Extract and Profit Operation" for a reason you're constantly on the move, always under pressure. And that's exactly what makes it so much fun. Gameplay R.E.P.O.'s gameplay blends co-op teamwork, strategic planning, and nerve-wracking tension. As part of a salvage crew, you and up to five other players enter abandoned industrial facilities, research complexes, or run-down residential areas. Your mission: find valuable objects, salvage them, and bring them safely to the extraction zone, all while maximizing profit. What sounds simple quickly becomes an intense balancing act. Every item has weight and physical properties. A TV rattles, a piano is to heavy to carry, and a dropped object can make enough noise to alert the creatures to your presence. They react to sounds and movements, so caution and coordination are everything. The proximity voice chat creates an authentic atmosphere: you only hear each other when standing close together. This leads to realistic, often chaotic moments, like when someone disappears into the darkness with a valuable object and frantically calls for help. Every mission becomes a mix of horror, tactics, and pure adrenaline. Development A major plus for R.E.P.O. is the active and dedicated development. The small studio semiwork clearly cares about the community: updates arrive regularly, and feedback from Steam forums or Discord is quickly addressed. The team listens closely and responds to player requests, whether for balancing, difficulty adjustments, or physics fine-tuning. Final words R.E.P.O. is an exciting, atmospheric co-op horror experience that excels with clever gameplay, physics-based challenges, and unpredictable monsters. The engine delivers realistic interactions and a dense atmosphere, while an active community continuously improves the game. Anyone who loves teamplay, thrills, and tactical horror will find a real gem here, remarkably polished even in Early Access. Cheers. If you enjoyed the review, check out our curator page! review_text: I do really like this game, but it desperately needs some balancing adjustments, especially early-game in the first few maps and in single-player mode. As it currently exists, I have a very love-but-mostly-hate relationship with it. The game is fine in multiplayer mode. It's silly, it's fun with your friends, and its mechanics aren't difficult to pick up and learn. However, it is JUST fine. The monsters need to be balanced much better than they are, ESPECIALLY some of the tier 3 monsters and ESPECIALLY for the first 1~4 levels of the game. You shouldn't be contending with a tier 3 headman monster in the first or second map of a new game when you've still got no tools, weapons, or meaningful upgrades to help you deal with it. Tier 3 monsters should not be spawning in the first couple levels of the game at all in their current state when they can be so abysmally difficult to deal with. If the devs don't want to touch any of that, then there should at least be vanilla tools that let you customize the game spawns or overall difficulty to your preference. It's not fun playing in a group of 5 where the same 1-2 players are the only ones left alive on every level because your more casual or weaker or simply misfortunate friends continuously just get totally annihilated by the floating head or a clown. Yes, I'm complaining directly from personal experience because it surely cannot be fun having our friends watching me and my one other friend have to struggle through each and every map by ourselves whilst trying to return our friends' heads to each extraction point because we just can't keep them alive against tier 2 and 3 monsters. This is supposed to be a fun and silly friend "party" game, not a sweaty GET GUD BRO game. Let us please make it more enjoyable for our friend groups to play. Finally, all of these complains extend into the single-player mode. In single player on the very first map, I should NOT have to be dealing with a headman and a bowtie with my vanilla butt with no upgrades, weapons, or tools to assist me while ALSO having no one else there to help kite the monster away or keep going if I die. That's just senseless. The single-player is far too annoying to bother with, and I feel like tweaking it to either incorporate more balance with the monsters or allowing more stable scaled progression would help tremendously. TLDR; I love the game but its lack of balance, difficulty scaling, and customization is extremely frustrating. This game has very high potential, but unless the devs start focusing more on making the game more balanced and fun instead of simply adding new monsters it will become a messy shell of a game past its initial "popular on twitch and youtube" prime. It needs some work to make it a genuinely GOOD game.

review_text: I love this game. It’s goofy and entertaining. It’s strategic but doesn’t take itself too seriously. My whole family enjoys both playing and watching people play it (especially when Grian, Geminitay, ImpulseSV, and Skizz play it). It has elements which are similar to Lethal Company, but I appreciate the differences between the games more than anything. I can’t play Lethal because it’s just a bit too creepy/spooky for me with clunky characters. Another big difference is the way you can “go out”. It’s very amusing to knock the other players off a platform to become “king of the losers”. I’ve seen people get out their frustration with this fun mechanic. And here’s where my suggestion comes into play: If there is a loser island face off, surely there should be a form of “winner face-off”. After who-knows-how-many levels (perhaps there could be a set goal in the settings?), the players could emerge onto that platform, not as losers, but as winners. They can sip tea (like eating a consumable), then take out their angst for certain monsters by placing toy-sized versions of them on an extraction table that smashes them. All of the while, credits can roll. And here’s another fun aspect to the idea. If they want, they can allow their teamwork to shine and all become REPO winners, or they can take each other out as with the other ending and become “king of the winners”. It could be an even better tag than losing because they reached a goal. So satisfying if you ask me. Reasons I think many people would enjoy an ending similar to this outline: I love setting a goal and reaching it. I love smashing and venting frustration on the actual monsters (hence the smashing of those silly things in an after-party). I like the idea of a celebration tea, whether it be a teacup, cake, oil can, whatever the lore would suggest. And then the opportunity to all be winners because it’s truly teamwork that gets many people through this game, is fun to me; of course, if they would rather be king of the hill, that’s their prerogative. If they can manage to get through the ongoing credits without taking out their friends, then they really deserve that cute crown. Yep. Those are my two cents. Love the game, but I’d prefer reaching a point where I can log off for the night feeling like I accomplished something, rather than have a bit of irk that we “lost” again. Edit: I do love some of the new features to become King of the losers. P.S. Once at the winner island there could even be a red button called Hard Mode which uses a trap door to send players back to the truck with their [previously purchased] stuff, because people who reach the winner island are likely to be more confident and eager for another challenge.

review_text: I do like REPO, but there are so many frustrating things in this game that have ruined me enjoying this game as much as I'd want to enjoy it. There IS a good game here, but I don't see many people pointing out the MANY negative or frustrating aspects of this game, so I wanted to point some of these out and I hope the developers see this so the game can be the best that it can be. Firstly let me talk about maybe my biggest issue, the Huntsman AI. I don't know why many people think he is ok, but I've heard it's worse on the host's end and I host often so maybe that's why I have such an Issue with it and others don't. I have had MANY times where he shoots me either across an entire room where I could not hope to react and get one tapped, or he shoots me when ANOTHER sound source made him trigger and he shoots me anyway. I've had times where I tap a object on the ground to bait his shot, and instead of shooting the object far away from me he shoots me instead. This makes absolutely no sense and I personally think he should not work this way, he should always shoot the sound source not the nearest player like how he does at times. I suggest taking inspiration from the Eyeless Dogs from Lethal Company, just make him not instantly shoot at the first sound he hears and make him have an audio cue where players can be aware they are making too much noise like a sound of him grumbling or him going "huh", and if they continue he then shoots them. I also think his idle sounds should play more often and have more range so you can hear him before you get in his range so less unfair deaths where you didn't even know he was there at the edge of your vision occur. I think in general the monsters in this game are too quiet/don't have idle sounds that are good sound cues. Besides some exceptions like the Loom/Robe, them being quiet is part of their design. This is a little less important but, WHY DO SOME COSMETICS GIVE YOU ONE OUT OF A PAIR?! I genuinely don't understand why they did this, because I've had so many times where I get a cosmetic that looks like I'd use it... IF ONLY I GOT THE PAIR AND NOT ONE FOR A SINGLE SHOE/LEG. Some cosmetics do look cool asymmetrically, but (in my opinion) most don't and this just makes cosmetics grindy for the ones you want because the chances of getting the other one in the pair are low. I just don't see any positives to it being this way because if you wanted to just use one, you could just equip one out of the two if you got the cosmetic in a pair anyway. But I do like everything else about the cosmetic system they did a good job on how they work in every other way. I just really disagree with it working like this with pairs of cosmetics. Back to another big issue (again in my opinion). The physics system is WAY to janky in some areas, mostly with big items. Big items take damage for absolutely no reason very often. Sometimes you'll just touch it to check the value... BOOM -$2,377 for no reason. Sometimes you'll slide it across the ground gently... BOOM -$5,078 for no reason. Sometimes you rotate it slightly... BOOM -$3,980 for no reason. The big items really need to be less janky because a lot of the time they quickly become not worth it because it randomly took damage from sliding on a carpeted floor. When moving big items is a main game mechanic, it should be polished. Also I'm not sure whether to call this a physics issue or not but, you also should not be able to hit yourself with a melee weapon so easily. Many times I've needed a melee weapon quickly and hit myself while pulling it out, getting me killed. I also have an issue with the early levels having a tier 3 enemy like a Trudge or Head, which would not be an issue if the levels had more paths. What often happens (especially when I played solo with the Trudge) is the monster blocks and camps where you need to go and they waste your time, and because its early game (especially bad on the first level) you can't deal with these guys and just have to wait 4-8min just for them to leave. I think this is worse with the Trudge because he is so slow and takes forever to leave and it's difficult to run past him without getting one shot. In the later levels this is not as bad because you and the monsters have more paths to go, but in early game it really can be frustrating and slow down the game more than it should. I would just make the early levels have more pathways to counter this issue. Also because I'm talking about the Trudge, I think he should not be able to kill you through walls and suck you in through walls either. But this could be a bug and not an intentional gameplay mechanic. I've also been killed by the Cleanup Crew (UH OH guy) when I was enclosed in a safe through the wall from the head explosion. Another thing is the weapon spread from some ranged weapons (mostly the handgun and similar weapons). Some weapons have insane bullet spread (even after they buffed it). They already have limited ammo, why do I have to be in hugging distance to make sure I don't miss? It makes the weapons feel a tad underpowered. The stamina system early game is a pain to deal with as well, mostly the recovery rate. The amount of stamina you get early game is barely enough to survive and if you aren't in a good spot, don't have full stamina or don't hide perfectly; you just die to some enemies without a chance(head, duck, Robe etc.). You can upgrade both of these aspects, but in a game where you're playing with multiple people you don't get enough till very late because everyone needs it. I think they should AT LEAST make stamina recovery faster with no upgrades. But that's all. I do enjoy this game, but I don't see people talking about these issues, (even though some can be seen as nitpicks) some can kill the fun of the game (Huntsman). It's ok to criticize a game, it can still be good. It helps the game be the best it can be. For anyone who read this, thank you for reading my rant/critique. I hope the developers take this feedback because there is a really good game here held back by some frustration, and unfair AI, mechanics or bugs. Thank you for reading!

review_text: “Friendslop” is a term that has been becoming increasingly popular lately, and I feel like it diminishes something very valuable: a game that makes you laugh with your friends. A game like R.E.P.O. In R.E.P.O., we have to collect a series of objects, fit them into a small, limited-space cart, bring them back to the base, and sell them for enough money to advance to the next level. The more objects we put in the cart, the less space we have, and questions start to arise: Will this object fit? Could I make it work if I rearrange everything? Will I be able to move the cart without everything falling out? Now add the fact that every object has its own size, shape, durability, weight, and behavior. And, to add even more tension, there are monsters capable not only of killing us, but also of destroying what we are carrying in the cart. Each one has its own unique way of interacting with us and our environment. As we progress through the game and heavier objects start appearing, we are (almsot always) forced to work with someone else to carry them and figure out how to get them back to the base. It is similar to moving houses, where a couple of people have to figure out how to carry and fit some enormous piece of furniture through a tiny doorway. Except here, you cannot just sit down and think about it or stand still for too long, because you might get hit with a jumpscare that makes you drop the object, break it, or simply die. With all these variables, it is no surprise that R.E.P.O. has become the clip-generating machine that it was—and still is. But these moments are not simply the result of putting realistic physics into a game and waiting for something funny to happen. They are the result of good design. And even its premise fits into this. The “story” is basically about a greedy tax collector who sends us out to repossess things, while we carry out the job as the result of an “apparent debt.” It is about greed and ambition. And believe me: many times you will find yourself wondering whether what you are carrying in that cart is really worth it. Whether it is worth risking everything for one more valuable object, even when you already have enough to finish the level. (Spoiler: greed comes at a cost.) R.E.P.O. is not particularly visually creative, it does not have a deep or terrifying story, and it does not even have an ending. . And it does not need any of that to convey a feeling. All it needs is its own language: physics, order, and strategy in an arcade game, with money essentially functioning as the score. The language of video games.

review_text: I decided to check out R.E.P.O. because, well, everyone and their grandma was posting about it. You know how it goes: trending everywhere, gotta see what the fuss is about. And yeah, it’s got flashes of “this could be fun,” but also enough quirks to make you raise an eyebrow (or ten). What grabbed me first was how fast-paced and chaotic things get. There’s an energy to the matches that feels raw: weapons fire, grenades fly, and decisions are split-second. When things go right, you and your squad breaching a room, nails hitting the wall, hearts pounding, enemies dropping, there’s a real sense of "we did it, lads." It’s the kind of rush that makes you remember why shooters can be so addictive. But here’s where R.E.P.O. stumbles: sometimes the chaos is too chaotic. Guns feel inconsistent; a spray-and-pray might work once and flop the next time. Match balance can swing wildly, one moment you’re dominating, the next you’re getting fragged by someone who moves like they’ve got a jetpack. The learning curve and randomness make it tough to feel like skill is always rewarded. On top of that, a few bugs and lag spikes popped up during my sessions, nothing catastrophic, but enough to remind me that this game is still a bit rough around the edges. All jokes aside, R.E.P.O. is a “love-it-or-leave-it” type game. For a casual go-at-it-with-friends shoot-em-up, it’s got some fun in it. Just don’t go in expecting the most polished shooter out there, treat it more like a wobbly roller-coaster: exciting, unpredictable, and maybe a little nauseating after a while. If you’ve got time to spare and tolerance for mayhem, give it a shot. But if you're picky about balance and consistency, maybe hold the trigger finger.

review_text: If you're looking for a co-op horror game that delivers pure chaos, tension, and nonstop laughter, then R.E.P.O. is an absolute must-play. This game perfectly balances horror and comedy in a way that feels fresh and incredibly addictive. Every session turns into an unforgettable experience where teamwork, panic, and stupidity collide in the best possible way. The physics-based gameplay is what truly makes the game shine. Carrying valuable objects carefully while terrifying monsters hunt your team creates constant tension, but somehow the funniest moments happen when everything goes horribly wrong. One second you're silently coordinating with friends, and the next someone accidentally destroys the loot, slams a door into another teammate, or screams while running for their life. It never gets old. The atmosphere is also surprisingly immersive. Dark environments, unsettling sound design, and unpredictable enemy encounters keep you constantly on edge. Even after several matches, the game still manages to create genuine fear and adrenaline. At the same time, the proximity voice chat makes every moment feel natural and hilarious, especially during panic situations. What makes R.E.P.O stand out from many other co-op horror games is how replayable it feels. No match ever plays out the same way, and the randomness of player behavior creates endless entertainment. Whether you’re playing seriously or just messing around with friends, the game is ridiculously fun. Overall, R.E.P.O is one of the best multiplayer horror experiences in recent years. Funny, stressful, chaotic, and incredibly memorable. If you enjoy co-op games with friends, this is easily worth your time. This is a perfect mix of horror, teamwork, and comedy chaos.

review_text: REPO has been some of the most fun I’ve had in co-op gaming in a long time. My friends and I dumped endless hours into it, along with several years off our lives from stress, laughter, and complete nonsense. Most of the tears were from laughing so hard we could barely function. The rest were from those moments where everything goes catastrophically wrong, the run implodes, and you are kicked all the way back to the beginning, which is the exact point where you start considering whether gaming is really your hobby or if maybe it’s time to take up knitting. That is the magic of REPO. It is absolute chaos. Beautiful, stupid, panic-filled chaos. One second your group is locked in, focused, and working like a machine. The next second one bad move turns into a full collapse, everybody is screaming, someone is dead, someone else is blaming the wrong person, and somehow it is the funniest thing you have ever seen. Even in a small group, this game was incredible. But once we added a few mods, it really became dangerous. Health boost, store expansion, buff sharing, all great. But the true gift from the heavens was the LEVEL SAVE. That mod deserves a shrine. Once we could save progress on a level instead of getting launched back to level 1 every time the game decided to beat us with a chair, that is when the real fun began. Suddenly the suffering had structure. The pain had purpose. And that is the thing, REPO somehow turns failure into bonding. Through the jump scares, the laughter, the yelling, the tears, and the absolute nonsense, I genuinely bonded with people through this game. Few games can say that. It is frustrating in the exact right ways, hilarious in ways you cannot plan for, and unforgettable with the right group. Hats off to the devs. REPO is chaos, comedy, suffering, friendship, and questionable decision-making wrapped into one beautiful package. Easy 5/5.

review_text: There's a good core game here, but unfortunately it's not built for solo gamers at all. It very much requires you to have a multiplayer group. Which if you don't have any gaming friends and you don't like randoms, means you're out of luck. The fact that the game deletes your saves when you die is also a horrible mechanic intended to create false difficulty. The monsters are not balanced for single player, the maps at a certain stage become almost unplayable due to the amount of random death pits that spawn alongside the monsters, and even if you somehow clear a map, the game will typically spawn or teleport every monster in the map to the extraction point and then they just sit there and spawn camp it, making it impossible to win. It's a shame because when the game is working well, the collection mechanic is really fun and addicting. There's just unfortunately all the other bad stuff that is built around it. Fans of this game will defend it by saying 'well its early access', but...Game has been out for a long time and the developer isn't adding anything actually needed by the game, just for fun, silly stuff. Most of the stuff the game needs are done by player mods, which is not acceptable. Overall, really fun core mechanics and gameplay that is addicting, but there's just too much other unfair stuff built into the game to make it a must have. Especially for solo gamers.

review_text: Welcome to Repo, the only game where beating a child with a bat is not only morally acceptable but also financially profitable. There's no plot, and no desire to find one. Instead, there's chaos, monsters, strange companions, and a complete lack of the concept of "normal." In short, it's another drug addict simulator, like in Lethal Company—you're ripping out everything, both bolted and unbolted, from the house for a fix. The atmosphere is like a crazy old man's house everything breaks, everyone's screaming, constant self-talk, someone's forgotten how to play again, the feeling that the map has a life of its own, and no one controls what's happening, and it all ends with you dragging all your companions because, well, someone has to. Here, every other moment feels like a scene from a dream with a temperature of 39°C you roll under a table while your partners are killing gnomes with screaming soundpads, and the guy with a gun in the corner is taking out everyone with a Nouscope 180, including you, because he's ♥♥♥ awesome. The truth of life is this: a crowd can take out even a blind guy with a gun. A separate art form—your partner's face after an encounter with some evil spirit—is truly the most devastating (literally) thing you'll see while sitting in silence at the blind guy's feet. You can also destroy a store with just a rubber ducky, or buy a bat and the monsters will run away screaming. With each new level, your moral compass decreases. The less shame you feel, the better your experience will be. And despite all this chaos, you feel like you're actually doing something useful. Even if you're just carrying your fallen partner's head through this madhouse, even if you've been lying under the table the entire game, that counts as a contribution here. And remember: don't trust the cute ducks and stay away from the crazy Wolverine woman on the minimum settings with your cart. Even if you die, it's no big deal. They'll find you, report you, resurrect you, and throw you back into hell. The game is great—four ducks and a head raped me. Special thanks to the developers for the ability to flush your partner down the toilet. 10 flushed partners out of 10.

review_text: This is the kind of game that starts with “okay, just one quick run” and somehow turns into hours of screaming, laughing, and blaming your friends for everything that goes wrong. The premise is simple: grab valuable stuff and get out. But the monsters make even the easiest task spiral into absolute chaos. One wrong move and suddenly all your friends are dead, you are panicking, and a baby is throwing your loot into a pit. What really makes this game shine is how naturally funny it is. The physics, the timing, and all the little disasters don’t feel forced at all, it’s just pure comedy gold. You don’t even need to be good at the game to have fun; honestly, being bad makes it better. Every failed run turns into a story you’ll be laughing about later. The proximity chat adds so much to the experience too. Some of the funniest moments I’ve had in co-op games came from yelling half-coherent words to my friends while running for my life. It’s not overly scary, but it definitely has its moments where you jump, panic, and immediately regret your life choices. This is an absolute must-have for any friend group. You’ll spend half the time screaming and the other half tripping over furniture, flinging priceless items, and accusing your friends of sabotage. Pure chaos, pure fun.

review_text: Had high expectations, and this game still exceeded them. review_text: Downloaded this with high hopes after a masterpiece like Hollow Knight. At first, I was thrilled to rediscover that familiar hand-crafted atmosphere. The map, dialogues, and atmosphere lived up to the first game. But then the boss fights started. Finding that satisfying character progression and power curve from Hollow Knight is quite difficult in Silksong. After a point, I started playing just so it would end and I could uninstall it. Unnecessarily over-difficult bosses and the constant spawning of secondary minions turn the boss fights away from the sweet, familiar challenge we knew. Instead, they transform into a Dark Souls 3-style finger-exercise that tests your stress levels and drains the joy out of playing. After a while, you realize that the charm system from the old game is very weak here. No matter how brilliantly you explore, strengthening your character requires a much more detailed and grueling exploration, and it doesn't unfold naturally alongside the story like it did in the first game. (And I'm a player who combs through every inch of the map.) I’ve already put over 30 hours into the game and I have no idea how much is left, but this is the first time I’m struggling this hard not to uninstall a game before finishing it.

review_text: Hollow Knight is a masterpiece, Silksong is just miserable. It's not the difficulty, it's the tone. Everything is more grotesque, baroque and overwrought than the last game, from art to story, NPCs and biomes have all had a significant charisma downgrade, to the point where I no longer care about exploring, because every area is just another boring slog with little sense of wonder or mystery. HK had a big infusion of the Studio Ghibli magic, and that's almost all gone in this sequel. I have never put so much time into a game I enjoyed so little. What's left is a masochistic slog, with a downgraded gamefeel in the character to increase the difficulty of combat. While Hornet is technically more mobile, the jump and basic attack have been mildly nerfed which means more precise timing and movement are required for all things. The game is harder and just feels noticeably worse than HK for the minute to minute gameplay, like a shoe that just slightly doesn't fit. Is the justification for this significantly more interesting challengers? Not really. While the behavior of the enemies has been made far more complex, which seems better at first, it's still not really interesting most of the time. The largest issue is that the more complex attach options for the enemies often results in awkward pairings of enemies. Two enemies attacking at the same time and being able to pass through each other with semi complicated attack options often leads to situations where avoiding one attack simply means you will almost definitely take contact damage from the other (the damage type that makes you feel stupid). There's no way to strategically deal with both at the same time, so most often you just try to aggro one away and deal with them individually, reducing the complexity of every fight as much as your can, but even with the multiple attacks many enemies now have, few are particularly interesting one on one. Hollow Knights comparably simple enemies were often full easy 1 on 1, but could create interesting dynamics when paired together or with environmental challenges. Speaking of environmental challenges, the main one in every biome is that you are on the ground and most of the enemies can fly. They all hover just barely in reach of a single swing at the height of your jump, and some will dodge away when possible. Will a single swing kill them or change their behavior? No, they'll be a slog, you'll need to jump and hit them multiple times, constantly, in almost every biome, throughout the entire game. And remember, jumping and attacking feel fundamentally less satisfying than in HK, and the risk of contact damage and feeling stupid are way higher. It just makes you wish you had a gun to shoot them out of the air, and when I got a tool that basically let's you delete more basic flyers, I realized how little I enjoyed engaging with any of them, and they are all over every biome, cluttering up boss runbacks, just being a pebble in a shoe that doesn't quite fit for almost every step you'll take. And their placement is consistently in places that mean you have to stop to deal with them, no matter how boring and difficult it is. Difficult because it will always require some level of coordination, but boring because it's the exact same behavior and strategy for almost all of the flying enemies. Hard and boring is a rough sell for something I'm choosing to do with my free time. Some enemy placements feel like the are suggestive of an almost "Lisa" like contempt for the player. People have made a lot of the difficulty and stingy economy, and while those are issues, the bigger issue to me is still the tone. Pharloom and the Citadel are both just miserable places that I don't enjoy traversing, in pursuit of a story I don't care about. I kept pushing forward hoping for bit of the Hollow Knight magic to start to sparkle again, but at 60 hours with enemies I hate dealing with, uninspiring NPCs and environments, and all of that on top of an incredibly punishing difficulty, I just don't care enough to push any further. While it's an insane amount of content for 20 bucks, and a ton of hard work and care have clearly gone into it, I can only say that I just didn't really enjoy almost any of my time with this game.

review_text: Fantastic combat, atmosphere, graphics, environmental story telling, MUSIC (the music is insane). This game is a beast. The boss fights are amazing, and each level having its own theme, enemies, collectables and shortcuts to connect the entire thing together is very satisfying and fun to explore. However, It is very difficult. I feel like it's too difficult, especially for most people. Bosses and most enemies dealing two shields of damage is frustrating, especially since this is also the case for contact damage. The game economy seemingly doesn't have enough rosaries , which means if you want to buy all the cool things in the shop on one save you are going to have to farm, a lot. There are also some runbacks which need not exist and simply drag out the experience which makes me just want to end the fight as fast as possible instead of enjoy the experience. A lot of the quests are ambiguous, with no hints or clear guidance on where to go. Means you are going to have to Google stuff, a lot, unless you want to aim around mindlessly. Unless you are a god who can memorise every location they've gone to in the past and realise where the NPCs are talking about. I feel like the game could do with some tweaks and it would become even better than it is. I would like to see an easier mode difficulty settings so my noob friends can actually play it because in its current state I can barely recommend it to anyone because of how sadistic it is lol. And some more benches (bile water please). Anyways just some random thoughts. Will be back for the DLC

review_text: Harsh, but not fair Hollow Knight was harsh but fair. Silksong is harsh and nothing else, and that difference is the whole of my complaint. I knew what I was buying. Nobody picks up a Team Cherry Metroidvania expecting a gentle stroll. I accept the beating. What I don't accept is a beating handed out by a referee who has quietly left the building. I'm about halfway through and going for 100%, so treat this as a report from the trenches, not the summit. The arithmetic of suffering Ordinary enemies hit for two masks. Not bosses, not armored brutes, but things that look like mice. Meanwhile early mice, frogs and birds take around four needle hits each, which is what genuinely dangerous enemies took in Hollow Knight. The needle upgrade arrives deep into Act One, so your damage stays stunted for hours. You hit like a wet noodle, and the noodle is fighting rodents in plate armor. A hoarder's economy of silk Bind heals three masks, even midair. But when everything hits for two, you're never actually back on your feet. So you hoard silk, and the counter, needle throw and the rest of Hornet's kit sit unused. A toolkit you're afraid to use is a display case. Some stretches practically require you to cheese enemies for silk, stepping in and out of a room until the meter is full. I never once had to farm soul in Hollow Knight. Benches, runbacks and trap benches In Hollow Knight, a bench ahead meant trouble was coming, and the Dreamgate covered the few brutal runbacks. Silksong has neither mercy. Benches sit far from where you die. In Sinner's Road there's a bench you have to repair by crossing a deadly gauntlet, and if you die the nearest bench is back in Greymoor. Twice I found trap benches that kill you for sitting down. Hollow Knight never pulled anything like that. A bench there was a promise of safety. Here it's a punchline. The bosses are fine. Getting to them is not. The bosses are hard, about regular-Grimm hard across the board, but none I've faced has been unfair. What ruins them is the runback: a platforming section you have to clear without taking a hit, because one lost mask can decide the fight. Then a five-to-six-minute boss fight, death, and the walk again. That's not a challenge. It's a humiliation ritual. And no, runbacks don't need to "train" me. The rest of the game can do that. Poverty as a design pillar Everything costs rosaries and you're always broke. In Hollow Knight, being broke was your own fault. In Silksong it's a toll booth on every road. Sadism, itemized Platforming that wants near frame-perfect play. Enemies parked in your jump path so you have to eat the hit. Mount Fay's falling pillars, which you have to touch to make solid ground, with zero hint from the game. And Bilewater, which earns every bit of its reputation. I'm a player who never uses exploits or god mode, and I've had to look up guides and YouTube videos to get through sections of this game. Pain without payoff Yes, Hollow Knight had the Path of Pain and the 15,000 Geo Unbreakable Strength. But that suffering was rare, optional, and paid off with a cutscene and arguably the best charm in the game. Silksong is full of mini Paths of Pain that reward you with a flea, a rosary, or some craft metal. Hollow Knight charged a lot for something great. Silksong charges a lot for pocket change. A confession, without honor When I sense death coming, I now pause, quit and reload so I wake up at a bench instead of chasing my cocoon over lava or spikes. I'm not proud of it. Worse, plenty of YouTube guides from regular players tell you to save-quit at the end of long sections just to skip the walk back. In Hollow Knight, the end of a long trek gave you a shortcut. When the community's best practice is stepping outside the game to skip the game, something is wrong. To the "get good" crowd Hornet being "tactical" doesn't explain why a frog needs four stabs, and "it's a different world" doesn't explain an economy built to keep you broke. Those are excuses for tuning. "Get good" isn't a rebuttal, it's declining to have the argument. Credit where it's due Silksong is gorgeous, the soundtrack is incredible, the bosses are memorable, the story is good, the world feels more alive than Hallownest, and it's genuinely funny. Those things, plus my own stubbornness, are why I'm still playing. The machinery underneath is the problem. Verdict Difficulty is a contract: the game gets to be hard, and you get a fair shot at winning. Hollow Knight honored it. Silksong keeps the first half. Hollow Knight was a hike up a mountain. Hard, beautiful, and people say "I might try that someday" when you tell them. Silksong is walking barefoot on hot coals with no camera rolling, and people just ask why you'd do that. Hollow Knight I finished out of love. Silksong I'm finishing out of spite.

review_text: two days ago, i beat silksong 100% on steel soul mode, giving me the steel heart achievement. i feel obligated to write a review just because of how much this game has changed my life. tl;dr + spoiler free part: this game is stunning. if you like exploring, always finding new things you never would have thought you've learned regardless of how many times you replay the game, if you have time on your hands and don't mind spending it on mastering a beautiful system of combat that makes you feel like you're dancing with your opponents, this game is absolutely for you. i do have to warn you, this game is not for people who don't have free time on your hands. this game does not respect your time. if you live a busy schedule and just want to play games for the fun of it, silksong is not that. it is an all-consuming beast that will rot your mind with rage and anger and will likely ragebait you into giving up (similar to rain world, in which i come from.) a perk is that this exposure therapy will make you immune to future ragebait, though! if you are a busy person and you plan on toughing out silksong regardless, please be patient. there's so much to this game and you will die a lot but it's all so incredibly beautiful. i would highly recommend it to anyone who has the time, patience and curiousity to explore and save a dying kingdom. upcoming marked spoilers for ALL of silksong + yap incoming! when i first got the game back in last year, november, i started out without much combat and platforming experience. yes, i played silksong before i even touched hollow knight (skipped the supposed tutorial for this game, i know). i come from rain world, which is quoted by many to be another similarly difficult game, but in terms of skill i wasn't that good! sure i spent a lot of time playing the game but i had a lot of mods installed that made the game way easier for me. and trust me! silksong is difficult. it was immensely difficult for me. each boss would take on average 2-3 hours for me to beat. platforming sections would always take me so long to figure out. this game has brought me to tears, so many times. i remember crying because of how genuinely difficult the (act 2 spoilers from now on) clawline gauntlet was to complete. there were tears in my eyes when i fell to the lava again just because i forgot i had to wait for the silk heart to regenerate. i cried at the end of the high halls gauntlet , both because my suffering and torment were finally over, and also it broke my heart to hear the conductor sing that raspy, broken melody whilst on his deathbed. however feeling the joy of seeing the summit of mount fay after a 4 hour climb, the satisfaction of being able to aura farm with a push of a button (cross stitch my beloved) , and dancing with the silly butterfly trobbio ... this game has also made me feel so much, especially the feeling of accomplishment. growing up i could never really have the determination to 'git gud' with video games. but now after more than 500 hours of silksong i understand. in my first playthrough, i was stuck on (act 3 spoilers from now on) skarrsinger karmelita for days. it genuinely came to a point where i thought it was impossible to beat her, or the abyss climb , or the dreaded final fight of the game... but i toughed it out. i beat karmelita , i did the abyss climb , and i beat lost lace despite being five hits away from death at any given time and unable to heal. (i used the shaman crest glass cannon build, because i genuinely wanted to learn the fight without cheesing, and actually beat the game.) so many of the achievements were so nerve-racking - i literally gave up on the speedrunner and twisted child achievement beacause they were too hard to do, only to convince myself to have another shot at them once i was more experienced, and i went ahead and got them! steel soul was a run where i felt i was riddled with anxiety at every turn. i even had to use a guide run to help me practice the parts of the game that I was the most unfamiliar with. but surprisingly, trusting my gut and just dancing with these bosses carried me such a long way. if there's one thing this game has taught me, it's that achievement is possible regardless of how much prior experience you have, and that the route to mastery is tedious and filled with tears and pain. but it works. eventually, as long as you keep coming back for the love of the game, find a breakable wall that you didn't know existed until your 7th playthrough, and find a hidden room you didn't know until your steel heart run, you will just keep getting better and better at the game. you will git gud, just by coming back and refusing to give up. thank you so much, hornet for being with me at every step of the way, all the angry garamas and all the double damage you've taken with me throughout my silksong journey. i'll see you again in sea of sorrow and future dlcs. :) and if you've read this review to the very end, thank you! please consider buying this game if you haven't already. :D

review_text: Hollow Knight: Silksong | Complete Game Review (100% In-Game Completion at 60.7 Hours) I thought Hollow Knight: Silksong would make me feel like a nimble warrior but in reality, I’m just a very determined pinball. Gameplay: Compared to Hollow Knight , Silksong is faster, sharper, and more aggressive, pushing you to stay on the offensive. Hornet’s mobility opens up combat and traversal in a way that feels incredible once mastered, but the game leaves little room for error. Early on, the game can feel difficult and punishing but once it finally clicks, the gameplay becomes one of the most fluid and satisfying systems in the metroidvania space. ★★★ Graphics: Hand-drawn and absolutely dripping with personality. The new world of Pharloom trades the decaying loneliness of Hallownest for something more vibrant yet no less haunting. Every area feels distinct, detailed, and alive in its own strange way. I kept pausing just to take it all in... right before the game reminded me that standing still is a terrible survival strategy. ★★★ Sound: The soundtrack matches the pacing perfectly and adds real weight to both movement and combat. Not every track stuck with me the way the music from Hollow Knight did, but Silksong still nails the atmosphere where it counts (pun intended). ★★★☆ Story: Just like its predecessor, the narrative is fragmented and intentionally vague. You’re given various goals throughout but the ‘why’ is buried in subtle clues and environmental storytelling. It’s intriguing if you enjoy piecing things together, but if you want a clear, direct narrative, this won’t give it to you. ★★★☆☆ Replayability: A variety of builds, tools, and hidden paths provide some incentive to return. However, unlike its predecessor, the absence of pathway split-route achievements reduces the drive for meaningfully varied re-runs. Beyond optional challenge playthroughs involving steel soul mode and speed running, its long-term pull feels more limited. ★★☆☆☆ Final Thoughts: The game refines what made the original great while demanding more from the player in return. Silksong is faster, tougher, and—in the wise words of Hornet—expects the player to ‘git gud’. Nevertheless, it also feels incredibly rewarding once you start to master the movement and combat mechanics. Overall Rating: 8/10, gorgeous, unforgiving, and definitely worth the inevitable suffering.

review_text: This game is Art - and like all Art, it's not for everybody. Team Cherry has created an uncompromising masterpiece aimed at players who've delved deep into Hollow Knight and enjoyed mastering its combat. These players will likely adore Silksong; the skill ceiling and combat depth are way higher now, both regarding Hornet's moveset and enemy difficulty and complexity. Hornet handles like a dream and requires a higher degree of mastery to keep up with all but the most basic of enemies. This is great for players like me who enjoy the process of "gitting gud" but brings us to why some players won't enjoy the game, quality be damned. Silksong is hard. Not just that, but punishing as well. This is very deliberate, and feels incredibly rewarding once you overcome what the game throws at you, but it comes at the cost of accessibility. If you play games to chill out and relax, chances are that the frustration factor may be too high for your tastes. Even if you liked Hollow Knight, if what kept you playing was mainly the exploration and atmosphere, and you preferred a more shallow involvement with combat, snubbing the Colosseum and Godhome, Silksong may end up being "too much". A tragedy, given Silksong's excellent worldbuilding and ludonarrative harmony (translation: you'll get to intimately feel the pain of what it means to be an inhabitant of Pharloom). If you are new to Hollow Knight and Silksong and want to give them a go, I would recommend playing Hollow Knight first. Silksong was designed to give veteran Hollow Knight players the "first time spankings" experience all over again, with all that entails.

review_text: Silksong is like a dream that you never want to wake up from. It's easily the best indie game I've ever played. It's one of those rare experiences that makes you sad when it ends because you know you'll never be able to experience it for the first time again. I truly believe Silksong deserved to be Game of the Year 2025. Many people ignored it saying it's just another Hollow Knight,but for me it's so much more than that. It's the ultimate GOTY. I've also played expedition 33, which is fantastic in its own right, but it didn't come close to the impact Silksong had on me. The credits soundtrack was absolutely beautiful. It genuinely made me cry as I reflected on my journey from the very beginning to the end. Few games have ever connected with me on that level. Silksong is a masterpiece and a perfect 10/10. It's a game that every gamer deserves to experience at least once in their life. Now all I can do is eagerly wait for the dlc and hope it isn't too far away.

review_text: Even when the road appears to climb toward the peak, its true destination lies buried deep within the mountain’s darkness After I got the platinum in Hollow Knight, I was waiting for the sequel. And I’m going to say it straight: it was 10/10 experience . Not because I’m trying to be dramatic, but because this game didn’t just meet my expectations – it blew past em and gave me one of the strongest gaming experiences I’ve had . Tbh my first time with the game wasn’t what I expected at all. I finished Silksong and thought like "yea, kinda ok," but it didn’t hit me the way HK did. I was honestly a bit disappointed. Then, while watching some random Silksong video, I learned one key thing: what I considered as completin the game was basically only about 50% of what the game actually offers – and not even close to the ending Team Cherry clearly treats as the main one. That instantly hooked me. I got curious and motivated, and decided to beat it properly: go for 100% and grab the platinum (I’m still finishing it up, but I’ve only got a couple achievements left near the end). And after that second, let's say "real" run, everything clicked. After completing Act 3, this game became not only my favorite in its genre, but one of my favorite games overall. And i put a ridiculous amount of effort into it. Clearing all three acts on Steel Soul was brutally hard af, and I genuinely went through the full range of emotions while doing it. It’s also the first game that made me plug in a controller just to finish Act 3, because the final missions were simply unreal (at least for me, prob skill issue) on keyboard. And still – that’s exactly why it stuck with me. It ended up being one of the best experiences I’ve ever gotten from a game . I expected a lot, seriously. But I didn’t expect my expectations to be exceeded this hard . And the cool part is that at first I was disappointed, and after the second playthrough I only regretted not doing it in the right way earlier. One of the biggest wins by TC for me is how the game feels more dynamic while also being bigger . Combat, playthrough, even just exploring the world – everything feels faster, more alive, and as a result more exciting . At the release, the difficulty felt like it was intentionally over-the-top(which was frustraitihg as hell tbf), but it got nerfed pretty quickly, and now the game is in a near perfect state . Yes, it’s harder than Hollow Knight – and for me that’s not a downside. That’s one of its main advantages . And then there’s the thing that really surprised me: the world and exploration . If the first game was built almost from nothing, the sequel takes the best parts and turns them into something far stronger . Yeah, it’s subjective, but while Hollow Knight is comforting and pleasant in my memory, the locations and the whole of Pharloom didn’t just impress me – they absolutely floored me. The world design feels unmatched, and the best part is that even near the end of Act 2 I kept finding something new: new areas, new characters, new events, new experiences. During 3d Act I went through Craw Lake purely out of curiosity and discovered a whole new location with its own story and interesting things happening there. And moments like that happen a lot . The game actively encourages you to explore – and it’s worth it , because exploration here (mainly) isn’t for the checklist. It actually rewards player's curiosity . On top of that world sits a constantly gripping atmosphere . The bar is just as high as in the first game, and it syncs perfectly with everything that’s happening – it boosts tension, highlights key moments, and makes the journey feel more real . Huge respect to Team Cherry for that – and especially to Christopher Larkin for another incredible and atmospheric soundtrack. Another improvement I loved is the way the story is presented . Hollow Knight feels very Dark Souls-like: you walk in silence, explore, collect lore piece by piece, and do all the work yourself. Silksong tells its story in a different way – more like a typical story-driven game – and because of that, Hornet feels more alive, so does the world. For me, that’s a big plus: it’s not just lore in the background, it’s a more direct connection to what’s going on and you actually understand it . There are cons, but to me they aren’t very noticeable: except for one thing . Some side quests/wishes can feel very repetitive : find-kill-bring,find-bring, take-deliver, and so on. It’s not something that ruins the game, but at times it does feel like routine. That said, it’s easily outweighed by how many strong moments and advantages the game throws at you along the way till the very end. So yeah. I expected a lot – but I got more than I was ready for. Silksong is the kind of game that might not hit the way you want on a first run, but if you actually dig into it, push through the acts, commit to exploration, and really finish what the game has to offer – it pays you back with such a level of emotion and reward that you just sit there thinking: Alright. This was something special.

review_text: It's very rare for me to write a review, but for Silksong I feel compelled to. To start, the art is stunning. There are some truly beautiful areas in this game with small attentions to detail that make the world feel more alive. Like the small ants carrying away the bodies of defeated foes. The same, if not better, little particle effects with the grass and bugs in each area. Not to mention the flying bugs that go past after you climb out the starting areas. The characters are made with such love; not just visually, but their animations, voice acting and overall design make each character so endearing. You'll fall in love with them, even your fast travel bug has one of the most impactful scenes in the game. From playing dice with a lonely bug in a cave, to battling the beasts of Pharloom side by side with a trusted NPC friend you're going to feel at home in these hostile lands. Not to mention an item you get later that allows you to hear all of the bugs singing. Some of the bugs even sing terribly which is somehow more charming. The music is breath taking. So many tracks have been so carefully and thouroughly crafted to represent each area. Sometimes you'll wonder (in two specific areas) why the music is so sad, and the more you find out about them, the more you'll realize exactly why it sounds like that. The final final boss (two finals on purpose) has one of the most amazing tracks in the game. I get chills just hearing some of the tracks, let alone that final theme invoking such strong emotions. Speaking of emotions, the story and lore (which I won't go into for spoiler reasons) is so wonderfully portrayed. With some moments that made my cry outright and moments of peak joy and wonder when you piece it all together. The traversal in Pharloom vastly outmatches anything in any other metroidvania style game I've played, there's always somewhere else to go if you're struggling. There are hidden paths to get to your objectives that are so mindblowingly considered for, it makes the kingdom of Pharloom feel like a living, breathing place. The platforming is brutally difficult on a first playthrough especially but so rewarding. The bosses are mindblowing, very often I'd say to myself, "There's no way they can top this boss." Only for the next boss to somehow be even more amazing. You'll never tire of the spectacle. With all this glaze, it's time to talk about difficulty. I'm on the fence here. On the one hand, I personally do not mind the difficulty but I also understand that some people want to just chill on their couch and unwind after a stressful work day and not want to bash their head against a wall. So if you're not ready for what feels like the fight of your life at times, with some truly brutal run backs and such. Then I'd say it's probably not the game for you. However this is a game that challenges you but also, there's always somewhere else to go that will make what you're struggling with. A new tool or weapon upgrade, sometimes a utility tool that makes the situation easier. When it comes to the difficulty: Team Cherry was very particular in how they crafted the encounters, I wouldn't want the game to play any other way. Each enemy, boss and obstacle is teaching you how to play better. It'd be like if I tried to play guitar and got frustrated it still sounded bad after a few weeks. Skill at a new game takes time. It won't be for everyone but I think it's worth it. I do think the game would benefit from having accessibility features like Celeste, where they're actively discouraged but do exist for those to just see where the game goes. But that may ruin the intent behind the design so maybe the "art" is more important here. All this being said, the game is a steal at the price tag. I hope you enjoy your journey in Pharloom everyone!
