review_text: Silksong does what Hollow Knight did well way better, and some things it did badly worse. Positives: • Fantastic art design on just about everything, far more varied than Hollow Knight and full of little details. • Very satisfying and varied platforming. While there isn't a full on White Palace/ Path of Pain section, similarly challenging platforming bursts are weaved throughout the game. • The crests, Silk skills and tools offer great gameplay variety. • Very well designed world packed with NPCs. • Enjoyable questing system although it does accentuate the backtracking and back & forth aspects which I don't like very much but it is nowhere near as bad as Hollow Knight. • Intuitive world design. In Hollow Knight, if you are playing without a guide, it is incredibly easy to get lost for hours on end, trying to find the next upgrade. So much needless backtracking and padding because of that. Not a problem in Silksong. Mixed: • The soundtrack is great BUT tracks are on average shorter than Hollow Knight's. Not sure why the composer chose to go with that direction but I'm hoping it'll change for the updates/ DLC. Negatives: • Near every negative in Silksong can be chalked up to what I call excessive TCT - Team Cherry TrollingTM. It is there on every step of the way whereas in HK such moments would be a little less frequent: - Traps/ even more enemies after already arduous platforming or fighting sections, you don't get a single break really. - Bosses that have arenas with debilitating effects (like Maggots, preventing healing), no platforms to stand on at all, add spam DURING boss fights and whole Colosseum-like gauntlets before you can even fight the actual bosses. Other bosses that'd be finely designed, have some extreme visual clutter (Trobbio) or otherwise poorly visible attacks (Lost Lace). - Extremely and I mean incessantly annoying flying enemy design, I do not understand what they were thinking when they made enemies that fly away from you constantly, input read your jumps and movement direction for their projectiles and freak around like they are on meth. - Cumbersome design = difficulty, apparently. The lack of QoL is very real. I do not understand why Team Cherry still think not displaying your position on the map or withholding the ability to autocollect resources that drop from enemies, basic game features present in like every other game, should be locked behind equipables? Why don't maps update in real time as well? Just unnecessary padding. • A negative that isn't specific to Team Cherry as it is present in other 2D games as well, it is however handled horribly in both Hollow Knight games: contact damage. In most other games that have CD, you have to misplay really badly and find yourself inside the enemy to be damaged. Or it could be the version of contact damage I actually like, where it is only active around whatever enemies/ bosses use as a weapon. In Hollow Knight and Silksong on the other hand, touching any single pixel of any enemy or boss at any time will immediately hurt you, sometimes even for 2 Masks worth of damage. You do not pair a system like that with enemies that move erratically and love to jump/ teleport on you, it cheapened the difficulty in HK, Silksong is no different in that regard. All in all Silksong is an amazing game that is well worth your time when the experience isn't being dragged down by Team Cherry's juvenile trolling attempts, that I honestly thought they'd grow out of considering they were working on Silksong for near a decade, but nope, if anything they got worse with it. I've been playing Fromsoft games since Demon's Souls and have played pretty much every Soulslike there is out there as well so I have quite a bit of patience when it comes to petty trolling, only the most egregious instances get a reaction out of me but I can imagine how infuriating it would be for others that aren't used to stuff like this, so I absolutely understand the negative reviews and those that ended up dropping the game because such sections/ moments do make Silksong feel like a chore to play, especially throughout Act 3. However if you have the patience to overcome the nonsense, I can't recommend the game enough. Or just mod it out! 🔳 Broken 🔳 Shovelware 🔳 Awful 🔳 Bad 🔳 Mid 🔳 Okay 🔳 Good 🔳 Great ☑️ Excellent

review_text: The real GOTY Modern games' sequels are usually bad news, as they are more often than not just a cheap cashgrab that butchers the original, but Silksong is the exact opposite, improving upon it's predecessor in almost every way. You can clearly tell this game was made with a purpose different than just making money. Same with Hollow Knight, it's already very clear what makes this game so good, so i'll keep it short. Probably the only complaint i've heard people say is that the combat is too punishing and difficult, which is totally not true, the difficulty is just right. Sure, some enemies and bosses may seem to be the way they are just to give you a hard time, but when you push through, it is incredibly rewarding. Instead of soul spells like in the previous game, you get to adjust your strategy using crests, tools and skills, allowing you to try out many different combos and finding your optimal playstyle. Though i must say, not all of the options are very good or fun to use, especially the tools. Exploration has massively improved, thanks to Hornet's (the playable character) many abilities. All of the locations are unique and beautiful (except the mist, f*ck that place), and always have a lot of hidden paths for you to uncover. As for the story and characters, both of these factors have also been improved, with many charming side characters, which was lacking in HK, but that's subjective. Despite the huge success HK had, the devs were still very generous and set the price for this masterpiece to mere 20€, which is an absolute steal, considering the amount of quality content you get here. Silksong deserved to win GOTY, Expedition 33 doesn't even come close to this absolute gem of a game. Overall, a 9.5/10, definitely try it if you loved HK and have atleast a small amount of patience.

review_text: "This is like when the smug kid (you actually want to hate) is indeed the best in class". I never jived with Team Cherry's silent treatment during Silksong's development, to the point I didn't even buy the game for a good while, but now that I've played it... man, this is a total masterpiece, it surpasses the original Hollow Knight (and that was the best metroidvania ever at the time) and it is maybe matched only by Nine Sols in recent years. Silksong is a crazily big, dense and rich game, and it's also polished to near perfection. Everyone's favourite bug in red, Hornet, is captured by strange bugs and finds herself in the kingdom of Pharloom, drawn to the citadel high above the land to understand who wanted to kidnap her and why. It's a setup with just the right intrigue to give you a clear objective throughout, but also vague enough that you're free to just go nuts. Much like HK, the storytelling in Silksong is actually super interesting. You're basically witnessing the death throes (maybe) of another kingdom, but you learn more about its history and its structure by multiple sources: dialogues (many NPCs this time around), bestiary entries, collectibles, and just the environments themselves, which actually could be playing the biggest part. The story you get out of it is tragic, dark, incredibly captivating and not too esoteric to understand. The sense of history the game world has is unparalleled in the genre, better than the first HK (and it was one of its selling points even back then IMO); the same is true for the world design and its impeccable sense of geography. Pharloom is a fantasy bug kingdom alright, but it feels rich, complete, believable, one of gaming's most exciting worlds. Plus, Hornet is great as a protagonist, she has a personality which is expressed in different ways and she's a total and utter badass. I loved playing as her. The gameplay has familiar foundations, but many improvements. It's metroidvania perfected. Combat is snappy, fluid, fun. Hornet has incredible agility and almost all of the traversal abilities can be incorporated into combat. You have different Crests, classes of sort that alter your basic needle moveset and some core abilities, and also have different notches to equip tools. Tools are an evolution of HK's charms and come in three colors, with red being akin to the Castlevania subweapons. Add into the mix some Silk Skills that act as HK's spells and you have an incredibly rich, flexible and customizable setup. You could have different Crests for bosses and exploration, or hone on your one favourite and master that. Up to you. The exploration is similarly incredible. Pharloom is nonsensically large, and there are a ton of areas to explore, each completely unique and each brimming with countless secret passages, setpieces, collectibles, subtle stories to tell. The sense of wonder and discovery is one of the game's biggest strengths for me, and the basic game loop that comes from it is intoxicating. Even when the game doesn't reward you with something tangible (like a new tool), you can almost always find something unique and strange. Now, something about difficulty. I don't know if the game's difficulty has been significantly patched since launch, but I just can't see the problems people talk about. Silksong is a hard game for sure, but it always keeps a sort of openness. Most tricky situations have unconventional solutions that reward exploring (High Halls gauntlet? You have two NPCs that can help and you can permanently disable an enemy type. Bilewater boss runback? There's a hidden bench to find. Etc.). Also, you have so many options to tackle a boss or an arena. I've seen that many people really hated the arenas, especially before bosses, and it's true they're way more common in this game but I found them fine? Like, instead of a boss fight, I saw those instances as a mix of different challenges and I found them very stimulating. Then again, I might not be a good average case for this. I've played tons of metroidvanias and had 100% completion in Silksong in 36 hours, which is way below the average. So I don't know, it was a tough game, but always completely fair and never frustrating for me. Zero. Nada. Artistically and musically, this has few rivals. The art style is immaculate and so full of unnecessary details that bring the world to life. Animations are painstakingly crafted, the visual theming is so strong. The artists at TC are savants, and the same can be said about maestro Christopher Larkin for having crafted - once again - one of the best soundtracks of all times. There are SO MANY incredible tracks here, and the contribution of the music to the mood and atmosphere can NOT be overstated. It clicks all the pieces together. Overall yeah, I am FUMING to say this, but Team Cherry did go above and beyond and did craft a complete masterpiece. Just don't be quietly smug about it next time, eh?

review_text: Hollow Knight Silksong is a step above the original Hollow Knight in many ways, but in my opinion, the thing that Silksong does best is it's platforming and movement. In a world of metroidvanias that often recycle the same methods of movement, Silksong innovates by changing the world you explore and how you interact with it. The world is focused on wall climbing, becoming a core mechanic early on and being extraordinarily helpful, considering Silksong's focus on verticality. Platforming with the harpoon is a dream, the dash feels great, and no part of my kit went neglected. The game constructs areas for you to use and learn your new abilities, making you commit them to memory. Eventually these inputs become second nature, and you're moving Hornet in flourishing and beautiful ways that make you (truthfully) feel more skilled than you actually are. As much as I had to say about the movement, there is an unfortunate downside. The game is too dark. This may sound like a trivial complaint, but more often than not, for large portions of Act 2 you are exploring areas that don't encourage movement. Across act 2 you are presented with endless ways to get around, sure. However, when a good bit of these places to explore are either enclosed areas or platforming puzzles where you can only see in a two foot radius around Hornet because of said darkness. While one can argue a lot of these darker/enclosed areas are optional, a statement in which I agree, I don't think that's a valid criticism. If presented with an opportunity to explore and upgrade, you'd be foolish not to, especially considering the difficulty of the overall game. Making these secrets and areas that often times rely on platforming with INCREDIBLY reduced visibility and maneuverability, makes the experience unfun. A general rule of thumb with Silksong is that reward rarely meets effort. If there is a potential platforming puzzle well out of your way, you'll most likely be treated with a handful of rosaries or shards. However, if a random breakable wall you missed has a challenging gauntlet of buzzsaws and traps you'd never see until you've already died on them- those are your moneymakers. Your mask shards, spool fragments, etc. To upgrade in this game, you have to suffer, and in most cases, really put up with a lot of challenges I would consider unfair. It really disturbs the overall beautiful flow of the platforming that Team Cherry found. Visually, this game is amazing. Each area carries its own distinct atmosphere between music and visual identity. Platforming makes sense in these areas- in universe, the objects you to and fro from don't stand out in any particularly offensive ways, and usually add to the world, which I personally think is a very impressive feat. Inflating balloons to hop on, bells to ring and bounce from, traps on the walls of sketchy areas- all of these examples and more establish a beautiful world that I almost didn't want to leave. After I completed Silksong, I revisited Hollow Knight to compare the games, as I'm sure a lot of people did. It is, and I say this truthfully, just how much the art improved between these two games. The difference between animations, personality, and world is very visible. Hollow Knight was already a world that was very alive, but Silksong improved without overdoing, and has wormed its way into one of my favorite settings. There is bad to this world however. Nothing immersion breaking, but a complaint I couldn't help but think about. Hollow Knight had fewer areas, however, these area's were important. Each bit was connected to the story in meaningful and insightful ways. Silksong, sadly, doesn't commit to this. There are areas like The Sands Of Karak or Deep Docks that grow and change as the story continues, however, there are also areas like Wisp Thicket or Wormways. While being interesting areas that work well as setpieces, they have very little to offer in terms of actual reason. Wisp Thicket is a random area that holds an effigy to a god. That's it. Wormways just... Has worms in it. Things occur there later, but nothing that warrants the area really existing at all. To me, these aspects are very shallow and underthought, making them stand out in aways that don't always feel great. It's time that I officially talk on the biggest complaint I've seen about Silksong; the double damage. Contrary to what I said earlier, I do not have a big problem with the double damage. The game introduces it in a way that makes sense. Fire hurts more than a normal attack. You go to Deep Docks, see that the game is choosing to escalate in difficulty, and that's it. Hornet's 3 mask container heal is enough to deal with this, as well as her air heal, which puts an emphasis on understanding opponents before finding your room to make a move. Opponents who deal double damage are often built on skill, and the game rewards you handling them. You are supposed to pick your battles, and the game is sure that you know it. There are aspects to the double damage debate that I do want to bring up however. Firstly, they make upgrades feel minor. Increasing your health often feels like a waste of time. If you reach an even number of hearts, you've gained no reward. What problem is this if the double damage makes sense? Well, sadly, the double damage really doesn't always make sense. An enemy half my size that I've been seeing since the game started doesn't need to deal 2 masks of damage and I say that with full confidence. Once you make it to act 2 and on, the game gives up on dealing only single mask damage. it's double damage from there on out. Working with Hornet's limited health pool you get steamrolled. You'll get mad, but it's still WORKABLE. At points though, I found myself fed up with tanky enemies that dealt 2 masks of damage, and at those points, I found myself diving into spikes or other hazards to avoid them, because taking 1 mask from a hazard was better than dying. That should never be the case in a game like this, where the fights are supposed to be challenging and meaningful, not dragging and annoying. Then you get to a point when all enemies deal 2 contact damage on top of their two mask attacks, and the game loses a lot of the 'challenge' and begins to be hard for the sake of being hard. I have one final ending point I'd like to go over before wrapping this review up. The final boss of the game. This was frustrating for me, and I must admit, it did not feel like it was through much fault of my own. The final boss has a handful of attacks, but any and all attacks from the first phase are the main culprits to this conversation. Without spoilers, they have about 3 or 4 separate attacks, all telegraphed relatively well so you know what you're expecting for the first half of the attack. The second half of the attack is RNG based from what I can tell. Sure, they may be using the charge attack, but instead of finishing the charge, they could randomly hop in the air and dive back down on you. There is no indicator of this, and all of these attacks have at least 3-4 variations that are randomly picked. It was this that kept me stonewalled at this fight. It was not fun to be randomly deciding how I should try to avoid an attack that may not come at all. Sadly, this is the only time the game does something like this, and it's at the very end. It left a bad taste in my mouth, and I hope that Sea of Sorrows takes time to go over this with a fine tooth comb. Silksong is an amazing game. Sadly, it's not better than Hollow Knight in my opinion. A more potent story didn't make up for the faults I had with the gameplay. However it's an experience I wouldn't trade for anything despite the faults. That's the beauty of this game though. Everyone's playstyle is so different, that they all struggle and succeed in different ways. I've never had a more adaptable gameplay experience, and I encourage you to try it for yourself before trusting my opinions over your experience.

review_text: This game is absolutely incredible. I can honestly say it's one of the best Metroidvanias I've ever played. If you like the genre at all, you owe it to yourself to play it. An Outlier In a time were most new releases are either $100 CAD with micro transactions, filled with bugs, or have horrible performance, this game feels like a breath of fresh air. There had been nearly no information about Hollow Knight's sequel for many years. Then they just drop this thing for 25 bucks. It's bigger and better than the critically acclaimed first game. It's extremely polished, looks great, movement feels better than any other games like it... It's just... A very very clean experience. The game they wanted to make One thing that surprised me about the game - And I honestly don't know how to say it any other way - is this disregard of game design "best practices". We see more and more AAA developers tooting their own horn about how great their UI & UX are, how sleek and streamlined their gaming experience is etc. There seems to be this obsession with simplifying games, removing friction and maximizing dopamine. And I feel like there are many things in Silksong that are not things you would see in modern games, like a boss with a longer / tougher runback for instance. But not even necessarily with regards to difficulty or convenience. It just feels like they stayed in their corner and made what they wanted to make exactly the way they wanted to make it, without trying to please everyone, which results in a very cohesive experience. Exploration Few games have given me the same feeling Dark Souls 1 has. And you may jump to the obvious conclusion that I'm talking about difficulty but it's not about that at all. One of the aspects I appreciate the most about both games is how vast the world feels. And it might sound strange, considering there are a ton of open-world games out there with larger maps. It's about how it feels . If I could sum up that feeling, I would say that whenever you think you've seen all of it, there's more. You start off having no sense of the game's depth and the more you play, the more you think to yourself "There's another whole area here? What??". I'm sure (or at least I hope) you've had that feeling before. Gameplay The character is an absolute treat to control. I like exploring in HK but it could feel a bit slow at times. Silksong feels fast . It feels snappy . I love it. Gradually unlocking new methods of moving around is really exciting and by the end of the game you're zooming everywhere and feel in perfect control of the character, it feels incredible. If you've seen anything of the game, you might think it's all about the bosses. And while bosses are indeed a big part of the experience, I think I appreciated the platforming aspects just as much. I'm a big fan of platformers and I honestly miss them. And this game has such good platforming sequences. The kinds where you're jumping, dashing, bouncing, double-jumping, dashing again, wall jumping... It feels awesome to pull off. There is a degree of customization with combat. I'm honestly a bit boring and just did the whole game with the default setup but you do unlock quite a few options throughout the game, which I know quite a few people appreciate. Bosses The bosses are obviously the big highlight and a big part of what the game is about. The game is faster and quite a bit tougher than Hollow Knight in general. So even the very first boss will likely be a challenge to most people. And listen. It's a specific kind of game. You need a specific kind of mindset going into it. It's going to take you time to truly get it, to really appreciate it. You're going to fail a lot. But it's through failing that you improve until you prevail. And I promise that once you do, the satisfaction you'll have will be proportional to how tough it was to get through it. You will feel completely hopeless against some of the bosses. You will die within seconds of the fight starting and think you've finally met your match. That you won't be able to progress past that point. You know the fight is probably a lot longer than what you've seen, but have no sense of how long it is because there are no health bars. You might get frustrated. Think that it's ♥♥♥, that the runback is long and annoying and unnecessary. But then it clicks. You enter this flow state. You start improving, getting further in the fight each attempt. You stop thinking about beating the boss and start enjoying participating in the dance, learning each attack and finding a way to avoid it, react to it. Even when you die, you start appreciating the brief moment of respite you get as you make your way back to the boss. You take a deep breath, push through the frustration of failing and transcend it. You embody the spirit of an immortal warrior that is destined to battle for eternity, be it futile or fruitful. Losing is no longer an option, because there is no such thing as losing. It's just part of the process. Then you make it. And you press forward. Story This is one of those games where the story is a bit abstract and lets you piece things out without overexplaining everything. How much you're willing to invest yourself into it is entirely up to you. Just know that you're not really missing out on anything if you're not remembering every single little detail. I'm the type to take things in as they are and just enjoy the ride, without digging too much about lore. Much like FromSoftware's games, I love the atmosphere in general and everything feels immersive, credible and well-pieced together, even if much of it ends up going over my head. I appreciated the dialogues and cutscenes nonetheless! Is it too hard? There are a few aspects that I found frustrating at first but that I eventually just learned to accept as part of the experience. It's something that I thought about a lot and I think that it's specifically those frustrating experiences that make the game, moment to moment, that much more memorable. The most vivid memories I have of games I played when I was younger are typically the biggest challenges I was able to surmount. It's a tricky balance. Would giving me more health, having fewer / shorter runbacks, more benches, taking less damage each hit, lowering bosses health etc. have made me appreciate the game more? At some point I might have said yes. After going through it... I don't think so. I don't think I would change anything about the difficulty. Whether you're willing to put up with it is ultimately up to you. But know that it's not a relaxing game where you sit back and enjoy pretty visuals. It's meant to be challenging to people who beat the first Hollow Knight, so it's definitely going to be extra challenging for anyone not familiar with the genre or who do not usually play more difficult games. But I sincerely don't think it's too hard or unfair. I think anyone can do it. It really is only a matter of patience and perseverance. If you absolutely cannot stand the idea of retrying an area or a boss 10-20 times, or if you hate having to take a break and trying again the next day because you can't beat a boss... Then you probably won't have a great time. If you're on the edge about it... I strongly encourage you to try and change your mindset. You absolutely can do it. You just have to keep going at it and you'll make it the whole way through with great satisfaction. I sincerely think it's worth it. Conclusion Absolutely loved this game, the amount of content you're getting for that price is completely ridiculous for a new release. I really hope you'll enjoy it as much as I did.

review_text: very good game that dwarves its predecessor in a lot of aspects but also makes really questionable decisions regarding the ones where it fumbles in: the last stretch of the game is kind of disappointing and not particularly interesting to actually play through, relying on rehashed enemies for the most part with a few boss fights that do bring back some form of excitement before ending in a final boss that's just kinda alright even if the character it's attached to is really good (though severely lacking in screentime for what it feels like team cherry wants to do with them). furthermore, durability is awful. I understand the desire of making the player feel like their resources are ephemeral but rosaries already do that perfectly: the player is constantly wringed out of resources for basic commodities (maps and benches) to say nothing of any equippable tools (both red tools, which require a second currency for maintenance, and blue and yellow tools which are passives). Speaking of, that secondary currency is extremely obnoxious to farm; the only real way to actually get shards in a timely fashion is to buy them for rosaries, which further puts strain on the rosary economy. I understand what the game is going for, but the end result turns out to discourage players from using one of the core mechanics for a vast majority of it, which is a shame. lastly, this game is Secrets as all hell. this is a more neutral point and your mileage may vary since this kind of gameplay might strike the fancy of a manner of freak different of my own, but I personally am a bit fed up with secret walls by this point. as for positives, well, the fact that there's multiple movesets, and that hornet controls really well, as well as the fact that acts 1 and 2 are the most fun I've had with a videogame in recent memory all definitely more than justify my time with the game. I would not have finished it nor written this review if I didn't have strong feelings about the game, but nonetheless I cannot hide the fact that I have some misgivings regarding it, which sour my enjoyment of the full experience, even if I still think it's deserving of praise for the majority of it, with only the last stretch feeling tacked on whereas the rest of the game had such high peaks they concealed the lows of the game dramatically well. strongly recommended, in spite of its flaws. As an addendum, Lace is perfect and deserved way more screentime. She is the only thing I'd add more of to the game, honestly; while I could enjoy some of the fat being trimmed, I think the game would be better with more of Lace in it, both because I quite like her and because the game's plot would work better (not that it doesn't already) with her having a greater role.

review_text: Hollow Knight: Silksong I am reviewing this game based on my own personal experience and taste. At the end of this review, I'll also provide some important tips and guidance for playing Silksong to help you on your journey . So, this is both a review and a guide! Gameplay Given the previous game, player expectations for the gameplay are incredibly high. However, it's clear that the gameplay and mechanics this game puts in the player's hands are incredibly varied and unique. Silksong's build system and Crests help you progress according to your own playstyle, allowing you to create your own personal build. The diverse abilities you acquire over time and through progression make the gameplay significantly smoother and more engaging. Silksong map is considerably larger than Hollow Knight's, and you'll encounter many different environments and enemies. You'll face over 300 different types of species in this game, which shows its sheer scale. The quests you encounter can be engaging at times, but some can be tedious and boring, and the main purpose of these quests is to reach Act 3 and, consequently, the true ending of the game. Silksong is divided into 3 Acts. Act 3 actually appears based on your choices in completing certain quests and the final boss of Act 2, and it's in this act that the true ending and the entire story the player has been seeking unfolds. To prevent the game from becoming repetitive, Team Cherry has designed specific mechanics and systems for each act. For example, the travel system in Acts 1 and 2, as well as how you purchase maps, is different, introducing the player to a new way of interacting with the environment. Also, in Act 3, you'll get a new ability for reaching travel stations that is really fun and cool. The platforming in this game is so flawless and special that it needs no explanation. Overall, the gameplay and mechanics, aside from a few minor bugs, are outstanding. Story The story of the Hollow Knight series is one of my personal favorites, and in my opinion, few games in this genre have such a deep and beautiful narrative. In Silksong, because Hornet can actually converse with NPCs, the storytelling process is incredibly endearing and understandable. However, unlike the first game which had a more direct narrative path, in Silksong you have to explore and investigate more to follow the story. Of course, this very thing makes players more curious to continue. Silksong's cutscenes are thoroughly exciting and cinematic, getting you hyped to keep playing. The story also answers questions from the previous game and serves as its complement. Be sure to play Act 3 to fully understand the story and get the true ending. Graphics and Art Style Overall, the graphics and visual effects of the Hollow Knight series are incredibly creative and captivating, and Silksong is even better than its predecessor, leaving nothing to be desired. The thematic design of the different map areas, enemies, and bosses is executed perfectly. In short, this game has a beautiful and delightful art style. Soundtrack I have immense respect for Christopher Larkin for composing the soundtracks for the Hollow Knight series, and I congratulate him on creating such masterpieces. The soundtracks in some map areas are very calming and enjoyable (like Bilewater, Cogwork Core, Bone Bottom, ...) and are perfectly matched to the theme of that area. The soundtracks for some bosses are incredibly unique and exciting, filling the player with tension. In my opinion, the soundtracks of the first Hollow Knight is on another level, but also Silksong's soundtracks has its own charms, and we should be grateful to Christopher Larkin. Some Negative Points (Common Player Feedback) It's necessary to mention some of the negative points that players have pointed out: 1. Excessive damage from simple enemies, which makes the beginning of the game more difficult and frustrating for players. Some basic enemies can take 2 mask shards from you! 2. Long and tedious runbacks to bosses waste a lot of time. The best solution is to always rest at the closest bench to the boss. 3. Unnecessary challenges for some upgrades and quests, like upgrading Hornet's needle. You have to find pieces of "Pale Oil," and for the last 2 upgrades, you face very difficult challenges. For the final upgrade, you must find all the Fleas in Pharloom and then complete all the Flea-Festival challenges, which takes a lot of time. 4. The extreme difficulty of some bosses and arena fights when you face them without upgrades. You can finish the game without getting the double jump ability and many other skills. In this state, you might face some bosses with low equipment and weak builds, which will give you a very hard time. I strongly recommend having a suitable build and, as much as possible, getting upgrades, Mask Shards, and Spool Fragments before facing bosses. Silksong is designed so that as you upgrade yourself (most importantly, leveling up your needle) and gain different abilities, the bosses become easier. They only seem extremely hard at the beginning. One of the arena fights I faced very early and without good equipment was the one in the top left part of the Citadel (High Halls), and I spent a lot of time trying to beat it. Worse yet, if you want to speedrun the game, this arena fight is a truly difficult challenge. Tips and Guidance I highly recommend that you finish the game on your own for the first time so you don't get spoiled on this amazing game and can have a pleasant experience with the story. But for your second playthrough or subsequent ones, I recommend the following tips: 1. For a checklist of things you've found, bosses you've beaten, quests you've completed, or anything else, you can use the following app. It's extremely helpful in this regard, allowing you to have a cleaner map and progress in a more organized way: OGM: Map for HK Silksong 2. Make sure to buy (unlock) the game's benches and travel stations as much as possible to have closer checkpoints to the bosses. Also, a tip you might already know from the first Hollow Knight is that you can quit to the main menu and reload your save to return to your last checkpoint (the last bench you sat on or the last location where you received an ability or Crest). This is useful for shortening your path or preventing death and the loss of your rosaries. (Of course, whether you like this method or not depends entirely on your playstyle.) For me, just walking through the Silksong map was enjoyable enough that I didn't need to do this, but it became extremely necessary for finishing the game on Steel Soul mode. 3. Each Crest has its own specific gameplay and mechanics, and you should choose one based on your playstyle. For me, the 'Wanderer' Crest (I recommend getting this early on after getting the Cling Grip ability) and the 'Architect' Crest were very good. equipping a few good tools will help you immensely during the game. I recommend using the 'Cogfly' tool along with 'Pollip Pouch' . This combination is very helpful. Also, use the 'Warding Bell' to protect yourself while healing. In the end, I have to tell you that you are facing an incredible game and you are going to have a wonderful experience with it. Silksong is highly optimized and also has a low price compared to other games. This game is really worth your time. I highly, highly recommend it.

review_text: There really isn't much on this game that I can say that hasn't been said already, with that being said I'm going to praise every single aspect of this game. Hollow Knight: Silksong is what every sequel should strive to be. It expands on quite literally every aspect of the original game in such unique and interesting ways that allows it to have its own identity while still having all the core aspects of what make Hollow Knight well, Hollow Knight. Take the tool system for instance. It's this games twist on the charm system from the original, separating them into three types. Red tools which are combative weapons to attack the enemy with, blue tools which help in combat with effects like a longer needle or extra healing, and yellow tools which are there to assist with exploration. It's such a simple change from the original system yet it adds new layers of depth with the builds you're able to make and massively changes how you play the game depending on what you equip. This game is absolutely massive too. Hollow Knight had 19 distinct areas to it, each and every one of them feeling distinct with their own unique identities, enemies, bosses, puzzle, and items to pick up. Silksong on the other hand has 32 UNIQUE AREAS. That's just the size though, every area is squirming with things to discover, secret rooms, relics, new tools, skills, it just goes on and on. Every area in the game feel so fleshed out with how much there is to do in each of them, and even the ones that might be lacking in content compared to the rest make up for it with their atmospheres and lore that makes them a treat to go through, especially on repeat playthroughs. And the music, oh my god, the music. Christopher Larkin absolutely hit the ball out of the park once again the soundtrack to this game is stunning. The music serves it purpose so well in this game. Amplifying the mood of an area or the intensity of a boss fight to perfect degrees. Speaking of bosses, the bosses in this game are a step up from the ones in Hollow Knight. After taking the time to fight every boss in both of these games again and again I cannont understate how much of an upgrade the bosses are in Silksong compared to Hollow Knight, and the ones in Hollow Knight aren't even remotely bad! The bosses in Silksong are just THAT good. Lace, Fourth Chorus, Moorwing, Widow, Last Judge, Phantom, Cogwork Dancers, Trobbio, Karmelita, the list just goes on and on there are maybe only 3 bosses in this entire game that I'd say aren't at the very least "good" which there are definitely more than 3 in Hollow Knight that I'd consider bad. I'd also like to add another perspective here that just to praise this game a little bit more. You see I've done quite a bit of speedrunning for this game, and while I didn't ever speedrun the original Hollow Knight I get the feeling that this game is even better for that purpose than the original. The movement in this game is some of the best in any game I've ever played, and it makes for such a clean, satisfying game to play through or speedrun if you're into that. Seriously, I'd highly recommend learning the any% speedrun of this game if you're even remotely interested. There is so much more on this game I could write about, and maybe I will in the future, but to wrap this all up... Hollow Knight: Silksong is a perfect sequel, and I'd never change a thing about it. 10/10 no questions asked

review_text: I've obtained 100% game completion but am still missing a few achievements (steel souls, speed and true hunter). It was an incredibly amazing sequel to hollow knight. I'm not sure how to put into words my experience in a way that justifies the game or is fair to other people. Is Silksong truly harder than Hollow Knight? That's a good question and I don't think there's a simple answer. I think the fairest answer is that they are completely different games in the same universe created by Team Cherry. If you only play Silksong like Hollow Knight it will be more difficult. But if you embrace Silksong for what it offers you, I think you will find a new love for it that can coexist alongside Hollow Knight too. I absolutely love silksong and, dare I say, I love it more than hollow knight. Silksong symbolizes my growth from a rather terrible unskilled gamer that struggled even properly jumping from platform to platform in the beginning section of Hollow Knight. I wasn't good and it would have been painful to watch. Hollow Knight is a place I grew from nothing to horrible to eventually 100% all achievements, completing radiant hall of gods. I also needed more so I did all bindings in pantheons. Playing Silksong, completing a gauntlet, I remember putting my controller down and exclaiming, "Wow, I love this game so much!" Who would have known that someone like me could actually complete the deeds I have done in Hollow Knight and Silksong?! Initially, I was worried about silksong because people said it was frustrating, difficult, punishing, and that Team Cherry made gauntlets, runbacks, and 2 mask damage which will make you want to stop playing the game. Admittedly, when I first started I went "the wrong way" and I hadn't gotten a key traversal ability. This made traversal in this optional area a nightmare. I also didn't really "need" to go there yet. While there. I made it to a gauntlet that I definitely should not have been doing without my traversal ability. That gauntlet plus the runback to it definitely made me frustrated. That's probably what made me stop playing the first time. That along with I was already in the middle of playing another game when silksong released that I wanted to finish. In retrospect, I wouldn't go there first and will avoid the area on my speedrun/steelsoul until I do get the key traversal ability. As for the 2 mask damage, I initially was upset about that too. However, I just beat the game (100% completion) and I was thinking. I would never have beaten the final boss SPOILER Lost Lace as quickly if this game was Hollow Knight and not Silksong. I think I would have taken many more attempts. Why? Because Hornet is so incredibly agile and acrobatic. Most importantly, I can heal quickly and while airborne. I recorded the fight I finally beat the game with and it was far less impressive than the fight I beat Hollow Knight with. However, I'd argue it was also more fun because of Hornet's quick movement. I took so much damage in Silksong at the end but I was able to heal while remaining mobile, switching between being aggressive and defensive until healthy. I never really was able to do that in every fight in Hollow Knight. There were some fights I knew I could heal up in Hollow Knight but in Silksong? It's almost every fight I have an opportunity to weave (get it?) heals in while fighting. In Hollow Knight, I usually just fought until I died and only in Pantheons with bindings, radiant fights or speedruns did I actually use my heals (if I messed up) but in silksong healing became a natural part of my rotation during combat. I always sought out heals since they were so accessible. That to me, is the reason I'd say the 2 masks of damage make sense. Lastly, I know originally when comparing the game to hollow knight, I was mildly upset that I couldn't heal 1 mask at a time because I hated the silk waste of overhealing without it not costing less silk (or refunding it). However, after finally beating the game, I feel like that point doesn't matter as much to me anymore especially if you have 3 blue slots filled with specific options. In conclusion, I love Silksong and it is absolutely worth the purchase but only if you commit to playing it with an open mind. If you struggle and find yourself frustrated, you should consider trying to go a different path because there might be an easier one. Once you finish the game, you could try harder paths earlier but for a first time I wouldn't recommend it. That being said, you will die, often times a lot before "it just clicks" in bosses, gauntlets, the environment, and maybe even to your electricity going out or your controller dying. That is definitely something you have to accept. But if you look at the game and ask yourself if it's worth it? I absolutely think it's worth it. It was an incredibly amazing ride just like Hollow Knight was. Silksong is definitely one of my absolute favorite games ever and Team Cherry deserves the positive review for the game. Wonderful job Team Cherry! Thank you!!!

review_text: There's an argument to be made that games don't have to be fun to be good. If I were inclined to make that argument, Silksong would be at the center of it. It's a mechanically polished experience with a great presentation, and a decent, if standard, Souls-like story. It's got a large expansive world -- one of the largest in any Metroidvania. There are moments, where the gameplay is sublime. If you like Souls-likes, difficult games and precision platformers, then this is for you. It used to be for me too, but now it's not. As I near the end I have been forced to reckon with the fact that, when I assess the time I spent with this game, it was not an enjoyable experience for me: on the contrary, this was a pretty miserable time. There were sparks of joy, but the majority of it was spent frustrated and if I'm honest, underwhelmed. When the game wasn't testing my patience, it merely felt like a pretty by the books Souls-like, of which I have played many many times before. The highs I usually get from overcoming these types of games never came, and I am now left wondering if I even like the genre anymore. Perhaps it's just burnout. Perhaps I'm getting older. Perhaps I just wasn't in the right mood. After Silksong I fear I'll never be in the right mood again. And I'm sad about that.

review_text: Beating Steel Soul in Silksong feels less like finishing a game and more like surviving an ordeal you’ll remember forever. This mode takes everything Silksong already does: precision platforming, brutal bosses, and tight combat. It removes your safety net. One death and it’s over. No excuses. No “just one more try.” Every room becomes a risk assessment. Every heal is a decision. Every new enemy makes your palms sweat. What really shines in Steel Soul is how well the game supports mastery. Enemy patterns are readable but punishing. Bosses demand calm, not mashing buttons. By the end, you’re not stronger because of your upgrades. You’re stronger because you got better. When I finally cleared the last stretch without dying, I had to just sit there for a minute and breathe. Exploration feels different too. In normal mode you wander. In Steel Soul, you plan. Do you detour for resources and risk an unfamiliar area, or play it safe and fight underpowered? That tension is constant, and it’s intoxicating. Is it stressful? Absolutely. I lost a run deep into act 2 (you'll see which boss I mean). Considered calling it there. But really the magic is just that: Steel Soul turns Silksong into a personal challenge, not just a metroidvania. When you win, it feels earned in the purest sense. If you’re the kind of player who loves high stakes, clean mechanics, and the quiet satisfaction of overcoming something genuinely hard, Steel Soul alone makes Silksong legendary.

review_text: A Great (But Flawed) Masterpiece After finishing one of the endings, then the true ending, and defeating Lost Lace multiple times, I think I can finally put my thoughts into words. Let me start with the obvious: Silksong is an excellent game. I spent dozens of hours exploring Pharloom, fighting bosses, uncovering secrets, and pushing through some extremely demanding encounters. Team Cherry once again delivered a huge, ambitious metroidvania that will probably remain a reference for years. But I also think the game is being treated as if it were flawless, and I strongly disagree with that assessment. What Silksong Does Right The world is huge and packed with content. Hornet's mobility is fantastic. Several bosses are among the best Team Cherry has ever designed. The Act III twist is genuinely excellent. Exploration remains addictive from beginning to end. The overall production quality is remarkable for an indie game. Had this review only been based on content quantity, ambition, and production value, it would be an easy recommendation. Unfortunately, I believe some core design decisions hold the game back. Boss Design: Harder Is Not Always Better Silksong often feels more difficult than Hollow Knight. The problem is that it does not always feel difficult for the right reasons. Several bosses rely on: Extremely fast attacks with limited telegraphing. Attacks dealing 2 masks of damage. Sudden repositioning or teleportation. Anti-air options that leave very little reaction time. Enemies or hazards appearing directly on the player. Yes, these encounters can be learned. Yes, they can be mastered. But mastering something does not automatically make it good design. As someone who defeated Nightmare King Grimm, Pure Vessel, Absolute Radiance and completed Pantheon 5, my issue is not difficulty itself. My issue is that Hollow Knight's best bosses usually felt fair. Silksong's hardest bosses often feel punitive first and fair second. Progression Feels Weaker One thing Hollow Knight did exceptionally well was making every major upgrade feel transformative. In Silksong, I rarely experienced that feeling. I became stronger. I unlocked new tools. But I rarely felt that my relationship with the world fundamentally changed. The sense of growth never reached the same level as Hollow Knight. Crests Are Disappointing This may be my most subjective criticism. I simply never found the crest system particularly interesting. Many crests feel like minor adjustments rather than meaningful playstyle changes. Compared to the charm system from Hollow Knight, the result feels less impactful and less memorable. The Soundtrack Lacks Standout Moments This was perhaps my biggest disappointment. Hollow Knight gave us unforgettable themes. Years later, I can still hear City of Tears, Greenpath, Sealed Vessel, Grimm, or Hornet in my head. After finishing Silksong, I struggle to recall a single track that left the same impression. The music is good. But for me, very little of it is memorable. Characters and Story This is where the gap with Hollow Knight becomes the most visible. The original game gave us characters like Quirrel, Cloth, Elderbug or the Last Stag. Silksong introduces many characters, but very few left a lasting impression on me. Sherma and Shakra stood out. Most others felt surprisingly flat, including some characters that seemed positioned to play a much larger emotional role. The story is not bad. But unlike Hollow Knight, I found myself caring more about the next boss than the next narrative revelation. Final Thoughts Silksong is bigger. Silksong is harder. Silksong is more ambitious. But I am not convinced it is better. Hollow Knight felt meticulously polished in almost every aspect. Silksong often feels like a brilliant game that reached further, but not always with the same level of refinement. I absolutely understand why many players will call it a masterpiece. I simply think it is a masterpiece with very real flaws.

review_text: I want to love this game so so bad, and so many things about it are so so good, and better than Hollow Knight (which is one of my top 3 games OAT) but if you came into this game because of HK just expect a completely different playstyle. The fantastic: Music is just as good as HK IMO, i think across the board music is maybe not as good but omg the ones that are fantastic are better than HK top tier songs. World/Art IMO is probably better than HK, Team Cherry really outdid themselves making a compelling world that is more lively than the first game. Hornets kit, in general feels so lively and fast. Definitely fits her character. The okay: Tools are a mixed bag for me, I like that she has the tools and they fit her character, but ultimately I'm going to put them here for a reason I'll expand on below. Enemies in general. Some enemies are so so much fun to fight, and feel so much engaging than HK, but this game has such an obsession with "boss" rooms that are literally just waves of enemies, that are just no fun. Some bosses also fall into this category as well, fights like lace were super fun but savage beastfly, brood mother, and splinter sister just kind of leave me with a sour taste in my mouth. Double damage. This one is probably controversial, but honestly I wouldn't mind double damage half as much if it wasn't on what feels like every enemy. The radiance had DD and it felt fitting as it was the final test, this game it's seen as a way to make every fight just annoying. The bad: First problem is more of just an overall feeling of playing it. This is completely my own take of the game as a whole, but it feels *mean.* The whole point is being taken to a foreign land against your will and I understand that, but there's been countless times I want to progress in the story but I find myself booting up a different game due to just not wanting to fight whatever boss room or enemy wave I'm on. Shards/rosaries. Everything in this game feels like it's in a capitalist hellhole. Benches, doors, cost money, shopkeepers nickel and dime you, and overall up until a certain part of the game when you need money, it's hard to hold on to. The shard system is always flawed IMO because you just spend most of the game not using them due to the fact you want them for bosses, and common enemies you need to be farming to get more. No difficulty settings. This is the one I'll probably get the most flak for, but this game needs it. HK did not as that game was end game probably a similar difficulty to this in act 1. I'm not the best player on the planet and the last thing I want to do after work is fight the same fight over and over again for a full play session, some people that sounds fantastic and that's why there should be more than one difficulty. No/less double damage, a rework of the shard system, and just overall less enemy swarms would go a long way to add additional difficulties. Overall this is a fantastic world with so much good about it, that I just don't find fun a solid 60 to 70 percent of the time, so ultimately I made the decision to not recommend since steam doesn't have like a out of 10 rating. If you like incredibly difficult games this is 100 percent the game for you, but if you're like me and played HK not because it was hard but because of everything else this game might just be a bit too much.

review_text: TLDR: A great game and an excellent addition to the Hollow Knight saga. The gameplay is fantastic and the worldbuilding and artwork are excellent. When it comes to the genre metroidvanias we should just ditch that name completely and call them Knightlikes from now on! A true paragon and a great example of a game that makes me question both my sanity, and the virtue of patience... First and foremost, following up on the masterpiece that is Hollow Knight was never an easy task and the overwhelming hype that surrounded this game with its silkposts and neverending memes made this release somewhat of a climax of 2025. However, despite my hesitation going in I can safely say that despite some minor flaws, Silksong is another defining masterpiece from Team Cherry that will stand the test of time.. For context, I have finished the game on all endings and did most of the achievements, all in all 80 hours of gameplay. I did not touch steel soul so I can not comment on all the extras added through that route but I have heard it did spice up the game with more secrets and added characters. I did take my time exploring all the nooks and crannies in this quite enormous world and never once did I feel like I got enough of this games gorgeous and remarkable worldbuilding that both expands on the lore from Hollow Knight, but also carves itself a brand new niche in the story of the fallen realm of Pharloom. To give this a fair rundown I have ordered my humble opinions in an internet-friendly structured list. The great The worldbuilding of Team Cherry is the stuff of legends. The various areas and their interconnected stories make for a sublime journey through a realm of twisted nightmare and horrible beauty. Travelling through Pharloom and its delicate handcrafted environments is an amazing experience and despite the sheer scale of it all you never feel lost or confused. Each area has its specific enemies and tells a different story about the fall of the empire and how its inhabitants struggled to survive the aftermath. The overall gameplay is sublime in its excellent and precise combat and movement and I really love how different Hornet handles versus The Knight. In the beginning it took a bit getting used to but the end result of the tools combined with the variation in crests were perfect and I truly enjoyed feeling the combat being just right during some of the bosses and challenges. The crests that give you your attack pattern are diverse and varied, and even though I ended up using the standard crest most of the game, the diversity and intricate differences are a brilliant way of seasoning the already excellent gameplay. The bosses were great, each telling a different story and fighting perfectly into its domain. In the end I faced them all and had a great time challenging my own lack of reaction. The music is bloody great. Simply perfection! The not equally great The many arenas where you are swarmed by a ton of regular dudes felt alright at start but quickly turned into a chore. I get it, we need some breakpoints to try out our skills and an arena where you throw in a couple of enemies can be great, unless they get too regular. Not a great annoyance, but quite remarkable in its “mundanity” compared to the great bosses! The improvements to be made (IMHO) The extra “layer” of currency. Now you have to juggle Silk (soul equivalent), Shards and Rosaries, each filling a certain niche that quickly made me fall back into a weird grindy loop that felt awful. The Silk powers your abilities and heals you, but if you, like me, need to heal a lot, this is what you will invest the majority of Silk into. I have heard arguments for the fact that using certain abilities speeds up encounters, but since most of them are just technical dances you really do not need the speed, only the health for these misjudged dodges and strikes... Shards are used in some quests/wishes and to recharge your tools, something you tend to need to do a lot if you keep bouncing off bosses. Early game you will drown in shards, late game, not so much. Rosaries are my main gripe since they are not dropped by all the enemies, yet are used to unlock benches, fasttravel, gadgets and much much more. Did it really need to be so many different currencies? And do you really want to use those fancy tools knowing you will run out of gas if you fail too frequently? To me this felt poorly executed and ended up being a grind, something that actually might be highly thematic in this dystopian bug-riddled fantasy. Conclusion: So with that said, I really REALLY love Silksong with every fiber of my being, and yet it makes me feel so frustrated and horrible at the same time. This game has my highest recommendations, but be aware that it is a hard game. Not in an unfair way but in a highly challenging and truly rewarding sense. I had my rough spots with this wonderful game and it really tested my sanity during some of the more mindrending parts, but in the end this was a game that truly captured the wonders of storytelling and gaming as an artform. Silksong will definitely (unless something obscure shows up from the sidelines!) be my personal Game of the Year (2025) and if you have any love for metroidvanias this is truly a must buy.

The amount of breakable walls and hidden passages at unassuming locations is crazy. I immensely enjoyed the game up until Act 3. I wish I could experience the true ending of the story, but im not good enough, the game simply wore me down to the point that completing it feels like a chore. This is a very good game. I'm only giving it a negative review as a warning.

review_text: How would you rate a game, where 80% are awesome and 20% make you question the sanity of its creators? There's a saying that if you put a spoon of ♥♥♥ into a barrel of honey, you will end up with a barrel of ♥♥♥. This is how I feel about Silksong. It has very high highs and extremely low lows. It's a masterpiece in world building, the level design to some extent, the atmosphere and environmental storytelling are great. Unfortunately, all of it is ruined by game design decisions, which just make the game straight unfun. The main issue is that game does not respect your time, and overstays its welcome if you decide to 100% it. In act 2 I installed the teleport mod (and it was the only change I made to the game), because I was just tired of running around the same areas dozens of times. I get it that it's a metroidvania, and you're supposed to explore and do multiple runs of the same areas, but backtracking is really pushed into the unfun zone, especially if you're not following any guides and try to figure everything out on your own. This could have been mitigated by more generous fast travel system, like, porting to benches, or at least having a build in teleport in the game. Second issue, and it's a big one, is how the game tries to make you feel. It raised a lot of discussions in the media regarding what makes the game fun, where lies that boundary where game's challenges are to its detriment. There was one video which made a good point, IMO, that we rarely mind the games which are difficult, but not punishing (e.g. Elden Ring), or the games that are relatively easy, but very punishing (most roguelites). Issue with Silksong is that it's both difficult and punishing. Dying is very real, happens often, and the progress setback can be tremendous. A lot of game design decisions are aimed at forcing you in a constant state of anxiety, where you are afraid of losing your progress and resources. Platforming sections can go for a long time without checkpoints, and death can set you a few minutes back. Bosses have notoriously long runbacks, and often require you to clear a gauntlet before you can even fight them. Your tools use a resource which is not replenished after death. All of this puts a real weight on you to stay alive, and it's not a game where you can one-shot all encounters just by being cautious. A lot of platforming sections and bossfights require you to gradually learn and progress them. The idea here is that the more you build the anxiety up, the better it will feel when you finally overcome challenge or reach safety. Problem is that I don't feel anything apart from relief. I kill a boss and my only thought is: thank god I don't have to do it again. The game annoys you more than it makes you feel good. There are also smaller game design decisions that just make you annoyed or frustrated. The design of flying enemies, for example. They always try to stay out of your melee range, either doing ranged attacks from the corner of the screen, or just sweeping across with a melee attacks immediately moving out of your range. It can be fun trying to figure the tactics out when you fight them for the first time, but you encounter them just so much and so often that dealing them becomes annoying simply because of how much time they waste. The fact that TC loves to put flying enemies in gauntlets or in the middle of the bossfights does not help either. A lot of encounters end up very chaotic, and you're practically forced to tool dump if you want to keep your sanity, and it puts even more weight on you to stay alive. I think, there's a universal agreement that double bossfights don't work unless boss movesets are fully synchronized, or AI is built in a way that it's unlikely that you're ♥♥♥ by overlapping attacks. TC made masterclass double bossfight in their previous game (Mantis Lords) and some good ones as well (God Eater, Watcher Knights), it's incomprehensible to me how they managed to drop the ball in Silksong so spectacularly. There are a lot of fights where you're not methodically learning the complex movesets, you're just trying to survive the chaos and clutch victory by some luck, without really feeling that you even deserved it. You're just glad its over. IMO, the main issue of the game is that Team Cherry worked in isolation for so long. They had no outside input, they did not know whom are they balancing the game for, and they ended up making a very niche product which caters either to people who were very good at the original game (speedrunners, pantheon players), or to people who can't have fun without high stakes and anxiety. I absolutely loved Hollow Knight and finished it 4 times. I managed to 100% Silksong, but I kept going on pure spite. I am done with it, and I am never touching it ever again. I love difficult games, but I prefer my skills and wits being tested, not my patience or tenacity. Unless you know what you're getting yourself into, I do not recommend this game. If you still decide to try Silksong, and you don't find some aspects fun, or feel overwhelmed, try out mods. A lot of people reported that they made the game better.

review_text: I really enjoy the game, but some of the design choices are legitimately irritating. For example: 1. The game starts you with 5 masks, yet something that becomes quickly apparent is that many enemies and nearly every boss deals 2 masks of damage every time they hit you. This makes the first mask feel significantly less impactful to earn, since Hornet goes from dying in 3 hits to still dying in 3 hits. 2. Grinding is practically a requirement if you want to regularly use your tools or the architect crest. In general it feels like this game is significantly more willing to waste your time than the original was. 3. The runbacks are unnecessarily long. For one boss in particular the runback is longer than the boss fight itself. Team Cherry did an amazing job with the narrative and the environmental story telling was top notch. Many of the moments I find frustrating do a fantastic job at conveying the horrors of Pharloom. Nevertheless, from a gameplay perspective, they still feel bad.

review_text: Is the game easy to recommend? Hell no! But why the positive review still? Well first thing first I enjoy the game immensely for few reasons: 1) The art direction is exceptional, from the music and sound design to the background art. 2) The levels are very fun if you like high-octane 2D action games like Dead Cells or 2D platformers like Rayman Origins or Legends. 3) There is huge build variety that even influences on Hornet movesets which encourage multiple playthrough to try different items or crests. 4) Hornet is super fun to control and move around. I definitely prefer her to the knight in the first game. 5) Most of the bosses feel like real skill checks, which I prefer. This is something that can't be said of the first game, where most bosses felt like random enemies with high HP bars. The enemy variety and density also makes each new zone unique and fun to discover. That's where the positives end. Now, on to the criticism. It seems like Team Cherry has a major issue by confusing difficulty with lack of quality of life. 1) I don't understand why we still have to waste a slot just to see where we are in the map. 2) there are way too many secrets. And worst of all, many of them lock game content, such as biomes or bosses. Some even lock progression to more game endings. Other Metroidvanias have an item that you can unlock at the end which hints at a secret when you enter a room. 3)While tolerance may vary from person to person, I find that there are too many gauntlet rooms. It doesn't help that most Silksong enemies are not only fast but also register your inputs just to walk, fly, or dash away from your attacks. This brings me to my next point about runbacks. A handful of bosses are not only locked behind a runback, but also behind waves of enemies. Nine Sols has bosses that are as hard as or harder than those in this game, but the runbacks are super short. In many difficult precision platformers and boss rush games, you respawn immediately after dying. It makes the experience more enjoyable and encourages you to Git Gud. In short, the game hides a lot of content behind secrets. It's also an endurance test because you have to go through the same long obstacles multiple times to improve. In my opinion, the game actively discourages players from progressing just for the sake of "difficulty." Team Cherry allows this because their loyal fanbase will defend their unfriendly design decisions. If another development team wanted to design a mechanically challenging game without considering quality of life or accessibility, I bet their game would be criticized and ignored. Oh, and 99% of the quests are boring, yet you need them to progress. Rather than balancing the game's pacing with peaks and valleys, the developers included quests similar to those in Power Washing Simulator to slow down the high-octane action. These are the same kinds of quests that were criticized in MMOs, gacha games, and poorly received Nintendo games. Now that you know the caveats, hopefully you'll enjoy the game!

review_text: Having finally beaten this game (and 100%'d it - technically, there's still a few things I should go back and do), I can safely say this has become my favorite game of all time. I loved the world of Pharloom and getting to know Hornet was great. The combat of this game felt incredible. Everything was snappy and responsive, and the new Crests system really helped to differentiate this game from Hollow Knight and expand upon the already-fun combat of that game. I really felt like I got to express my "identity" within the game picking the crests that felt best for me - and even using them like "loadouts" for particular situations like platforming segments versus combat potential. My only "complaint" would be that sometimes there's *a lot* of buttons to be worrying about moment to moment which can lead to some missed inputs from time to time. I'd have liked if the silk skills / tools were a little more spread out. It felt too easy to accidentally throw a tool when I just wanted to do whatever I had on my RB button at the time. My other complaint relating to combat, however, is the runbacks. Some of these fights had some of the most insane runbacks. To me it felt like it really just interrupted the flow of the fight to die, return to the bench, and have to do some kind of platforming segment or dodge a bunch of enemies risking taking chip damage just to return to the fight. Also on some fights I found myself frustrated just by tiny time-wastes here or there. Like it taking Hornet a good few seconds to sit up from the bench and be playable again. Or certain fights requiring a particular skill usage I won't spoil that makes it take a good 15-20 extra seconds of just sitting there to re-enter the fight. When you're already getting a bit tilted from the fight those few seconds of "please just let me play the damn game again" really start to grate on you. The platforming felt really good though. Definitely very tough in some segments but finishing them was very gratifying. Don't have a ton to say here other than that everything felt very well-executed for the platforming. I think my favorite part of this game was Hornet's journal entries. In Hollow Knight the entries being the hunter's that you were revealing was interesting and sometimes entertaining, but it was so cool to me to be learning aspects of Hornet's personality from the entries. If you don't want spoilers on Hornet's personality stuff I'm gonna be discussing that next here. Her character design is incredible here. I love that she has this incredibly confident, tough attitude. Some of her lines in this game go *incredibly* hard. And then comes the journal. We get to read a lot more about Hornet's softer side here. There's so many remarks about how soft a particular enemy looks and how it's s shame she can't pet them, and even small bits about how a particular bug would have been a good pet in the courts back home. These little bits just felt like I really got to know who Hornet is beyond the no-nonsense exterior. Her reaction to the relic-collector finishing the collection and how she'd appreciate some thanks showed a very "human" side to her too. This game differentiated it well from Hollow Knight for me in that I actually got to know the character, versus the Knight being a relatively "blank slate" type character seeing as he never talked so we only got passing moments of any kind of personality if any at all. Hornet felt like she was bursting at the seams with personality from every moment we saw her talk. I found myself looking forward to talking to just about every NPC so that I could see what Hornet might say to them and glean just a bit more about her. I'm really looking forward to the DLC so that I get to experience more of Silksong. Also the art of this game is gorgeous. Fantastic job there, Team Cherry.

review_text: Hollow Knight: Silksong is a sequel that I had frankly a lot of expectations for, and if I am honest... This game exceeded all the expectations I had. Story-wise , one thing I instantly noticed is how much more present the story feels during gameplay. While I’m not entirely sure how to explain it, but the best way I can describe it is that it feels like you always have a certain goal in mind, and that goal constantly shifts as you progress. Now, this is a goal largely set by yourself, so it can be quite personal, but I personally felt like I always had some idea of what I was searching for or what I was working towards. It made the story feel more integrated into the actual gameplay than it did in Hollow Knight. Hornet also feels much more alive as a protagonist. Obviously, a large part of this comes from the fact that she actually speaks, unlike the Knight, but I think there is more to it than that. Atmosphere-wise , I think Silksong stands just as tall as Hollow Knight, if not slightly higher. The locations throughout Pharloom feel much more alive, which creates a noticeable contrast with Hollow Knight. In that game, Hallownest was intentionally designed as a fallen and decaying kingdom, so much of its atmosphere revolved around ruin, isolation, and the remnants of a world that had already collapsed. Pharloom, by comparison, feels far more active and inhabited, giving its environments a greater sense of vitality. Detailed background lighting, sharper animations, and a more dynamic audio design all contribute to this. Traversing through Pharloom feels more reactive. These elements make the environments feel more like living spaces that exist independently of the player that it did in Hollow Knight. Personally, I prefer the atmosphere of Silksong over the original, but I think this ultimately comes down to personal preference. The two games are clearly going for different atmospheric identities: Hollow Knight embraces a melancholic, decaying world, while Silksong leans more toward something vibrant, animated, and constantly in motion yet still quite melancholic. Gameplay-wise , Silksong is a massive step above Hollow Knight for me. Hollow Knight already has incredibly satisfying movement, but the Knight generally feels more grounded. His movement is deliberate, and while abilities such as Mantis Claw, Monarch Wings, and Crystal Dash give him considerable mobility, they often feel more like tools for navigating the world than direct extensions of his combat style. Hornet, by comparison, feels as though her entire moveset has been designed around movement and momentum. One of the biggest additions in Silksong is the Tool system, which feels far more active and gameplay-focused than Hollow Knight’s Charms. In Hollow Knight, Charms primarily modify the Knight’s existing abilities, affecting things such as damage, spell efficiency, movement, or healing. Tools, by comparison, feel much more like actual pieces of equipment that you actively incorporate into your gameplay. Rather than simply altering how Hornet’s abilities function, they can give her entirely new ways to attack, defend herself, or interact with enemies. What I particularly appreciate about Tools is how much more connected they make preparation to your actual playstyle. A Tool isn’t simply a passive bonus that you equip and then forget about. Many of them provide abilities that you can deliberately activate during combat, effectively making your equipment another component of your moveset. This creates a much greater distinction between different playstyles, because changing your Tools can fundamentally alter how you approach an encounter rather than simply making the same strategy slightly more effective. Another particularly interesting addition is the Crest system. Crests essentially function as different loadouts that can fundamentally change the way Hornet plays. Rather than simply providing passive bonuses like Charms, different Crests can alter aspects of her moveset, attacks, and overall combat style. Then there are Silk Skills. These are special abilities that give Hornet additional ways to utilize her silk during combat. What makes them particularly interesting is how distinct they are from one another, giving you a variety of active abilities that you can incorporate into your playstyle. Now all I said is mostly scratching the surface of the difference in gameplay and I truly think that gameplay wise, this game is miles better than Hollow Knight Overall, Hollow Knight: Silksong takes everything that made the original special and expands upon it in meaningful ways. Its story feels more integrated into the gameplay, giving Hornet a stronger sense of purpose as she moves through Pharloom. The atmosphere is just as impressive, trading Hallownest’s decaying isolation for a more vibrant, active, and living world without losing the melancholic ton. Most importantly, the gameplay feels like a major evolution, with Hornet’s movement, Tools, Crests, and Silk Skills creating far more depth and freedom in both exploration and combat. While Hollow Knight remains an incredible game, Silksong feels like a genuine step forward rather than simply a bigger version of its predecessor. After all the expectations surrounding it, the fact that it managed to exceed mine is genuinely impressive. If you enjoyed Hollow Knight or simply love challenging Metroidvania games, Hollow Knight: Silksong is a must-buy .
