review_text: Hollow Knight: Silksong has made it clear to me over my many hours of play that it is among the best sequels to ever be made. There are many things Silksong improved upon from the original Hollow Knight; foremost among these being the boss/enemy design. Silksong's bosses are varied, exciting, and a constant highlight of the game. Each one has a unique set of attacks which don't feel like they were designed in a rushed manner (save for the enemy summon attacks which I'll come back to). Personally, I felt as though every boss had some amount of merit to it, which is more than can be said of the some of the bosses from the first game (I'm looking at you Flukemarm). Fighting against any foe in Silksong felt more strategic and, in many cases, more fluid than the original. I will also add that the actual visual designs of each boss were stunning and a perfect reflection of how much the art has improved as well. As far as criticism of the boss/enemy design, I am generally of the opinion that enemy summons are something that should be avoided in most bossfights. There are certainly bosses where enemy summons make sense (Brood Mother and the second Great Conchflies fight being two examples which come to mind), but why is Savage Beast Fly summoning random-ass bugs to help him? I just don't see a good reason for that attack. Another criticism I'd make is rewards. Most bosses in Hollow Knight gave you something as a reward upon beating them, but in Silksong, rewards are often just allowing Hornet to move on. A quick note: a lot of people seemingly dislike the sharp difficulty curve, but I didn't find it all that extreme. As I stated previously, there is a lot to be praised about Silksong which include how great it feels to play as Hornet, the area design being gorgeous, the characters being all around fun and charming, the story feeling connected to Hollow Knight's, and so on and so forth. A few more quick notes: I appreciated the system of acts which was used, however, I hope that the DLC brings with it a new act so that I don't have to walk around such a depressing version of Pharloom. Actually, I would really like to see how Pharloom begins to improve after Act III, especially Bellhart (my decked out Bellhome needs to be surrounded by more jolly scenery). I have no clue what went through Team Cherry's mind when they gutted the Red Choral Gorge (yes, I know the Choral Tower is a thing, but it wasn't enough) for the Blasted Steps and the Sands of Karak. During the trailers it just looked sick af and it was really disappointing not getting to see more of that.

review_text: So the first Hollow Knight is probably one of my all time favorites. Beautiful ambiance, beautiful storytelling, both in lore and visuals, and the gameplay was a perfect balance between challenging and 'peaceful' exploration. The game could be hard, but it felt balanced and never too much. Music was phenomenal. This game, I don't know... I really want to like it, but over 30 hours in, I just can't say I do. The story-telling is ok, except it lacks the depth and inspiration of the first game. Graphics are nice, although I feel a certain charisma is not quite there (except the first area, with all the moss; loved that). The music doesn't nearly dress up area's the way the original did. But that would be totally fine and enjoyable, weren't it for the gameplay. The gameplay is just mean. Platforming is FULL of 'gotcha' moments. You walk into a screen just a touch to fast, you slip into spikes. You traverse a difficult area full of spikes and wall clinging, then in the last room you jump up - spikes on both sides - and in the time it takes your brain to register, a rock falls down on you and you have to do the whole thing again. Bouncing projectiles in rooms so dark you cannot respond by the time you see them. Platform sequences that just go on and on and on and on. Often you'll get hit by an enemy (lose 2 masks) which bounces you into spikes (lose another) and makes you redo a huge chunk of trajectory. Then, since you'll only have between 5 to 8 masks at this point, 3 such mistakes and you restart, having to platform your way back there. You might not make it as far and lose all your monies. Yay. Combat is definitely more refined, but I am enjoying it less too. So many misses that then lunge me into the enemy, enemies constantly flying just out of reach while throwing things at you that will bounce around too long, and get used to almost everything costing you two masks rather than one. The amount of backtracking and redoing the same area again and again just feels wasteful. This game is exhausting.

review_text: I do sort of like this game but with this title Team Cherry has confused "hard" with "tedious". There are definitely fun moments in this game but sometimes it can be a real slog. These aren't just isolated cases either it feels like an overarching theme of the game. It's by no means a horrible game but steam only allows yes/no and on balance Team Cherry have had too much focus on making the game "hard" but not enough time on making it a fun "hard" instead of a tedious "hard". Even with some very good moments you're left wondering if you've actually enjoyed the game.

review_text: Silksong might be the greatest game I cannot recommend. Hollow Knight is one of my favorites of all time, and I wanted to love this one, but it was just really hard to do. By the end I had more or less accepted it with all its flaws, and the game does eventually shape up to be enjoyable, but I still wouldn't recommend it. In order to critique this game without it being a skill issue, I'd need to complete it right? So I 100%'d it trol. There's genuine stuff to like here, so let's start with that. Visually this game is stunning. There's a variety of regions, each with their own look and feel, and the art direction is just incredible. Some areas feel reminiscent of the first game alongside completely new environments, and both work really well. Enemy designs look great, the visual effects are clean, and the whole aesthetic meets the bar the first game set. The world also feels more alive this time. There are a lot of entertaining NPCs, and the addition of proper questlines makes interacting with them enjoyable if you want to fully immerse yourself in the world, though they don't always feel worth doing. The gameplay takes some time to ramp up, but when you reach that flow state after unlocking more abilities, it feels great. Silksong builds on the first game's moveset through the introduction of Crests, alongside expanded movement options. It makes movement faster and allows for levels of skill expression. The boss fights are a lot of fun for the most part, there's a good range of them and some are genuinely great. That's kind of where my positives end though, and that's the frustrating part. The most straightforward way I can put it is that a lot of Silksong feels designed to be annoying first and challenging second. Enemies hit considerably harder than feels fair (with double mask damage) right from the start while your own damage feels very underpowered, basic enemies take too long to kill, and the world is densely packed with them. Staggering enemies is also practically non-existent, so unless you dodge in time you're almost guaranteed to get hit from a lunge attack. Getting around makes everything worse. The game is more linear than its predecessor, so when you don't know where you're going you end up grinding through the same areas while you try to figure it out. Exploration feels unrewarding more often than not, and if you're not heading in the right direction you've just put yourself through a gruesome journey for nothing. The region layouts are a pain to navigate, bench placement can be punishing featuring some of the worst runbacks known to man, and the game has a habit of throwing in cheap traps. Bilewater in particular may be one of the most frustrating areas I've played through in any game. It wasn't fun, I wouldn't even call it difficult, it was just tedious in the most unearned way possible. Then there are the bosses. In isolation a good number of them are solid and some are excellent, but compared to the first game they fall pretty flat. Hollow Knight's best fights had a real sense of grandeur that made certain encounters feel like genuine milestones. Silksong doesn't. The ceiling of what Team Cherry can do is on full display in a handful of late-game encounters from the first game, which just makes the lineup of endgame bosses in Silksong feel like an even bigger missed opportunity. This game really feels like it's playtime padding with annoying design choices disguised as difficulty. When it works, it really works. The problem is that it doesn't work consistently enough, and the stuff that doesn't is too frequent to overlook. I completed it, I wouldn't recommend it, and that sucks to say. If you want to play it, find a friend to suffer through it with. Then it's not so bad.

review_text: After playing Hollow Knight, it was time to give the sequel, one of the most praised games of 2025, a chance. It had everything going for it: I was excited to play it, I was a big fan of the first game and I was also well aware of the overwhelmingly positive reception. I went in expecting something great, and honestly, it did not disappoint. The world is beautiful, all the characters you get to meet along your journey are great, and the music and atmosphere are incredible. It was exactly as you would expect the successor of Hollow Knight to be. From an artistic standpoint, the game is, just like the first one, an absolute masterpiece. But...this is still a game. And games, for me at least, are supposed to be fun, and Silksong miserably fails at that. I was expecting a masterpiece, but it ended up being one of the worst gaming experiences I've had so far, made even worse by how disappointed I was, given the respect I had for the devs and how much I loved the first game. This is one of the most tedious, pretentious and exhausting games I have ever played in my entire life, and it got me so bored and tired to the point where I simply didn't want to keep playing. The double damage is absolutely pointless and incredibly punishing, especially in early game, the runbacks sometimes are too extra and stupid, some bosses feel ridiculously overpowered, and you're constantly taking damage from everything around you. Instead of feeling challenged, I just felt worn down. It's not that I couldn't play this or kill the overpowered mobs or get over the stupid long arenas, because I did beat the game in the end. It's just the fact that when something feels artificially hard, I just lose interest. review_text: This is the type of game that makes the limitations of Steam's review system apparent - Whether or not I recommend this game depends a lot on who you are as a player and what you like to play. Hard to capture any kind of nuance like that with a simple boolean "yes"/"no" review rating, so I'm settling on asking the question "Would I recommend this game to anyone?" with a thumbs down. The TLDR on why is because most people are going to be turned off by this game's brutal level and enemy design. You can get around this with the help of mods on PC tbf, but the average player isn't going to do that - either because they're not on PC, they lack the technical knowledge, or they're simply just not interested in altering the artist's original vision for the game. This is coming from someone who calls Metroidvanias and Soulslikes their two favorite genres, who fully completed the original Hollow Knight multiple times and calls it one of their favorite games of all time. I don't mind a difficult game; in fact I cherish them when they're done right. This game is a polished work of art, but one that seems to take sadistic pleasure in it's difficulty, on a level above the first game. Don't get me wrong - the first HK has some of the most challenging bosses and levels I've ever encountered in a game, but crucially this kind of content is off the beaten path and optional (for the most part). The main game was also challenging, but reasonably so, rarely to the point of feeling unfair. Silksong on the other hand regularly feels unfair along the main path; I can't imagine what playing it must be like for a newcomer, but even as a metroidvania/soulslike/HK "vet" I've been struggling to continue with it because of how frequently it just doles out unreasonably challenging sequences for the surrounding level context. It does help that you can take multiple paths, and that everything is so well polished mechanically and with how it's presented - but multiple paths don't do you a ton of good when all of them end with brick walls that you're expected to either hurtle flawlessly or smash into repeatedly. As a dev myself I can't help but notice all of the little details that add up to paint the picture of what the devs were trying to create, and I can't help but feel like Silksong paints a clear picture of a dev team that spent too long in isolation and relied too little on outsiders for QA/testing. As you develop a game, you tend to lose sight of what that game is like for other people because of how creating it affects your perspective; but also because they tend to get incredibly good at their game (natural result of playing and testing it constantly, for 7 years in this case...). If you don't get people with fresh perspectives to test it enough along the way and you don't iterate enough on that feedback, you risk making a game that pisses people off more than it gives them that satisfying feeling of overcoming a challenge. And to be fair, this stuff is incredibly difficult to get right. I'll also concede that although I've made it through a lot of the game (seems I'm about halfway through?), I haven't finished it, so this is a "review so far" and I might change it by the time I finish it, or if they manage to patch these problems out and give it a better balance. The world is gorgeous, the characters are full of personality, the toolset Hornet uses is really fun (moreso than the first game in a few ways, I love her agility and mobility for instance), the SFX and music are haunting and beautiful, and all in all you can tell the devs poured their hearts and souls into this game... So it hurts a bit giving it a thumbs down after this long wait, but I feel obligated to warn newcomers with how big the game has become, and I hope that can change over time so I can recommend it more broadly. In the meantime, if you love these types of games and don't mind an imposing challenge of an adventure, you'll probably find yourself loving this game and I can give it a thumbs up for it to you in it's current state.

review_text: After 68 hours and beating the game at 93% completion, I feel quite confident in my following review: Silksong *can* be a fun game. The art, the story, the explorable map, the combat. It's all great. But silksong is full of many baffling decisions and a completely different design philosophy from Hollow Knight. If you really like Hollow Knight enough to have the patience to legitimately complete the true godseeker pantheon: Only then I would recommend you Silksong. If you otherwise thought that the godseeker pantheon was too hard and too punishing to bother with, that's exactly what awaits for you in silksong. Silksong is HARD and PUNISHING. I do not say this as a good thing. Hard games can be fun, and so can punishing games. But both combined veer into the territory of extreme tedium and frustration. I will now point out specific things that I did not like: - The early game does a poor job at easing you into the game. The game starts hard, to the point that the midgame will feel a lot easier in comparison because its not really all that harder than the very first bosses of the game, except by then you'll have a lot more items and upgrades to suit the situation. - As a continuation to the previous point, the biggest culprit is the fact that throughout the entire game, everything the player touches will remove 2 masks of health, out of the 5 you start the game with, and you may very well spend your first 10 hours of the game before you collect enough masks shards to upgrade that to 6. At all points in the game, you have half as much health as your health UI would suggest. To the point team cherry has realized they overdid it and have slowly been patching certain enemies and environment hazards to deal only 1 mask of damage, but they're very tentative in their approach, so don't expect patches to eventually fix the early game difficulty more than they've done so far, which in my humble opinion has been far from enough. - A lot, and I really do mean a lot, more than half of the bosses have incredibly lengthy runbacks. Expect to spend more time running back to the boss than you will spend actually fighting them. And the runbacks get worse and worse as the game goes on, every time you think "God this runback was the worst", you'll be surprised to see theres one even worse a few bosses down the line, with mandatory path-of-pain levels of parkour and multi-round normal enemy guantlets before each attempt. Some of the worst runbacks can take upwards of 4-12 minutes just for the priviledge of one attempt at the boss. - Contact damage is still a thing in this game, despite how much people pointed out that it sucked in hollow knight. Except this time is way worse because the game is way faster and so are you, so running into the enemy by accident, or the enemy teleporting on top of you, or randomly deciding to jump when you try to pogo, are all massively more likely in this game than it ever was in hollow knight. - Act 3 feels like a slog. Every enemy gains a MASSIVE pool of HP, to the point that even after upgrading your nail at its maximum possible damage, overworld enemies still feel like HP sponges. And the difficulty spikes massively with the mandatory bosses, to the point they stop feeling like challenges and more like frustrating hurdles to get over with. - The last Item needed to fully upgrade your nail is locked behind getting a high score in several different minigames you only unlock after rescuing all of this game's equivalent to grubs. The minigames are fine, but locking such a valuable item behind them makes them feel mandatory, which massively diminishes any enjoyment you could've gotten out of them. The minigames would've genuinely been a lot better if the reward was worse or none whatsoever. - This game contains lots of dead-ends that literally contain nothing, and never contain anything. Only exist to make the map appear larger and waste time. Extremely disappointing whenever I found one. - Mount fay is an area of the game where its really cold and you take damage if you stay too long on it. And there is nothing in the game that tells you that you have to defy common sense and actually go exploring it while taking constant environmental damage, instead of the logical and intuitive alternative that would've been finding an upgrade that lets you enter the cold area without taking cold area damage, because said item is found at the very END of the cold area. - The beast crest, one of the equipable movesets that you can learn, is really underpowered despite being fun and unique in concept. A super aggressive moveset that loses the ability to heal on demand for a damage buff that lets you steal health from foes. Sounds awesome until you realize that the life-steal effect is capped at 3 masks only, so at best you're getting just as much healing as usual, and more often than not you're spending exactly as much silk (this game's soul meter) to heal LESS or NOTHING AT ALL if the boss decides to stall out the buff, which happens a lot because the duration is very short and is cut even shorter if you take damage, which you will if you're playing aggressively as the mechanics encourage you to. If that wasn't enough, it also has no blue item slots, which contain 90% of the good passive items that would've synergized excellently with the crest, giving you only two red slots of which there are exactly 2 items that synergize with the crest so there's zero build variety there, and two yellow slots, which contain some of the worst items in the game, to the point that even after you've unlocked every yellow item in the game, sometimes there might be a slot that could just as well be empty because there is nothing useful to put in there that will have an effect whatsoever. - Overall I just really don't like how hard it is compared to hollow knight. The difficulty in that game was perfectly fine, it didn't need "improving" by making it harder, specially *this* hard. Silksong is a game that demands you grind many hours banging your head against a wall, rather than a smooth sailing main story that slowly ups the difficulty and offers you some optional hard challenges to prove your skill. Silksong completely breaks a perfectly good difficulty curve in favor of unforgiving difficulty; Which admitedly, can be fun, sometimes it was fun, but is not what you would've expected coming fresh from Hollow Knight, and ends up being very jarring.

review_text: i hate to do this as much as the next guy but i genuinely felt like this game was actively trying to get me to stop playing from almost start to finish, spoilers ahead! before i begin let me clear up some things: this isn't a "waaah game's too difficult / everything does double damage / savage beastfly" review, i overall found the game's difficult to be mild at best and for a majority of the time easier or comparable to base hollow knight, just about everything dealing 2 masks of damage is a necessity as the game would just be pathetically easy otherwise, without the high damage you could quite literally tank and outheal bosses entirely, something i was STILL capable to in most mid to late game; i also don't think that everything about this game sucks or that silksong is the worst game ever, far from it, the art and music are fantastic, quite literally what you'd expect if you were to think of an enhanced hollow knight, perhaps i may be mis-remembering but it overall felt like the npcs in silksong were much more "alive" with many more player interactions which i appreciated; as for the story i can't really say much other than it's ok... but certainly didn't make me salivate to get into the lore and by the end of it i was so exhausted from everything the game pulled that i really just couldn't bother anymore; have you noticed how i haven't talked about the actual GAME yet? yeah let's talk about it. Hornet's base moveset feels amazing to play with, both fast and versatile, even equipped with a fancy new diagonal pogo move! surely the game is built around it yeah? nope, absolutely not even close and the hitbox of it is absurdly miniscule that using it in combat felt like a hindrance than an actual combat choice, in general the moveset just felt like it didn't belong in the game it was in and i couldn't help but feel that team cherry felt the same, what do i mean by that? well notice how i said "base" moveset, Hornet will gain access to different "crests" that change her moveset completely apart from meta-movement abilities, most of them are trash compared to the starter crest (keep this in mind), but one crest in particular... just gives you the hollow knight moveset and pogo, with a built in quick slash... the BEST tools (charms) distribution out of any crest AND a 2% chance to deal triple damage for no reason, wtf? i feel sorry to the 90+% of players that used this and robbed themselves out of experiencing silksong, you just played hollow knight 2. well ok surely that's not a complete deal breaker right? unfortunately it kinda is? remember how i mentioned almost every other crest just feels useless, because this is a big trend in this game, you'll feel weak no matter what, what do i mean by this? lightning round: -an impressive amount of tools are completely useless, there's no variety to builds as once you have the best stuff that's what you'll use and what everyone else will tell you to use. -upgrading your needle literally might as well not be a feature since enemies get a secret damage reduction, because why should you ever feel powerful traversing through early areas in a METROIDVANIA. -defensive upgrades like extra masks or max silk (soul) are so unbelievably far and few between that by the time you get your 7th mask, which is a huge deal when everything does 2 damage you're probably already done with 60% of the game, the 7th mask would be your SECOND HEALTH UPGRADE. -the only thing that "MAY" make you feel powerful, and this is a BIG may, are red tools, think of them kind of as one time throwing items, again most of them are dogs*** while 3-4 are actually worth using, problem is they require shards to craft, one of the 2 currencies in the game which... i really don't want to get into it but do know that despite making currencies more plentiful and stuff overall costing less in a patch i was STILL grinding for them deep into late-game, (this is accounting never losing ANY on dying twice before retrieving them); anyways, shards have a max capacity and if you're trigger happy with your red tools you've got 4-5 attempts at any given boss before you run out and have to grind because of course you don't get anything refunded if you die, great, safe to say i only ever used red tools when encountering particularly annoying bosses. (tl:dr) there is still a lot of stuff that i'd like to discuss in detail but it'd be a never-ending loop of things and minor design choices that ticked me off while i was playing so instead, i just want you to know this: this game hates you, the player, you WILL be inconvenienced at every step of the way, you WILL be ridiculed and made a fool of in practically every stage of the game, and just when you're about to say "surely it can't get worse than this" for the 4th time, it'll find a way to one up itself once more; Pharloom is an exceptionally dark and depressing place in the hollow knight universe, and so too will be your experience with it.

review_text: There are a lot of things to love about Silksong. Highly detailed, smartly designed areas, beautiful music, intricate and complex fighting system, the lore that was developed with sincere care, a ton of secrets to explore... So much truly fantastic stuff that was spoiled for me by a stupidly over-the-top difficulty. I get it, there are games that are made to challenge players – and I'm not a stranger to loving such projects. Sekiro and Lies of P made me swear and sweat so much that at some moments I wanted to quit them – or smash my gamepad against the wall. Some episodes of Silksong's predecessor, Hollow Knight, were extremely unforgiving and took everything to beat them—such as the White Palace or the Colosseum final stage. But every time my character died in those games I felt that was fair. It was the lack of skills from my side, my impatience, my misunderstanding of games' rules. Those games were very hard – but fair and rewarding. Every victory in them felt well deserved, well timed and brought something cool as a prize – from a new tool to a cool plot turn. But Silksong... It is just a challenge after challenge after challenge. Like everything the game designer cared about was how to make player's experience more difficult. Enemies have a ridiculous amount of health, and needle upgrades don't help much — especially in the third act. Most of them are almost unreachable for your attacks, since those are pretty evasive fliers. And there are a lot of them. A LOT: developers are obsessed with locking you in in a small room where you have to fight one wave of enemies after another. Bosses constantly spam their minions, so in addition to dealing with one lethal threat with quirky attack patterns you have to monitor another 2-3 less dangerous enemies, wasting your focus in the process. Using combat tools in such situations sounds like a cool concept, but they require resources to craft — and you'll find that you are out of those pretty soon, and must tediously farm them. Now add the fact that almost everything in this game could kill you in 3-4 touches (hi, dear contact damage), polish it with the lack of checkpoints and the need of going through a boring runback across the half of the map on some bosses. And, finally, put some bugs with controls which aren't very user-friendly from the get-go. Now you see the whole picture. Silksong is a great game for competitive players whose life is dedicated to gaming, I guess. Unfortunately, I'm not one of them – and can't recommend Silksong to any relatively casual gamer, such as myself. If you are ready to dedicate a huge chunk of your time and energy to master it, and okay with all the pain of this process, you'll be highly rewarded with the things from the first paragraph. Otherwise, just save your money.

review_text: This is an incredibly well polished game, but playing it is just... not fun. Due to how small your effective health is most obstacles don't feel like challenges, they feel like chores that you need to keep redoing until you finally learn to do them perfectly. I hoped this would fade with unlocks and experience, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Every new encounter is a test of memorizing what spawns where and how to deal with it rather than testing the player's proficiency with the tools they're given, which makes overcoming them feel like passing an exam rather than proving your skill. And with the variety of options you get for equipment it's really a shame how little these choices change in that matter. Everything aside from the gameplay is exceptional, so if you just want to see more of Hollow Knight's world this game may still be worth picking up.

review_text: This is such a great game in terms of the world, story, visuals, music and gameplay mechanics (and the cost of the game is almost ridiculously low) but it’s massively let down by what I am going to call overly sadistic game design. I almost stopped playing the game completely at one point because I was getting so tired of one punishing challenge after another (honestly think I should have just dropped it there for good). I actually said out loud "I do not play video games to feel this frustrated." Worth noting I'm not a slouch when it comes to games, I've beaten plenty of hard ones. I cannot in good faith recommend this game to most players as this feels tailored towards the elitists who loved the hardest and most punishing challenges in the original HK and wanted basically an entire game's worth of that. In the original the especially hard parts were largely optional whereas here it’s the entire game - it's unrelenting and I felt exhausted by the end of it. I also think the way in which the game is hard feels very unrewarding: Regular enemies are annoying - they have bloated HP and too many deal double damage. Flying enemy AI is beyond frustrating - they always hover just out of reach and pelt you with projectiles. Too many hazards deal double damage - it’s overly punishing. No contact damage with a stationary enemy should do double damage. Too many platforming sections have annoying flying enemies midway through who will almost inevitably hit you while you are trying to navigate the platforming. Far too many bosses have regular enemy gauntlets before them. Rather than this be a rare occurrence that fits thematically, it feels like most of the time. It’s just tedious. Too many bosses also swarm you with regular enemies and at times you can have almost literally nowhere to go without getting hit if the enemy AI moves in a certain way. Bosses have too much HP and become an endurance test unless you start utilising most likely one of a few handful of tactics to eat away at their health (I'm looking at you cogflies, tacks and poison). Shard and tool balance is off. I think ideally the game would just be better if you could use your tools to their limits after every bench rest without any shard economy at all, as it can lead to mind-numbing grinding if you use your tools on a boss too many times and fail. And using tools on the bosses feels mandatory when they start getting harder. The additional allowance in tool use could make fighting regular enemies less frustrating as well. Some rewards were really underwhelming, consisting of a few beads or shards that were pitiful in quantity. I felt like maxing out everything in prep for the final bosses / final boss was mandatory rather than optional, especially given some of the above points. Team Cherry - I think you came extremely close to making an amazing game but lost sight of what is fun and enjoyable. I could happily replay the original HK any time, but I won’t be touching Silksong with a barge pole unless you make serious changes to the difficulty (just add a separate "hard mode" for the elitists keeping it as-is).

review_text: I think this game is too punishing It relies too heavily on bosses and combat arenas. And for the game that does that, it really puts save points far away. It gets quite repetitive and even physically tiring get through the same platforming section from the bench to the arena Damage is cranked quite high. A good chunk of mobs even in early game deliver 2 masks of damage, That makes meaningful mask upgrades take 8 mask fragments, which are quite often locked behind boss arena or a platforming gauntlet. Each individual upgrade feels less substantial compared to the difficulty you made to endure. Mobs early game seems to be able to tank more hits, than player does. Like I get what developers trying to do, to make player be more thoughtful with each mob, making it like a miniboss of its own, like in Dark Souls, but it doesn't feel all that great, and in Dark Souls encounters kinda feel more manageable, since you're rarely forced to take more than one mob and end up in a situation, where is no way to go unscaved During exploration you always wary and discouraged, especially early game, when your margin for error is lower, because of earlier mentioned mob difficulty, but also because how hostile traversal often is. For example, it might be a weird specific complaint, but if you traversing downward, you better bet, that spikes are off screen and you better pay full attention, even if this is a transition area, that you will traverse a hundred times Shells mechanic is questionable. It kinda encourages to be less reliant on tools during the boss fights, because of how difficult bosses are, you're likely to ran out of ammo between attempts. And before mentioned far runs don't alleviate this issue. In the end, if your play style relies on tools, like with architect's crest, you're encouraged to grind. Interestingly enough, those flaws were not present with some specific late game bosses. Checkpoints were close and ammo were replenished between battles (for in universe reasons), that makes me think developers were probably aware in some sense about those things At times I've been frustrated by the game to a degree I can't recall being frustrated before. The game felt like a test of endurance more often than not. It is a shame, because the game is compelling in a lot of ways. Controls feel great for the most part. Visual style is top notch. Game starts more interesting and compelling compared to Hollow Knight, giving player more moves right of the bat. World is interesting to explore For music my expectation were pretty high, after we had some demo tracks released. And although the music is absolutely beautiful at times, it feels deliberately less memorable than in Hollow Knight and the tracks released prior to the games released seems to be exceptions from the general trend and probably the best of overall soundtrack, which was quite disappointing So overall, to use a food analogy, this game was like a delicious dish otherwise, but so much red pepper is added, that you can't even feel the taste anymore. Frustration outweight enjoyment by around 53% to 47%, so I can't wholeheartedly recommend

review_text: This game is pretty good, but disappointing compared to Hollow Knight. I adore Hollow Knight but Silksong is a mixed bag. Enemies are almost unilaterally more tanky, so fighting them often becomes a chore, even after damage upgrades. They also often feel far cheaper, because they have more erratic movesets, so engaging with them feels more random and the insane frequency of two mask damage is stupid. In the original, that was reserved for major bosses and stuff like that and there you became far tankier far more quickly. It ends up that most of the time, enemies you're fighting literally take more hits than the player, even when the screen is full of them. So you are a 2-3 hit glass cannon, except you're not a cannon, you're a peashooter. More of the encounters also feel cheap. Several "lock doors till you kill all the waves" feel half luck-based with how the several enemies choose to attack. In other places, darkness makes it so enemies jump in from out of view, making it almost impossible to avoid the enemy except by tedious baiting. Bosses also feel pretty tanky, which means the fights often end up becoming more about endurance, which feels worse. In short, it is far harder to avoid damage, because enemy movesets are far more erratic and with shorter tells and most things feel more random. This is made worse by the way the basic attacks also seem to have far shorter range. It also kinda feels like the hitboxes of player and enemies are too large, to the detriment of the player, so that being within attack range is almost always a hair's breadth from collision damage. The reduced freedom in how to use charms is also a letdown, particularly when they are mostly so insignificant that the "balance" of charm types feel pointless. The items are the only innovation I like, as well as the varied movesets. Overall, the game is a very mixed experience for me. The style, story and atmosphere are all great. I want to keep playing and there is a lot to like. But it feels far more unfair, in a bad way, more luck-based. Not helped by how, with such high damage from everything, you barely get the chance to learn enemy movesets before you die. Particularly because the movement feels less controlled. Honestly, it feels like the developers lost sight of what a good progression is and what a good balance between player and enemy power is. Ultimately, it almost feels like they were more interested in making "super-hard game for hardcore players" instead of something polished and fair. I really hope they tweak it. In Hollow Knight I would sometimes go "Gah, dang!" when something went wrong, but then think "OK, fair". In this game, I find myself way too often going "oh, come on, that's just stupid and random." I've never felt compelled to review a game before, but this got me over the edge. I want to love this game, but in most ways, I'd call it worse than Hollow Knight. So Silksong gets a like but honestly not a recommendation.

review_text: Team Cherry delivers another beautiful game. One of the best games of the decade. It's a very well made experience all around, with very few niggling gripes. The map design is great, it's a solid metroidvania style game with plenty of secrets, unique areas that don't feel too generic. The OST is once again great, not as good as Hollow Knight's personally, but still very fitting for the game and the occurrences within. Gameplay is still pretty tight and responsive. It all comes together to be a complete experience, and an enjoyable one at that. I personally found the dive kick instead of a down slash made platforming harder and a bit more tedious in some instances, it felt less responsive and consistent than Hollow Knight's version. This rings true for a lot of the movement options given to the player, a lot feel similar to what was given to the player in Hollow Knight, but they're a little less consistent or general purpose. A good example is the Silk Soar compared to the Crystal Heart. One sends you up, the other sends you horizontally, and one of those is a lot more responsive and frequently used that the other. The entire game felt like this. A lot of it felt like Hollow Knight, but a bit worse. That being said, it's still a fantastic game, well worth the price for it, and I look forward to Team Cherry's future endeavours wholeheartedly, no matter how long they take to make them. I'd much rather a good game than a rushed game. Thank you for the experience.

review_text: Hollow Knight: Silksong pushed me to the absolute limits of how hard a game can be and still have me WANT to keep trying. It demanded possibly too much in some areas and I reached my personal breaking point during Act 3 and the Coral Tower. At this point, I was trying to prove i could complete Act 3 and get the true ending and that I was a good enough gamer or something... But it finally hit me that I wasn’t having fun anymore. It pains me to say that because I felt like getting through Act 1 and Act 2 was hard and challenging but doable. Exploring the world and meeting the characters enjoying the soundtrack and the character voices. That was all peak gaming for me, and once I rolled credits twice to do the (2) different actions with the fake end boss... I thought ok maybe Act 3 will provide some memorable bosses or something NEW. I was disappointed to find its basically the same game but less fun and more fetch quests and more gauntlets where waves of enemies with annoying flight patterns and cheap feeling tactics. I know many people explained in greater detail why they love or hate the arena style gauntlets with waves of enemies, and the reasonable ones I found a nice challenge, and the unreasonable ones made me hate the game. I think that is the real tragedy of this game is that I LOVE this game in its beautiful brutality and it’s demanding near perfection from me. But the final taste in my mouth will be the Coral Tower and that stupid gauntlets of waves of annoying enemies where I could only get through 3 waves without dying. I could not get to the boss of this section which seems like a cool boss from the videos I’ve seen, but I won’t get to experience it or the other Act 3 bosses. I am left with ironically a HOLLOW feeling inside of me that I wasted 90 hrs on a game that wanted me to fail and in the end, I did fail to complete Act 3. Was this because I am terrible at action games or metroidvania style games? No. I’ve played and beaten everything from Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne, Sekiro to Elden Ring. But with those games, I walked away feeling amazing and that I did something really special. In the end, Silksong made me feel hollow inside and made me think I wasted 90 hrs on something that was designed to make me fail anyways. Even though I loved the score the look and feel of the world and the way the game played, the difficulty just always kept me at arms length when I was trying to LOVE this game, it kept telling me it only wanted me to fail. review_text: I am 40+ hours into Silksong, and while I genuinely love the atmosphere, the characters, and the sense of discovery, I am experiencing more frustration than joy. It is a stunning game, like it's predecessor, which I really loved 10/10, I feel Silksong is bogged down by mechanical "friction" that feels like it was designed purely to annoy the player rather than provide a fair challenge. The main issues: Cheap Contact Damage: Simply touching an enemy—even if they aren’t attacking—costs you 2 or 3 masks. Because Hornet is tall, the tips of her ears often clip an enemy's hitbox. It feels terrible to be penalized so heavily for a pixel-perfect error while enemies feel like poise-heavy tanks. Input Conflicts: Mapping the Special Move (Silk) and Tools to the same button (RB) is a baffling UX choice. In high-stress fights, it is far too easy to mis-input a tool and accidentally waste the Silk you desperately needed for healing. The "Parachute" Dress: The flutter mechanic is way too sensitive. It frequently activates when I’m just trying to tap-jump, killing my momentum and floating me directly into hazards or enemies. Mechanical Inconsistency: Ledge grabs are unreliable compared to the first game, and the constant "pogo" parkour feels like a tedious chore rather than a rewarding test of skill. My Advice to New Players, specially if you are a casual gamer: The world is worth seeing, but the "cheap ♥♥♥" in the base game can be soul-crushing. Ive never used mods in a single player game, not even with Silksong, but for new players I highly recommend looking into the modding community, maybe with mods your experience could be better than mine. Final Verdict: Good game, beautiful art, but questionable design. Feels designed to be frustrating instead of joyful. I can only recommend this to hardcore players and for players who want to see more of Hollow Knight world, but if you are just new... then forget about this ♥♥♥ and buy Elden Ring or something else.

review_text: TL;DR: Great game, worse Hollow Knight. 8/10 For context: the original Hollow Knight is my favorite game of all time. I've beaten it deathless and without upgrading my character. So when I say Silksong frustrated me, it's not a skill issue rant. If Hollow Knight gives you a wall and tells you to go find a pickaxe, Silksong expects you to break through it with your head. The good Movement is god-tier. Hornet glides through levels like a ballerina. Traversal is so fluid it's basically its own form of fun, so the huge map never feels like a chore to cross. Combat has depth. Pogo, parries, deflecting projectiles, tools (spears, knives, potions, grenades), and Crests that completely change your moveset or healing. You can build a mage, a tool spammer, whatever you want. Exploring new areas is the best part. Almost every biome brings new enemies, mechanics and upgrades. Greymoor, Shellwood, Deep Docks and the Citadel are phenomenal, classic Metroidvania design. Art and music are stunning. Tons of tiny details, multilayered backgrounds, and another incredible Christopher Larkin soundtrack. Story and lore are coherent and well thought out, and Hornet actually talking makes the narrative much easier to follow. The bad Less Metroidvania, more Souls. Many areas are fairly linear with shortcuts. You clear them on the first pass and never come back. Backtracking often leads to a room with a handful of rosaries. Some secrets are absurdly hidden , Dark Souls illusory wall style. Good luck getting 100% without a guide. The balance feels like a stream challenge run. HK's endgame damage (2 masks per hit) becomes the default a few hours in, while your HP stays at base level. Getting knocked into spikes by a boss can take 4 masks in a second. The new healing (3 masks at once, but only with full silk) is the only thing that makes this work. If you get chunked with no silk, you need 9 hits on 1 HP to heal. Stingy direct progression. Twice as many silk upgrades as HK for the same endpoint. Your first needle upgrade is basically it until Act 2. One extra mask barely matters when you die in 3 hits anyway. "Rage-game" design. A bench that's a trap (the only one in the whole game, using the same assets), a boss that explodes on death and nearly one-shots you, flying enemies that fall on you for double damage. Consequences way out of proportion to the mistake. Gauntlets everywhere. Locked-arena wave fights every 15 minutes against enemies you've already beaten, often copy-pasted arenas, often with no reward at all (drops disabled). One mandatory 10-wave gauntlet ends in a boss, so every death means 10 more minutes to try again. Lazy bosses. Few of them, many with 2 to 4 attacks spammed at high speed and high damage. Lots of them spawn random adds, so RNG decides how hard the fight is. Some are recycled up to three times as mandatory fights. Broken economy. Paid benches are fine (rosary strings exist for that), but shop prices are huge and about half the enemies drop nothing. You WILL farm rosaries, and shell shards too if you rely on tools. Little to no rewards. Many bosses give nothing, one 30-minute area gives you... a Steam achievement. Clearing a zone for an hour gets you 30 rosaries. For a game with speedrun and deathless achievements, this kills replay value. Quests are MMO-style fetch/kill tasks, a leftover from when Silksong was a DLC, and they're mandatory to reach the endgame. Courier quests are basically mini platforming Death Stranding: you'll either love them or hate them. Minor bugs : bosses vanishing between phases and just dying, broken scripts, inconsistent hitboxes. Rare, and the devs are patching quickly. Act 3 (spoilers) Story-wise it's great fanservice that ties up most threads from HK. Lace's arc feels chaotic and underexplained, and Grandmother Silk appears in like two scenes, so the antagonist never really lands. Gameplay-wise, the jump to the endgame is barely noticeable because the whole game already had endgame balance. Most side bosses give nothing or near-useless items. And the final boss of a multi-dozen-hour game is... a third Lace fight with extra AoE attacks, partly recycled from other enemies. Seriously? The whole act feels rushed and done on the cheap: barely any new areas, recycled enemies, and the difficulty bump is just the same modifiers slapped on everything. Verdict The core gameplay is impeccable, and most of the problems show up only when you dig into the details, so you might not even notice them. This is for HK veterans who want a bigger challenge and Souls fans who like platformers. If you're new to hard games, it might break you. Hollow Knight is a 9/10 for me. Silksong is an 8/10 , and at its price it's still one of the biggest, highest-quality games you can buy.

review_text: I really, REALLY wanted to like it but the game tried it's hardest to discourage me by constantly annoying me during play and implementing stupid game decisions every chance it had. I've heard people say it's GOTY easily but I can't really say the same. The combat feels good but it's kinda jarring how much they abused double damage dealing enemies to the point where you'll get clipped by 2 masks of damage often in places where it doesn't feel like it should happen (For reference, at the point where I stopped playing, 35 hours in, I had 7 total and I was pretty thorough exploring everywhere, you start the game with 5 ) and it just creates a frustrating experience when you're going on long stretches of gameplay looking for a save point just to get hit by double damage from an environment obstacle. The exploration is one of the aspects I really enjoyed at first but I feel the more I explored during the latter part of the second chapter, I started to hate it more and more cause the game overuses hidden passages and destroyable walls to the detriment of the player experience. There was an extremely egregious case in (spoilers for Chapter 2 about THAT ♥♥♥ place) Bilewater, where to find the bench, you're required to look for a barely visible passage that's juuust above the maggot water that locks you out of healing when you touch it. This area is already really punishing, long and tedious to go through- and if you don't find this save point, you'll be doing 10+ minute runbacks to arguably the worst boss in the entire game (which already wastes your time by having an unskippable horde fight BEFORE even being able to attempt the boss) This was probably one of the most frustrating experiences I've had in my life and it wasn't even because of the difficulty, at every turn it felt like the devs were focused on ♥♥♥ with me to the detriment of their own game and when the buffed enemies started appearing I honestly lost all the interest I had in continuing to play. I wish I could call it GOTY like everyone else but honestly I can't and it was the most disapointing game of 2025 for me. I envy the people who enjoyed the trip cause there's an amazing game buried under all these dumb decisions, but for me it was a "death by a thousand cuts" kind of situation and I can't really recommend it.

review_text: Worst PvP experience I've had in years. I have 5000 hours in Escape From Tarkov and thousands of hours in other games. Man, this PvP is AWFUL. To be able to get any guns that stand a chance against players you need to invest dozens of hours of grinding to upgrade your crafting stations. If you don't do that you cannot buy or use good weapons, unless you randomly find one in a match. 14 shot kill AR, 20+ shot kill SMG, 20+ shot kill semi auto weapon, 4 shot kill sniper... Every level 1 and level 2 weapon takes more shots to kill than your magazine can hold. If your magazine holds 14 shots then it will take 16 shots to kill someone. This is extremely annoying because even when you get the jump on someone, the absolute worst players still have more than enough time to turn around, locate you and then 3-5 tap kill you because they have good guns and you don't. The quest design is atrocious. You have to go to 4 different maps for one quest that only gives 2500xp (not even 10% of a single level). The guns feel so weak it's like slapping people with a pillow. Headshots do no bonus damage. There is a sniper that is completely useless because by the time you get a second shot off the guy already had more than enough time to regen his entire shield. To be able to get kills as a low level you literally NEED to camp, third party or get insanely lucky. There is no skill here. I am dying to some of the worst gamers I have ever seen in any game. People who do not take cover, who do not control recoil, who do not listen to audio, who camp for 45 minutes to get 1 kill can and WILL defeat you. Over and over again. When you get a kill in this game you won't feel like you made a play or had skill. When you get killed you will not feel like you did something wrong, or learn anything. Buy this game if you want to grind for 50 hours before you get access to any guns that actually allow you to compete. I do not get the heart-pounding feeling (like Tarkov or Dark Souls) when playing this game. It feels like I am playing Fortnite but every gun is worse than the worst weapon in Fortnite and when I win I feel nothing. It is genuinely like a more casual version of Fortnite. I cannot express enough how bad the guns in this game are. 14+ shots is absolutely ridiculous. Especially when that person will have time to heal before you reload. GARBAGE. Save your money man, don't buy a game that kills you in unfair ways over and over again. Don't buy a game that is specifically designed to waste as much of your time as possible. If you want an extraction shooter, play Tarkov. Literally all of the other ones are just bad games.

review_text: There is something empowering about giving your players the option to choose the way they want to play the game. PVE mode detractors will say that it separates the player base and that the whole point of the game is the potential threat of PvP. While I agree with this, there is something that they are overlooking completely. There are people out there who derive enjoyment from ruining the experiences of other players. It is this small portion of the player base that must not be encouraged or rewarded. A large portion of the more casual, less competitive players have voiced their frustrations about this and a toggleable PvE mode was implemented as a test. Good on you, Embark, for doing this and listening to your players. Now the power of choice is given to the players and they can choose how they want to play. Now players that want a chiller experience can get what they want. Players that still want PvP can still have PvP. I suspect that most of the PvE mode detractors are simply complaining that easy prey is no longer available.

review_text: I honestly believe separating PvE and PvP into different modes is a huge mistake, and I really hope you reconsider making this change permanent. One of the things that made ARC Raiders special was the balance between trust, tension, and unpredictability. In my experience, most of my lobbies used to be relatively chill. I rarely shot at other players unless I had a good reason to, and there was always that underlying tension of not knowing whether an encounter would turn hostile. That uncertainty was a huge part of what made the game so unique. Since this PvE/PvP split, my experience has changed dramatically. Now, it feels like five out of every six players are immediately shooting at me or actively looking for a fight. Why? Because many of the players who previously preferred peaceful encounters have moved to PvE. This creates a serious problem: players can now farm resources, accumulate wealth, and progress in a much safer environment, potentially without even needing to bring proper weapons. They can then enter the standard PvP lobbies fully equipped, with plenty of resources and money, while facing an environment where almost everyone is ready to shoot on sight. In other words, the players who helped make the original PvP experience more varied and unpredictable are being pulled out of it. The result is a much more aggressive environment, where peaceful interactions become increasingly rare and combat becomes the default response. **This isn't simply about preferring PvE or PvP. It's about how separating the two fundamentally changes the ecosystem of the game.** The tension between potentially friendly players and hostile players was part of the core experience. You never knew what kind of encounter you were going to have, and that made every decision meaningful. By allowing players to progress in a low-risk PvE environment and then bring that progress into standard PvP raids, you risk creating an imbalance between risk and reward while also removing a significant part of what made the original experience engaging. Personally, I believe this change could seriously damage the game's economy, its risk-reward loop, and the social dynamics that made ARC Raiders stand out from other extraction shooters. I understand the intention behind offering players more choice, and I appreciate that you're testing different approaches. But I strongly believe that making this separation permanent would do more harm than good. Please consider the long-term consequences before committing to this direction. The beauty of ARC Raiders was that peaceful players, opportunistic players, and aggressive PvP players all shared the same world. That mix was what made encounters feel organic and unpredictable. **Please don't remove that dynamic from the game.**

review_text: Leaving a review to mark that whilst I enjoy (and would love it to be permanent) the PvE mode, it needs some adjustments to be really good, and here is my wacky take on it. Overall, I hope it stays in and just is iterated upon. I played this game on launch, and I lost interest because the stress of PvP (even with ABMM) was not worth playing this game. I love this game, I love the vibes, I love the feel- But I do not like PvP. This is a subjective opinion, a lot of people love the anxiety PvP adds to the game (since you never know what other people are gonna do), I am not one of them. I play games to have fun and relax with friends. Including a mode for people will never be an issue as long as the player base is large enough to support both sides, which many o' game has done in the past. People saying it has to be one or the other are really only correct if this game truly loses it's playerbase. Issues with PvE: 1. The PvE mode as is, is obviously not fully done. I think the main thing that feels "missing" is the need to be quiet or stealthy; In PvPvE lobbies, your gunshots not only cause ARC to come over- But other players. Making noise is a problem, choosing to not fight ARC is a choice not just because of the ARC- But because you'll draw attention to yourself. That entire choice is missing from PvE. People are loud, it feels like the map turns into all out warfare. And it ruins the "vibe" of the game and some of the good decision making. - My on the spot solution would be to make ARC better at hearing things at a distance in the PvE modes, not only to add to the danger of encounters but the choice of "Do I really wanna shoot at this wasp that will probably fly overhead, or do I need the materials and am willing to risk a Vaporizer coming by?" - I understand it could be not only complicated to have different ARC difficulties across two modes, but I think it's the only viable way to keep the fear of "noise" in the game in-tact. Also, the fact ARC shoot at downed players is already a thing in PvE- And should definitely stay there; If not get harsher. 2. Rats still exist, in a way. My friend and I spent multiple expensive explosives and ammo taking down a Bully on Pandola, only for a cluster of people to run over from the shadows and strip the thing of everything valuable before we had time to even heal up. Even worse, there were flying ARC choosing to ignore them and shoot at us- So our Bully was completely dismantled by the time we got to it. This is a problem. I believe there seriously needs to be a system in place that dictates if you *didn't* help take down boss enemies, there is a set timer on the corpse before you get to dig at it. Not that you can't ever get to it, just a timer that keeps you from taking the loot from people who poured resources into taking something down. If people help provide a certain percentage of damage to the bot in question- Then the timer isn't a thing and it's free reign. I think that hits a good in-between. The way it is now, you no longer can defend your loot like you could in PvP. If someone tried that stuff there, you could blow their brains out and move on. I can't do anything here. 3. This attaches on to the fact that "noise" is no longer a fear factor. Everyone in the PvE modes is moving at mach-3 to get to the buildings before anyone else can, it's no longer "fighting" over buildings, it's rushing them. It causes people to not engage with the game or it's mechanics (fighting, traversal, cooperation) and just sprint to hot spots and strip it clean before others can get there with zero fear or hesitation. It's just bum-rushing. My main "fix" to all of this is the most simple; PvE lobbies have less people in them. I know this could cause server issues, but with some expanded slots in this field, just simply having less players to deal with ARC (less players to be nearby when you take one down, less players to help you, less players to rush loot before you) could fix all my issues I have with PvE in it's current state. All of this said, I love the fact the devs are checking it out, I literally would not be playing this game without this PvE mode right now. I hope it stays in, even in it's current state. The game is better with, rather than without. Have a fantastic day if you read this I love you.

review_text: I’ve been in the game for a while, so I can give you a balanced perspective on both sides of the negative opinions. First, let’s talk about the addictive nature of the game. It’s definitely a game that keeps you hooked. Now, let’s get into the PvP and PVE aspects. I’ve been on both sides, and both sides are what you expect. In PvP, you have to be cautious of camping players and getting shot in the back. But you don’t have to worry about fake friendly players. You know what you’re coming for, and so do they. It’s always fight on sight now. In PVE, the “friendly lobbies” are exactly how you’d imagine them: people running around carelessly. You do run into rats, but from my experience, the ratio is about 1/10 raids. I’m completely fine with that. You don’t have to constantly watch your back while looting. At the end of the day, you can’t have it your way all the time. Finally, let’s talk about cheating. There was a time when cheating was bad and extremely noticeable, especially in PvP. But PVE players don’t tend to cheat. I’ll say it has cooled down, but if they don’t get the ESP wall hacks taken care of, this game is dead to me. I’ve lost a lot of stuff to cheating players and have only gained a tiny fraction of what I have lost.

review_text: I don't like multiplayer games so much. I'm more of a single player guy, but I took the plunge on this game because of all the positive press it has been getting. And they weren't wrong. This is a very fun MP game. What I like about it coming from a single player mindset is that you can actually play this single player and have still have fun in a multiplayer world. More so, in fact. As a single raider, I had to sneak around firefights and patrols. It was pretty intense and felt like I was in the world of Terminator, scavenging for survival. I was practically crawling through dilapidated warehouses and buildings searching for loot, sometimes picking pieces off dead corpses. When I did see other players, I kept my distance. I felt like I was really struggling to survive. And not all player encounters were bad. In fact, some players even helped me along the way. This game makes for some great experiences. So as a single player preferred person, I would definitely recommend it. It's not perfect: some levels look too pretty to be post-apocalyptic, the loot can be overwhelming, and the progression can be slog at times. But overall, this is a fun experience that should keep you entertained for a long time.

review_text: ARC Raiders has an incredible amount of potential, but right now the game is being seriously damaged by cheating, exploits, and the overall PvP experience. The game feels completely infested with wallhackers, cheaters, exploiters, dupers, and players who abuse every possible advantage they can find. It is becoming harder and harder for legitimate players to enjoy the game when they constantly have to wonder whether the person who killed them was actually better or simply using cheats. The developers need to take a much stronger and more aggressive stance against cheating. We desperately need a reliable and powerful anti-cheat system, better detection, faster investigations, and much harsher punishments for confirmed cheaters and exploiters. Temporary bans are not enough if the same players can simply return and continue ruining matches. Cheaters should face serious consequences, including permanent bans when they are caught. Cheating doesn't just affect the person who gets killed. It affects the entire player base. Every legitimate player who gets repeatedly killed by a wallhacker or exploited out of their loot eventually becomes frustrated and may stop playing altogether. Once players lose trust in the fairness of the game, it is extremely difficult to get them back. On top of that, ARC Raiders desperately needs a proper dedicated PvE mode with NO PvP interruptions. Give us a friendly PvE-only lobby where players can focus on fighting ARC machines, exploring the maps, completing objectives, collecting resources, farming loot, testing weapons, and enjoying the world without constantly worrying about another player hiding somewhere waiting to shoot them in the back. A dedicated PvE mode would not have to replace PvP. Keep the existing PvP extraction experience for players who enjoy that style of gameplay, but give PvE-focused players a legitimate alternative. There are many players who genuinely enjoy the PvE side of ARC Raiders—the robots, Queens, exploration, looting, missions, builds, and progression—but don't enjoy being forced into PvP encounters every time they enter a match. Right now, PvP can feel extremely frustrating, especially when you combine aggressive players, rats, exploits, and suspected cheaters. A PvE-only mode would give players another reason to keep playing and could help retain people who are currently getting burned out by the PvP environment. ARC Raiders has a fantastic foundation. The atmosphere, world design, ARC machines, gunplay, movement, looting, and extraction gameplay all have huge potential. But the developers need to protect that potential before the problems become even bigger. Please listen to the community. Improve the anti-cheat system, take cheating and exploiting much more seriously, punish repeat offenders permanently, and seriously consider introducing a dedicated PvE mode with no PvP interference. The player base is already showing signs of dropping, and if legitimate players continue leaving because they feel the game is unfair or unenjoyable, that decline will only accelerate. Don't wait until the community becomes too small to recover. We want ARC Raiders to succeed. We want to keep playing. We want to support the game. But we need to feel that our time, progression, and effort are respected. Please take action before it's too late. ARC Raiders has the potential to be an incredible long-term game, but the developers need to address these issues NOW.

review_text: ARC Raiders, much like The Finals before it, is a game fighting against itself. Embark has proven that they know how to make engaging worlds with satisfying gameplay, and they have that in spades. Where they seem to struggle is designing systems that don't actively push you away from engaging with the mechanics they've created. They did this in The Finals, creating a ton of interesting gameplay choices with its items, weapons, and classes, only to pair them with such aggressive matchmaking that even in unranked modes, you'd be hard-pressed to use anything but the most optimal combinations. In ARC Raiders, they've fallen into a similar design trap. The world is incredible, the gameplay loop is fun, and the ARC themselves are some of the more interesting enemies I've seen in quite some time. Upon release, the game was lauded for having a PvPvE environment where the E part is fun, unlike say Scavs from Tarkov. So what's the issue? To put it plainly, there often isn't much reason to engage with the PvE. Bosses require significant amounts of ammunition, healing, durability, time, and often some of your best gear. But because this is a PvPvE game, you have another option: wait for someone else to start fighting the boss, then kill them and take their weapons and loot, often a better return than just killing the boss in the first place. So why go through a difficult, lengthy boss fight when you can use third-person peeking (yes, in a PvP game) to get the drop on someone who's already half-dead and has spent all of their resources doing the difficult part for you? Once again, Embark has created a gameplay loop in which the game's design actively discourages you from participating in the content they've built. The problem isn't that PvP exists, it's that the incentives make exploiting someone else's engagement with the PvE more attractive than engaging with it yourself. Because you're discouraged from engaging with the exceptional PvE gameplay in favor of the mediocre PvP gameplay (again, third-person peeking), the game ends up being less than the sum of its parts. PvPvE is a balancing act, and it's one that ARC just can't seem to get right. Embark really knows how to make a game at their core. I just hope they eventually stop shooting themselves in the foot before this one dies completely.

review_text: ARC Raiders is a phenomenal game. Unfortunately, there's nobody steering the ship. Make no mistake, ARC Raiders is a fantastic game. Even if you're joining the party late, you'll still have a decent time for a while. You will not, however, get anywhere near the ~600 hours worth of value I got. The game was able to sustain its appeal for that long through frequent fresh content, along with consistent small tweaks and additions to what was already in the game. Less than 10 months post-launch, Embark Studios have publicly announced that that era is decidedly over. At its October launch, Embark claimed that they had 10 years worth of content and support lined up for ARC Raiders, and that the game would receive weekly updates. By January, Things were starting to look shaky. The studio collectively took a month off of work for Swedish reasons during one of the worst periods of the game's PvP balance, leaving huge swathes of the player population unhappy. When the developers returned, it was with the bitter pill that updates were being scaled back to be once a month, and significantly smaller in scale. Not wonderful, but survivable. In May, Embark dropped the catastrophic news that from now on, the game will only be receiving updates once every six months, with bug fixes sprinkled throughout and a new paid cosmetic weekly. To say that this decision was poorly calculated or came at a bad time, would both be incredible understatements. ARC's Steam Charts speak for themselves. As it stands, what you see is now what you get with ARC. There is no compelling late-game loot. There is no endgame to speak of, nothing to surprise a long-time player, and nothing to look forward to for months at a time. On top of that, if their previous "big updates" are to be our measuring stick, there's no compelling reason to believe these twice-yearly updates will add more than a couple hours of worthwhile content. Past a point, all that's left for a player of this ostensible "live service" is the exact same PvE content on loop, or a PvP experience where day by day the number of cheaters rises, and the number of legitimate players dwindles. ARC Raiders is a really good game. There is absolutely no chance I would recommend it to anybody at the moment. See you in October, I guess.
