review_text: "Wanted to feel like a raider? Sorry, bro — that moment is gone. Now you are just meat for f***ing content." For the first two–three weeks, ARC Raiders was that rare case: a game about raids, atmosphere and survival. Now most matches feel like an arena for aggressive streamer content (and other content creators), where a normal player is just expendable. · WHY I LIKED THIS GAME SO MUCH Visually and atmospherically, ARC Raiders is honestly a piece of art. Concrete brutalism that feels like a Soviet–era architecture fever dream, mixed with industrial aesthetics in the form of rusted structures; post–apoc–punk clothing with retro–futuristic elements that could be ripped straight out of old sci–fi – it all works together as one coherent style. The sky and distant vistas are the kind that make you want to just stand there and stare. Sound and audio design set the overall feeling of a raid and give that rare sense of: “I am actually in another world.” The developers themselves called audio one of their “strategic pillars”, and you can feel it: this is a game you first play with your ears, and only then with your eyes. The raid atmosphere and the map as a sandbox: tension and unpredictability, a world you genuinely want to explore, where every run can feel unique. All of that existed in the first phase of the game’s life (those early weeks) – the game really did deliver that experience, until it became flooded by mass PvP purely for content. · WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED I want to freeze in time the moment when it was still possible to play ARC Raiders “normally”. For me, this was that rare case when a game actually gave me a feeling of happiness and deep engagement. ARC Raiders could easily have become one of those games I come back to for years. But right now it is being buried by one specific thing – an aggressive meta pushed by streamers. · HOW IT LOOKED BEFORE THE “EVENTS” Not that long ago, matches looked roughly like this: – you drop into a raid; – sometimes you run into other squads; – some players choose to interact, some choose to avoid you; – there were tense moments (“is this guy a d***bag or actually a decent dude?”), but you did not have the feeling that every single person you met was a f***ing psycho sprinting at you and screaming for “content” on TTV or TikTok. You could: – team up and destroy ARC machines together; – loot buildings (there really is enough loot for everyone); – help each other with quests; – sometimes extract side by side with total strangers – and that felt great. Now it is a completely different story. · WHAT CHANGED After one particular streamer (TheBurntPeanut) decided to start his “war” and hyped his audience into playing as aggressively as possible, this started: Every encounter = automatic KoS gameplay. (For clarity: KoS = Kill On Sight.) No attempt to communicate (I literally carry defibs just to pick random people up), no reading the situation – just instant deletion of anything that moves. Or they hard–ignore you until you get knocked, then suddenly turn on their mic to brag about being from some “faction”. Bro, we are in solo. What f***ing faction are you talking about? Camping exits and key locations. People sit on extracts and quest spots not for loot, but for “clean frags” for recordings or streams. And it is not even impressive – the shooting in this game is extremely simple; this is not CS or PUBG, where gun skill actually matters a lot more. Matches feel less like raids and more like BF/CoD with extraction sprinkled on top. Instead of tense PvEvP, you get a pure PvP arena with some running to the exit. On top of that, depending on luck, the surrounding PvE can either screw you over or bail you out: bots aggro whoever they see first and often end up helping your enemy. Naturally, part of the community picked all this up: people watch how their favorite streamers or YouTubers play and simply copy the style. As a result, a normal player (or a newbie) who came for an extraction adventure, not for a never–ending circus of clips, just stops having fun. Friendly or neutral players slowly turn toxic too. As we all know, evil breeds evil: if you get ratted out ten times in a row, your hands start itching to play the same way. If it keeps going like that, we might as well rename the game to RAT Raiders. · WHY THIS IS NOT JUST A PROBLEM FOR “SNOWFLAKES” I am not against PvP and I am not asking for some “hippie chill–only mode” (I can play aggressively – I just keep hoping the person in front of me will turn out to be reasonable, not an a***le). But right now: The game is losing its identity. Instead of a unique mix of co–op raids and risky PvEvP, we are getting yet another simulator of “shoot everything you see” (well, except ARC, apparently). The experience is dictated not by design, but by streamers and their fanbases. Today they feel like “playing like psychos” – and the whole server turns into a toxic festival of aggression, and everyone else is basically forced to live in that format. New players are thrown straight into the most toxic version of the game and make the only logical conclusion: this is just another toxic KoS trash pit – so they uninstall it, or in the worst case, go straight for a refund. · WHERE THE DEVS COME INTO THIS The problem is not just one freak who started a “war for content”. The problem is that: The game has no tools to balance player behavior or dilute the total KoS clown meta: no karma, no reputation, no rewards for helping others or for non–aggressive behavior, no real tools for peaceful interaction, no convenient signaling or identification systems, and so on. There is no clear stance. Is this a game about raids, survival, adventure and destroying ARC – or about “shoot everything that moves”? Right now it feels like the developers themselves have not fully decided what they want from their own creation, and that empty space has been filled by streamers. They are effectively the ones setting the tone. If you let streamers and content creators define the behavioral meta, be ready for your game to become a hostage to their moods. That is exactly what is happening right now. · WHAT I WOULD LIKE TO SEE If the developers really want to keep ARC Raiders as an interesting extraction experience, and not just another PvP arena, we need at least some of this: – Systems that reward a variety of playstyles, not just brain–dead total KoS shooting. Yes, technically something already exists (killing raiders gives less XP than killing ARC), but that is nowhere near enough. – Counter–measures against constant extract camping and stream–sniping for highlights. Shoutout to that “Partisan” from EFT – at least there, there is a dedicated NPC whose whole job is to hunt down ratting campers. In ARC Raiders, there is not even a hint of that kind of counterweight to this playstyle. – A clear communication stance: what kind of game this actually is and what behavior is considered “normal”. – Basic boundaries for friendly play. For example: if you signal “I am friendly”, get a clear “yes, me too” back, and then the guy just shoots you in the back – that should be reflected somehow: karma hits, reputation loss, something. And honest play, on the contrary, should be rewarded. You could even go for a more radical approach: put the “bad boys” in lobbies with other bad boys, and sane players with sane players, with some kind of redemption system if someone decides to start playing normally. The online population allows this – there are enough people to separate rats and normal players into different lobbies. [ My final verdict is in my last comment at the bottom of this thread. Also look for my “Update after ~200 hours played” comment — it has important extra observations. ]

review_text: Arc Raiders is a great game...but here's a caveat... At launch, AR was fantastic, both in solo mode and with friends. In solos, you would mainly come across friendly players who would help you out with quests, fight Arc for you, rez you when downed or at least help you to an extraction zone if they weren't carrying a defib. Squads was also full of topside fun as you occasionally ran into an aggressive team and have a gentlemen's agreement that the best team won - 'gg gl next' <3 Fast forward 8 weeks. The game dynamic has drastically shifted in the opposite direction. Everyone has completed the arduous quests, have a totally stacked inventory, completed the Raider Deck, grown tired of the constant daily Feats, completed many pointless Trials and even pulled together enough resources over 5 phases to prepare for the optional Expedition on the 22nd Dec... Now, I'm NOT saying that there isn't enough content in the game, there is...IF you are a casual gamer who only gets the opportunity to play a few hours a week. But for the majority of players who CAN play most evenings (plus the sweats who play 16hrs a day), the ONLY thing that remains is PvP. Of course, AR is (essentially) a PvP game, so I don't sign up to the "this game should have a PvE mode" mantra...get over it...but that also gets boring for a large majority so they revert to what gamers do best...toxicity. And it's RIFE! Extraction camping, fake friendliness, and even players who watch you crawl to extract after downing you, watch you call the elevator, watch you wait for the elevator, watch you dial for Speranza and THEN kill you so you leave with nothing - these are the sort of players who burn ants with a magnifying glass just for fun; and it isn't just every few raids either, it's 9/10 raids...this breeds a 'shoot-on-sight' culture which will haunt the less-skilled gamer who will simply stop playing. Is AR a good game and do I recommend it? Absolutely! Is it worth your time and money? Also yes! But just know that you are going to have to deal with meta shifts from time-to-time, not with the game state, but with player attitude...

review_text: **187 Hours Played | Recommended? Not Right Now.** I have 187 hours in ARC Raiders after buying it on June 12, 2026. I didn't casually play this game—I no-lifed it because I genuinely believed it had the potential to become my next 1,000-hour game. That's what makes this review so frustrating to write. At its core, ARC Raiders is one of the most immersive extraction shooters I've played. Think Escape from Tarkov with a bit of Destiny and Helldivers mixed in. The gunplay is phenomenal, movement feels smooth and responsive, the lore is interesting, the AI is challenging without feeling unfair once you learn the mechanics, and discovering new blueprints and crafting equipment is incredibly satisfying. The maps are well designed, dynamic world events keep raids fresh, and most of the community is surprisingly friendly and cooperative. The foundation of this game is outstanding. Unfortunately, the developers keep getting in the way of their own game. The biggest issue is matchmaking. Recent changes completely destroyed what made the community special. Friendly players, cooperative players, and backstabbing "rats" now feel like they're thrown into the same matchmaking pool. Instead of rewarding cooperation, the game constantly rewards betrayal. I went from being ratted a handful of times over my first 170+ hours to getting betrayed nearly every other match after the latest update. It's exhausting and completely changes the atmosphere of the game. Unlimited free kits make this even worse. They allow players to risk absolutely nothing while killing fully geared players who spent hours earning their equipment. They show up at endgame events, wait for everyone else to do the hard work, then shoot people in the back and walk away with the rewards. The developers tried to address this by banning free kits from night raids, but that simply pushed the problem into every other mode instead of fixing it. Beyond matchmaking, the game is filled with frustrating quality-of-life problems. Inventory management is honestly one of the worst I've experienced. I have easily spent 20-40 of my 187 hours just organizing my stash because there isn't enough storage space, there are too many crafting materials to keep track of, no item locking system to prevent accidental selling or recycling, and no bulk recycling or selling options. These are basic features that should already exist. Technical issues don't help either. I encounter game-breaking bugs almost daily, from ADS glitches requiring a full restart to visual, audio, and gameplay bugs. Network performance is also surprisingly poor. My friends and I all have solid internet connections, yet we constantly experience lag, rubberbanding, and connection issues. Balancing is another recurring frustration. Instead of bringing weaker weapons up, the developers repeatedly nerf everything else. Attachments often come with bizarre durability penalties that make little sense, and weapon durability itself feels overly punishing for some guns. Another baffling design choice is joining raids that are already 10-15 minutes in progress. The best loot has already been taken, objectives are already completed, and you're left running across an empty map hoping to salvage something. At one point I had 12 raids in a row where I spawned into matches that were already halfway over. What hurts most is that none of these problems come from the core gameplay. The actual gameplay is fantastic. The shooting, movement, atmosphere, PvE encounters, exploration, progression, and world design are all excellent. The frustration comes almost entirely from avoidable design decisions and updates that consistently seem to create bigger problems than they solve. I wanted this to be my next 1,000-hour game. Instead, after 187 hours, I'm stepping away until the matchmaking, free kit system, and overall balance are seriously reworked. ARC Raiders has lightning in a bottle. It just feels like every major update moves it further away from what made it special in the first place. **Verdict:** Incredible foundation. Frustrating execution. I'll happily come back if these systems are fixed, but in its current state I can't recommend it.

review_text: There is nothing to be afraid of. This game is very new player friendly, solo friendly, duo and trio friendly. It runs well on old hardware unlike a lot of recent popular games. You can use a free load-out of gear for any game if you want to just casually loot and explore. You will keep your free load-out gear if you safely extract from a game. Making it a simple way to replenish guns and equipment. The environment and soundscape is crafted well with hidden things to find. If you have been apprehensive about trying a game that falls within the category of PvPvE extraction for the first time, this is the game you should start with. The AI (Arc / robots / drones) are designed well and play an important role in balancing out your interactions with other players. You can easily keep to the outskirts and focus on missions, feats and casual looting. You are not supposed to go in guns blazing (you can if you wish). You should for the most part be avoiding contact with AI and working your way around them and other players. Most players don't actually want to fight you. Sometimes the initial fire is just reactionary. Set the proximity chat button to something you can easily access. Every time you are trying to extract with or around other players, call out "friendly, friendly". But still be ready to fire and take cover as needed. You are safer playing solo with how the matchmaking works. If I cross paths with players while traversing the map I often allow them to carry on past without them even knowing I'm there. You will eventually find your own balance of when to shoot first and follow through, hide or communicate. Go into a game with a general idea of what you want to do (quests, feats, explore, loot specific items). Look at the map as soon as you spawn and plan a route and extraction location. Change your plan based on where you spawn and what you encounter. Take cover and hide after you call for extraction and wait for the doors to open. Don't be afraid to extract early. Use your microphone. If you find a snow globe, put it up your bum. It won't always go well for you but that's just how it goes sometimes. Try to adapt and fall into the flow of the game and don't expect the game or other people to adapt to you or your desire to not be shot. Tension and risk is important. It won't always be friendly in every encounter, sometimes you gotta do what you gotta do for those credits. The calls from some people for a PVE only mode or complaints about the third-person view partly come from not understanding how the game is designed and balanced. Having a first-person view as optional would be fine, but the maps are designed with third-person in mind and work well with avoiding drones. As for a PVE only mode, the game would not be as great or appealing to so many people as it is now if it was anything other than PvPvE. Maybe it would be viable a very long way down the line when the game has been around for a while and needs something else to keep it going or an end of life patch for offline or co-op so the game is still playable far into the future unlike some other games that have been shutdown. Some things I would like to see: Additional larger maps that would allow four player teams. The current maps should remain restricted to three and bellow as that is what they were designed for. Being able to see what items recycle into when mousing over them. More items, more enemies.

review_text: As of writing this review, I'm still playing this game to complete my first expedition and see how it goes. Uncertain if after doing the expedition I'll decide to continue or not. However, I don't recommend new people buy this game for the time being for the following reasons: 1. In hostile lobbies, there's ~80% chance your lobby will have cheaters in it. 2. If you're a social player and want to play in duos/trios with your friends, you'll be forced into lobbies where people largely shoot on sight. Most social players stopped playing with their friends months ago for this reason and they only play solo. 3. While solo social lobbies are still good, the player count is still declining and once it reaches a critical point where even solo lobbies can't be match made with social players, the social community will either leave or convert to shoot on sight and ARC will just become another sweaty death match extraction shooter like the rest. ARC being a social game is the main attraction for it. That's what made it special. I'm sad I didn't jump on it when it first released because it was reportedly even more social than it is now and you could actually play duos/trios with other social players. Once ARC loses the social community, the only people left will be the (heavily cheating) sweaty PvP community and I've already played enough Tarkov to burn out on that. I'll change this review if the developers make changes to the game to make it last long enough to be worth purchasing. Until then, while the game is still steadily cruising down to a point of total collapse of the playerbase, I can not recommend purchasing this game if you intend to play it for a long time. Unless they make changes soon, the ARC experience will soon be lost forever.

review_text: Absolute masterpiece, I strongly recommend however lets get into the nitty gritty Pros: -Insanely stimulating gameplay loop -tasteful and enjoyable progression -Voluntary wipes that if committed to grant slight bonuses and rewards -Challenging enemies each with separate approaches for taking them down to get their loot -lively and entertaining community -Gun feel and gun play is easy to use and enjoy with enough nuance to have attatchment combinations good for different things as well as each weapon serving different purposes -genuinely useful utility items in their designed scenarios -free random loadouts to avoid being shut out completely from being able to compete if you have lost all useful gear -Nice cosmetics to give the game a sense of style -anything you can think of trying has a decent chance of working -Definitely scratches the gear fear itch -team fights feel fairly balanced -incredible map designs and environments -Being downed and still being able to extract and operate the controls is genuinely god tier QOL -Game is designed for exploration and does a very good job at explicitly and subliminally incentivizing it (keys, quests, hidden high tier loot locations and random higher tier loot drops) Cons -stat tracker bugs do not track stats appropriately -Some shared missions do not update when completed by teammates as intended -some puzzle pieces become unable to be picked up and transported to intended locations (I believe this is an issue with pinging those pieces erasing the pickup prompt however I am unsure) -some priority issues with firing weapons such as being hit behind walls -Audio balancing is a mess, although directional audio is top notch the balance between ambient noises and noises you want to listen for such as nearby footsteps definitely feels like it needs some tweaking, as the number of times I have been stock still and someone has ran up on me without a sound is frankly absurd -repairing weapons costing the same as a full weapon upgrade I believe is a little gratuitous but that's more of an opinion on my part -plant spawns outside of baskets are incredibly low (with exception of the herbal bandage plant) despite most plants being green tier items, I spent 8 hours looking for 6 prickled pears before finally locating them -tool-tips do not tell you of all uses of an item such as use of workbench upgrades -being low on a certain craft-able item quantity and not being able to click on it to craft it despite having the needed raw materials makes crafting a very jarring menu searching simulator, a change to make this more convenient would be a really nice QOL change -Quests do not feel very engaging and can become fairly tedious, however the rewards are fair All in all I really do love this game, the negative things I have about this game are more an attempt at constructive improvements that can be made and are in no way game breaking or experience ruining, and I do plan on using as much of my time in this game as I can (Addendum) After playing this game for a few more dozen hours I have new things that have come to light that if you're thinking of buying you should be aware of -Mid Match spawns: You will frequently find yourself spawning middle of the raid timer with no warning or noticeable cause which will impact how you are to approach your raid in a significant way given how the locations that you may want to go to will more than likely have already been hit unless you have found small secret loot deposits that tend to have the things you are looking for. I have no idea why this happens so often as they have enough players to keep queue times down and even if that weren't the case, I personally am okay with waiting the extra 30 seconds to a minute to queue into a potentially 30 minute raid -Gun play desync and lag compensation: There is an EXTREME disconnect between where you are and where the opponent sees you in gunfights and will very often result in you ducking behind full cover and even moving a few feet away from the edge of cover and still getting hit by rounds because your opponent still sees you out in the open on their screen, there are many videos you can find this online where you can watch as the bullet traces by the players body by a large gap but their shield still breaks and they take damage. This is a very disheartening and extremely frustrating phenomenon

review_text: ARC Raiders is, hands down, the best thing that’s happened to multiplayer shooters in years. As someone with over 2K hours in Tarkov, playing ARC has been a real breath of fresh air. The game is accessible for casual players but still keeps the challenges and that endless gameplay loop that can keep you hooked for hours if you’re a tryhard. Ever since I tried the TT2, I’ve been waiting for this game with a level of excitement I hadn’t felt in years, and the final version has not only met expectations but completely surpassed them. The visuals, performance, sound, atmosphere, animations, physics, gameplay, the feeling of landing a shot, whether it’s on an ARC or a Raider, the tension during extractions, the ability to fight your way out of any situation or simply socialize with other players in the match, the solo matchmaking... everything together makes ARC Raiders the best example of how a studio can truly listen to players, take the best from every shooter sub-genre, mix it perfectly, and create a unique experience that makes many veteran players feel like kids again after so many years. Embark, thank you for this masterpiece. And please, don’t stop creating content and refining the gameplay loop so the game doesn’t fade away too soon and stays alive for years to come. I think the biggest challenge right now is keeping a community that’s devouring quests motivated to keep going on expeditions over and over again, with rewards interesting enough to make it worthwhile. If you can pull that off, ARC Raiders will become a legendary game.

review_text: From Addictive to Completely Stale – They’ve Ruined What Made ARC Raiders Special This game used to be brilliant. Genuinely addictive. I absolutely loved the mix of PvP and PvE, the challenges, the tension of extracting, building up your gear and never quite knowing what was going to happen when you dropped into a raid. It had something special. Unfortunately, that game feels like it has disappeared. ARC Raiders has gone downhill so badly that I honestly struggle to recommend it anymore. Lobbies feel emptier, matchmaking can take forever, and cheating has become so common that some sessions feel virtually pointless. Whether it’s a lack of enforcement or simply not enough being done, from a player's perspective it feels like Embark has completely lost control of it. Then there’s the gear system. They keep talking about reducing “gear fear”, but instead they’ve gone so far the other way that gear barely means anything anymore. Free kits everywhere, completely mismatched loadouts and very little sense of progression or achievement. At the same time, actually grinding for the materials you need can be painfully slow. It somehow manages to make gear feel both worthless and tedious to obtain. The bigger problem is that the game has completely lost its identity. Embark seems determined to please every possible type of player, and in doing so they’re pleasing nobody. ARC Raiders cannot survive pretending it is some deep PvE experience. It isn't. There isn't enough story, meaningful mission progression or endgame PvE content for that. You aren't working towards some huge conclusion. There isn't a compelling campaign. You're essentially repeating the same loop over and over again. The PvP is what gave that loop its excitement. So where are the clans? Where is the meaningful competitive progression? Where are the systems that give long-term players a reason to keep logging in? Where is the evolving endgame? Instead, we seem to keep getting slightly different versions of the same content. And from what I've heard about the October update, it sounds like more of exactly the same. More content layered onto a fundamentally stale gameplay loop isn't going to fix the problem. One of the most frustrating things is that players have repeatedly asked for a proper PvE option where they could gear up, gather materials and then take that equipment back into the main game. Apparently that couldn't be done — yet a PvE implementation can be considered for the Chinese market. That tells you everything about how disconnected the direction of this game has become from the community that actually supported it. Whoever is ultimately directing ARC Raiders needs to seriously reconsider what this game is supposed to be, because right now it genuinely feels like the people making the big decisions either don't play their own game or simply aren't listening to the people who do. A year ago, I would have recommended ARC Raiders without hesitation. Today? Don't waste your money. There are better games competing for your time, and ARC Raiders currently gives you very little reason to keep coming back. The gameplay loop is stale, cheating destroys far too many matches, progression feels increasingly meaningless and the game has no clear long-term identity. To take something that had this much potential, this much atmosphere and such an addictive core gameplay loop and drop the ball this badly is genuinely impressive. Embark had the magic. Well done for ruining it.

review_text: Almost never review games, but this one deserves a review. I know the developers are kind of hesitant about making the game PvE because they originally sold it as a PvPvE experience. But, to be honest, I played for almost an entire month when the game was released, and the main reason I stopped playing was the campers and the really bad experiences that came with them. I would spend hours farming, fighting, and preparing just to take down a big ARC, only for some guy with a free loadout to take everything from me—or, more often than not, kill me while I was extracting. I also remember reading for months about the really bad hacker problem the game was dealing with. I never personally played during that period, so I can't speak from experience about how bad it actually was, but seeing all the reports and discussions about hackers definitely made the situation look even worse. I get it. PvP is part of the experience, and for some people, that's what makes the game fun. At first, I was like that too. I think that's how most people feel when a cool and innovative game like ARC Raiders first comes out. There's something exciting about the constant risk of losing everything and getting into fights with other players. But at some point, I realized that wasn't what I wanted anymore. I just wanted to experience the game for what I personally found most enjoyable: fighting ARCs, exploring the world, completing quests, and enjoying the vibrant world that Embark Studios created—a world that, in some aspects, feels more alive than our own. I actually downloaded the game again after deleting it many months ago, simply because they announced a PvE experience test that will last for a week. They have said that it isn't a permanent update, but honestly, all I want to say is that, for that week, I'm going back to dust off my Raider gear and spend as much time as I can killing ARCs and enjoying the world without having to worry about another player waiting around the corner. Whatever happens after that week, I'm just glad I get to experience ARC Raiders this way again, even if it's only temporary.

review_text: I’ve played over 400 hours and earned all 50 achievements, and I can honestly say that I love and hate this game at the same time. The core gameplay is excellent. The gunplay feels good, the movement is smooth, and fighting the ARC is genuinely fun and challenging. The PvE side of the game is where ARC Raiders really shines. Where the game struggles is PvP, and the issue isn’t the mechanics themselves. The problem is that the community has split into two completely different types of players: Players who want to play mostly PvE Players who want to play mostly PvP For solo players, the developers actually stumbled onto a surprisingly good solution. If you play solo and avoid PvP, the matchmaking tends to group you with other players who also avoid PvP. What you end up with is a cooperative environment where people: Share items Help with quests Fight ARC together Leave each other alone instead of killing on sight The game is already challenging enough just fighting the PvE, and there’s plenty to do without needing PvP. It’s genuinely fun to work through the weekly challenges, complete expeditions, finish quests, hunt down blueprints, upgrade your workshop, and slowly build up your inventory with better and better gear. That progression loop feels rewarding and gives you a lot to work toward. Another interesting side effect is that there are basically no cheaters in this environment. The reason seems pretty simple: if you kill players you get grouped with other PvP-focused players. Since the friendly solo players aren’t killing anyone, they naturally get grouped together and separated from the PvP crowd. Cheaters tend to end up in the PvP pool where the competition actually matters. The real problems start when you play duos. Duos mix PvE-focused players with PvP-focused players, and that’s where the experience becomes frustrating. PvE players usually ask if other players are friendly before getting close. Unfortunately, many times the answer is yes... right up until the moment those players betray them. That dynamic creates a very toxic environment. PvE players feel tricked and betrayed, while PvP players often get shamed and harassed by the people they down before finishing them off. A lot of PvP players don’t even enjoy the experience because dealing with constant insults and accusations just isn’t fun. Neither side ends up happy. The design unintentionally pushes players toward either betraying people first or trusting no one, which slowly makes the social side of the game worse over time. Both styles of player should be able to play the game the way they want without being harassed by the other group constantly. The biggest frustration is that if you want to play with a friend, you’re forced into duos, which means you’re automatically thrown into this toxic middle ground. The solution seems obvious: the game should offer a PvE-only mode and a PvP mode so players can choose the experience they actually want. At least then everyone would know what kind of interaction to expect. Despite all of this, I still put 400+ hours into this game, which should say something about how strong the core gameplay really is. But at this point I’m leaving a negative review and uninstalling. I kept hoping the developers would fix this dynamic, but lately I find myself finishing sessions feeling worse than when I started. Gaming is supposed to be my time to relax and have fun, and this game increasingly just leaves me feeling frustrated and unpleasant. I don’t need something toxic like that in my life. So I’m done. review_text: Post-script edit: The charm of the game does come back when you play it solo, it's a shame that I prefer to play these types of games with a group, which is where it gets extra-sweaty. Even with the charm of playing solo, it's still just getting worse. Every waking decision we're seeing from the devs is a massive fumble; Free loadout guns are meta in PvP, the rewards for wiping your profile are too much take and not enough give, and overall the game ENCOURAGES gear-fear and hoarding your best stuff as opposed to bringing it into raids for fun. After all, the rewards you get at the end of the season are based on your stash value... So why take the valuable stuff out of your stash? It just makes no sense, and I hope the devs get their heads back on soon. The honeymoon period is over, and now that there's no more high to chase, it's just... Another PvP game. Another return-to-lobby simulator where any semblance of progress is torn away by the most braindead of bottom-feeders that sit around and do nothing until you're unfortunate enough to walk into their sights, or make enough noise for them to catch you wounded. There's no incentive for PvE once you've gone far enough, the community has gone to shambles at the hands of streamers, and now it's nothing but throwing yourself at a wall until something sticks. As with every PvP game, the casual playerbase is getting filtered out by the no-lifes and leaving no fun left to be had.

review_text: Arc Raiders launched with something genuinely special: a fun and interesting world that felt worth exploring. The ARC were unknown, clever, and dangerous. They presented problems that required some thought before approaching them, and part of the fun was learning how they operated. PvP wasn't initially the sole focus either. A lot of people seemed genuinely excited to explore the world and help each other survive, which created some really memorable encounters. The players who did decide to go looking for fights were often outnumbered and dealt with accordingly. For a while, the game felt like an actual adventure. Then we learned everything. Once you understood how each ARC worked, they stopped being particularly threatening. Most of them became predictable, especially one-on-one. The ARC went from being something you had to think about to being another obstacle you knew exactly how to deal with. With the ARC becoming a minor threat, the game gradually turned into a massive grind for loot. And the loot itself became incredibly stale. Eventually, most matches stopped being about exploring or scavenging and became a rush to specific locations to get whatever targeted materials you needed for your next Project or upgrade as quickly as possible. Then came the blueprint system, which completely destroyed what I thought was one of the core ideas behind the game. Scavenging and looting should be the reason you enter a match. Instead, blueprints turned the game into a speed-running exercise where everyone races to specific containers hoping for a particular item. You can walk into room after room and find containers already opened and stripped of anything valuable, with the garbage left behind. At that point, you're not really scavenging anymore. You're just farming a loot table. The blueprint system feels archaic and lazy, and it actively works against the original appeal of Arc Raiders. The other major change has been the player base. The "friendly" system has been completely abused by players whose only objective is to get into friendly lobbies, gear themselves up, and kill people who trust them. But only when those players are alone. That's where the term "rat" really comes into play. These are some of the worst people online gaming has to offer: act friendly until you see an opportunity to stab someone in the back, but only when you're certain there's no risk. Then suddenly you're friendly again when you need to escape with the gear you were too lazy to acquire yourself. The problem isn't that PvP exists. PvP was always part of the game. The problem is that the game has gradually lost the sense of wonder and cooperation that made those interactions interesting in the first place. Gone are the days when you could encounter an entire lobby that would team up and run around killing ARC together just because it was fun. Now it feels like most people have simply been playing for too long, and the game has devolved into optimization. And unfortunately, the ARC themselves haven't really evolved in a way that improves this. Instead of introducing machines that are interesting to fight and reward you for understanding their behavior, new ARC often feel like increasingly annoying, heavily armored versions of the things we already know how to kill. Comets are basically a larger, more annoying version of a Pop. They don't add much to the game beyond creating another problem that you often can't realistically deal with unless you're properly geared for it. Heavy armor, ridiculous speed, and an enormous AoE explosion make them miserable to fight if you're not prepared. And if you're caught in the open? Good luck. The "strategy" often boils down to baiting them toward you, hiding behind a wall, and waiting for them to explode. That's not an interesting encounter. That's cheesing an enemy because the alternative is simply eating unavoidable damage. Fireflies are another example. They're more heavily armored, more aggressive, and constantly dealing damage while flying alongside Hornets and Wasps. Their flames obscure your vision, they don't offer particularly satisfying weak points, and even their exposed fuel tank takes multiple shots to destroy. The propellers are technically a target, but they're even harder to hit than the weak points on the Hornets and Wasps. It's difficulty for the sake of annoyance. The Vaporizer, on the other hand, is one of the better examples of how new ARC should be designed. It's incredibly powerful, but actually fun to fight. Its shield creates an opportunity because it can't attack you while it's active. You can reposition, find better cover, bait out an opening, and then punish the weak point. It's dangerous without simply being a massive bullet sponge. That's the difference. The problem isn't that ARC are difficult. The problem is when difficulty comes from armor, damage, speed, and inflated health rather than interesting mechanics. And the recent events have only amplified the worst parts of the game. Massive grind-fests filled with huge numbers of some of the most annoying ARC, encouraging players to smoke out areas just to loot under cover while other players take advantage of the chaos to shoot them in the back and steal the loot. Then you have the "boss" ARC that can be trivialized by Deadmine junkies while being absurdly resistant to almost everything else. At some point, it stops feeling like the developers are designing encounters and starts feeling like they're just increasing the numbers until something becomes difficult. And then there's the live-service desperation. This is probably the most frustrating part for me now. After losing the overwhelming majority of its player base, the game is constantly shoving itself back into your face. Forced update screens. Forced event screens. Constant notifications about Trials — a part of the game that I couldn't care less about — being pushed in front of you over and over. And then there's the ♥♥♥ store. The constant store pop-ups don't feel like a game confidently presenting something I might want to buy. They feel like the developers are begging me to spend money. And that's what makes this so disappointing. Arc Raiders had an incredible foundation. The world was interesting. The atmosphere was great. The ARC were fascinating when they were still unknown. The player interactions could be genuinely memorable. But instead of building on those strengths, the game has gradually become a grind-heavy loot treadmill wrapped in increasingly aggressive live-service systems. It's the second live-service game I've seen from this development group that had an incredible foundation and enormous potential, only to be handled in a way that burned through its audience. It's sad watching something with this much potential get reduced to grind, optimization, engagement systems, and increasingly desperate monetization. I've uninstalled Arc Raiders, and at this point, I don't think there's anything they can realistically add that would bring me back. Another dead live-service game. And this one didn't have to be.

review_text: 👍 What I like: The core gameplay is genuinely fantastic. The PvPvE concept works. The gunplay feels good, the atmosphere is great, progression is satisfying and the risk versus reward gameplay loop is addictive. When everything works, this game creates some of the most intense and memorable moments I've had in extraction shooters. I enjoy building up my stash, upgrading weapons, planning routes, fighting over objectives and extracting with valuable loot. Losing gear doesn't bother me. In fact, gear loss is what gives successful raids value in the first place. The gameplay loop is simple: Loot. Fight. Win better loot or lose your gear. Rebuild. Repeat. That's the magic of extraction shooters. 👎 What I don't like: The cheating situation in aggressive PvP matchmaking is awful. Most cheaters are not farming robots and avoiding combat. They want kills, gear, K/D and the feeling of dominating other players. That's why many PvE-focused players have a completely different experience from people who actively seek PvP every raid. The obvious rage hackers are not even the main issue anymore. Most of what I encounter are players who seem to have way too much information. Always knowing the correct flank. Always rotating to the correct exit. Always pre-aiming the exact angle. Always making the right decision with no information available. Maybe some are legit. Maybe some aren't. The problem is that it happens often enough that you start questioning every fight. Another issue is the community constantly trying to pull the game into one extreme or the other. I am completely in favor of PvE. I am completely in favor of PvP. What I am not in favor of is turning a PvPvE extraction shooter into a pure farming simulator where people spend hours shooting wasps, filling their stash, avoiding players and then wondering why they are bored. Of course your stash is always full if nothing ever threatens it. Of course the gameplay loop eventually feels stale if there is no risk. The entire point of the genre is that players are the danger. The loot only matters because somebody can take it from you. I genuinely don't understand buying a PvPvE game, reading that other players can kill you, and then spending months complaining that other players kill you. That's like buying a horror game and complaining that it's scary. Or joining a boxing gym and being upset when someone throws a punch. ⚖️ Final thoughts: Do I recommend the game? Right now, no. Do I still play it? Yes. Because underneath the cheating issues and community arguments there is a genuinely excellent game. The frustrating part isn't that the game is bad. The frustrating part is that the game is good enough to become one of the best extraction shooters available if its biggest problems get addressed.

review_text: ARC Raiders: A Breath of Fresh Air for Extraction Shooters When I first played The Finals, I was blown away by Embark’s attention to detail. The intuitive UI, the weighty sound design, and the overall polish. So, when I learned they were creating their own extraction shooter, my excitement skyrocketed. ARC Raiders doesn’t disappoint. Its PvP is intense, the gunplay feels powerful, and the world-building is distinct and atmospheric. Even the AI demands respect, creating encounters that rival those against human players. Like all good extraction shooters, it’s unforgiving. Losing a gear set you’ve carried through several raids hurts every time, yet it’s exactly that risk that keeps you coming back for more. Naturally, comparisons to Escape From Tarkov are unavoidable. While Tarkov wasn’t the first extraction shooter, it defined the genre with its realism and punishing mechanics. Having spent nearly a year’s worth of hours in Tarkov, I can confidently say that while the gameplay loops are similar, ARC Raiders and Tarkov diverge in design philosophy. Tarkov itself is brilliant yet demanding. Being difficult to run on older hardware, time-consuming, and endgame achievements being inaccessible to casual players. ARC Raiders, on the other hand, feels like the genre’s evolution: it opens the door to a wider audience without sacrificing depth. With crossplay, a strong foundation, and Embark’s proven passion, ARC Raiders could be the bridge between hardcore and mainstream extraction shooters. If Embark continues to nurture it with the same care they gave The Finals, we might be witnessing the next defining title of the genre.

review_text: After 430 hours, I don’t really feel like I can judge ARC Raiders the same way someone would after playing it for a few hours. At this point I’ve spent enough time with the game to see both why I keep coming back for another raid and the things that start getting annoying when you’ve played the same loop for a very long time. The core gameplay loop is probably what keeps me here. You go in, look for loot, deal with ARC machines, keep an eye out for other players, and eventually try to get out with what you’ve found. It’s a simple idea, but the decisions become much more meaningful once you’re carrying something you actually don’t want to lose. Do I stay a little longer and risk everything for more loot, or do I just leave while things are going well? That risk/reward feeling is a big part of why I can still enjoy the game after 430 hours. I also like how the PvE and PvP don’t feel completely separate. You’re dealing with ARC machines while also having to think about what other players might be doing nearby. Hearing a fight in the distance or suddenly realizing another player might be around can completely change how you approach a situation. Sometimes you don’t even want a PvP fight, but the possibility of one is always part of the decision-making. For me, that’s one of the strongest parts of the extraction gameplay. Looting and managing your gear become much more important the longer you play. You can’t take everything, and you shouldn’t. What you decide to carry, what you leave behind and how much you’re willing to risk all become part of the raid. The classic extraction game problem is always there: a raid is going really well, you already have enough, but you think “I’ll stay just a little longer.” That’s usually when things get interesting. The weapons and combat feel good to me overall. Winning a fight isn’t only about aim. Positioning, awareness, knowing when to push and knowing when not to fight matter a lot. The ARC machines also help keep the game from feeling like it’s only about PvP. They can be a direct threat, but they can also affect how you approach other players and how a fight develops. The maps and atmosphere do a lot for the experience too. There’s a constant feeling that staying in one place for too long might be a bad idea. Sound design is especially important here. After enough hours, you start recognizing sounds and paying attention to things you probably wouldn’t even notice when you’re new. Solo and team play also feel noticeably different. With a squad, communication and coordination become much more important. Solo, you’re responsible for reading almost everything yourself, so mistakes feel more personal and every encounter can be a little more stressful. I enjoy both, but they definitely don’t play the same way. Of course, after 430 hours, the weak points are easier to notice too. The repetition becomes more obvious, and not every raid has the same level of tension or excitement. Some runs are incredibly engaging, while others can turn into slow, overly cautious sessions. Losing a good haul after spending a long time collecting it can also be genuinely frustrating, especially when it happens because of one bad decision. Still, I’ve put 430 hours into this game for a reason. It isn’t perfect, and I definitely have moments where I close the game annoyed. But somehow I still find myself thinking about doing “one more raid” and loading back in. After this many hours, that’s probably the most honest review I can give it.

review_text: The game has promise, but the players don't. Look, this game can be REALLY fun - taking down massive machines is an absolute thrill. Hiding, sneaking about, scavenging, surviving against malevolent overlords - it's all the hallmarks of an enjoyable game... ...until you're shot in the back of the head by a rat. Look, I get it, this game has PvE and PvP elements. I've never been opposed to testing your mettle against another player, but this isn't what's happening here. This isn't glorious combat - this is spineless backstabbing. People saying they're friendly and then shooting you in the back. People seeing you're using a Hullcracker and knowing you can't hurt another raider with that weapon. It's predatory nonsense, and it pulls me out of the excitement of the game every time without fail. I want to drop in and TEAM UP with people to bring down the enemy. I don't want to have to listen for every footstep and think, "Oh boy, time to die". And I know what comes with a complaint like this, and yes, it IS a skill issue. I will be the first to admit that I do not react as quickly as others, but I also don't WANT to. You can check my achievements if you want - you'll see that I have no achievements for taking down a fellow raider, because that's not what I want from this game. I promise you, if they brought in a PvE only mode, their numbers would JUMP - because some of us just want to enjoy the area, the fight against the REAL enemies, and then extract without a rat waiting in the shadows.

review_text: At the beginning, ARC Raiders was designed primarily as a PvE experience. Later, PvP was added, and the game evolved into a mix of PvE and PvP. The idea behind that balance made sense: create a system that could match players based on aggression level and play style, allowing different types of players to have different kinds of experiences. On paper, that sounds great. The problem is that some PvP-focused players appear to have learned how to manipulate that system. They figured out how to play in a way that gets them placed into more passive or “friendly” lobbies. Once that happens, especially on boss maps, the experience can feel broken before the match even really starts. Players come in prepared to fight the boss, often bringing their best gear and setting up for a PvE-focused encounter. Then someone who has no real intention of helping with the boss waits for the right moment, shoots them in the back, and extracts with the loot. They contributed almost nothing to the objective, but they still walk away with the reward. There are also players who run around claiming to be “friendly,” only to attack once someone lowers their guard. I am not saying players should never watch their backs. This is still an extraction game, and risk is part of the experience. But when people are intentionally gaming the matchmaking system to get into easier lobbies, that feels less like normal PvP and more like exploiting the system. After the expansion, I started seeing this happen on boss maps far more often, especially in friendly lobbies. Players load in with good gear, ready for the PvE fight, only to get quickly taken out by someone whose entire strategy is to prey on the lobby rather than engage with the actual boss encounter. At that point, it becomes almost impossible to enjoy the boss content the way it seems to have been intended. I liked the algorithm-based matchmaking idea at first. I thought it was a smart way to let different play styles coexist. But once players learned how to abuse it, the system became unreliable. It now feels like the algorithm has been figured out, manipulated, and effectively broken. What makes the issue worse is that the same players abusing these lobbies often argue that “this is a PvP extraction game” and that this is simply how the game is supposed to be played. But if that is true, then why would they oppose a PvE/PvP switch or separate queue? A switch would not hurt players who genuinely want competitive PvP. They could still choose PvP. The only people it would really affect are the ones who rely on getting easy kills against players who are not looking for that kind of fight. That is the real issue. It is not about removing PvP from the game. It is about stopping players from exploiting the system to target friendly or PvE-focused lobbies for easy loot. ARC Raiders needs a proper switch, separate mode, or stronger matchmaking protection because the current algorithm is no longer working as intended. The system has been exploited, and it is damaging the enjoyment, achievement, and balance that made the game feel exciting in the first place.

review_text: I bought this game little over 4 months after the release and my experience with it was very good, since I was mostly playing solo. In my experience, most people in solo lobbies were cooperative, didn't want to kill me and were sometimes even helpful. I advise you to avoid fighting Arc robots in the start (low levels), since you will be very weak and every battle can be lethal. You will become stronger as you progress through the game though. Playing with a friend was not so carefree, because most people in duos are not friendly from my experience and want to kill you, which added another level of complexity to the game. The graphics is very good, but I was experiencing a 2 second lag occasionally while playing the game, though the game seems to be well optimized. There are not many bugs, the gameplay is fluent (no missing animations) and sometimes even scary or thrilling. The game may feel grindy and repetitive sometimes, if you are playing one map only, or grinding resources for a project like the Expedition, but some aspects of the gameplay are randomized, so it doesn't become too boring too soon. I became addicted to it for a while, because it was nice and I wanted to become good at it and I still have a lot to learn about other maps. If you are looking for an extraction shooter, this game delivers what it promises and a little more, because it is receiving regular updates based on player feedback. There are plenty of guides online to help you improve in the game, some things in the game are similar to other games you might have played, but ultimately it is up to you see if you like it or not. This game is not for people who give up easily though. It rewards good strategy and map knowledge, good use of utility like grenades and so on. I recommend this game based on my very positive experience with it. It reignited my love for gaming too. I guess there will always be people who talk about more PvE or more PvP, but you can safely ignore that and see for yourself if you like the game. That is it for my review now and I wish you good fun!

review_text: I got enough enjoyment out of ARC for what I paid for it (around £30) but have decided to pack it in. A bit of background, I've 2k+ hours on Hunt:Showdown, and untold hours gaming in general over the past 40+ years - and whilst I had a nice honeymoon with ARC, it wasn't long before the sheen wore down and the ugly parts began to show. - On release we had absurd hit registration, they addressed this is patch 1, so good on them, it's still not amazing, but it's better. Expect to be hit round corners, play with jiggle peeks and see how they work for you; I think the server predicts you'll keep moving and gives the peek-ee chance to hammer you. - There are no loadouts - what I mean by this is the only quick way into a game is to take the free loadout, which hands you a random tier 1 weapon, a full stack of ammo, a basic shield, no safe slot, and a random assortment of consumables which can contain useless items, like binoculars. If you want to take another loadout you build it all from your inventory, and if you need to craft some of that well get comfortable because you'll be here a while navigating menus and remembering which bench it is that crafts ammo (no, it's not the gunsmith bench) This process is painful when you're on a loosing streak and you quickly run out of resources so resort to the free loadouts. In Hunt:Showdown a free hunter would be chosen from a small roster so you could pick the best one for your playstyle, strengths or team makeup. You could also augment the hunter with odd items you had in your stash, in ARCs case - more bandages and shield rechargers are pretty bloody basic items - especially when the game can spawn you right next to other raiders or AI. - You are also massively undergeared to PvP with a free raider, that wasn't the case in the beta or early days, but now we begin to see that with tier 3 guns, shields more commonplace - remember you have a single shield recharge and bandage - a single shot from another raider and you're on your last legs. - Even getting the drop on another raider, you'll empty the clip into their heads if you happen to get a good close range option, reload, and they'll drill through your level 1 shield in 3 or 4 shots, bam, dead, back to crafting menu. And so it suffers the dark and darker issue all over again, a failure to balance or match up vs players of similar gearing. - You will also spawn into a round halfway - this means the dynamic of play is changed, you have no idea where anybody might be, where they might have been, what loot places are taken or trapped, oh that quest you wanted to do that needs 25 minutes? Nope, not enough time friend, extract, back to menu. - Searching items is just watching progress bars, then more bars waiting for the items to appear, it's like my guys got cataract or something, I can just imagine him squinting into the drawer he's searching trying to make out the mix tape they've just found. - Certain items and weapons are locked behind bench upgrades, and some of the items you need to do that are stupidly hard to find, i.e rusted gears, this further separates the lower and higher players since higher level weapons make a big enough difference to turn the tide in a fight. I don't even want to tell you how long I tried finding prickly pears. Embark have made a good game here, it's styled very 80's / star-wars to appear to us 80's kids - and I enjoyed the time I spent discovering the game - after a night of repeated losses I recognised something I'd felt before with Hunt... crippling lows to the feeling and flow of playing the game, but this time, without the highs of landing that headshot with the worst weapon in the game - Hunt became an unhealthy habit for me, I know that ARC becomes that for me, it becomes an abusive relationship and I'm not blindly in love with Arc, I'm sorry but you just don't do it like Hunt did it for me, it's not worth it. I do like how lethal the Arc can be, the maps are pretty, the guns and stuff feel good, the setting is fleshed out and the lore compelling, the store isn't obnoxiously placed in the menus or anything though the prices are steep. Later in the evening I played other games I'd put down because of ARC and as fate would have it, ended up in tears of laughter with friends just enjoying my free time. I left for the evening feeling good; That's what gaming is for me, ARC cannot reliably deliver that.

review_text: If the Steam comments section is like every other comments section for this game, I expect to get flamed for this negative review, but the lame PVP ruins solo play. review_text: This game is fantastic at its core, but I cannot recommend it in its current state. This game was marketed as both a PVP and PVE experience, yet the reality is that the PVE side has been almost completely erased by the way the community and loadout system function. The overwhelming majority of players have adopted the kill-on-sight or worse, the befriend and betray mentality, which wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the risk and reward were balanced. Right now, there is little to no incentive to bring high-tier gear into a raid. Any player can load into a game with a free loadout and still reliably kill someone who is risking valuable gear. This creates a situation where hoarding gear isn't just encouraged, but required, because bringing anything good almost guarantees you'll lose it to someone with nothing to lose. As a result, the PVE content suffers immensely. ARCS are actively avoided because engaging them requires gear that is too risky to bring. This problem is even worse for new or casual players, because they cannot acquire and retain the gear needed to take down bigger ARCS. This means a lot of quests cannot be fulfilled unless you are blessed with a kind lobby, or you simply join the rats and steal from others. The PVE aspect essentially becomes useless then, and you are left in a frustrating loop where ignoring half of the advertised experience is the only way to progress. The longer this continues, the worse this problem will become. As the weeks go by and the player base becomes more established, new and casual players will have an increasingly difficult time acquiring the materials needed to upgrade their workstations. Without upgraded workstations, they cannot craft better gear, meaning they cannot engage with PVE content, which is required for the majority of quests. This leaves them effectively stuck at the start of the game. The aggression-based matchmaking does little to alleviate the loadout problem, because in most matches, there are still multiple highly aggressive players who camp the spawn and extraction zones and kill Raiders, again risking little on their part. Some of these spawn camp deaths also occur while the players load in, as mid-game spawns are enabled and poorly protected from trolls. If this game were marketed as a PVP extraction shooter or a PVE co-op game, there would be no problem with either playstyle. However, the current blend of both creates an unfun, toxic and exhausting loop full of childish people who cannot work cooperatively and who believe that shooting people in the back while risking none of their own gear is the only way to enjoy the game. And any attempt to raise these concerns is routinely dismissed as a skill issue on the new player's part, despite the fact that the game actively rewards low-risk griefing over meaningful cooperation or PVE battles. TLDR - ARC Raiders is supposed to be a blend of PVP and PVE, but its current systems reward zero-risk PVP with free loadouts while punishing anyone engaging with PVE. This makes progression nearly impossible for new and casual players, and any criticism is brushed off by the community as a 'skill issue', despite the issue being rooted in the poor balance and design. Edit - If you're still not convinced that the community has a problem, just take a look at my comments. And shout out to all you people proving my point, your lack of basic reading comprehension makes my day.

review_text: TL:DR - I'm conflicted I've followed the game for some time, ever since I heard about the AI/reinforcement learning implemented for the ARC machines. I normally would not play an extraction shooter/looter, but reconsidered purchasing after I heard about ABMM (Agression Based Match-Making). The idea behind it is, that if you don't shoot at others you will be put in the lobbies with more friendly players. This is where problems start; it created a division within the community. Some people really like it, some despise it - and there is a group that even gambles this system. The so called by the community "rat players" would attack unsuspecting players just before extracting, either posing as friendly players or hiding in a corner. This results in you being shot from behind, with no counter play - dead before you can respond. While this seems fun for the first few hours, it gets old quickly. Responding to human threats, ah! Here's another problem - if you shoot back, your ABMM raises and you get put into mixed lobby of peaceful players and aggresive players. Continue to shoot back, and you will be put in kill-on-sight lobby. In the end I just don't shoot back and write off every 6-10th game as a random loss. Not fun. The PVP crowd would say, that this is a part of the game and you should "get better" in PVP as it is a part of the game. But to get better you have to start shooting back, which will put you in strict PVP lobbies you might hate. The PVE crowd would say, there is a need to split PVE and PVP lobby to prevent this behaviour. But this would result in almost no challenge after you learn how the ARC machines operate and pointless resource grind. I don't know what is the right option, I don't want to guess. I can just say that whatever it is currently it is not it. Which is a shame, because the game is really good otherwise - good graphics, really well optimized. The machines are really cool. Should you choose to buy it, at least now you know what it struggles with.

review_text: Arc Raiders This game is amazing. From the moment you drop in it’s clear that Arc Raiders is something special. The sound design and overall audio quality are absolutely top-notch. The AI is some of the smartest I’ve ever seen in a game. For example if you mount a Rocketeer or somehow manage to climb on top of it, it will literally try to throw you off. There are tons of little reactive behaviours like this that make every encounter feel special, for better or worse. Playing Solo If you plan on playing solo, the game leans toward a more peaceful experience. Players are generally more open to interaction, many won’t shoot on sight and there’s a real chance for friendly encounters or temporary team-ups. The solo matchmaking keeps things fair by pairing you only against other solos which makes exploration and looting tense but not overwhelming. You’ll often find yourself emoting "dont shoot" or teaming up briefly with others desperate for an extraction escort. Playing Duos They added a dedicated duo queue in the recent patch! Playing Trios In trios teamfights become much more possible and coordinated groups can dominate. It feels like a completely different game from solos, faster, louder and way more chaotic but also incredibly fun even if you’re filling with randoms. What’s great is that cycling between solo and trio sessions keeps the experience fresh, it genuinely feels like you’re playing two separate games each with its own vibe and pacing. I’d recommend Arc Raiders to anyone. It’s a surprisingly “easy” game in the sense that no loss feels extremely punishing, you can always recover. The upcoming Prestige system adds even more replayability, letting you reset your character for small permanent buffs like extra skill points or increased stash space. [UPDATE 2025/11/14] Embark Studios continue to suprise the playerbase. They reduced store prices for cosmetics, dropped a new map + a free reward "track" for just playing on it plus a bunch of new arcs and items. If you're still considering the game, it's never too late to jump in!

review_text: Well, as much as I hate to write this review, I can't recommend the game at its current state. To start off, the community is literally doomed, the game has lost around 90% of its player count. Now, how does that affect the game? Let me explain. You see, back when the game launched, there was a lot of hype and talk about Arc Raiders, because it was truly a special experience. As a player, you could never really know who you might run into: whether the person was a casual player who wanted to team up and uncover ARC's mysteries, or a die-hard PvP enjoyer. That uncertainty was one of the things that made Arc Raiders special in the first place. As time went on, the community got split up by something called "aggression-based matchmaking," a system designed to make sure players who seek PvE end up in "PvE lobbies," while players who seek PvP end up in "PVP lobbies." Because of that, you now basically have to "choose" a playstyle to reach your goals: want to do quests and farm ARC for workbenches or projects? Go be a PvE player. Want to take other players' loot and hunt them down for fun? Go be a PvP player. This system doesn't sound bad on paper, right? Every player gets a lobby that matches their playstyle. Well, not quite. Because the community got split into two separate sides, both sides ended up worse off, not better. I'm a mixed playstyle player myself, I enjoy both sides of the game, and honestly that's exactly why this split bothers me so much. Neither side feels fully rewarding right now. On the PvE side: progression feels painfully slow. New projects, the main thing that gives PvE players a real long-term goal, only show up once in a while. You can spend hours doing quests and grinding ARC kills, and still be left waiting for the next project to actually drop. It just doesn't feel like there's enough consistently to chase. And in my opinion, the rewards you actually get from those projects aren't that good either, I'm not the only one who thinks so, from what I've seen a good chunk of the community feels the same way about it. On top of that, the Expedition system kind of sucks too. The only reason it's even worth doing, in my opinion, is the 5 skill points, some extra stash space, and the repair percentage buff, the repair buff being my main reason honestly. Everything else about it barely feels worth the trouble. And what makes it worse is that once you start an Expedition, you can't skip it, you're locked in and have to keep starting over again and again, or your progress and buffs just reset. That's especially painful in the game's current state, where you're already short on reasons to keep playing in the first place. On the PvP side: things aren't much better. A huge chunk of the players you run into are using free kits, meaning there's barely any risk on their end while you're the one putting your actual loot on the line. On top of that, cheaters are still a real problem. To be fair to Embark, they have been trying to do something about it: they've been testing map conditions that affect free kit availability, and they rolled out Denuvo Anti-Cheat alongside their existing Easy Anti-Cheat and Anybrain ML-based detection to try to catch cheaters earlier. It's a step in the right direction, but from where I'm standing, it still isn't enough to fix how the PvP side actually feels to play. And then there's Stella Montis, the map everyone knows as the PvP map. For some reason, every time my friends and I decide to risk our good loot and queue into a Night Raid there, that's exactly when things go wrong. We get picked off by campers or cheaters, and to make it worse, there's no hatch key available to fall back on for a safer extraction. So if the fight goes bad, we're stuck fighting our way out through the front door with everyone else. And if we instead queue into a regular match to avoid that? It barely helps. Almost everyone we run into is still using free kits, and on top of that, the match itself frequently spawns us in dark, Night Raid-like conditions anyway, so we end up dealing with the same visibility problems either way. Now, I want to be clear about one thing: I don't want Embark to rush out updates just to fill the silence. Rushed content usually means more bugs and half-baked features, and that's not what I'm asking for. But there does need to be a little bit more happening between these long update windows. Right now it just feels like too much dead time where both sides of the community are left waiting, one side for content, the other for the game to actually feel fair. Until PvE gets more consistent things to work toward, and PvP actually deals with free kits and cheaters in a way that holds up, I can't recommend Arc Raiders in its current state.

review_text: Not Recommended (after 600+ hours... and it hurts to say that) I’ve put 600+ hours into Arc Raiders and unlocked almost all achievements, so this isn’t coming from someone who just tried the game and quit. I’ve been here since the early days, when the game felt fresh, cooperative, and full of potential. And that’s why this review is so difficult to write. Because I love this game at its core. The atmosphere, the beautiful environments, the map design, the social aspects and the intensity of fighting ARC enemies... when Arc Raiders is at its best, it’s one of the most immersive multiplayer experiences out there. But the game today is not the game we started with. The playerbase has gotten worse... Much worse... Over the past few weeks, the experience has taken a serious downturn. The number of “rats” is out of control, players pretending to cooperate, acting friendly, then shooting you in the back the moment it benefits them. Yes, betrayal is part of the game. But when almost every interaction ends this way, it stops being an interesting mechanic and becomes a toxic default behavior. Instead of tense cooperation, the game has become a constant trust-no-one simulator. Cheating Is still a big problem (and penalties feel weak). Cheating and exploiting haven’t gone away, and honestly, the response to it feels far too lenient. Right now, it feels like cheaters get nothing more than a slap on the wrist. Whether it’s exploits, suspicious gameplay, or outright hacks, there doesn’t seem to be a strong enough deterrent to stop people from doing it again. And in a game where you can lose everything in a run, that completely kills motivation to keep playing. Nothing feels worse than losing progress not because you got outplayed, but because someone decided to cheat. Player experience Is declining, you can feel the shift in-game: - Fewer genuine, cooperative players - More sweaty PvP-focused players (with cheats) - More toxic encounters overall The early magic, where players would sometimes help each other, improvise alliances, and focus on surviving ARC together is almost gone. What Is Embark even doing? This is the most frustrating part. It feels like Embark is listening to the hardcore PvP minority, instead of the much larger group of players who enjoyed the cooperative PvE aspects of the game. Most updates focus on: - PvP balance - Weapon tuning - Bug fixes But the core issues such as lack of incentives to cooperate, toxic player behavior, weak anti-cheat impact, remain largely unaddressed. The game has changed... And not for the better I was here when: - Encounters felt exciting, not exhausting - Cooperation was common - Fighting ARC was the main focus - The world felt alive and unpredictable Now it feels like: - PvP dominates everything - Trust is gone - The social experience has broken down Final Verdict: I’ve invested hundreds of hours. I’ve unlocked almost everything the game has to offer. And I still believe Arc Raiders has insane potential. But right now, it feels like an amazing game being dragged down by: - A toxic player meta - Weak enforcement against cheating - A direction that doesn’t match what many players actually want (mind you, 90% of the playerbase are casual players) I really want to recommend this game. But I just can’t anymore. I hope Embark turns things around... because this game deserves better. EDIT: Didn’t expect this review to blow up. Thanks for all the comments, positive and negative. It’s clear a lot of players feel strongly about the direction the game is heading. Quick clarifications (since there’s been confusion): 1. About the extra hours Those hours were added after my original review because: - The Riven Tides update released, and I needed time to properly test the new content. - Embark Studios made last-minute changes to Expeditions. What was expected to be a coin grind became a damage grind, forcing players to put in extra hours just to secure 5 bonus skill points. Extra hours don’t mean the game is fine, they reflect testing new content and reacting to sudden changes. 2. I’m NOT asking for a PvE mode Some people keep assuming this. My feedback is about how the playerbase has shifted and how recent updates seem to reward “rat” behavior and pushing towards PVP. That’s based on experience, not a request for PvE-only gameplay. 3. Enjoying the game ≠ positive review I enjoy the gameplay and can put in many hours when I want to. But that doesn’t override the current experience. A review reflects the state of the game right now, and at this point I can’t recommend it. 4. “Casual players” ≠ PvE players “Casual” refers to players who simply have limited hours to game, often working adults or people with other commitments. They can still enjoy the game, but they don’t have the time to constantly grind sudden changes, adapt to shifting systems, or re-do progress every time the game direction changes. Hope that clarifies things. Would be good if the comments stayed respectful and on topic. Thank you
