review_text: Having played nearly 100 hours to really get to know it I can say it has MASSIVE potential, but is ruined by how it works most of the time and feels 99% of the time, which is to say a depressing, shallow, pointless effort because whatever progress you make and whatever good experiences you enjoy will be mostly undone and/or out-weighed by the constant fear (and actuality) of being shot in the back. If I could give it a mixed recommendation, I would, but since it's "yes" or "no" I have to recommend, "no" for most folks. You end up making progress and getting better gear but hardly ever using it because you will almost certainly lose it when you do. Some advise you just forget the 'gear fear' and that it's your choice, but the problem is the balance in PvP is awful. A bushwacking rat can have a free load-out and kill you with just a little knowledge, planning and sociopathy or even just luck/surprise. The game (and gear) is balanced when fighting ARC. There is little advantage in using good gear unless you are going up against ARC and this is one of the favourite points at which the rats will sneak up and murder you - when you've just fought a dangerous ARC and worn away the minimal PvP advantage your good gear might have gotten you. This is a PvPvE game. People don't seem to understand what that means. To be fair, I don't think the devs know what it should be either, so it's understandable that players are confused. What PvPvE in ARC Raiders means is there is a CHOICE. PvP is OPTIONAL. Very optional in fact, since the game lore, story, events, mechanics, etc are all based around anti-ARC co-op PvE, but unfortunately too many simply appear to have psychotic tendencies and when given the choice of attacking other players and looting everything they have earned, they kill on sight or worse, befriend and betray. This is even though it is actually more beneficial and lucrative to work together... The psychos will tell you "it's just a game" and "don't be a care-bear" etc to cope with the feelings of being a scum-bag, but fully sane and well-adjusted people know that, yes, it _is indeed_ just a game and when it doesn't matter either way but you _still_ choose to murder and steal, then there is something a bit weird about you. The lore/story of the game is that humanity HAS pulled together to survive. They HAVE formed communities for the betterment of society and to give themselves a future. They train and supply raiders to go to the surface and retrieve supplies essential to the survival of all. Life is tough so, sure, if there is 'bad' behaviour up there, like stealing someone else's loot, then the threat of violence is a good balance, but when it becomes the default with no consequences whatsoever it is an utter chaotic imbalance. In any cohesive narrative raiders that choose for no reason to kill other raiders would be at best sanctioned. Traders would refuse to help them. There would be no free load-outs from those running the raids. What would probably happen is they get ostracised or even exiled and hunted down. In game terms what we are talking about is a notoriety system that would give some depth and meaning to the choice to attack other players instead of it being meaningless and with zero repercussion or consequence. Also, it seems the devs are intending to push this further. In the up-coming expedition where players can choose to start over but with advantages, the most important of those advantages (a raising of the skill point cap) depends on gathering together up to 5,000,000 cash/stash - 1m per skill point. In fact it's _much_ more than that because to even take part you have to commit probably 1,000,000 worth of gear to build your caravan. One obvious and immediate upshot is that players become even more greedy and pressured to murder steal. They get into a raid at 15 to 20 minute mark and they know all the good loot has been taken and is probably being carried by other raiders. The devs know this. There are other indicators that they don't care, such as some Feats relying on damaging other raiders. I have lots of free time at the moment and have put in nearly 100 hours and have built the caravan and saved up maybe 2,500,000. Only the very hardcore players will be able to get the best from the expedition system. Those players that already have advantage in a way that is at least 'natural' - if not totally 'fair' - will be handed further advantage every expedition. For those that have less time to play and probably care more about their progression and the feeling of becoming better equipped to survive and maybe begin to take on the harder ARC events, they will get pushed further and harder away as time goes on. TLDR: The way this game currently is and seems to be planned to be, wanton PvP with no repercussion or consequence will ruin it. The inevitable baddies that infest and ruin most games with griefing and ganking will find a very comfy home here and everyone else will get depressed and bored and find a game where the co-op PvE actually works and/or there is some depth and meaning to the PvP. It's a shame. This could have been so much better. It could _still_ be made better. Servers with different rulesets. Match-making based on behaviour. Notoriety system of some kind. But until then I will do the expedition just to say I did and recommend people with less stamina for grind stay away. P.S. Just had a look at the comments. Lol. Unsurprising. Some people feeling the same making cogent comment and lots of others showing the same dumb toxic attitude that makes them KOS psychos and scumbag rats in game. Thank you all for proving my point. OK some actually did make sensible comments defending ARC Raiders as an 'extraction shooter' or a PvP game. But, to them I'll say what I pretty much already said: It's not just an extraction shooter. It's not just a PvP game. Many people are playing it like it is just like any other and it is so much more, or at least it could be if they quit ruining it or Embark bother to put in some kind of calming influence on the wanton mindless PvP.

review_text: A Masterpiece of Optimization, but a Crisis of Progression and Purpose The game’s foundation is rock-solid: smooth optimization, beautiful visuals, and satisfying gunplay. However, once you peel back the layers, the core loop suffers from a severe lack of rewarding content and a disconnect between developer intent and player reality. The "Exploration" Paradox: Snap and Salvage The developers clearly want us to "explore and absorb the atmosphere" of each map. However, quests like "Snap and Salvage" achieve the exact opposite. By forcing players to find a single Epic item with an abysmal spawn rate in the tiny, cramped map of Stella Montis, they aren't encouraging exploration—they are forcing monotonous farming. Instead of interacting with the map, players are locked into a 2-minute "speed-run" route, clearing the dense loot rooms before anyone else can, then extracting to repeat the cycle for 10+ hours. This isn't exploration; it's a chore. Weapon Meta & The "Coin Hoarding" Simulator The equipment balance is currently upside down. When Common and Rare weapons consistently outperform Legendaries, the motivation to grind disappears. Tier Disparity: The Bettina is essentially scrap, while the Aphelion (Legendary) is outclassed by a Ferro. Economy: Because high-tier gear isn't worth the investment, the game turns into a "Coin Hoarding Simulator." You reach the 5-million mark for the expedition with nothing meaningful to spend it on, as your mid-tier gear is already "BiS" (Best in Slot) for all practical purposes. Broken Challenge: The Wolfpack Problem The game offers a decent challenge until you unlock the Wolfpack recipe. From that point on, the survival horror and tactical elements vanish. By carrying 6 Wolfpacks into a raid, you effectively turn a high-stakes extraction shooter into a "Walking Simulator." Bosses and drone swarms that should be terrifying become minor inconveniences that you simply "delete" with a button press. Community Events & Social Integrity The Queen and Matriarch events are meant to unite the community, but the lack of a contribution-based reward system turns them into a toxic sprint. It’s a race to see who can loot the carcass first, regardless of who did the heavy lifting. Furthermore, the daily influx of RMT (Real Money Trading) friend-request spam suggests that the social and economic integrity of the game needs urgent developer intervention.

review_text: Embark just achieved something I don’t think any other developer truly has — and most of us haven’t even realized it yet because we’re too busy nitpicking. They’ve created a game that’s actually fun and accessible to every kind of gamer. They know our gamer instincts perfectly and hinted they monitor behavior for a better matchmaking... Want to sweat in PvP? Go for it — it’s a blast. Want to mess around? You can do that too. Feel like role-playing? Absolutely. Craving a tough PvE challenge? It’s there. Want immersion, emotional highs and lows, moments of celebration and bitter losses? All of it exists on the same map, at the same time, for everyone — with matchmaking that somehow makes it all work. I always wonder what it would be like to experience a moment in gaming history — how players of that time reacted. Some complained, some celebrated, some didn’t even notice what they were part of. With a new Cold Snap update and added guitar I`ve seen Arc Raiders form a music band: guitar, flute and shaker. Those boys played music all the way until extract...we thought this is what it must've been like before the machines... for a brief moment... topside was ours again. This feels like one of those moments. I LOVE IT. See ya topside, Raiders!!

review_text: I really enjoyed ARC Raiders when I first started playing. The gameplay was fresh, the atmosphere was fantastic, and every raid felt exciting. It had me hooked for quite a while. Unfortunately, the more I played, the less I wanted to log in. PvP has become the focus of almost every encounter, making it feel like you can’t enjoy exploring or completing objectives without constantly being hunted. Instead of feeling tense and rewarding, it often just feels frustrating. The community hasn’t helped either. It’s incredibly difficult to find friendly or cooperative players. Most encounters end in kill-on-sight, and the overall experience feels much more toxic than enjoyable. I know that’s part of an extraction shooter, but there needs to be some room for different playstyles if you want to keep a broader player base engaged. I still think the core game is excellent, and that’s what makes this so disappointing. The world, gunplay, and overall design have so much potential. But right now, the constant PvP and the lack of positive player interactions have completely killed my motivation to keep playing. I hope the developers find ways to encourage more meaningful interactions and make the experience feel less like a nonstop PvP deathmatch. I’d love a reason to come back, but for now, I’m moving on. Right now I can’t recommend arc raiders... maybe after some updates.

review_text: I’m honestly starting to hate this game. Every single time I finally secure high-value loot, I get wiped by rats and free-loadout players camping in corners like that’s the entire meta. It’s not skill. It’s not smart play. It’s low-risk behavior that the game actively rewards. What’s the point of grinding for gear, planning routes, winning fights, and taking real risks if someone with nothing to lose can sit in a dark spot for 20 minutes and delete you in two seconds? That’s not “hardcore.” That’s broken design. The risk-reward system feels completely backwards. Players who bring real gear and actually engage are punished the hardest. Meanwhile, people running free or disposable kits have zero fear and zero consequence. If they lose, nothing happens. If they win, they walk away stacked. That imbalance ruins the competitive integrity. Instead of rewarding mechanical skill, smart rotations, and tactical decision-making, the game rewards patience-abusing campers who avoid interaction until the easiest possible moment. It turns intense raids into coin flips. You can do everything right and still lose to someone who contributed nothing to the match except hiding. That’s not tension — it’s frustration. A hardcore game should reward risk, skill, and confidence. Right now, it rewards passivity and cheese tactics. The balance feels off, the flow feels stale, and the overall experience feels more unfair than challenging. If this is the intended gameplay loop, then it’s a serious design problem. Because at this point, it doesn’t feel competitive — it feels punishing for anyone who actually tries to play the game properly. Fix the risk-reward balance. Stop incentivizing rats. Reward actual engagement. Until then, this just feels bad.

review_text: Arc Raiders has a lot going for it- the world looks great, the gunplay feels good, and the PvE is surprisingly well-designed. The AI forces you to think, position, and play smart. Every encounter you take needs to be deliberate, and beating a tough fight is genuinely satisfying. But then there’s the PvP- and that’s where the game loses its footing. The problem is twofold: - There’s almost no real incentive to PvP. - Despite that, everyone still does it. I join maps expecting fights, but 9 out of 10 players I kill have nothing worth taking- usually the same salvaged junk I already have. So you engage in pvp fights for basically no gain and then punish someone else. That leaves PvE as the only real “progression” loop, primarily against higher level AI mobs. It’s fun, it’s challenging, and the rewards make it worth your effort- until someone camping in a bush ends your run and walks off with everything you just earned. So you end up in this weird middle ground: PvP isn’t rewarding, but PvE isn’t safe. The systems constantly clash instead of complementing each other. And that’s a shame, because under all that, Arc Raiders is actually a great game- it just doesn’t seem to know what kind of game it wants to be. and i think unless this is fixed, the game will spiral downwards

review_text: ARC Raiders has huge potential: gorgeous visuals, smooth movement, satisfying looting, and a community that’s often more chill than average. That said, some current design choices really hurt the experience: Frustrating matchmaking: spawning at 18 minutes out of 30 in several matches in a row... often in areas already looted within a 400m radius → you’re basically playing archaeologist of missing loot. Broken passive/aggressive system: if you defend yourself against a hostile player, there’s a high chance the game “rewards” you by putting you into much more aggressive lobbies. Surviving becomes a strategic mistake. Unrewarding quests: vague directions + weak rewards = no real motivation. Unbalanced wipe progression: dozens of hours for ~5 skill points... the time-to-reward ratio feels rough. The game is good, but right now it challenges you more through its systems... than through its enemies. With a few adjustments, this could become a true standout. For now, it’s an excellent game that mostly tests your patience.

review_text: Game Strengths • Features engaging PvEvP gameplay with beautiful graphics and enjoyable gunplay. • Offers decent progression and a satisfying crafting loop. • Arc enemies provide a challenging and lethal combat experience. • Finding blueprints, weapons, and loot, then successfully escaping a raid, is highly rewarding. Major Issues • The game does not respect players’ time investment: o High-end gear and epic weapons offer no real advantage over basic equipment. o Players can be easily killed by anyone, regardless of gear quality. o Extremely fast time-to-kill (TTK) leaves no time to react, even with strong shields. • Lack of social and gameplay structure: o No factions or bounty system to identify enemies, leading to a “kill on sight” mentality. o Defensive actions are penalized the same as aggressive PvP due to aggression-based matchmaking. o Even looting dead raiders can result in being sent to aggressive servers. • Limited defensive and escape options: o Few ways to disengage from combat; smoke screens are ineffective. o No viable defensive tank builds to enable escape. o Extraction points are heavily camped, especially on night servers with the best loot. o Players often escape with only minimal loot. • Tedious recovery and crafting: o No ability to save loadouts or craft full replacements quickly. o Dying means spending significant time crafting basic supplies before re-entering a raid. Overall Impression • The PvP element adds excitement but currently feels frustrating. • High-end gear’s poor performance makes grinding feel pointless. • The game needs better defensive options and ways to survive extraction/loot area camping. • Without improvements, the game risks becoming ruined by aggressive PvP and losing its main player base.

review_text: Only 13% of raiders are responsible for 80% of all homicides. With that out of the way. The honeymoon phase is officially over... it was fun while it lasted. It took only 18 days for the community to shift from 70% friendly players to a full shoot-on-sight mentality. ngl I’m impressed. I expected the decline to take at least a month. Granted, this applies mostly to the EU servers. The biggest issue the game faces right now is the fragile balance between PvP and PvE, which has completely collapsed over the past few days. Ideally, the game should sit around 70% PvE and 30% PvP to keep tension high without turning every raid into a deathmatch. Instead, it has become pure PvP with the occasional sparks of PvE. A major reason for this is that both systems feel half-baked. They work well enough at first, but over time PvP eclipses PvE in rewards, incentives, and overall impact. Sadly, the game offers almost no real motivation to play cooperatively and PvE only, except your own moral compass. Right now, PvP isn’t even enjoyable. It’s completely stormed by players who run free loadouts nonstop. It’s normal to kill four of them per raid, because they rush aggressively in hopes of a lucky kill on someone with actual gear. In our last four raids, our group killed more than 16 free-loadout players who immediately attacked on sight. After a while, it stops being entertaining and just becomes annoying, especially because you gain nothing useful from them. So here we are. Thanks to the sociopathic players from EfT, Rust, DayZ, Scum, etc... that are well known for all kinds of sh*tty behavior over the years. Community trust went down the drain. It started declining around November 10th and hit rock bottom between the 15th and 16th. Now the community adopted one simple rule: shoot on sight or be shot first. No one is to blame except the players with over 2k hours on the mentioned games that probably at the mildest case need psychological evaluation and have some degree of school sho*ter aura Cheaters are starting to show up, so the moment you spawn into a raid you already need to be on high alert, because wallhack users will rush anyone nearby instantly. On top of that, regular players are also trying to jump unsuspecting spawns, hoping to score easy gear with minimal effort. It’s especially brutal when you’re playing with someone on a slower PC. If they load in 30 seconds after you, they’re basically seconds away from being in a firefight after loading in. Soon the casual players will start leaving, followed by the rats and griefers who won’t be able to keep up with the PvP sweats. And once the PvP diehards move on to the next big thing, only the most diehard fans will remain. Unless Embark introduces something that actually attracts and protects casual players like a dedicated PvE-only mode... this pattern is pretty much inevitable :P

review_text: Arc Raiders: A Masterpiece Undone by Human Nature Arc Raiders delivers on its promise of a high-stakes, visually arresting sci-fi survival experience. From the moment you drop into the devastated, vibrant world, the game’s core loop scavenging resources, battling menacing automatons, and barely escaping with your life is meticulously crafted, offering some of the most satisfying risk-reward gameplay of the year. The aesthetic is stunning, the sound design is immersive, and the feeling of overcoming a seemingly insurmountable threat with a few trusted comrades is, quite simply, exhilarating. This is, without a doubt, a great game, built on solid mechanics and a compelling atmosphere. The problem isn't the Arcs we fight; it's the dregs of humanity we encounter under the guise of the PvP aspect. The inclusion of player-versus-player combat was intended to introduce tension, complexity, and emergent rivalries. Instead, it has become a corrosive excuse for ruthlessness, seemingly allowing players to shed all pretence of sportsmanship or simple decency. In Arc Raiders, the competitive loop is not about skill meeting skill; it’s about exploiting a system to justify casual cruelty. Every hostile player interaction feels less like a calculated tactical move and more like an exercise in gleeful malice. They hide behind the thin veil of "It's PvP, what do you expect?" to justify behaviour that drains the joy and cooperative spirit right out of the environment. You might be low on ammo, cornered by a group of heavy Arcs, and desperately need aid, but the moment a fellow player spots you, the survival instinct is overridden by a lack of humanity. They seize the opportunity not because it’s a smart strategic move for the greater good of their own run, but because the system grants them permission to be purely selfish and destructive. This toxicity is a heart-breaking betrayal of the game's cooperative potential. The game is designed to celebrate survival, ingenuity, and teamwork against a mechanical threat, yet the player base often transforms it into a miserable, dog-eat-dog failure of a social experiment. Arc Raiders is a brilliant machine whose heart is being slowly ripped out by the very people meant to inhabit its world. It is a masterpiece let down not by its code, but by the community that uses its PvP mechanics as an excuse to unleash their worst impulses.

review_text: I really enjoy Peak at its core. It's a fun climbing game, relatively relaxing and with a focus on figuring out a solid path forward. Or, at least, that's how the game started out as. I was never a hardcore player of Peak but now I never will become one. Every time I get the urge to come back I'm reminded of all the new biomes that I just don't find fun to explore and thus any desire I have just evaporates. If you want something with wacky, crazy moments to play with friends then I can see the appeal for you. If you are like me though, stay away from this game unfortunately. Which sucks because there really isn't anything else like it.

review_text: Having just summited my 100th Peak, now finally feels like the right time to leave a review for this incredible game. I bought this originally with the intent of just adding it to my friendslop pile for a few hours of silly co-op, but it only took a few runs for me to quickly realise how much care went into the design of this game. It's had me tearing my hair out in frustration, sweating, and heart pounding so many times (and I'm a big Souls fan so that's saying something). I've enjoyed co-op but I'd say about 80% of my peaks were solo and not a single moment was dull or felt lonely - the beautiful soundtrack and biome designs have you fully immersed throughout your journey. I've been playing since the original biome setup and have thoroughly enjoyed the additions and can't wait to see the teased biome that is yet to come. You'd think after 100 Peaks (and that's not counting my many failed attempts) this game would start to feel a bit stale but the new map seeds every 24hrs and biome rotations keep things feeling fresh and exciting and importantly, offer a new challenge each time giving unlimited replayability! review_text: I know a friendslop when I see one. Everything feels intentional and none of them is frustrating, the gameplay loop is interesting, challenging, and full of variety and surprises. Other than that, its extremely rewarding and keeps you determined through all those challenges to reach the top to see the tail of that campfire smoke. Other than that, the gameplay mechanics like the stamina bar getting replaced with various debuffs is very interesting and fun. I think that part of the survival gimmick is what makes the game so interesting in the first place, and the way that survival mechanic is neatly bound to everything that happens in the world around you is really complemental because it makes you feel more connected and inside the biome. Obviously its way more fun with friends, obviously its way more unforgettable with friends. But that doesn't make it a friendslop. Not every coop game is friendslop and this game is a good anectode for all lazy friendslop developers out there trying to make a quick buck out of your 5 second reactions with simple gimmicks.

review_text: With the final update dropped — final ascent, final badges, and a secret ending — my journey on PEAK has officialy come to an end. What started as my bro's recommendation turned into hundreds of hours of climbing, challenges, fun, and chaos. I didn't expect it'd hold my attention for hundreds of hours, so I'm glad this game has a good longevity to keep player's attention. To my bro, my friends, every stranger I just met, and of course everyone who's been part of PEAK's journey, thank you for playing. Also, shoutout to Keimorizh for opening up sessions to help collect the badges hadn't gotten yet. This chapter's closed, but I'll see y'all when I see ya! Friendslop I know there's been lotta debate about the term "Friendslop" ever since co-op games like Lethal Company, Content Warning, R.E.P.O., PEAK, and you name it, started being labeled as Friendslop. Even older games before the term existed are somehow being considered "Friendslop". I understand why lotta people who love these games feel disrespected by the term. The word "slop" already has a pretty negative connotation. We hear it in things like "AI-slop," where it usually describes something cheap, low-effort, or mass-produced. I use the term because I see it as a "new genre" of co-op games, games designed around playing with more than 2 people. Just like how we use terms like "Metroidvania," "Souls-like", "Simulator", or "Incremental". They are genre that help us describe games that share certain characteristics. Not to mention I don't use "Friendslop" as an insult. I hope it finds a new term that fits better. And you'll see comments like, "You just hate it because you don't have friends or a group to play with" or, "Your group probably gets bored with these games easily." But I don't think that's necessarily true. Games like R.E.P.O. and MecCha Chameleon have public servers, so you aren't completely locked out of the experience just because your usual group isn't online. You can drop into a random lobby and play with strangers. Or you can find people through the community (discord, example). And maybe you might get along with them. And then add each other afterward, play again, or move on to another Friendslop game. Now, let's say you already have a group to play with. Another comment pops up. "You paid for a Friendslop game and only got an hour or so of fun. Is it "wasted" your time?" How about I ask you a familiar question, amigo. 1. What's the difference between that and going to the cinema, where you pay for a 2-3 hour movie? 2. What's the difference between that and going to a concert, where you might pay even more for a few hours of show? Is it waste your time? i don't think so. I don't think the value determined by its duration. What makes something worth it can be the moment, the experience, or the memory. When I think about the value of a game, I usually look at what the game itself gives me, "How much content it has, how many hours I can play, how many mechanics it has, or how much there is left to discover?" Let me take examples from my 2 friendslop games, R.E.P.O. and PEAK. After hundreds of hours spent in both, I've noticed that they share a lot in common. But there's one major difference: One has an endpoint, one does not. 1. R.E.P.O.'s core is on moments with people. The gameplay itself is just the medium. No matter how many levels you clear, it just keeps going. It runs on an endless loop. The levels get harder and harder until you eventually fail. "Winning" a round just unlocks... another round. 2. PEAK, has an actual endpoint, an achievable finish line, and that is reaching the peak. Once you're up there, the run is over and you did it. Because of that, its core leans more toward its gameplay mechanics. Stamina, hunger, health, weight, items, and even reading the routes through each biome all matter if you want to reach the peak. If you fail, you can restart, find another route, and plan a new strategy. These two games have different focuses, but they still share a similar experience. And I'm glad that both managed to achieve such good longevity. Updates like cosmetics in R.E.P.O., or new biomes in PEAK. Also, the modding community that can completely change the way you experience these games, adding new mechanics, challenges, and making the game even more fun and chaotic. I believe what Friendslop really about is not the "Slop". Sometimes, you just want to hang out with other people. And video games happen to be one of the places where we can do that. The game becomes a social space. With friends, the game becomes a frame for shared memories. With strangers, every lobby becomes a kind of social experiment. You don't know who you're going to meet. You play with them and maybe you'll never see them again. Or maybe you'll add each other afterward and end up playing together again later. These games can even give you a reason to bring your old friend back from the grave. Someone you haven't talked to in months suddenly texted, "Wanna play?" And for a few hours, you're just hanging out again. Until eventually, the time ends. The updates get old. The server closes. And one day you stop playing entirely. Maybe your friends do too. But you still remember what happened. The dumb decisions. The accidental betrayals. The screaming. The unpredictable one. The game was never the entire experience. The people are too. The game becomes a place where you make the memory. R.E.P.O. Click for Review

review_text: For newcomers, the concept of the game sounds incredibly simple: Climb through different biomes, manage your wounds and hunger. Sounds easy, right? Well... achieving it with my bro took nearly 20 hours. (I died, but hey, at least one of us made it out.) Now sitting at around 40 hours with most of the achievements unlocked, I can safely say the real fun isn’t in collecting them. It’s in the memories we made along the way. The laughs, the happy moments... and even the times we were raging and arguing. Because we didn’t give up. We kept trying, climbing again and again until we finally made it. Each day, a new island is generated procedurally, ensuring no two runs are the same. It constantly forces you to rethink your decisions, because even the tiniest mistake can ruin your run. Sometimes the path that looks like the best one ends up being the worst, and the smartest thing you can do is turn back before it’s too late. Or risking a climb that seems safe, only to slip and fall to your death... or barely survive, but with so little stamina left that the rest of the run becomes a struggle. Or misusing an item because you had no idea what it actually does, only realizing your mistake when it actually mattered. Would I board that plane again, crash onto an abandoned island, and try to reach the peak? Absolutely. And my bro is coming with me too. No arguments. Period.

review_text: Was waiting until the final update to make this review. PEAK is one of the most fun, creative, and unique indies to come out within the past couple of years. With a randomly generated map every 24 hours, and different luggage contents every new run, the game manages to make every new run feel unique but also not feel too reliant on RNG. Whether you're just BARELY scraping by or making the comeback of a generation, every run is different and interesting, and as long as you play smart and react effectively with the items you DO have, you WILL make it to the top of the mountain. It's a tough balance that the PEAK Devs NAILED. Probably my favorite thing about PEAK is that even when you're failing, you're having FUN! You can have a really rough run, or make a dumb mistake that costs you the run, and you're still having a good time. Most of the time failure also feels earned and feels like YOU did something wrong, and you know how to react next time to avoid it in the future. And the rare times a death wasn't necessarily your fault, usually it's something so ridiculous you can't help but laugh. Getting to the top of the mountain and beating the run feels satisfying, rewarding, and so so so deserved. While PEAK is obviously best played with friends. Despite that, the exploration, resource management, and constant decision making are satisfying enough on their own to make just a really solid roguelike, even while playing solo. Also it has pretty neat lore hidden, which you can find if you pay enough attention. It's pretty cool. Anyway all this to say, there's a reason the friendslop genre hasn't really gotten much bigger than this game. This game is truly and utterly, PEAK

review_text: PEAK is one of those games that looks simple at first, but quickly becomes an unforgettable experience. Climbing a massive mountain with friends sounds straightforward, yet every step feels tense, rewarding, and sometimes hilariously frustrating. The physics-based movement creates plenty of funny moments, but beneath the chaos is a surprisingly satisfying survival and teamwork experience. Communication matters, mistakes have consequences, and reaching a new checkpoint feels like a genuine achievement. What I enjoyed most was how naturally the game creates stories. Whether it's a perfectly executed rescue or watching a friend fall after confidently saying "I've got this," every session feels unique. It's not perfect—the controls can occasionally feel awkward, and some failures may seem unfair—but those moments are part of what makes the climb memorable. If you enjoy co-op games that test teamwork, patience, and friendship, PEAK is absolutely worth the climb.

review_text: PEAK is a physics based adventure game, where you alone or with others suffer a plane crash and wake up on a mysterious island. In order to get away from the island you need to climb to the peak which you can reach by going through the island's different regions, surviving the nature and the climb. The graphics looks cartoonish, but fits perfectly with the game's style. It's colorful and sometimes detailed enough, but only for those things which needs the extra details. Also, the characters and the customization is alright, you can change 6-7 different things on your character, additionally you can unlock some new things which you can acquire to your own avatar. Controls may seem difficult at first, but after some time the player easily can get into it. Soundtrack is okay, usually there are not many music tracks to listen to as the game's ambient takes the leading role, however any other sound effects and especially the in game voice chat is really well done. Especially the voice chat, which can change the voice of the other players depending on their location, if they are moving or what place they talk at, like if they are in a cave there is reverb in the voice and so on, which is pretty cool and can make some fun moments. Finally, one of the best thing in this game is the gameplay. Even though this is just a climbing game there are many game mechanics, items, regions and a few secrets which the player going to explore and figuring these things out, and that is so much fun in PEAK. I could details what things I like in here, but I really do believe it's best to explore this game without "spoiling" some of these things. Even figuring out how to play game: there is no tutorial for PEAK, however the very first region, which is the Shore, is constructed in such way that the player can check and try the fundamentals which gives a directionless tutorial mode basically, and with this you can enjoy the game in your own pace and won't be slowed down by the game itself. It can be considered as a trial-error type of gameplay, but I believe this is how PEAK needs to be experienced. Once you figure these out then you start thinking about how to optimize your climbing, which is not that straightforward as you may think and to me that's also pretty cool thing to do. Not even mentioning when you can play with your friends, which make the game such a chaotic fun in some cases, or it can feel good when the group works together and reach the top of the island. You can also play it alone, which also works, but in the long term this game works best with others. Also, every day the island is going changing, so even if you played through the game once you can play a new map with new regions and generations again, which can give additional challenges. Even if you see a region which you already overcome, the regions have different types in itself and also the generations can make different map basically, so there is more than enough replay value in this game. Also also, you can unlock additional difficulty levels which can give extra challenges in future run. I also want to mention the in-game accolades, which are basically the achievements for PEAK. In my reviews I really don't highlight achievements for a game, because I like to play it in my own pace and do what things in the game which I feel like to do, but in PEAK these accolades unlock new character customization items if you complete them, but also they give incentives to try out new things in a run, which is also interesting to explore. There are many positives things about PEAK, but there are a few negative things too. There were a couple of times when I got disconnected from an online match, due to timeout... which is weird, because I did not lose internet connection and this happened randomly, and to others in my lobby. You can invite players mid run, but this can be annoying to get into, as it comes up out of nowhere. One thing which is good to know, is PEAK is a 4 player game. If you have more people to play with, the vanilla game don't have the option to play with more sadly, however there is a mod which can delete this limitation and play with more people. Also, occasionally there are some weird generations which can make the game more broken, like when two objects is generated in each other or when certain items are in one location. So far I did not encounter anything game breaking, and also as far as I know the devs checks the maps beforehand, but this is something which is good to keep in mind. And I hope there will be more regions to explore or new things to find in existing regions, because even though the regions have different generation types in itself, after a couple of hours they might start to feel flat for some people. When I first tried this game I thought it will be an over hyped something, but I did not expected to be this fun to play and even more fun to get into it more. I would definitely recommend to get this game, especially if you can get someone else along with you to play. 7.5€ is honestly a decent price for this game too.

review_text: I love PEAK. I’ve played it since launch and always look forward to new maps, achievements, and mechanics. It's obvious how much time and effort "Team PEAK" has put into this game. The devs are very community-oriented, respond to player suggestions and improvements and fix minor bugs and errors within a few days. I haven't seen any bug that negatively affected the gameplay which hasn't already been removed, except the well-known backpack glitch. Backpacks ragdolling under the map as soon as we put 'em down. Very rare, but still happens. (Mostly in the tomb, when the entrance is nearly fully covered by sandstone and you're putting down a backpack to get past a little hole, you got a huge chance you'll never see that lil baggy again. Since the tomb is optional, not that dramatic, but still room for improvement.) Another thing I'd love to see is the ability to create lobbies larger than four players without the need for mods. I personally love to use mods in general, but since PEAK is also a very family-friendly game and many people don't like using mods, I'd like to see the option to create bigger lobbies without them. Especially because we all know that new game updates + old mod versions aren't the best friends, and PEAK literally gets updated nearly every week. All in all, PEAK is an incredibly funny game and I can highly recommend it to anyone who's searching for a quirky alternation with friends and randoms, or an adventurous, almost meditative single-player experience. Not to unmention the various ascents (difficulties). They force you to try different packing methods, adapt your typical climbing tactics, use new paths to reach the peak, and in the end, get another cool cosmetic as reward for each ascent, which also definitely increases the replayability. No matter if you just wanna reach the Peak a few times with your friends, or go all in for achievement hunting and the full adventure trip, it's worth the price with or without a discount.

review_text: -Quick Review- I’m resisting the temptation to make the joke about how “PEAK is Peak”. PEAK is a climbing game, it’s best experienced cooperative with friends, however you can play by yourself too... but with voice proximity chat, extra hands, extra inventory space, sharing the load, huddling together for warmth, pulling up a friend that extra couple of inches when their stamina runs out, PEAK really is more geared towards a cooperative experience where you summate the mountain together. Review Video: If you don't like reading, or are curious about watching gameplay check out my video here: -Detailed breakdown review- Story: You are a scout... I mean obviously you are a scout, but I mean in the game you play as a Scout. Kinda like “Boy Scouts”, “Girl Scouts”, “Junior Woodchucks”, or “Junior Chipmunk”, go on hikes, learn how to tie square knots, camping, sit in a classroom and do underwater basket weaving... if that last example seems odd, it’s because my time in boy scouts wasn’t stellar. Anyway, you’re all on a troop adventure and... ...Oops! Looks like the plane crashed and only you and your friends survived. It’s up to You and maybe Huey, Dewey or Lewy (friends sold separately) to make it to the PEAK where some idiot lost all of the flares to summon the helicopter to escape. But to get to the Peak... ahh, that’s where the story truly is. Gameplay: For a game about hiking... There's a fair bit to explain about the gameplay. First thing you should know is if you want to climb something you walk to a tree, rock, wall or something, click and hold the left mouse button to climb. General movement is with WASD, and when you’re climbing WASD translates to the wall the same way, W is up, S is down, D is right, and A is left. After movement is figured out, the next concept which is CRITIALLY important to master is Stamina. It’s definitely a case of “Easy to Learn, Hard to Master”, at the bottom left of the screen you have a stamina bar, once this bar empties you stop climbing and start falling, if the gods of PEAK really hate you, the mountain will slope away and you’ll just fall thousands of feet to unceremoniously hit the floor and bounce once before you drift into unconsciousness. So you want as much stamina as possible, right? Right! But it’s more complicated then that. Things eat away at your stamina bar, like poison, injuries, burning, freezing, weight from items in your pockets or backpack, and hunger too literally takes chunks out of your stamina bar. Some food items, or cooked food, or Campfire checkouts will give you bits of a second stamina bar. This second stamina bar is “Bonus Stamina”, if you use up your normal stamina you’ll dip into these reserves which are quite literally CLUTCH. That being said, try not to use bonus stamina unless you need too, everything on peak becomes an exercise in weighing the risks vs rewards... Do you want to use your bonus stamina to clear this part, and then drop a role for your friends? Or do you want to use a rope cannon and save your bonus stamina? Maybe you don’t have much to work with at all and you should try looking up another side of the mountain... for a potentially easier path? At the end of the day that’s where the real challenge in PEAK is, it’s planning and using your tools effectively and efficiently. Conclusion: PEAK is really fun! The MESA update was... frustrating. Sometimes you’ll get a generated seed which is just god-awful, and you get to quit the game sad on that day... but you can know tomorrow there’ll be a new generated seed to try out and maybe that one will be easier? On the whole PEAK has been a fun game, I look forward to any future updates the game might have. I can easily suggest the game for anyone looking for a cooperative game to play with friends. PEAK is very unique, I haven’t played any other game like it, and it’ll sit in my list of “favorite co-op games” probably for the rest of my life.

review_text: I used to play games to relax. I thought to myself, "Man, modern gaming is too sweaty. I just want a nice, colorful co-op adventure where my friends and I can chill, enjoy nature, and look at some cool low-poly scenery." Then I booted up PEAK and realized it is actually a psychological horror game disguised as a cute scouting trip. Now, three hours later, I am dangling by a single pixel off a sheer cliff face. My entire life depends on my buddy, who is currently hyperventilating into his mic because his hand is slipping on his desk. "HOLD ME," I’m screeching, watching the literal lava at the bottom of image_69df55.png mock our existence. One tiny, microscopic slip of the mouse—one minor physics jank—and we are both plummeting 40 minutes of vertical progress straight back to the lobby. I haven't blinked in ten minutes. My hand is actively cramping from gripping my mouse like my actual life depends on it. I came here for a "co-op physics adventure," but my heart rate is higher than it’s ever been in my life. We started the session as a tightly-knit squad; we are ending it as bitter enemies who can't even agree on which rock to grab next. Verdict: 10/10. It will completely destroy your trust in human nature and test your grip strength to its absolute limits, but reaching that next checkpoint feels like conquering the world.

review_text: I played this with my wife’s boyfriend and had a lot of fun. He talked sh*t to me the whole time. Super funny. Peak wife’s boyfriend experience! It's the only game where my hands and butthole sweat simultaneously while playing!! It makes me a nervous wreck! I love that this game is forcing friendslop enthusiasts to stare god in the face and stop using that term. It’s so much fun. It’s another one of those fun, “let's get three idiots together and have a good time” games. By idiots of course. I mean friends. Of which I don’t have any. Thank goodness for my wife’s boyfriend. This game is the epitome of "it's the journey, not the destination." I've played around a dozen sessions with my wife’s boyfriend and we've rarely made it to the top. We just end up tormenting each other and bantering. Safe to say that this game is Peak. This game is actually brilliant. It's so simple in premise and so perfectly executed in practise. A simple goal, with simple game mechanics and an environment that encourages silly moments. Tons of fun, actually quite challenging once you start getting more ascent levels. A lot more strategizing with your friends for what to carry, and having to throw things ahead of where you're going just to keep your carrying weight lower. Me and my group wife’s boyfriend can’t put it down. Me and my wife’s boyfriend played the other night and we were on the last portion of the mountain. My wife’s boyfriend made it across and lowered a rope for me, as I didn't have enough stamina to climb the route he took. It required a clutch jump to pull off, and I missed it. My wife’s boyfriend heard me screaming "NOOO!!!" a thousand feet down, and I was gone. (Afterward, I found out he didn't extend the rope all the way... and that made it even funnier!) It's a surprisingly thrilling game for being something that seems so mundane. There are times when I'm genuinely white knuckling it, thinking "I can't go back down, and I don't see a way up except this one, stressful move!". The fact that the mountain randomizes every day also just lands so well. The experience varies depending if you play with others or just by yourself. When I play solo, the games are relaxing and when I die it’s no big deal. I made a mistake, I learn from it, my next run will be better- sort of thing. When I’m playing with others it’s a different story. I tend to get stressed out if someone else is taking the lead-and I can tell we’re headed the wrong direction. Or if I’m leading, it becomes stressful if I make a mistake, because I don’t want to be the reason we fail. This is definitely just a ME problem. However, the feeling you get when you peak with your group is 10x better than doing it alone- so it’s a trade off. A little stress for more satisfaction is sometimes what I prefer, but other times I just want to cut on a YouTube video for background noise and climb by myself and figure out the puzzle. The game is meant to be played however you play it, don’t beat yourself up over it- stress is totally natural, so is being chill. This is easily my favorite climbing/obstacle game I've played. The rules are simple, but it's so addicting. I encourage anybody who's on the fence to give it a shot. It's not just a "have a quick goofy time with your wife’s boyfriend " game that you'll play once and put down, it's actually just a well-designed, engaging game that leads to moments ranging from hilarious to ridiculously intense. I also advise everyone to play with in-game chat; the proximity chat and vocal effects like echoes and reverb really add to the experience. God I love this game. Over the moon that it caught on so much, super happy for these guys. Overall I'm just glad that this means Aggro Crab will have more cash for Another Crab's Treasure 2. Hell, if they aren't already, they should bundle ACT and Peak together for the Summer Sale to get more eyes on it. 10/10

review_text: Mixed Feelings – Fun concept, frustrating direction PEAK is, at its core, a co-op game meant for laughs, teamwork, and the shared struggle of the climb. When it’s working, it’s a blast — the silly moments, the coordination, and the feeling of slowly overcoming obstacles together are genuinely enjoyable. The problem is that the game’s balance seems to be moving in a direction that punishes rather than empowers players. Most people play PEAK for the goofy co-op experience and a sense of progression with some challenge, not to be endlessly punished by near-impossible climbs. Right now, many players struggle to complete even a single run after several hours, and yet updates seem to focus on making things even harder. There feels like a disconnect between what the players want — fun, teamwork, and steady progress — and what the developers are delivering — harsher mechanics and more frustration. I hope future updates focus more on keeping the experience enjoyable and achievable, rather than just increasing the difficulty curve.

review_text: PEAK is a mountaineering, survival platformer. Balancing resources, helping one another in co-op, and taking risks to ascend up towards your goal is all part of the fun. There is a lot of artistry and effort put into this wonderful game with its straightforward objective to reach the top. While the game is designed with multiplayer in mind, it is also incredibly good even when trekking it alone. The game is well crafted visually in its daily random map generation and character designs. Biomes have distinct aesthetics which come with their own unique set of hazards. They challenge players with different kinds of environmental obstacles -- including various fauna -- and weather conditions. The terrain for each biome never look out of place due to the excellent use of shadows and lighting, and objects and flora are seamlessly integrated into the environment. In addition, the sound design really lends itself to the tone and atmosphere of each biome in its ambience. The music, or lack thereof at times, also emphasizes the feelings of isolation (especially in solo expeditions) or the pressure to continually move upwards and onwards or face dire consequences. A lot of care was also put into characters as well with player characters having charming and expressive designs. Their colorful, cartoony look makes players easy to spot from the environment. The effort put into making visible responses for various player actions and gameplay movements make things feel more natural in co-op sessions. Mouths that move while using proximity chat and eyes that follow you when you're close are nice touches. The addition of emotes and the ability to point things out for everyone are appreciated. As a survival platformer, the game can be unforgiving. You and your group's pathfinding skills will be put to the test as you ascend towards the peak. Whether going in alone with no others to rely on or as part of a group of friends (and setting aside any hijinks between players), balancing cautiousness and speed will be essential and you must use items and tools as efficiently as possible and take risks when necessary in order to proceed. The goal of reaching the summit can be a puzzle all on its own while minimizing injuries but there are also various ways how each biome can throw debuffs at you with its challenges such as hunger or poison. They will impede a player's stamina which makes climbing more difficult. In later difficulties the game not only makes climbing harder to do, but it also adds pressure on players with a long-term doom counter that forces players to race against time as well or die. Yes, dying sucks but the variety and ways players can overcome challenges keeps things interesting. In a group it's best to work together, share resources, and help each other by literally lending a helping hand to pull friends up. But if someone does die and have not yet been revived, then it's not the end for them. Dead players will return as ghosts to haunt your friends. Though ideally they'll help their living counterparts by pointing out the best routes or items. (Who packs a cannon in their luggage anyway? On a side note though, I love how the game incorporates the tutorial by way of minigames and the player lobby seamlessly into the game's world. I also love how Steam achievements are directly tied to the badges on a player character's sash.) Thankfully, the game eases players into the world of PEAK with smaller challenges before the bigger, do-or-die challenges found later. Players always start on the "Shore" after waking from the plane crash to get them rolling. PEAK is an excellently designed game for both single player and multiplayer. The game makes players think about their pathfinding and how to use any found tools in the best possible way. review_text: TL;DR: Fun and colourful but sometimes frustrating coop game about climbing and finding your way through worlds that change daily. This review is written from a "pre-finished" viewpoint (at the time of this review, I haven't played through the whole game). From Team PEAK and the publishers Aggro Crab and Landfall comes PEAK, a coop climbing/find your way game for up to four simulatenous players. The premise of the game is that you and your fellow players board a plane and tragedy strikes. The plane crashes and you're stranded on some unknown island. Suddenly, you're fighting for your survival and trying to reach civilization once again. Not only do you have to scale difficult terrain, you also have to find some food to keep going. The better you're fed, the more stamina you have to tackle your challenges. And on top of that - at least with the Roots update - you will also encounter enemy-type creatures that are out to get you. And then there's some additional "natural" obstacles and conditions like heavy wind which will hinder your progress, so you'll have to learn how to deal with that. Also... you can slip on some objects, so watch your step! You have to get to know your surroundings, learn which plants might be safe to eat or which herb does help in certain situations. There's some help if you keep your eyes peeled: you can find some written tips to help you understand what's what. You can also find items that may help you on your way through the game - or some that might just be cluttering your inventory, depending on your playstyle. Think of ropes you can use to help your fellow players reach areas they might not be able to climb anymore because they are hurt or out of stamina. Or think of noisy little trumpets you can use to annoy your friends. "Ah, there's an inventory?" you might ask. Yes. But it is limited to three slots plus a backpack. And you have to search for those backpacks, since they're not too easy to come by. The graphics are colourful, the player characters being depicted in a cartoonish style with some customisation options like diverse facial expressions or different clothing (some of which needs to be unlocked by playing the game). The areas you reach are kind of themed, starting you in a rocky beach area and encountering others like a huge mushroom forest (this came in with the roots update) or lava areas - among others. Each "biome" has its own difficulties and quirks you have to manage. I have to say the music seems relaxing most of the time and since the situations can get a bit tense that's very welcome. As I use to say: if the sounds don't feel out of place for you, they did a good job. And as of now I don't feel that the sound effects are misplaced at all. Also I didn't notice any "too loud/too silent"-type problems. Aaaand of course the game has microphone capabilities, so... just mute your discord if you want to use the in-game voice chat options. This is fun because sometimes you get lost or separated and can listen for the voices of your fellow players in the distance. Or listen to their screams when they plummet to their deaths. Yes, there is a "death mechanic". Players who suffered heavy injuries will KO and be able to follow the other still alive players around and talk to them, so you're not completely out of the game. If your friends reach certain areas you can get revived and continue the stressful journey. Earlier I wrote that the game can get "frustrating". Yeah, I've stood in front of some walls/mountains and asked myself: "How? How in the hell should this be possible?". And I'm not sure if every scenario is "doable", but that's kind of the design I guess. You will fall. You will reach dead ends. There will be environmental hazards that will neutralize you at the worst timing possible. If you can live with that, you're fine. At the time of this review, the devs still care for the game, putting out bug fixes and additions to the game. We all like that, don't we? For you achievement hunters: currently there are 54 steam achievements you can work towards and none of those seem too over the top, although a lot of them are circumstancial. The friends I'm playing with and me still have to finish the game, so I don't know everything yet. There's still a lot for us to find out about the game so I guess this review isn't too "spoilery". Thanks for reading, Ossel PS: I might edit this review if there should be any questions or if I should feel like I forgot to mention something.

review_text: PEAK is a cooperative climbing adventure where you and up to three fellow scouts attempt to conquer a massive, ever-changing mountain. Blending physics-based movement with light survival elements, the game creates a mix of chaos, tension, and unexpected comedy. From scrambling up cliffs to scavenging strange food and yelling at your friends through voice chat, every climb becomes its own story. Summary After your scout troop becomes stranded on a mysterious island after a plane crash, you awaken at the mountain’s base with only minimal gear and questionable rations. Ahead of you lies a towering summit shrouded in fog, divided into four distinct biomes—each more unpredictable than the last. With stamina dwindling, hazards lurking, and the environment shifting daily, you and your fellow scouts must climb, slip, fall, laugh, and improvise your way toward the Peak. Overall PEAK is charming and chaotic. The physics-driven climbing feels tactile and fun, especially when paired with friends who can rescue or sabotage you and daily rotating mountain layout help keep the game experience fresh. Though the survival mechanics are intentionally light and solo play can feel tougher, the game delivers a memorable co-op journey packed with emergent moments and shared laughter. For its price, PEAK is absolutely worth it. Rating: 10/10 [Follow Curator] [Steam Group]

review_text: The gameplay itself can be quite fun. The gunplay in general feels good and satisfying, and plenty of the maps flow well and make for fun, intense engagements. To this day, though, matchmaking is probably some of the worst I've seen in any AAA title. A good 40%-50% of lobbies, since launch, will start populated with bots. These may fill up over time, but there's no reason why a game as large as this has been sees bot-populated lobbies during peak hours. The constant back-pedaling with promises made during the advertising run prior to release (more grounded and realistic skins, no emphasis on collaborations, etc) is egregious. Certainly better realistic skins compared to recent CoD titles, there are still plenty of weird, unrealistic kits. More and more skins are being released with bright colors, and recently, GLOWING colors. These are, at the end of the day, nitpicks, but still highlight a lack of a consumer-friendly backbone. AI-generated skins, models, and emblems, especially with the release of Season 5, also plague the game's marketplace and earnable rewards. That is money siphoned from the actual developers and into the hands of the already-rich CEOs and AI companies. I can't in good conscious recommend this game anymore. Dice and EA prove time, and time, and time again that they are spineless entities that do not care about promises made or a positive consumer experience.

review_text: It's really the last Battlefield game I will ever purchase, unless they sell the franchise to people who know what they are doing or will hire proper people and get rid of all current people involved with this game, as they are incapable of making a proper battlefield game. It's a shame that they fail so hardly to deliver the classic battlefield experience. You have all the previous battlefield games, codes, mechanics and feedback from players on what was good, great, excellent, bad and terrible, yet you fail to put all of that into a package. The monetization is also ridiculous. They sold the game (STANDARD EDITION) for 70€ already. Then we get the Battlepass nonsense, skins here and there and other crap. Ridiculous. Back then, for Battlefield 3 and 4, you would gladly start to buy expansion packs to also support the game. Why? Because the games were great and fun. Sure, it also did split up the Playerbase because of people who cannot or did not purchase them and then people who bought this or that pack, would play different maps the standard edition did not have. But that was not too much of an issue, as the core gameplay was so much fun and the base game had so many fun maps included already, that you would often just play on a server with base maps. Now we can also mention the server browser which was amazing back in battlefield 4. I mean, battlelog wasn't my best friend in battlefield 3 mainly, but it also did an 'okay' job to find and pick from servers at ease. With battlefield 4, yes, there were issues and people would question, why? You already had battlefield 3 as a solid foundation, how do you mess up the netcode and other obvious things, but the developers at least worked on it for about 1 - 2 years continuously to make it greater and they delivered. Battlefield 1 was good for what it was, not my type of game, as I am not too much into world war 1 weapons as well as world war 2 weapons for battlefield 5. But even Battlefield 5, as many weaknesses as it had, was more fun than this game. And yes sure, not everything about Battlefield 6 is utter garbage either. The graphics are fine at least. The Campaign as in most battlefield games (If available) is not good, but in battlefield 6, as trash as never before. Maybe this next opinion is more controversial to some people, as they get sensitive about it and try to defend this nonsense, but that's their issue not mine(And trust me, you got some serious problems if you defend this, boy): Keep women out of Military games! There are definitely environments where you want women in and definitely women making certain noises, but definitely not in a Battlefield game. It's disturbing, annoying and makes no sense. Not to mention that women would never have the physical capabilities to keep up with any man, be it when it comes to sprinting, sliding, shooting under pressure and many other things I could mention. Now you can come with: This is a video game. Yup it indeed is one about war, killing, destruction and having fun with your boys. It kills immersion and fun by putting nonsense into it, just like what I mentioned about women. Battlefield was always a franchise for the male audience and there was nothing wrong with it. If a girl wanted to play it, she could, but if she complains there aren't any women in this military game, then she can play Fortnite or Call of Duty Mobile or something else. Simple as that. And Electronic Arts should have told developers, who really want diversity or whatever in Battlefield to either do their job as they are told (including the simp guys or the low testosterone guys) or leave the company once and for all. We also do not need 'characters and their faces' to be identified as something, it simply shouldn't matter. In Battlefield 3 and 4 you mostly played as a generic soldier, whether it was a black dude or a white dude. No issues at all(Even if I personally would be a black OR a white dude). The focus was the gameplay, awesome maps and sound as well of course and it delivered!(Men screaming and being badass not some try-hard masculine woman) But here, the focus is monetization, skins, diversity(diversity dialed back compared to the previous failure of battlefield 2042) and other crap nobody needs in a battlefield. (And for the people who just cannot get it: I have no issues with women in games and I play as women characters in various games and I enjoy it that way, because it just fits, makes sense and everything is developed to make it work fine). About customization: A little bit of customization is fine sure. Personalization for weapons, like in the older battlefield games. Platoons with their own platoon icons which then are on your parachute, vehicles etc. But having everybody walk around in weird different outfits just kills it for me. This should absolutely not belong on the battlefield and not in battlefield. And you know, I think it's even okay if you want to start adding character generators, where you can customize your individual MALE soldier, but keep it battlefield suitable. Also I did not mention the older battlefield games including the Hardline one. Hardline was a good game, but should not have been included in the battlefield franchise. Bad Company, Bad Company 2, Battlefield 2, Battlefield 1942 etc. all had amazing gameplay and were super fun to play. Yes, playing Battlefield 1942 today, will be not as much fun, as there is a lot of nothingness and other things to complain about today, but back in the day? How amazing it has been! Battlefield 2 gets mentioned less by people, which I cannot understand, as the game was solid too. Especially later on with mods. Boy was it great. Now I got to phrase it carefully: It had those 'special soldiers' in one of these amazing mods, which would 'blow up' themselves with the classic phrasing a certain religious group loves to use a lot. Hilarious and fun to play, really. But yes, this might be too much to talk about now, whether mod support is really necessary or not. Anyway, Battlefield Studios, should not be allowed to make any more Battlefield games and Electronic Arts, get rid of your corporate nonsense (So get rid of all top / leading people within your company) and let the company be run by people who really would bring honor to the name 'Electronic Arts' and especially the Battlefield franchise. Cheers.

review_text: I’ve been playing **Battlefield** for pretty much my entire life. My first Battlefield game was **Bad Company**, then I moved on to **Battlefield 3**, **Battlefield 4**—still the best one in my opinion—and I’ve played basically every Battlefield game all the way up to **Battlefield 6**. I love this game, and I’ll always love this series. My kids are going to play Battlefield, their kids are going to play Battlefield, and I genuinely don’t care what the haters or naysayers have to say about it. To me, Battlefield is the greatest first-person shooter franchise ever made. Better than Call of Duty, better than any one-off FPS that comes and goes. Nothing else gives me the same feeling. Battlefield is the best. Always has been, always will be.

review_text: A Mechanically Revived Titan Being Cannibalized by Its Own Publisher One year after its October 2025 launch, Battlefield 6 stands as one of the most frustrating paradoxes in modern PC gaming. On the surface, it was hailed as the grand course correction the franchise desperately needed after the disastrous missteps of Battlefield 2042. And in moments of pure, unscripted squad combat, it genuinely earns that praise. Yet as its first year wraps up with recent Steam user reviews tumbling to a polarizing 50% "Mixed" rating, it is impossible to separate the game's solid mechanical foundation from Electronic Arts' hostile technical policies, creeping live service rot, and a historic $55 billion leveraged buyout that threatens to hollow out the entire company from the inside. The Nuance: Best in Class Gunplay Meets Creative Hollowing To give credit where it is due, Battlefield Studios and DICE nailed the kinetic fundamentals of infantry combat. Shooting in Battlefield 6 feels phenomenal. Every weapon class carries distinct weight and mechanical personality: assault rifles demand disciplined burst-fire rhythm, marksman rifles punish rushed follow up shots, and staged partial reloads force split second tactical decisions in the middle of a firefight. The audiovisual engineering is equally triumphant. Rather than relying on the obnoxious, Vaseline smeared screen blur of past entries, suppression is communicated through visceral acoustic cues and subtle camera shake. Firing a sidearm inside a concrete stairwell produces a sharp, metallic echo that sells the physical scale of the space. Combined with a return to defined class identities and a reactive destruction system where blowing open a load bearing wall isn't a scripted cutscene, but a tactical choice that permanently alters sightlines and cover for the rest of the match the core multiplayer loop Across maps like Cairo, Brooklyn, Gibraltar, and the reworked Golmud Railway can still deliver spectacle no other shooter matches. However, the cracks appear the moment you look past the physics engine: * A Glorified Tech Demo for a Campaign: After a cinematic, rain soaked opening mission that screams big-budget confidence, the six-hour solo campaign collapses into a repetitive corridor slog. The geopolitical plot exists almost entirely as disembodied radio chatter, and the AI is shockingly primitive enemies spawn on predictable timers, sprint blindly into gunfire, or break completely on ladders, while friendly squadmates routinely block doorways and ignore revive prompts. * Eroding Identity and Balance: Over its first year of seasonal updates, the grounded military atmosphere promised at launch has increasingly given way to twitchy, Call of Duty chasing pacing. Vehicle combat historically the glue of the Battlefield sandbox suffers from erratic balance swings and handling quirks, while inconsistent netcode frequently leaves firefights feeling like a coin toss. The Linux Exile: EA Javelin and Unjustified Hostility Nowhere is EA's anti consumer stubbornness more glaring than in its deliberate lockout of Linux, SteamOS, and Steam Deck players. While the rest of the PC gaming industry has spent the last several years embracing Valve's Proton compatibility layer, EA has doubled down on EA Javelin, its proprietary kernel level anti cheat that mandates Windows, UEFI Secure Boot, and TPM 2.0 while refusing to provide Proton or native Linux support. EA executives have publicly patted themselves on the back, claiming Javelin has blocked 2.39 million cheat attempts and framing the exclusion of alternative operating systems as a necessary sacrifice for security. That argument collapses under technical scrutiny: * Collective Punishment of Legitimate Players: EA didn't just lock Linux users out of Battlefield 6; it retroactively forced Javelin into older legacy titles like Battlefield 1 and Battlefield V, revoking access from paying customers who had been playing those games flawlessly on Linux for years. * The Technical Excuse Is Hollow: Treating Linux as an inherently insecure "cheater haven" ignores reality. Modern Linux distributions can utilize UEFI Secure Boot with custom signing keys and verify system integrity through TPM attestations in user space without turning the operating system kernel into a proprietary black box rootkit. Furthermore, competitors have long supported user space anti cheat modules inside Proton with minimal friction. * Security Theater vs. Hardware Cheats: For all of EA's insistence on invasive ring-0 kernel access on Windows, serious cheat developers didn't stop they simply moved to Direct Memory Access (DMA) PCIe hardware cards with spoofed device firmware that read memory externally, bypassing software kernel checks while legitimate Linux and handheld PC gamers are left out in the cold. The $55 Billion Guillotine: How EA's Buyout Spells Its Downfall If Battlefield 6's post launch trajectory already felt increasingly predatory, the corporate seismic shift that closed on August 4, 2026, explains why the worst is still ahead. In the largest leveraged buyout (LBO) in corporate history, EA was taken private in a $55 billion ($210-per-share) deal by a consortium consisting of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (holding roughly 93.4%), private equity giant Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners. To understand why this buyout is an existential threat to EA's studios and franchises, you only have to look at the balance sheet math: * Crushing Debt Placed on EA's Own Books: In a leveraged buyout, the buyers use the target company's own assets as collateral. To fund the takeover, roughly $18 billion to $20 billion in high-yield debt (with bonds priced between 6.25% and 8.75%) was dumped directly onto EA's balance sheet. * Interest Payments Exceed Profits: Servicing that debt requires roughly $1.8 billion per year in interest payments alone. In its prior fiscal year, EA generated $887 million in net income. In short, servicing the debt used to buy EA now costs significantly more every year than the company actually earned in profit. * Layoffs and "Organizational Efficiencies": Because the debt must be repaid out of EA's operating cash flow, the gutting started immediately. EA executed three separate rounds of layoffs in February, March, and June 2026 before the deal even officially closed, and subsequently promised debt investors $700 million in annual cost cuts, including $170 million in "organizational efficiencies" corporate speak for mass studio layoffs, alongside aggressive mandates to replace human creative workflows with generative AI. When a publisher is saddled with $20 billion in debt and stripped of development staff, margin expansion can only come from one place: squeezing existing players dry. Battlefield 6 has already become the testing ground for this desperation. Players who already paid full price for the base game are bombarded with prompts for a $24.99 cash-only "Battlefield Pro" tier (which cannot even be bought with earned in-game currency) that gates basic community infrastructure—like hosting 100 player persistent Portal servers behind a recurring paywall. Prior to Season 3, EA even began pushing $24.99 Battle Pass pre-orders before announcing what items were actually inside the pass a move that solves zero problems for players, existing purely to pull revenue forward for debt ridden financial reporting. The Verdict Battlefield 6 proves that the engineers and artists at Battlefield Studios still know how to build a thunderous, tactile military sandbox. The gunplay, soundscape, and environmental destruction deserve a spot alongside the franchise's golden era peaks. Yet it is impossible to wholeheartedly recommend a game whose publisher treats Linux users like criminals, locks community server capabilities behind multi tiered subscription passes, and is now chained to an $18+ billion private-equity debt bomb. Battlefield 6 isn't dying because of the developers. It's EA.

review_text: Very disappointed with the game, and that's coming from someone who've played 2042 for almost 200 hours (whilst it was really not good, I still gave it a fair shot). We were promised a return to the roots, we've basically got COD. Gameplay is okay, don't get me wrong on that, far better in fact than what 2042 could propose (although BFV stills clears every other BF games in terms of gameplay). But, the maps are SO restrictive I feel like we're playing in a very tiny portion of a larger potential map, spawn zones are an absolute joke, and the Season 5 is by far the worst announcements they could possibly have done. Who the ♥♥♥ asked for a Dead Space collab ??? Where's the "boots on the ground" approach we were promised ? The guns have this "you must play the meta" ♥♥♥, the UI is bloated from the menus to the gameplay, and the game whilst looking worse that previous entries such as BFV and BF1, runs very poorly on optimized settings with measurments i've made. At least, you could have proposed an option to turn off skins and reactive skins. Don't get me wrong, I definitely didn't want BF6 to be a mil-simesque game, I've got Arma covering for that. But this game does NOT feel like a Battlefield game at all. I legitimately feel scammed and sadly won't trust anything else BF Studios might promise in the future, depsite my many fond memories i've had with this series (since BF2).
