review_text: Now that all the content updates have been released, meaning the base game is effectively complete, it felt like a good time to revisit my thoughts on Wilds' base game. For some context, I've been playing Monster Hunter games since 3U released in 2013, and the first ~230 hours of my playtime on Wilds were built up in the initial two months after launch. To quickly summarize my most important thoughts: I think this is the strongest High Rank game we've ever had in the mainline series and one of the strongest High Rank experiences in the franchise. The monster roster is very good and the gameplay feels like a significant improvement from its World/Iceborne roots, which are the two most important parts of a Monster Hunter game. However, even for a High Rank game, it does feel abnormally easy until you start hitting the endgame (HR50+), where it ramps up and starts feeling much better. Performance is acceptable in its current state, though it still leaves a lot to be desired considering the level of fidelity on display. The main story is ♥♥♥, the prodigal child it revolves around is annoying, and there's several lengthy auto-walking segments that always drag the pacing to a crawl - but that all becomes irrelevant once you finish Low Rank (which should take you 15-20 hours). You suffer through it once and then basically never worry about it again. The game is in a fairly good spot now. While I always hesitate to recommend any $70 game at its full price, I think that most of the potential for buyers' remorse has been eliminated by now, and if you're comfortable paying that much then you won't regret it. If you can get the game on any kind of discount then it's much easier to endorse. Unless these sorts of grind-focused action games just aren't something you get along with, I guess. I'm eagerly awaiting the G Rank expansion. If Capcom can come back with a roster of additions that's a similar size and quality level to that of the base game, then Wilds will probably dethrone GU as my favorite title in the franchise. But that remains to be seen. If that's enough information for you, great. If not, here's some additional detail for each of the points I mentioned above. Gameplay This feels like a refined and more responsive version of World/Iceborne, which makes sense as the two entries share a director in Yuya Tokuda. In many ways, Wilds is like a spiritual successor to World. I main Hunting Horn, and in my opinion this is easily the best iteration of the weapon we've ever had. It restores the emphasis on positioning and predictive play that had fallen by the wayside in Rise/Sunbreak, while doing a better job of incentivizing aggressive play than previous entries. I've also logged a few dozen hunts with most of the other weapons, and those too feel like improved versions of their World counterparts. Safe to say that unless the only way you could have fun was spamming SAEDs with Charge Blade, you'll probably be happy with how your main feels right now. As I said before, I think the monster roster is very strong. That isn't to say that there are no weak links; rather, that even the most forgettable fights are still enjoyable in the moment. There aren't any true stinkers in the game right now, no equivalent to World's Lavasioth or Rise's Almudron. Nothing so unfun or annoying that it makes you want to stop playing for the day after a handful of hunts. For me, the closest thing to that is the returning siege monster you'll find after reaching the endgame. It's another one of the heavily scripted pseudo-raid fights that World became somewhat infamous for, and it just makes me sad. The original version of the fight wasn't exactly exciting either, but loading the cannons and activating various arena traps was still more enjoyable than any of the bespoke mechanics created for Wilds' rendition of it. Around launch, the game received a lot of criticism for being too easy, and it's not entirely unfounded. Even though this is just a High Rank game and those are always on the easier side, the power delta between your hunter and the various monsters is much higher than it's been in the past. Focus Mode gives you the ability to freely aim all of your attacks with very little downside, meaning that mistakes are punished less harshly. The wound mechanic allows smart players to chain flinches and knockdowns together in ways that we've never been able to before. The effect is frankly comical on some monsters. And wounds are very easy to exploit as you progress through the game, it isn't until the endgame hunts that wounds become noticeably harder to create. I made it all the way to HR50 before failing a quest for the first time, and my weapon has historically been the worst out of all melee options. Outside of the 9- and 10-star endgame hunts, which are properly hard, the difficulty just isn't going to be there until G Rank comes out. If you want a hard Monster Hunter experience right now, the Risen Elders and high-level Anomaly fights in Sunbreak are your best bet. You could also go load up GU's Hypers or EX Deviants. Hell, if you really get off on putting your genitals in a bench vice then go look up how to play on a Frontier private server. I've done all of those and had a blast in each of them. The weakest aspect here is how large some of the maps are while not having enough points of interest to justify the size. Just flat open spaces for the sake of encouraging you to ride your mount. It's also annoying that several shortcuts between zones are inaccessible if you're on foot, particularly in the early maps. The game conditions you to enable full self-driving, and that makes it harder for you to feel connected to the world like learning maps in previous games could. Story I don't have much more to add here aside from it being ♥♥♥ and feeling like a slog because of the regular autoscrolling segments. The story in a MH game being bad shouldn't surprise anyone who's played one before, it's always been an afterthought and it wasn't until World that they tried upping the production value, but this one really left a bad taste in my mouth. The prodigal child it's supposed to revolve around is distinctly unlikable and annoying every time he's on screen. The main story beats are nonsensical and the conclusion is very underwhelming. Thankfully you only have to do it once, and it doesn't take very long to get through (despite how it feels at times). Performance Most areas of the game run acceptably in their current state. I play at 1440p and average 60-65 FPS on mostly High settings with FSR running in Native Anti-Aliasing mode, however some parts still drop into the low 50s or even mid 40s. One thing to note about my specs is that my 6800XT is overclocked to 2.5GHz, so if you have the same card then your performance may be a bit worse than mine. The heavier parts of the game still seem CPU-bound so it might not make a huge difference either. Fact is, the RE engine doesn't cut it for open-world games, which is something that Capcom has known for some time. They couldn't get the upgraded REX engine ready in time, and having to backport a ton of work to the RE engine was one of the biggest contributors to the game's myriad of issues at release. Hopefully REX will be ready for MH7 (or even Portable 6th). Even on a mix of High and Highest settings, including the optional high-res texture pack, the game really doesn't look good enough to justify being so hard to run. It's certainly an upgrade over World, but it's not a huge one in terms of actual visual fidelity. Fur looks much better, textures are noticeably sharper, characters and environments are more detailed... however there's still a certain blurriness to the presentation even with all the usual suspects disabled (upscaling, motion blur, TAA, volumetric fog, DoF, etc). You won't always notice it but it sticks out every time you do. I've never had any significant crashing issues.

review_text: There are already many negative reviews that give very valuable feedback on the game. For whatever reason, it does not seem that anything is done to directly address issues raised by the playerbase. Rather, the devs have dealt with them peripherally, or just straight up insulted the playerbase with collaborations nobody asked for when technical issues are the most salient. There is nothing wrong with introducing new content, and it can be good when the game works. But the game barely works for most. Furthermore, its gameplay is decent, but highly overrated. There are many glaring issues with it: - The wounds mechanic. Some weapons rely more on the wounds mechanic to be effective. The wounds mechanic works in a "zero-sum" manner. Meaning that if one person takes the wound, everyone else in the session is deprived of it. So, for example, if you are a charged blade user and you're paired with bow users, good luck trying to activate savage axe mode. And when you can do so, you would have done so with great anxiety and at a cost to proper strategy and timing. There are other things to say about the wounds mechanic, such as the insane stunlock on monsters. - The maps are picturesque, visually stunning, but lacking in substance and/or complexity. On this note it is important to compare it with Monster Hunter World (it's predecessor). The maps in Monster Hunter World may not have been as big, but there was more "content" packed into its area compared to the ones in Wilds. For whatever jank it had, MHWorld had more complex maps, and interactions with the environment that seemed more organic- not just pretty but flat maps with theatrical QTEs. So the end result is you have spaces that look good but feel hollow. - The weapons don't feel great anymore. So many weapons have glaring issues, and those who main each respective one will tell you exactly what is wrong with them. Many changes to the weapons from previous titles don't make any sense on the whole. I myself stopped using the charged blade entirely in MHWilds, which was my favourite weapon in MHWorld. This is not to say that no improvements could have been made to the weapons in MHWorld, but the way they approached it in MHWilds seems to lack careful evaluation of feedback provided by fans of MHWorld and MHRise. The crux of the matter is, in their effort to streamline and "improve" the accessibility of the game, many weapons have a more fixed way of being played, or have simply been dumbed down in general. Some changes to the weapons render certain moves pointless altogether. MHWilds had every opportunity to take from and improve systems from its predecessors (MHWorld and MHRise). MHRise for example allowed Hunters to customise weapon movesets, which introduced different ways to use the weapon and adds more satisfaction because of the variety and added flavour. You would think MHWilds would adapt something similar to this, considering its much bigger scope, budget, prior material, and scale, right? Nope. After all those years of development, and the insane starting price of the base game, this is how they justify it. Nothing really new or innovative has been added to the mix. No real substantial additions. No new weapons. No new ground-breaking fun ways to use already existing weapons. - Difficulty and accessibility. The Monster Hunter series has always featured the balance between preparation and execution. MHWilds undermines this balance by becoming the most forgiving entry in the series. There is often little consequence to mistakes, paired with overpowered blocking and the heavy emphasis on perfect blocks. The point of Monster Hunter was never about artificial difficulty, but rewarding mastery and deliberate play. In MHWilds, that diluted sense of mastery, alongside the overly-simplified weapon systems and rigid playstyles, makes combat feel flat and less engaging. - Loss of tension and identity. As an extension of the previous point, MHWilds lacks a genuine sense of danger- something that heavily characterises all its previous titles. Previous titles excelled at making monsters feel intimidating and memorable. First encounters with monsters like Nergigante, Bazelgeuse, etc. were tense and overwhelming. Monsters commanded more respect with their presence. But MHWilds rarely achieves this. Encounters with monsters feel a lot more choreographed and less threatening. What comes from this is a game that has monsters with superficial spectacle, but no real threat substantiating it. Aside from problems with gameplay (and I'm sure I've also missed out on many other important ones), other issues abound: - Technical issues. Ironically, while the game attempts to become "accessible" to players by dumbing down mechanical depth and punishment, it becomes less accessible in practice due to its technical state. MHWilds places extremely heavy demands on hardware, effectively locking out many players (and long-time fans) who use systems that don't cost you a kidney. In contrast, other modern titles (such as the free game Where Winds Meet) has both smooth gameplay and very decent graphics without requiring top-end GPUs. - The story. The Monster Hunter series was never known for having the most compelling stories, but again, with all the resources they had, whatever you see in the game is an absolute joke. For the record, there are games that cost a lot cheaper, with much smaller teams, that have way more compelling stories. Even a free game like the new Where Winds Meet has a story so much more compelling. - Monetisation. For reference, the starting price of the base game is already extremely high. It was 70 USD, 60 GBP, 100 SGD, etc. And yet there are still features you would expect to not cost anything additional... that cost additional. For example, the game charges you real money each time you edit your character after the first time you do so. There's also a sneaking suspicion that they would intentionally make "free" gear/layered armour unattractive, just to compel players to spend real money on cosmetics. - Messaging. Referring to updates as "Free Title Updates" is extremely disingenuous, as it frames essential fixes and late-arriving features as "bonuses" rather than necessary completions of an unfinished product. This ranges from technical to content issues (or the lack of content altogether). After almost 10 months, its players are getting late-delivered fixes (which haven't really worked at this point in time) for an extremely high-priced game that really needed more time to cook, and they market it as exciting content drops. Furthermore, capcom's fiscal year ended on 31 March 2025, while MHWilds launched on 28 February 2025. This timing allowed Capcom to record roughly 10 million unit sales in its final report. Coupled with the technical state at launch, and its severe lack of content, it would be reasonable to infer that Capcom prioritised corporate goals at the cost of severely undermining the quality of MHWilds. Gamers/Hunters lost, and the shareholders won. In July, Capcom also issued a formal policy warning that it would take legal action and pursue criminal proceedings against customers whose feedback exceeded "socially accepted standards". Capcom is happy to take premium prices for an unfinished product, but considers it a breach of social standards when the fans who funded that success express dissatisfaction with the result. (See also RainbowKrampus’ 12 December review for a critique of MHWilds’ PC performance) Regardless of whether the issues ultimately stem from the developers or the corporate leadership, the end result is that players were charged a premium price for a product that was neither finished nor honestly presented at launch. This conduct is predatory and exploitative. What is most disappointing, however, is not merely the presence of technical or design flaws. Capcom eroded trust- trust that was built over years and then severely undermined with this release cycle.

As someone who started with the first game in MH1 and played each new title from there it brings a happy but somewhat bitter feeling within. Don’t take this the wrong way I still love the franchise all warts and all, this is me dissecting what gave me mixed feelings along with the well earned praise. Mixed feelings - Sadly I must confess about my Wild problems First, Asinine inconsistent multiplayer structure - had 2 crashes, friends and I tried to play multiplayer for the full base game from the start and it was just constant complaints. Group play was fantastic as always, but the gears of starting and over-complicating the multiplayer features always slicing our knees everytime we played is brutal. Let me walk you through the process of why the multiplayer from just starting in low rank to end credits. 1. Start game 2. Enter game 2.5 wait for godawful loadingscreens to finish before main menu appears 3. Invite friends from steam list/or join a squad then join lobby 4. Make sure all friends are in a link party 5. Start main quest 6. Cutscene! 7. Forced on a mandatory escort mission EVERYTIME 8. Large Monster appears, fight just a bit to have notification quest sent out to all in link party 9. 3 of your party have to QUIT their own MAIN QUEST. To join the 4th player’s MAIN QUEST 10. Fight large monster with everyone! Yay! 11. Finish quest, watch new cutscene! 12. Repeat steps 5 to 11. Process repeating the cycle from steps 5 to 11 until you get to end credits which in my group was just shy of 15 hours or just a bit over. Absolute madness! Such an insane, bewildering, exhausting, and quite frankly horrible experience. Our group came back from Monster Hunter Rise + Sunbreak where we would literally. Do step 5, but we all can see the cutscenes and we ALL ENTER THE SAME MAIN QUEST. How the fudgeruckers did we regress from this peak form in multiplayer to separate instances by comparison. God, it infuriates me with salt tsunami’s coming from every pore of my soul. We don’t need to send an invite everytime nor do we need to quit our own quest to join our 4th player’s quest. MH Rise multiplayer infrastructure by comparison was near flawless. Everyone loads in, sees cutscene, no need to wait until you can send everyone a notice saying “Hey yall can join now!” no fuss or muss. MH Wild Multiplayer? Oi devs get back to work fixing this. 2nd, Forced Cutscenes and lots of guided forced walking while admiring the indigenous life. Aside from the multiplayer. I also found to my absolute flabbergast most if not all story missions were forced walking while admiring the wildlife. More often than not you couldn’t venture out and had to focus following a linear path in an other wild large world hearing your constant companions yapping while you unbearably have to listen to them through the day. Third, I don't like how large monsters are permanently visible, specifically on the minimap. And more often than not close by the base camp. I love the MH series for the simple act of finding where the monster is through hunting their familiar routes either. Feels good to paintball them once you succeed in finding them by trekking through the terrain into their habitats and thus can track their status if you have a special skill. Fourth, not a fan of how the base game’s story is structured. Particularly an annoying lackey who tags alongside us but also the main premise where we, a newly promoted hunter of the guild has to escort said annoying lackey in the Forbidden lands, an uncharted region of the old world. As usual something strange is occurring in these lands and its up to us to find out why. I’ll be honest, I find the narrative of introducing us to these new characters to be flat, uninteresting, predictable and beyond some cool climactic moments of ‘hype’ and ‘aura’ they ultimately dwindle my interest. Perks of Monster Fighter Wild Off the bat, I appreciate the auto-pathing quite a bit. Helped tide over my frustration at times with the forced walking segments when I could set auto-pathing to move my character already and when I needed to go somewhere I can easily set my character to go there while I move the camera and admire the view, reminds me a lot of Jurassic Park films of the ‘tourist’ sections, in a way where our cast is viewing the landscape and indigenous life while we enjoy the ride. I adore the wound system which reminds me a bit of Xenoblade Chronicles X’s parts destroying system, for a similar surface level comparison I suppose one could think of it like the Fallout VATS system , though with no slow mo. Love how the dev’s incorporated companions we can bring to missions from Sunbreak. Now with flares we can bring AI companions to fill in the slots for a party. Not mandatory(except some story missions) too! Seamless biome integration, this is something I wish MHWorld had innately at launch. Where we the player could travel to any biome and back without any loading screen at all. Wilds finally fulfills this feature, where each zone is connected and we could travel from one area to another via mounted or plain good o’l running. Useful to have two weapons we can change once we mount rides, very nifty if we are engaged against 2 or 3 enemies and they have opposite elements they’re weak against. So I can change my Fire charge blade for a Dragon element charge blade. The days of having to lug one weapon for all engagements during a quest are no more! Performance is now Gucci. Back when MH Wilds first launched I tried the demo benchmark and GOOD LORD, faces were melting, crashes galore, egregious texture loading, horrible frame drops, and overall a miserable experience. Now with the latest updates as of June 2026 I can confirm and with my friends who tried the game alongside me, we are finally in pretty good state. Great title updates even better than Rise base content and post game grind wasn’t grindy! This was a main criticism I had back in Rise, where I felt the content was lacking and a weak majority of exclusive mons. Here? we don't have that problem, I felt the free quests updates given were a suitable amount of old and new integrated well enough for me to be in awe. Despite my rating being in the situational range according to my scoring system, i still generally think Monster Hunter Wilds is a fine entry for newcomers to try. Veterans may hm and ah like I did for sure, but it doesn’t detract from my overall pleasure seeing the franchise flourish so hard when it was a niche JRPG decades ago. Honestly Wilds has a lot of forward steps I very much like, but the fact it missteps quite a sizable scars left me in dire straits, more so than my time in Monster Hunter Rise , a game I also finished their fair of postgame in the base game. Yet, when I think about my experience in Wilds, I have to confess I did enjoy a lot of quality of life it offers, I suppose now I must accept the fact the series will inevitably experiment perhaps in a similar manner as to how each new entry in Final Fantasy always shakes up the formula in some way. And while the series has maintained a core identity from gen1 to gen4, the shift from gen5(World) and up have largely diverged in concepts so we’ll see how the future goes! The upcoming expansion Ascendance looks super hype since they're bringing my OG big daddy back from MH1 and I cannot wait to experience that fight once again! 5.9/10

review_text: Going into this game I was eagerly excited. How could hunting monsters be anything other than extraordinarily invigorating? How could one possibly ♥♥♥ this up? I knew there were performance issues people complained about, but I was undaunted. I decided to support this franchise, one of the last that still sparks dopamine in me. Against common sense I bought the deluxe edition as a token of good faith to the dev team. Performance issues for me were rare, so I assumed it was just people with outdated rigs trying to squeeze performance out of their decaying GPUs. My friend had issues with his semi-old setup barely hitting 30 fps despite tweaking his settings. I got 60 fps with my 4060 TI. I’m not a max graphics kind of guy, so it was good enough for me. Where everything fell apart was in the core gameplay. I consider myself a seasoned hunter, not a speedrunner. So when I started killing monsters in five minutes flat, I thought something was wrong. I told myself it must be because it’s low rank. Surely high rank would ramp up the challenge. Right? Right?? No. It didn’t. What I found was a game on rails. Beautiful worlds, sure, but they mean nothing when your mount takes you directly to the monster every single time. I don’t even count travel time anymore because it’s automatic. The real fight starts when the laser pointer stops, and that’s about five minutes of empty motion. The fanbase calling this “rewarding” or “respectful of my limited game time” absolutely baffles the ♥♥♥ out of me. I haven’t suddenly become a god-tier hunter overnight. The problem is the monsters hit like toddlers. There’s no fear, no tension, no need to respect them. You can play recklessly and win. The older games punished greed. One bad swing could send you back to camp, forcing you to think and adapt. Here, the monsters might as well have foam teeth. You can stun-lock them in half a dozen ways. You can play with your eyes closed. The game inflates everyone’s skill by making failure nearly impossible. And the fanbase cheers like cattle for being bottle-fed easy mode, insisting, “It’s just low and high rank that’s easy, wait till G rank!” I was so disappointed that I went back and replayed Rise, then World. Within an hour I realized how far the series has fallen. There’s no auto-find. My weapons have weight. I can’t greed attacks because I’ll actually get punished. I got carted several times adjusting back from Wilds’ hand-holding design and I laughed. The contrast was that stark. Rise reminded me what risk feels like. Wilds feels like a padded room where you’re not allowed to fail, not allowed to feel. In Wilds you can hunt two monsters of any type and already have everything you need to craft a full armor set. That’s about five to seven minutes per hunt, tops. Ninety-eight percent of the game is you coasting half-awake, waiting for the credits to roll. Once you’ve crafted your weapon, armor, and decorations, you’re done. There’s no drive left. God forbid the FOMO-afflicted crowd actually face something difficult. Finding the monster is automatic, fighting it is a formality, and gathering loot is guaranteed. Why stop there? In the next installment they might as well add an “auto-hunt” feature, and the fanbase will probably call it “a quality-of-life improvement.” And yeah, I’ve seen the noise about how there are no strong male characters, how the cast is full of girls and one brown kid who won’t stop whining. Sure, that’s annoying, but it’s not why this game fails. I don’t give a ♥♥♥ about the story. I’m not here for politics or representation debates. I’m here to hunt monsters. I’m here to feel challenge, danger, and triumph. Instead, what I got feels hollow. The gameplay loop is soulless. The fights have no tension, no grit, no weight. Every victory feels unearned. Every monster feels defanged. And the fanbase’s defense—that “a couple of late-game monsters are hard”—is the most damning thing of all. You’re telling me I need to mindlessly wade through hours of filler just to finally experience the ghost of what Monster Hunter used to be? This isn’t evolution. It’s lobotomy. The spirit of Monster Hunter wasn’t just about the grind; it was about struggle, tension, and mastery. That’s gone. What’s left is an empty shell of a once-great series made safe for people who don’t actually like difficulty but still want to feel like they’ve conquered something. Monster Hunter Wilds doesn’t respect your time. It drains it. It flatlines your passion. It turns the hunt into a checklist and the player into a consumer. And the saddest part is that people will call this progress. I can't in good faith suggest this for anyone until they address the core gameplay loop...which won't be happening because they want to appeal to new hunters and not actual hunters.

That said the cutscenes are really damn good, and the monster encounters in them are cinematic. every time the handler authorizes a hunt i bust a lil I really like the Focus system and the new wound system conceptually, but they currently feel overtuned. Hunters are way more op than before but many monsters don’t seem to have been given enough new tools or reaction speed to compensate. Some monsters feel too slow and end up getting stun locked for large portions of the fight due to constant wound breaks This is most noticeable in lowrank but Once the real game begins after finishing the low rank story, difficulty does improve and monsters become more threatening but the Focus system still feels stronger than it probably should be. Good systems overall, but they need tuning. Specs: RTX 4080 / AMD 5950X 64 gigs of DDR4 At launch performance was rough even on highend hardware. After the January patch, it’s a completely different experience. I’m now running at a smooth 120–140 FPS at max settings, native resolution. Major improvement. here are some Criticisms i have I don’t like the Seikret mount. Default controls are poorly mapped and require adjustment. Auto movement being enabled by default is ass. I dislike the removal of traditional tracking mechanics. Always seeing monster locations makes paintballs feel pointless. The pack mechanic is a good idea but feels underutilized. I haven’t reached endgame yet, so I can’t comment on that portion of the experience. Despite some questionable changes to the classic formula, Capcom has improved what they built in world/iceborne with this release. i would say Wilds improves upon Monster Hunter in most areas that matter. Highly recommended. Hyped for the next expansion

review_text: Monster Hunter Wilds is a fantastic action game, but it's one of the least satisfying Monster Hunter games I've played. Wilds absolutely nails the presentation. The environments are beautiful and the monster animations are the best they've ever been including a great roster with returning community favourites and awesome new additions. The game is packed with little details that make hunting feel alive. The problem is that almost every system surrounding the combat pushes the game toward being faster and easier. Wounds let you deal massive bursts of damage for very little effort, monsters spend huge amounts of time toppled over, Seikrets remove much of the commitment from actions like healing and sharpening, and hunts are often over just as they feel like they're getting started. I don't want a hunt to end in ten minutes. I want a struggle that lasts for a decent amount of time and leaves me feeling like I genuinely overcame something. My biggest criticism isn't that Wilds changed Monster Hunter—it's how it changed it. Older games asked you to commit to your decisions. If you wanted to sharpen you had to find an opening. If you drank a potion you stood still and would get rocked if you didn't do it at an appropriate time. If you got hit you had to deal with the consequences. That slower pace made every success feel earned. Wilds smooths away so much of that friction that the highs don't feel quite as high anymore. It's far too easy of a game for people who have played an entry in the series before. Monsters feel like they struggle to fight back and the player has an answer for every situation. This problem is exacerbated in multiplayer where it feels less like a hunt and more like beating on a crippled puppy for 5 minutes until the quest complete message shows up. The only fights that consistently run up to the 20+ minute mark and pose an actual threat in multiplayer are endgame encounters like omega and gogmazios and even then they still go down really quickly. Performance is also a big sore spot with the game, I am able to run the game at mostly maxed out settings and no upscaling with a semi consistent 60fps but in places like the jungle in Plenty season certain areas can cause that to go down into the low 50s. It's clear the game wants you to use upscaling which is an industry direction i don't really agree with as i prefer games at native resolutions and no fake frames with framegen. I don't agree with the steam page listing a 2060 with a Ryzen 5 3600 as "recommended" you are certainly gonna want beefier hardware than that. That's not to say Wilds is bad. Far from it. It's polished, incredibly fluid to control, and probably one of the easiest Monster Hunter games to recommend to a newcomer. Layered armour and weapons being here is always awesome allowing you to make the hunter of your dreams and the new fluffy palico option is so cute. Add on their adorable new voices and i became obsessed with my little partner and wanted to support him just as much as he supported me. I just think it lost a little of what made the series special to me. I don't want Monster Hunter to be faster. I want it to make me think, commit, and struggle. Overall: 7/10. A great action game, but not the direction I personally want Monster Hunter to continue in.

review_text: Having given it some thought, and having 100%'d it, Monster Hunter Wilds might be my least favorite game. I'm an old hunter. I started with Monster Hunter Tri back on the Wii and I love that game to bits. But I'm not some jaded old gen guy who hates everything new; Monster Hunter World is another of my favorite games, and though it had its issues, namely the uninteresting story and AWFUL endgame content, the game was still Monster Hunter at its core and I still enjoy playing World to this day. I'm saying this as context when I say that Wilds was one of the worst gaming experiences I've ever had. Almost nothing about this game works. I say almost because there are legitimate improvements in Wilds worth recognizing; the ability to use your binoculars to check the sizes of monsters is something that should have been in the series years ago, as is the ability to skip the 60 second end of quest timer. These are good changes. Unfortunately, they're subsumed by a cavalcade of baffling game design choices. Let's start with the least of my issues; the pacing. To the game's credit, the pacing of the game is, at first, pretty good! Monster Hunter has always had issues with getting players into fighting big monsters and this one does it the fastest, and after the intro you're already fighting a boss. However, afterwards the game's pace rams straight into a brick wall and doesn't pick up again until the third act. Until then, you are railroaded on these truly - and I do mean this - TRULY boring walk and talk scenes where nothing happens and the characters talk about the most boring things imaginable. If these dialogue segments were written well, I wouldn't have minded so much, but almost every bit of dialogue in this game is stilted and uninteresting to listen to, much like the story. It's not the absolute worst story I've ever had the displeasure of sitting through, but it is still a boring, melodramatic mess that cuts into time I could have been spending slaughtering the local ecosystem for new boots, and while yes, the cutscenes are skippable, the frequent walk and talk scenes are not and you have to sit there on your mount as the characters around you drone on about nature or whatever. Have fun! Let's get into why this game really grinds my gears. The gameplay of Wilds was gutted from previous games. Hard. Monster Hunter's combat has always been about proper positioning; knowing where you should be to hit a monster's weakspots while not getting killed yourself. It was simple, it was engaging, it was unique and it was fun. Monster Hunter Wilds introduces new mechanics that remove all of that; Focus Mode and the wound system can effectively stunlock monsters to the point where they are a non-threat and almost laughably easy to kill. You don't need proper positioning when the answer is always aim for a wound and pop it with focus mode, which means you can basically just wail on a monster and kill it in five minutes. What made Monster Hunter's combat so unique has been replaced by hack and slash gameplay and I think that is unbelievably disappointing. Continuing from monsters being a non-threat in this game, returning monsters from older games have been slowed down significantly or gutted of their moves to the point where they're hardly the same monsters anymore. Even new monsters have attacks that just leave them wide open for several seconds, and it comes off as unnatural and video game-y, which is ironic considering the story of Wilds. This is a nitpick, but for as much as folks like to rag on Capcom for reusing assets or recoloring monsters in older titles, this is the game that feels the most like I'm just fighting the same monsters over and over with different body shapes. Wilds is also painfully easy. I was killed one time during the entire low rank campaign, and it was because of a camera issue. Monsters simply do not do enough damage to you throughout low rank to justify getting new armor past, like, the midway point, it's pathetic. Preparation, a key component in older titles, has been streamlined to the point where it's almost unnecessary. Your cat friend can heal you, buff you and cure you of all statuses the instant you get them, removing any urgency you may have getting poisoned or burned, and unlike previous games, your cat always has access to all of their tools, removing any semblance of customization for them. Luckily the cat can be turned off, but the random endemic life that does the same will always be out in the open for you to use, removing the point of half of this game's items. Connecting to friends has never been made harder. Instead of the simple act of selecting a lobby and then joining, Capcom thought that process wasn't complicated enough and introduced several friend code and friend list systems that muddle the joining process and make connecting with your friends way more difficult than it needs to be. Even once you're together, God help you if you picked the option "environment link" because now you're all stuck in the Windward Plains with nothing but a Chatacabra, a Balahara and absolutely no way to initiate quests. What the hell was wrong with the old system? This is the big one: Your mount will automatically take you to your quest target, removing the need to learn your environment and understand a monster's behaviours. This is one of the core components of Monster Hunter and it was completely removed: Actually HUNTING the monsters. Now you just always know where your mark is, you go to it and you hunt it. Yes, it's more convenient, yes, it's easier to get into playing the game but it removes so much nuance and charm and uniqueness the older games provided to the point where Monster Hunter Wilds doesn't even feel like Monster Hunter anymore. It feels like just another action game, its individuality and personality torn to shreds and its mechanics broadened to make Capcom as much money as possible from as many people as possible. And it worked. Capcom will never learn from this because it sold like hot cakes. They will never make another Monster Hunter game again, but they will keep making games like Wilds devoid of what made Monster Hunter, well... Monster Hunter. And I think that is a genuine shame.

review_text: I think it’s time to add a more grounded perspective to the discourse around Monster Hunter Wilds. Some of the criticism it’s getting is fair—but a lot of it feels like long-time players complaining about changes that don’t meaningfully harm the experience and, in many cases, actively improve it. For context, I’m not a diehard fan of the series. I played Monster Hunter: World, skipped Monster Hunter Rise, and came back for Wilds specifically because it addressed some of the friction points I’ve always had with the series. Focus Mode: Focus Mode doesn’t “ruin” the game—it’s optional. If you don’t like it, don’t use it. That’s the simplest reality. For many players, especially newer ones, it improves responsiveness and reduces the feeling that you’re fighting your own character instead of the monster. There’s a recurring mindset in parts of the gaming community that clunkiness equals skill expression. It doesn’t. Sometimes something just feels bad—and smoothing that out doesn’t dilute the experience, it refines it. If someone finds themselves using Focus Mode despite claiming to hate it, that says more about how it improves gameplay feel than anything else. Wound System: If there’s a system that actually impacts gameplay balance, it’s this one. The Wound System was over tuned at launch and, even after adjustments, still leans toward being too strong. It can trivialize encounters by enabling repeated staggers and high-damage windows with minimal risk. As a result, fights often feel shorter and less dynamic than they should, with monsters going down in just a few minutes. This is where criticism should be focused; not on optional quality-of-life features, but on mechanics that meaningfully affect combat depth. Mounts and Travel: Auto-travel isn’t particularly exciting, and it does feel like a convenience feature rather than a meaningful addition. That said, the argument that it “removes the hunting from Monster Hunter” doesn’t really hold up. The series has never truly been about hunting in a simulation sense. Monsters are marked almost immediately, and the gameplay loop has always been about engaging them in combat rather than tracking them in a systemic or emergent way. There’s no real risk of losing a trail, no deep ecology systems to learn, and no meaningful punishment for poor tracking. At its core, Monster 'Hunter' is more-so just a name than it is a suggestion of its gameplay loop and has always been closer to an arena-based action game than a true hunting simulator. Certainly not like something even somewhat controversial in hunting communities, like theHunter: Call of the Wild. Where its seen as a watered down hunting game, this one doesn't even barely begin to reach the basic foundations to be really considered one. You're chasing after a monster to fight it, you aren't exactly hunting it when there's nothing but surface level flavor text outside of missions to give an illusion of that. Alongside that, I highly doubt that a large portion of players are sitting here taking in the vistas. Monster Hunters in any form aren't exactly pushing the graphical boundries and while the set pieces of their world can be cool to see, like any game's environment, it's guaranteed to get old for the vast majority of players by even the 5th time going through it, so I don't feel like this is any better of a complaint. There are few if any exploration rewards or reasons to spend a load of time in these zones beyond fighting the monster or grinding ingredients to fight the monsters and the zones themselves aren't to the quality or beauty of something like RDR2, Dark Souls titles, Crimson Desert, and more which all focus more on the exploration quality than this series ever did and likely ever will. These maps are just that: Set pieces to an epic battle between some giant beast and a human. That's why most players got into this series and most players will keep playing it, not because the tiny map you can run around in 15 minutes looks nice. Grind: Complaining that the game doesn’t demand excessive grinding is hard to take seriously. Reducing artificial time sinks isn’t a flaw. If players can build viable gear without repeating the same hunt dozens (or hundreds) of times, that’s respecting their time. Players who enjoy grinding can still do so voluntarily—but designing progression around extreme repetition shouldn’t be the baseline expectation. A better direction would be adding meaningful challenges—harder variants, unique encounters, or skill-based rewards—rather than padding playtime through low drop rates. Broader Issues: Where Wilds, and frankly, World before it actually stumbles is in content and post-launch structure. Both games launched feeling incomplete, relying heavily on updates and expansions to reach their full potential. There’s also a noticeable reliance on reusing monsters to stretch content. This pattern suggests a broader issue with how Capcom is managing the series, rather than any single gameplay mechanic. Final Thoughts: A lot of the backlash toward Wilds feels less like thoughtful critique and more like resistance to change—especially from players whose experience and identity are tied to mastering older, clunkier systems. But improvements to responsiveness, accessibility, and pacing don’t invalidate the series—they modernize it. And if those changes are optional, then they’re not even taking anything away. Criticism is important, but it should be aimed at systems that actually affect the game’s depth and longevity—not features that simply make it feel better to play.

review_text: I'm not gonna comment on performance because you'll likely read more than enough about it in the reviews. All I'm gonna say is I have a pretty beefy rig myself and experienced some pretty bad drops in performance which isn't exactly ideal when the game looks fairly muddy when you start looking up close. That being said. I think what killed MH: Wilds the most for me was how trimmed down everything felt compared to previous titles. I'm not one for artificial difficulty but if I don't have at least some challenge, then parts of the game just feel boring. There's no researching monsters to identify more things about them to aid in hunts, there's no expeditions to stock on needed supplies for hunts, there's just nothing to add to the hunt other than breaking out a stick and whacking away at it. This might work for the people who want nothing other than a monster arena style game but I don't think those types dominate the franchise. Another glowing problem with the game is the absolutely boring level design, it's not even close to other games and those who say otherwise are straight up lying. Windward Plains is a wide and empty desert with very little visual variety, you have a small oasis, some caves, lots of wide open spaces, and just overall nothing else going on. Compare this to Wildspire Waste which has the same desert style areas and caves, but also a riverlands, an isolated swamp, some steppes, and more. On the surface they seem similar but it comes back down to how EMPTY the worldspaces of Wilds feel. You have the same issue with Scarlet Forest, Oilwell Basin, Iceshard Cliffs, and the Ruins of Wyveria. But what feels worse is that each respective map starts to feel small and more like a corridor than a map which is a stark contrast to the prior games which were either much more open or at least had more flow to them with intertwining paths. Not to mention a total lack of unique locales such as Coral Highlands or Rotten Vale. It took me a relatively short time to become bored of the world it was making me inhabit. I hope the expansion truly breathes some life back in the game but I honestly don't have much faith that they will. What a monumental fumble of what could've been a title that surpassed everything before it.

review_text: I'd like to start this off by saying I'm going to try to be pretty transparent about the issues, negatives, and positives of this game - *However* I think the positives far outweigh the negatives. My only real major gripe with the game when it came out was the lack of difficult and engaging content, and bad performance on high-end hardware. Even though the monsters at launch were quite easy, the fights still felt deep and interesting compared to previous titles. Now jumping to the current state of the game, and the game is nearing exactly what I wanted it to be. My opinions on difficulty: All the 9* versions of monsters are a blast to fight, with interesting move sets and weaknesses you can exploit at the right times, like any other monster hunter game. Nearly all 9* monsters in this game are much higher quality fights than anything I experienced in either base Rise, World, or even GU. (The only games I've actually put a fair amount of time into). The new monsters and variety of returning monsters from old games and their upgraded move sets and gimmicks are fantastic. Unfortunately if you're a somewhat skilled player, most monsters outside of 9* monsters, don't really put up much of a fight at all. Wounds open instantly and they all get focus strike stun-locked until they die. Unlocking 9* monsters doesn't really take that long in the grand scheme of things and 9* monsters are the endgame and what you should be fighting the most of anyways. Focus Mode makes the combat extremely seamless, although it does remove the aspect of positioning yourself perfectly to land hits. Personally I think Focus Mode should be the future direction of Monster Hunter. Having the pace of the combat be controlled by what I find to be somewhat dated mechanics is just not something I want to see going forward, I want it to feel fresh. I feel as though designing every monster around the hunters' limited control was holding the fights back from ever evolving or changing in any meaningful way, though I can fully understand why people might enjoy the slower paced, more methodical combat of some previous titles. Savage Omega is one of the most unique and interesting fights in a Monster Hunter game to date and nearly forces you to fully utilize all the mechanics Wilds gives you to take it down easily. I will admit, before 9* monsters the game was quite easy, but I really don't understand the difficulty complaints of Wilds. 9* Monsters are both challenging, and fun and rewarding to fight. When a tempered wound pops up on a 9* monster, it actually feels rewarding to focus strike and get that opening, unlike the monsters 8* and below that just become punching bags. Playing through base game GU, Rise, and World, I do not remember a single fight that felt much more difficult or memorable than anything in Wilds, the only thing that actually felt more difficult about going back to those games again after Wilds was the lack of focus mode and trying to re-adjust. If you know how to lock down a monster in one Monster Hunter game, you can do it in any game. When it comes to performance: After the recent performance patch for Steam, the game has become a lot more stable. Personally my FPS didn't *increase* all that much, but the stutters and hitches are basically entirely gone, and it runs a lot smoother. Overall I have to say the future potential of Wilds, and it's expansion are only looking pretty high upwards. Most of the weapon kits in this game are fun, some could still use some adjustments to flow better. All the monsters are fun and engaging to fight, there isn't too much of a grind but the grind also isn't nonexistent, endgame difficulty is just about right, unique and fun new skills. The only thing the game really lacks right now for me is a couple more 9* versions of some of the existing monsters, a bit more balancing around the main gimmicks of the game (wounds and focus mode), and possibly a bit more options while mounted on a monster than just doing a mounted finisher. (I really liked when you could bonk the monsters into each other lol)

review_text: Played every game since MH3, with World being my favorite. I was ecstatic about Wilds being essentially World 2.0, but it has been largely a disappointment. Unfortunately, there's too many glaring issues to recommend the game. My gripes have nothing to do with performance. I had around 60 fps on launch, and after toying around/light modding to get DLSS and frame gen to work with my GPU, I had a consistent 80-120 at all times, which I was fine with. My disappointments were mainly with how much Capcom has dumbed down the game. They started adding QoL in World and Rise, and while some vets complained, most welcomed them. They saw the success those games brought and pumped that QoL up to 1000 for this game. Focus mode completely erases the methodical nature of MH combat, gathering or even grinding for monster parts (outside of ultra endgame gear) is a thing of the past, getting hit goes unpunished if you call your loyal steed to swoop in and save you, and my personal least favorite - the beautiful, sprawling maps the series has come to be known by have turned into glorified cutscenes. I wasn't a fan of the mounts in Rise for a similar reason, but at least you were looking at the screen while riding the palamute. Now when the monster goes to a new area, you literally press tab and pick up your phone, alt tab, do WHATEVER YOU WANT, because the "hunting" part of monster hunter is a thing of the past. Why do monsters even change locations anymore? Or why not just fight everything in an arena and load in instantly? Some of these maps are gorgeous but I couldn't tell you a single thing about most of them. Besides that, the endgame Artian weapon system (that they double downed on with TU4) is so mind-numbingly boring to interact with that I haven't bothered. I lost all interest when I saw multiple endgame build guides recommending savescumming to get the desired pieces. The game has a lot of great stuff- in particular I loved the ambitious approach to the MSQ. While it could've been much better, I've never been a huge fan of the "do this list of instanced quests" approach MH has done until now, and appreciated them trying something new. Furthermore, it has a great roster of beautiful monsters to fight, and the maps are on par with World for the most part. But too many poor decisions took away from the magic of MH and make it a chore to play.

review_text: I want to like it, I think. The game would not even run on my PC in Windows, it only works on Linux on a RX Vega56 which is an older obsurce card, but thats more of a driver issue as the card is no longer supported directly by AMD. Pacing is quite slow, unlike parts of World the game is very easy; 20 hours in and I have not carted at all playing solo. I feel as though it is missing those 'breakpoints' that other MH games had where you had to either learn or die. If you are a new player to the series this is probably not the case and it might actually draw you to the series. The 'on-rails' experience of the story so far is a little frustrating and I'm not a fan of my own Hunter having voice acting. You gain so many materials from a single hunt of a monster early in the game that it kind of takes the charm away from doing multiple hunts to gain that next big upgrade. The Seikret being able to remove you from any bad situation is wild, on the ground? press up on the d-pad, I feel as though it should probably be more 'afraid' of the monster that the hunter is engaged in a fight with. So many of the smaller nuances have been 'taken away'. Picking the correct potion was replaced with an 'optimal health/status recovery' option. Automatically picking up materials from broken parts of a monster rather than having that moment when you need to decide if you want the mat right away or to wait until its safe. Palico starting with so many available skills rather than gaining them through progression. The smaller mystery of each early hunt tracking the monster in the area, they are just always present on your map at all times. I realise this is just a stream of unfettered thoughts, I will add more once I encounter more ingame. Overall I think it would be a great experience for someone new to the titles, but just the lack of nuance and charm being replaced with single button presses and removing the draw to veteran players, especially in the early game feels detrimental. I have yet to encounter a moment where I felt I needed to SoS flare. I'll return and update the review after credits roll with my thoughts of the game as a whole.

review_text: Alright, I'm going to keep this short and sweet(This was not short at all). I don't really like the current negative reviews of the game, so I want to write my own that testifies against them. Anything I say should be taken with a grain of salt. I can very well agree that the story of the game is very underwhelming, and I basically snoozed my way through it. It felt like a forced session of constant walking. There are more reasons why I disliked it, but I can't pinpoint them. PERFORMANCE A constant dislike with the game is the overall performance; it has come an insanely long way if I am honest. From beta, where I'd always get 34 fps with a lot of laggy frames, to now, where I am at least averaging 50+ fps in even the highest quality of areas, is amazing. I've had my current pc for a few years, and it only cost a thousand dollars, the literal bare "minimal" for a gaming pc. If I can run this game with zero crashes, then maybe those people crashing should really study their pc's better and find the issue. DIFFICULTY SCALING A lot of old Monster Hunter players are sh*tting on Wilds for being too "unbearably easy" in the early game, when the game's difficulty is literally scaling in the same way as any other Monster Hunter game. My first game was Rise, and I solo'd every hub quest, not knowing that the monsters had buffed hp there without a hint of struggle. For MH:WLD, I haven't got stuck in it's early game once either, I have only quest failed on Nergigante, a built different monster. And even then, what's wrong with a game's early game being easy? Everyone's experience with a game's difficulty is subjective. Is that not what an early game is? Why is Wilds being sh*tted on for being easy? Positioning has never been hard in world or rise until MR, so that doesn't make sense either, really. I can completely understand the dislike of focused slash attacks; however, they completely trivialize the game against monsters that aren't arch tempered or certain tanky tempered monsters. This crutch is almost non-existent in the endgame, though, against monsters that are arch-tempered. Also, a quick nitpick that people make, auto-moving seikrets are optional; if you hate them so much, then don't use it, stop whining about it. If you like exploring so much, then turn your map off. You bought the game, you can make it more enjoyable for yourself, but you just don't. VISUAL APPEAL(Very subjective subject) Artistic value can be very subjective, yes, but many argue that Wilds has by quote, "the most unoriginal coloring and scheme of any other monster hunter game," which is plain out exaggeration. Wilds takes place somewhere in the New World that is completely unknown, with a very low human population. While world is the "First time exploration OF THE NEW WORLD", it's of course going to look very colorful and bright because that's how it literally felt like to the hunters. It's like a child wandering into a candy shop for the first time. Wilds takes the view of an experienced hunter wandering through unknown lands with different locales and monsters, everything is gonna look like a single color and look exactly what it is. Another negative thing that people have been saying is how uninspired the areas look. I personally disagree; the simplicity of the areas is exactly how they should be. Not every forest is shaped like World's Forest, which becomes a glorified maze or a ♥♥♥ treacherous climb up a tree just to reach a Rathalos. A desert/plains biome looks exactly how you'd think it would look. As the name suggests, "Iceshard cliffs" is a very cold frozen area where monsters matching the environment's elements thrive. Oilwell basin is a...Oilwell basin that is very hot. To me, there is nothing wrong with this simplicity. The art style from World and Wilds is two different things and was made this way purposely.

The characters are certainly more interesting than MH: World, who were already LEAGUES above the previous games in terms of personality. Because who can forget, uh... "Caravan Leader". Yeah... Newcomers don't know any of this stuff, so its all new, interesting, and highly valuable information... But veterans don't care, because "me, me, me, me". Well, some veterans. All the new Monsters are fun, and the old monsters' reworks are either great, or flat-out better than they ever were. If anybody tells you, "Oh, spams [one move] over and over again, its ♥♥♥!" and they're not new? ...Remind them of Rathian and Rathalos in the old games. Remind them of basically EVERY MONSTER IN THE SERIES. Its nothing new. They're just whiny because people like to complain about "new thing bad and old thing good". I've got my issues with the game, but, overall? ...Aside from the initial optimization issues and bugs that come with every game nowadays? ...S'pretty good game. DLC's approaching soon, too.

review_text: I have approximately 1,200+ hours across the franchise, including time spent arguing about motion values in spreadsheets that absolutely should have been used for real employment. I say this not as a flex, but as a warning: I am exactly the target audience for Monster Hunter Wilds... and this game still managed to exhaust me in a way that feels less like hunting apex predators and more like debugging a group project where no one read the design doc. Monster Hunter Wilds is what happens when you take a historically tight gameplay loop built on deliberate friction, weighty combat, and systemic interdependence — and then sandblast all the tactile feedback off it while loudly insisting this is “evolution.” It is not evolution. It is feature creep wearing a photorealistic skin suit. Let’s start with performance, because performance is not a “technical issue,” it is the substrate on which the entire Monster Hunter experience rests. Frame pacing here behaves like a heart monitor during a jump scare compilation. You are not reacting to monster telegraphs; you are reacting to whether the engine decided to remember what time is. Input buffering becomes interpretive dance. I have had smoother combat interactions with laggy MMO raid bosses from 2007. When your game’s central fantasy is “precision under pressure,” you cannot have the renderer spontaneously deciding to roleplay as a slideshow. And yes, I’m aware of the usual PC optimization discourse. I tweaked settings. I adjusted configs. I performed the sacred rituals. The problem is not hardware. The problem is that the game’s technical foundation feels like it was stress-tested exclusively on optimism. Combat — historically the crown jewel of the series — feels like it has been run through a “broad appeal normalization filter.” Weapon identity is still present, but the kinesthetic feedback has been diluted. Impacts lack conviction. Hitstop is inconsistent. Animations communicate motion but not force. Instead of that signature Monster Hunter rhythm of commitment and consequence, we get something closer to “suggestive contact.” I should not be wondering whether my Great Sword connected. That weapon is supposed to feel like it alters local weather patterns. Monster behavior also suffers from a strange design contradiction. We are told this is a living ecosystem. In practice, it’s more like a carefully scheduled theme park parade where each creature has a designated time slot to appear relevant. Emergent interaction is implied, not realized. Systems exist, but they rarely produce surprising outcomes — they produce curated outcomes. It feels less like hunting in a dynamic world and more like triggering pre-approved environmental cut-ins. The maps are gorgeous, yes. They are also overdesigned in the specific way that confuses scale with engagement. Verticality exists, traversal options exist, environmental hazards exist... and yet the moment-to-moment decision making rarely deepens. The world is dense with elements that look systemic but behave decorative. It is environmental aesthetic masquerading as environmental mechanics. UI/UX design continues the long and storied tradition of Monster Hunter interfaces feeling like they were designed by an academic committee studying menu theory from first principles. Information hierarchy is an afterthought. Workflow friction is abundant. Routine tasks require enough navigation overhead to qualify as light clerical work. I should be preparing for hunts, not filing paperwork in a fantasy bureaucracy. Multiplayer — the literal soul of the franchise — feels like it was engineered by someone who conceptually understands cooperation but has never tried to coordinate four human beings in real time. Session friction, connection awkwardness, inconsistent flow between activities... it’s all just slightly more cumbersome than it needs to be. And “slightly” repeated across every interaction becomes death by a thousand loading prompts. Progression is where the existential dread sets in. Historically, Monster Hunter progression is a dopamine engine fueled by mastery and meaningful gear differentiation. Here, upgrades frequently feel incremental rather than transformative. Builds lack dramatic identity shifts. The reward loop hums, but it does not sing. You know that feeling when you craft a new weapon and immediately want to test it because it meaningfully changes how you approach a hunt? That sensation has been replaced with polite acknowledgment. “Ah yes, numbers increased. How reasonable.” The tragedy is that the audiovisual craftsmanship is genuinely impressive. Creature design is phenomenal. Environmental art is absurdly detailed. Audio during peak combat moments can be outstanding. There are flashes — sincere flashes — of brilliance that remind you why this series commands such loyalty. But those flashes exist within a framework that feels structurally undecided about what Monster Hunter is supposed to feel like. Wilds appears determined to reduce friction without understanding which frictions were essential to the identity of the experience. In doing so, it neither preserves the old intensity nor fully commits to a streamlined alternative. The result is a game that is technically ambitious, aesthetically impressive, and mechanically... curiously weightless. This is not a bad game in the catastrophic sense. It is far worse: it is a game that is persistently almost great. It is the ludonarrative equivalent of an asterisk. If you are deeply invested in the franchise, you will find moments worth dissecting, optimizing, and debating online for hundreds of posts. If you are looking for the next defining Monster Hunter experience, this currently feels like an extended beta for an idea that hasn’t finished deciding what it wants to be. I wanted to be obsessed. Instead, I am... academically disappointed.

review_text: Not recommended and here's why As someone who has spent a few thousand of hours in Monster Hunter: World, Monster Hunter Wilds feels less like an evolution and more like a regression. The biggest difference is that World respected the hunt. You had to learn maps, track monsters, pay attention to footprints and environmental clues, and gradually master each locale. In Wilds, your Seikret automatically takes you wherever you need to go, monsters are immediately marked, and gathering materials is reduced to scrolling through a menu and pressing a button while riding. Exploration has become little more than a loading screen you can control. Combat has undergone a similar simplification. World rewarded positioning, commitment, and knowing when to attack or back off. Every swing mattered because overcommitting could get you punished. In Wilds, attacks are far more forgiving, weapons can correct their direction mid-combo, and perfect guard trivialize attacks that previously required proper preparation or skill investment. It feels like the game constantly tries to save you from making mistakes instead of asking you to improve. Additionally the Seikret also ends up feeling like a safety net rather than a meaningful gameplay mechanic. Being able to instantly mount up and ride away from danger makes avoiding attacks far too simple in a hunt. Another step backwards is the decoration system. Splitting decorations into weapon-only (offensive) and armor-only (defensive) slots sounds like it should encourage build variety, but in practice it does the opposite. It makes min-maxing far more restrictive and limits player creativity. In World, you could fine-tune your build however you wanted depending on the slots your armor provided. In Wilds, the game decides where entire categories of skills are allowed to go, making builds feel more rigid and less rewarding to optimize. One of the most satisfying parts of Monster Hunter: World was being able to squeezing every last bit of efficiency out of a build. The new Wound system only makes this worse. While it's satisfying the first few times, it quickly becomes repetitive as monsters spend huge portions of hunts staggered or knocked down. Rather than learning a monster's moveset, you're often just waiting to pop the next wound and continue the chain of free damage. Then there's the atmosphere. Monster Hunter: World had Astera and later Seliana—hubs full of personality that felt alive. NPCs had memorable dialogue, quest descriptions added personality, and the world itself encouraged you to slow down and appreciate it. Wilds replaces much of that charm with long, unskippable story sequences filled with constant dialogue that rarely says anything interesting. Instead of feeling like a hunter carving out your own adventure, you often feel like you're being dragged through someone else's movie. The maps themselves are also a step down. Beyond their appearance, the environments lack the layered design that made World's locales so memorable. Areas don't feel like interconnected ecosystems with unique landmarks and routes to learn. Instead, they often come across as broad, simplified spaces. The maps may be bigger on paper, but they feel shallower in practice, making exploration far less rewarding. Instead of making you feel like the hunter driving the story forward, Wilds often makes you feel like a bystander following NPCs from one cutscene to the next. Major plot points happen around you rather than because of your actions, leaving the overall narrative feeling disconnected and surprisingly forgettable despite the amount of time it demands from the player. To be fair, Wilds isn't a bad game. The core Monster Hunter combat is still enjoyable, the monsters are well designed, and the visuals can be impressive. The problem is that Monster Hunter: World already exists. World asks more of the player, rewards mastery, and gives every hunt a stronger sense of purpose. It has more personality, more memorable environments, and a gameplay loop that remains satisfying even after hundreds of hours. Wilds feels streamlined in almost every aspect, but in doing so it also strips away much of what made Monster Hunter special. It's smoother, more accessible, and more cinematic—but it's also less rewarding. If you've never played either game, I'd recommend Monster Hunter: World + Iceborne first without hesitation. It's cheaper and, in my opinion, delivers the better Monster Hunter experience.

review_text: The biggest problem with Wilds is that it removes almost all friction and with it, a lot of what made Monster Hunter feel like Monster Hunter. Almost every mechanic that used to require preparation, decision-making or knowledge has been streamlined away. You barely walk anymore. Seikret handles most of the traveling, lets you heal and sharpen on the move, and even gets you back on your feet after taking a hit. Items don't need to be picked up anymore, just shoot them with the Slinger. Monster drops teleport straight into your inventory. Resources are basically infinite. Money, points, consumables and materials never feel scarce. There is almost no grinding. Most monsters only need to be hunted a few times to get everything you want, and even decorations and Artian gear are extremely easy to obtain. The Palico handles healing and status recovery for you, capture thresholds are practically impossible to miss, and mechanics like tremors, wind pressure, blights and especially stun barely matter anymore. You can cook and restock whenever you want, even during a hunt. Fainting barely has any consequences because you keep your food buffs. And then there is the actual combat. There is almost no challenge. Monsters spend huge amounts of time knocked down or locked into wound-break animations. You don't really have to learn their moves or earn openings anymore, just attack wounds and the monster falls over. Triple-carting feels almost impossible because the monster will often die before it can seriously threaten you. The result is that you don't really need to learn the maps, prepare for hunts, manage resources, understand monster behavior or grind for gear. You just fight the monster, collect everything automatically and move on. And that's the biggest disappointment for me. Wilds is polished, beautiful and fun, but it has streamlined so much of Monster Hunter that it removed a lot of the reason I loved the series in the first place.

review_text: After 200 hours I haven't had any performance issues, I don't know how the other players with much better spces than me leave negative reviews talking about poor performance, the game works completely fine for me. I've only had some connection issues but that gets fixed just by updating my dirvers so I wouldn't say I've had any perfomance issues so far. The combat is really fun and the monster fights are great, there are many mechanics that I like for example being able to aim your melee attacks to target a specific part of a monster and it complements the wound mechanic perfectly. You can also use the environment at your advantage by creating hazards to trap or damage the monsters and use the endemic life in your favor in order to heal or inflict status ailments to the monsters. There are many weapons to choose from and everyone plays very differently so there is a weapon for any playstyle; one thing that I really like about it is that no matter if you choose a simple or a very complicated weapon because once you master it any weapon could be as good as the next in my opinion. The bosses are well designed and are very distinct from one another so there will be a lot of variety in the many different hunts that you can take once you hit High Rank. The main story can feel easy at the beginning for some players but the late game bosses have more advanced patterns of attacks and it could get really dangerous if you mess up. The developers clearly wanted to make a fast paced and action packed entry on the series; while MH WORLD has a more slow and meticulous approach that a lot of people liked becuse they felt like actual hunters WILDS gives you a bird like dinosaur that automatically rides you through the map so you can focus only on fighting and so removing the elements of exploration and monster tracking that makes World so appealing for most people. I think that it is a valid criticism and I actually agree with the players who feel that way but I also feel that they are too harsh on this game just because is different while it clearly has no intentions on being like it's predecessor. In conclusion, old school Monster Hunter players may not like the newer games and specially this one either for the easier difficulty or the quality of life that removed some elements form previous entries but every Monter Hunter game is very different from one another and everyone of them are able to excel on their own despite their differences. Honestly this game is a 10/10 for me and I highly recommend it to any one who likes action/adventure games and to anyone who wants to get into playing Monster Hunter.

review_text: Upsides: - This is the most beginner friendly Monster Hunter game. All of the menus are also easily understandable and responsive (even though having like 5 submenus for everything is annoying at times). - Good roster. Only a few boring monsters and 1 terrible (Congalala). - Good environment, huge attention to detail. Iceshard Cliffs is the only area which I've found annoying to fight in - The story is fine. Nothing groundbreaking but entertaining enough. The final boss of the Low Rank quest line is very good. The kid character did not annoy me unlike some other players who foam at the mouth the moment his name is mentioned (I really do not get the problem). - After 3 Title Updates the endgame is very solid and the difficulty is there. The "star" system is confusing at first but not that hard to understand, the difficulty progression is solid with 6, 7, 8 and 9 star monsters. Downsides - Of course, performance. Even people with good PCs still struggle with this game because the release was rushed so the optimisation is poor. There have been updates improving it a little but the game still struggles. The devs promised to improve the performance on December 16th with the release of Title Update 4, I hope it will actually be substantial (improving the performance of your game almost 1 year after release is kinda crazy not gonna lie) - In my opinion, the game lacks art style. The previous games were a product of their time and that gave them a certain style, the way they look is memorable. In Wilds they just went with super realistic, I wish there was more to it than that. The monsters are gorgeous, perhaps the playable characters could've been more cartoon-y. - The amount of handholding during the story gets tiring. Multiple missions where you gotta ride on your mount and you cannot stray from the path (your character won't let you), it's all mostly on walking speed. It wasn't the worst thing in the world and it was probably done to show off how much work they've done on the environment but at some point you've just had enough. - More of a late game issue but I wish Artian weapons weren't in the game until like Title Update 3. For most weapons, they are the best option so the Rarity 8 weapons you can make out of the hardest monsters in the game are mostly useless. Yeah, of course I could just not interact with the system, but it would be stupid to deny their advantage. *Update*: The game has received its final update. So, after the update and the TU4 from December last year, I can confidently say: Monster Hunter Wilds is a good Monster Hunter game. It has a slow start, however, the endgame is rich with content and variety of monsters to fight. The difficulty is all there, Gogmazios is alright, Savage Omega is still one of the craziest fights, the new 10* monsters pose a great challenge while not being too much of a slog (except the ever-boring Uth Duna), Arch-Tempered Arkveld is Cinema. The TU4 Gogma weapons have introduced even more annoying rng but it is what it is I guess. The artstyle is still my main downside, focus mode feels very handhold-y, other than that I have no complaints. The performance issues were fixed (at least for me), the game runs great. I have genuinely enjoyed playing this game and cannot wait for what the DLC will have in store.
