review_text: I've been playing this series since Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate and have played every monster hunter that released after 4U. I absolutely adore and love this series, its my favorite. However, I do have my gripes with it. Throughout my journey this series took a noticable shift with the gameplay and other details, many are positives, there are however also negatives. Starting with the core gameplay and the hunts: They're great. Despite some people swearing that the gameplay isn't. I personally don't have many issues with it. My only dislike is the new focus mode and other minor changes that I will get to. Disclaimer: I have ONLY played hammer as of now (and I plan to ONLY play hammer) so I can not talk about weapons that heavily rely on wounds to go into different modes or to fully use their moveset (eg. Charge Blade). The additions of wounds are great, they give a good feeling when used and open up opportunites to punish the monster or to reap your rewards when you successfully damage a monsters part more than enough times. I do however dislike the fact how much mobility focus mode gives you as a hunter. The fact that you gain more reach with your weapon while holding down the button to activate focus mode is ridiculous. As well as how good your hunter is able to turn around attacking while holding down the focus mode. While I do not dislike the fact that our hunter gets stronger, I do dislike that fact that the monsters don't. Im unsure if its because I know my way around this game and some monsters-moveset after years of experience with this franchise, but I honestly fail to see if Capcom ever designs monsters around our hunter and our possibilites with our weapons and environment. As of now, the only difficul fights have been monsters where their damage have been sky-high (Tempered, arch tempered) and Omega (Which is a very fun hunt, but the design is sadly from Final Fantasy). Another point are the monster designs. They're phenomenal. Stunning even. Weapon designs are also absolutely amazing. They fit right in and are a treat to fight against and use. BUT, as a hammer main...why can you NOT break the head of Rathian and Rathalos? Seriously? It has been a real head scratcher for me since I first fought them in this addition. Is it because they don't want us the break the "beautiful" faces of their flagships? Is the reason really that silly? Im furious about this change. Another great gripe I have is the whole Gravios hunt. Coming from 4 Ultimate, he was never my favorite (don't remind Capcom that black gravios exists). But he never felt...lazy...in a sense, unlike here. 2 Things I want to point out. He has a very basic design. Big rock with flesh under. But this design opened up many opportunites for the team in 4U, and by god they took them. Mounting him in 4U was fun because you could mount him on two places, the back and his chest with different animations. In this game its only the back, which is disappointing but Im not as heartbroken about it as the other change. His roar. They took a bear mp3. and made it his roar... Im jawdropped. His original roar is still in Wilds but sadly they didn't make it his only roar, so you sometimes get thrown out of the immersion when the mp3 plays. Why make it that way? You have the blueprints already there. Seregios (My favorite monster god bless him) also got a more Falcon-esque cry which you can sometimes hear. His cry isn't a bad change, its nice but the bad change is definitely the change they gave Gravios, they must hate him. Rewards are not as rare to come by like in older games which is very nice, now that I have less time to play due to busy days it's nice to ask friends if they have investigations with the items I need. This nice change is however instantly thrown away and stomped on by Artians weapons. Basically the gacha and grinding mechanism they have in almost every game for some gog-foresaken reason (Word/Iceborne decos and guiding lands, SunRise talismans and and augments). They're a nightmare to grind if you want to best possible weapons since you can't choose which augments you get on your weapon (Safi-weapons were better in this regard and design wise) and you have to destory the weapon if you don't get the right augments (you get back the upgrade materials you use for the augments, thats very kind). The worst thing about Artian weapons is sadly the upcoming Gogmazios. Unless they give us a way to upgrade monster-part-weapons, I fail to see why you should even use them since Gogmazios will upgrade your Artian weapons EVEN FURTHER, they will become the best weapons you can get (if you're lucky at the slot machine) and nothing will even compete against them. This however is pure speculation. Lets get into the world of Wilds. Im not commenting on the story, Im only saying that Monster Hunter isn't a story game and they shouldn't push it to be one. This game further enhances my opinion. Characters in Wilds are good, I like them a lot. Im super happy to see the Ace-Lancer and Little Miss Forge back, here's me hoping that we get to see the rest of the Aces or other characters from 4U when Gogmazios releases! Overall I do not dislike the things that we have on this topic, what I dislike are the things that are missing. You're forced to listen to languages, there isn't the option to let the cast speak the "Monster Hunter language" like in World/Iceborne, thank gog that we're able to let our Palico speak in only meows (Hopefully they won't take this away from us in future games). Speaking of cats, there aren't Palicos/Felynes cooking for you in this game. The villagers and your hunter cook the meals. Perfomance wise I can not complain, I don't have the best or the worst system but the game runs, even tho it doesn't have the best graphics and framerate, its playable (we apparently reached the point where good enough is acceptable). They made a good job optimizing the mess they created, it was almost unplayable when I played the demo-version of this game. I am a bit disappointed in the art-design choices of this game however. Monster Hunter for me was always a very colorful game. Even darker places like castle Schrade or Dundorma had a nice color palette in previous games. Iceborne was gorgeous and looks (and runs) way better than Wilds. Wilds however...Im disappointed. It looks very monotone and grey. Areas don't stand out since every area of a map looks almost the same. Music is phenomenal like usual, great job on this one. Even tho this review has been focusing on the negatives, Im still giving this game a good review. Its a great game, its fun, I don't regret buying this game and I will maybe buy the expansion. I am however very sad that Monster Hunter has lost so much of its soul and things that made me personally fall in love with it. I hope they change their ways, but from the way things are and how much money they made with the game already [(and the in-game mico-transactions which are purely cosmetics) (Im also part of the problem for supporting Capcoms greed, Im sorry)] I don't see a light at the end of the tunnel. This is a very backhanded recommendation from me.

review_text: Amazing game held back by technical issues and jarring design decisions. Performance is rough even on my high-end rig (RTX 5080, R7 7800X3D, 32GB RAM). Playing the game at 3440x1440, DLSS Quality, 2x Frame Gen, and most settings including textures at high, I get 90–120 fps. Turning down the graphics settings doesn't meaningfully improve performance on my PC, except for the high-res texture pack. Never use that, at least until they fix it in a future patch, as it causes stutters and basically maxes my 16GB of VRAM. Without ReShade, the game still looks fine at resolutions higher than 1080p, but it's still blurrier than any other game I've played with DLSS. So to make the game look truly great, I use a sharpening filter and a LUT to slightly alter the colors to make the game more vibrant. The HDR implementation is also quite lacking, though it is fixable by using RenoDX with ReShade. With all this combined, it's one of the most beautiful-looking games that i've played on my OLED monitor. Disregard the recommended specs on the Steam page; I'd say you'd need at least either a 4060 Ti at 1080p or a 4070 Ti at 1440p to get an acceptable experience, unless you don't mind your game looking like a blurry, pixelated mess. As for the non-technical problems the game has: The difficulty is all over the place. While I do agree that the game was a bit too easy at launch, the devs could've done a better job at integrating the new difficulty levels. For example, 8* Arkveld is significantly weaker than the rest of the 8* monsters, and because Arch Tempered Rey Dau and Uth Duna were released before the 9* difficulty, they were shafted too. I still don't get why they had to make the remaining AT monsters 9* while the first two are still 8*; it makes no sense. At least I hope the devs now know what difficulty level to target for the Master Rank expansion so that we don't get these shenanigans again. Another problem I have is the extreme RNG endgame weapon and talisman system. Honestly, getting the materials isn't even that bad; it's the abysmal chances to get good rolls on Artian weapons and talismans. I've probably hunted over 40 9* tempered monsters at this point, and I still haven't gotten a talisman that's worth using. Same with Artian weapons. Since I despise having to sit in the menus clicking the same 3 buttons for over 3 hours a day to complete endgame builds, I'll just admit I have installed mods to edit Artian weapons and talismans. Though I do still upgrade each weapon to the max first before editing, so it's not completely free. So why do I still recommend this game even after all these issues? Simply put, the combat in this game has been the most fun I've ever had in a third-person action game, even surpassing MH:World and Elden Ring. Though my all-time favorite is still MHW:Iceborne, I feel like that'll change once Wilds' expansion comes out.

review_text: When I think about Monster Hunter, I think of having to explore a map, learning the layout, find and keep track of the monster I need to fight, being careful about my positioning and commitment to moves, and having to fight a monster more than once or twice to finally get the equipment pieces I want or need. This game does nothing of the sort, and what is still present here, is heavily disincentivized. Maps are uninspired, uninteresting, just a blur of a single color, nothing striking, nothing cool. Which would be an issue if you had to learn them, but "luckily" mr. Capcom is here to save you from a problem they themselves created: here is a mount that will automatically Uber you to your destination, no need to find the monster, it does that for you, no need to stop to gather materials, you can do that from range by selecting what you want from a list of nearby sources, you dont even need to aim at them you just need to press a single button. Combat is laughably easy at the core, are you using a weapon that can block? You now have perfect blocks, and even the strongest attacks can be nullified completely that way, no need to get points in guard or guard up skills. Attacks can be redirected and corrected, even mid-swing in some cases, you don't need to position yourself, to consider what the monster is doing or could be doing, the game simplifies everything for you. This time, as the awful gimmick that every monhun game must have, we've got Wounds. You hit a part enough time and it gets wounded, which makes it take more damage until the wound is destroyed, making the monster fall down or flinch. The issue is, you can just stunlock a monster to death with this, from the weakest of them to the final monster of high rank. But hey at least there's no wirebugs. All in all this is just a mediocre game, but just that would be not enough for me to just tell people to not play it, these are my thoughts, other people might like the extreme streamlining of the game. What definitively tips the scales to a "don't bother just grab World+Iceborne its cheaper and better" is how the story is done and the complete removal of flavor from the game: The game is on rails for quite a long time, you are very often stuck walking or riding along your marvel quips-dialogue riddled npc characters, and you cannot skip these sequences that last for a relatively long time. And they must've thought they really were cooking for this one because they removed the monhun language so you get to experience all of it in an actual language of your choosing. Flavor text from the npcs in quest boards? gone. A village like in every single other game? hope you weren't expecting Pokke or Seliana, gone. The music is nice but few tracks manage to stand out, the rest is okay, not bad but nothing that makes you go WOW or look it up on youtube. It really gives the feeling of shareholders meddling after seeing that MHW was their best selling game ever, and devs somehow being confused and maybe scared about what to do with this one. It's not awful, it just feels flavorless, there's no seasoning. It just feels corporate. Your money is better spent on Monster Hunter World + Iceborne, or if you already own that, just go back to it, there is a reason that game still has as many active players as this one does.

review_text: I'd rather give this a neutral rating but since I have to decide I'll go with negative. I enjoy the game and will keep playing it but there are some things that just keep bothering me. The expansion may be able to address some of those but not everything can be fixed. I'd say post Title Updates Wilds has the better endgame than the base games of its modern predecessors but that wasn't exactly a high bar to begin with. Is the game worth a purchase? Honestly Rise and Sunbreak together offer all in all the better experience if you don't mind graphics and multiplayer. However if you're looking for multiplayer and your rig can handle it I'd take Wilds over World and Iceborne. For the things that bother me: - Graphics: it's true they patched the performance to some extend but there are things they couldn't patch like the blurriness, the fog and the brutal post processing. The game lacks visual clarity and as consequence it can be hard to tell what's going on. Their pinnacle of design is literally an all grey zone with terrible lighting where you fight a grey monster. - floaty controls: Capcom has multiple motion cap studios and it shows. They felt like they had to animate everything but as consequence your character feels unresponsive thanks to additional intermediate animations. It's especially bad after getting hit when you're on the ground and try to get up just for some struggle animation to play. People would say old generations were clunky and had idiotic extra animations but even with things like the superman pose the controls itself were crisp and not as muddy as they are in Wilds. While it doesn't affect me frame gen will introduce additional input latency making it even worse. - Weapons: Some are good, some are bad, at least one is so awful you could just remove it. I hated the counter focus in Rise however there you had alternatives. In Wilds they are forced upon you. I don't even get the point of 14 weapons when everything is a counter stick. A lot of people will point out that focus mode killed positioning but as someone who plays a lot solo I never need to position anyway as I'll just wait for the monster to attack me and then counter it. For me the biggest loser is the Insect Glaive even post patch as Capcom doesn't seem to know what it should be. Hammer is now "what if we turned that youtube hammer slowmotion Tigrex video into a weapon" however offsets become pretty awful once the monster have high hp and buildup resistance and outside of them at least slower weapon have a hard time dealing damage. I wouldn't even say hammer is gameplay wise bad cause I enjoy it but all the extra steps you have to do just to get the same damage as other weapons in total is frustrating. All in all if hunters weren't so absurd strong maybe monsters wouldn't require all this extra crap either. - Seikret: They wanted a combination of Palamutes and Wirefall but made both strictly worse. Palamutes were more interactive and they weren't forced upon you. You could always bench them and use Wirebug movement as alternative. Something similar isn't possible in Wilds at all and maps are clearly designed around the Seikret. The worst is the Seikret pickup is just bad. In order to pick you up the Seikret has to physically run to you from its current random location while having collision with the monster, can be knocked over by monster attacks and will jump over ledges so the pickup will always fail at a ledge. How long this takes and in what direction the journey will go? WELL you will see. It works in the early game but once monster deal damage it can flat out cart you if you accidentally use it. - Ecology: I don't care about corpses rotting. I don't care about the pack monster interactions that requires you to stalk them for 10 minutes. Endemics were a nice touch in World but you would see them while traversing the map. Captured endemics you could place in your room and interact with. Here the Seikret strikes again as it walks you just past all of them with the maps not being designed around seeing endemics anyway unless you search for them. You catch them? They are just an entry that's it. I don't want ecology to be removed as whole but it should be a nice to have and not the main focus. The game is called MONSTER HUNTER and not some pseudo realistic bird watching simulation. - Maps: the desert is unnecessary big with anything other than the north-eastern area being awful to fight in thanks to slopes resulting in sliding and mini jumps when dodging. Forest and Oilwell are OK but Cliffs and Wyveria are two awful maps as they are cramped, visually monotonous and full with ledges, slopes and other crap. - Too much random grind: this used to be a franchise about killing monsters and using their skin for armour and weapons. The materials being random drops was plenty honestly. Sure some parts were hard to get but hunting the monster again and again was the game. Now? Random decorations, random talisman, random weapon parts, random weapon bonus, random weapon set bonus. You want to try a new weapon? Too bad now go through absurd amounts of randomness cause the crafted weapons cannot compete with the randomised ones. An appealing grind has progress but here you just bash your head against the wall and hope you will eventually get what you want which can be never.

review_text: As a huge Monster Hunter fan for a long time, I understand all of the criticism coming for the game, but I want to break it down into a handful of points. So if you don't mind a moment of your time, I would love to give an extensive review on the game after many many hours, and having played the beta, and been at one of the events showcasing the game to be playable to the public before release. 1. "It's too easy" Something I find with a lot of people when it comes to MH they play a souls-like and expect Monhun to be the same. I know this isn't everyone and I'll get into that, but first I wanna say that Monhun is a Monster Hunting game, I know shocker but that's why the game doesn't feel like some story of these over the top proportions. The lore and game is all about living with monsters and the balance of it all so applying a souls-like onto it doesn't work. On the other hand, for those who just say it's too easy, stop referencing Wilds to World, one of the biggest things in the community is saying "World is better and harder, Wilds is too easy" and truth be told, right now, it is. Because subconsciously you're relating G rank/Master rank to Low and High Rank. World had the exact same "issue" at launch for vets of the series, it's just what happens when you get good at a game comparing the skill ceiling between two games, even if in the same series is hard if you've played one before the other. I can say World is easy because I play MHG from time to time, or I could go back and play MH Tri and say it's too hard, but a Tri player could play World and say it's too easy. It's not about your skilllevel, it's about the overall level that is comfortable for casual and hardcore players. If you want a challenge, enjoy the challenge quests, or do the arch-tempered quests or fight Savage Omega. 2. Lack of Content Jumping off of my final point on the last part, lack of content is really overstated. For all games not just Wilds. If you look at any new release now, people are BEGGING devs for content updates almost all the time. I've seen it with this community where they release a huge update and instead of enjoying it and being happy, they request more. I understand it's a large company with lots of people, but the entire company is not working on that game, a small portion of the company is working on wilds still. "well just put more people on" -you can't exactly do that when whole entire games and systems need to be made. It's a lot for a team to concept, dev, texture, everything for an update. World had just about the same time for these content updates, but now people are so pushy for things here and now to get it over with and done. This gives the game more time to breath and allow newcomers to come in and not feel overloaded, I think that's what people are forgetting. 3. Performance I understand the issues people are having, and I get it, but i can also say I have been able to run MH Wilds on a laptop for months now just fine. It's not a gaming laptop, it's not some custom-built model, it's a Lenovo Thinkpad. My pc which is damn near 6-8 years old and about $1000 can run wilds on high just fine with a hiccup now and then when loading zones. A game of this size, with so many well-crafted zones and thought put into every nook and cranny is bound to be powerful like this and hard to optimize. I've talked to people who want to get into game dev who have said they have no idea how Capcom has even been able to optimize so far. If you really believe games like these, of this scale aren't going to be optimization hells at launch you're mistaken. A company can't make it optimized for every single person out there because they don't know every single person's setups, so they have to try everything and see what does and doesn't work. They need player feedback, not hostile player feedback, not kind, professional feedback. So I want to close this off by saying if you really aren't enjoying the game in its current state, take a break from it and come back. I adore this game and want to play 100s of more hours, I really do and I know I can. But I also know I want to take breaks as well to keep the spender of the game in my mind. It's such a beautiful game and not once have I felt taken out of the experience, sure when I first load in, one or two things may be polygonal, but that's also cause my GPU is old, but once it all loads in I'm right back into the immersive world that has been crafted and I've been allowed to venture into and enjoy. If you're getting tired of the difficulty of monsters, take a stroll and do some fishing or just watching the monsters and endemic life interact. That's not just a fun detail, it's apart of the game's experience, it's built for Monster Hunter. If you die and spawn at a camp, follow the palico that heals you, if you do, they run all the way back to the base camp of that area, best seen in Windward Plains. Amistrigian have an entire life cycle, Gelidron switch from oil to land to sunbathe and moisturize, the list goes on. Monster Hunter Wilds, and for the series in general has never been so alive than before in Wilds. It's not just about hunting the monsters or killing the boss, it's about those little moments in life that you would usually miss if you weren't looking hard enough. It's a great representation of nature and life itself, and looking past that and only staring at the flaws of the game is going to ruin the experience. I understand if its hard to see because of performance, but don't forget these are real people working on this game who have passion and love for this game just like you do. If they didn't they wouldn't be working on it in the first place. With that, a send off, Happy Hunting to all!

review_text: Mixed Reviews — and honestly, that’s probably a good thing. Monster Hunter Wilds is worse than some people expected, but apparently that’s enough to declare the entire franchise a disaster. The mixed reviews are actually doing the community a favor: they help separate people who genuinely enjoy Monster Hunter from those who apparently played for five hours, got mildly inconvenienced, and immediately became professional game critics. Is Wilds perfect? Absolutely not. It has technical issues, questionable decisions, and plenty of things that deserve criticism. But somehow, every minor flaw has been treated like Capcom personally cancelled someone’s childhood. As an actual fan, I’d rather see honest mixed opinions than a sea of exaggerated praise. Criticism is useful when it comes from people who understand what they’re criticizing. The rest is mostly entertaining background noise. So yes, Monster Hunter Wilds is not the masterpiece everyone wanted. It might even be worse than previous entries in some ways. And that’s okay. We can criticize it, enjoy it, discuss it, and still play the damn game. Some people just need to remember that a game can be flawed without becoming a personal tragedy.

review_text: I cannot recommend this game to anyone because the idea of rewarding Capcom with another seventy dollars for this product makes me feel physically ill. My stomach genuinely turns when I think about how much fun this series was when it wasn't awful live service slop with the gameplay loop and the weapon movesets and the monster movesets and the progression dumbed down to the point of putting you to sleep. You can spend 90 hours in a second or third generation Monster Hunter game without beating the game and you can feel like you're progressing at a completely fine speed. The only reason that this game takes 20 hours to beat is that for 17 of them you are trapped in utterly excruciating unskippable cutscenes. Turning Monster Hunter into live service slop was bad enough, but Capcom has interpreted the existence and widespread acceptance of Title Updates into an excuse to release blatantly unfinished and untested games. The performance was bad on launch, and Capcom promised that it would fix the performance, and then it said "we will finish fixing the game in December," and now it is December and the performance is not fixed, and now it has said that the performance will be fixed in February. A year after release. A YEAR. And I just don't believe Capcom. If you do, that's wonderful wishful thinking on your part, and it brings me some happiness that you haven't got a pit of emptiness where your hope for this series once was, and that some light yet exists. But even if the performance is fixed, too much is wrong with the game besides that. My favorite weapon, the charge blade, has been completely ruined by its moveset changes. The weapon designed to function in a switching capacity that was once considered to be the most complex weapon asks you to press the circle button and nothing else. Focus mode, in conjunction with more consistent invincibility frames, mean that positioning your character is not nearly as important as timing dodges. This was once the case only in a select few fights, and now it is the case in nearly all of them- at least, it would be, if the monsters in this game spent less time lying on the ground incapacitated and more time actually fighting you. Which they cannot. They are entirely too weak in comparison to the garbage the player is allowed to do. The retroactive adding of more 9-star monsters did not matter: their movesets were unchanged and they are still incapable of actually hitting a player who is not drooling all over his keyboard or who can't see the screen because the helmet his doctor told him he has to wear keeps slipping in front of his eyes. I think I am only writing this review now because I heard the quest completion theme from an actually good video game when I beat the (added nine months later) final boss in what was an extremely transparent attempt to "recapture the magic" or "inspire nostalgia" that fell completely flat, having been at the end of an extremely scripted and therefore extremely uninteresting quest that was completed by mandatory NPCs who do the whole thing for you. I couldn't decide what was sadder- the thought that the developers were deliberately trying to nostalgia-bait me, or the thought that even the developers are disappointed in this game (and interviews with them give me that impression) and that it was their attempt to try to remind themselves of what great things they did in the past. I am probably going to keep playing this game on occasion, but with nothing close to the regularity that I shall play the other actually good Monster Hunter games. There is a genuine fear in my heart that I will FOMO myself into buying the expansion, which will almost certainly be 60 USD, even though I know that the game will not be fixed by it. Wilds cannot be fixed- it is a symptom of a deeper disease: complacency- both the consumer's complacency with bad business practices and the developers' complacency with their own bad work.

review_text: I waited until a few patches (and a hefty sale) to get this, and I'm glad I did. Because now I can give this a positive rating! After over 1000 hours in MH:World, I'm finding Wilds a fun experience for the most part. Visually, a side-grade. Things seem a bit easier than they were in World, but the combat is a definite upgrade. I was a bow main in World, and the bow feels even better than before with the additional mobility we have in Wilds. You also don't need Crit Ele any more, so you're not locked into the ugly Rath set for half the game. We have a much better jump attack, and popping wounds is a fun (albeit OP) addition. DP-spam is finally a valid strat. Bows are in a fairly decent spot. Though, FYI: if you're playing multiplayer as a bow user, maybe don't go quite so wound-pop crazy, as other weapon types need wounds to build combos. Anyhoo... Performance is fine. Story is, ya know... usual MH story-level. I don't like how the camera constantly robs you of control (it does this frequently), but I think that's just during the main campaign. Minor complaint either way. All in all, it's pretty fun so far! Edit: end-game is brutal, man. That difficulty curve is quite something!

review_text: I tried to give this game a fair chance. I really enjoyed playing it up until TU1. Starting with TU2, however, I began experiencing FPS drops and performance issues. I have an i7-12650H and an RTX 4060 laptop GPU, not top of the line, but still decent and I was getting around 40–50 FPS without frame generation. But since TU2, performance has gotten so much worse that I eventually had to stop playing and uninstall the game. When TU3 was released, I decided to give it another shot, but somehow it ran even worse. I ended up wasting my time downloading and installing it again. Still, I wanted to give Capcom another chance since they promised “performance optimizations” in TU4. I waited patiently and was excited to try it. Today, TU4 finally came out, and after downloading and installing it, I launched the game, only to find the same old issues. In fact, it seemed even worse. Before TU2, I had never seen polygonal textures in the game, but today, for the first time, I saw polygonal monsters. It’s a great game in terms of gameplay, but poor optimization completely ruins the immersion. So my recommendation to players is this: if you have a really powerful gaming PC, go for it. Otherwise, I wouldn’t recommend the PC version due to its poor optimization. If you own a PS5 or PS5 Pro, just buy it there, it performs much better on those consoles.

review_text: After much consideration, I can't help but recommend this game despite my issues with... many things. I've been playing since 4U and I cannot bear to "hate" a MonHun game. Without getting too far into the critique, do not buy this at full price! Especially in the current state, and because you can't guarantee you will like the endgame loops, it's not worth spening 70€ on this game. Get a key, get it on sale, and play with friends. The endgame here is truly the meat and potatoes of Wilds, including a HR100 grind that is supposedly becoming easier in TU4 with an event quest. The soundtrack, the combat (with a new wound mechanic) and the monster designs and areas are incredible, the performance issues almost make sense when you see the beautiful landscapes you commit mass genocide in. The monster designs range from a monster with a face AND tail that look like a drill to a railgun and the most unique ones of all, big squids that WILL use all of their tentacles fully. The compositions for this game are exactly what I want from a MonHun soundtrrack, true heroes are the Jin Dahaad and of course the Rey Dau theme, but the main menu of all things has stuck with me as well. The ecology, the story, the DAMN SEIKRET BABIES. I love so much on display here. I'm glad that 6th gen looks this good, we've come a long way as a series. The story mode! It's... really short for a game of this price. I really like the characters having names, personalities and motivations in this one. The fact your handler FOLLOWS you onto a HUNT? God, is that what we were supposed to be seeing the whole time? The Seikret mechanic surely makes this much easier to implement, but every character is so... involved in this world. Nata as a central character you can periodically check up on optionally adds some tonal depth and his arc of revenge to compasion towards arkveld is truly sad when you eventually have to put it down. At least it would be sad, if Alma didn't have a kill phrase implanted in my brain that makes me feel like a hitman towards my target monster (I'm joking of course, but I do feel awesome when she says it). This is by far the best monster hunter in terms of characters, bringing back many themes and people from MH4U and its own original ones, joining you on hunts for dialogue before you start fighting that big spider. Your hunter talks, by the way. Most well known is the final boss of this game, Zoh Shia, which acts as an interpretation of the equal dragon weapon. If you don't know that concept, look it up. Seriously. This may or may not be the case but the fact the devs took that concept, made it even cooler and then made it the most awesome fight in this game (arguably) is a surprise to me. I could go on about my absolute love for the game, talk about the endgame grind of talismans and artian weapons (I'm still waiting for craftable decorations, capcom.), I didn't even mention focus mode or the crossover... I think I would rather mention some negatives. The multiplayer is a little odd, you need to join link parties and, while an option, environment links are as fragile as a nerscylla hatchling. This pales in comparison to the performance. Please fix, capcom. This game has some serious potential to have the impact world had, bringing in a whole new generation of players to this beast of a series, but that one snag... the performance. It held even me personally back until recently where I upgraded to a 4060 and I can run the game fine. I did go into the files and edited a lot of visuals though, the windward plains still lagged me. I think the "difficulty" discussion is a little overdone. It's on the easier side, sure, but WOW this game can hit you between the legs just as much as one thinks back on their first MonHun game kicking them. Chances are you are not a Sixer but rather a Fiver who plays this game, comes from having learned mechanincs in World/Iceborne, and blasting monsters with the wounds and your main weapon you already found. I have a Fiver friend who I play with and, while they played all the way to Fatalis in World, much prefers Wilds *because* of the faster hunts. And this is not to say that even AT Uth Duna is fast, those take your usual 20-25 minutes. Even normal Tempered hunts (not even double ones) can take 20-30 minutes, at least for us two. If you want some difficulty you truly do need to get further into the game, but once you hit a 9-5 Star Tempered Gore Magala you will SCREAM and CRY. This may not be everyone's cup of tea, but to those true diehard MonHun fans who want difficulty: Try savage Omega Planetes, have yourself a 9-5 Tempered Seregios hunt. It's hard! and with AT monsters and Gogmazios on the horizon I only see the endgame getting spicier. Let the early game be easy, I'd much rather blast through La La Barina in 5 minutes and genuinely struggle on High Rank Zoh Shia. This game suffers from performance issues and a community that cannot decide what difficulty it wants. I have VERY high hopes for this game and its eventual DLC, and I will continue to support this series into any generation as long as it's not completely terrible. This can become the 6th-Gen game we all wanted, and I hope the team of talented individuals realizes this reality! Can't wait for TU4.

review_text: The Sad End Of An Era I never thought I would be writing a negative review for a Monster Hunter game seeing as it was and still kind of is one of my favorite video game franchises, but here we are. In my opinion, Capcom has completely and utterly dropped the ball on this game and ruined what was once an incredibly compelling and deep gaming experience. In this review, I will illustrate my thoughts on what went wrong and why this game should be avoided for the time being. The Gameplay Since the release of Monster Hunter: World there has been a slow shift to make the series more accessible to newcomers with the introduction of streamlined mechanics. As someone who started with World and went back to play older games, I can say that most of these changes were welcome additions, moving the series forward from its slow and sometimes clunky roots. Wilds tries to continue this trend, but I feel as though it streamlined some mechanics too far, trivializing the experience. Take the new Seikret for example; what should be a fun tool that makes map traversal easier is immediately ruined when you realize that this creature knows where the monster is on the map at all times and is able to automatically take you to its location with very little input from the player. At that point, it really doesn't feel like you are hunting the monster anymore and it gives the player very little incentive to explore the map or study monster behavior which used to be a core mechanic of older games that was beloved by fans. Another drastic change that’s been made was the decision to split defensive and offensive skills between armor and weapons respectively. I am really not sure what Capcom hoped to accomplish with this choice, because all it really did was make builds way more rigid and took away a lot of freedom when it comes to armor skills. This has resulted in an endgame build that basically fits every weapon with not a lot of deviation which feels very boring. Speaking of endgame, that is another thing that Capcom has completely neutered. I’m not going to beat around the bush here and say that this game was unfinished at launch. Monster Hunter has always been a series praised for its deep and complex endgame grind, but there has been a concerning trend that started with Rise where they release the game with only a couple of monsters to hunt for end game gear, and slowly add more monsters with content updates. This trend has continued with Wilds where, at launch, this game had 2 endgame monsters to grind. There is also the aspect of the special weapons that players are able to make from grinding these endgame monsters, which are also incredibly flawed. Basically, you get these weapon pieces from high powered endgame monsters and can build weapons out of them. You can then “reinforce” them which is basically rolling augments for more buffs. Here’s the thing though: if you don’t get the right stats for these weapons, you have to Disassemble the weapon, losing those parts that you worked hard to grind for. That is an insanely unsatisfying and unrewarding system that is basically just straight up gambling for the right augments. I know the Monster Hunter series is known for its RNG-based systems, but this is getting ridiculous at this point. The Story Monster Hunter has never been a series known for its riveting plot lines or deep character arcs but over time it seems that Capcom has been wanting to remedy this. In World we got fully animated and voice acted cutscenes which deepend our connections to the world and characters. Then there was Rise which gave all of the NPC characters names rather than just their job title which I thought was nice. But then we come to Wilds, where the team seemingly decided to put even more emphasis on the story while simultaneously not putting any effort into making these characters memorable or have any sort of character arcs. This is the first time where I would say that the story of a Monster Hunter game actively got in the way and hindered my enjoyment. First of all, the story overall felt very rushed. You are moving from one locale to another at a breakneck pace with barely any time to get familiarized with the towns and locals. But at the same time, your crew of NPC friends that you’re on this journey with are constantly gathering with you for mandatory “yap sessions” where you all stand in a circle and talk about what has already happened in the story so far. It is so beyond frustrating because I want to take my time and get to know the locations and monsters of the area, but it feels like the game is shaking me by the shoulders and yelling at me to just get on with it. The story is basically the same as every other entry in the series, but I really feel like the developers are trying too hard to make me care about these plot points and characters when that was never really why I played these games to begin with. It makes the whole experience feel like it was born out of corporate greed rather than passion. The Performance I will include my PC specs in this review to show that I’m not working with the best or worst hardware here but also to illustrate that the PC launch of this game was rough. From day one, I have experienced several stability issues that have made playing this game quite frustrating to play. Frequent crashes, long load times, and graphical bugs have made me dread booting up this game because it just becomes a production. Not to mention it has that classic modern gaming touch of having to preload shaders before it can actually start. This is super frustrating, especially if I haven’t touched the game in a while because it will now take 20-30 minutes to actually load into this game. I don’t know if the RE engine is just bad when it comes to PC gaming, but so many important aspects of this game's performance just don’t work. The worst part is that this is all for a game that doesn’t even look that much better than World. Now, credit where credit is due: CAPCOM have released several stability updates that have improved performance significantly. But the damage has been done and the game still sometimes has stability issues. It’s a real shame because up until now Monster Hunter games have had pretty rock solid performance. I just hate to see one of my favorite series in such a state. Conclusion Like I said at the beginning: I don’t like having to make a review like this. I spent about 5 years playing these games religiously. There really is no other franchise that even compares to this unique living world that the team has created. So it breaks my heart to see it like this. I have watched this series slowly but surely fall into the trappings of greedy modern gaming practices that it has become a shadow of its former self. Fortunately or unfortunately depending on how you look at it; a lot of these issues will be fixed with the DLC expansion that was recently announced. It’s just a shame that we will have to pay extra to get the “full” experience. You know, there’s a part of me that wishes this series never expanded, that it never broke free of its slower, more methodical if not clunky roots and stayed a niche series. But Monster Hunter is a series that loves to experiment; that’s something I love about it. Wilds, however, has been a clear failure.

review_text: Pros: Cross-platform. Most of the weapons are easier to use. Cons: As a long-time Monster Hunter fan, this game felt like a slap in the face. The worst part about the game is probably the ridiculously bad difficulty scaling. Past Monster Hunter games gave you tough hunts from the start, making the campaign fun and engaging. In this game, none of the fights are difficult until you get to end-game, which means the first 30+ hours of the game play like a boring slow-paced tutorial. Was this game made for toddlers? I genuinely don't understand how the designers could have messed up the difficulty this badly. There is a magical feeling that Monster Hunter games used to give me. This game doesn't do it for me. Even though the graphics are probably technically higher definition, I still found this game the most visually ugly Monster Hunter game I've ever played. The environments, weapons, and armors look bland and dusty. The characters look boring and lifeless. It looks and plays like it was made by a massive corporation trying to make money rather than a game design studio that actually loved and cared about the project they were working on. Also I hate that there is more cleavage and immodesty in this game than any other Monster Hunter game. I recommend Monster Hunter World if you want an epic Monster Hunter experience more like AAA title games. Monster Hunter Generations Ultimate if you want to really experience old-school Monster hunter at its best. Monster Hunter Rise if you want a super fun fast-paced experience that basically gives the player super-powers. I love all three of these games and I'd probably choose MH Rise as my overall favorite.

review_text: Review done after getting all achievements. MH Wilds is a good MH game. It has beautiful maps, diverse and huge. Even the "dessert map" or the "snow map" are now huge chunks of terrain with lots of details and different areas. The forst area is incredibly detailed and beautiful. The monsters roster is great, they've avoided the usual "elder dragons" and what they're have the usual mechanics and gimmicks but with the new additions (focus mode, parrys, gear skills, etc) it feels really fun. The QoL improvements are there. It feels like an improved Worlds in terms of gameplay and hunts. They took some combos and attacks from Rise but none of the gameplay mechanics, which I think is very good. I'd wish and hope they added Rise monsters (specially sunbreak) in the game, or at least in an evet quest... something. The negatives are quite common as there are there since day 1. Mainly, the performance (specially in the forests areas) and how unpolished the game feels with RE engine. On a personal level, the hitboxes feels very wonky, specially with huge monsters but, in general, in wings and tails. I also don't like how some weapons feel a step backward, even if they're fun and competitive (Insect Glaive, for instance). Then, the lack of a "fixed base camp" where you can show your hunts... I've got a Cactilio for nothing! I hope the expansion brings new monsters, less focus on focus mode (heh) and, overall, better performance. If the game would be better optimized I think Wilds would be the best monster hunter.

review_text: Overall, an underwhelming entry to the series. First off, why on earth is there no option for the audio language to be classic Wyverian anymore?! The hell do you mean, "we wanted to make people pay more attention to the dialogue." ?! While the changes made to the weapons move sets are overall welcome and extremely refreshing, amping the tempo and dynamic ways of engaging your target, it doesn't take long to notice the cracks in the game's overall structure. The game has been simplified. Now, don't take this as a "this is an insult to my intellectual capability!" type of complaint. I'm a simpleton at heart, but even I think some of the simplifications in this game's gameplay loop feel just dull and unnecessary. The story, unsurprisingly, isn't the main reason for people to buy into this thing. But if you make it feel like an overgloryfied tutorial, that neither respects your will to learn from experience nor your time, it will just become a massive eye roller after another, and even a reason for people, not to buy it. While the online play was serviceable at best, it got the job done. In Monster Hunter World, that is. Many were hoping for a more seamless online experience, with friends and strangers alike. You know... for the next game to improve on the predecessor's shortcomings and make the already good stuff even more enjoyable. Instead, they just cramped the round based matchmaking of World into the now more open world oriented gameplay of Wilds. How there isn't a persistent party system yet, I don't know. The only noticeable attempt at changing the structure was the dynamic hunt mechanic, allowing you to join another player in your lobby, should he engage a roaming monster in combat. As for the story... yes, you still have to start the mission alone and have to wait for the contained cutscene to be over, so you can invite your friends or even allow strangers to drop in. The roster of monsters is solid, but still sort of underwhelming. While it's great to see some older monsters return, the overall selection of monsters seems to be suffering from the usual live service mentality of modern triple-a companies. And paying full price, just to wait a year or two for a multi-billion company to hand me a bunch of new monsters, which should've already been part of the "newer, bigger and better" set of promises they lured my money out the wallet with in the first place. The only nail, missing in this coffin, would be another Iceborne move. And don't even get me started on the horrendous technical performance. Even after all this time, you're still required to buy expensive, top of the line hardware just to run this game. And the sad part? It doesn't even look wort the money you spend to run it. I wish this was taken like one or two more years trough development, instead of being released as a half-hearted excuse for a so called tripple-a title, being a live service game in disguise. I really hope they'll finally pull their head out of their ass and fix this mess, to bring people the well deserved polish and excitement, they expected from this full priced title in the first place.

review_text: Fully recommend this game. Right now it’s in a really good state, and the devs did a great job with optimization. It feels like an upgraded version of World where almost all the monsters feel unique and fun to hunt. The maps are really immersive, and it’s a big jump compared to World/Rise. But... even though all that is true, the game also has some downsides. At least for me (LS main), the game still feels clunky in a way, similar to how World did. The combos are boring and it often feels like you’re just spamming the same attack over and over. Also, the autopilot of the Seikret can ruin the exploration since it's a no-brainer mechanic. It’s a shame that, with such complex and well-designed maps, they ruin it like that. It doesn’t have the same level of dynamism that Rise has to offer with LS, where you have a lot of combos to do, skills to choose from, and more entertaining gameplay overall. Of course, this applies mainly to LS and maybe some other weapons (I don’t know, since I haven’t played any others), but it could be the opposite for some players. I have a friend who mains DBs, and he tells me the opposite: in Rise he spams the same attack, while in Wilds he does crazy combos and the gameplay feels much more dynamic. I know Capcom can’t make everyone happy or make all 14 weapons perfect, but I hope this gets improved in a DLC. Other than that, the fights are pretty good and enjoyable. Maybe there are some monsters that spam attacks that one-shot you, but that’s just bad design and it only happens in the endgame. About 95% of the fights are really good. Overall, I recommend this game to both new players and veterans. It will only get better over time with updates and DLC, and it has the potential to become the best MH ever. 9/10

review_text: I like Schedule I. The core gameplay loop is genuinely fun, and the first playthrough is a great experience. Building your operation, unlocking new products, and gradually expanding your business is extremely satisfying. Unfortunately, the game’s post-launch development has been disappointing. Content updates take far too long to reach production, and when they finally arrive, they often feel shallow and disconnected from the rest of the game. The mushroom update is a good example. It gives you another product to manufacture, but it does not meaningfully affect the game. It does not change how you operate, introduce interesting decisions, or interact with the existing systems in a meaningful way. You can ignore mushrooms entirely and lose virtually nothing from the experience. The cartel update was a fantastic idea with poor execution. A rival criminal organization should create pressure, competition, danger, and meaningful rewards. Instead, the cartel mostly adds more chores and obstacles without giving the player much to gain. It feels less like a dynamic rival and more like an artificial way to slow progression and stretch out the existing content. There was so much potential here, which makes the final result especially disappointing. I understand that this is largely the work of a solo developer, and that game development takes time. However, that explanation becomes less convincing after a game earns millions of dollars. Players bought the game in Early Access to support its continued development. At some point, it is reasonable to expect some of that success to be reinvested into additional development resources, faster production, and more substantial updates. Early Access was originally presented as a way for players to fund promising games while developers continued building them. Increasingly, it feels like a way to earn most of a game’s revenue before delivering a finished product. Players are not simply buying what currently exists; they are buying into a promise that the game will continue growing. When development slows down and updates feel minimal, it creates the impression that the game has entered maintenance mode before it is anywhere close to finished. I love Schedule I, and I want to see it reach its potential. That is exactly why its current development and management are so frustrating. The foundation is excellent, but the time, money, and momentum generated by the game’s success do not seem to be translating into the depth or pace of development that players were led to expect.

review_text: I’ve been playing Schedule One for a while now, and overall I genuinely enjoy it. The core gameplay loop is solid and it’s easy to sink hours into without noticing. If you like grind-heavy progression systems, this game will absolutely hook you. Watching your operation grow from nothing into something profitable is satisfying. That said, the grind can feel excessive at times. A lot of the gameplay relies on repetitive manual tasks, and while that works early on, it starts to drag in the mid-to-late game. There needs to be deeper automation systems, something that lets you scale operations more efficiently once you’ve proven yourself. Right now, it feels like you hit a ceiling. The game hints at building a serious empire, but you never quite reach that “kingpin” level. It would be great to expand progression so players can go full Tony Montana. Bigger networks, ability to export large quantities, larger territory control, higher risk/high reward systems, and more strategic management instead of constant micromanagement.

review_text: Schedule 1 is a crime sim that mashes its dark subject matter and dirty jokes with surprisingly cozy management mechanics in a way that works really well, resulting in an extremely unique and highly amusing crafting game I happily sunk 100 hours into. review_text: This is a super interesting game that will hook you for a few evenings—perhaps a few weeks, but not much longer. It’s rewarding to develop and create your own laboratories, interacting with the world. But at some point it becomes too easy: once you have a couple of labs, you quickly start farming dealers, and the game loses its angle due to the sheer abundance. I know the developer does it all by himself, and I have a lot of respect for that. Yet it seems that introducing new cities as you level up and expand your territory would significantly boost the interest. It’s worth noting how fun the game is. Overall, the map could use a bit more space: after a couple of gaming sessions you know every corner and feel like there’s nowhere left to grow. My take: adding a couple more cities you can relocate to after gaining full control over the previous ones would restore the hype and give the game a fresh breath of air.

review_text: The community votes are pointless. The game needs more polishing and improvements to features that have already been implemented. I don't care about new customers—right now it feels pointless because the gameplay is still the same repetitive cycle. I can stack all my deliveries after midnight and finish them at the 4 AM mark, which completely freezes the game... WHY?! It's incredibly stupid. The police need improvements, gangs need improvements, and THE MAP NEEDS TO BE BIGGER!! There are many other issues that should be addressed before adding more content. The game also needs more side activities besides the casino. Even after the nerf, the casino is still overpowered and can make an insane amount of money. There should be more profitable and engaging alternatives so players aren't forced to rely on the casino as the best way to earn cash. I bought this game on day one, so I know what I'm talking about. This is Unity, not Unreal Engine. Stop pretending the engine is the reason basic gameplay improvements are taking so long. I don't want to hate on the game, but I'm tired of all the unnecessary glazing. The game is still way too easy, and it WILL STILL be easy after the customers update if nothing else changes. That being said, I still think the game is fun and has a lot of potential. The biggest issue isn't that the game is bad—it's that the gameplay becomes repetitive after a while. Discovering new drug combinations and seeing all the hilarious effects they create is one of the most enjoyable parts of the game. The humor is one of its strongest features and keeps the experience entertaining. Even though the casino is overpowered and needs better balancing, it is still a fun activity. The problem is that there aren't enough other activities that are just as enjoyable and rewarding. More variety would help keep the gameplay fresh and give players more reasons to continue playing. I bought this game because I saw its potential, and I still believe it can become much better. Instead of focusing on community votes and adding more content, the developers should focus on fixing and expanding the core gameplay first.

review_text: I really want to recommend this game, I spent quite a bit of time playing it and enjoyed some of it, yet I can't because it has glaring issues that aren't addressed. And with each passing update this game recieves I doubt they will if Tyler will continue making updates for the game based only on the community updates that add new mechanics that are barely fleshed out, instead of polishing already existing stuff and making it more enjoyable. The game says that the whole drug dealing business in it is "dangerous" but the entire police department can be killed off on the first day if you put a tiny bit of effort, and the cartel barely does anything do hinder your operations. And even during the occurences during which the cartel actually DOES something besides leaving a graffiti or doing a deal (both of which I have seen like occur maybe 3 times through several of my playthroughs), like the gang jumping you or robbing the dealer, it usually happens so late into the game that it is barely an inconvenience. Speaking of murdering the entire police station, the fact that you can steal the guns off of officers this early in the game completely destroys the balance of the game in two ways. 1. You get late game weapons on practically the first day of the game which make any combat encounter trivial 2. The weapons can be sold for a ridiculous (for the earlygame) price, which gives you way too much money than you should have in this stage of the game There is no reason to diversify your products, as it is too much of a hassle for way too little of a return, and making one good product can practically catapult you to the endgame with the amount of money it can make. And from one point of view it might seem weird of me complaining for having too much money, but the whole point of the game is to be making money, so getting so much early game makes the whole goal of the game nonexistant. Even if you consider destroying the cartel to be the main goal of the game, with the amount of money that you get from even just slightly optimising your operation makes it completely trivial and unrewarding (might be overexaggerating here, but I only got the satisfaction from the first time, because it was a tidious grind to get there). The workers are just unfun to use. The only ones that are somewhat okay to work with are the botanists, and even then I wish that they weren't locked to only one locker for all of the resources that they need, because it makes organising how much each of the botanists need a chore, and handlers, but they have their own issues. The chemists feel like a downgraded version of the botanists but for chemistry work stations, in a sense that they can only have 3 work stations assigned to them, and they can't even bring the ingredients from the lockers to the work stations, making you have to manually put the ingredients into their work stations, and then manually take the output out. I would've understood if you could've assigned handlers to do the moving between stations, but you can't. Also the mixing abilities of chemists are abhorrent, so the fact that they can use the mixers is completely irrelevant, because if you want to make a mix that has more than 1 ingredient in it, you will have to do it manually as you can't just assign the chemist to do the proper mix because there is just no such option. I understand that the workers are limiting so that we have to interact with the production of the drugs, but it fails at that, because at a certain point in the game all you do is order ingredients, repack the stations, deliver the product to dealers, repeat. Which makes for a very dull endgame that otherwise has a lot of potential. And I know that the counterargument to bad workers is "just make the product by hand" but doing so is giving me carpal tunnel having to manually move 20 leaves into a cauldron to make cocaine, and if I miss a single leaf I have to restart the whole process. The early game suffers from the same issues a bit too, especially when you don't have a mk2 packager and mixer, but it makes sense as you have to work hard in the early game to make money. But the same doesn't apply when I am a rich cartel boss and can't for some reason just carry 20 leaves at once. Also I wish that there was an actual time limit on doing the deals, because the night doesn't progress after 4 am, the deal timer is essentially endless (unless you forget you have deals and go to sleep), which removes all the pressure you did have on quickly finishing the deals. I believe that the game can improve on every single one of the listed aspects, like making the police stronger, not letting you sell the guns you got from the cops cause I don't think a pawn shop should buy stolen items, making the cartel much more aggresive, having a supply/demand system where the products lose value the more of them you sell (also on a side note, please let us rename products, it is so infuriating when I misspell a product name and have to be stuck with it), make the workers consistent all around by letting for instance chemists pull ingredients from shelves and putting the finished product on shelves (like botanists do), make it so that the deal timer goes out before 4 am so that it is not endless. I know that maybe some updates in the future will address some of the issues that the game has, like the police in the upcoming (hopefully) police rework update, but that should've been one of the first updates to come out. I really like this game, but it's very depressing to see that the game's health isn't prioritized in the current updates that it recieves (that also take quite a long time to come out, but I don't judge here because I know that game development takes time), and instead the priority is on more side content instead of polishing the existing stuff.

review_text: I love the game, I really do. It's already become a go-to comfort pick for me and my boyfriend to just banter on with good vibes. Despite giving it my thumbs up, I still think there could be some genuine improvements to the game. I am sorely disappointed in the presence of the Cartel, or lack thereof, once unlocking them within the story. They barely show up and to decrease the influence of the Cartel in certain districts, we had to camp certain doors at midnight to kill a Cartel dealer that only briefly would leave the building and go back inside, unless you managed to knock them out in time. It wasn't long after until we realised that having the influence completely down to 0 had little to none impact on the story. Of course I know the game is still in early access and being fixed, though, the longer we played the same game file, the more things got buggy. We had to abandon one of our save files because eventually cars were literally flying, turning upside down, doors that shouldn't be open were open, etc. We usually played through the bugs and didn't mind them all that much, though some of them were quite frustrating and so unavoidably frequent, it almost got us to ragequit a couple of times; Sometimes my friend would get arrested by police and captured even if he wasn't anywhere near them, needlessly losing bagged products and money in the process. The game would often crash for the person who wasn't hosting the game and upon getting back into the game, items and money would have disappeared from their inventory. We grinded so hard for the manor, I was so hyped to see it and did everything in my power to explore it myself before looking at it online or anywhere else. But my disappointment to see the manor so empty and bland, with nothing inside like a kitchen or a bathroom or anything that could've been built in (like the bungalow's kitchen) was so disappointing and such a let-down, it was so anti-climactic that I closed the game without saving it and haven't been back online yet. I do feel like the manor shouldn't be unlockable after the end of the game, once you've fully gotten rid of the Cartel. I felt like there was no point to the manor because the game was already done. Regardless of all my criticism to the game, I still enjoyed my time thoroughly on it and it's got a cosy vibe to it that I will definitely revisit again at some point. Keep up the good work!

Presently, while the game is a lot of fun for a while I had banked my goodwill toward the game and returned to it on the premise that eventually they would flesh out the base systems in the game but instead we keep getting semi fleshed-out content expansions which, while cool, takes the game in the opposite direction of feeling complete in my opinion. review_text: Would be closer to neutral review but no such option exists on Steam. Honeymoon phase is neat and exists for every game but unfortunately tedium gets worse and worse over time. It feels like a DarkRP drug role that received its own game - with decently fun minigames. But they quickly overstay their welcome, especially when scaling up operations it isn't simply fun to do this ♥♥♥ tens of times over and over, and some parts of the drug manufacturing that are annoying cannot be skipped over. The balancing with cash/credit is terrible - I unlocked cocaine before I even managed to afford the barn. Mushrooms have weird place where they are located after meth and shortly before coke is available, require more hands-on than even weed while barely more profitable. Robbing guns from cops feels like an exploit given how much money it can give so early on. For most time, I was artificially blocked from buying new ♥♥♥ and having to carry tens of thousands of dollars while money laundering drip-fed me credit balance that was being taken by some produce that you HAVE to buy for credit balance until much later on. Cartel was non-existent for me through my gameplay. I seen TB roll up to me, told him to ♥♥♥ off becoming enemies with Benzies, never seen him ever again nor my dealers were attacked even once. Combat is a meme in this game in general, even before guns you can easily whack entire police force with a baseball bat. Mixing anything 'fun' and expensive takes far too much time if playing 'by the rules' turning a single 20-piece batch can take total in-game day. The experience could be less miserable by having either a feeder-hopper with ability to queue up to 8 ingredient 'batches' or bundled together for tier 3 of the mixer. Automation feels clunky and handicapped - the amount of objects that the workers handle is miserable. I seen guides explaining how to automate the mixing and there is no way to just set a recipe and let workers handle the recipe until the final product is reached, it requires some stupid daisychaining that I would expect to be done from a mod, not an official paid game. It's understandable that this is EA and 'this is done by a single guy and they just got the studio' yaddayadda I get it, but does not help that this concept generally does not feel fun beyond few hours in. I've tried multiple runs to 'finish' the game but i got tired of it each time because it turns into a boring slog at midpoint. I think fixing balance of drugs and income first, maybe making police less of a pushover, would actually be more healthy in long run than adding new content that essentially sits on islands. Beyond design issues, there are a lot of technical issues as well - police respawning after reloading a save, laundering operations disappearing or being rollbacked, vendors dialogue prompts disappearing and trash items getting stuck on objects that cannot be picked up until the object is redeployed. Those are the things that I've experienced myself in the latest run. If the Cartel is supposed to appear more often and not that I accidentally curbstomped them so hard they just hid 24/7, I guess that is a bug too. The performance for the game with graphics that is on the level with Unturned is atrocious. I have no idea why this game runs like ♥♥♥ until everything is set to lowest and even then it stutters during combat. Hoping the developers make priority of making game feel like a proper game and not just a tech demo - I appreciate them taking the 'community votes' as a way to be close with players and let them decide what comes up next, however the devs still need to have a solid grasp what actually game needs the most given technical and design issues will just permeate to every next content update.

review_text: I wanted to come back and re-review Schedule 1 since I recompleted the 100%. For context, I bought this game right when it dropped in Spring 2025 and have loved all, if not most of it. I did take a long break from playing and the last time I played was prior to shrooms and weather being added (among other additions). The hype and community around the time of release was insane and it was so fun to be a part of. That said, I think the only issue I have with the game is the same as I did back then; the mid-to-late gameplay is slow and a bit boring at times (for me). You can definitely progress the game far enough and still have fun (it is a sandbox game afterall!) but for me it just lacks something. I’m not sure if the map isn’t interactive or even immersive enough or if it’s something else that isn’t yet fully fleshed out. But once you get to a certain point financially and with automated farms/properties, it just fizzles out for me. I thought going into my most recent playthrough that the addition of the Cartel would make things interesting, but it honestly didn’t. At first I was taken back by their presence, but I was then quickly able to overpower them and they truly posed no challenge to me or my dealers. I know that the game is made by one developer/a smaller team, so there’s absolutely no hate for them because I’m happy with all they’ve done thus far. I’m looking forward to future content updates since I know the community is active and TVGS truly listens to and involves the community in the update progress. So trust me, I’ll inevitably be back to re-complete the 100% if and when new stuff gets added. Since I know several people on my friends list have played the game, I wanted to share a few ideas I had for future updates and would love to hear anyone's thoughts or any ideas you’ve had. So far I’ve thought about: - Being able to go into more buildings, especially residential (not having to call someone down from inside like the Apartment Building) - Bikes or scooters for cheaper transportation - Backpacks for more storage on your person - Can eat items like donuts or addy (and they give special effects like mixed products do) - Can throw or drop items from your inventory - Can sell items to more than just Mick (why can’t I sell clothes to the lady at Thrifty Threads?!)

review_text: I honestly can’t tell if the developers are genuinely this delusional or if they just think we’re all braindead enough to swallow this garbage. Seriously, how did this game get so much hype? The story is ♥♥♥ a joke. ♥♥♥ Charlie Cox dies at the end of ACT 1, wtf? And it gets worse. Look, the whole game is a total scam anyway. The entire world and Expedition 33 are just a giant hallucination inside a magical painting created by a dead guy named Verso. There is no evil Paintress erasing humanity, as she is literally just a pretentious metaphor for the terminal illness that wiped out Verso's family. Your entire party consists of fake ghost clones based on real people from Verso's life. His ♥♥♥ toxic parents literally trapped their surviving daughter, Alicia, inside this depressing art world because they couldn't handle real-world grief. In the end, you either delete the canvas so everyone vanishes and Alicia cries at a real graveyard, or you keep it and watch Alicia go completely insane and get terminally ill inside a fake reality. It is just an overpriced, edgy therapy session about coping with death. ♥♥♥.

review_text: 8.75/10 This game gripped me basically from the moment I opened it. I genuinely sat on the title screen for like two minutes before pressing anything because the art direction and music were that good. Probably the best first impression a game has ever given me. The story kept me interested throughout and Verso was easily my favourite character. The combat took me a little while to get used to, but once it clicked it was sick. Having an RPG combat system mixed with dodges, parries and almost Naruto Storm-style quick-time events is such a good combination. I also really liked how the levels were designed. They're linear enough that I always felt like I was progressing somewhere, without being Devil May Cry levels of "walk down this corridor and fight." It was a really nice middle ground. I unfortunately had to stop playing for a while right after finishing Act 2 because of other commitments, which was probably the worst possible place to take a break. Act 2 almost feels like a resolution in itself, so I struggled to get back into Act 3 afterwards. Once I actually did though, I finished the rest of the game in about three days. My biggest criticism is that the game somehow feels a little small despite having basically the perfect runtime. I finished it at around 30 hours and wouldn't really want the main story to be much longer. I just wish the world had more characters outside of the main cast who were properly developed, and I would have loved more combat options or some genuinely weird builds and abilities to play around with. By the end I was getting a little tired of running variations of Maelle, Verso and Sciel. But those are pretty minor complaints compared to how much I enjoyed everything else. Incredible art direction, incredible music, a great story, fun combat and characters I actually cared about. Peak game. Would recommend it to basically anyone.
