review_text: NO SPOILERS - 7/10 TL;DR - I played almost 100 hours in the span of a single week, defeated almost everything except the very last 3 super bosses in the Endless Tower. The game is really fun but the combat is unbalanced and broken, I don't think it deserved "Game of the year 2025" (a lot of hype), and it definitely did not deserve "Best Role Playing Game 2025" award. Short version Pros: Amazing graphics (I also played with DLSS 5 and it looked like cinema), the story and acting are really good, they make you actually care for the characters. The combat is entertaining but has a huge RPG balancing flaw that was simply never fixed, I also had lots of fun making builds and whatnot ( I highly suggest to not Google for builds, simply do them yourself ) Cons: There are a lot of areas that required "Quality of Life" updates that never happened, like a much better loadout system (skills, weapons, luminas), features for organizing pictos, lack of meaningful side quests, and most importantly the damage balance is just non-existent. Verdict: 7/10 , the game is really good and entertaining, however its most important RPG aspect which is combat is simply broken and was never fixed, it did not deserve "Best RPG 2025" award. Long version The game performance was really good compared to what we have nowadays, I played with High settings and DLSS 5 balanced (Neural Rendering), I was playing at 80 FPS, which by comparison in other games under the same settings I was getting around 50 FPS. Visually speaking, the environment and characters are out of this world, even more so when using DLSS 5 Neural Rendering, I spent a bunch of time taking screenshots as it looked completely astonishing. The story and characters really captures you as a player, you can feel their fear, anguish, joy and sadness. It's among the few games that actually manage to transmit the character's feelings to the player, they did a perfect job on that. However, the game was overly-hyped, in my opinion. I very much enjoyed the game up until half way through the story, at which point the game allowed me to finish every single encounter in 1 to 3 turns max (including bosses), and that went all the way through finishing the story. Then it only got more absurd after finishing the main story (one-shots). review_text: One of the Best Gaming Experiences I've Ever Had! This is actually my first ever review, and I couldn't think of a better game to write one for than Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of those rare games that makes you feel as though you're genuinely part of its world rather than simply playing through it. The immersion, atmosphere, and storytelling drew me in so completely that I found myself invested in every moment. As someone who usually dislikes cutscenes and tends to skip them whenever possible, watching every single cutscene in this game says more than enough about how deeply it captivated me. The soundtrack deserves special recognition. I genuinely loved every song in the game, and the music plays an enormous role in making the experience so memorable. Combined with the incredible art direction, beautifully designed environments, and compelling characters, it creates an atmosphere that is difficult to put into words. The gameplay was another major highlight for me. The ability to experiment with different builds, mix and match abilities, and develop unique strategies makes the combat incredibly engaging. The variety of encounters and the design of the bosses kept me invested throughout my journey. What surprised me most was how much I enjoyed the turn-based combat. The game almost feels like a turn-based Soulslike, combining strategic decision-making with challenging encounters and rewarding progression. It's a concept I hadn't fully appreciated before, but Expedition 33 has opened the door to an entirely new style of gameplay for me. It's also one of the few games I've ever committed to completing 100%, earning every achievement along the way. The journey was certainly not without its frustrations, though. My biggest complaint is that completing every achievement requires a New Game+ playthrough. Having to go through another playthrough solely to finish the achievement list was disappointing, and I wish everything could have been completed in a single run. However, this is my only significant criticism, and it hardly diminishes the overall experience. Everything else came together exceptionally well. From the world design and characters to the soundtrack, combat, bosses, and sheer atmosphere, Expedition 33 delivered an experience that genuinely resonated with me. It reminded me of what makes video games such a special medium: the ability to immerse yourself in another world, become invested in its journey, and walk away with an experience that stays with you long after the credits roll. I know I'll remember this game for a long time. It has not only become one of my favourite games of all time, but has also changed my expectations of what a game can achieve when its different elements come together so beautifully. For my first review, I couldn't have asked for a better game to write about. Thank you to the developers for creating such an unforgettable experience. An unforgettable experience, and one I would wholeheartedly recommend. (:

Like stun was a 5 turn build up just to have it wear off after a turn most of the time, Lune and Gustave felt similar. Sciel was a mid range option with ons and offs of high dps, Verso was even worse than everyone else as he lost progression as he took damage and the move sets for all the enemies were so varied that it made it really hard to maintain a decent rank. MONOCO was the most fun for me to play. Collecting moves from downed enemies was a rather novel mechanic and gave him a more readily available skill tree. Maelle was my most consistent damage doer but even she would struggle to get her moves off the ground sometime. Yes I played on easy as this game was already out of the spot light when I mostly played it for the story which didnt make sense for the first 8/10ths of the game. That was annoying. A story driven game like this should have a more clear story at the beginning. I do like dramatic reveals and unreliable witness based perspectives but I had no motivation to fight past the vagueness of the depressing story. By the way SF... That first epilogue was not an epilogue! 1 Epilogues take place after the main game and are story exits for every character usually. 2 You cant have an epilogue after an epilogue. That just proves that the first one was not an epilogue. 3 If understanding your whole game only happens in the epilogue then you will have discouraged most of your gamers from finishing the game and truly appreciating what occured in the main story. For me, your game only really happened in the first epilogue. which is not how epilogues work. I almost just put down the game at the 10 hour mark and said, 'nope, its a random depressing story that is beautifully rendered but ultimately pointless. dont buy.' BUT! because of how it ended, (and I think I picked the better ending,) it ended up being a powerful story about dealing with grief and loss and the effect of a loss on everyone it touches. For me it ended well, but sucked the life out of me up until that point. Maybe that was the point... or maybe I was just bored on easy mode. 7/10. Could done this with less fighting. review_text: Clair Obscur feels like one of those games that shouldn’t exist, but somehow does because a bunch of passionate weirdos decided “yeah, why not?” The dev story alone is wild: A French dude who speedruns Sekiro gets tired of his job at Ubisoft and just... quits to make his dream game. He calls his old university buddy, who ends up becoming the lead tech. He finds a musician on SoundCloud who makes the entire OST. He finds a girl on Reddit who agrees to voice the demo for free and she eventually becomes the lead writer. Then they hire like thirty fresh grads who are all in over their heads but clearly giving it everything they’ve got. And member number thirty-three? A dog. Literally credited as the Happiness Manager in the end credits. And the crazy part is: the game actually turned out great. Stylish, unique, full of heart, exactly the kind of thing you get when people make something because they want to, not because some exec told them to. Clair Obscure is a win for gamers and a big, beautiful middle finger to AAA companies that fill their games with garbage and micro transactions.

review_text: "When one falls, we continue." This review is going to sound like it was written by a kid who just finished their very first video game. Which is funny, because it's exactly the opposite. After being a gamer for almost 40 years, I rarely get seriously impressed by a game. If anything, they often feel like a chore, just because of the "been there, done that" effect. But this? This is... Wow. Or should I say "owowow?" Anyway, our story begins with Ubisoft, the company known for its greed and copy/pasted games. And our hero, Guillaume Broche, grew tired of that. He wanted creativity, not just a paycheck. He left. And he wasn't alone. Another Ubisoft employee, Tom Guillermin, left with him, and since Tom knew Unreal Engine, they started fooling around with it. Things started to take form, and we got an early draft called Sandfall (originally, the game was supposed to revolve around time). But clearly, they needed more people, so... they wrote on Reddit (that was the scale, a bloody Reddit post). They looked for voice actors, but instead, they found their lead writer—Jennifer Svedberg-Yen. And she... OK, it's hard to describe the story of the game without spoiling it (actually, the one who included certain scenes in the trailer is a criminal). Again, with too many games behind me, I'm rarely excited about stories in video games. Heck, I'm one of those people who hated Last of Us, just because of all the "Will you shut up already? I want to shoot something!" Clair Obscur? Blew me away. Think MYST. Think Cornelia Funke's Inkheart novels, but also think something absolutely unique and beautiful. And also sad. Very sad. Like Cyberpunk 2077 (you can say a lot of things about that game, but it had some really good characters, and its story made a lot of impact because of how things were never fair), Clair Obscur pays so much attention to characters (without making things boring) that it's literally impossible not to care. And when you begin caring? The game will break your freakin' heart. Welcome to Clair Obscur, guys. A world of infinite sadness. Sadness so thick you can feel it with your skin. Which is... Shocking. Not because it's good (it is, though; both the story and atmosphere here are absolutely amazing), but because... Jennifer never wrote for video games. Heck, her previous job didn't even involve writing! Yet here we are. One of the most beautiful stories I've seen in ages. And you know what? It wasn't just Jennifer. Sandfall (even though the game wasn't about time anymore, Guillaume and Tom kept the name and gave it to the company they co-founded) hired another person with no experience—Lorien Testard. Who's Lorien? Well, he's a guitar teacher who worked on music for fun and posted tracks on SoundCloud. That's it. That's our guy behind the music. Means we've got a cute, yet simple soundtrack, right? Wrong. No, seriously, you couldn't be more wrong. With the help of soprano singer Alice Duport-Percier, Lorien created one of the most beautiful soundtracks I've heard in my entire life. It's not a paid review, but honestly, it's one of those cases when you simply must buy yourself a soundtrack. It's one of a kind, and it's impossible to forget it. You will keep listening to it long after you finish the game. Finally, a couple of words about visuals. And it's yet another name that changed the project's look entirely. Originally, in its times as Sandfall, Clair Obscur was a Victorian steampunk. Hence, hiring Nicholas Maxson-Francombe, an illustrator known for such stuff, was logical. I mean, he's another one with no experience with video games whatsoever, but it still made sense. The thing is though, while looking at some random pictures he made, Guillaume understood that those are much more beautiful than what the team had in mind originally. Nicholas for the game's visuals is what Jennifer is for the story. It's hard to describe what he did specifically, but... let's just say he somehow captured a certain kind of magic in his design. Thanks to him, the game has its own face, its own signature design. Unique and instantly recognizable. But OK, for a person who believes that gameplay is the most important part, I talked too much about story, music, and visuals. What about the gameplay? Well, what we have here is JRPG. And yes, this game is not Japanese. It's French. Very French. A French aesthetic is everywhere. It's so French that, exactly like I recommend playing Japanese RPGs with the Japanese voices, I recommend playing this one with the French ones. And yes, thanks to the publisher and other financial incomes, English voices here come with the Hollywood cast, but still, I can't imagine this game without the French cast (since you can simply switch to it in options, it looks like it was suggested by the devs too). Yet it's JRPG. Because somehow JRPG became a genre's name, and JRPGs that were not made in Japan have been a thing for quite some time (Septerra Core anyone?). And you know what? It's yet another cool thing about this game. Let's just admit it, JRPGs are struggling now. Lots of them feel exactly the same (like those games from the Idea Factory, for example), while major franchises like Final Fantasy are going through one heck of an identity crisis. Personally, I used to love those up until PS2 times, where the gameplay changed so much that the games became something entirely different. Clair Obscur? In a way, it's what Final Fantasy wants to be but fails. It's also important to remember another Square-Enix title – The Legend of Dragoon. Remember how that game used a smart workaround to make turn-based battles more dynamic? Clair Obscur does the same. And it goes all the way into that direction. Despite being turn-based, it wants you to dodge, parry, and even jump during the battles. Which makes it feel almost real-time at times. And it feels... Awesome. No, seriously. The battles here feel almost like something from the rhythm games. Remember good ol' Patapon? That's the stuff. When it's about those big bosses, you either pon-pon-patapon their attacks or die. And it's not just a coincidence, it's by design. On many occasions, the characters will compare battles to dances. Like everything else in this game, battles are bloody art. And so is the leveling mechanics. Personally, I don't like overly complicated mechanics. Sitting on my butt and doing micromanagement for hours instead of exploring and fighting? Not really my thing. Clair Obscur? It can pleasure both people like me and the micromanagement crowd. Long story short, things revolve around some items called "pictos." Those are the things you can equip on your characters for certain effects (like Materia in Final Fantasy). What's interesting here is that those chain. Here's an example: There's that ultimate boss who can and will one-hit-kill you. What can you do about it? Well, you can equip certain pictos. One will instantly resurrect you and give you a second chance, another gives you some buff upon being resurrected, and the third one will give the boss a debuff. Do pictos right and you'll be able to one-hit-kill every single enemy in this game, including that ultimate boss. Which is extremely satisfying. And again, it was intentional. Clair Obscur's developers weren't just making a game. They were making a game they wanted to play for themselves. You can feel it everywhere. In how very special and personal the story is, in how beautiful the music is... Even the gameplay is full of some little touches it's hard not to praise. For example, my biggest problem with the genre is that battle animations are very long and the UI is too bulky. Sandfall guys? They felt the same. Thanks to which battles, despite being extremely spectacular, are also pretty fast-paced. So yeah. What we have here is not just GOTY, it's the best game I've played in, like, a decade. You either love Clair Obscur or you just didn't play it yet. It's simple like that.

review_text: See things as they are, not how you want them to be... The most beautiful game I have ever played, in every aspect! I think by now everyone has played or at least heard about Clair Obscure: Expedition 33, but I'm not going to spoil anything about the game in this review. The story is about a group of people living in an isolated town called Lumiere, inspired by France during the Belle Époque. A huge number can be seen on the monolith that the Paintress paints every year, which affects them, so they form a team of expeditioners to sail to her in hopes of killing her and stopping her from harming the people in Lumiere. This year, Expedition 33 is gathering to start the adventure. Will they be able to stop her and live life normally? The gameplay is like that of old RPGs, where you explore a world map, travel from city to city, meet people, kill monsters, and upgrade your weapons. The fighting is turn-based, which I'm familiar with. Think of old Final Fantasy games when you play this game. It is clear it was inspired by those old games, and the atmosphere is similar to NieR, which is one of my favorite games. However, there is no manual save; the game autosaves regularly. Whenever you find a flag checkpoint, it will save automatically and let you fast-travel to another checkpoint. Make sure to touch the checkpoint flag whenever you want to save. The combat is turn-based with QTEs, which you can set to auto in the settings if that's not your thing. Each character has a different fighting style and set of skills. The only things I had to do repeatedly were parrying attacks and dodging. I found out that by learning and hearing the attack, it would be easy to parry it. It frustrated me a couple of times, especially with some bosses you can't kill unless you parry them, but you can always fail and learn how to do it next time. The game needs some grinding to kill some bosses. Try not to skip any monsters you see around; kill them to level up and earn new weapons. The artwork is outstanding, and every detail in the game is beautiful and meaningful. The color palette chosen for each area is mesmerizing, and the character's design is memorable. This game did something other games in my opinion failed to do. There is no UI and clutter while you are exploring the areas; you just walk around and enjoy each detail without having a health bar, a minimap, or a distracting list of objectives. You have the full screen to yourself and your character, which is a huge plus for me, as it lets me enjoy the environment. The characters' animations and facial expressions are on point; you can see the emotions in their gazes, posture, and voices. The voice actors did an outstanding job capturing the essence of those characters. It felt like watching a movie; in each scene, you could see how they reacted, what they looked like, and how they received each piece of information. This alone makes you want to replay the game to watch those little details. The dialogues are extremely well written. Music is breathtakingly beautiful; each soundtrack is meaningful; the lyrics tell a story and capture the characters' emotions. The game has 154 tracks on the main album alone, worth listening to, and they will actually stick in your head after playing the game. Character development is one of the strong suits of this game; you can see and feel how they bond, how they become stronger, how they hate, and how they grow suspicious. The writing of each character is phenomenal, especially in Act 2. Pros: +Emotional beautiful story. +Outstanding soundtracks. +Beautiful graphics and animations. +Great characters and monsters design. +Phenomenal voice over. +Turn-based combat. +World map. +Fast traveling. +Journal. +Multiple endings. +Collectables. +Cosmatics for each character. +Auto save. +Steam achievements. Cons: - No manual save. The game is unique in that it doesn't explain the story to you directly; it wants you to follow it emotionally and logically, forming theories about what is going on before the grand reveal. I highly recommend not charging and just killing bosses without exploring the world, reading the journals, or speaking to the characters. Those interactions will give you different layers to the story, and you'll understand it more, especially in the last act, where you'll be able to explore the whole map to read more information and learn more about the characters. The game has two endings; it is up to you how you want this to end. For more reviews check my curator page Feena's Choice Follow IndieGems for more reviews like this one.

review_text: I’m playing games for 3 decades now, and Clair Obscur is one of the best I experienced in all of this time. Of course I got all the excitement about it, and all the positive reviews and how much people loved it, but I honestly still did not expect it to be this good... Story The game takes place in a surreal, painterly fantasy world, where art, architecture, and technology mix together in an elegant and dreamlike way. But as beautiful as the world is, it comes at a steep price. Society is built around a single horrifying phenomenon: a mysterious being called the Paintress. Each year, the Paintress paints a number onto a distant monolith. When that happens, every person of that exact age instantly disappears turning into a cloud of flower pedals. Because of this, humanity lives with a constant sense of countdown and inevitability of when their deaths will happen. Families know the year their loved ones will disappear, and the world has reorganized itself around this grim cycle. To try to end the curse, the remaining cities send out Expeditions - groups of volunteers who journey across the dangerous lands toward the Paintress. But so far...none have succeeded. Expedition 33... The story follows Expedition 33, the newest team sent to attempt the impossible: find the Paintress and stop the cycle before their own time runs out. Members of the expedition know they may not return, but they still set out across a strange continent filled with ruined civilizations, bizarre creatures, and environments that feel like living paintings. On their travels they uncover fragments of past expeditions and clues about the deeper nature of the world and learn more about the fate of the expeditions that came before them. Gameplay It is a mix of talking to your fellow expeditioners, and learning more about each other, exploring big, semi open world levels. (I say semi open world, since there are different routes, but most level contain several routes you can follow that loop back on each other, which is by no means a bad thing!!!, quite the opposite) The different areas are connected via an overworld map, which you unlock more and more of, while you progress the story. When it comes to battle, Clair Obscur turns into a turned based battle mode which happens in the world, but can involve different number of enemies, from my experience it isn’t always just the ones you see. For each character you have different options, either attack normally to increase your AP (which is needed for stronger skills), use items or execute one of your many skills. Nearly every skill in this game different effects added to it, like for a simple example, cause a burn status effect on the enemy, while other party members have attacks that do more damage on enemies with this status effect. But of course, there are countless different combinations and possibilities to take into consideration when making your moves, which makes the battle system very intuitive but also adds a lot of complexity with time. Furthermore, another big part of the fights are the active dodging mechanic and quick time events for your skills. Many skills allow for increased damage, or extend buffs when you hit these. Once an enemy starts attack you, you have the option to either dodge the attack or parry it, which happens in real time, it can take a while to learn the right pattern for each attack, but once you figured it out and managed to actively counter or avoid the enemy attacks, it feels extremely satisfying! Graphic/Audio/Atmosphere Clair Obscur has probably the best and most creative level design I personally ever experienced. The amount of love, creativity and details flown into the look, feeling and environment, and animations to make the world be more alive is second to none. They went all out with the concept that this world I painted. Absolutely every area of this game is an absolute masterpiece, I can’t describe it in any other way. And oh my gosh...the soundtrack, to say it is stunning and beautiful is an understatement, each song is sung with so much passion and fits so perfectly all the time, sometimes you just stop, close your eyes and listen. Same can be said for the general sound design of the game, attacks, environment, character movement, etc...it just all fits perfectly and sounds amazing, they hasn’t been a single sound that I started to dislike, even when hearing it countless times...it is hard to call something like this perfect...but for this game, I would go that far. Tech The game is, from what I experienced of course, very well optimized, and mostly ran fluently, I had like 1 or 2 crashes in over 100 hours of gameplay, and I think even these are mostly because of my system. So no complains there. Final Thoughts Even if turned base combat isn’t your thing, I would argue Clair Obscur: Expedtion 33 is one of these very rare must-play games. The world, story, characters, creative ideas, world design and combat system mix so well together. Clair Obscur is one of the rare cases where a game will stay with you for a while, even after you watched the credits. One of the best gaming experiences I had in my entire life.

review_text: Alright. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is done and dusted. For me, this game mostly lived up to the hype, which is always nice to see. It had some incredibly intense holy -ish moments, some tear-soaked moments, and just some all-around crazy moments. Often all three crashed together, lol. The game itself is an interesting mix of open world and linear JRPG with a WRPG flair, FromSoft style Soulsborne concepts and UI, and The Last of Us 1/2 Influenced writing. The prologue itself gives you an inkling of the emotional roller coaster ride you are about to embark on. You play as Gustave who is about to watch as the woman he loves but had broken up with, is about to be Gomagged (erased). Which is this world's version of people dying when they're a certain age, on the day the Paintress reduces the number on the horizon by one. So, this year, everyone who is 34 dies when she changes the number to 33. Next year, it would be 32, and so on. So, you are given an emotionally heavy moment from the very beginning of the game, lol. To me, this prologue was equally intense compared to TLOU 1's prologue, and I can't think of another game that even comes close. The day after the Gommage each year, the people of Lumiere send an expedition to try and stop the Paintress. This is the 67th year they've done so. This expedition, Expedition 33, features Lumiere's bravest from the group of 33-year-olds who will of course be Gommaged next year anyway. So, Gustave and his friends, along with his 16-year-old ward, Maelle, set off on said expedition. When they finally land on the mainland, things get completely insane. You are treated to the first of many holy -ish moments right there. And then the prologue ends and you are properly in the game. With the impression the prologue leaves, you already know this game is going to be insane, and by and large, that holds true. I thought the writing was stellar most of the way through the game. And you know what I said about the Prologue being insane. That can't even match what happens at the end of Act One, lol. I was actually stunned by that transition and had to stop and reflect on it for a bit. Again, the Druckmann influence shows up in spades here. I actually was in disbelief of what had just happened, and I was impressed that Sandfall was gutsy enough to take the story there. Where I think there is a drop off in the writing is in the game's conclusion. It's not bad by any stretch of the imagination. Actually, it's quite good. But...I think it lost a bit of the seamless progression that the writing enjoyed prior to that, and kind of bogged down a bit. I kept thinking during Act Three that the pacing shifted a bit too much and dragged on more than I would have personally liked. It was important to have this conclusion and the two end story options, but the pacing definitely suffered for the final reveals and overall exposition. Memorable, but not on par with the rest of the game. In my opinion. Gameplay is a mix of overland open world travel; and linear exploration with a few branching paths to find secrets and items, when in specific areas. As you expand your list of companions, and their power grows, your ability to unlock more of the open world map really starts to show off the size of this world, which is reasonably large, with plenty of required AND plenty of optional areas to explore. I have 29 hours put into this game, but if you are thorough, you can easily get 70+ hours out of the game just based on exploration alone. The named areas in the game are mostly linear, as mentioned above. There is always a main path to follow with maybe a couple side path shortcuts included, and a degree of interconnectivity within each map that touches on the FromSoft formula of world building a bit. There will typically also be side paths that lead to secrets, be they items, past expedition logs, and even optional bosses. And some of those side paths actually lead to what are essentially full dungeons. So, it's not a bad idea to try and explore as much as you like. Scattered along the way in each area, you will find past Expedition flags. Those serve as traditional Soulsborne bonfires, where you will level up, learn new skills, rest and heal; and late game, they are also used to upgrade gear AND your party member's Lumina/Pictos, which is basically a set of innate combat skills/buffs that can be unlocked by spending Lumina points. Prior to gear upgrades and Lumina unlocking at the flags, there will be an NPC that shows up at your camps after a certain point in the story who will handle those two things for you. That NPC can also upgrade your flasks (basically the same system you find in Elden Ring, but with the addition of a resurrection flask as well). You can only camp on the overland map, but it is important as, in addition to upgrading your Lumina and weapons (and flasks), this is also where you will build relationships with your companions, get some more lore about the world, and a couple other camp options that will be unlocked as well. You also have a record player in camp and can enjoy any music you may have found in your travels already. Which, the soundtrack for this game is flat out stunning. Unquestionably one of the best OSTs to ever grace a video game. And since we're talking audio, everything was as good as it gets here. From the voice acting to the in-game sounds, the sounds in combat...all of it was top top tier. Sandfall put the industry on notice with the excellence of the audio in this game. And the exact same is true of the visuals. I defy you to play this game and not take several hundred screenshots. This game is literally THAT gorgeous. This was an amazing job the artists for Sandfall did here. Again, they pretty much put the gaming industry on notice with this one. Sandfall talks about the reactive turn-based combat system on the product page. This was a pretty innovative system IMO. It is standard JRPG shootout style, BUT...it features attack and defense QTE's and an action point system. The QTEs mirror the type of combat options you directly get in Soulsborne games. Dodging, parrying, jumping, timing your attacks properly, and so on. It's a little jarring seeing those systems implemented in a turn-based game, but it definitely works. That said, I didn't love the attack part of this. Which Sandfall clearly understood would be a sticking point for a lot of gamers. So, there is an option to disable the attack QTEs. Which I did. You can't disable the defense QTEs, however, and actually as I played, I really started to understand why. The dodging and parrying (and jumping) is integral to other mechanics baked into combat. So, you will just have to learn enemy movements and windups and do your best to get your timing down. Which wasn't really so difficult IMO. You won't always be right, but it's incredibly satisfying when you get that chain of parries, and doing so gives you enough action points to pull off one of your epic nine-point abilities. This was a pretty robust and fun system. Obviously, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is a must play. And it's definitely priced fairly for the amount of content there is in the game, not to mention the absolutely industry breaking sound and art design. Is it flawless? No. And in reality, I was exhausted by the end. But I'll also remember this game and think back upon it often. review_text: I've played a lot of games that deal with loss. Most of them tell you about it. This one makes you feel it in your chest. MAJOR SPOILERS WARNING On the surface it looks like a gorgeous game about stopping an apocalypse. But underneath that it's a story about a mother who couldn't let go of her dead son, a father destroying an entire world to save his wife from herself, and a daughter caught between two lives wondering which one is actually hers. Nobody here is a villain. Everyone is just broken in their own way and trying to survive it. Then there's Verso. A painted copy of a dead boy, fully aware that he is not real. He never asked to exist. He just woke up one day inside someone else's pain and had to figure out what to do with that. He spends decades watching people die, loses the person he loved, grows tired of everything, and eventually decides the kindest thing he can do is end it all. Not out of hatred. Out of pure exhaustion. And his own mother, when she finally sees him, looks him in the eyes and says: you are not my Verso. After a century of feeling and losing and carrying all of it. Still just a copy. And somewhere in the canvas a faceless little boy wanders alone, painting endlessly, keeping the whole world alive. Everyone made decisions around him, about him, for him. The only one who ever bothered to ask what he wanted was Verso himself. The game never lets you feel comfortable. It builds people you care about and then asks you to decide their fate. Do you save a painted world full of people who laugh, love and die just like anyone else? Or do you free a soul that has been trapped inside it since the day he died? Neither answer is clean. The game doesn't pretend otherwise. Life keeps forcing cruel choices. No other game has made me feel the weight of that sentence the way this one did. See things as they are, not how you want them to be.

review_text: Tl;dr: Very few games have moved me so much that they've left me feeling empty once finished. This is certainly one of them. If you enjoy RPGs, give this game a chance. Even just on story mode, it's absolutely worth it. As a fan of RPGs, I can say that Expedition 33 is incredible and I wasn't expecting it at all. Turn-based games are usually hit or miss for me, but this one was so good that it kept me hooked. If I had a list of boxes to check for every aspect of the game, I think E33 would tick a lot of them. From the very beginning, the game hits hard with its Prologue, which is just a glimpse of the emotional journey ahead. The world is beautiful to explore and the story is incredibly well-written from start to finish. The osts are so good that I want to buy the soundtrack album asap. I was also happy to learn that their composer was found randomly on SoundCloud, what a nice thing to happen. I never expected to enjoy the turn-based combat here this much, but the parries and dodges make it feel fresh and dynamic. I really like that you can adjust the difficulty at any point in the game, it's a nice touch. Personally, I chose to play on Expert from start to finish. The extra challenge added weight and meaning to every encounter, effectively turning it into a Souls-like experience. I get that this level of challenge isn't for everyone, but honestly I believe that the game has a lot to offer even if you don't want to play this way. Even if this game had zero combat and was just a graphic adventure, I would have loved it just as much. I believe that E33 is so special that it will become a landmark title: it's an ambitious project from a dev team that started without knowing how to create a game, yet I could feel every bit of the passion and dedication they poured into creating it. Against all odds, they delivered a masterpiece. "For those who come after, right?"

review_text: I genuinely believe that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of the greatest video games ever created. Not one of the best RPGs. Not one of the best games of this generation. A huge piece of art. A triumph of creativity and passion. If video games have a Mona Lisa, this belongs in the same gallery. No bugs. No filler. No wasted moments. No compromises. Just perfection. Years from now people will look back at Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 as one of those rare landmark titles that defined an era and demonstrated exactly what this medium is capable of becoming. A masterpiece. 10/10 doesn't do it justice.

review_text: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 | Perfect Game Review (100% Completion at 62.1 Hours) With Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 absolutely cleaning up at the Game Awards and invading my social media feed, I figured I’d finally see what all the fuss was about. Fast-forward to the credits, and I’d spent the entire game whispering “this is absolute cinema” at my screen like I was personally responsible for the standing ovation. Gameplay: As a fan of both genres, combining souls-like mechanics with turn-based combat was a real treat. The huge range of builds and smaller playable cast let me experiment without feeling overwhelmed. But if we’re being honest, about 95% of my squad decisions were just Maelle and Lune taking turns carrying the team. ★★★ Graphics: The character designs are fantastic, the cinematics are peak, and every area across the continent is ridiculously detailed. I genuinely didn’t mind getting lost without a map because there was always something gorgeous to stumble across. Even that creepy face-mask island looked incredible... although I’d happily get lost somewhere else next time. ★★★ Sound: I have far too many tracks permanently stuck in my head to give this anything less than a perfect score. Even the water level theme was an absolute banger. Now, I may not understand French, but that hasn’t stopped me from sneaking songs into my playlists and telling my family it’s just French pop music. ★★★ Story: I knew this was going to be top tier when I got emotionally attached to the characters within the first 30 minutes. Packed with twists, humour, heart, and plenty of emotional damage, the story keeps you invested from start to finish. The characters are bursting with personality, while the cinematics and storytelling are on another level. There were moments I wasn’t even sure if I was playing a game or watching a really good movie. ★★★ Replayability: With multiple builds, challenging encounters, collectibles, and a substantial post-game, there are plenty of reasons to return. And once you’ve finished everything, there’s also New Game+ for those who apparently haven’t suffered enough yet. ★★★☆ Final Thoughts: Expedition 33 combines stunning visuals, phenomenal music, satisfying combat, and an unforgettable story into one hell of an RPG. It takes familiar ideas and somehow makes them feel fresh. It is also one of the few games I’d genuinely pay to have my memory wiped just so I could experience it all over again. ★★★ Overall Rating: 10/10, the Game Awards had me curious, the 9,999 emotional damage had me convinced.

review_text: Without a doubt a game of the year contender and honestly a winner. What Sandfall Interactive created here is an absolute masterpiece. I never played turn based action games before and this was a perfect introduction. I would highly recommend it to anyone who wants to get into turn based action or turn based JRPG style games. It feels welcoming but still deep and rewarding. The visuals are stunning. Face capture animations feel incredibly real and expressive. After watching some behind the scenes videos it is honestly insane how much work went into body language and facial mimics. Areas like Lumiere and the Forgotten Battlefield look breathtaking and make the world feel heavy, alive and meaningful. The art direction deserves special praise because every location feels hand crafted with a clear emotional tone rather than just being pretty. Performance was smooth for me and the UI is clean and readable without breaking immersion. The music is a masterpiece on its own. I constantly paused the game just to listen to the beautiful menu soundtrack. My favorite tracks are Gustave theme, The Departure and the absolutely goated Monoco theme. The soundtrack elevates every emotional moment and stays with you long after you stop playing. Gameplay wise the game does a great job. Some mechanics do get repetitive and certain broken builds can make the game feel repetitive in terms of moves and animations. Seeing the same animations over and over can get a bit stale. That said the dodge and parry mechanics combined with the aim system add enough engagement to keep combat exciting. Enemy variety is fantastic with so many unique movesets to learn and overcome. Simon stands as the pinnacle of everything the game teaches you throughout its length and is an unforgettable challenge. Story wise this is straight up peak fiction and it leaves you wanting more. I got deeply invested in the world of Expedition 33 and tears were definitely not rare while playing. The game celebrates victories and mourns losses in a very human way. If I learned anything from this journey it is the importance of caring for those who come after us. I will not spoil the story or its twists but witnessing it all made me rethink what makes a person real, what it means to be alive and what consciousness truly is. The more I write the more memories come back and the more I want to say, but out of respect for the story I will stop here. My absolute favorite characters are Sciel and Gustave. Sciel really clicked with me and offered a powerful perspective on death and the afterlife that will probably stay with me for a lifetime. If there is an afterlife then I will see everyone after death. And if there is not I will simply join them in death. I will be with them either way. Gustave on the other hand teaches the importance of caring for others and working on yourself so you can help people in the long run. Campsite interactions are a brilliant feature that truly helps you connect with the characters and understand their motivations. I am genuinely grateful that I got to experience these characters and their stories. All in all this game is an emotional rollercoaster that deserves to be played. It is without a doubt a game of the year winner for me(2025). I heavily recommend it even if you are not a turn based enjoyer. Buy it at full price and you will not regret a cent, at least I did not. Or wait for a sale, either way you win and gain an unforgettable memory. Tomorrow Comes.

review_text: I just finished the game. Honestly, it’s clear GOTY material: the narrative and its cast are beautifully crafted, the world-building and visual design are stunning, and the soundtrack -what can I say- pure cinema. If you’re searching for an experience like that, I wholeheartedly recommend it. That said, I did run into a few drawbacks. For starters, the battle system isn’t for everyone. It blends traditional turn-based mechanics with parry elements similar to those found in Soulslikes. It feels satisfying and fresh at first, but over time it starts to feel monotonous, so that’s something to keep in mind. Additionally, while the first two acts are engaging (particularly the second) the third chapter loses some momentum. The encounters grow predictable, enemies lack move-set diversity, and the endgame introduces optional bosses that can be overwhelming without proper preparation. All of this makes the final stretch feel drawn out and draining. By the closing hours, I even lowered the difficulty because I was having trouble mustering the drive to see it through. Even so, the plot remains deeply impactful and encourages meaningful reflection on life’s purpose and the value of learning to let go. In short, it’s an outstanding title and it undoubtedly deserved to win GOTY 2025 though it won’t resonate with everyone. You need to connect with its atmosphere to truly appreciate it. 8/10

review_text: I expected this game to be good, especially considering how many awards it has won, but it still managed to exceed all my expectations. What started as curiosity quickly turned into one of the most memorable experiences I’ve had in a long time. Graphics Absolutely stunning. The lighting, environmental design, effects, textures, and animations all come together beautifully. The level design, in particular, sometimes pleasantly reminded me of Alice: Madness Returns, with creative layouts and visually striking areas. Every location feels carefully crafted and visually unique, and I spent a ton of time in photo mode capturing the world from different angles. Audio One of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard in a video game. My personal top tracks: Aria pour un Masque de Colère Lumière The Reacher – Orphelin Sound design is also top-notch; everything feels crisp and impactful. Gameplay Very good. Each character has a unique combat style, which really reinforces their personality. The gameplay feels like it has two layers. On one hand, you can build a powerful setup and dominate enemies. On the other hand, even without optimal builds, you can rely on skill, dodging or parrying with good timing to win fights. I really loved how they implemented it. Despite the large number of battles, combat never got boring throughout the entire game. Story Hard to talk about without spoilers. All I’ll say is that it’s unique, engaging, and memorable. The main characters are charismatic, each with their own personality, motivations, and backstories, and they act in believable ways. The ending leaves a strong impression. Cons Lumina progression system I didn’t really like how Luminas are leveled. You need to use a newly obtained Lumina in several battles before it becomes permanently available. This makes build-crafting awkward because you constantly have to swap them in just to level them up. It would feel much better if they could be upgraded using Chroma instead. Too many Luminas / balance issues By the end of the game, there are just too many Luminas. They become hard to manage and, more importantly, they break the balance. Characters become extremely overpowered, to the point where story bosses, which are supposed to be important and strong, feel easier than early-game enemies when you had almost nothing. Meanwhile, the “hardcore” bosses in the Endless Tower feel less like a fair challenge and more like a clunky way to counter overpowered builds. World map navigation Not very convenient, and could be better. A minimap or markers would help a lot. Final Thoughts These minor flaws didn’t stop me from enjoying the game at all. Most of the time, I didn’t even think about them — I was too engaged in the story, combat, exploration, and the beautiful world. For me, this is a solid 10/10 and one of the best games I’ve ever played.

review_text: This game is a masterpiece. I have been on Steam for 16 years and I have never written a review, but I feel compelled to say SOMETHING about this game. It just excels everywhere: story, gameplay, level design, music, art, sound design, graphics... on every single metric, this game is outstanding. There is no room for improvement. Back in the early 2000s, people used to debate about whether video games can be art. This game is art. It is a piece of art that will make you think and feel things, all while being one of the most fun experiences you will have in a modern game. Show anyone this game, and you are showing them a masterpiece. I don't like to throw around phrases like "best game ever made" or "one of the best games ever," because you're comparing apples and oranges when it comes to different games (like, how could I possibly compare this with a game like The Last Of Us? It stands on its own alongside the rest of the best games you've ever played. 10/10 perfect, no room for improvement.

review_text: Sandfall Interactive has created one of the most artful and inspired games in years with E33, which is peak irony considering this studio is made up of former Ubisoft devs. It shows just how much corporate money men and playing it safe can stifle creative expression and freedom, as when set free to create this is the kind of masterpiece Ubisoft developers can create when unleashed. I do think this is one of the few games of each generation that is a must play, from the music to the artistic styling, this game is a beautiful experience that feels fresh in a sea of generic and safe AAA and even AA products. This is high praise from me, someone who doesn’t really enjoy turn based combat (outside of deck builders). At least you have dodging, parries and QTE interactions (that I admit I lazily chose the auto option for), along with an absolutely massive selection of potential builds to keep the combat feeling interactive and varied. By the end I had so many ‘Pictos’ (abilities) mastered the build potential was overwhelming – perfectly set up for a future play-through. Though after a 100% play-through, I likely never will do NG+, for reasons mentioned later. Overall I quite enjoyed the story, it has everything from highly emotionally charged moments, to humour to anger inducing desires to see revenge carried out. Though I do think it falls off a bit in the later parts and after the main story it is mostly nonsense, to be honest. I really have to give credit to both the music and artistic styling in this game, it really is stunning and I enjoyed every aspect of these. It again highlights how talented devs are so often creatively stifled when in big companies like Ubisoft, but can produce incredible content when they are allowed the creative freedom to do so. On the downside, many of the enemies feel repeated and some are pretty much all the way through the game. If you dislike the combat, you’re going to be really drained by the end of the game. I chose to get 100% on this game (special thanks to Optinoob on YT for his guides!) and honestly by the end I was so over it I was literally avoiding combat unless absolutely necessary. That being said, if you absolutely loved the main campaign, then you’re getting an absolute bargain with the huge number of optional areas and bosses to fight. I have to be clear, my fatigue was result of going for 100% achievements and most people will never feel this way just playing the main story part of the game. I would recommend the main campaign to anyone and everyone, if you love gaming and appreciate artistic styling with very quirky music accompanying the journey, you will love this and again I do think this is one of those rare ‘must play’ games.

review_text: I bought this game to cope with the fact that I will lose a parent within the next couple of months. review_text: I literally had no idea about this game last year when it released. I just thought it would be a random turn-based game from unknown developers. There was little to no hype for this game, as it wasn’t one of those AAA IPs we are already familiar with. But then came The Game Awards 2025—this game got nominated for Game of the Year. I was shocked, as it was competing with some of the greatest games released that year, like KCD 2, Hades 2, as well as Silksong. But when the day came, it literally swept almost every award, and the next month it overtook Elden Ring to become the most awarded game of all time. My mind was completely blown away by the success of this unfamiliar title, so I decided to give it a try through Game Pass. First of all, if you are planning to buy this game, play it for free on Game Pass first to get a basic idea of what it’s all about, because it’s not for everyone. Many people may find its real-time turn-based combat boring and repetitive (which is not true in my case). I played Pokémon games for years, and this was a huge upgrade for me, as now we are parrying and dodging enemy attacks rather than just taking them. I never found this game’s combat boring; it always felt fresh to me. Getting new pictos, trying new skills, and making different builds for characters were engaging. This game has so much content—even after finishing the main story, there are many locations, side bosses, and mysteries left to explore. That’s why I purchased this game on Steam even after finishing the main story on Game Pass. And then comes its music—"OH MY GOD." Every soundtrack in this game is GOATed. Literally, when I opened this game for the very first time, I just sat watching the main screen, listening to its music. From there, I knew it was going to be one of the best games I have ever played, because I absolutely love listening to video game soundtracks. I didn’t understand a single word from it, but the feelings it gave to my ♥♥♥ ears were incredible. It’s also shocking that such great soundtracks were composed by an unknown artist hired from SoundCloud. Sometimes I just hum the music of this game when doing nothing. For the story and characters (NO SPOILERS), it’s the same as the music—"PEAK." I don’t remember the last time I had tears in my eyes while playing a game, and that too within the first hour. There are some games that start off slow and rough but make sense in the end; this game, on the other hand, literally hooked me from start to finish. No fillers—just absolute cinema moments every time. You are not playing this game but living in it. And OMG, the cast—Ben Starr, Jennifer English, Charlie Cox, and Andy Serkis—such a packed lineup. You already knew this was going to be peak. The emotions I felt for them—their fear, joy, and sadness—touched my heart, and I will never forget the beautiful experience this game gave me through its story and characters. This is the pinnacle of storytelling in this form of media. If you play this game in the future, just don’t rush through the story. Always engage in character conversations and optional cutscenes. Even if you completely move on from this game, its story and characters will stay with you forever in your heart. Now, the gameplay, as mentioned earlier, will not satisfy everyone. But if you have played turn-based games in the past, this game is definitely for you. The Lumina system is excellent—you can stack different abilities and effects to create an OP build. After all the positives I mentioned earlier, the only weakness I feel this game has is that by using the Picto and Lumina systems, the difficulty can feel weak. You become so strong that you can easily beat the main story without even dying. However, the post-main-story content gets a bit harder, and that difficulty spike compensates for the earlier limitation. All I can say is: don’t look for guides—they can ruin your experience. As this game is made in Unreal Engine 5, it looks visually beautiful, but it can be demanding in terms of hardware. Still, it is optimized—no bugs, glitches, or performance issues. Everything is fine. I can’t believe this was their first game, and they delivered one of the masterpieces of this generation. Now I hope the developers can maintain this level of quality with their future releases. Final Verdict— This game is easily in my top three of all time, second only to Elden Ring. The experience it gave me will forever remain in my heart. I wish I could erase my memories of this game so that I could feel those emotions again for the first time. After playing this game, I now understand why it won nine awards at TGA—it completely outshined its competition. Even if you don’t like the gameplay, play it for the story. It is what everybody says—"Absolute Cinema." It’s one of those games you should play before dying. As a wise man once said: "FOR THOSE WHO COME AFTER"

review_text: This game is an incredible JRPG experience with so much heart and soul, so much polish, it puts the entire triple A gaming industry to shame. Clair Obsecur sculpts its lore around the most core of human emotions. It is a story about the meaning of stories, it is art about the power of art. it is an experience that demands we collectively return to it again and again, not for entertainment, but because it is a story about grief. And our need for art about grief will never disappear. And with grief at it's center, the narrative introduces so many concepts whilst still managing to keep them so meaningful. It grounds them in people and in metaphor, bringing them to life on your screen. Its remarkable writing adds a sense of beautiful sensitivity, delicateness and humanity to the characters and their personality. It creates a world so big in its scale of breadth and imagination, yet so small in its emotions and experience. And it does it all without ever losing balance. The combat is so satisfying, it revolutionizes the turn-based system, polishing its fundamentals and adds upon it in ways that modernizes the experience. The open world is so thoughtfully constructed, it's directed enough that you always know where you should go and yet open enough that exploration still results in a delightfully earned sense of power fantasy. The Environmental story telling is similarly phenomenal. Every detail gives you a clue into the world and it's history/stories. It rewards you for paying attention and makes your surroundings come alive as you traverse through them. This game should not exist. It is a project that accomplishes so much with so little. It is an outlier. A droplet of innovation in a sea of soulless corporate mediocrity. Its existence is a contradiction to the industry giants that have long replaced art in video games with corperate greed. This game, by all definitions of the word, is art. But even art can never be perfect. The combat balance tends to be weak at times. The item descriptions tend to be vague and unclear. There's a lack of quality of life features to help streamline navigation and exploration. The level design feels more like a maze then organic terrain. It's these small details that add up to make a big difference in the overall experience of this game. It is what stops Clair obscur from living up to it's immeasurable praise. And while it's far from a true flawless masterpiece, it's short coming does not come anywhere near enough to take away from its accomplishments. This game is a rare achievement. It’s ambitious, heartfelt, and unforgettable. And despite its rough edges, its creativity, storytelling, and soul more than makes up for it. That's why I highly recommend this game. 9/10

review_text: I shudder at the knowledge that it took me this long to get around and play this game. I had it on my radar, of course, but at the sudden announcement of FF7 Rebirth, I caved. And this game has spent the last 60+ hours making me regret that decision. Multiple times. A blank canvas Sandfall Interactive is a relatively small studio, and while some work has been offloaded to external companies, it's impressive that such a small team was able to accomplish so much. The story behind the team is nothing short of inspiring. From a single person leaving Ubisoft chasing a passion project and opening a new studio, to the process of hiring the talent from social media and Reddit posts, and lastly obtaining funding, it's genuinely a level of dedication you don't see often. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 (E33) is their first title, and, my God: what an opener. I won't get too much into the story, as I believe anything I say might ruin the - and I'm mincing my words - masterfully crafted narrative, but I can say the writing has been up there with some of the best work I've had the pleasure to experience. I have always been on the edge of my seat, while having a laugh, as the game doesn't always take itself so seriously, abeit it is, being unequivocally French in themes and humor. A story this captivating isn't something that often happens, and while E33 does not reinvent the wheel, the wheel is perfect as it is, and it's presented incredibly. The cast of characters, especially, are a standout. Well written, and with their own point of view, coherent for the entire runtime. I've loved the night camp mechanic straight out of Dragon Age Origins and the relationship tiers of Persona, which made me fall in love with them even more. A stellar cast, and an even more stellar performance from all of them. From afar, the game seems to be a turn-based game heavily influenced by the Persona series, especially in its UI, but when looking harder, the influence of other titles can be seen. For example, the timed attacks and dodging were a defining aspect of Mario and Luigi RPGs, and the addition of a parry Sekiroes up the experience, differentiating it from any other game in the genre I ever played, where I often end up somewhat distracted during the turns of the enemies, especially later in the game. The combat is genuinely addicting, and with the way the game is structured, I never found fighting a drag, but always something I engaged with as much as possible; although I must say the lack of a way to avoid low-level fights like in Metaphor Re-Fantazio, or the Persona series when unlocking the ability, was definitely felt. I especially enjoyed how different each character's skill set is, covering many roles for each of them, and yet allowing huge build variety. The amount of Pictos - abilities that can either be slotted when unknown, or equipped at a cost freely once mastered - is honestly overwhelming. Especially when considering that everything stacks cumulatively in the game, an aspect I don't believe many players, unless they interact with the endgame, ever come across. This goes to show even more how tailored to many different people the game is, from story-focused to hardcore endgame, there is something for everybody. Especially since additional content was released with the Thank You update. The art style of the game seems to have taken a page out of From Software's handbook, with each area looking straight out of a painting, and with a very strong design identity, making the more realistic presentation everything but bland. There are many ideas that stand out as fitting and clever; for example, the traversal of the world map happening in a pseudo-diorama of the world has to be my favorite. It really helps to feel the dimension of the continent, while providing character to something that usually has been just functional. Last but not least, the soundtrack is a magical 8h of composition. I am, weeks later from my completion of the game, still listening to. It establishes itself with some motifs that are then used during the entire game to communicate to the player, subconsciously, things that they are not aware of yet. A little bit like the Advent Children's musical cues and motifs when Sephiroth appears in the new FF7 Remakes; it hints at something that, if you know: you know. Additionally, carefully hiding the meaning of the game in many lyrics, behind not just the French language, but a cypher built from pseudo‐Latin phrasing, invented vocabulary, and layered symbolism designed to obscure the narrative, is the cherry on top. Unreal, despite Unreal The game has been developed using Unreal Engine 5, and while I appreciate that its existence is allowing small teams such as this to develop a title of this caliber that in the past we might have seen only from AAA studios like Naughty Dog, I must say it has to be its biggest flaw, while not being of the game in the first place. The thing is this. There aren't many options on the market, besides UE5 and Unity; the latter could never have delivered at this level. Indeed, there are other engines that can compete well with UE5. For example, Anvil by Ubisoft has implemented virtualized geometry, or Decima used by Kojima and Guerrilla, and the RE Engine - when Capcom optimizes their games. But all of them have one thing in common: they are non-licenseable. Could Sandfall have spent years making an engine? Sure, but that wasn't profitable for Konami with MGS:V, let alone a brand new studio. Therefore, UE5 is the pick, and while Sandfall tried their best to avoid many of the common issues like just-in-time shader compilation or traversal stutters, with it come many of the issues of the engine. Please bear in mind, I do not fault Sandfall for them, as these are present in all games made in the engine. Character motion, while well done, results in floaty and imprecise. Especially when turning, the characters lose no momentum whatsoever. Far from me to say that every engine should break the ankles of its characters like From Software does to establish contact with the ground, but even in the intro of E33 it's possible to see Gustave's feet are clipping in the slightly angled roofs; something that wasn't an issue in 2009 . Clutter around the map has very precise collisions, which, combined with the motion, often end up dead-stopping your momentum, for example, on a candle holder. Additionally, a lot of items have been made using virtualized geometry - nanite. For example, the stairs in some buildings or small decor, that, because of nanite collapse logic, end up looking more poligon-y than a PS2 game. There are not a lot of physics-enabled items, besides boxes, making the world of the game stunning to look at, yet not so interactive. Lighting is handled via Software Lumen, and somehow, in 2025, the abovementioned minor items are not being properly ambient occluded or shaded, leading to a lot of clutter that looks floating because they are not included in the simplified SDFs used for the lighting. All things considered, the cost of rendering versus the - stunning - end result, especially for a static world, is just bonkers. Especially when a simple option in the engine to rasterize all this real-time info would have solved it. And while I don't agree with many of his takes or tone, this video goes in depth about the rendering issues the game has, despite Sandfall's efforts. Varnished As a final note on the review, despite the engine limitations usually being a turn-off for me, the game exceeded my expectations and has become a magical experience that, honestly, I will think fondly of for a long time. I'm glad they were able to bring this to life, and I can't wait to see what they work on next. 10/10

review_text: Overall this is a great game, and if you can get it on sale it's definitely worth the money. At it's core this game is just like any other traditional RPG game with menu fighting. It's similar in that regard to games like Final Fantasy, or older games like Chrono Trigger. In the menu RPG category what this game does differently is add a lot of quick time events (QTE) and timed parry requirements to fights. A lot of people enjoy those menu fighting RPG games because of how relaxed they can be since they give you the ability to calmly fight and pay less attention to the screen. The QTE and parry requirements do make it so you are encouraged to stay focused and react quickly which can turn some people off. There is an easy mode where if you crank up your defense you can ignore a lot of things, but even on easy there are encounters and bosses you won't be able to do unless you can nail those timed parry events. The world and soundtrack are amazing. Many will find the story to be great, but others will find the story slowly gets worse over time and lackluster at the end. I found the story gave a lot of plot slowly in the beginning, then it was like all characters for the longest time refused to talk about anything story related with substance until it was nearly the end of the game. It dragged out the mystery so long that I personally lost interest, which made the ending a little more underwhelming. For me the best part of the game was the beginning, and then being allowed to explore such a beautiful world. I had fun taking my time exploring every area, killing every monster, and enjoying the beautiful sights. The people who made this game clearly did so with a passion. The soundtrack often matches perfectly with the vibe of the world. The character's facial expressions are animated wonderfully, and they are all impactful to have around. All my complaints are minor, and I still plan to go through the new game+ soon. Great game.

review_text: ⭐Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is a masterpiece.⭐ This game won 436 Game of the Year awards, making it one of the most awarded games in gaming history, and after finishing it, I completely understand why. I have played around 500 games in my life across many different genres. You can even see my complete game list on my profile. I have experienced so many different types of games, from action games to RPGs, adventure games, platformers and many more. I am also someone who pays a lot of attention to details in games. The atmosphere, the music, the world design, the characters, the gameplay systems, everything matters to me. Because of that, it is honestly very difficult for a game to completely surprise me and make me fall in love with it. But Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 did exactly that. I never expected a game to surpass some of my personal favorites like Assassin's Creed 2 or Life is Strange. Those games always had a special place for me. But this game changed everything. This is the best game I have ever played. I cried multiple times while playing this game. I even cried when it ended, not only because of the story, but simply because the journey was over. I was genuinely sad that this incredible experience had come to an end. I am still not ready to let go of this game. I will get all achievements and probably play through it again because I just cannot move on from this world yet. The music is absolutely incredible. It is so good that I actually listen to the soundtrack on Spotify in my free time. The gameplay is addictive, creative and something I never expected to enjoy this much. The funny thing is that I was extremely skeptical before playing this game. I never really got into JRPGs or turn based combat. I tried games with similar systems before, like Mario & Luigi and Paper Mario, but it was never really my favorite genre. I started this game with a lot of doubts. And then it immediately pulled me in. The story is so creative, complex and interesting. From the very beginning, I wanted to know more about this world and its mysteries. Even when I was still learning the controls and combat system, the game did an incredible job introducing everything naturally. The characters are written beautifully. The voice acting is amazing, and every character feels unique, understandable and memorable. The enemy designs are some of the most creative I have seen, the attacks are exciting, and the abilities are incredibly well animated. The whole progression system with Pictos, Lumina and the different builds is so creative. You are always thinking about your next combination, your next upgrade and how to make your team better. My biggest recommendation is to not look up guides for the strongest builds. Just experiment and create your own experience. The world design and graphics are also unbelievable. This is easily one of the most beautiful games I have ever seen. The environments, the atmosphere and the art direction are absolutely breathtaking. I took countless screenshots because I was constantly amazed by the world. The game also had almost no bugs for me, which is impressive. I could honestly talk about this game for hours. There is so much more I could say, but words are not enough to describe how special this experience was. I recommend this game to everyone. It does not matter if you usually like JRPGs, RPGs or even turn based combat. Give it a chance. This game is worth every single euro. Looking back, I would have easily paid 100€ for this experience. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is not just a game. It is a special experience that I will remember for a very long time. A true Game of the Year winner for a reason. I will never forget this experience 10/10⭐

review_text: I honestly feel like I am crazy for not enjoying this supposedly "game of the decade". I want to love this game, and I was sure I would, yet somehow this game managed to bore and disappoint me. I love story driven game. I love turn based RPG. I love parrying. But this game made me realize that just because the two things are good, doesn't make it a good idea to smush them together. It reminds me of that one Family Guy meme with Noah saying "What the hell is this?" to a child product of an elephant and a penguin. The long wind up of some of the attacks to bait your parry/dodge drove me crazy. It's almost impossible to tell what's the correct timing for them, unless you memorize each of these attacks. The lack of camera angle freedom means that some attacks does not telegraph well which "phase" it's in at all. Also your character is locked to one place, so that stripped away any decision making ability you can have in a normal dodge/parry fighting game and turned the whole system into a glorified QTE. Even if you decide to ignore the mechanic and just focus on the turn based strategy part, you still have to sit through this slow ass animation every turn. It's excruciating. Speaking of strategy, there is no strategy. I quickly realized this when I ran into a miniboss way over my level that can one shot my characters, but was able to win on the second or third try anyway thanks to well timed parries/dodges. What's the point of building for anything else if your characters are able to be impervious to all damage? Just optimize for big damage and git gud at dodging. Somehow they made the QTE the most powerful ability you can have in a turn based game. I am not against dodging but I'd rather take a 5% chance dodge/counter armor over this mechanic. That being said, the world is beautifully crafted. The story is intriguing - the prologue was a super strong opening. It even managed to make me re-examine and look back at my relationships with some of the people around me and that's really something. The music was haunting. But all that couldn't save this game from boring gameplay. Maybe I will revisit the game at a future time, but right now it's a pass from me.
