review_text: This review contains no direct spoilers. It's nearly impossible for me to say why I don't like E33's story while being vague, but I'll try. "I'm not angry, just disappointed." A quote from a character in E33 which happens to describe how I feel about the game. Giving a negative review to a game that many consider "life-changing" and a "masterpiece" will probably make me seem contrarian for the sake of it. However, given the direction the story went and some of the more atrocious dialogue, I think E33 earned it, which is a shame because I thought for sure I'd love it. If you're thinking about buying it, I'd say be at least a little skeptical of the hype and consider whether or not the dialogue, the game's final act, and the ending all being "bad" could ruin the game for you before you do. If you expect a journey from E33, you'll probably get one, but a journey is remembered less fondly when the destination turns out to be ♥♥♥. Starting with the obvious positives, E33 is extremely cinematic and well-presented, the environments are stunning, and the music is amazing. Given these things, it isn't hard to see why someone would call E33 a genuine masterpiece. That said, I think this game deserves more criticism than it gets, particularly story/writing-wise. The boss Sirene feels like an unintentional representation of the game itself and how people feel about it (iykyk), and given the praise this game gets, I've had to ask myself whether or not I played the same one as everyone else. The gameplay of E33 should technically also be a positive since I do like it, but I do have to critique it a bit. Combat has a central focus on parries. This in mind, you'd think parrying would be rewarding, but it really isn't. If you parry all 7 hits of a combo string, what do you get besides AP you can easily get anyway? You get a single counter. And if you miss a single one of your parries, you are denied this small luxury. And because Elden Ring and its consequences have been a complete disaster for the human race, the developers looked at that game and really admired how many obnoxiously delayed attacks were in it and copied some homework. Have fun waiting a full 5 seconds for that one attack to land only for it to come out instantly on the 6th second. So while I like the combat on paper, and most of the time in practice, it does walk a line between being satisfying and being annoying. The dialogue in this game is usually good/fine, but weighed down by Marvel-esque quips and forced humor. You'll eventually hear characters use modern speech patterns and slang (I ♥♥♥ you not one of the characters says "Bromantic" + another moment where someone says "So which one is it?" only for another character to respond "Yes" in that funny internet way) to be "funny" and "lighten the mood." It's like the writers were told "make these characters feel real" and then they decided "characters feeling real" must equal "talks like a modern day person," which definitely doesn't break the tone or take you out of the setting or anything. The multiple palm prints on my face are the result of humorous dialogue, I assure you. Humor has its place in a dark story and I don't dispute that fact. The problem with E33's "humor" is that it's so desperate to be funny that it constantly breaks the tone of the story and doesn't care that it does. It irked me to the point where I legitimately did begin to care less about the story/characters after one too many forced attempts at a laugh. Some of these moments land and feel like they have a place, but the vast majority don't. Hell, even a few of the expedition journals you can find about people who died are played off as jokes, and when you compare those journals to the intro of the game, you'll probably just narrow your eyes or cringe if anything. Now for the story, as spoiler-free as possible: You're introduced to the world with some good hooks, but sadly this game peaks at its intro and goes steadily downhill. Things are fine for a time until act 1's finale, during which some events take place seemingly just for cheap shock value (plus characters acting stupid for the sake of the plot) and fail to justify themselves any other way. Actually, it isn't even that shocking - odds are you'll be able to predict what happens long before it does, so it doesn't justify itself that way either. The events aren't "bad" in the moment, but looking back later in the game, you realize they happened for no reason other than to set the stage for a ♥♥♥ plot twist. In the context of where the game goes, act 1's finale is garbage. It feels like someone said "Hey wouldn't it be cool/funny/random/shocking if we did this at this moment in the game?" and everyone just unanimously decided to throw it in for how quirky of an idea it was. Act 2's finale is even worse and tries too hard to pull off an M Night Shyamalan twist to the point where it just feels super jarring and random. Think of the dumbest, most random plot twist a story can have and there's decent odds you just guessed THE major plot twist of E33, or close enough to it that I wouldn't be able to say you were wrong. Act 2's finale pulls the rug out from under you so it can say "Ha, gotcha!", then takes the story in a bizarre direction and proceeds to hide behind annoyingly contrived twists. And despite the fact that these events are the storytelling equivalent of upending a set table for fun, you're still expected to care about what happens next and participate in like 60 hours of sidequest hell to provide explanation as to what the ♥♥♥ you just witnessed and learn more about things you have no reason (and/or no longer have reason) to care about. Lmao no - I rushed the final boss because I was that out of ♥♥♥ to give. E33 was so focused on painting a plot twist that it didn't care whether or not what it painted made sense. The start of act 2 and onwards feels like it was taken from a separate game idea and inserted clumsily into this one, with no regard given to whether or not it'd fit with the rest of the game, and all regard given to how unlikely it'd be for someone to guess the plot twist(s), which is obviously stupid writing that is doomed to sabotage any story and E33 is no exception. Given the previous points, my capacity to care about the rest of the story was already getting low, but I pressed onward hoping I'd see that life-changing masterpiece everyone talked about on the 25th hour or so only to run into act 2's finale and the game's ending(s) and encounter two middle fingers from the story as my reward. I wish my $40 a happy Gommage. Act 2's finale punishes you for caring, and so do the endings, both of which are bad, but one of which is "moral"/"good" by the game's standards. That ending finishes what act 2's finale starts. To continue my "set table" analogy at risk of spoilers: It lights the upended table on fire because you were too attached to it and it wasn't a "real" table anyway. The other ending is resetting the table but putting mannequins in all the seats. Both defeat the purpose of having a table. With how often you hear "for those who come after" in act 1, you'd think the story would continue that theme, but nope, it just shreds that in favor of a dumb plot twist that makes it ring hollow. The messages of the final act should flow well with the messages of the first but they're conveyed in the form of such convoluted twists that it feels more like the final act overwrites the first and doesn't pay off the story's hooks in a satisfying manner, destroying all intrigue, and rendering previous stakes and tension pointless. And that is the most I can say spoiler-free. Everything else about the game is so well-presented, but the story and some of the dialogue are the exact opposite. I guess you could say that's a very "Clair Obscur" contrast.

review_text: A game that makes nearly everything right and somehow still fails. for me I went into this game with optimistic expectations. I like turn-based games such as Divinity and Baldur’s Gate, so the turn-based combat looked promising. I also loved HiFi Rush and Sekiro, so the QTE dodge and counter system sounded like a good addition. Unfortunately, it was not. The constant flux between slow motion and normal speed during attack animations was annoying, and most animations are very hard to dodge based on telegraphing alone. As a result, it feels more like a rhythm game without music to follow the rhythm. Throughout the entire playthrough, I never once entered a flow state. Not a single boss fight made me feel hyped in the way Sekiro did against Genichiro. The rush when you perfectly deflect every strike of Floating Passage or the epic moments in Metal Gear Rising. Simply put: the combat was not fun at any point in the game. The story is very cunning in how it plays with your emotions by making you experience the same feelings as the protagonist. It can be deeply upsetting (All of Act III) but that is clearly the intention. So while it made me angry, it is actually a positive. Well played, writers. The dialogue is, for the most part, very high quality and often genuinely funny. Good Humor is rare this days. There is also the typical video game contradiction of “Hurry up!” while the game simultaneously says, “No worries, just explore and grind levels.” The story constantly implies hard time pressure, but mechanically there is none. This happens quite often? Which always pulled me out of the experience it wanted to give me. Visually, the game looks impressive...when there is no clipping. Unfortunately, the game has a a big clipping problem, even during cutscenes. Gustave and the legendary Flying flower The music is very good on its own, but many of the “fun” tracks lose a lot of momentum midway through, shifting into slow jazz or even sad classical vibes. This feels very strange? But "epic" "sad" and "serious" tracks are awesome. The tutorials are bad: large popup text walls after popup text walls. This was fine for me. I am the dude who reads board game rulebooks and teaches them at the table, and most of the game systems are close enough to other RPGs to feel familiar. But, someone not used to this type of game will likely have a rough time. Exploration is fun as long as there is no parkour. This game is not a platformer, and it shows. Every time it tests your platforming skills, it feels like someone poured sand into your controller. Overall, this game has a lot of great elements, which makes it even more frustrating that the most gameplay-heavy parts were the least fun.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of those rare works—part storybook, part symphony, part duel of wills. From the first step into its world, it’s clear the game has a painter’s hand behind it. The art, the music, the direction—everything feels crafted with the precision of someone who understands that style means nothing without substance. The story unfolds like a slow-burning folktale: tragic, strange, and full of humanity. Its pacing gives you room to breathe, to wander, to meet memorable faces—each one sketched with personality rather than clichés. I came into this as a Souls veteran expecting familiar rhythms, and instead met a combat system that challenged my muscle memory. At first I doubted it. Then it swallowed me whole. The turn-based combat is nothing like the genre’s usual autopilot; it demands presence. Parries require timing as sharp as a razor, and a perfect parry feels like striking a bell in a cathedral—clean, resonant, earned. Dodges exist not as panic buttons but as teachers, helping you learn each enemy’s cadence. Over time, the combat becomes meditative. In no-hit attempts, it borders on transcendence. You fall into a flow state where patience becomes your shield and emotional control your lifeline. This synchronicity between player and enemy is unlike anything I’ve felt in a turn-based system. It’s a combat language you learn, not a mechanic you exploit. Exploration carries the same duality: grounded and playful. You can roam freely as any of your party members—up to three—and the game lets you switch perspectives at will. One moment you’re behind your character in third-person; the next you’re hovering overhead in a perspective reminiscent of classic RPGs or World of Warcraft. It’s a small touch, but it breathes life into wandering. The RPG layer is surprisingly robust. Every character can be customized with outfits, hairstyles, weapon upgrades, and stat allocation. “Pictos” act as passive traits—tiny fragments of power that shift combat in clever ways—and choosing who gets what feels meaningful rather than obligatory. The game quietly encourages experimentation, offering multiple approaches to almost every encounter. Performance? Impeccable. On my setup (i7-13620H, RTX 4060 Laptop GPU, 32GB DDR5, 1.5TB NVMe), the game didn’t flinch. No stutters, no hitches, no excuses. In a year full of broken releases, this one arrived polished and confident. Here’s one nitpick: there’s no proper navigation or area map. Oddly enough, the absence of a good minimap or level overlay is that it forces you to pay attention to the streets, the architecture, the rhythm of each zone. Still, a few more environmental cues or subtle hints would’ve saved some backtracking. The compass is kind of useful and yes, there is a world map, but it's barely useful. So here’s the truth: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 doesn’t just entertain. It moves. It offers a story worth hearing, music worth remembering, characters worth caring about, and a combat system worth mastering. It delivers challenge without cruelty, beauty without pretension, and heart without melodrama. This isn’t simply a game; it’s an experience. A rare one. A memorable one. If you care about games that try something bold—and actually succeed—then don’t skip this. Every penny is justified. Make the purchase. Step into the painting. Let it echo in you when it’s over. And as for me—I'm currently on the quest of platinuming the game, because an experience like this deserves to be completed to its final stroke. Very well deserved and yes, it was an experience worth having! FOR THOSE WHO COME AFTER!!!

review_text: Great game, hands down. I heard a lot of praise for this game since the beginning so I always wanted to give it a try, glad I did now. All the animations were great and enemy attacks were telegraphed quite well so things didn't seem unfair most of the time. review_text: Context of the Review As someone who came into KCDII without playing the first game, I did not have any expectations beyond the media and user reviews. I also purchased it about 9 months after release, so I played a version built upon months of patches and DLC releases. Additionally, I played and finished the storyline of KCDII almost one year ago, so my memory is fuzzy. However, I stand by my opinion that KCDII is a fantastic game that I highly recommend to any fan of open-world RPGs. Narrative and Characters The narrative of KCDII delivers in spades. I possess no applicable knowledge of 15th-century European history, so much of the first act had an air of mystery as I navigated interpersonal relationships and alliances. The characters presented to you are ALIVE! From Hans Capon and your immediate circle to the smallest of side characters, the world is rich with characters of depth. Even the characters you grow to despise are only able to elicit this reaction because of how well they are written and performed. Despite the time since I played, I can still remember three specific characters off the top of my head who had me imagining how Henry was going to deliver their comeuppance. To emphasize the depth of story, two of these are side-plot characters! I would often walk away from quests feeling satisfied. Many plotlines and side characters, no matter how small, were impactful to my playing experience. RPG Elements The RPG elements of character progression may be the magnum opus of KCDII. Never in a video game have I genuinely felt so immersed in a character. In the beginning, without mentioning any plot points, you are a feeble, inept commoner without any notable skills. Alchemy is a new domain to you, social situations are a minefield, and you'd best forget about posing any kind of threat in combat. However, at the same pace you as a player learn and develop your skills in the gameplay mechanics of KCDII, Henry also learns and develops his own ability. While it can be boiled down on paper to "do X thing Y times to unlock Z ability," this was not my perception of the gameplay progression. Perhaps others can articulate my experience better than I can, but I truly felt rewarded for my efforts to get better at the game, and it seemed deliberately built as a shared journey between me and Henry. Combat Combat is clunky, and I won't pretend otherwise. Early fights can feel awkward and punishing, and it takes time before anything clicks. But learning it is genuinely satisfying. Unlike most RPGs, where you eventually out-level your enemies until fights become trivial, KCDII made me feel like I won because I'd actually gotten better at fighting. By the late game, I felt like I had mastered the combat myself, and that sense of earned skill is something few games deliver. The DLC Issue - A Personal Gripe with RPGs in General No spoilers version Many aging RPG titles suffer from blending DLC perks (typically equipment) and storylines into a world, story, and character/equipment progression that were designed without them. Low-level characters have OP equipment and storylines make less sense because of conflicts between the base-game narrative and expansion storylines. I wish there had been a way to toggle the introduction of certain DLCs to later points in the game, or to have them locked behind a small gate of accomplishment to better introduce them. KCDII does this to some extent, but not enough. Of course, a player can choose not to use the OP crossbow and armor that inexplicably found their way into my chest, but the intentional choice to not use it is more immersion-breaking and distracting than if it had been introduced in a way more in line with the rest of the game. Spoilers for mid to late game and Legacy of the Forge I cannot remember exact specifics, but I really feel like the final act of the game was worsened by the existence of the Legacy of the Forge expansion, or at least its prominence. At the same time that you are an outlaw in the land with powerful figures wanting your head, you are an established, well-known blacksmith in Kuttenberg. I mean, I quite literally killed dozens of men defending the Jewish Quarter and had been ousted from town, but then I just waltz back in the front door of the city and go about my blacksmithing trade. I also made copious amounts of money from selling my works, and even fixed the clock tower, but when I return to the main story I am an underground vagabond plotting the heist of the century. Had I known how it would influence the game by giving me a home base in town, and how it would break my immersion in the story, I would have chosen to not pursue its questline as early as I did. Verdict My DLC complaints are minor next to everything KCDII gets right. It has memorable, well-written characters, a story that kept me invested down to its side quests, and a progression system, combat included, that made me feel like I was growing alongside Henry. If you enjoy open-world RPGs, it's well worth your time, even if you've never touched the first game.

review_text: I have a deep love hate relationship with this game. I have never completed a game and felt such complex emotions. It is one of the most rewarding, realistic, and incredible games I have ever played. At the same time, it is one of the most difficult, frustrating, and overwhelming games I have ever played by far. The ability to save is few and far between and the devs make it much more difficult than it needs to be which does take away from the joy and fun of the game. I am extremely disappointed by the unnecessary amount of violence towards dogs in the game. It does not impact the story, has no point, and should not be in the story at all. It took away from the beauty of the game for me and the enjoyment I got out of it. It was not needed and I hope whoever added those moments into the story does not have animals of their own. There is clearly something very wrong with them. Overall, the story was rich and incredibly detailed. It was inspiring and breathtaking. Graphics are great and the intelligence of the NPC's is scary good. They are highly intelligent and observant. Some of the best NPC's I have ever seen. Very similar to RDR2 in that way. I loved Mutt and what he brought to the experience, it would not have been as good as it was without him. Not even close. It was so cool to have a partner in crime. I loved the depth of the lore and the tedious process of building your character. My favorite part of the game was stealth and stealing. Every chance I got, I would have fun with sneaking around, stealing stuff, and seeing how much money I could get for it. I really enjoyed outsmarting the NPC‘s and seeing how much I could get away with. I absolutely loved the challenge of figuring out people’s schedules and how to get in and out of houses or businesses and how to navigate that entire process. It never got boring for me. The game is extremely detailed, very difficult, and at times mind numbingly frustrating. I have never been so frustrated playing a game in my entire life. You truly have to grind and survive in every sense. Nothing will come easy. You will die more times than you ever have in any game you have ever played. You will feel like an idiot. Constantly. It will test your patience and you will have to google A LOT to figure out what is going on, where you are supposed to go, and what you are supposed to do. The devs do not explain much and I think that is another unfortunate issue with this game. If i did not look up all that I did, I would have missed a tremendous amount of story telling and I truly do not think I would have completed the game. It was that hard. I have never not completed a game. I have been gaming for 25 years. Every genre you can think of, I have played it. This game almost broke me. There are so many mission that leave you very stuck, confused, overwhelmed, and frustrated with little to no guidance. Combat is a nightmare. It is the hardest combat I have ever encountered. I never really got better lol. I just some how got by (or lucky). I think there is a fine line between overwhelming the player to the point that they do not want to go back to the game and creating a challenging game that is enjoyable. Not going to lie, when the main story was over, I was relieved. Sad that the story ended, but glad that the grind was over. I don't like feeling that way at the end of a game. I want to be left wanting more. I hope this is something they work on in the future for KCD3. The entire game should not be an extreme grind. The point of playing a game is to escape and have FUN. I hope the devs keep that in mind and listen to the many players that feel the same way I do. I love this game and I hate this game. I am glad I played it because it did help me through a difficult time in my life. I put nearly 200 hours into this game and I still have a few more quests to do after finishing the main story. This game will always have a special place in my heart and I am glad I played it. The characters are wonderful and the story telling was epic. It truly pulls you in and takes hold of you. There is nothing quite like it.

review_text: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a direct sequel to the original game, taking place shortly after the events of the first game. You once again play as Henry of Skalitz, and you are sent by your lord as an envoy/diplomat to deliver a very important letter to a neighboring town. However, things don't go according to plan, and sh*t hits the fan really quickly. Story: The story is really compelling from start to finish and takes place across two different regions: Trosky, which serves as the beginner zone, and later, Kuttenberg. I was surprised by the massive scale of the game and its attention to detail. The game also features a lot of choices that affect how things play out, and I think there are around three different endings, depending on what you do throughout the game. When it comes to romance, there are also a lot of different characters you can court and romance. I recommend getting the Legacy of the Forge DLC, which features a hilarious and insanely long questline. The 10-minute ending cutscene almost made me die of laughter before nearly bringing me to tears at the end. Characters: I honestly can't think of a single bad character in this game. Every character you meet feels fleshed out and interesting in their own way. The main characters are really intriguing, and the quests are a lot of fun. You also get to meet (and, at times, play as) Godwin, the priest from the first game, which is great since he was one of my favorite characters. The overall dialogue is fun and engaging, but can feel a bit stiff sometimes. Combat: The only real downside to this game is the combat. It's a bit better than in the first game, but the lock-on fighting system made me rage so many times. Every strike can be lethal, and timing, blocking, and riposting are crucial to making it out alive. If you miss once, it could be game over. I eventually just ended up poisoning my blade to take down my enemies one by one. Otherwise, I'd resort to using a longbow or crossbow with poisoned ammunition. Overall: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is hands down one of the best medieval action RPGs out there. The attention to detail is beyond anything I've ever seen in a game. I waited a year before playing it, so my experience was pretty much bug-free (apart from a few crashes during loading), and the game ran smoothly throughout my playthrough. The atmosphere, historical accuracy and overall setting and vibe of medieval Bohemia are insanely good, and the best I've ever seen. I highly recommend it if you're a fan of games like The Elder Scrolls (e.g., Oblivion and Skyrim), but be prepared to get a bit aggravated by the melee combat and fighting system. Then again, the game has access to the Steam workshop, so you can mod it how you like it.

review_text: This is my love letter to Kingdom Come Deliverance 2. This game is a masterpiece, my absolute most favourite video game ever made! Of course this is a personal opinion, MY OPINION and how I FEEL about this game. That said, I started a new game in hardcore mode which should be a worse experience because of the debuffs. But man It just makes the game more realistic and it slows down the game so much! Which sounds like a bad thing, IF you don't love every little detail. This way you need to walk around the wilderness, witness details you never noticed before. Slow down and take in the games towns, villages, NPCs and small details. It is a totally different, better experience to the base game. Well of course, for certain people, I admit it's not for everyone. So let's get into the review. Gameplay wise the game is a huge improvement form the first one. The first game was an Indie game made by a small passionate studio. The second the in fact was made by the same little passionate studio BUT with the budget of a TRIPLE A game. That means it's just so fluid and every little mechanic feels just right. I did not feel anything would be forced, everything fell in place. Dialogs and choices are made so well, you can solve encounters with so many options, stealth, strenght, wit or speech. You're choice, the game let's you decide, it is just a bloody awesome RPG what more do you want? It does not feel like you are the main character you are a nobody in a medieval setting. Grunt fantasy in medieval bohemia?! Sounds lovely doesn't it? Of course it is. You do not feel overpowered, more underpowered to be honest. Especially if fighting outnumbered without gear. You WILL die. But after struggling through and learning and getting armour. You will be able to fight outnumbered and it will feel so satisfying. The game is a struggle especially for beginners but that makes it more fun, you will enjoy the boring bits, brewing potions and crafting, walking from places discovering the map. This is what makes KCD2 feel so different. It makes you slow down and enjoy boring tasks. Sounds weird but you need to experience it to understand. Combat is a little dumbed down from KCD 1, but it feels better, easier in way because of the decrease of attack angles, combo wise I feel it's about the same. The sword is absolutely broken compared to other weapons. Better said masterstrike is broken, you can easily beat the game by just using masterstrike. Polearms are a cool such as crosbows and guns. Battles feel better and yes bigger as well, sieges are absolutely cool. There are people who prefered the harder KCD1 combat but this is a mainstream game meant for wide audiences, combat was change for this reason. If you want harder I am sure there are mods for that. Graphics are godlike I played on one below the max settings. Everything is just so pretty, this is probably the biggest change from the first game. Trosky region is a nature powerhouse, you just want to take a forest walk after a forest walk and go down to the ponds, follow the rivers climb up the mountains go trough the valleys and so on. It just feels real. Like you are in medieval Bohemia admiring the beauty of the region. Sounds, I played it in Czech but I know the English dubbing is awesome as well. The actors just nailed everything, hungarian needs some improvements in some aspects. Music, Jan Valta made an absolute banger soundtrack. Capturing the vibe of medieval Bohemia. Ambiences of regions of places, battles suffering and prosperity. DLCs, the first one Brushes with death is alright it is a good quest line to finish and if you are into ART it is super cool but it's nothing mind blowing. Now LEGACY OF THE FORGE, omg this is sooo good you have a forge and you are an official blacksmith with quest and upgrades to the forge and armor and customization and everything, absolutely lovely. The third one Mysteria Ecclesiae is the mission from KCD 1 where you were a monk, just in a bigger map and you are basically a detective not a monk. Absolutely lovely the setting is stunning, quest is awesome and activities also. All in all DLC are bloody awesome. At the writing of this review I have 184 hours in the game finished it once and began a second playtrough in hardcore seeking 100% achievements. I will finish the second playtrough around 250-300 hours in. After that I can play it with my friends in multiplayer which I am excited about. Because there is new MULTIPLAYER mod made for this game. I am so thrilled. I don't know why, but I can feel the love which was put into this game by the devs and also by the community and it feels just right.

review_text: KCD2 is a masterpiece I have sunk an unhealthy amount of hours into the game but somehow still find myself discovering new things. Little interactions, hidden details, unexpected consequences storytelling that makes one stop and stare at a random corner of the world like one has just unearthed a lost Shakespearean tragedy. This game is so ridiculously rich in detail that I genuinely wonder how much of it I will have to play before I can confidently say I have seen everything. At this rate I will be on my deathbed finding the first time NPC unique dialogue. The characters are phenomenal. They feel like people rather than glorified quest dispensers with their own personalities, motivations, flaws and peculiarities. The writing in the game is consistently brilliant. The story manages to be compelling without sacrificing the grounded human quality that makes this world so believable. Even the mundane interactions have a certain charm to them. Warhorse somehow made talking to people walking around the countryside and getting absolutely demolished in a fight feel like components of an unforgettable experience. The mechanics? Magnificent. The combat has weight the progression feels earned and the sheer number of systems that interact with one another makes the world feel genuinely alive. Every action feels like it belongs in the setting and every little thing you learn makes you feel like a player manipulating game mechanics and more like an actual person learning to survive in medieval Bohemia. The immersion is borderline absurd. I don't merely play this game; I temporarily relocate to the century and develop personal grievances against people who probably died six hundred years ago. The environmental storytelling deserves recognition too. The world is not a pretty backdrop for your next objective. It is a place with history, character and a life of its own. There are stories told through architecture, landscapes, the placement of objects and the little details you would miss entirely if you were sprinting from quest marker to quest marker like a dopamine-addicted lunatic. Kingdom Come: Deliverance II rewards curiosity in a way few games do and that is perhaps its greatest achievement. What impresses me most is that despite the hundreds of hours I have poured into it the game still manages to surprise me. There is always something to discover some mechanic I haven't fully appreciated some detail that makes me reconsider an earlier experience. It is the sort of game that reminds you why video games can be an art form in their right. Warhorse Studios has created something special here. Not just a great RPG, A world I genuinely love spending time in. The passion, craftsmanship and sheer ambition behind this game are extraordinary. I could spend another thousand hours in Bohemia. Still find reasons to come back for more. If Warhorse Studios ever asks me to sacrifice my firstborn in exchange for Kingdom Come: Deliverance III I will need three seconds to consider the offer.. Those three seconds will be spent checking whether the sacrifice is a mandatory quest objective or an optional side quest. 10/10. A monumental achievement, in RPG design. Henrys come to see us. I have absolutely no intention of letting him leave.

review_text: In short: this is an amazingly detailed, large and fun game that despite some minor shortcomings you should definitely play. The long version is that KCD2 is the successor to KCD1, which I feel people forget because of all the hype and awards KCD2 has gotten at release. If you are on the fence of playing KCD1 or not, definitely do! It introduces many of the characters you meet, is maybe a bit less polished but equally fun. While I agree you won't miss that much, a lot of details will go pass you, and the devil is in the details :) Back to KCD2, so you continue off as Henry from KCD1. The story is much more different compared to the original. You continue your revenge story, but aside from that you are heavily mixed up in the war between Wenceslas and Sigismund. Aside from those 2, there are dozens of other characters involved that in their turn involve Henry. I honestly gave up on the story half-way through because I just couldn't follow what we were actually doing. The scope of things diminishes near the later quests and I felt the story got better their. The side quests are much more enjoyable and personal, while not being repetitive or fetch-quests, so go out of your way to do them, since there are a lot. I got the achievement for doing most things in the same about 40 hours from actually I did everything, so there is plenty of choice. Graphics and music are great; the game looks really beautiful and performance is rock solid. Not much to add in that department. Its an RPG with a plethora of skills, so you have great variety in how you want to play. Using your sword/mace/axe/hammer and bash skulls in, optionally boosting your skills with alchemy. Or being a sneaky guy picking people of with a (cross)bow and dagger. Or just talking your way out of everything. Its all possible and rarely are you forced to a single solution (minus some stealth-only segments here and there). Most other skills take a backseat and usually come in handy but don't influence the general flow of things much (like dog/horse handling, reading, crafting, survival or drinking). The one other useful - if not the most useful - is thievery. Even if you want to roleplay as someone who never steals or pickpockets, its very handy to be able to open certain doors and chests with a high enough lockpicking skill. Medieval people like fighting, so you will have to pull out your weapon eventually. The combat is probably the most divisive element of KCD2 and most negative reviews are about this. Its not a hack and slash you have to approach combat with a bit more realism and fighting anything over 3 enemies at the same time will probably result in a death screen. There's essentially 4 directions you can attack from and parrying and countering are important skills to learn. Learn the masterstrike early to make things easier but its definitely nerfed coming from KCD1. I wouldn't call the combat bad, but I agree with people saying it's annoying at times. The DLC's are also worth. If you were to pick one, I would say Legacy of the Forge since it has the most to offer but Brushes with Death and Mysteria Ecclesiae are equally good. I see some people hating on Mysteria but I really enjoyed it. You can play most DLC's as you encounter them - especially Legacy - but I would keep Mysteria for after the main quest. So yeah, aside from the combat being a bit flaky at times and the story being real convoluted halfway through, everything else is just fantastic and you should play this game.

review_text: I came here to live A lot has changed between the time I played the first game and the second. Funnily enough, given the setting, in the meantime, I got into historical reenactment, larp and fencing. I became a bit of a handcrafter, a bit of a historian, and a bit of a swordsman Naturally, I approached KCD2 with a much more critical eye than I did the first game. Honestly, I never even considered the KCD a masterpiece, so the sequel didn't exactly have an enormous amount of goodwill to burn through. KCD was solid, sure, but it never lived up to the “second Witcher” hype people kept throwing around at the time. And then KCD2 somehow became that game. It completely surprised me and made me fall for it hard, even though I was looking at it with way more skepticism. Once you get invested in the story, it doesn't let go until the very end. This is storytelling in the truest sense of the word. Not just some excuse for the protagonist to exist in an open world, as is the case with so many games, but one coherent, genuinely compelling story. It has fantastic twists, memorable characters, moments that are both heartbreaking and hilarious, and dialogue that rarely lets you get bored. Every second or third cutscene had me going "♥♥♥, how the hell did they pull that off? These absolute madmen" Taking this story in felt as good as it must have felt for the developers to make it. This is genuine art. It's not another game that sucks the life out of you in exchange for a hundred pointless activities. This thing was made with love, and it lets you feel as though you're living another life. And that "another life" thing applies to the characters too. You can feel that the actors weren’t just playing these roles, they were living them I randomly stumbled across videos and streams featuring Tom McKay (Henry) and/or Luke Dale (Hans), and ♥♥♥, these guys seem to live and breathe this game even outside of work. Luke Dale genuinely seems to identify with the character he played, even in real life. That's an incredible level of commitment to a role. That kind of dedication is rare, and from what I can tell it was shared by a huge part of the development team and cast. That’s what makes this world feel alive. The more you dig into the people behind the game and watch stuff about the development process, the more you realize just how much love and soul went into it. That said, it wasn’t all smooth sailing. The game still has bugs and some unbalanced, poorly thought-out moments, although far fewer than the first one. Combat is still far from perfect. What really pisses me off is the continued existence of "ice skating" - when your positions sync up for animations. If an opponent parries your attack from a distance, he’ll just slide toward you like he’s on ice so the animation can play out. It completely kills any sense of weapon range. Polearms especially feel pointless; a guy with a short mace or sword will just skate right up into your face so he can ignore the reach advantage your longsword or a spear is supposed to give you. From my own time spent fencing, I’ve learned that not only the length of your sword, but even your height and the length of your arms actually matter in a fight - but none of that matters in the game. On top of that, Henry constantly gets stuck on branches and rocks in fights, his movement becomes sluggish, and since you can’t look down at your feet during combat, it gets really annoying - especially when you’re trying to backpedal while fighting ten guys at once. Some quests are needlessly, almost sadistically convoluted. It doesn't happen too often but sometimes you’ll get something like: "Find Zbysek. Last person who saw him was Jesek. Jesek has disappeared, so go talk to Pasek. None of them will tell you anything until you talk to ♥♥♥, and ♥♥♥ first. They're all in different towns, so enjoy running around the map talking to fifteen different people who have nothing more interesting to say. Congratulations, you've finally found Zbyshek." It was annoying, but truth be told, there are only a handful of quests like that. And that’s pretty much the entire list of real complaints. For a modern AAA game, that’s a short list. It’s a price I’m more than willing to pay for the immersion this game delivers. The game is worth almost every single hour you put into it. In the end, I din't play this game. I lived here Because even when you're not following the gripping main story or doing interesting quests, Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is one of the best immersive sims out there. When you boot it up, you won't be thinking "I’ll just knock out a couple of quests" or, worse, "I’ll clear a few outposts and do some dailies" You will be thinking "I’m going in there to live" Because ♥♥♥, you really do live in this game. I don’t know how these absolute maniacs pulled it off, but sometimes it’s pure joy just walking through a medieval town, stumbling into random events, taking part in this life, competing in tournaments, walking into any house and looking at how people live, then riding out into the fields, finding a pasture full of cows and going up to each one going "hello, cow" chasing around ridiculous squealing little piglets, or just looking at the beautiful horses. The only thing missing is the ability to set up camp like in RDR2. And a special mention goes to the blacksmithing. As someone who genuinely appreciates the craft, I spent a ridiculous amount of time in this game just forging things. That's the magic of it. There's always something to do, but you don't always need a quest marker telling you what it is. Sometimes you just want to exist in this world for a while. That's ultimately the best thing I can say about Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2. It's a literal window into another world. It has a gripping story and a living, breathing environment that's a joy to immerse yourself in, even when you're doing absolutely nothing of importance. In the end, this game completely won me over. My appreciation for it is on an entirely different level. It's earned a place among my all-time favorite games. I'm genuinely happy I got to spend time in this world. And someday, I'll be back.

review_text: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is my game of the year for 2025. I have played the original game and have also really enjoyed it, so this is not the first time that I’m exploring Medieval Europe as Henry of Skalitz. Since first playing KC:D II on the day, it was released on February 4th, 2025, I have been playing it all year. The 145+ hours that I played it was on just one playthrough, so you know this game has a lot of content. This game features a beautiful large open world to explore with the help of your trusty steed full of historical Medieval landmarks in the Kingdom of Bohemia. As someone who has visited Czechia during the 21st century not 15th century. I don’t have access to a time machine...Yet. 😊 Warhorse Studios did a great job capturing the feel of Czechia’s countryside. Many fans have visited locations from the game and compared them with real life. Here is an example of Trosky castle which plays a role in the game’s story. Speaking of time machines, the game’s soundtrack is very appropriate and gives you the feeling that you have traveled back in time to the Middle Ages. Warhorse Studios spared no expense and had an Orchestra perform some of the games most memorable music. Regarding the gameplay itself, it feels like the first game but more streamlined and simplified compared to the first game. I still find it highly enjoyable! Even if it is simplified by the standards of the first game, I still found the combat in this game is still much better than in most action RPGs that use Medieval inspired weapons that I have played. After experiencing combat in KC:D II, I found it hard to go back to other action RPGs that focus on combat with swords and other weapons that you would find during the Middle Ages. Games which still use simpler “hack and slash” style gameplay which just requires you to click your left mouse button repeatedly instead of the more complex and realistic combat mechanics that requires more practice like KC:D II has. Combat is not the only part of the game, KC:D II is a story driven RPG in the truest sense. I will not post any spoilers but the games story and especially the ending does a fantastic job of concluding the story of Henry of Skalitz. Even half a year after finishing the main quest I found the ending very satisfying and is still in my memory. Interesting fact, the games script has over 2.2 million words, making it the longest script in video game history! Talk about a milestone for gaming as a form of sophisticated storytelling. Overall, I think that this game stands out from the rest of the RPGs on the market. In an industry where it feels like we have a sea of RPGs with fantasy settings it is refreshing to see a more realistic game that explores real historical locations. I hope the industry takes notice and more role-playing games with historical settings are released. For the Czechia-based Warhorse Studios making a game about their nation’s Medieval history was obviously a labor of love and it shows in the finale product. If you are interested in the Middle Ages and like action RPGs this is not a game, you should miss playing. Whatever game wins GOTY on Steam this year Kingdom Come: Deliverance II will be the game of the year for me. Audentes Fortuna Iuvat!

review_text: There are so many things I love about this game, but many other reviewers have already gone into great depth about its many amazing qualities, so I'm not going to repeat them much here. Instead I am going to address some criticisms I see (and sometimes agree with), but also address why those criticisms shouldn't prevent you from playing this great game. One criticism I see and that I agree with is that the requirement of brewing potions in order to save your game outside of save points can be annoying. Luckily there is a way to get around this requirement. After installing the game, go to your steam library, right click on KCD2, and select "properties." Then, in the properties window go to "launch options," and add the command "-devmode" (not including quotation marks). Now, whenever you launch the game, press the tilde key (~) and enter the command "wh_sys_nosavepotion 1" (not including quotation marks), and now you will be able to save your game without needing a saviors schnapps potion. Another complaint that I see is that the combat is annoyingly difficult. I agree that its difficult, but I don't think its annoyingly so. In my experience most RPGs fall into one of two combat formats. The first category would be games like Assassin's Creed and Witcher 3, where where one button attacks, another blocks, and maybe one dodges. The second category is souls-like combat where you have to be super strategic and any mistakes are punished harshly. The KCD franchise doesn't fit into either of those categories. This might not be the best way to describe it, but I'd describe it as needing more real-time combat strategy. Button mashing won't get you anywhere because if you keep doing the same thing your opponents will learn your pattern and block it. Unlike souls-like games where you have to plan your combat in advance and learn an enemy's patterns, in KCD you have to be continuously watching your enemy to see which attacks and strategies they favor, but also how they respond to your attacks and strategies. Its an innovative system which I think makes combat more engaging than in games like Witcher 3, and difficult in a way which I appreciate more than souls-like combat. A third complaint I see with irritating frequency is that certain people don't like that there are Jewish characters and the option for a same-sex romance in this game. They seem to think by including that the devs are putting modern politics into the middle ages and breaking immersion or some other such nonsense. Judaism has existed in Europe for longer than Christianity has, and there have been LGBTQ+ people for just as long as there have been straight people. If that's a deal breaker for you then I'm not going to try to argue with you, and please don't try to argue with me.

It's like if you took an Elder Scrolls game, removed all the magic or fantastical elements, and replaced them with realism and historical accuracy. My wife’s boyfriend says it’s like if Project Zomboid was a medieval FPS. KCDII makes every Bethesda game look like a child’s crayon drawing. It is better in every objective measure from graphics to stability, and it’s better in most of the subjective ways too. They have surpassed Bethesda by a country mile in the 7 years from their start-up release to their second game release. They've surpassed a whole lot of studios who are stuck in the mud, tbh. They deserve ALL the credit. It’s insane for a game of this scale to have so much detail and charm. It has set the standard of modern open world RPGs. God, what a game. I love this company. I hope they stay true to their visions and keep making great games. It's incredibly hard to make dynamic choice based, dialogue heavy games with consequences for your actions all inside a living world. And they have achieved it in one of the better looking games that's ever released that runs on all current gen and older gen GPUs. And it's also a cinematic AAA story driven game on top of that. Only Sony first party studios tend to release games in this state, and their games are on-rails for the most part, and designed to run on one bit of hardware. Mind blowing, really. Warhorse. 👏👏👏 This game, to me, is perfect. The stories are amazing, from the smallest interaction or conversation to the side and main quest. Combat, alchemy, SMITHING, all of it is fun. They have taken everything that was cool, and made it 100 times better. I am so f**king happy after playing this and I'm still thoroughly addicted. The music is amazing, world and exploration is breathtaking. I cannot praise it enough. It was so worth the wait, and it's making me so excited for the future. I'm just so damn happy Warhorse made this game. It puts Bethesda (who I love) to shame in so many ways. I played Skyrim often for a decade, I see myself playing this for far longer. I love so so much about it, I love its commitment to realism and aversion to fantasy (I love fantasy, but the hard commitment to realism is a breath of fresh air). I love the character writing, I love how Hans grows on you like a mold, I love how naive and hopeful and just young Henry is, there’s so many gruff jaded protagonists that having him freak out at the mention of the devil or just blindly believe random sh*t or just refuse to compromise on his morals is so endearing to me. I love the world and systems for stealth and stealing and character schedules, just a pleasure to be in and play around with. But by far my favorite part of the game are the side quests, they’re so unique and fun, the rewards are universally bad but it genuinely doesn’t matter, you just go somewhere and you watch some weird, funny or creepy medieval drama unfold, and it’s different and interesting every time. I also love how your different character stats can also play into it New Vegas style. I loved how small things in this game had a level of challenge to them. You have to watch your characters hunger, and at the beginning of the game it's a bit hard to find food without stealing. Your equipment wears down (especially boots), and your character can stink if you don't visit the bathhouse. I laughed when an enemy found me while I was crouching behind them just because they could smell how bad my character stunk. I also really enjoyed learning about medieval Europe as a lot of it is historically accurate with an in-depth codex’s detailing events, real noblemen, and general things like historical professions and the like. I could never in a million years have imagined that a game this hardcore and slow paced could have as few rough edges as KCD2. The fact that myself, and seemingly most of the people that are still talking about it online drop 40-60 hours into the game before starting the first real main mission is testament to how well designed, integrated and engaging all of the systems in the game are, which for a game with such a large amount of very in depth systems is a straight up masterstroke of game design. I've played countless open world RPGs and no game has come close to getting me this deeply invested via its gameplay systems alone. Just existing as Henry, building up his stats and gear while also improving my own understanding of the game and combat evokes a feeling I can only compare to the "one more turn" feeling you get from the Civilization games. There is always something to do and a reason for me to want to do it and that feeling seemingly just never stops. It's a lot like RDR2 for masochists and if Arthur was 15 again. It's not a "fun every minute" kind of game. It's immersive and challenging, and there's a great satisfaction loop as you improve at various things. I think it requires a bit more nuance and preparation than a lot of modern day RPGs, which can be frustrating to people expecting more of a Ghost of Tsushima type game, or a game with fights every 5 minutes. Let's say that where in RDR2 the immersion stuff felt rapidly like a chore here is linked to actual gameplay mechanics and not just for the sake of it. Personally, I think KCD2 does a great job of rewarding the extra effort that it asks of the player. It's one of those games where the positives far outweigh the negatives. The game can be quite buggy especially in the second map, the story drags on in certain parts (especially those extended sections where you can't explore freely until you complete the quest), pacing is inconsistent, good loot is easy to obtain early game, etc. However, the writing, characters, voice acting, visuals, soundtrack, realism and detail this game has far compensate those issues. In a way it reminds me of The Witcher 3 10 years ago. I put about 100 hours into the game and don't regret a single minute of it. I'm looking forward to a second playthrough in the future, trying different choices and gameplay styles. It's GOTY contender for sure, though Clair Obscur has a strong case to win as well. I have not felt like this about a video game since crawling out of the prison in Bethesda's Oblivion and discovering a sprawling world rife with adventure and nature. This game is not for everyone, the combat takes patience and finesse, it is a survival sim and you are not the chosen one and you will fail at conversations constantly, but this is a game for me and I'm so thrilled to have played it. I know I'm rambling here but the best comparison to make my point is Larian Studios: Divinity Original Sin 1&2 are some of the best games made for CRPG fans. Baldurs Gate 3 however is a game that creates CRPG fans. Similarly KCD1 was a very good game made for a specific niche of hardcore immersive RPGs. KCD2 I think has the potential to create fans of such games, in a way that I don't think we've seen since Skyrim. In conclusion, I've never felt more immersed in the Middle Ages. The graphics are stunning, and the level of detail is astonishing. Everything just feels right. Even walking through the forest is so immersive it's breathtaking. This level of detail, combined with the vast possibilities the game offers, makes it an experience you don't want to miss out on! If you’re willing to sit down, take things slow, and just get lost in it, there really is no game that does it better in my opinion. I can wholeheartedly say that if you want to experience an amazing campaign set in a perfectly recreated version of life in 1403 Europe, give it a try you won't regret it. 10/10 JESUS CHRIST BE PRAISED!

review_text: I got jumped by three barefoot peasants with sticks. 10/10. Other RPGs: "You are the Chosen One, savior of the universe, slayer of gods!" Kingdom Come Deliverance 2: "You smell like a sewer, you don't know how to read, and the local baker won't sell you bread until you take a bath." I didn't think it was possible to make a game where getting aggressively rejected by a bathhouse wench feels like a core gameplay mechanic, but Warhorse Studios pulled it off again. I spent three real-life hours practicing how to swing a mace properly. I walked into the woods feeling like an absolute medieval badass, only to immediately get beaten to death by two drunk bandits wielding literal tree branches. It was a humbling experience. I loved it. I recently upgraded to an RTX 5050, and let me tell you, rendering 15th-century Bohemian mud and horse dung in ultra-realistic ray-tracing has never looked so incredibly glorious. The optimization is actually pretty solid, though my CPU is definitely working overtime just to calculate the physics of my character getting thrown into a wall. My buddy Mojtaba keeps spamming me on Steam to go play multiplayer shooters, but I had to put myself on 'Offline' mode. Sorry man, I can't rush B right now, I'm busy brewing a single health potion for 45 minutes in real-time and trying not to burn the tavern down. Pros: You can actually hit things with a sword now (after 20 hours of crying). The world feels incredibly alive. NPCs will literally insult your fashion sense. "Jesus Christ be praised!" Cons: I am quite feeling hungry. I am STILL quite feeling hungry. This isn't just a game; it's a full-time medieval job. Buy it, suffer, learn to read, get rich, and then lose all your money playing dice. Best historical RPG ever made. Jesus Christ be praised.

review_text: I remember booting up KCD2 expecting a bigger, prettier version of the first game. What I got was something that pulled me in and did not let go. One moment I am riding through the countryside just to see what is over the next hill, and the next I am three hours deep into a side quest I never planned on starting. It has that same soul the first game had, just polished to a point I did not think was possible. Bohemia in KCD2 does not feel like a game map. It feels like a place. The villages have their own rhythm, the forests feel like you could actually get lost in them, and Kuttenberg is easily one of the most impressive cities I have walked through in an RPG. Henry's story grabs you early and it never really lets go, and the way KCD2 treats Czech history gives the whole thing a weight most games do not even attempt. What surprised me most was how much the small things added up. Just riding back to camp after a long day, with nothing but the music playing, ended up being one of my favorite parts of the game, and that music never once felt like background noise. Combat still has that same bite from the first game, but it is smoother now, easier to pick up if you want to keep things simple, or deep enough to master if you want real combos. Side activities like alchemy and blacksmithing pulled me in more than I expected too. KCD2 is not perfect. NPCs sometimes forget something happened right after a quest ends, the pacing dips depending on how you play, and Mutt got nerfed, which still stings a little. None of that changed how much I enjoyed the ride though. As for the DLCs, the first one brings in a mysterious painter character and a string of fetch quests with a surprisingly dark undertone, and it fits nicely into the main story if you run them side by side. The second is more of a quality of life add-on. You finally get a home base with your own customizable forge to craft and rest at, though the quests tied to it can feel a bit repetitive after a while. The third DLC leans into a monastery based stealth and investigation, with strong characters, great cinematics, and a story that is decent on its own but really shines through the atmosphere. It is shorter than the others, but it is put together really well. Finishing Kingdom Come: Deliverance II did not feel like closing out a sequel, it felt like picking up right where the first journey left off and finishing it properly. Without exaggeration, KCD and KCD2 together make up the best RPG series I have ever played. Overall, KCD2 gets a 10/10, easy recommend.

review_text: Finished Dec 7 2025. Earlier in 2025, I finished KCD1 and found myself enamoured by the game's dedication to put you in Henry's shoes, the level of immersion, details that actually affect the gameplay, the fair amount of freedom of choice and of course the clunky combat. All of which that helps culminate the KCD experience. So I was genuinely excited for the sequel the way everyone hyped it up to be a clear improvement from the first game. And while it isn't a huge departure, the improvements are worthy of every praise. These past 140 hours have probably been some of the most fun I've ever had playing any game. My biggest fear was that, since KCD2 is much larger, they would dumb down core mechanics for "quality of life" or to appeal to a broader audience. I’m glad they didn’t, for the most part. While there are some much needed QoL upgrades, it still feels like Kingdom Come, just more expanded and refined. Just like the previous game, this one also takes place in Bohemian countryside and wilderness. Where the first game took more photorealistic approach with the graphics and vistas, KCD2, though still being photorealistic, has more colorful, painting-esque visuals. I really appreciate this direction, since so much medieval media is obsessed with trying to look "gritty" all the time. Dividing the game into two regions was, in my opinion, a great decision. It keeps the first region from feeling overwhelming while giving you enough time to complete quests and prepare for what’s ahead. One of the coolest moments is when you feel like you've experienced the peak of the game, only to get hit with the, much bigger, denser, second region. And then there's also the massive living, breathing city with unique npcs, vendors with life cycle or their own and random events. It's easily one of the most impressive cities in any game. Talking about the world, I can't forget the npcs, your attire and reputation still affect your charisma and how npcs treat you, just like the first game. But now, they are much more dynamic mixed with the in-depth crime system. You can get punished accordingly or if you have high enough charisma or speech, you might get away with it. The persuasion system is more interesting than ever now with few more options, so passing and failing them can result in different outcomes which are always fun to see play out. Reputation also plays a big part who you're talking to and now some NPCs have they're own individual reputation meters. On the topic of speech checks, perk system is much better integrated in the dialogues this time. For example if I have high scholarship, I can choose the dialogue that rely on it, letting me argue better with an educated npc and so on. One of the biggest highlights of this game is the way you can meet alot of characters through pure exploration, only to meet them again in important quests. Where they'll often refer to earlier events which just adds to the immersion of making the world feel lived in. Or some minor npc that you helped long time ago will run into you and thank you. There are lots of moments like this and it really feels fulfilling to see your efforts gets recognised. Most of my playtime was me doing side quests and thankfully a very good amount of them were much better this time around. Alot of them had choices that reward out of the box thinking and different outcomes which lead to different side quests. So the whole thing feels like a side story rather than running errands for npcs. It also helped that a lot of them had cutscenes and good voice acting on the same quality as the main quest. Side activities were also alot better now, often having their own quests that make them feel personalized rather than just grinding for rewards. The best example is the sword fighting tournament and how we go through a whole quest to set it up with some beloved npcs. Then of course there's the whole blacksmithing business which is a really great addition that just enhances the game's life-sim experience. Which also has a great quest with it that strengthens Henry's character. KCD2's story is one of my favourite in gaming. Many of the themes that were established in the previous game are carried over and expanded upon in this sequel which I really like. The pacing never breaks, even at the slower missions, you always feel like you're going somewhere. The story being great is also a result of how masterfully some missions were made with hundred ways to approach them. There are big twists you can easily discover if you explore enough and the game rewards you for it. While some missions are a bit on the on the rails, they're never bad. The final stretch was a genuine masterpiece. For the characters, Hans, Godwin are here. Who were easily my favourite in the first game, now joined with the colorful ensemble of characters that enhance the experience. There's also a gang dynamic in the story which makes Henry feel like everyone's equal compared to the first game where he was just an underling. There's simply way too many people you care about in this game that fixes my issues with the first one. The returning antagonists were also done really well, now showing more human sides compared to the first game where I didn't really care about them. Whenever they were on the screen, especially with Henry, you know it's going to cinema. As a protagonist Henry is now alot better this time around. He has more agency and there's a fair amount of choice in the main and side quests with consequences that help shape his morality like you want. There were some choices that had me think for a bit before acting, all of them are enhanced by the wide range of characters we have and the dynamics they share with Henry that makes him better as a character. All of these story related stuff wouldn't be as good if the VA, mocap and cinematics weren't as phenomenal as they were. Everyone in the main cast went all out and the cinematics were so good it was hard to believe they're all made in-engine. Easily the some of the best cinematography I've seen in any game. There's also the soundtrack that consists of LOTR inspired themes, whimsical tavern music to accompany you on travels or a Mozart piece, Jan Valta did an amazing job. Issues About some issues, combat is much more streamlined this time, which is a double edged sword. There's 4 sides to attack from compared to 5 of the first game, so the combos are much simpler(it doesn't matter bc you're just gonna spam master strike anyways). But just like the first game it's easy exploit it by learning master strike and getting stronger very early. So it becomes pretty brain dead. Crowd control is much better here but still kinda flawed. Some combat perks are genuinely very broken that you pretty much become invincible. On the topic of perks, it's pretty easy to just max out on everything so you are an all rounder by the end of the game. The new additions which were the crossbows and guns were also very situational, one takes half a minute to reload and the other has half the accuracy (I know, realism). So I got stuck with bows and longsword, which are very busted btw. Balancing is basically broken after some point into the game. Another thing is there isn't much to spend your in game money on. After doing the main quest for a bit you can just have about everything you need for the rest of the game without spending much money. The two unique swords and one armor set I had were from the forge dlc. These are just some issues I had. Though, they don't erase what Warhorse had managed to do with this ambitious sequel. This was some of the most fun I've had playing a game. Nobody is making a realistic rpg based on historical setting with immersive systems like this, so I'll be very much looking forward to their next game.

review_text: After having played the first Kingdom Come: Deliverance , my expectations were high for the second iteration. My expectations were not met, they were shattered. The sheer amount of stuff to do, the gorgeous landscape and the detail that went into creating this medieval masterpiece are just incredible. It improved on about everything from the first game, and it feels like a labour of love. Keep in mind, I am playing hardcore mode, which means - amongst other things - no compass, no map marker of your current location and no fast travel. It makes you pay more attention to your surroundings, and you end up navigating via landmarks. I also make it a point NOT to run / gallop all the time, as I want to immerse myself into the universe created by Warhorse Studios. And yes, it is an entire universe. The research done and all the info found in the codex really give you a good impression of medieval Bohemia. When they took some liberties for the sake of the game, they will actually mention that in the codex entries along with the reasoning. I love that meticulous approach to designing a world inhabited by NPCs who - mostly - will react in a manner you might expect. More so than in the first iteration. Then again, this also falls short on a few occasions. For example, when I ride on an old mare, just about every NPC I come across feels it is their duty to inform me that they would never be seen dead on a shabby horse like that. Keep in mind, most are peasants who couldn't dream of ever owning a horse. And after 10 minutes of being shunned by people this gets on your nerves. And it certainly doesn't feel immersive. Same goes for all sorts of interactions initiated by NPCs in order to make the world feel more "engaging". This is an issue with nearly every single open world game. And one I think they could have improved by simply realising that a lot of times you will pass people without them feeling the need to comment on your lovely dog, your shabby old horse or the fact that your clothes are slightly dirty. The fact that this irks me so much is less an indicator of the actual nuisance of this particular little annoyance. It rather shows how little I have to complain about so far in this game. Yes, I would like the tasks to be less "gamey" and more real-life like, but I assume that 90% of gamers would hate to do mundane stuff and rather have their adventures, regardless of whether they are super immersive or not. And I have no intention to die on that particular hill, as I still like doing some of these tasks and I have the option to ignore the rest (which I do on some occasions). So, the fact that I am nitpicking at tiny stuff should give you a good idea about how much I actually love this game. Please, please, please, let there be a Kingdom Come: Deliverance III.

review_text: Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is one of those rare sequels that makes the original feel like a proof of concept. You can tell Warhorse had a much bigger budget this time around because they took everything that worked in the first game, refined it, polished it, and somehow managed to make it all come together almost perfectly. The biggest difference for me is just how smooth the game feels to play. I enjoyed the first game, but there was always a layer of jank sitting on top of everything. Here, almost every mechanic feels refined and far more intuitive. The movement, combat, exploration, conversations, progression, it all flows so much better than before. What really elevates the game though is the immersion. This is genuinely one of the most immersive games I've ever played. The world feels alive in a way very few RPGs manage. NPCs follow believable daily routines, the day and night cycle affects how people behave, and everything feels grounded enough that you start treating the world like a real place rather than a video game map. One of my favourite memories was passing time blacksmithing weapons and horseshoes under shelter while it was pouring rain both in the game and in real life as well. Moments like that completely pulled me into the experience. Kuttenberg is also one of the most impressive cities I've ever seen in a video game. The sense of scale is incredible, and walking through it genuinely feels like exploring a real medieval city. Even outside the city, the smaller villages are packed with personality and are fun to wander through. The forests deserve special mention too. This might genuinely have the best vegetation I've seen in a game. Walking through the woods, hearing the wind, birds, distant wildlife, and all the environmental sounds creates an atmosphere that's hard to describe unless you've experienced it yourself. The story is fantastic as well. Both the main quest and side content are consistently well written, and I loved how often the game plays around with morality. So many quests avoid obvious good and bad choices, forcing you to think about what the "right" decision actually is. Henry continues to be a great protagonist, and after spending so much time with him and the supporting cast, I became genuinely attached to these characters. I spent over 90 hours in this game and still have content left to do along with the DLC. Somehow those 90 hours absolutely flew by. Looking back, it's only when you start remembering everything you've done, every place you've visited, every character you've met, and every story you've experienced that you realise just how massive the journey actually was. This is one of the best RPGs I've ever played and an absolute must-play for anyone who loves the genre. 10/10 (Masterpiece)
