review_text: How do I begin? KCD2 is a very refreshing AA game for the longest time in the midst of AI, remaster, and gameplay replayability. It has been nominated and won several awards in 2025, and now I can see it why. Like most people, I'm one of those who feel playing game nowadays seems like a chore or doesn't feel fun anymore because as a "GaMer" (*hur-dur sarcastically*), I always think how I want to win it ASAP or if I already have the prerequisite knowledge of similar games. Initially, I went blind into KCD2 while avoiding spoilers because I already played KCD in the past...and I'm glad because I feel something that I haven't felt for a long time...I'm actually having fun in single player game. I actually DESIRED it to play more, and that's not an easy exaggeration. KCD2 is an open-world first-person RPG medieval game where you play as Henry, a friend and squire of Sir Hans Capon. The game sets heavily in historical timeline of Late Middle Ages of 1403 in Bohemia with succession war looming across the Holy Roman Empire. Your role might seem insignificant at first, but you actually play parts in the bigger picture. Positives: + Very good optimization: Warhorse Studio optimization has come a long way since first KCD. I gotta say, at launch, first KCD was not the most optimized version. Even after I played it again somewhere this year, it's still not as optimized as KCD2. But KCD2 actually surprised me with 100-150 fps in Ultra 2K with FSR. There were stutters if you went into some heavily guarded areas if you are running too fast, but it's quite mild. With my PC specs, I never went under 100 fps, so the result might be varied. + Great story-writing and easter eggs: you will laugh, you will feel joy, you will question "what if?", you will feel sadness/empathy, but the outcome will be decided by...some dice roll. Yes, that's true. some conversation actually strike by dice rolls similar to DnD. Not too many which feels random, but it's there. Dialogue mechanic options aside, the writing in this game is...very good. Again, it's an RPG game, therefore there are some limitation with to what-if dialogues by the dev, but they basically give Henry options to be an absolute menace or good boi. Sometimes trollish even. And for modern audience, the dev understood perfectly when they put hilarious meme references you saw in internet. Very cultured indeed. + Gameplay mechanic and contents: since you could say KCD2 is a game which is quite close to medieval realism, it doesn't need to be as close as historical as possible. But they did. Which feels more fun and less of a medieval history simulator. That doesn't mean the content is not authentic, it's just presented as simplified history version. What I mean is, you must remember this is a GAME and not historical simulator, it doesn't have to be perfect, but at least tolerable to some degree of realism. With that put aside, the content in the game were beautifully designed than I expected and it's hard to mention it without spoiling some story or content. You want to save your game? Too bad you need to brew a Schnapp for it. You want to buy something? Too bad you are branded now because of your past misdeed. Did you get food poisoning? Better have antidote or you will die in the next 5 minutes (accurate irl too). Ohh, you better check that grave, might be have some quest item for later. Sometimes some quest puzzle like a riddle need an ACTUAL BRAIN to solve it out. Yes, it was that detail. And I love how Warhorse gave insightful Codex to player who are interested in this periodical of time. It's like you are learning and playing at the same time (watching Ubisoft games with face palm). Like depicting NPC's daily life in medieval time of what not and what does. From the architecture of Trotsky castle to Kuttenberg city and (arguably) accurate armor and clothes in the 15th century. There will be lot of historians who will debate this, but still, kudos to Warhorse studios team for putting tremendous effort in the game for the sake of authenticity. In short, yes there're lot of contents in the game and justify the price tag. + - Good music and sound effect: I don't have lot to say. The music in the game fits perfectly on every action sequence. For example, if you are on the road, you will hear the standard lute and pandeiro so Henry won't be so lonely. Or if you are in Italian quarter, you will hear funny Italian pizza medieval music. For most part, the game will give you sequence of music based on the cinematic, location, and your action in the game. Overall, very good choice of music. That said, the SFX might need some variations. Because most of the SFX sound so high or doesn't have lot of grumble or "thump" variation except the horse hoof gallop. It's not bad per se and certainly won't affect your gameplay, but it's there. Negatives: - Minor bugs and soft lock: unfortunately even though I have been such a fanboy about this game, it's with heavy heart that I also must come clean that this game is not without bugs. No game is perfect, and KDC2 is one of those. For example, Kuttenberg Tournament quest notification have such infamous bug where you need to return the gears but it won't allow you, therefore you could just leave the tournament or pay the gear to remove the notification. It's a minor bug I say, but it's annoying because it's such a wake up call. Another example is an investigation quest in Forge DLC where you need to investigate lost materials or schematic for the guild. If you "accidentally" learned one of the required schematic, it will count as lost item and you couldn't lie nor decline the quest to fail it. So the notification dangling there awkwardly and you can't finish the quest. Or maybe you met with strangers in Kuttenberg street, but you couldn't see who you are talking to because they already gone behind the cart in marketplace. For completionist, you better make some Schnapp in case you soft lock some choices (or maybe that's part of the gameplay?). - Limited save slot: this is just me being very picky. Like aforementioned above, I need to save a lot because I want to try to finish all the side quest first, then the main quest. Therefore I need to save a lot. Turn out, you only could have 500 slots or you need to overwrite the older saves. - Questionable decent-ish stealth mechanic: this is more like a complaint. Since it's very weird that sometimes enemy could have x-ray vision to see the body inside the building or night vision which could see a body from far away even though it's so damn dark unless you need to get close to it. It's not bad, but it's not good either. And that's probably it. Kudos to TomMckay (Henry VA), rest of the casts, professional sources, and the developers, you all did brilliantly. Go give KCD2 a try. It's worth the full price, and even better on discount. Edit: "AAA" to "AA".

review_text: Possibly the best game I've ever played and the best game humanity has ever seen. It has the best RPG mechanics of all time for sure. You can be whoever you want and the game allows it, because you can complete every quest through various routes depending on your character. I'd say they took everything that was already good in the first game and even improved it. Also, I'd like to thank the developers for adding the Ukrainian language to the game. review_text: This is my first ever public review of a game, and for a damned good reason. I will address both KCD1 and 2, because you’re mistaken if you think you can fully enjoy the second game without playing the first. Earlier this year, I played KCD1 at the behest of my friend. It was unpalatable to me. The combat was clunky, the graphics were dated, and the overall gameplay was otherwise cumbersome and difficult. The map, its large swath of characters, the various choices I could make – it all felt too big and overwhelming. I never thought I'd fall so deeply in love with it. I thugged out the initial discomfort, and before I could say " are you yanking my pizzle? ", I was burning an egregious amount of midnight oil toiling away at side quests, sharpening my skills, and immersing myself in the breathtaking world of 15th century Bohemia. As a history nerd, KCD scratched an decades-old itch in my brain that was last tended to when I played Assassin's Creed 2 as a kid. Its deep realism doesn't just start with its historical storyline, though. KCD features a challenging uphill climb where you grow from a naive peasant boy to a skilled and noble warrior. It doesn't hold your hand, and refuses to mollycoddle you under the pretext that you're the protagonist. It is precisely this unforgiving aspect that earned this franchise my deep and profound respect. If KCD1 is an antipasto , KCD2 is the primo , secondo , and dolce all wrapped up in a platter of seamless gameplay, engaging storylines, clever humour, BAFTA-worthy voice acting, and environments so alive and detailed that you can almost smell the tavern mildew through the screen. The beauty and diversity of KCD2’s world frequently compelled me to slow down and watch the sun setting from the hills, saunter through the woods, or sit inside a chapel for a moment of repose amidst the swashbuckling, gritty realism of medieval wartime. Through its many, many quests and NPCs that feel like real, relatable people, KCD2 commands a level of immersion and realism unparalleled to any RPG game. KCD’s combat is demanding, to say the least. Reminiscent of For Honor ’s combat system, KCD practically screams medieval immersion. With combos, parries, and feints running alongside a ridiculous amount of gear and weapons at your disposal, you’ll spend what seems like a frustrating (and oftentimes embarrassing) amount of time trying to take down a couple of lightly-armoured bandits. It’s for this reason that it feels so exceptionally rewarding. KCD2 does simplify the combat system from its predecessor, but does so without sacrificing the fundamentals that made it so great in the first place. I could ramble on and on, but I think I’ve made my point. KCD swallows the RPG genre and spits out its best qualities in spades. I’ve dedicated over 200 hours of my life to this franchise, and I still find myself hungry for more. Jesus Christ be praised, and may the Lord watch over Warhorse Studios for creating such a masterpiece. 1000/10. Audentes fortuna iuvat!

review_text: After playing the first game I felt quite hungry for another game and a conclusion to the story and Jesus Christ be praised Henry has returned with a new jawline in Kingdom Come Marmite II. I actually pirated this game first as I'm sceptical thanks to game creating a-holes like ubisoft and EA but it was so good I had to buy a real copy with all the DLC to support the dev and to make sure they make sequels or other games for me :p BTW If you do make any sequels think about going back in time please not forward (Hussite's being slaughtered with guns would be a very different game). I'm not a fan of the combat, I understand the mechanics, I just personally don't like it much within an open world. It's a bit like a QTE mini-game where stamina is king. I like how it tries to go it's own way and against 1 opponent but most of the time you're fighting multiple opponents and it's designed for 1v1 you're locked onto a single opponent, you can argue realism all you like but if 3 enemies come at you IRL would you only concentrate on only one and let the other 2 hit you? In the later game I was shouting "Kurva!" at the screen. Henry can only see at about a 90° angle and doesn't have the capacity to block or parry from opponents he's not locked onto but it's improved from the 1st game and there's others ways around it like using the doggo, blunt stuff works better on armoured opponents, sharpened weapons are more effective, potions & poisons can help, specific perks etc. it's also worth bearing in mind that combat can be avoided sometimes with talk or stealth, you could read/watch some guides to get more info as the game doesn't explain it all well. There's some new weapons including hand cannon's but if I wanted guns I'd play some junk like COD or battlefield not a game about knights. You can fight on horseback too but it's not good with mêlée weapons and you can't joust with a polearm (that might have been too overpowered?) but archery works well. The loot is not distributed in a balanced way, after my second bandit encounter in the open world I found one of the best longswords in the game that I didn't need to change until the end game. A lot of the bandits I encountered had a full sets of plate armour worth thousands which apart from not very immersive made making money way too easy and no need to purchase any. I had fairly regular crashing until I disabled Shader Caching in the NVIDIA control panel. Found a few other bugs like wonky NPC pathing and events not triggering most of which were fixed by reloading, this would have been less annoying with a different save system, particularly annoying in the early game until I stocked up on saviour schnapps. I noticed a lot of the problems I encountered have been patched and it was in a better state on release than KCD1 was. It's a big, detailed game with hundreds of hours of content and I'm not yanking your pizzle, exploration is good, it's not an empty bloated map like a modern AC game, some of the side quests have depth with multiple ways to complete them some of which are not even listed in the journal. Be a thieving murdering intimidating bastard, be a noble charming literate knight. One thing that wasn't well thought out though was the timed quests in an open world with no proper warning which can result in you having to go back to earlier saves, you can lose a lot of gameplay if you're not careful. There's some clever mechanics that make the world feel more real, reactive people going about their daily medieval lives, if you steal someone's clothes then wear them in front of them they will recognise them. Stealing too much in a specific area will result in people becoming more paranoid, using harder locks, guards will search more, prices may even go up. Your rep and appearance changes how NPC's treat you; when you're the outsider you're treated like one (eg: the first person they blame for any crime) but when you have a good rep some speech skills and the right outfit you can get away with murder but be warned crime has consequences such as fines, jail time, whipping with no safeword, branding and even death. Rep makes a huge difference for example try walking around a town with your weapon out with a low rep and guards will immediately approach you and tell you to put it away and if you ignore them they will attempt to arrest you and shove you in the stocks but if you have a good rep in the same town guards will tell you to put it away but won't chase you and just go about their shift because they know and trust you. Alchemy and blacksmithing has some mechanics, not just gather materials/ingredients then click a magic button and your done you have to brew potions properly and hammer the metal on an anvil, you can't forge armour only weapons which is a shame but still better than other games. The soundtrack and visuals are good. The perk system is improved from the first game, be sure you exploit the right ones for your playstyle and you can eventually unlock everything with a few being exclusive/opposites. The VA is generally good with unfortunately the occasional Yank showing up 400 years too early and no Brian Blessed but an improvement on the first one which I recommend you play first if you haven't already to enjoy the full story (it's also a good game), there's some really good performances from the main cast (at least in English) combined with good writing makes me forgive the little mistakes. All the miners have scouser accents to represent the cultural divide between them and the rest of society (Bohemian's didn't go to Liverpool and kidnap a bunch of them). Story and side quest actions and dialogue have some consequences, there's some character development that made me question who is good or evil and I don't mean a blue Marvel villain, it's deeper than that, I even found myself giving a Toth about the fate of some of them. There's some optional romances for Henry in there too, you can even take Henry and Capon's bromance to the next level (with a different kind of swordplay) or easily avoid that without being mean or affecting the plot, it's all very clear (and doesn't feel "woke" or like pandering, if anything it's the devs throwing a bone to the fan art that came out of the first game). The plot can be serious, heartfelt and tragic at times but it has a nice balance as there's also some funny moments too such as getting drunk, a Muslim claiming they treat women with greater respect, Henry's excuses for committing crimes and more. It's not perfect of course but there's no such thing. It takes a large chunk of poetic license for obvious narrative reasons it also tries to be historically accurate too such as the weapons and armour of the time, historical events and characters, a slimy Frenchman who's talk is far greater than his actual deeds and everyone (regardless of culture) having a huge drinking problem and btw alcoholism can be a very useful tool if used correctly. The developers unfortunately used AI translation rather than humans so bare that in mind if you're against the replacement of human beings but you're getting plenty of human-made content for your groschen here and it's clearly a beautifully crafted game made with passion but this game is not for the instant gratification generation. It's a medieval life simulator. What you need to ask yourself is: Are you okay with hardcore roleplaying? Do you mind taking care of your gear, sharpening your weapons, washing yourself and eating food regularly, carrying a lot of sacks? Are you okay spending time making stuff rather than a simple click? Are you prepared to level up both Henry (to make stuff like lockpicking easier) and level up yourself (to get the hang of some systems and combat) Do you like a bit of medieval history? Is patience one of your virtues? If not you're going to find this game an annoying awkward slog but if you like all that you're in for a real treat. Btw if you ate Man's best soup you're a monster.

KCD2 has all the necessary elements in place - impressive world, captivating story, likable characters, and a ton things to do. Core mechanics are great, good balance of stealth combat and dialogue, and many interesting quests with none feeling arbitrary or dull. review_text: It took me a while to come around to KCD2 because I usually prefer a bit more fiction and fantasy in my open world RPGs, but there's a great world to explore here that you can really get lost in for a while. Got myself hooked on blacksmithing early game, scrounging for materials I could hammer into something useful to sell, then whatever I had left after paying for my essentials I gambled away. Higher stakes gambling led me to a life of crime, building a second set of gear so I could better sneak around at night. I'd been sticking to the non-combat stuff because after a few very bad combat experiences I thought I must have been undergeared, after training up my skills and getting some adequate gear and a bit of sparring in I tried again, but still ran into major difficulties. Later found there's a target lock-on system and a controller has a much easier time with the quick directional inputs needed for the ultimate combat technique, an ability called master strike, basically a perfectly timed directional parry that counters an enemy for big damage. I felt a bit more confident in combat for a time, until unnamed forest bandits started using master strikes against me. From then on I stuck mostly to melee grapples and master strikes, there's a whole system of combo attacks for all the different weapons you can find, but the problem with any enemy able to pick up a sword being capable of hard countering any attack you can do and often one-shotting you leads you to feeling forced into playing a defensive game of master strikes, just so the enemy doesn't master strike you! After a bit of investigation it seemed a lot of people felt the same way, and modding out master strikes looks very popular. That was the biggest downside I found to the game, the world is gorgeous and interesting to explore, systems of wear and dirt and blood have you cleaning up your appearance to boost your charisma before talking to others, or you might want to keep some dirt on if you're going thieving at night, there's even a talent to make you stealthier when you're dirtier. Oh I should mention the save system, I absolutely appreciate the intention here to prevent savescumming by tying saving to a consumable item, resting or exiting the game, however in practice it means a cautious player like myself ends up spending a lot of time harvesting herbs and crafting save game consumables to the point that it feels a bit too grindy for my taste. Fortunately one of the most popular mods available adds a quicksave, while this does go against the intention of the developers, losing hours of gameplay because of stupid human mistakes felt a bit too punitive for me. Whether the solution is timed autosaves, regional autosaves or something else I don't know, but as somebody with twitchy mouse button fingers from an injury earlier in life where I can accidentally click the wrong dialogue option more than I'd like, having that quicksave mod was a lifesaver for me. The ownership system of stolen goods impressed me, where an item description would mention which town you stole an item in, so you would know where NOT to wear that stolen hat. The whole thievery system felt like a big step up from the elder scrolls system we're all used to, and I'm glad to see that evolution. Audio is excellent allround, it was cool to hear birdcalls I'd never heard before as I explored forests, the soundtrack was memorable and the voice work ranged from good to excellent. One minor complaint would be that the pool of voice actors could have been a bit larger, you will hear the same voice actors a lot, but hey that's still infinitely preferrable to AI voice acting. I'm not usually one to get super excited by historical settings in my games as I prefer a bit of fiction and fantasy, but the lands of Bohemia grew on me over time, and I'm definitely interested in a possible third Kingdom Come game. I suppose to summarise, KCD2 stepped into the open world RPG void left by Bethesda and in many ways showed them how to do a better job of it. I got this on sale for half price and that's a great deal for the experience I got. Recommended.

review_text: A fantastic sequel. Kingdom Come: Deliverance is a rare example of an RPG based on medieval historical events that doesn't make you want to stick two fingers down your throat and lose your lunch. And while it takes plenty of liberties with history, the game still brilliantly captures the spirit of the era and manages to tell a far-from-boring story about a certain bastard. Let me state right off the bat that I do not recommend playing the second part until you have finished the first. Franchise games are usually designed so that a player can jump in at any point and fully enjoy the experience, but that is not the case here. Even with the inclusion of flashbacks, there is still a wealth of information that requires having played the first game. That isn't a bad thing, though it is a relatively risky move for a big-budget project. Fortunately, the risk paid off. Compared to the first game, the combat system has been slightly simplified. Henry can now wield early gunpowder pistols, crossbows, and polearms. While the gunpowder weapons and crossbows are fun to use, I can't say anything good about the polearms. As for the main storyline, it is every bit as good as the first game's. There is still plenty of room for tense moments and drama, as well as a touch of comedy. The finale is particularly intense, though I do have reservations about the narrative's moral stance. Let’s just say I don’t quite subscribe to the philosophy that Henry should always turn the other cheek whenever possible. The game tries to teach that revenge is always wrong, yet the issue of impunity is never addressed. But that is the developer’s worldview — their message. There is nothing to be done about that. You’ll find a handful of interesting stories among the side quests. Most of them didn't really stick in my memory, though. There are a great many tedious "fetch-and-carry" tasks that serve only as a means of earning money — honestly (or close enough to it). Speaking of the economy, getting rich in the game isn't particularly difficult, provided you don't mind looting fallen enemies and selling off the gear. Your main obstacle is simply the limited amount of Groschen in the merchants' purses. As for the DLC content, I was largely disappointed. I can only praise *Mysteria Ecclesiae* for unlocking a new location and offering a reasonably interesting storyline. *Legacy of the Forge* failed to impress me due to its guild reputation system; I simply had no desire to grind just to complete a mini-storyline, especially since the opening setup made the ending all too predictable. As for *Brushes with Death*, it struck me as the most tedious and awful DLC of the lot. Instead of a mysterious artist, you get an annoying, schizophrenic whiner who constantly demands you complete the most boring tasks imaginable. His personal story is simply uninteresting. The remaining DLCs offer no narrative content — only gear that makes the early game significantly easier — so I chose not to use them. I highly recommend the game, if only for its main storyline. It is superb — as are the antagonists and allies Henry encounters along the way. Clearly, the developers left room for the franchise to continue. I look forward to the third part of the story.

review_text: Casual playthrough ~70 hours No spoilers in this review! @MatureContent ─── KCD1 was a fantastic game with its incredible story, gameplay, visuals and immersion and KCD2 is whatever is better than all that. I feel like I should start out by saying that I have seen a lot of people ask if they should complete the first game first or if they can just jump directly into KCD2, and I would highly recommend completing the first game first. It is important to understand the story and that you have developed a bond with the recurring characters in the world. The story in this game is just as important as everything else. Story The story in KCD2 takes off right after the end of KCD1, after ending the siege on Talmberg Castle, rescuing Sir Radzig and Lady Stephanie and witnessing Istvan Toth's peaceful escape. Henry and Hans Capon are sent to the Trosky region of Bohemia on a diplomatic mission to find further support and allies for the imprisoned King Wenceslas IV and this is where KCD2 takes off. Right after the opening scene, Henry and Hans Capon's party enters the Trosky region, meeting Captain Thomas and his party. They warn them of a dangerous bandit group who has been terrorizing the land. I won't say anything more about the actual story to avoid spoiling anything. Just know that it is great and a big part of why this game is so good. Combat I know there is a mixed opinion on whether or not the combat in KCD2 is better or not than in KCD1 and while I do agree that it is more nuanced, less abusable and maybe more realistic, it does have issues that the combat in KCD1 didn't have. They changed how combat works in KCD2 and it did throw me off a bit at the start. The big problem with it is that there is no good way to train combat early on. Yes, you can duel Tomcat, but it isn't a repeatable tutorial that teaches you blocking and how you keep distance and it is only just him, what you really need to train early on is how to beat multiple opponents outnumbering you. This makes combat quite unpleasant for the first many hours of this game. I guess the best advice I can give is to be patient, most of the time I died in combat it was because of bad stamina management, being too aggressive and not keeping distance. Footwork is actually very important in KCD2 combat, especially when you are alone against multiple opponents. It is very important to learn how to move around so that they do not encircle you and hit you from all sides, you want them always to be in front of you. So, I would train that first if you are struggling. However, it is also important to know, that you are very weak in early game KCD1 and you will encounter a lot of enemies you aren't necessarily supposed to beat, so it is totally okay to just run away. If you want some video tutorials, I did find these two videos helpful: Where this combat system has taken a hit in my opinion is with masterstrikes and overpowered swords. The developers really want you to play with your father's longsword in this game and therefore they made it so that masterstrikes are only possible while wielding a sword. This really sucks, if you like me don't like swords much. My preferred weapon throughout both games was the warhammer and in KCD2, while it is still very strong, it can be really hard to dodge sword wielding enemies, you will pretty much have to rely on dodging instead, but even that has its issues, especially when facing more than one opponent. Out of the swords, the two handed swords are definitely the most overpowered. From my experience, the two handed sword opponents were by far the scariest. They block better than any shielded opponent, they all masterstrike almost perfectly, they hit really hard and they often also block strikes after dodges. I can't count how many times I got knocked out after only 2 - 3 strikes from a two handed sword while wearing some of the best heavy armor in the game. It also doesn't make any sense why so many opponents wield two handed swords when it wasn't a particularly good weapon and therefore not a commonly used one in the Middle Ages. They were more of a status symbol rather than a good weapon. We should really see more polearms and maces than swords around. But two handed swords aren't the only issue combat in KCD2 has. Fist fights are utterly broken. It doesn't matter how much steel your fists are covered in and how many deadly blows you deal to your unarmored opponent's face, if the game considers him high level and skilled, fist fights can go on for minutes with your opponent showing no signs of loss of fatigue or injury. It is funny that fist fights are made this badly when they throw you into fist fights a lot throughout this story. Gameplay Beside combat, the rest of the gameplay is very similar to KCD1, sometimes maybe a bit too similar. Mission directives are still as bad as they were in KCD1 and it really makes no sense, since it isn't like they tried to go overly hardcore on the realism to where you have to always find your own way, because they will still show you on the map where to go. There is just a lot of missing and hard to read markers and badly worded descriptions in the quest log that sometimes makes it really hard to understand what to do, it is just badly designed. What I do really like though, is that this game has a lot of different quests with choices that really matter on the outcome of the world and Henry's story. You are actually given choices in this game through dialogue that might not seem like much at first, but then it turns out that if you had been more careful with your words or kept certain things to yourself, it might have saved entire villages worth of civilian lives, and I really like that. Another great change is that the AI is now a lot smarter and way more careful with you sneaking around and entering their property. They can hear and spot you from pretty far away and if they see you sneaking around, they will check if you stole anything and report your behavior. This goes hand in hand with the reputation system in all the cities where you can see how well liked or hated you are. I will say though, it is a major oversight not to have added a preview for your horse when shopping for horse equipment. It was so annoying having to make a save every time I wanted to shop for horse cosmetics. Visuals The first game was impressive for its time and still looks good today a decade later, but this second game isn't just impressive visually, it is truly breathtaking at times. The attention to detail in the environmental design is really admirable and sometimes when there is no one around and the light is just perfect, the scenery can almost look like a real picture. Conclusion Even if it isn't perfect, this is still one of the best games I have ever played and I have it ranked 6 on my top 100. It has a high learning curve, but it is so worth the time you invest into learning it. Please add jousting tournaments in the next KCD. ─── Help me out by following my Curator, I’d really appreciate it!!

review_text: Open worlds nowadays are something that actually scares a gamer like me away. You know - all those points of interest, outposts, and often pointless exploration that gives you nothing but the feeling that you just wasted your time. Well... I can say that this world sucked me in for about 90 hours before I realized I no longer wanted to explore it, having completed most of the content and then focusing specifically on the remaining main story. Compared to the first game, KCD2 is much more player-friendly. Throwing Henry into a village where it is simply easier to start was definitely the right decision. In the first game it took me about 10 hours to settle in and understand how to actually play (after which KCD2 was announced and I dropped the first game) , while here it took me only around 5 hours after the prologue. The game's meticulous mechanics initially scared me off - where after a real-life workday you basically do another job inside the game: forging swords, brewing potions, doing routine tasks. But in practice everything turned out to be much more engaging than expected. Some clunkiness and slowness are still there and do stretch the playtime (for example, the lack of auto-brewing) , yet at the same time they undeniably enhance immersion. Once you start treating it as part of the gameplay loop, the game fully pulls you in. It was a rare case where at the beginning, out of pure ignorance, I searched for videos not about quest walkthroughs, but about how to even start playing the game properly. I admit - I have become a bit too casual as a player these days. I spent around 40 hours in the starting area, either enjoying or suffering through the local rules and life simulation. At some point I got used to it and even started enjoying it. Probably because the level of detail and immersion is so high that it simply does not get boring - at least not too quickly. I would say the game strikes a very well-balanced mix of medieval simulation and gameplay, where routine itself becomes a core mechanic. Around the 40-hour mark the game started to feel slightly repetitive, and the initial excitement slowly began to fade. After the mid-game, interest in exploration unfortunately starts to decline (especially if you complete all side quests before unlocking a new region) , because there is no longer a real need to clear everything, and you become so experienced that the challenge decreases. Those tense moments - like trying to perfectly handle three opponents at once or cracking a valuable lock - become rarer, and those were some of the most memorable parts for me. Eventually you move from petty thievery in villages to infiltrating castles and estates. Still, even with the best equipment you can absolutely get wrecked by bandits, so player skill and experience still matter a lot. Around the 70-hour mark the game started to feel slightly repetitive, and the initial excitement slowly began to fade. I was honestly surprised to see that the game still runs on CryEngine, because visually it can easily rival what once was the technological benchmark - Crysis. Lush green forests, excellent sound design (although some tracks do become repetitive if you stay in the world for too long) , beautiful lighting - especially in HDR mode. The work of the artists and designers deserves special applause: you can easily get lost just admiring the scenery and architecture. This will be particularly enjoyable for players interested in medieval history. For those who want to dive deeper, there is an in-game codex and even a very entertaining official YouTube channel. The life simulation aspect, which perhaps impressed me more when I was younger, here simply works naturally and convincingly, making the world feel believable. All gameplay systems feel carefully balanced to keep the player engaged. Around the 100-hour mark the game started to feel slightly repetitive, and the initial excitement slowly began to fade. Overall, I would say the quests are about 50/50. Half of them are just regular tasks without anything particularly special, while the other half are genuinely memorable and interesting stories. There are many side quests, and some of them are surprisingly intricate in unexpected ways, which is a definite plus. Closer to the end, some narrative patterns start to repeat, but it is hard to complain too much about that. It can be frustrating when a quest has a hidden timer and you miss a trigger that locks certain content. Even after completing quests, some consequences can later be encountered in the world, which is a nice touch. Still, I occasionally had to check guides to avoid wasting too much time searching for solutions. The good thing is that most quests are not just "map markers" - they are actual stories: funny, sad, or dramatic. Some of them genuinely give you goosebumps. To avoid making the game sound perfect - quest rewards often feel more symbolic than truly useful, although this depends on your playstyle. And when the game makes you travel back and forth across the map multiple times, it stops being amusing quite quickly. The infamous "bag-carrying" quests are funny the first couple of times, but by the eighth time it becomes a bit too much. The city is huge and changes the gameplay significantly, but you will spend a lot of time running through it, and fast travel points are somewhat limited, which can feel exhausting. The game's budget occasionally shows through, mostly in the reuse of character models. And of course, the ultimate highlight of the game is its story. Everything related to the main quest and cinematic set-pieces (which are generally great even in many side quests) deserves nothing but praise. Acting, camera work, cutscenes - all are top-notch, and it is hard to believe this is all done within an in-game engine. The meticulous attention to detail in many scenes makes them truly memorable. This is exactly the level of immersion you expect from a large-scale RPG so it does not feel like just another disposable blockbuster. The story is both fun and heavy, and brutally medieval at times. The characters are memorable, and it feels genuinely sad when the adventure finally comes to an end - which is a clear sign of a truly great game. P.S. I would also like to highlight the localization - the richness of the language is conveyed very well, and native speakers will likely be satisfied.

review_text: I actually finished this game a long time ago but never had the time to talk about it. But still, this is the best RPG of 2025 in my opinion. The RPG vibe in this game is really strong. It reminds me a lot of Baldur’s Gate 3 where you can approach situations in many different ways and basically do whatever you want depending on how you want to handle things. But just like the first game, this isn’t a game for everyone. There are a lot of improvements compared to the previous game, both in graphics and overall quality of life features. Story-wise, it continues directly from Kingdom Come Deliverance 1, where the main character and his friends are tasked with delivering a letter to the lord of Trosky. A lot of people might ask if you need to play KCD1 first to understand the story of KCD2. My answer is yes and no. If you played KCD1 before jumping into KCD2, you’ll definitely feel a sense of familiarity and connection with characters like Sir Radzig and Sir Hanush. After everything the main character goes through in KCD2, there’s this feeling of relief when those characters finally show up, like you just want to say “finally.” There are also moments where you don’t only play from the main character’s perspective, and I think that part makes more sense if you already know who that person is from the first game. If you jump straight into KCD2, the game does give you short flashbacks explaining the story of the first game. But in my opinion, you won’t really feel attached to the returning characters, especially the important ones. Gameplay-wise, there are a lot of important additions that really improve the experience. One of the biggest ones is the new detection system called the Behaviour Indicator with a hare icon. It helps a lot if you want to play stealth. You can see when someone is looking for you, when you’re entering restricted areas, and other useful indicators. The combat mechanics in the sequel feel easier compared to the first game. That’s actually understandable because the story continues from KCD1 and the main character is already more experienced with combat. It only starts to feel challenging again when you try using the new weapon introduced in this game, the handgun. But still, don’t get overconfident and try fighting a big group of enemies alone. One thing I noticed in combat is that the attack directions are simplified compared to the first game, and switching stances to choose attack directions feels much smoother now. This sequel also has a lot of quests that are surprisingly funny, both main quests and side quests. The humor doesn’t always come from actual jokes. Sometimes it’s just the stupid things the characters do that make the situation awkward and funny at the same time. For example, there’s a side quest where you help two musicians get a lute. There are multiple ways to solve it. You can either steal the lute or buy it. If you buy it, the musicians will arrive safely at their destination city. But if you steal the lute, both of them end up getting arrested when they reach the city, and you can find them again later being punished there. There are also a lot of new activities added to the game. You can do horseback archery, participate in horse races where you’re free to take any route as long as you reach the checkpoints, work as a blacksmith, customize your hairstyle, mustache, and beard, and many more. With so many side quests and activities, it’s honestly hard to get bored playing this game. Most of the downsides I found are pretty minor. For example, the romance system isn’t as deep as it was in the first game. In this sequel, romance mostly leads to a single sex scene, while in the first game you could go on multiple dates with Theresa and even give her gifts. Another small detail is the alchemy system. In KCD1, when you added herbs into the pot, you could actually see them floating in the liquid. In KCD2, no matter what ingredient you add, you only see the color of the liquid and nothing else. There’s also the removal of the automatic potion crafting feature. In KCD1, once you reached a certain level you could auto craft potions. In KCD2 you have to craft them manually again, although at higher levels you can produce around five or six potions at once. But again, despite the flaws I mentioned, I had a great time playing this game for a very long time. I honestly think this game deserved to win at least one award, especially for Best RPG.

review_text: I really wanted to like this game, I gave it 32 hours of my time. As I say the game is immersive, but most of the time it feels like you are doing chores, many of the features are fun and novel but become very tiresome when done repeatedly. For example the alchemy is incredibly cool but there is no reason to make the player do the same recipe repeatedly ad nauseum because I want to save the game or make poison to make the combat playable. Allow the player to do things faster the more they do them and this would be a minor issue. I want to give the game some kudos, the main quest has some really fun stealth missions and the crime in this game genuinely feels risky and interesting in a novel way, people are quick to accuse you of things and they will put 2 and 2 together if you were sneaking around and something goes missing. However, It has to be said that 90% of the quests in this game are mind-numbingly tedious affairs; "go speak to Gerald", "I don't know nuffin about that, go speak to Jemima", hmmm where is Jemima she isn't where Gerald said she would be, guess ill aimlessly walk around looking for her where the useless map has given me a pointer towards (the entire town), 20 minutes later googles where Jemima is (in an attic only accessible from one entryway), "hmm I think I heard Jim say something about that", also cannot find Jim so you need to ask around "Ill tell you where Jim is but first please follow me and do 5000 chores while we go and walk around the countryside at 1mph". IT IS INFURITATING, this game has so little respect for my time that I just got burnt out and decided to do the main quest only (which is also plagued with these tedious mandatory quests which amount to nothing more than long dialogue chains, searching for NPCs to speak to, and hauling things around). The combat is god awful, and I say that knowing what I was getting in for. I knew the original game had challenging combat and I knew this one was supposed to be similar, but the combat isn't hard it is just either tedious slogs of blocking an NPC with limitless stamina and them blocking you, or getting ganged up on by a group of enemies which this game is NOT designed for. You might think, "well I want to use bows anyway so that shouldn't be a problem" well that has even more problems as you shoot a bandit in the leg and they sprint at you at 30mph and stun lock you to death as you try desperately to switch to your melee weapon faster than a snail. Now you can make poison that stops them from doing running (which I did) but as I mentioned previously it takes forever to do that. That said even if you do jump through those hoops, the main quest forces you into ALOT of situations where you are literally unable to use your preferred fighting style because the quest you are in is borderline impossible with a bow or any other approach than just using a sword. You will get surrounded and die or the NPC you are with will walk away and die. You might say "okay why not just use the sword", to that I say this is an RPG or at least it says it is so I should be able to approach things in different ways and not just arbitrarily lose because the game was designed with only one playstyle in mind half of the time.

I highly recommend Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, even at full price, which honestly isn’t that high compared to other games.

review_text: I'm going to get my value out of this game, but there have been some things which are quite irksome which overall give the sense of the game being an unfinished product, and at times a nuisance to play. There are many aspects about this game I really like, but at this stage I honestly don't get the hype. - Quite a misleading trailer: this feels like a medieval simulator more than an adventure-rpg I was expecting. This is done for realism according to the internet, but the following points completely break any realism in the game which makes it feel quite slow, lame and boring to play at times. - Horse combat sucks. Any mounted warrior was a fearsome opponent in those times. In KCD2, charging down even a bandit feels unintuitive, and lacks all the power and fun of smashing into an unarmoured enemy I was hoping for. - That same bandit will have unlimited stamina to chase you on your horse, at times I've galloped down a path, turned to charge the opponent, and I don't have enough time to even fully turn before he is making a swing as he has somehow managed to keep up as a fully armed and armoured "bandit" with a galloping horse (but you swing a sword 3-4 times and you are breathless on horseback). - On the note of bandits, it's not long into the game you will be heading down a path thinking "ah a fellow knight, good day sir" for it to turn out to be a "bandit" in full chainmail/armour. Going back to the "realism" aspect, it just feels immersion breaking to have such heavily armed and armoured opponents so early on (unless potentially this ties into the story somehow). The next section down you will see a man/woman travelling solo in full cloth. If the roads were that dangerous, not a single person would leave the villages/towns. Again, immersion breaking. - So much filler dialogue. While it's awesome to have the game fully voice-acted, it feels like low quality dialogue. As someone that is a huge fan of following a story in many games (disco elysium, cyberpunk, elder scrolls, Baldurs Gate 3) and will quite happily sit through hours of compelling dialogue, in KCD2 it feels lacking. Uninspired quantity over quality type of deal. So much jargon and even foreign languages are thrown in that sometimes you feel you need a translator to get the context. - Unskippable "walk/ride through the forest" scenes. Replaying this game must be so draining. Games like Skyrim you could enjoy this as the landscape was shifting and was interesting to view from different angles and kept these sequences relatively short, with a lower frequency. For KCD2 it's the bread and butter of the game: go for slow walk through repeating landscapes of thick forest, grassy meadows, more trees, more grass, pond, small pond, rocks. - Very grindy, I play on hardcore and you must create potions to be able to save. It seems the places you can stash your gear are nowhere near where you can craft items, which is even further away in the opposite direction to where you can sell them. You can’t carry all your items with you, yet you need different armour sets/crafting mats for say combat and/or speech. So before getting the horse early on it brought me close to tears with all the running up and down the same old paths to maybe sell 3 items or crafting a few potions. To gather the crafting mats you must press E on them 100 times. When you do craft items to sell, you will get next to nothing for them. At which point you are exhausted and hungry so you need to travel to fix that. This is all before you can set out to do the thing you wanted to do in the first place. I’m a fan of the hardcore experience, I love a good challenge and consider it my go-to in games and typically really enjoy the experience, whereas in this game they feel like frustrating slow additional labour that has no respect for your time. - Selling items, it is unclear who will buy/sell what and to travel for 20 mins to a town who is a blacksmith that will only buy a few weapons and none of your armour you've just lugged halfway across the map is a pain. - Part of the "realism," will be starting a fair duel with someone where they are swinging a sword at you before the game has even fully faded from black after a load screen. Or if you started the dialogue from horseback, you are being pulled off horseback. Ive tested this by saving before hand and starting a duel, even if I'm smashing the block or attack button nothing has time to prevent this first bit of damage from being taken. You have to be immediately sprinting away. Why would these combat sequences not start a few paces away from each other with your weapon already drawn? Features that are missing that makes the game feel like it's in beta stage and/or immersion breaking: - Inventory management sucks. You can design “outfits” that can be utilised for various situations (e.g. speech outfit), but as soon as you store it, the game will “forget” it was part of your outfit. No ability to mark items for sale. No ability to sort-by weight to value ratio. The armour organisation is poor considering how many slots there are. - Hardcore mode compass (that doesn’t provide cardinal directions) that can not be switched off - No auto-run feature - NPCs will go from thick eastern European accent to Obi-Wan "Hello there" as you pass them, or someone in pillory going from grovelling ruffian to "Ah, God grace us today, friend" - Sound design feels lacklustre at times. Swing a huge crushing blow to head with your sword? Sounds like someone hitting a teacup with a spoon. - A huge amount of the game mechanics are not explained in the slightest and require extra-curricular learning or forum trawling to discover. Very punishing and time consuming to get wrong. - Combat feels jank, clearly designed for a controller. Moving the mouse to change direction of a swing only to end up looking off to the side to then get your head smashed in. The tab-targeting, quick time event, run away circle back to swing once or punch once feels lame and boring. - Horseback combat sucks outside of horseback archery competitions, which I really enjoyed - Marksmanship combat is not viable in the slightest, even after being patient and levelling it. review_text: This winter holiday I took time out of my incredibly busy schedule of playing video games for half of the the day to instead play Kingdom Come Deliverance 1 and 2 for half of the day. It was meant to be, because I love both clunky RPGs and ambitious eurojank, and I ended up enjoying the first one so much that the potential review for that game that I was floating about in my mind was instantly discarded as I wanted to play the sequel that much, and here I am now, 80 hours later. While I was initially somewhat worried about the simplification of the skill system and combat system, I was very pleased that the simplification actually did things for the core systems. Combos are actually finally doable instead of being something you pray to god will happen. Combat is thus basically the same but actually works all of the time instead of when Czech Catholic Jesus decides to smile upon you. The combat system is much improved, and weapons other than longswords feel very fun and good to use, but it's insanely easy to cheese with the masterstrike and you once again end up using basically nothing but a longsword. Sometimes the perk system is quite boring, the survival skill for an example will at times just give you one hunting and one herbalism skill to pick between, instead of giving me two hunting perks to choose between to give more depth. But hey, I would much rather take three steps forward one step back than whatever slop is pushed out by triple a these days. The game is fully voiced and so is your protagonist, and as always it comes with some tradebacks. You often times only have two-three things you can tell characters and it can lead to some conversations feeling short, but on the flipside the actual voice acting is excellent so it's not a huge deal. As far as I understand this is the longest video game script in history so they tried their best, and mostly succeeded. I'm not fully convinced that RPGs should be fully voiced, but this is a game which proves what can be done with a fully voiced cast. The writing is sharp and fun. This game could've very easily fell into the trope of making everything grimdark and having everything sucks because you're in the middle of an enemy invasion, but instead the game perfectly balances it with the good in humans. Humans are complex beings and the game knows this, every good person you meet has their flaws and every bad guy has depth, no expense is spared in drilling it into you that you're simply taking a side in a civil war. I very much enjoy how every derived stat in speech this time around got a bad version. You don't just have speech but also coercion, impression has domination as its counterpart and presence has intimidation as its counterpart. This is quite honestly ♥♥♥ ingenious design by the devs, it gives real depth to the conversations in a way that never quite existed in the first one. I quite enjoyed how many different groups of Bohemian society were included in this game. The jewish community of Bohemia finally played a large role which is fitting considering how large and old it is. Due to the game taking place in larger urban settlements the game features much more Germans than the first one, both german speaking Bohemians and people from the Holy Roman Empire at large. Bohemia at this point was quite cosmopolitan and it's cool to see it reflected in the cast. A nice touch is how Moravians are always shown to speak Scottish, reflecting how they speak Czech but a much different dialect than the Bohemians you meet. Quest design was KCD's greatest strength and they don't disappoint me here. I don't think any quest really hit the highs of The House of God or Plague, but I do think overall the quality is close to those two across the board. The bar for quest design is permanently raised by KCD2 and that's probably the highest praise I could give to any game. I'm gonna go into spoilers here to skip ahead if you haven't played the game. I did enjoy the main quest and most of all I absolutely loved the encounter with Von Aulitz. You've spent two games chasing him and he admits that he's sorry about wronging you. Not only that, but he admits to remembering your entire family. The man who's been built up to be a horrible villain says that he remembers everyone he's killed, because well, it's such a rare occurance. Henry having lost any moral high ground as by this point, he had already waded through an entire ocean of blood to confront him. Absolute cinema. While the revenge plot was handled well and gracefully, I don't think the part about war being hell is particularly well handled. Every time you have the ability to actually act in an honorable way you are either paying a massive price or it bites you in the ass. I understand where they're coming from since doing the good thing is usually harder than taking the easy route, but at least give my boy Henry /some/ victories on this front. It ends up slightly muddying the message. The music and sound design are very good in the game. I wish I had more to say about it lol. I recommend this game with all of my heart, and I recommend KCD too. If you can't handle KCD's more hardcore systems I want you to know that it's totally doable to start with this one as it allows you to recap at your own pace, although for someone like me it was quite nice that aside from the start I could simply go "Yeah I know I did that in the last one, so why are you bringing this up?" in basically every conversation that required prior knowledge. Still, I do think everyone should at least try KCD, so don't be afraid of what people say about it, it's clunky eurojank but clunky eurojank are some of the best games around.

review_text: I finished Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2, and overall the experience was great. Another negative point is the limited in-game translations and the lack of official Arabic support, which makes following the story and fine details harder for many players. review_text: Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 is my favourite game of 2025. I started playing the first game this time last month, and finished with the second game just now. Daniel Vavra's experience as an industry veteran, plus unshakeable belief in their game has given us two of the best RPGs in gaming. While KCD1 was a proof of concept, KCD2 is a celebration that their concept works, and how well it can translate to being one of the best games of all time, if not the most important game of 2025. Gemini said Review: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II – A Beautiful, Tedious Mess If the goal of Kingdom Come: Deliverance II was to make me feel the crushing weight of 15th-century peasant life, then it is a resounding success. However, if the goal was to provide an engaging, functional gaming experience, it stumbles into the mud and stays there. Ambition Over Execution Developer Warhorse Studios clearly doubled down on the "hardcore realism" that defined the first game. While the scope of Bohemia is breathtaking, the performance is abysmal. Even on high-end hardware, the frame rate chugs in dense urban areas like Kuttenberg, and the pop-in is so aggressive it feels like the textures are being delivered by a medieval courier who keeps getting lost. Clunky Combat and Artificial Difficulty The directional combat system remains a polarizing nightmare. What is marketed as "skill-based" feels more like wrestling with a shopping cart in a hurricane. Henry’s movements are agonizingly sluggish, and the lock-on system is a death sentence when facing more than one opponent. The game mistakes tedium for depth; having to manage every minute detail of hygiene, hunger, and sleep doesn't add immersion—it adds chores. I spent more time looking for a bathhouse to wash off bloodstains so NPCs wouldn't scream at me than I did actually enjoying the narrative. Buggy Bohemia Then there are the bugs. From quest-breaking NPC pathfinding to physics engine freak-outs that launch Henry into the stratosphere, the game feels undercooked. It is frustrating to lose an hour of progress because your horse clipped into a fence and the "save-anywhere" feature is still tied to a limited in-game item. Final Verdict The writing and historical authenticity are top-tier, but they are buried under a mountain of technical instability and archaic design choices. KCD2 feels like a game built for a very specific type of masochist. If you enjoy fighting the controls as much as you enjoy fighting bandits, you’ll love it. For everyone else, this is a beautiful, bloated, and deeply frustrating experience that desperately needed another six months in the oven. Score: 4/10

review_text: The first time I played the original Kingdom Come game way back when it launched. I love the world, simulation but the janky combat very quickly ended my run. Then I came back years later and last month I was able to finish it. I enjoyed it but equally had a frustrating time with it. With KCD 2, things are different. Sure the combat still carries the jank and there are situations the game throws at you which is frustrating, but only this time the good parts massively outweighted the bad parts. The combat is tweaked to be faster, a bit simpler. Against one on one, it works really well, but when the game throws you 3 or more enemies, it can be frustrating super fast. Luckily enemies sort of take their turns in attacking you, unlike KCD 1. One design decision they carried over which I am not a fan of at all is their save system. I lost almost 2 hours of gameplay in KCD 2 because of it. I am absolutely not a fan of their quite to save loading, sleep or drink specific item to save. This is an open world simulation driven game, so if the stars alaign, death can come hard and fast. I immediately installed the F5 save mod, cause with it I would not have continued. The game's story, characters are signficaintly better than the first game. This is where game truly shines above the original. I cared about the characters and the plot a lot more than I did in the first game. Well written with great cast of supporting characters. The open world also took a big step up. The regions feels much more handcrafted with more attention to detail and diversity than the first game. Every where feels unique, which the first game didd not have. Also the game's biggest town, Kuttenberg is one of the most impressive medieval cities I've ever seen, bustly with life with npc's having their own schedules. All these running on a very impressive performance thanks to their modified Cryengine. The world looks stunning, only the character models and their facial expressions looks dated. Where the first KCD felt like a 6-7/10 game depending on the day. This game is easily 8-9/10 game. Really enjoyed it. Warhorse Studios, please go away from this restrictive save system, thank you.

review_text: This is, without a doubt, up there in my top 3 games in all of gaming history. Kingdom Come Deliverance 1 was certainly a sensational game which tested the boundaries of what an open world RPG truly could be, and KCD2 became the masterpiece, sanding out any rough edges of its predecessor and refining everything else. If you've come for Balder's Gate style fantasy and Skyrim magic systems, you will be disappointed -- at first. But once you gain an understanding for what this game aims to be, you will be instantaneously hooked. I've played this game four times start to finish in 2025, it's release year, and I still haven't done everything yet across all four playthroughs. If you're a history buff like me, you'll enjoy the historically accurate setting of Bohemia in the year 1403. It's a game that does very little to hold your hand; instead, it trusts YOU, the player, to set out into the world, learn and grasp the games mechanics, and understand that you are NOT "The Chosen One", the "Main Character" -- you are Henry, just a peasant, elevated to squire (from KCD1) and have an inkling more status than that of the common farmhand. Nobody cares who you are and you wont be the One Man to Save the World. You're another nameless person who will not have a page in history, but you will witness it unfold in real time and even take part in it. Real life names and real life events from 1403 history are painted seamlessly into this world while you survive inside of it. Real locations that still persist to this day are fully explorable, most NPCs (and especially named ones) have a 24 hour schedule that push the immersion even further. Everything you do from how you dress to crimes you've previously committed (...and got caught) are remembered or taken into account when people deal with you. Combat is what you make it; if you focus on swords, you'll excel with swords. If you're an archer, you'll be Robin Hood in no time. Focus on everything? You're a literal God ... with a rather small health bar. Even if you've played KCD 1 and felt that it was a bit too challenging, try KCD2 -- the devs put blood, sweat, and tears into making it accessible for everyone, but still maintained the core aspect of what makes this game stand out even among the best of the best that gaming has to offer.

review_text: I genuinely enjoyed the first 6-7 hours of the game. There were moments where Warhorse's bad habits bled through, but it was redeemable. Two key examples of that are instances where you are locked off in a zone without any items, or access to the world menu filled with 1) timed quests with poorly indicated criteria and 2) forced 'sneak' scenarios where the AI tracks you through walls. There's jank, such as from the collision physics (e.g. weird invisible walls, or major rebounding events) to the interactions with characters (e.g. in a fit of frustration I killed a citizen in a town, expecting to reload a save; instead nobody cared, the guards walked right by). The start of the game is clearly more polished than after hour 8 and lately I've found myself sipping savior flasks like they're water in a desert, just to stay ahead of the jank. What's oddest is that this doesn't feel like a sequel to Henry's journey. Yes, it's him from a story perspective, but the game literally has you 'take a bonk on the head' and lose all your levels. So things like lockpicking, which you levelled up in the previous game are suddenly frustrating again. I picked starting options for charisma, however after 12 hours I've won about 2 charisma checks (less than 5% success rate). Partially this is the heavy weighting on the choices matching the situation... That's where Mass-Effect-Syndrome kicks in. I can't read the developers mind and choose from 2-5 word options what Henry will actually do with my choice. Often the dialogue that emerges from my choices is unreasonably disconnected from my expectations when I chose it. If you don't mind the fourth wall crumbling away, roleplaying to be more about 'watching' than 'embodying,' and having an open-world of options which are suddenly restricted to 'what the devs want you to do this 5 minutes' - You could find some great experiences here. Like I said, the first 8 hours were brilliant fun (minus some janky 'Monestary-like' event; if you know, you know). [Removed recommendation to buy this on discount] Did not try the DLC, none of it appeared to be meaningful if I wasn't going to get far in the main story. And I regretted my previous Kingdom Come DLC purchases, so trust is shaky. Edit: Played a little more. The amount of 'Lock you into a zone with no items stealth missions' is out of control. The save function through 'saviour snapps' has completely broken down, because you have none! This reduces every forced stealth mission to little more sophistication than Mario World; die, reset at save point (minutes, hours ago?), attempt to recreate the last scenario that almost worked and try again. At least in Mario the AI doesn't telepathically transmit your detection to foes throughout the map that drop what they're doing and sprint straight at your hiding spot. The argument for realism falls apart with janky and outdated mechanics. I miss choices. I miss open world. I miss roleplaying. I miss realism. The only tag for this game you can trust is 'single player.' After about 12-20 hours you arrive in an actual open world game. It's grueling to get there (unless you love Stealth games like Thief, but then with this games marketing why would you have bought this?). A few hours later the game unveils Masterstrike, just like in KCD1, and the same crippling combat jank that overtook KCD1 propagates like a plague through this rendition. Farmers, bandits, drunkards all with Masterstrike. It's modestly turned down in KCD2 versus KCD1 (happens less than every single attack). Nevertheless it negates any concept of combination strikes. It's unclear what, if anything, is going through the minds of the developers. They wasted wages for their team to develop combo systems that were ultimately 'scrapped' by the Masterstrike. Last straw Warhorse. I'll buy no more games after this one. Coffin is all nailed up. Maybe try making point and click adventures where you don't need a combat system?

review_text: 💬For the past few days/weeks, I've been completely immersed in Kingdom Come Deliverance 2, and the game has captivated me in almost every aspect. 🎮The storyline unfolds somewhat later from the climax of the original story. Henry as well as Jan Ptacek are trying to communicate a vital message regarding the insurrection against King Sigismund, but a robbery of their property leads them to the Trosky Castle's fortifications without any gear or official papers. The narrative develops through three parts: Trosky, Kutná Hora, and the end. The tale is rich in tension, treason, and sensational scenes - the whole spectrum from the saving of Ptacek to the stunning conclusion with the coming of the allied army. The account is made in a way that follows a logical sequence and is easy to comprehend even if one is not very familiar with the political situation of the medieval times. The siege of the fortress is definitely striking, especially when there isn't much hope left and the supplies are close to being exhausted. It does not exclude anyone, the audience has to sympathize with the characters for they are in the same situation as the characters have to go through their hardships. The whole storyline could be compared to the movies of Guy Ritchie. A bunch of robbers with a good heart comes up with the most extravagant schemes, but everything ends in chaos! The main combat system has undergone minor changes in its design. Moreover, it has been enriched with the addition of new weapons such as polearms, crossbows, broadswords, and boomsticks (squeakers). Henceforth, combat has been more dynamic - leg strikes have been changed to abdomen thrusts, and counterattacks demand higher skill levels. The interaction of the enemies is more natural and the impact of damage is quite apparent. To summarize, the whole combat experience is more dynamic compared to the one in the first game. The new features consist of weapon forging, the option to walk through bushes, and various random encounters along the way - from unfortunate bandits to a frightening meeting with the "Death." The world's response to your actions is, in fact, the most remarkable part. Support a needy person - he could come back to you later with a good deed. Misbehave with a trader of great importance - expect to be charged extra or to lose completely your access to scarce items. Your adventures are talked about everywhere, and the quest choices (even insignificant ones) can surprise you with their consequences at the most unanticipated times. I helped some refugees to get rid of the bandits once, and then they took part in the defense of a castle - such events are just too intriguing for me. The ending and the fate of certain characters hinge on past choices even in situations that initially seemed to be of little importance. This gives the impression of a genuinely vibrant world, not merely a list of missions. Although the graphics are not significantly different from those in previous versions, the Czech scenery still looks great. The atmosphere is especially created by the towns and fortresses. The music is right on spot with the plot, and the optimization is really great - the game works without a hitch even on average computers. One curious thing is the different menu splash screen that changes according to your level of play. Additionally, the technical side has almost no problems, thus being considered almost perfect. 👍Positive. - Immersive, historically grounded world - Deep, skill-based combat - Rich narrative & meaningful choices - Huge open world with lots of content 👎Negative. - Learning curve - Combat can feel inconsistent - UI or menu navigation may be clunky - Some minigames or mechanics feel fiddly 🧾Summary. Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 is a one-of-a-kind RPG that features not just profound gameplay but also an absorbing narrative. Here everything is of the highest quality: an interesting storyline, thoroughly designed characters, enticing adventures, and a lively universe. 🎯9/10 💬The game really is a delight to play; the developers' commitment is evident in every aspect. I would not be shocked if it gets the title of Game of the Year - it is really worthy. Naturally, there will be some that will not appreciate the medieval setting or the RPG style, and for total immersion, it's recommended to start with the first part. However, if you are in doubt about its worth, the response is a loud Yes!!, without a doubt!

review_text: Kingdom Come Deliverance II is one of those rare RPGs that feels less like a game world and more like a time machine. From the very moment you step back into late Medieval Bohemia, the game’s commitment to the historical time period is obvious. Landscapes and towns are modeled on real locations, armour is modeled from surviving musuem pieces of that era, Peasents/nobles in towns have daily routines mapped out, heck even the night sky has been modeled to be somewhat accurate to early 1400 Bohemia. This is not absolute however, balancing historical accuracy with enjoyability is always a tricky affair, and unless you are in the minority and you are a hard core history buff some things always get sacrificed to make the game enjoyable for all. It could be major things like there not being any children in the game at all, or smaller things like carrots anachronistically being orange. Where the dev's focused their efforts on being historically accurate they did so with spades. It’s this obsessive attention to detail that gives the game its immersibility. Getting back into the saddle with Henry is as punishing at times as it is rewarding. The combat is deliberate and skill-based like the first game. Positioning, stamina, and timing matter. Do things right and you feel like you can cleave your way through an entire army, but miss the parry or allow yourself to get riposted and you find yourself getting sent straight back to the load screen. The continuation of Henry's story feels natural and is very well written. The game excels at making large-scale events feel personal. You’re not saving the world you’re trying to survive and find your place in it. Choices matter and the story is filled morally ambiguous choices for the player to make, and they rarely feel simple or clean. The two regions are a big step up from the first game, The regions are overall quiet and beautiful to traverse, the notable fortresses are very well detailed internally as well as externelly but these pail in comparison to the standout location Kuttenberg. A bustling silver-mining city and economic hub, packed with shops, guilds, quests, and citizens which make the city feel dense and alive. These elements come together to make Kuttenberg arguably one of the most detailed cities ever built in an RPG. Overall, KCD2 to me isn't just a sequel, it’s a refinement of a very specific vision. A grounded, historically rooted RPG that prioritizes immersion. One that if you’re willing to embrace, it will offer you one of the most authentic RPG experiences ever created. 10/10
