review_text: Game of my life so far. It's like Stardew Valley for me in the sense that I play it in game day by in game day. I have a clear idea of what I want to achieve in the current day, but in medieval bohemia and in first person. My early game routine tends to be waking up, drinking alcohol (responsibly of course, because being addicted is a thing), selling potions, brewing the same amount of potions that I sold, working on quests, sleeping for 8 hours. While working on with the day, random encounters - most of them are hostile -are scattered in the map too. The minigames are robust, my favorites are alchemy and forging weapons. This game is a big canvas to do stuff. I love that the npcs have routines, that they gossip as to what you've been doing - if you've been such a menace or a helpful person, i love that the npcs may actually die and that they cry over their loved ones dying, I love that when I meet them later on, they may be more trusting of me because of what i did for them or did for their neighbor. etc I love that the quests have multiple solutions to them, even having unique dialogs about it. If you ever wonder "what if i do this instead?", you'd be surprised that the game accounted for it and would allow you to do it that way. I love the stats and perk system in the game, it's rewarding and feels good. You just keep on playing the game, and the respective stats will increase. You don't have to grind anything, but you can if you want to, and it doesn't break the game that much, there is a bit of scaling happening: some npcs would have better armor/weapon depending on how high your main level is. For combat, it caters different kinds of people: It caters to people who enjoy using unblockable attacks, it caters to people who wants to be fancy and do flashy combos, it caters to people preferring to kite enemies with ranged weapons, the combat lock on can be misunderstood at first making it super frustrating at first, but once you understand what the lock on is for, how to unlock it, how to have it etc, you'd understand that the combat system is really fun and fair. For weapon choices, they're really good: swords are the best because of the unblockable attack, but they're the worst without it. Polearms are ok now, but the combos are still lacking, you can only have 4 combos with them, 2 combos are free lol. The main quest is really good, the sound track amplifies the moment in this game a lot it takes them from 90 to 200! I'm not elaborating on it more, I just hope people pushes through and experience all of the main quests. They can feel tiring because the main quests go on bulk, you will have open world privilege most of the time, but when you don't, that means you're locked in to doing main quests only for a certain amount of them. This game is wonderful, it looks great, it runs great on my budget desktop from 2020. 80-120fps dlss quality, high and experimental settings 1080p. Highly recommend.

review_text: At 129 hours at the time of writing this, I think I've seen just about all the game has to offer on a single playthrough. That's not to say I've seen it all, as there's quite a bit of variety in the delivery and handling of much of the dialogue and missions can play out. It's a bit hard to wrap my head around all my thoughts on the game after weeks of play, but I can safely say this has been one of the best titles I've ever played and the game was done a disservice in the 2025 awards. The game looks great, runs great and has a solid, history influenced narrative that both keeps you moving along while at the same time giving you plenty of room to breathe and explore. Most of the gameplay mechanics are great and the attention to detail is constant. Voice acting is delivered well by the main cast, though there are a handful of actors that have a ton of multiple parts; a little more variety there would have been nice. Combat is challenging and something I never truly excelled in, but, much like the first title, it is something you tend to grow into with both practical experience and in game skill growth. The tale of frail to menace is just as strong in KCD2 as it was 1. I also enjoyed the little mini games, alchemy and following cooking instructions was particularly intersting, though I imagine some might find tedious. It's particularly fun to see just how many of your actions large and small impact things: little things like stinking to high hell can ruin your stealth missions as they smell you coming, wearing freshly stolen goods in front of their owner won't go unnoticed and major plot points in a few missions can change based on how thorough you are beforehand. As far as technical issues, there were little. One constant one I had was that all cut scenes would run at near 0 FPS until I broke and returned focus to the game; double tapping the windows key was enough for that. Also had one CTD in my playthrough; not too shabby. When it comes to the DLC, I'd highly recommend the complete package. The two narrative based ones add probably 20-30 hrs of additional content and the blacksmithing one is a bit narrower in focus and a bit more open ended grindy, but if you tackle that one during your playthough it is far more enjoyable than I imagine it would have been on its own at release after beating the game before it. There is no drop in quality throughout the title and the DLC continues that trend. One last little point worth mentioning that you don't see much these days is how friendly the game is to pausing the title. Mid cutscene, mid sentence in dialogue, mid combat, whatever; very convenient when interrupted by work, spouse, kid, bad weather, whatever. This is a lot of words not necessarily saying a lot in particular, but the game warrants a thumbs up and all the praise people can heap on it, so I'm adding some more. Get the title and enjoy it; I'd strongly recommend playing through the first one though first. While not required (the game will use some flashbacks and dialogue to broadly fill in the player to the broad strokes of the first title), KCD2 is simply KCD1 improved, so if you're likely to enjoy 2, don't rob yourself of playing through 1. The end.

review_text: I can honestly say that I have fallen in love with "Kingdom Come: Deliverance II". From the moment I stepped into its world, I was hooked: the attention to detail, the freedom to play Henry however I wanted, and the way the world reacts to your choices just made me feel like I was living in it, not just playing a game. I’ve lost track of hours wandering, experimenting, failing, and figuring things out, and every session still feels fresh. Few games have grabbed me this deeply, and I keep finding new little details that make me appreciate it even more. // Review after 100% completing the game. // Gameplay The game is honestly a lot of fun, but it definitely leans heavily into realism, so I can see it not clicking with everyone. Combat is slow and deliberate, more about timing and positioning. You can't just mash buttons and expect to win. It has a noticeable smoother feel than the first game, with less clunkyness, while still maintaining the heavy, grounded feeling. Controls felt good to me on both mouse & keyboard and controller, which was a nice surprise. There are a wide variety of mechanics to explore: alchemy and survival, gear maintenance, reputation, and crime system - and they all play a meaningful role in how your journey unfolds. The game rarely holds your hand, which is great if you like figuring things out on your own, but it also means you’ll probably mess up a few times before things begin to make sense. Quests are easily one of the best parts. They're open-ended, with multiple ways to handle them, and rarely feel like basic "go there, kill that" filler. You can talk your way through situations, sneak around, or just force your way in, and the game actually reacts to what you do. It makes your choices feel meaningful, and sometimes the consequences don’t show up until much later. Story & World The story remains true to real historical events, which makes it believable, but it still manages to tell a more personal story through Henry. His journey is becoming more complex this time around, and your choices can have an impact on how people perceive and deal with you. The world itself is probably one of the game's biggest strengths. It actually feels like it's alive. NPCs go about their daily routines, react to your reputation, and remember what you've done. If you cause trouble, people notice. If you build a good name for yourself, that can open doors later on. It all comes together in a way that makes the world feel alive, not just something you're passing through. The writing is nicely balanced too. It handles the heavier historical side of things well, but still leaves room for smaller, more personal moments. Even side quests feel worthwhile, and a lot of them put you in situations where there isn't a clear "right" choice, which makes them more interesting. Visuals & Audio The game's visuals are incredible, and it's easily one of the most realistic worlds out there today. The environments are packed with detail, whether you’re walking through thick forests, muddy villages, or busy towns, and everything feels grounded and believable. The lighting and weather also play a significant role in making the world feel more alive from one moment to another. Animations are noticeably better this time around, especially during conversations and combat. Characters feel more natural and expressive, which helps a lot during the more emotional parts of the story. The sound design is just as solid. The small details like wind in the trees, people talking in the distance, and metal clashing are enough to draw you in without being overwhelming. The music is a perfect fit for the setting, adding to the mood when needed and never getting in the way. Performance & Technical Quality Overall, the performance is fairly good, especially considering the size and detail of the game. Frame rates stay consistent most of the time, and it feels well-optimized on modern hardware. I was getting around 80 FPS on High settings, which is honestly great for a game this big. The game has some minor issues, such as textures popping in late or small AI issues, but nothing that really gets in the way. Compared to how the first game launched, KCD2 feels a lot more polished and stable. Design & Balance The game really leans into realism and allows you to do things your way, which can make it feel tough at first, especially if you're new to this kind of RPG. It puts a lot of emphasis on preparation and role-playing. What you wear, how you talk to people, even how you act in general all have an impact. The game's difficulty is largely influenced by how you approach it. If take your time to train, earn money, and improve your skills, things will go much smoother. If you rush in without being prepared, things can quickly go wrong. One nice thing is that it doesn't lock you out of the main story based on your level, so you can move things forward at your own pace without being forced to do side content. Some of the systems can feel a bit unforgiving, no doubt. But if you stick with them and give them time, it ends up being quite rewarding. Replayability Replayability is without a doubt one of the game's biggest strengths. You have a lot of freedom in how you shape Henry: whether you play him as an honorable knight, a sneaky thief, or something a bit more shady. Your style can have a significant impact on the outcome of every walkthrough. Quests can play out in different ways, there are usually multiple ways to handle objectives, and you can interact with (or even get rid of) a lot of NPCs if you want to. Because of that, each run ends up feeling a little different. Add in how much content there is, and you’re looking at dozens, if not hundreds, of hours if you really get into it. Value for Price Great value for what you get. There's a lot of content here, and it's not just filler - it's detailed, well-constructed, and worth the time. There are few games that go as deep with immersion and player choice at this scale. Overall Impression & Recommendation In all honesty, it's a 10/10 if you're a fan of immersive RPGs. It takes what the first game did and improves on it in all the right ways, feeling more polished and detailed without losing what made it special in the first place. That being said, it's definitely not for everyone. The game relies heavily on realism, has a slower pace, and doesn't simplify its systems, which may be a bit too much if you're used to more straightforward RPGs. But if it resonates with you, it's something special. If you're willing to follow its rules, it can be a game that can truly stay with you.

review_text: Recommended: Yes (Base Game) / DLC: Optional "A thrilling Souls roguelike loop, but chaotic timers and brutal RNG demand frequent breaks." With just shy of 200 hours logged alongside my co-op partner, I can say Nightreign offers a genuinely exciting, high-stakes spin on the Elden Ring formula. The transition into a roguelike structure brings a lot to like right out of the gate: built-in cooperative play without hoops to jump through, an intuitive button layout, zero fall damage for high-mobility traversal, and that unmistakable, exhilarating rush when you finally topple a brutal boss. However, the frustrations here hit very differently than they do in standard Elden Ring. In the mainline game, hitting a wall rarely kills your momentum—you can always explore elsewhere, level up, and feel continuous progression. In Nightreign, the combination of harsh timers and wild RNG can make a bad run feel intensely discouraging rather than rewarding. What Works Smooth Co-op & Mechanics: The built-in multiplayer makes tackling runs with a dedicated partner seamless (and spares you from rolling the dice on random matchmaking). The controls feel tight, and removing fall damage lets traversal stay fast-paced and fluid. The Boss Rush High: Overcoming the initial slate of bosses through coordinated team play delivers that peak FromSoftware satisfaction. Addictive Run Variety: When the loot RNG aligns and your builds click, hunting down targets across the shifting landscape is a blast. What Frustrates Brutal RNG Meets Strict Timers: When drop luck goes south while a countdown forces your hand, the resulting pressure shifts from fun tension to outright demoralization. Losing a run simply because the loot refused to cooperate stings a lot more than a standard death in Elden Ring. Map & Loot Segregation in the DLC: Separating the expansion locations and gear pools from the base map feels counterintuitive for a roguelike that thrives on variety and synergy. Steep Wall for Added Bosses: While we conquered the base game bosses, the expansion's added encounters are tuned to an extreme level. They currently feel out of reach without near-flawless RNG, leading to long breaks away from the game rather than the eager "one more run" feeling of earlier hours. Final Verdict: Nightreign is an easy recommendation for fans of tactical co-op and roguelike runs who want fast-paced, high-stakes combat. The base game is deeply satisfying to clear, but be prepared for heavy RNG fatigue. The DLC is fun if you want an extreme challenge, but it is entirely optional to get full value out of the game.

review_text: What to say about a game while having 1300+ hours in it, not even 1.5 Years after its' release date... The Nightreign team has developed a simple yet beautiful gameplay loop capable of giving FromSoft's Classic formula of incredible frustrations, skill issues, and sweet hard-earned victories - but within a typically 1 Hour game cycle. Hosting a beautiful cast of playable characters (and the amazing Iron Menial), all equipped with interesting mechanics and storylines - I had the best time coming to further understand each of them and what they stood for within the context of the greater plot. You may not enjoy playing some of them as much as others, but all their stories are a beautifully-weaved narrative set in this (supposedly) alternate-ER timeline. Deepest thanks and respect to the dev team - I hope you enjoyed making and maintaining this game as much as my friends and I enjoyed playing it. Can't wait for ED Heolstor, right guys? (':

review_text: Something tells me this one was forced upon FromSoftware, kind of like how Marathon and Anthem were forced on Bungie and BioWare. But it seems like the team still managed to make it unique in some way. The characters are cool, and the new bosses are sick. Still, it really makes me think: what if this had just been DLC for the base Elden Ring? Or a separate game series? Or hell, what if they'd worked on it more and turned it into a full-fledged Elden Ring 2? Instead, we have what I'd call FromSoftware's introduction to speedrunning. If you're not playing optimally and using the characters the way they're meant to be played, you'll struggle. It's not that you can't succeed, but it won't be easy, and sometimes it won't even be fun. 6.5/10 I still have fun but i don't think i can recommend it to just anybody.

review_text: Awful experience for someone new to the game. You will feel basically useless as you hope someone has a clue where to go, and what route to take. If you try to pick where to go, someone else will decide to go to another spot. Knowing where to go, and the proper route basically decides if you are going to win or not, since you won't be nearly as powerful as you should be, and you will be less familiar with the bosses as a new player. Figuring that route on your own is nigh impossible given the time limit. You will basically have to learn from other people, and hope you can actually keep up. Identification of where teammates are is really difficult. The compass isn't enough, and if your teammate is close by, but above or beneath you, it's difficult to tell where they are, without looking all over the place. It would be nice if there was an icon on the edge of the screen to help point out where they are, when they go running off ahead, thinking they are leading, but leaving everyone else behind instead. The name above their character isn't enough for this type of game. Since it's geared towards co-op play, it will be difficult to learn what you are doing because you cannot respawn and replay the boss. You have to go through the whole run and then get another try. I pretty much felt like a burden. I consistently never get anything geared to my character. I'll play duchess and end up with a colossal sword in each hand. The vertical traversal feels awful. The constant button mashing to jump up tombstones feels ridiculous, like this is some mario platformer. One of the most frustrating parts of this game is missing some jump, and falling a massive distance that basically makes you useless to your teammates as you try to find a way to where they are. I feel like this game requires you to study videos to have a chance of being competent. Either that or you have some friend show you through it. Not really enjoying it as much as Elden Ring. I'll play it more I'm sure, but I wish there was an easier entry for people trying to learn how it works, and how to route properly.

review_text: How big is the gap between Depth 4 and Depth 5? In my personal experience, the main difficulty of Depth 4 lies in the Night King battle. As early as Depth 3, players have figured out how to farm by fighting Sinners. Unless you mess up extremely badly in the early game, you can almost always get through the opening phase. However, starting from Depth 4, squishy classes can no longer tank certain moves from the Night King—sometimes you still die even with full damage reduction stacked. By the time you reach Depth 5, most players have fought the Night King enough times. Apart from the Ice Dragon and the Fairy boss, it’s really hard to wipe on the other fights. The only thing I fear about the Ice Dragon is the unmarked ground spikes—the ones that only pop up right under your feet the very second they’re about to hit. The other nightmare scenario is just bad RNG: no good damage-related relics, and your teammates are playing classes like Snail or Hermit that can’t interrupt the big cast. Once the Ice Dragon gets its second ultimate off, it’s basically a slow, guaranteed wipe. Some people say Depth 5 feels no different from Depth 4. If you’re playing squishy classes like Hermit or Snail, you still die from one single hit either way. The only real difference is that Depth 5 drops way better relics. After all, a truly skilled player can clear Depth 5 even without any relics at all—it just takes a lot longer because of the lack of damage.

review_text: tl;dr - CONDITIONAL RECOMMENDATION: recommend if you value atmosphere, soundtrack, cryptic storytelling, and artful landscapes, characters, and weapons on the same level as gameplay. Colorful and deep design on the nightfarers and nightlords. Elements of soulslike, survival, roguelike, and open world (among other genres) come together in an experimental, cluttered way. Although the game is intended for 3 players, it features a solo-mode that feels rather unbalanced due to certain bosses being spesifically designed to be taken on by a group of 3 players. I like the game for its artistic presentation of its story and themes (the soundtrack is very good as well), but from a gameplay-centered perspective, I didn't really vibe with the messy genre blend. Having the last 45 minutes of my life wasted because I got jumped by an off-screen Gladius isn't a good time. I wonder how it feels to play this as your first fromsoftware game. That must be immensely painful.

review_text: I loved Elden Ring so I bought this game. It is fun at first, the initial standard boss fights are all possible without really having to worry about relics. There's a character for each playstyle and you can further customize them with said relic effects. However once you beat the standard bosses and get into deep of the night as well as the ever-dark variants relics become absolutely necessary. If you don't enjoy grinding you likely won't get really good effects for your relics. As far as I can tell no additional bosses or items are coming to the game anytime soon and that leaves a-lot to be desired in terms of adding things from the other souls games. Overall, Solid game would recommend to pick up with a friend on sale.

review_text: While this game does suffer from a lot of missed potential, ELDEN RING NIGHTREIGN and its DLC provide hundreds of hours of fun; it easily kept my friends and I hooked and grinding for months. The main idea of NIGHTREIGN is to condense the classic ELDEN RING experience down into a 45 minute run with randomized bosses, points of interest and weapons, and make it cooperatively playable up to 3 people. ELDEN RING NIGHTEIGN isn't exactly a roguelike, but it definitely plays like one. And a kind of weak one, at that. It's not a big deal at all when you first start playing, but becomes more apparent as you rack up hours. This game's biggest flaw is its lack of randomization in its experiences, leading to fatigue and runs ultimately not feeling significantly different from each other. This problem is helped by the addition of the DLC's content, but there are still many "What If?" moments. What if they could have added Shadow of the Erdtree weapons? What if there were twice as many legacy Dark Souls bosses? What if the POI's weren't so formulaic? If you are a massive roguelike fan, you may find other games in the genre to far surpass NIGHTREIGN's random elements. Basically everything else is so great though. The FROMSOFT combat and gameplay formula is more fun than ever, with new additions to the sandbox unique to NIGHTREIGN. The super sprint added brings the pace up to a blistering level and it's addicting to dart around the map. All playable characters are so much fun to play and master, with different costumes to acquire and relics to customize your loadout. All the bosses pose a feasible challenge and remain a blast to learn. NIGHTREIGN's best aspect are the ten final NIGHTBOSSES. They are completely original bosses with insane spectacle, challenge, and sense of reward for overcoming. Taking on each one and finally managing to conquer them alongside two friends still hasn't lost its luster. These are some of the greatest bosses FROMSOFT have ever created. Most of them have an alternate 'hard mode' version, with difficulty cranked to 11 and insane alternate movesets. Post launch, FROMSOFT added a "ranked mode" called Deep of Night, and it provides a massive challenge as well. This hard mode, alongside the added "hard mode" bosses offer tons of replayability. This game is an absolute blast, and will remain in rotation with my friends for a while. If you can't get enough FROMSOFT and you have a few friends willing to take the plunge, this is an easy recommend.

review_text: Man, this is a tough one. There is a lot to love here for Elden Ring fans, but I'd say the game misses it's mark overall. Obviously, you've got the same fantastic Elden Ring combat. Plenty of familiar bosses are here, and in particular there are a few from the Dark Souls franchise which I thought was an awesome addition. Characters are extremely diverse and allow you to approach your favorite play-styles in unique ways when incorporating the special characters abilities. There is a character here for most everyone, and its fun to switch it up and improve at all of them. Nightlords are, for the most part, really fun and engaging fights that demand your attention and teamwork (there are some stinkers though, you know the ones). Leveling system being more streamlined compliments the new faster-paced gamplay nicely. And skins are pretty cool overall too. BUT...there is not even close to enough variation in content here. Build variety is technically there but so many effects and passives are just boring and enhance your character in the most minuscule ways. Relics are just like the effects; there are a FEW interesting ones but by and large they are boring and unneeded for success in the game. Honestly, by the time you have beaten all the Nightlords for the first time, you will have seen basically the entire game. The amount of map seeds in the game is a JOKE, and the boss pool is laughably small considering all the bosses they could have used but didn't. The 'rare' occurrences in the game are quite frankly TOO rare, to the point where you almost never see them in any given session. Then, instead of maybe adding more stuff to the game, they made Deep of Night mode instead, which is an absolute grind-a-thon that gets unendingly frustrating even as early as Depth 2. We're SOOO close guys! This is a fun and engaging Elden Ring spin-off, but it is BEGGING for more variety. I have had fun with it, enough for me to still leave a positive review, but saying I recommend it would be a huge overstatement. Give it some time to cook if you are on the fence, hopefully the upcoming DLC will fix some of these problems.

review_text: Good Spinoff, Bad Roguelite I always have a mixed feeling towards Elden Ring Nightreign. The extraction-style gameplay shuns me away for quite a while. But after playing it through, I certainly feel less dismissive about it. On one hand, it's admirable to see FromSoft step out of their comfort zone and try something different. Yet on the other hand, Nightreign is not a particularly good roguelite experience. Even some of the indie brethren can eclipse its effort. Still, Nightreign is an interesting experiment on mixing up different mechanics from popular genres. It's better to bring a friend or two along. Solo is certainly doable, but the learning curve is steep. Thing I Like About Elden Ring Nightreign: The Raids: Now I think about it. The Radahn fight in the base game is definitely the prototype behind Nightreign. You and your friends working together to take on (or cheese the hell out of) a big boss is one of the best moments in the Souls series. Nightreign tries to expertize this experience, and I say it's a job well-done. Scout the map, plan the route, conquer locations, loot the gear, run away from the shrinking zone, defeat two ring bosses, tackle the Nightlord and fail miserably (prerequisite). A complex process on the surface, but with friends you can easily make it fun. Moreover, teamwork has never been more important than ever. Who draws aggro, who deals damage, and when to rotate the roles for breathing room, and stop going after the Bell-bearing A-hole are key to a successful expedition. Preset Characters: I am a little bit sad you can't create your own character, but at least the eight available ones are very unique. Each of them offers a distinctive playstyle and fulfills a certain role in your team. You can find your preferred playstyle in these characters. Moreover, their backstories are also interesting, told through FromSoft's usual storytelling shenanigans, except this time it's rather clear and more involved in the player's part. I like how these people feel like a bunch of misfits bound together by a shared goal. Yet, through remembrance you can easily see how their fate intertwined with each other. Combat QOL Improvements: Now these are something that sparks excitement not only for the game but also for future titles. Nightreign has a lot of improvements on both combat and movement. Instant sprint offers a new way to close gaps and make distance. Jump has been even better at dodging attacks since the inclusion of kick/wall jump. Enemies' grab attacks are now unifyingly color-coded for easier recognition. There's also a red marker on the character indicating who is being targeted by the boss right now. Performing a critical attack no longer makes the enemies invulnerable, meaning your teammates can continuously wail on their downfalls. Whips, shields, and even bows can now backstab, and so on. Things I Like And Dislike About Elden Ring Nightreign: Shifting Earth: Nightreign's map is pretty stale. The random generation doesn't alter the map layout much, so the developers create this feature to mitigate the problem. Unfortunately, Shifting Earth only achieved half of its goal. For the good parts, these new biomes drastically change parts of Limveld. They offer new terrains, special points of interest and a unique secret buff for you to uncover. However, the way the developers implement leaves a lot to be desired. They are randomized one "period" at a time. The game rolls one event, and the next few runs you will always have this event active (unless you sleep). These new terrains also suffer from the same issue as the mainland—fixed placement and fixed layout. I really wish their locations could be randomized, and the other terrains could have the chance to spawn as sub-areas. Nightlords: Just like the eight playable characters, all eight Nightlords are fantastic in their own way. The classic orchestral bombardment is in full force. Their presentations are easily the most stunning out of all the Souls series. Their move sets are designed to deal with multiple targets at once, and there are actual interesting mechanics woven in to make the fights more dynamic. The only thing I really dislike about the boss design is the cinematic attack—you know, the one where you see the boss fly away and you wait for almost 10 seconds until it lands that one attack. This is a trend I wish Fromsoft would refrain from using too much. It only works once. The second and third times onward just feel like a waste of time. Oh, and also fck Maris. Things I Dislike About Elden Ring Nightreign: Relics: It's farming blood gems in Chalice Dungeons all over again...except it's worst and takes longer to get. I believe the purpose of the relics is to make your early game as smooth as possible. If that's the case, then there are two problems. First of all, the pool is heavily diluted by tons of weak or borderline useless attributes. Even if you manage to roll a stat-boosting one, the number is still too negligible to make a difference. Second, everything is completely randomized. There is no way to reroll attributes, so the only way to get better relics is gambling. Builds: This might be me not adjusting my mindset accordingly, so take it with a grain of salt. Despite introducing character abilities and passive bonuses, the build flexibility is surprisingly rigid in Nightreign. One of the beautiful things in Souls games is how easily and freely you can change your build. Nightreign doesn't do that. All characters have set stats, and leveling up gives a universal increase to every stat. As a result, it's easier to lean into what the character is already capable of instead of exploring other possibilities. Passives on weapons might enable a certain degree of availability, but it will never be half as good as a dedicated build. 中文小簡評 一開始《艾爾登法環黑夜君臨》讓我五味雜陳,強調快速清塔撿裝躲圈的設計與FromSoft一貫照自己步調細細探索的作風大相逕庭,讓我望之卻步,直到夏特才決定入手來體驗,把玩幾場後我算是體悟出箇中滋味。《黑夜君臨》是FromSoft踏出舒適圈的一次大膽嘗試,將既有的魂系戰鬥與現今較熱門遊戲類別的機制加以融合,的確打造出獨具風味的遊戲體驗,這份勇氣值得嘉許。然而以roguelite的角度去看的話機制非常不成熟,幾乎被其他獨立同儕輾壓。不過最好還是拉個朋友一起入坑,單人打可行,就是學習曲線過於坎坷。 喜歡的點 現在想來,《艾爾登法環》裡的碎星Boss戰應該就是《黑夜君臨》的藍圖吧!和朋友一起挑戰(或用各種外鄉手段)打Boss絕對是魂系遊戲中最最棒的體驗之一。《黑夜君臨》在這點上就發揮的淋漓盡致,一起觀察地形、一起規劃路線、一起分工、一起跑圈撿裝、一起打黑夜王然後再一起被壓在地上磨擦。 這也是歷代魂系中最講究團隊合作的重要性,誰負責坦傷、誰負責輸出、何時要輪替吸仇恨製造喘息空間、誰要去阻止隊友在等級太低的情況下還敢去打鈴珠獵人和龍形大樹守衛,這些流程看似複雜,但和朋友一同經歷就能充分享受其中樂趣。 不能自創角色有點可惜,但遊戲提供的八位主角各具特色,各自擁有鮮明的定位與專精的武器,絕對能讓你找到自己心儀的玩法。此外,他們的背景故事也很有趣,除了FromSoftware一往的敘事手法外,也加入了許多互動要素,讓你能更清楚了解他們。我意外地滿喜歡這群看似格格不入的烏合之眾,只是因為共同的目標而聚集在一起。然而,透過追憶你就能明白他們彼此的命運緊密交織在一起。 不過我最喜歡的還是本作在戰鬥方面做的各種改良,像是瞬間衝刺讓你能快速逃離或拉近與Boss間的距離、、敵人抓技有用更鮮明的特效顯示、Boss打出大招時也能清楚看出誰被鎖定、爆擊或背刺敵人時隊友可以無視無敵禎盡情輸出等,這些都是很棒的設計,讓人非常期待FromSoft未來遊戲的走向。 又愛又恨的點 《黑夜君臨》的地圖變化隨機性低且非常單調,通常走過一次就能輕鬆記起來,因此製作團隊想用「特異地形」來做點變化,我只能說這項設計只做到一半。先說優點,特異地形的確有效改變部分主地圖的地形,加入了新敵人、新地點以及專屬隱藏增益讓你能在規劃路線上做些改變。但是呢,特異地形是以隨機「週期性」的方式出現, 一旦條件生成你接下來的所有行動都會是出同一個地形,而且這些特異地形也跟主地圖有同樣的問題:位置與分部始終固定,沒有隨機地點,也沒有隨機生成特殊子區域實屬可惜。 黑夜王的表現各有千秋,氣勢與演出絕對不輸FromSoft過去的經典Boss,配樂一個比一個還有特色,招式上不僅充分考量「一對多」的要素,也成功融入有趣且非一面倒的機制,這在正統魂系中可是非常少見的。缺點的話,我覺得FromSoft可以少用點浮誇的攻擊,這裡是指那種Boss會突然走遠遠的開始搞一些很炫泡的前置,然後過來打你一下。第一次感覺很新鮮很壯麗,但兩、三次後難免會覺得有點浪費時間。 不喜歡的點 遺物機制根本就是下位版的金盃刷血寶石啊!即使退一萬步說遺物的功能只是用來讓你前期好過一些好了,詞條全靠隨機生成,既沒有鎖詞條重刷其他欄位的功能,還將一些改變角色技藝或絕活的重要詞條與一堆非常無用的詞條放在一起,讓人刷起來非常氣餒。 這點應該歸究於我個人心境還沒調適過來。《黑夜君臨》看似有許多被動與技能可搭配,實際上角色流派的多樣性與變化性比想像中來的侷限。本作不像《艾爾登法環》可以隨時隨地改變配點裝備,角色初始數值固定,升等也自動幫你配好點,與其探索其他可能性倒不如更專心玩角色已經擅長的流派。 If you like what I write, please consider a follow to my curator page, thanks! 如果你喜歡我寫的東西,可以追蹤 我的鑑賞家 喔!

review_text: Nightreign is the premier "I want to play a SOULS game, but I don't want to commit to an entire playthrough" game. It's quick, it's challenging, it has enough content to satisfy people who get bored with things quickly, and it has enough depth to squeeze several hundred hours out of it for the people who really want to dig in. At the time of this review, I have a save file with 160 hours with all achievements that has reached Depth 4, without the Forsaken Hollows DLC. If the gameplay trailers don't sell the concept well: Nightreign is a fast-paced cooperative Roguelite boss rush where the core gameplay loop is a run that takes anywhere from 15 to 50 minutes (average 40 mins) depending on how fast or slow you win or lose. You select a Nightfarer, a character that comes with their own unique abilities and stat spreads, and then you group with up to two other players to challenge one of the Nightlords of your choice. During the run, you have two 'days' to search the map for ways to get stronger: enemies killed grant you level ups, and bosses killed grant you randomly generated weapons or permanent buffs. After 7 minutes of daytime, your play area will gradually shrink, forcing you to maneuver towards a zone where you fight a more powerful boss. After defeating the boss, the 'day' ends, your play area resets, and the next 'day' begins. On the third day, you do not get any more chances to grow stronger, and instead are thrown into a fight against the final boss of the run: a Nightlord. Regardless of win or loss, you are awarded with a currency and a few relics (permanent upgrades that persist through runs), though victory always rewards more. In the base game, there are 8 Nightlords, 5 maps, and 8 Nightfarers (6 at the start, two unlocked later). The Nightlords are tricky enough that they take multiple attempts to master, the maps have enough hidden secrets that you'll still find something new every run, and the Nightfarer's abilities provide a lot of room for mastery, such that even after 100 hours you'll still be learning new techniques. Seven of the Nightlords come with more difficult variants, known as "Everdarks", that pose a significantly greater challenge over their base form. The worst part of the game is easily the lobby area and the meta progression. The Roundtable Hold is a place where you spend resources earned in a run towards unlocking permanent power-ups for your future runs, or where you unlock cosmetic items for your Nightfarers. Each Nightfarer comes with their own mini-story, told in the form of "Remembrance" quests that have 4-5 steps each, and they're just long enough to give some charm to what would otherwise just be caricatures of popular Souls builds. However, there isn't as much depth-of-lore present in Nightreign as compared to other Fromsoft titles. After about 100 hours, the lobby becomes a place where you either spend all your currency on relic gacha where you have a miniscule chance to generate a random relic that synergizes well with itself, or a place where you parkour idly after having exhausted all of the NPC's dialogue as you wait for a match to be found. The late game experience revolves around a hard mode called Deep of Night, which features scaling difficulty and skill based matchmaking. Enemies deal more damage (and stronger variants appear), items found in a run have stronger text but also come with downsides, and unlike the regular mode, your map and your Nightlord (or Everdark Nightlord) are randomly chosen. Victory in Deep of Night will increase your rating until you eventually reach a greater Depth where the challenges scale up even more. Deep of Night runs grant you more currency and will generate more powerful relics that can only be used for Deep of Night runs. I have more than 1000 hours across the entire Souls series, and have beaten many of the games deathless or at soul level 1, but clearing Depth 3 has been personally more challenging than anything else i've done before. TL;DR this is a really great game to casually play with friends that does not require a huge time commitment, but also provides a seriously challenging experience to anyone who wants to lock in. HOP ON NIGHTREIGN

review_text: I really wasn't sold on the idea of Nightreign at first, but after getting into the game with a friend it's quite addicting. Nightreign condenses the fun parts of Elden Ring into a cheaper, bite sized adventure; I only wish they dedicated harder to the rougelite experience. I was really into Elden Ring when it first came out, I did about nine playthroughs back to back and did one hundred percent completion, though I've tried revising the game since and just can't get into it the same way. Open worlds never really were for me and upon returning to the game it's really pushed me away, I want to get to the fun stuff and not spend more time horsing around getting from place to place, collecting everything I need for my character. Nightreign is the solution to this; it sections off the map and shows you clearly where things are, minimizing the downtime and maximizing the fun stuff. Unlike Elden Ring, Nightreign isn't an RPG, instead of a custom character and build you have preset characters with specialities and unique skills, which like a lot of things in this game don't sound like they'd work but in practice really do. Each character feels unique and like they have a role on the team, my only issue in this department is the lack of representation of some build types. There isn't really a dedicated miracle character, you've got Revenant sort of but unlike Recluse there's no way for her to get mana back and while she is still my favourite character, she doesn't really feel like a second caster. More characters are promised as DLC but we're yet to see any so far. One big shortcoming of Nightreign is the lack of wack. Rougelites and roguelikes alike are typically full of upgrades that really let you push the game to its breaking points which is part of the fun; but here they're very shy and reserved about letting things get too crazy. The vast majority of upgrades you'll collect are very minor things like "stamina recovery +4" or "physical attack +6%," the craziest upgrades you'll find see is something like raining fire or magic stars when you're walking which is as useless as it sounds unfortunately. I would love to see stuff like faster attack speed or lower attack interval buffs, or even more out there things like leaving a trail of fire behind you when you run or something. Elden Ring Nightreign is a somewhat experimental game with a lot of ideas that sometimes feels like they were holding back. If you like soulslike games but don't always want to do a full new playthrough because the tedious parts weigh you down after doing it all multiple times already, Nightreign is the cure. It's got all the meat; plenty of huge, fun boss fights, unique abilities and weapons, and is still receiving free content updates. Unfortunately, no swimsuit outfit for Recluse and Revenant; oh, and we got Alva for Birdman but no Zullie skin for Recluse? Maybe one day...

review_text: I want to preface that while I don't recommend the game, I do think it is a "good" game. As a player with 1200+ hours on Elden Ring, thousands more consuming content, hundreds of hours on Nightreign, and 12+ years of FromSoft gaming, it's actually really fun to play. However, I can't recommend it for one reason alone, and that can be minimised to one word: undercooked. So while it comes up as red, it's not a BAD review. (This is not a spoiler-free review, in case you want to be surprised by the game) Gameplay You have two "days" to run around the map as fast as possible, killing any enemies in your path in order to gain weaponry and passives in hopes of eventually killing the Nightlord, who is the 'final boss' of the run. Each day is segregated by a major boss fight of its own, usually being bosses from Elden Ring and occasionally Dark Souls. Unlike other entries in the series, you can't make your own character and build here. You're playing as preset characters, all with their own stats, preferred weapons, abilities, and ultimates. You can't crouch and there is no Torrent/horse anymore, but you can sprint really fast and climb walls now. It's actually extremely fun to blitz the map like prime Wally West by yourself. Getting passives is very much a big part of the rougelike element of the game. Killing bosses, important enemies, and opening some chests will give you a drop that usually has something like two weapons (with minor passives) or a larger passive. Your survival really hinges on you choosing the right things, as these boosts can be extremely significant (like 18% more defense against holy damage, and this is stackable with itself and talismans). At the end of a run, you'll get 'relics' that are equippable passives for every run, like a loadout of sorts. It's pretty close to gacha and is definitely designed to keep you coming back for the perfect relic set. It's also multiplayer, up to 3 players (which is literally odd). Your success also hinges on their performance to a degree (you can solo carry if you never get hit, but everything has higher health scaling). As an extremely good player in these games, your average player is not going to be the greatest of help (which is fine) and will likely need a lot of ressurections. You can run duo/solo, but the game is definitely best with three. This is the very basic gameplay loop and doesn't cover everything, but that's the gist. The Map It places you in a map that isn't necessarily procedurally generated, as the main map is actually a large set of pre-made seeds. This means with enough playing you can start to recognise exactly what will happen, exactly what boss is behind that gaol, what 'random' events will occur, and exactly what the shopkeep will have. The game attempts to alleviate this by having a 'Shifting Earth' mechanic that heavily modifies a corner of the map. Day 2 will take place within it, so in a way it's a mini map to explore. The DLC is also a Shifting Earth, except it replaces the entire map instead of a corner and has its own music, enemies, etc. The problem with this is that Shifting Earths are usually random to get on a run (the DLC one can only be accessed if everyone has the DLC unfortunately), so 70% of the time you are still running around on the same map. Other It's hard to split this game up into different categories since so much of this game is both borrowed from other games and nebulous on its own, so I'll just throw in a few things I can think of. Firstly, the music is among some of the best in the entire series. It's like Bloodborne level for sure, surpassing even Elden Ring imo. Caligo, Augur, Balancers, DLC tracks, etc. Those tracks had me floating inside my room. The story seems pretty cool, but I haven't invested myself super deeply into it. The characters are sick and they're almost fully voice acted. Cosmetics are cool, love the Dark Souls skins. The actual character designs are some of my favorite in the series, you'll wish you looked as good and moved as quickly as you do in Nightreign when you go back to Elden Ring. The Elephant in the Room Nightreign wants to be a rougelike. This means it is competing with other ones. But I cannot recommend it as a rougelike because the content is so thin. Within 50 hours you will probably have beaten every Nightlord, seen most weapons, and have a gameplay loop. Nothing in the game will surprise you. Build variety is far less complicated here than in Hades, Risk of Rain, Gungeon, Binding of Isaac, anything. You'll run around on the same map, do the same things, and fight the same boss. Why did the DLC not add any weapons from ER/Dark Souls? The game isn't truly random. Base map is 20 seeds, Shifting Earths are 5 more each, and the DLC is probably another 20. The game gets so samey as a rougelike in a way that is so much faster than other ones. I also can't recommend this to new players as the game is more brutal than past entries. Everything is timed, stats seriously matter, bosses are brutal. I can't recommend this game before any of the original games (Elden Ring, Dark Souls, etc.) because it is more of a hodgepodge rather than a complete experience. This game sits in the awkward niche of players that loved the other games and just want more, even if it's pretty anemic. This game is an endless well of potential and it's fun as hell, but does absolutely nothing better than other games for me to tell you to buy it. My opinion could change if they update the game again, but who knows. This game is truly delicious stale bread, but it is stale bread nonetheless. Buy it on sale or if you REALLY feel like you are missing out.

review_text: First I was maidenless... now I'm friendless... there is no justice in this world. From Soft dropping the hardest boss ever: having friends. Great, I hope they add that “friends” thing as a DLC. YOU DIED (friendless and alone) It's 6AM on a Monday. I play with strangers and we beat the Night Lord. Dance and repeat. It's a fast phase Elden Ring, you get all the power ups and rush to the last boss. OG Elden Rign feels more solo, dedicated. Nightreign is Fast Food. Get guns, do the job John Wick style. If your friends are like mine though, it's gonna be a struggle... Fellow maidenless, Nightreign f**king rules. The game is experimental, flawed, but good. I personally don't think it should win GOTY or even get any MP awards at the VGAs this year (and I say this as a massive Fromsoft fan), but I definitely think the game is worth playing if you enjoy Souls games and rogue likes. It’s like Elden Ring Seamless Coop but you don’t have to actually go through the entire open world for an hour between each boss. Every character is well-designed and fun to play. The returning bosses are great and the new Nightlord bosses are some of the best in the series. THEY REMOVED FALL DAMAGE. I see a lot of negativity towards the game. Some of it is fair criticism. But the idea that this is just an asset flip cash grab or the beginning of the end of fromsoft is absurd. If you liked Elden Ring, it’s more Elden Ring, except without all the annoying busywork of Elden Ring, and you can play with your friends or wife’s boyfriend without a mod or the awful souls game co op mechanics. It's so good. Maybe the hardest game they've put out yet, at least on first pass when solo. It's brutal, but the satisfaction of overcoming a mere single run is enormous. At first, it can feel overwhelming for a solo player, nigh on impossible. Once you've figured out how to manage and coordinate your runs is when the game starts firing on all cylinders. And it's not even a full priced game. You can pick it up for 40$, which at this point, is becoming half the price of a new over budget AAA game. Nightreign shocked me by having lore and story as well. It has personal quests for each character, that include cutscenes and NPCs around the world's hub in addition to tasks to perform within matches. There are also quite a few endings connected to the remembrances, which are quite fun and interesting to complete. Additionally, there are static set pieces in the game that are added to maps as you progress the game forward, and those include interesting handcrafted level design. They are not as robust as a legacy dungeon, but they are very cool nonetheless. They scratch the itch and include some wild descents and boss fights, all pasted on top of the procedural maps. And lastly, all the original bosses I've encountered so far are fantastic. And each character has brand new move sets (in the form of tactical and ultimate abilities) that are unique to Soulsborne games in general. Oh, and many of the old bosses that are directly reused have new move sets as well. So, even their recycles have had a little bit of dev work. Honestly, the amount of new development for this game (that isn't even a full-priced game) has impressed me. To each their own, but Nighteign does not remotely resemble shovel ware. It is good and there is fun to be had for sure. But it’s also... a one note game. It does one specific thing and outside of that it is pretty sparse. Which is fine, especially for a budget title, but I have to say I’m pretty underwhelmed with it after beating the final boss in 40 hours. There’s really not much more to the game unless you just love dropping in and doing it all over again. I don’t feel the urge to grind skins or rng for better relics so there’s no real reason to keep playing. Some people will love just playing it over and over which is great but it’s definitely the quickest I’ve put down a fromsoft game. Still, overall it’s a great condensed version of Elden Ring that has you doing all the fun stuff that Elden Ring provides in a frenzy of fighting, looting, and building your character. It’s just a refreshing game in a sea of corporate slop. 9/10

review_text: Well I genuinely love the game, I cannot recommend it to others. The content is stale and after 9 months they have only added 2 new playable characters, 2 new nightlords, and one new map (shifting earth, not counting the night bosses and such because technically they are not new). The lack of new content is actually astounding. There have been NO changes to the loot since release and it is so basic that you get the SAME thing every run. Hardly any run is different from one another and the variation is tiny because for some reason each nightlord is tied to only 4 nightbosses (2 each night) and certain events. There is hardly any RNG to allow for runs to differ from one another, you will fight the same things in probably the exact same way over and over and over and over, especially if you like 1 or 2 nightlords, you will likely fight the same boring bosses again and again. Not to mention there is no crossplay. I think this game would be much better if: - more playable characters (or perhaps the ability to custom make a character to make ur own build) - more loot and bosses (actually criminal that every thing from elden ring is NOT in this game, its literally just a port of everything, in the right circumstances all it would be is copy and paste, the lack of content is inexcusable) - crossplay (would love to play with my console mates) - quit focusing on LAZY difficulty (i.e. deep of night) and actually add content - actuall RNG elements (to the point where you can never guess exactly what your fighting because rn its LITERALLY a 50/50 chance you are right) IMO, this game would excel if it was a TRUELY RNG based boss rush with ACTUAL MEANINGFUL roguelike systems, the only reason this game has any value is because the nightlords are awesome bosses and some of the best fights fromsoft has ever made The short time frame and the fornite wall don't install a sense of panic, but instead make everyone follow the same path every time because it is the only path to ensure victory, variation is rare EDIT: I started playing with mods and by golly I was right. All they had to do was add more content and variability to the weapons and enemies and the game got 100x better. The fact that these mods exist proves that it can be done but FromSoft doesn't want to, another negative imo.

review_text: Okay, after playing for a long time, I have a lot to say: It’s an incredible game and I hope other versions of the game come to PC (Sad that I can’t play Duskbloods on Steam) Let’s get to the review: Pros - 1. A wide variety of build options for all characters. 2. The launch POIs and the new ones from the DLC were a positive addition, though there could have been more. 3. First impressions of the new bosses are positive. 4. Impeccable soundtrack (kudos to the Straghess and Caligo tracks). 5. Item options and a variety of scaling opportunities during the match. 6. The skins look great, except for the Remembrances, which will be mentioned in the Cons. Neutral - The RNG is over-the-top, and you waste a lot of time searching for perfect rolls, but this is necessary to keep the attention of players who care about gear improvements for progression in the Depths; therefore, I consider this a neutral assessment for this requirement. Cons - 1. Multiplayer is lacking due to MMR distribution (I think that after D5, players with a similar MMR should be matched with you, not players with lower MMR or who haven’t reached a specific “cap”). 2. Fighting a single ED isn’t interesting, and everyone hates Algur. 3. The new invasions are bad, except for Tricephalos (I hate having to reroute my path just to land two hits on that damn Caligo). 4. Few skins available, and honestly? All the Remembrance skins are really lackluster. A skin that requires certain requirements to unlock should be better designed. 5. Number of characters (I honestly think there were more options in the catalog, and I hope they’ll be used in the future) Final Thoughts - If you’re here looking for reviews of this game, welcome but be warned: People take this game very seriously, and I’ll admit that can be frustrating for newcomers, especially if you’re planning to play the Depths. So my advice is: Study the game, because there’s a HUGE gap between a casual player and someone who really knows what they’re doing in this game. The gameplay overall is incredible! I feel like I’ve never spent so much time on a game that repeats the same things over and over, yet I had a different experience every time. Rating: 9

review_text: Looking back, I didn't care about 'Elden Ring Fortnite' before it launched and yet it is currently my most played game on Steam for good reason (which is why I felt like I should write a review.) The main selling point is the same as most games by FromSoftware: the sweet taste of victory after struggling against all odds versus brutal bosses through practice and mastery of game mechanics. It never gets old, and Nightreign further makes this even more addicting because you will strive for this with other players; especially ones who are willing to be cooperative and play together as a team. The whole movement and combat aspects are great, fluid, and you'll almost never have any moment to relax. Learning how to route properly and where certain chests/loot are placed takes a while but it never makes or breaks a run because in the end, your skills matter the most. You have 10? Different characters to choose from (DLC included), each with different playstyles which get even more customizable with the relic system. At this point I have played all of them and while some feels better to play than others, every character is viable even at the highest difficulty (Depth 5). Speaking of which, game difficulty is a tricky metric to measure. I will assure you though, that the base 'story-mode' game could be challenging yet very doable, even for casuals. Dying over and over is expected in these games and you will die a lot while learning how to play better, but when you see how much better you can dodge and punish boss attacks, you'd feel like the greatest player there ever was. A run typically goes for ~40 minutes so you can just jump in and get off the game without much time investment. Even less if the team wipes during certain mini boss fights within the run, or even longer if your team struggles at the final boss. What I can say is that in those ~40 minutes, you will focus so hard you won't even realize 40 minutes have gone by. I don't really have anything bad to say about this game, just make sure to have friends or a group to play it with. Random queue can match you with extremely laggy people; not to mention there are quite a few cheaters running about. All in all, the game is addicting because it's seriously 'dopamine rush' the game. I have 900 hours in the game, I still (mostly) play the same 3 characters over and over again, and I still die a lot :))

review_text: This is the first game that genuinely got me addicted to its gameplay loop. I've played a lot of action games, but nothing comes close to the combat fluidity in Elden Ring: Nightreign. Every dodge, parry, and attack feels so satisfying that even after hundreds of runs, I still wanted to jump into "just one more." The whole format is brilliant. Survive two increasingly difficult stages, then face the final boss. Every run feels different, and even when you fail, you learn something new for the next one. I honestly thought I'd seen everything after beating almost every boss in the normal runs... then I unlocked Deep of Night. ...and damn. That's where the game completely hooked me. Every run was intense. Getting clean kills, getting absolutely destroyed by new attack patterns I had somehow never seen before, learning, adapting, and pushing further every time. The adrenaline of trying to climb deeper into Deep of Night is something I haven't felt in a game for a long time. I made it to DoN 4, and I think I'll leave it there. 😂 It genuinely took a toll on my body with all the late-night runs and the constant focus, but every second was worth it. Massive respect to FromSoftware for creating something so addicting while still keeping that signature challenge. I really hope we get another DLC or more content for this game in the future. review_text: Preface Elden Ring veterans have almost nothing to complain about when it comes to Nightreign. In essence, this title provides more Elden Ring content with added variety, faster pacing, and easy-to-pick-up yet hard-to-master builds and playstyles that provides enough replayability with overall game design that makes it easy to get into another session whenever you have what I call the "Souls itch." Positives No Time to Waste Before delving into Nightreign, there were two primary concerns I had from what I knew about the game so far: time-limited runs and boss variety. The time-limited runs is a godsend for players like myself who want more Elden Ring but also seek a fresh experience. The exploration is there (albeit with less freedom from the vanilla title), but the balance between the need to explore and focus on boss fights is all in all well executed. Builds can shift drastically after one or two Nightlord kills and each run can feel unique simply based on how the player approaches each run. As with all games, it all comes down to mindset. Ten Nightfarers, Ten Playstyles By this point, most players will settle for the good ol' DR build with most Nightfarer they choose to run. I myself ran mostly solo (a primary reason I held off on Nightreign for so long since solo play was an afterthought a few months into the game's lifespan), and yet with choices like Wylder, Ironeye, and Raider, my runs were not as grueling as I thought they would be. Melee all-rounder, ranged archer, and heavy-hitting bruiser were all on the menu. Now upon completion, I look forward to trying the other Nightfarers to try more technique-based playstyles like the caster-based Recluse and parry-focused Executor. At the end of the day, Nightreign has something for everyone as long as you focus on building each Nightfarer the right - or maybe even wrong - way. Performance I rarely mention this as a forte for game reviews, but with all the performance issues AAA games have been launching with lately, a honorable mention is at very least in order. Nightreign ran flawlessly for me, and that may be due to patches that have been released since launch but the point still stands: FromSoftware rarely, if ever, misses in the optimization department. Combat is quick and responsive even more so than it was in vanilla. And in a title with co op multiplayer being one of its appeals, that's saying something. Negatives Day Phases This is highly subjective, but granting roughly 13-15 real-time minutes for the exploration cycle before the circle starts closing in might be a turnoff for many players. Time is your greatest enemy in Nightreign, and if anything this can simultaneously be considered a positive as it pushes you to think quickly on your feet and work on your decision-making skills/speed. Granted, you have unlimited time for night/boss phases, but a little more leeway might not have hurt for the less initiated. Just a minor gripe on my end, but not a gamebreaker. Feels...incomplete? Perhaps with more dedicated resources, a bigger pull towards ER newcomers, and I daresay more content & horizontal progression(?), I feel the game could have been bigger than it is. As successful as it may have been, many agree that Nightreign just kind of came and went; perhaps not off the grid, but now it's just there for people to enjoy when they feel like coming back to it. Arguably, Nightreign could have started a movement to take the Soulslike genre to the next level entirely, departing from the singleplayer experience we've had for the last decade and causing a chain reaction of games that could give birth to an entirely new genre. But alas, here we are. Nightreign, quite simply put: More Elden Ring . Conclusion Final Verdict: 9/10 A- Though not as deep and immersive as the original Elden Ring, Nightreign delivered on its promises and provided the on-the-go Elden Ring experience for veterans and newcomers alike. It may not have been perfect at launch, but FromSoftware has a healthy habit of always striving to satisfy their fans. Patch after patch, they improved solo play and fine-tuned everything they had in place for a memorable experience. Compared to many other companies that recently lose the faith of their supporters with every title they release in this post-2020 era of ongoing hit-and-miss titles, FromSoft remains faithful to its identity and to this day remains in excellent standing with the loyal fanbase. Now, once again, we look forward to what they have in store for us next.

review_text: Community Reign I am not the biggest fan of Elden Ring, Roguelites, or Battle Royale-esque games. . . So what gives? Nightreign falls into a strange realm of games I enjoy in the same way I enjoy Monster Hunter, Outer Wilds, and Peaks of Yore. The game thrives on being driven by a player's knowledge of it's semi-static map, enemy placements, PoI layouts, Boss patterns and weaknesses, and semi-obfuscated meta knowledge. When I first started playing I absolutely did not know how to manage the first day of the game, after another run I got to the second day, and after that I made it to the final day with a bit of flailing. After about 30 hours I can safely lead most expeditions in the base map to hit enough points on the map to make it close to max level, if not max, with a decent set of gear. The reality of this learning process is not done through in-game tutorialization or looking up guides, but by a natural learning process from letting other people lead me through the game. By making mental notes about how to better optimize my own time, and apply it to games that I'm in. That is the crux of this game's joy for me; it's silent community. Able to instill parts of their knowledge on me in order to collectively teach me to be a better player by paying attention to what they're doing that works, and the things that don't. Every run that I go on seems to teach me something new about the map that I didn't know of before, and that always feels like an absolute blast to me. Watching all of this come together to execute a plan driven by the collective knowledge of other players to get through the game's nights. Beyond that the exploration, combat mechanics, and bosses are all better designed and feel as though they have a bit more intent behind them than most souls games. The minimalistic building elements mean that you can get in and out of games relatively quick and will pick up on what works and doesn't work in a rather natural way. Being that this isn't a PvP game in the slightest the ability to cooperate with others is always fun for me, and I haven't had too much truly awful experiences to say that I've had a bad time outside of the occasional bit of frustration over failing a couple of clutch moments. Nightreign is a game that I think will hold a special place in my heart for proving me wrong about a great deal of apprehensions I had going into it, but I think it's worth people's time if they enjoy learning and optimization in games to try to attain a perfect run and mitigating the curveballs it throws you with it's shifting elements.

review_text: Elden Ring isn't just my favourite Souls game—it's my favourite game of all time. The biggest reason for that is the incredible amount of variety it offers. Whether it's the hundreds of unique weapons, countless spells/incantations, diverse enemy types, or unforgettable bosses, there is always something new to discover. That's exactly why Nightreign caught my attention. Instead of committing to a single build for the entire playthrough, this game gave me the chance to adapt and experiment with different weapons, while trying different characters, each with their own unique playstyle, abilities, and skills. It provides great replayability, and I genuinely enjoy my time playing this game. Positives/PROS Gameplay- Nightreign is much more fast-paced compared to Elden Ring. You have Surge Sprint, which lets you run faster (just like Torrent, but without him). You can actually climb walls and obstacles in your path, and there is the Spectral Hawk, which helps you traverse long distances quickly. I wish they had added these features to the main Elden Ring too :(. Every run feels different due to randomized loot. You also get different characters—each Nightfarer has a different playstyle. For example, Ironeye is an archer, while Recluse specializes in sorceries and magic. Every Nightfarer has its own passive ability, Character Skill, and Ultimate Art. After each run, you receive rewards, including Relics (items that contain passive bonuses, effects, and other benefits), which you can equip on your character to gain advantages, and Murk (the in-game currency), which can be used to purchase cosmetics, emotes, Relics, and other items. All of this makes the gameplay enjoyable and provides excellent replayability. Bosses- As this game reuses assets from Elden Ring, you will face many of the same enemies and bosses that you already fought in that game. The game also features six returning Dark Souls bosses that are not part of Elden Ring. You will encounter these either at the end of Day 1 or Day 2. But keep all of that aside—if you reach Day 3, you will face the Nightlords, which are completely unique bosses. There are eight of them in total (excluding the DLC), and they are much harder than the regular bosses you have faced in Souls games. They have diverse movesets and can wipe out your entire expedition with their devastating AOE attacks. And oh my God, the music for these Nightlords is just beyond this world. No other Souls game has boss OSTs of this quality. Special mention goes to Caligo, Fulghor, and Libra. I honestly don't know why this game wasn't nominated for Best Soundtrack at TGA 2025. Everything you do beforehand throughout your journey—your builds, upgrades, and teamwork—ultimately leads to this one final challenge, making it incredibly memorable. Quality of Life- This game still has approximately 20–35k active players every day. In my experience, Matchmaking usually took only a few seconds, with the longest wait being around 2–3 minutes. This game provides a smooth multiplayer experience with almost no connectivity or network lag issues. At least it's much better than previous FromSoftware games, where the co-op system felt like hell without mods. This was FromSoftware's first proper multiplayer/co-op game, and I think they did a pretty good job. The optimization is just okayish. During chaotic boss fights, or when a Nightlord gets mad and uses its "signature move," FPS fluctuations are very common. And just like Elden Ring, this game is locked at 60 FPS, which is pretty disappointing. Negatives/CONS Now this game starts to show its actual disappointments if you put its positives aside for a moment. -> This game is very fast-paced - You have to make decisions quickly because you don't get enough time for exploration. Each day lasts for about 15 minutes, and during that time you are under constant pressure to gather gear and loot as fast as possible while the safe zone continuously shrinks. You can miss a lot of things if you don't act quickly. This also means that even if you enjoyed Elden Ring, it's not guaranteed that you'll enjoy this game too. If you're the kind of person who likes to explore the world slowly at your own pace, then this game is not for you. -> The gameplay loop gets repetitive after some time- After you achieve 100% completion, which can take around 40–50 hours at most, there's nothing much left to do other than grinding in Deep of Night mode. -> You only get one map - Although there are variations with Shifting Earth events and changing boss locations, they don't make enough of a difference. After several hours of playing, you'll know the entire map, and it becomes very predictable and repetitive. -> No communication tools when playing with randoms - At least they should have added a text chat or voice chat because communication is very important in a PvE co-op game. Right now, the only way to communicate is by marking locations and equipment on the map. -> This game is not made for solo play - I know the game scales the health of enemies and bosses depending on the number of players, but solo play is still very difficult because you don't get revived. Although you can obtain Wending Grace, which gives you one extra life, the game can still throw two or even three bosses at you at the end of a day. -> Lack of content - As FromSoftware has now abandoned this game, there have been no updates regarding its future. The community has been asking for a new map, another Nightlord, or even SOTE weapons from Elden Ring (which I also want). But sadly, with the base game and the Forsaken Hollows DLC, Nightreign's journey seems to be over. There's still hope within the community for at least one more update... but for now, it's just "hope." :( Should you buy Nightreign if you want to play solo or with randoms? As I mentioned earlier, the game is not well-balanced for a solo playthrough. You have to act fast from the very first day so that you don't end up under-leveled or without good weapons and upgrades. It is very difficult, but some people still manage to do it. If you equip Relics with useful benefits and just "GIT GUD," you can even defeat the Nightlords solo, so yeah, it's ultimately up to you. Playing with randoms is also fun. Sometimes they'll carry you, and sometimes they'll rage quit mid-game lol. The lack of communication tools is the biggest problem when playing with randoms. Still, most players are cooperative and show good teamwork. But if this game had a chat or voice chat option, it would have been much better. Final Verdict- This game was just an experimental project by FromSoftware. I know it's not perfect and has many flaws, but this was never meant to be a live-service game. FromSoftware delivering multiple updates and a DLC is more than enough for what this game was intended to be. The community has its own demands, but I think it's time to move on from this game and let them focus on their future titles. I played this game for over 40 hours, but even in that short time, I made a lot of memories with the friend I played duo with. I still remember the day when we finally reached our first Nightlord together after so many attempts. Although we failed, that fight was absolutely dramatic, and I loved every second of that experience. I will still do at least one run every day because I genuinely love this game. I'm even thinking about starting another playthrough of Elden Ring because this game motivates me to do so. I love everything about the world of Elden Ring—the bosses, characters, music, worldbuilding, lore, and the incredible diversity of its weapons, skills, enemies, spells, and so much more. That's exactly why I loved Nightreign, even with all of its flaws. "In the end, it was never about surviving the night—it was about wanting to face it again." Rating - 8/10

review_text: This game has a strong hold on me. While I was only a relatively casual player of Elden Ring and wasn't well accustomed to Soulslikes, as soon as I started playing this game, it all clicked. You get one big fixed map with a few variations depending on where the night tide starts to come in. You work by yourself or ideally with two or three other Nightfarers, while runs are possible with teams of 2 or 3 of the same class, it pays to divide and conquer, get spells for your Recluse/Revenant, bows for your Ironeye, big weapons for your Wylder/Guardian etc. Certain points on the map can attract strong bosses which will grant you massive buffs if you're able to overcome them. The key to success is to stick together, take on the right enemies at the right time and focus on reviving teammates, taking pressure away from others when they're struggling and work on what equipment works best for you. There's a lot of replay value too with cosmetics to unlock, Relics which give you buffs and can be equipped on each Nightfarer along with some other unlockables too. I've been playing this game for a few hours every day and I feel like I may not win 100% of the time, but I'm doing the best I can and providing the firepower my team needs to give them a chance at beating the final bosses. I can say this runs well on a decently built PC and also runs nicely on Steam Deck (though you're mainly limited to 30-35FPS, at least on the LCD model). Well worth buying if you're curious about it. If you have friends to play with, even better! Update: I will say from what I hear in the DLC it's very much aimed at pro players and doesn't add a lot to the base game. I would advise against getting the DLC unless you're a super-fan and like a tough challenge.

review_text: I really want to love Nightreign. I’m a huge Souls fan with countless runs across the series, and I own hundreds of roguelikes, so on paper this should be perfect for me. But something just doesn’t click. The game throws you in fast and expects you to keep up. If you stop for even a moment to read new abilities or compare weapons, you’re either falling behind your teammates or losing levels because you didn’t rush to the next objective. The tutorial barely explains how the game actually works, so it’s easy to wander into bosses way above your level and lose both time and souls trying to recover. Meta progression is extremely limited for a roguelike. Each character has 3 rune slots, and those runes can roll up to 3 affixes, so your long-term progression is basically just 9 stat quirks. Some of them are cool, but it doesn’t change how limited it all feels. And because item drops are random, you can easily end up stuck with weapon types you don’t want, making some runs feel flat-out worse through no fault of your own. Communication is another huge miss. Outside of simple map pings, there’s no text chat, no voice chat, nothing. If you’re solo-queuing, coordinating with random teammates is almost impossible. There are great boss fights here, and moments that remind you why FromSoftware’s combat systems are so beloved. But getting to those moments means pushing through confusing itemization, a lack of build variety, shallow progression, and no real way to communicate. I want Nightreign to be amazing, but right now it’s unfortunately more frustrating than fun.

review_text: Nightreign doesn't reinvent the wheel, but what it does exceedingly well is providing a bite-sized multiplayer Souls experience. Though it does grab from other games' bosses that you may have already fought dozens of times, there still are a fair bunch of new bosses here too, with quite a few feeling pretty memorable to me! Atop the normal gameplay there's even an interesting "hard" mode. It's far from being just an "asset dump." Though I do wish Fromsoft would revisit the game's success and add another expansion or tweak some areas, there's genuinely a lot of love and content here and you could tell from my playtime that I'm a pretty big fan of what we have. The game is fun if you want a faster Souls game with arcade vibes. Grab some friends or make some new ones too, as the community is still pretty populated as of this writing :)
